Furthermore, although one should separately distinguish the six categories such as the ten-membered assembly (*daśavargīya*), there nonetheless exists a distinct essence of *karmavācanā*.
Answer: The seven means of settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamatha*) and the seven non-means of settling disputes constitute the distinction between the general and the specific.

This is like the sense organs such as the eye and their objects such as form (*rūpa*). When defining the category of form (*rūpāyatana*), they are collectively termed "form," even though the five sense organs and four [of the] five objects are separately distinguished.

Once the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) has been accounted for, there still remains a distinct substance of the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). What is now termed "karman" (action) refers to a general-and-particular classification, like a worldly army or a forest;
it is not analogous [to the case of the spheres], because apart from the people and the trees, there is no separate substance of "army" or "forest."
Just as within a boundary (*sīmā*), there are also indeterminate cases when the community is not divided, the Venerable One said:

"One should also say that the accomplishment of the formal boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) is likewise indeterminate, because both the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) and the precinct (*sīmā-maṇḍala*) are also indeterminate. The verse of the twenty-eight persons says:
"The remainder, the suspension, the extinction, the difficulty, the divine, the concealment, the separation, and the precinct."

Regarding the third section on the person who can uphold [the teaching], the *Mahīśāsaka-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) states that those who have personally realized the truths [attain it] by themselves. This does not fully accord with reason. As that treatise’s second [chapter] says:

"Six are obtained from others; one must be distinguished. Because they arise through the Buddha's preaching, they are called 'from others'; when they arise from one's own realization of the truths, they are called 'by oneself.'"
It is so; as explained extensively therein.

When the *Śāstra* says, "In terms of the fundamental [path]," and so forth, this applies the aforementioned dharmas according to the analysis of the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) found in other *Mahāvibhāṣā* treatises.
It does not mean that this specific text exists in that treatise (the analysis of the vision of the truths is as cited above from the second section of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*).

Regarding the phrase "when both dust and habituation are extinguished": if one follows the systems of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and other such treatises, "dust" (*rajas*) refers to defilement by dust, which is the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
There are three kinds of "habituation" (*vāsanā*): first, all seeds of the wholesome and the defiled are termed "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*);

here, however, "habituation" refers specifically to the seeds of the afflictions. Second, even though the afflictions have been severed, they still persist as something adhering within the body that serves as their basis.

It is incapable of functioning. Although it is incapable of functioning, it has no separate substantial entity. Third, all cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are also termed "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*);

therefore, the Sūtras describe them as the "habitual tendencies of ignorance. If one follows the intent of various sūtras and śāstras belonging to the Buddha-nature school, such as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, "dust" (*rajas*) refers to the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), encompassing both seeds and manifest states, collectively termed "defiled dust. As for "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*)...
This refers to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). It comprehensively includes all states of insensitivity (*akarmaṇyatā*), and is collectively termed "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*).
Since the Tang dynasty, those unfamiliar with that school have mistakenly assumed that the term "habitual tendency" was a wrong translation by ancient scholars; this is a profound error.
The intent of the present commentary is precisely the doctrinal meaning of the Buddha-nature school (*tathāgatagarbha*). This interpretation is definitive; it is only that people harbor doubts.
Regarding those who enter the Path through transformation: they transform their secular attire into dharma robes and the like. As stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
"At the mere utterance of the words 'Welcome,' their hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and the kaṣāya was donned upon their bodies."

Regarding the passage "The Dharma-treasury was entrusted to Ānanda; welcome": as stated in the first fascicle of the *Fu fazang zhuan* (Biographies of the Transmission of the Dharma-treasury), when Ānanda was traveling by boat down the middle of a river and entered parinirvāṇa, there were five hundred rishis in the Snowy Mountains who, having been saved by Ānanda, simultaneously entered nirvāṇa.
According to that account, this constitutes his "welcoming" of them across [to liberation]. This shall be fully detailed in the records of the third fascicle below.
This is distinct [from other cases].
As for Śāriputra, the son of a goldsmith, being taught the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), consult the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 26; the circumstances do not involve the Buddha.
"As can be known from the text": In the following passage, the Buddha was at that time traveling about and teaching the Dharma with one hundred and eleven arhats.
At that time, there were those who, having heard the Dharma and attained faith, desired to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

When the bhikṣus led those who wished to receive the precepts to the presence of the Tathāgata, they lost their original faith before reaching him midway and were unable to receive full ordination. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and because of it...
The opening of the Three Refuges consists of ten meanings, as explained in detail in the second fascicle of that treatise (*Mahāvibhāṣā*).

Regarding the "four unbreakable faiths" (*catur-avetyaprasāda*), in newly translated sūtras and śāstras they are termed the "four purities of realization" (*catvāri avetyaprasādāni*). According to the Mahāyāna, these are taken as faith...

As for their essence: it refers to untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) that takes the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, and the precepts as its objects. Because this faith cannot be destroyed, it is called "indestructible faith" (*avekaṃpya-śraddhā*).
Alternatively, because one has realized purity, they are called "realizations of purity" (*avetyaprasāda*). Since realization itself is purity, they are termed "realizations of purity."
There is no logical error here. According to the Sarvāstivāda, the essence consists of the two dharmas of untainted faith (*śraddhā*) and precept (*śīla*).

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 13, states: "Purity refers to faith and precept; because they are free from defilement and impurity, one attains this purity through the distinct realization and verification of each of the Four Noble Truths;
therefore, it is called 'verified purity' (*avetyaprasāda*). It further states: "In this context, 'Buddha' refers to all the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) within the Buddha’s body."
The untainted faith that takes those as its object is called "verified clarity regarding the Buddha" (*buddha-avetyaprasāda*).

Herein, "Dharma" refers to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and other *śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa* dharmas within the person of a Pratyekabuddha; the two untainted faculties and other various *śaikṣa* dharmas within the person of a Bodhisattva;

and the three truths of suffering, origin, and cessation. The untainted faith that takes these as its object is called "verified clarity regarding the Dharma" (*dharma-avetyaprasāda*). Herein, "Saṃgha" refers to the [Śrāvaka]...

Hearing of the dharmas of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) within one’s own continuum, the untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) directed toward them is called the "purity of realization regarding the Saṃgha" (*saṃgha-saṃpratyaya-viśuddhi*).

All untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) are called the "purity of realization regarding the Dharma" (*dharma-saṃpratyaya-viśuddhi*), because they are pure by their very nature (*svabhāva-viśuddha*) and because they arise based on realization; thus they are also termed "purities of realization.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-five, states: "The two—faith and morality—are the essence [of these purities]; all four are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). A detailed explanation is as found therein.

Regarding the first, the *Saṃpuṭa*: it is often said that once in the past, there was a bhikṣu who was destined to attain arhatship, yet because of an obstacle created by a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), he could not exhaust his outflows (*āsrava*).
The Buddha, wishing to remove this obstacle, performed the *saṃpuṭa* rite for him; the wheel-turning monarch’s merit was extinguished, and the bhikṣu immediately attained non-attachment (*asaṅga*).

Regarding the distinction between the universal and the restricted application of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), Jue states: "Prior to five hundred years [of the Dharma's decline], it applied to both ordinary persons and noble ones (*ārya*).

After five hundred years, since there are no longer noble monks, it is therefore restricted to ordinary persons. Now, considering that Piṇḍola has been responding to invitations to the meal offerings (*bhojana*), how can one say there are no noble monks?
Even if a noble monk were to come and preside over the rite, how could it not be accomplished? Why, then, do you say it is restricted? Venerable sir, [please explain].

It says: "Only the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is universal" means it applies to both ordinary beings and sages. "The restricted may be known" refers to the fact that the remaining four [types of karma] are restricted to those who hold office.
This concludes the section on the fourth gate.
Regarding the ultimate state of perfect compliance, there are further explanations by others that are entirely unfit for recording here.

Now, examining this in detail according to the tenet of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, one enters the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) by contemplating only the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and realizing the principle of signlessness (*animitta*). This is like an inner-worldly ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who repeatedly observes the Truth of Cessation through applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
However, at the time of initial practice, it is still interspersed with minds characterized by signs (*sanimitta-citta*). At that time, it is still...

When one has not yet reached the ultimate limit of "thorough compliance" (*anuloma*), but through long study has become pure and matured such that one perceives the cessation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) without being interrupted by [conceptual] marks (*nimitta*), this is called "entering the path of vision" (*darśana-mārga*).
Reaching this point is termed the ultimate limit of thorough compliance; it refers to the ultimate limit of thorough compliance characterized by the signless (*animitta*).

According to the Sarvāstivāda, one enters the path of vision solely through emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wishlessness (*apranihita*); they certainly do not allow entry into the path of vision by means of the samādhi of the signless.
This directly contradicts the *Tattvasiddhi* school. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"These two types of recipients of the Dharma are neither weak nor do they abandon [the roots of goodness]. Question: If it is said that those within the stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are neither weak nor abandon [the roots], why does the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-three, state:
"If one who has attained the stage of 'Heat' (ūṣmagata) falls away, they sever the roots of goodness"? Answer: That [text]...

Regarding the point that one who has regressed from *ūṣmagata* may sever the roots of goodness, the present intention is to state that for one who has not regressed from the stage of *ūṣmagata*, there is certainly no loss or abandonment [of the roots].
Therefore, there is no contradiction or error.

As for the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) being performed by those who have not yet attained the status of a superior person (*uttarimanussa*), it is as described in the *Upasampadā-khandhaka*: prior to the establishment of the formal rituals, [such acts were performed].
The bhikṣus wore their robes unevenly and went on almsrounds contrary to the Dharma. These individuals were all those who had taken the Three Refuges.

Since it is said that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) was established only after these people had committed such transgressions, we know that those who have merely taken the Three Refuges are still at the stage of ordinary worldlings (*bālapṛthagjana*).

Now, considering those who have attained the two lower fruits, they might still be liable to commit a *pārājika* offense; how much more so for one whose robes are not even worn? How could such a person...

This establishes that [the recipient] is an external ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana). Therefore, it would be better to rely on the second fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which states that the reception of the Three Refuges is neither weakened nor abandoned, and thus judge them to be internal ordinary persons (adhyātmapṛthagjana).

Regarding those who are universally encompassed, there are three types: first, the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*); second, the internal ordinary person (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*); and third, the noble one (*ārya*).
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, concerning the "Pure Brahmin" (*Śuddha-brāhmaṇa*), in the thirty-ninth fascicle of that sutra, the Pure Brahmin said to the Buddha:
"I have already attained the pure eye of the True Dharma and take refuge in the Triple Gem. I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me permission to leave the household life. The Buddha told him:

"Kauṇḍinya, listen to this brahmin as he leaves the household life and receives the precepts. At that time, Kauṇḍinya led him into the midst of the Saṃgha and performed the *karmavācanā* ceremony to ordain him as a renunciant. Fifteen days later, he attained arhatship.
The Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā. In the following text, she attains the first fruit [of the path] and is ordained by Vajraprabhā.
*Shizongyi Ji*, Fascicle 2, Part 1;
*Shizongyi Ji*, Fascicle 2, Part 2.
Regarding the gate of conditions (*pratyaya-mukha*): formerly, the Vinaya masters held that all five types of ordination (*pañca-upasampadā*) each possessed five conditions.

As for the five [conditions] for the "Come-hither" (*svāgata*) ordination, these combine the three and four [conditions] mentioned above into a single condition (namely, assuming the form of a Buddha and receiving the Buddha’s verbal instruction). To this, one further adds the correspondence between mind and object, as well as the completion of the act through speech. Now, let us examine this in detail.
It has already been stated that within oneself there exists the wholesome mind of renunciation, as well as the form of the Buddha and the Buddha’s holy teaching;
this thus reveals the correspondence between the objective field and the mind. Furthermore, the Buddha said that there is no fault in not falling away.

For what reason, then, is it said that the task is accomplished? Regarding the five conditions for the aforementioned Dharma: first, receiving the instruction of the Buddha (the same as the first condition in this chapter); second, establishing a vow and commitment; third, diligent application.

1. Diligent cultivation. 2. The exhaustion of the three poisons. 3. The manifestation of the knowledge of exhaustion (this corresponds to the third condition in the chapter). Now, examining this further, the "knowledge of exhaustion" already implies diligent cultivation and the exhaustion of the three poisons.
These three phrases combine the first two [conditions] to form a single condition (namely, assuming the form of a disciple and the teaching of the Three Refuges).
Second, the complete appearance of one who has left the household life; the scriptural text states that he was commanded to shave his hair and don the *kāṣāya* robes, etc. (The Venerable One...)

[It is] said: "Furthermore, this condition is excellent. The mind of the three refuges is accomplished by receiving the previous reliance [on the Triple Gem] (this is the third condition within the chapter).

Fourth, the mind and the object correspond; fifth, the words are completed and the matter is concluded. Now, upon detailed examination, these may also be subsumed within the third condition of reliance.

The eight respects and five conditions are explained identically to the three refuges, namely: first, the provisional form and the teaching; second, the possession of the marks; third, the existence...
One should eternally maintain the mind of precepts, receiving and practicing them. Fourth is "correspondence" (saṃprayoga); fifth is "completion of the task" (kṛtyaparisamāpti).

Now, examining these five, while it is good that the possession of the mind seeking [the object] is complete and one receives and practices it, I fear that "correspondence" and "completion of the task" may not be fully present.
For this reason, within the chapter, they have been revised to four conditions.

Regarding the phrase "the *karmavācanā* for receiving the precepts as established since ancient times," the Master’s intention has already been preserved in this interpretation. Now, I shall examine the four conditions in detail.

Although their meaning is complete, if they are applied to the scriptural text (*vinaya*), they seem to diverge from the textual characteristics. The intent of the textual characteristics is as follows:
"If one receives the full ordination (*mahāśramaṇera-vinaya*)"—this refers to the person who is capable of receiving [the precepts].

Regarding the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* being accomplished according to the Dharma: this refers to the complete fulfillment of all four conditions; therefore, it is called "accomplished according to the Dharma.
As for "attaining the proper location":

to be in accord with the holy teachings is what is meant by "attaining the proper location," as in the description of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*).
Regarding "power" (*bala*): "proper place" (*sthāna*) refers to that which accords with principle; "improper place" (*asthāna*) refers to that which does not accord with principle.
Because the Tathāgata has fully realized both and cannot be overcome, they are called "powers. Therefore, in this context, what is designated as "teaching" is termed "attaining the proper place."

Regarding those who abide within the dharma of a bhikṣu: this concludes the preceding ritual procedure. By invoking the name of the teaching, one achieves accomplishment and thereby attains stable abiding within the dharma of a bhikṣu.

Furthermore, one should carefully examine the four conditions. Although it is said that one must have reached the required age and be free from physical impediments or obstacles, one must still investigate in detail according to the lower sections of the Vinaya texts;

for if the thirteen *antarāyika-dharmas* (obstacles) are not inquired about, it is not called "receiving the precepts. Thus, even if one is free from obstacles, if they are not inquired about, [the ordination is likewise invalid].
The precepts are obtained. Regarding the point that "breaking the meaning of the four conditions is not in accord with principle," this does not mean that an obstacle is raised to refute them;
rather, it is a refutation consisting in the distinct establishment of another thesis while analyzing those four conditions.
Regarding the meaning of "otherwise" (*anyathā*) which should be explained, it is precisely what is briefly set forth below.

As for the "six conditions," Master Yuan states: first, the year [of ordination] must be completed; second, the person must be free from obstacles (*antarāya*); third, the boundary (*sīmā*) must be established; fourth, all [monks] must assemble;
fifth, the *karmavācanā* must accord with the text; and sixth, the number of the Sangha must be complete. This is based on the second chapter of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

There appear to be five conditions; yet the vow speaks of six conditions, which is likely established for the sake of the meaning. That text says "complete," meaning that it is not incomplete even if [the number] is not twenty (this likely corresponds to the first condition).

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu receives full ordination, he properly receives the full ordination through one motion and three proclamations (this corresponds to the fifth condition), being free from obstructing factors (this corresponds to the second condition), and having a harmonious assembly rather than a divided one (this corresponds to the fourth condition). If there are ten monks...

[The section] "Beyond Ten" (corresponding to the sixth condition). This constitutes the formal reception of the precepts (*śīla-samādāna*) [as recorded in the *Jiwen*]. Third, the establishment of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) is accomplished.
This was established by Master Yuanyue based on the underlying principles; since it must logically exist, it is necessary to add it here. In summary, the verse says:
"Twenty [monks], no obstacles, the boundary, the assembly, and the full quorum for the *karmavācanā*."

Regarding the interpretation of the meaning of the eight bhikṣus: in the second fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, there is only mention of a single type of *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) for a bhikṣu.

Why, then, does it speak of "explaining the eight bhikṣus"? Now, examining the intent of the commentary (*śū*), it says: "If you [refer to] the six conditions for the *karmavācanā* in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*..."
This also serves as an explanation of the meaning of the "eight bhikṣus" within this *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. How could it be compared to simply taking the text from one's own school?

It is not that the commentary states, "In that *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, there are eight bhikṣus. As for the phrase "though the words are extensive and bustling," this refers precisely to Master Shou’s five conditions.
Now, taking those five conditions of the Master, they are rendered in verse as follows: "The capacity to receive [the precepts] has five [factors]."

The seed. The human faculty, the pure marks, and the Dharma (the first condition). The seven so-called elements, the Sangha, the ten assemblies, and the requisites for the time of the *karmavācanā* (the second condition).

The request, the object, and the correspondence of mind (the request is the third condition; the correspondence of mind and object is the fourth condition). And the words "the matter is completed" (the fifth condition).
Now, the Master [Yijing] subsumes those five conditions within four conditions, exhausting them all. He further provides a verse: "The first subsumes the Sangha and the ten..."

[The section on] the Collection. Two *karmavācanās* and four and a half [verses]. Three realms, four capacities, five [factors]. At the time of the requisites, the request consists of four and a half [verses].
The commentary states: Regarding the "five conditions," the first is the one capable of receiving; the second is that which is opposed; the third is the request;

the fourth is the correspondence of mind and object; the fifth is the completion of the matter through speech. Furthermore, regarding the first condition—the one capable of receiving—there are five [requirements]. First, it must be a human being. This excludes...

1. Because they belong to other realms of existence. They must be endowed with both sexual organs; as the text says, those who are mute, deaf, and so forth are not permitted to receive [the precepts].

2. Because their physical vessel is pure. This excludes those subject to the thirteen difficulties. 3. Because they possess the characteristics of one who has left the household life. The text states that one should not confer [the precepts] upon those wearing secular clothing.

Fifth, the partial attainment of the dharma. This is because the text states that one should not receive [the full precepts] without first having conferred the śrāmaṇera precepts. Second, regarding the subject matter, it is further divided into seven parts:

1. The accomplishment of boundary-delineation (*sīmā-bandha*). As the *Jì* (祇) states in the eighth [section]: "In a place where the *karmavācanā* has not been performed, one may not carry out monastic affairs.
2. Being subsumed within the status of the Saṃgha, as it is not performed by an individual alone. 3. The number of persons. As stated in the *Campa* [Vinaya]: [The minimum number required is thirty.]
1. It is said: "If even one person is missing, it is neither Dharma nor Vinaya. Thus the text states: "From this day forward, we authorize a group of ten to receive [the precepts].

2. All members within the four boundaries must assemble in harmony. The text states: "There is no other expedient; for if the assembly within the boundary is divided, the *karmavācanā* cannot be performed.
3. Five: The teaching of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. The text states: "The three verbal proclamations cease, and the *karman* is established. 4. Six: The Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the timing: the *Cittaviparyāsa-śāstra* states that at the time when the Dharma has been extinguished, all boundary-markings (*sīmā*) and ritual acts (*karmavācanā*) cease;
therefore, those who have already received [the precepts] do not lose them, while those who have not yet received them cannot obtain them. Regarding the completeness of the seven requisites:

the text states that one should not receive [the precepts] if one lacks even a robe and alms bowl. Third, regarding the request for the precepts: the text states that one who does not request them is not said to have received the precepts. Fourth, regarding the mental state.
This is consistent with the scriptural text: "A person who is intoxicated or insane does not successfully receive the precepts. Thus, we know that the mind does not correspond to the object.

Furthermore, according to the text regarding the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), if the motion (*jñapti*) and so forth are not performed in accordance with the prescribed method, we know that the object does not correspond to the mind.
The fifth point states that the matter is concluded. When the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is complete and the procedure reaches its conclusion, if no one raises an objection or restrains it, only then—

The formal act having been completed, the Master now subsumes those four conditions. As the previous verse stated, "First, the ten members of the Saṃgha assemble," the Master’s first condition here—stating that "the number of monks is complete"—subsumes three of the former master’s points:

the assembly of the ten members of the Saṃgha and so forth. Second, regarding "the *karmavācanā* being completed by the fourth and a half [recitations]," the Master’s second condition here states the instruction...
Regarding the accomplishment of the Dharma: it encompasses the *jñapti-caturtha* (four-part motion) teachings addressed by the former masters;

and within the fourth [stage] of the correspondence between mind and object, the object accords with the mind (this fourth condition fully encompasses four-and-a-half [factors], hence it is called "four-and-a-half"); furthermore, it encompasses the fifth [stage], wherein the verbal action is completed.
Regarding the three realms: the third condition of the present master states that the boundary is established, and within the realm, [the practice] is not...
Regarding "separate from the assembly": this refers to the accomplishment of the boundary (*sīmā*) within the context of those whom the former masters confronted.

Regarding "the four capabilities, the five times, and the requisites for begging four or half [of the robes]": the present master’s fourth condition states that one's years are complete and one’s person is free from impediments or obstacles;

this encompasses what the former masters taught regarding the immediate reception of the five [precepts], as well as the fulfillment of material requisites during the time of the Buddha’s Dharma within the context of those whom they confronted.

Regarding the third request and the fourth, within the context of the correspondence between mind and object, the mind accords with the object (the meaning of "four and a half" follows the previous explanation).

As for the four minds all being attained, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*), Volume One, they are attained within the three natures of mind as well as in the state of no-mind; this should be understood as it is therein.

Regarding the first four [types of restraint] which take the mind as their condition, the fourth verse of the *Cittaviveka* states: "In accordance with whether the mind is superior, middling, or inferior, one obtains the three grades of discipline.
Therefore, following the *Cittaviveka*, we establish that the reception of the first four types of restraint necessarily relies upon the mind as a condition.

Although the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) does not explicitly list [the conditions] in its text for the single act of receiving [ordination], it means that within the context of eight bhikṣus, the Vinaya text itself explains the meaning of the complete set of conditions.

However, the text does not list them because it takes the mind as the condition. Even though they are not listed in the text, the mind is nonetheless essential, for one must conform to the discourse on the mind (*cittasūtra*).

Regarding what constitutes the four conditions (*pratyaya*): there are four kinds of conditions. First, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); second, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);

third, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); and fourth, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). However, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, these [four] subsume the five causes (*hetu*), taking all of them as the causal condition, while including only the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) within the dominant condition.
Therefore, one should first clarify the meaning of the six causes, and subsequently explain the four conditions, so that their meanings may be understood.
This is easy to understand. However, within the Mahāyāna there are also six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu*). Although the names are the same, their meanings are entirely different.

If one were to provide a detailed exposition, I fear it would weary the reader with excessive verbiage; therefore, for now, we shall follow the extensive explanations of the six causes found in the sixth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (fascicles 16 through 21).
I shall now briefly summarize them. The verse of the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)."
The homogeneous, the associated, the pervasive, and the ripening—these are accepted as the six types of causes.

To first distinguish the first, the *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient cause)—which was formerly called the *kāraka-hetu* (productive cause)—the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "Excluding itself, all else is the efficient cause. The commentary says:
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), excluding their own self-nature, take all dharmas as their efficient cause, because they arise [from them].

Because it abides without obstruction at that time. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Jianzong lun), in its ninth chapter, provides one interpretation, stating: "The cause itself is the 'efficient' (kāraṇa);

thus it is called the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*). Because this cause possesses the power to produce the fruit, although other types of causes are also efficient causes, they have no separate designation."

As in the case of the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth, the general term is used as a specific name (this indicates a *karmadhāraya* compound). Furthermore, it is said: "Alternatively, this enables another to perform an action;
that which enables another is the cause that performs the action, which is the fruit. This indicates a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Regarding the exclusion of itself:
for instance, when a single atom of form or a single moment of mind is in the process of arising, its own substance is excluded.

No. All other conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are acting causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*). This is because when those [effects] arise, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the causal phenomena remains unobstructed.
"Cause" here refers to abiding in its own state; it means that the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the causal phenomenon does not obstruct the arising of the effect.
However, to explain this in general terms: herein, the substance of the resultant phenomenon is narrower than the cause, while the substance of the cause is universally pervasive.

As for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), their nature as a fruit is restricted solely to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Nevertheless, there are briefly two types of efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*):
first, those that possess power, such as the eye in relation to visual consciousness; second, those that lack power, such as nirvāṇa in relation to conditioned phenomena.

The second is the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), which is what was formerly called the "shared cause" (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*). Of the five causes discussed below, the nature of four is restricted to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

To first distinguish the co-existent cause, the verse says: Co-existent factors are mutual effects, As are the primary characteristics (*mahābhūta*) and their secondary characteristics (*lakṣya*), And as the mind is to its concomitants (*citta-anuvartin*).
The commentary states: If dharmas are mutual effects of one another’s *puruṣakāra-phala* (human effort effect), those dharmas are also mutually co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another.

(This explains the first phrase of the verse). To illustrate by citing specific instances: first, "like the great elements" (*mahābhūta*), meaning as the four great elements relate to one another in turn.
Second, it further points to "the characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "the characterized" (*lakṣya*). "Characteristic" refers to the primary characteristics: arising, abiding, change, and cessation.

"The characterized" refers to that which is characterized, such as matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Furthermore, these [characteristics] are of two kinds: first, the "great characteristics" (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*); [the second is the secondary characteristic]. Regarding the characteristic...

Regarding the eight factors: second, the minor characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). They characterize only a single factor. With respect to that factor, the minor characteristics act as simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*); however, with respect to the factor, the minor characteristics are not simultaneous causes.

(By analogy, the primary factor is the cause of the minor characteristics, while the minor characteristics are merely the effects of the primary factor; the primary factor does not act as a mutual effect [with them]. Nevertheless, it is admitted that the factor acts as a simultaneous cause with respect to those minor characteristics.

Thus, we know that when the verse states "simultaneous causes are mutual effects," this refers to the majority of cases. As for the major characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), with respect to the primary factor and also with respect to the minor characteristics...

And these are both simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). Third, the subsequent reference concerns the mind that functions in accordance with the mind (*cittānuvartaka*)—that is, while the mind [itself] is a simultaneous cause in relation to its own concomitants, those fruits of the simultaneous cause do not necessarily all function as simultaneous causes in relation to the mind, as will be explained later.
Regarding those that function in accordance with the mind, the verse says: "Mental factors, the two types of discipline, those [factors], and the characteristics of the mind;

these are said to function in accordance with the mind. In total, there are three categories: first, mental factors (*caitta*); second, the discipline of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the discipline of the Path (*mārga-saṃvara*).
There are two kinds of restraint (*saṃvara*). Thirdly, there are those [factors] and the various characteristics of the mind.
"Those" refers to the aforementioned mental factors (*caitta*) and the two types of restraint. "And the mind" means including the mind-king (*cittarāja*).

Herein, by mentioning the mental factors, the two restraints, and the mind-king, the intention is to indicate and grasp the various major and minor characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of these phenomena. Thus far, such is the mind.

Regarding the *anuvartaka-dharma* (concomitant factors): if the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) serves as the cause for them, one must exclude from among them the mental factors (*caitta*), the two types of discipline (*saṃvara*), and all minor characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
This is because the treatise states that the mind-king acts as a simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) only for fifty-eight factors.
Furthermore, if those which were previously results of a simultaneous cause are in turn regarded as simultaneous causes toward the mind, one must again exclude the mind from among them.

The minor mental factors (*anuparivartin-caitta*) are not co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) that arise simultaneously with the mind. All remaining fifty-four dharmas, however, are likewise co-existent causes of the mind.
(This concludes the explanation regarding those said to "follow and revolve" with the mind, though it is not necessarily the case that all of them are co-existent causes.)
The third is the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). It was formerly called the "cause of its own part" (*sva-bhāga-hetu*) or the "cause of its own seed" (*sva-bīja-hetu*).

The verse says: The similar cause consists of similar [dharmas]; It belongs to its own category and level (*nikāya-bhūmi*), and is prior [in time]. The Path [is a similar cause] for the nine levels, Taking only equal or superior [dharmas] as its fruit.

The same applies to those produced by application (*prayoga-janita*), Such as those consisting of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā-maya*). The commentary says: Regarding the similar cause, it refers to similar dharmas that...
Regarding similar dharmas acting as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), I shall briefly summarize that treatise and explain it by citing specific examples:

namely, the five wholesome aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) act as homogeneous causes for one another in relation to other wholesome aggregates; it should be understood that the same applies to defiled (*kliṣṭa*) dharmas.

The first moment [of consciousness] also arises from a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). How could the second [moment] begin by adding a *jibun* [cause]? (As in the *Shiyi*, this must be examined. Now, let us examine the characteristics of the dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) in detail.
The principle is as Master Chong has explained. Prior to the three *karmavācanās*, there already exists a mind of aspiration that serves as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Furthermore, there is also the continuity of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) prior to the *karmavācanās*; although it is not yet the substance of the precept (*śīla-dravya*), it is nonetheless able to continue until after the *karmavācanās* have been completed.

It is sufficient to establish that they are of the same category (*sabhāga*). How can you say they do not exist? Moreover, prior to immeasurable past lives, the dharmas of one's own realm and stage were all of the same category.
Thus we know that the second [category] is added only for its own specific portion (*sva-bhāga*); therefore, your statement contains an error. Now, let us resolve this through reasoning.
This may also be without error. That is to say, for the time being, we speak of "homogeneous causes" (*sabhāga-hetu*) as those whose essence is identical to the immediately preceding moment;

this does not exclude causes whose essence is distinct but whose nature is the same. Therefore, there is no contradiction in principle. (That is to say: the preceding prayer-mind and the mind or matter have distinct essences; likewise, the preceding unmanifest precept [avijñapti-śīla] and other past dharmas separated by time have distinct essences, yet they share the same wholesome nature.

Because they are distinct, they are not discussed together [in this context], though in reality such cases are not excluded. This applies even to those with distinct essences that share the same nature.)
Regarding the section on the timing of attaining the precepts:

as for those who attain them when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) manifests, Jue says: "If one follows the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, one attains the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) at the time of the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).

Other schools maintain that afflictions are severed during the path of uninterrupted transition, and the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising is attained during the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*)."
[The Master] Zhi [says]: "Now, examining these words closely, there is no way to rescue them from error. I request all later students to be cautious and never transmit them.

Furthermore, according to most schools, the ninth uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga), the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), lasts for only a single moment. Immediately thereafter, the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) attains the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna).

For those of sharp faculties, at the time they give rise to the knowledge of exhaustion, it likewise lasts for a single moment, after which the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) arises; or else, [it may be] one..."
Whether it be momentary or continuous, subsequently one may give rise to either the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*) or a conventional mind (*saṃvṛti-citta*).

According to this, the acquisition of the precepts occurs at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), not at the time of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). If following the Mahāyāna perspective, other points may be the same as before;

however, according to the [distinction between] the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, their substance is identical while their meanings differ. Whether one is of sharp or dull faculties, all realize these two; thus, these two knowledges are permitted [to be the basis for ordination].
It is the same as the preceding [discussion on] mindfulness. As has already been analyzed in the section on the "Explanation of Names," one may refer to that for the analysis of the meaning.

Regarding the statement that because it is not produced through effort (*abhisamskāra*) there is no "action" (*kriyā*), yet one obtains the "unmanifest precept" (*avijñapti-śīla*) by the power of the Path:

this is based merely on its present lack of effort. However, prior to entering meditative absorption, the manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) of making a vow is capable of eliciting the unmanifest [precept], which then continues in a continuous stream.

Upon reaching the stage of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), it is designated as having the power of the Path (*mārgabala*) as its predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). Because the conditions are complete, it is called "precept" (*śīla*);

thus, one is said to have "attained the precepts. In reality, however, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) has already existed from the preceding moment; it was simply not yet called "precept" because the conditions were not yet complete.
This has been briefly analyzed above, and it has also been explained within the section on the "Goal of Wisdom and Teaching" (*jñāna-śāsana-uddiśya-mukha*).
Next, regarding the exposition of the Three Refuges: they are fundamentally for the purpose of receiving the full precepts, as discussed in relation to the five and eight precepts and so forth.

Furthermore, when examining the various masters of past generations, they collectively established five types of the Three Refuges: first, the Three Refuges for Renouncing Evil, which according to the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*, one must first perform the Three Refuges if one intends to receive the precepts, thereby overturning former false refuges to non-Buddhist teachers and the like; second, the Three Refuges for the Five Precepts; third... [text continues].
First is the eightfold precept; second is the tenfold precept; third is the full precept (*upasampadā*); fourth is the bodhisattva’s three refuges established according to certain interpretations;
and fifth is that, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, and other texts, the bodhisattva also receives the precepts through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).

Regarding a general explanation of the three refuges, Master Hui-ssu, relying on the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*, organized them into seven sections: first, the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the three refuges; second, the three... [text continues]
The meaning of "returning" (*pratyāgama*). Third, the breadth or narrowness of the realm to which one returns. Fourth, the authenticity or falsity of the realm to which one returns.

Fifth, the sequence of the general and the particular. Sixth, the distinctions regarding the various destinies (*gati*). Seventh, the gains and losses of the gradual and sudden approaches (referring to whether the gradual approach involves receiving [the precepts] with gravity or not, and whether receiving them with gravity results in their acquisition).

These are explained in detail in the first fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* and the thirty-fourth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Those who delight in extensive wisdom may consult these at their own discretion.

I have searched for it. Since that passage does not constitute a difficult point in the text, I have omitted it here. However, because the Venerable [Master] frequently recounted it, I have recorded it again.
Furthermore, there is an addition found in the first fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which states:

"Why is it that when a person enters the path, the upāsaka receives the three refuges, and likewise the śrāmaṇera and even those who observe the eight precepts all receive the three refuges? For what reason are they not called 'those who have received full ordination'?"
"Is it the precepts? The Buddha said, "The two meanings are distinct. One who is an upāsaka does not merely abide in the Three Refuges;
only when the five precepts are further added is one first called an upāsaka. It is the same for śrāmaṇeras and those who observe the eight precepts.

Receiving the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) is sufficient in itself, with nothing further to be added; therefore, it is called 'receiving the full ordination. (And so forth... At that time, the Buddha had not yet established the two hundred and fifty precepts."
"Up to the eight precepts. For this reason, by directly receiving the Three Refuges, one obtains the full precepts" (the above is from the *Śāstra*).

The commentary states: "Now, I shall explain: once the Three Refuges are completed, the Five Precepts are immediately generated. It cites the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* as proof, saying: "One who wishes to receive the Five Precepts first receives the Three Refuges;

when the Three Refuges are finished, at that moment one has already obtained the name of the Five Precepts" (and so forth). This is like [the case where] after the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) has been performed...
The characteristics [of the precepts] are explained for the sake of understanding; thus they are taught. However, consulting various treatises, there are generally three interpretations.

In the preceding chapter, the first interpretation has already been cited. Next, another explanation states: "Some say that when the Three Refuges are completed and the precept against killing is recited, at that moment one obtains the precepts;
this is because one is able to uphold one precept, which implies upholding all five. (And so forth... Others say that one obtains the precepts only after the Five Precepts have been fully received.

Among these various explanations, the first is definitive (the above is from the treatise). Although this chapter follows the initial interpretation of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, it contradicts the *Vibhāṣā* (volume 124).
As the orthodox position of the critics (*pūrvapakṣa*) in that treatise states: "According to this explanation, one does not become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) merely by taking the three refuges.
Why do these two treatises contradict each other in this way? Now, examining the translators of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*...
Excellent. This has caused the predecessors to develop somewhat erroneous interpretations. Now, according to the *Vibhāṣā*, it is indeed consistent with the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

For example, in the one hundred twenty-fourth [section], citing the scriptural passage from the *Upāsaka-saṃvara-vidhi-sūtra*, the text states: "I, so-and-so, take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
May the Honored One remember me: I am an upāsaka. From this day forth, until the end of my life, I shall protect living beings."

"Taking refuge in purity" (the above is from the sūtra text). In the treatise (*śāstra*), the interpretations of two masters from two countries are fully recorded. Now, the intention of the master from the country of Gandhāra is as follows:

"The phrasing of this sūtra text indicates that one merely wishes for the three refuges and personally undertakes the vow to receive them; these three refuges are themselves termed an *upāsaka* (lay follower)."
Yet, the precepts have not yet been obtained. Only after the preceptor subsequently explains the characteristics of the five precepts does one finally obtain them.
However, as for the scriptural passage stating, "One who takes refuge in purity must protect living beings," this is because if one does not protect living beings, one does not take refuge in purity;
thus, this sentence does not explicitly reveal the characteristics of the precepts. The masters of the treatises in Kaśmīra maintain that these scriptural words actually manifest the three refuges.

This also clarifies the characteristics of the precepts. As the Sūtra says: "One who protects living beings returns to purity. Regarding this, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* offers two explanations.

The first states: "Protecting living beings" means abstaining from killing; taking this as the basis, the other four [precepts] are established, because among the harms inflicted upon living beings, killing is primary.

The second states: Furthermore, the expression "protecting living beings" applies to all five precepts, because it involves protecting sentient beings by abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying.
Regarding the statement on drinking alcohol: once this vow has been made, one also obtains the three refuges and also obtains the restraint; only then is one called an upāsaka (lay follower).

Subsequently, the preceptor explains the five characteristics merely for the sake of understanding, not for the sake of obtaining the precepts. Therefore, the masters of the Kaśmīra school, whose positions we refute, state:

"There is no such thing as becoming an upāsaka through the three refuges alone. (In reality, the ritual formulas for receiving the precepts in both countries are identical, based upon the scriptural texts.)

(However, they differ because their respective exegeses of the sūtra differ). Now, examining the three interpretations of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Dolun), all are the correct positions of the *Vibhāṣā* commentators;
the intent of the two treatises is the same, and there is truly no contradiction. Furthermore, the meaning of the first interpretation in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* is clear:

it fully recites the sūtra text, stating that when the self-vow is completed, it is called the completion of the Three Refuges. That one who has completed the Three Refuges obtains the five precepts is precisely what the sūtra text says.

In the middle [section], because he vows to protect living beings, he obtains the five precepts. The second and third explanations clarify the original intent, merely explaining the phrase "protecting living beings";
they do not contradict the reasoning of the first explanation. It is the translators who have falsely judged right and wrong.
Regarding the initial explanation of the meditative determination (*niyama*): it is not that the Indic original contained these words of dispute.

Rather, since ancient times, masters of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma have failed to investigate the textual characteristics and have erroneously conferred the precepts upon others; thus, by failing to respect the wording of the sūtra, they certainly do not obtain the precepts.

The thirteenth chapter of the *Samyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* also relies on the phrasing of the sūtra text, stating: "I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, the Honored One among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma..."
"Homage to the One Honored by those Free from Desire; homage to the Sangha, the Honored among all assemblies. I am such-and-such a lay follower (*upāsaka*); may you bear witness to this.
For as long as life lasts, I renounce the taking of living beings; with a pure heart, I take refuge. This concludes the third [section] (the above is the treatise).

However, in the [text] numbered 124, it quotes the scriptural passage: "Protecting life and returning to purity. That treatise further states: "However, there is a different recension which says 'renouncing living beings' (*prāṇātipātād viramāmi*)... and so forth.

There are many such explanations, which I have not recorded in full. Thus, one should know that there are two different versions of the sūtra text. The *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* follows the version of the *Śasana-sūtra*.
Having thus thoroughly investigated and established the principles and meanings above, the arguments set forth in this commentary should now be concluded.

The Commentary states: "The answer to this refers to 'the mental aspiration' (心期). This is the heading. 'Because the amount of the characteristics explained varies, it causes the recipient to aspire to five or ten [precepts]' according to what the mind aspires to—this is the explanation."
Regarding the distinct phrasing for each [formula]: when reciting the two refuges and the five or eight precepts to overturn heterodox views, various masters of the sūtras and śāstras all say:

"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, the Honored One among Two-legged Beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the Honored One among the Assembly."
Recite three times: "I, [Name], have completed taking refuge in the Buddha; I have completed taking refuge in the Dharma; I have completed taking refuge in the Sangha.

From this day forward, I shall honor the Buddha as my teacher and shall no longer take refuge in other demons, heretics, or external paths. I pray only that the Three Jewels will compassionately accept me. (Recite three times).
Regarding the reception of the eight precepts, Vinaya Master Nanshan stated: "I, [Name], ... up to taking refuge in the Sangha for one day..."

One night, he became a *śīlavat* upāsaka. Now, to examine the term *upāsaka*: in the correct Sanskrit (*brahma-svara*), it is called *upāsaka*, which is translated as "one who serves closely" (*jin-shi*).
In Sanskrit, it is also called *upavāsa*, which is translated as "one who dwells closely" (*jin-zhu*). Since these two names are distinct, [their meanings differ].
One should not be called an *upāsaka* merely by observing the eight precepts; therefore, we shall now further examine the previously mentioned taking of refuge.

Regarding the phrase "no longer taking refuge in other heterodox spirits and demons," this merely serves to overturn heterodoxy. As for the five precepts, they have already been cited above, namely the passages from the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, and the sūtras.
Regarding the eight precepts and the three refuges, no such textual exposition has yet been seen. For now, following the model of the five precepts, one should say: "up to..."
May the Venerable One remember me: I am one who dwells in proximity [to the precepts]. From this moment until the break of dawn tomorrow, I vow to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Regarding the ten precepts and the three refuges, according to the subsequent text: "Up to taking refuge in the Sangha, I now follow the Buddha and go forth."
"Such-and-such a person is my preceptor; the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One.
Regarding the three refuges and the observance of the precepts, according to the text below, it says: "up to taking refuge in the Saṅgha. Now, one goes forth under the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One. (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Chapter 1). Question: If one receives the three refuges, or if one first recites...
Regarding the Dharma Jewel: if one subsequently recites "Buddha," does this constitute the Three Refuges? Answer:

If one lacks understanding and speaks out of order, one cannot personally achieve the Three Refuges (though the teacher incurs no offense, and it still allows the disciple to achieve the Three Refuges).

If one has understanding yet speaks erroneously, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense and the Three Refuges are not achieved (the teacher incurs a *duṣkṛta*, and it prevents the disciple from achieving the Three Refuges). Question: If one recites...
Regarding the Buddha and the Dharma, but not mentioning the Saṃgha: does this constitute the Three Refuges? (The remaining two phrases should be applied accordingly. Answer:

It does not constitute the Three Refuges (because the objects of refuge are incomplete, it is not established). Question: If one does not receive the Three Refuges, can one obtain the Five Precepts, the Eight Precepts, or the Ten Precepts?

If one does not undergo the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of four proclamations), can one obtain the Full Ordination (*upasampadā*)? Answer: None of these are obtained. (*Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, 34)
Question: If one receives the vows of discipline (*vinaya*) without having first taken refuge (*śaraṇagamana*), does one obtain those vows? Some say one does not;
others say one does. If one does not know the Dharma, or if one forgets or errs and thus does not take refuge, the recipient obtains them and the bestower also obtains them.
[This constitutes] an offense. If one possesses pride and does not receive the Three Refuges, but receives only the vows of discipline (*śīla*), that person will certainly not [attain the result].
(If the disciple forgets to receive them and the teacher remains silent and neglects it, the teacher incurs an offense. There are also two explanations regarding this, as previously stated;

one should know that the third fascicle of the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* says: "Either twelve kinds, or twenty-one kinds," yet it does not provide an explanation. One should follow [the standard interpretation] accordingly.
According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*: Because sexual misconduct, theft, killing, and lying are each associated with the wholesome root of non-greed, they constitute four precepts.

Likewise, for non-hatred and non-delusion, there are also four each; thus, there are twelve. If one abstains from the seven branches of unwholesome action through these wholesome roots, there are twenty-one.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states, etc. This refers to the first fascicle of that treatise.

Regarding "those with outflows and those without outflows," this is explained from the perspective of the training precepts (*śaikṣa-śīla*). Regarding "those who possess them and those who do not," this is clarified according to their respective stages (*avasthā*).

Regarding the statement, "However, because it is a constituent of the study [of the precepts], it universally conditions [the object]," the question is raised: If it were to universally condition the object, then the precepts should be universally produced;
that is, a śrāmaṇera should already have fully obtained two hundred and fifty precepts. If this were so, it would contradict the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 104, which states:
"When an upāsaka receives the śrāmaṇera-pratimokṣa-saṃvara, he does not abandon the five precepts but further obtains the ten precepts; at that time, he possesses fifteen."
Regarding the vows (*saṃvara*): when one who is already a *śrāmaṇera* further receives the *bhikṣu* vow, at that moment they accomplish more than two hundred and sixty-five vows.

Since the treatise is explicit in stating that there are only fifteen at the stage of the ten precepts, and their number is only increased upon reaching the stage of full ordination (*upasaṃpad*), how could it be possible for a *śrāmaṇera* to universally take them all at once?
Answer: The treatise bases its calculation on the fact that the nature of a *śrāmaṇera* is established by the ten precepts; it does not exclude [the possibility of taking more].

The universal production of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) constitutes these ten precepts, which are established as the restraint (*saṃvara*). All other non-informative wholesome actions are not "precepts";

even if one violates them, they are collectively termed *duṣkṛta* (misdeeds), but cannot be specifically termed the *duṣkṛta* of violating a precept. This is for the purpose of training the faculties of those who are suitable vessels, so that they may train universally.

Regarding why the Sages did not establish inquiries for those who receive the five or ten precepts, according to the *Śrāddhakarman-sūtra* (or *Susheng jing*), when receiving the five precepts, one must likewise undergo interrogation.
Every time the Venerable [Master] recounted this, he noted that the full scriptural intent cannot be recorded here in detail;

it states that one must first inquire of one’s parents, down to one’s slaves and servants, and then inform the king before seeking to receive the precepts. The Preceptor should then ask: "Do your parents, wife, and children..."
"Does the lord of the land permit you? Have you not incurred debt to the Three Jewels or to others? Do you currently suffer from any internal or external physical or mental ailments?
Have you never killed one who has resolved upon Bodhicitta? Have you never stolen the property of the Saṃgha present before you?

Have you never engaged in double-tongued speech or harsh words? Have you never committed unrighteous acts toward a human being, or toward your mother, sisters, or female relatives? Have you not [acted improperly] toward the Great Assembly?"
Does one tell a falsehood therein? To speak extensively, it continues until, having received the three refuges, one is called an *upāsaka*.
There are *upāsakas* who possess one part and those who possess many parts; that is to say, they observe one precept, or two, four, or five, respectively.

Furthermore, after the reception [of the precepts], the six grave and twenty-eight light offenses are explained for them. According to this, these are indeed the Bodhisattva precepts and not the Hinayana school.
As for what is clarified: the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that bodhisattvas have ten grave and forty-eight light precepts, which differ from those in the *Śrāmaṇera-śikṣāpada-sūtra*.
This is like the case where an upādhyāya may be either fully qualified or not; both the ten precepts and the full precepts require an upādhyāya, according to the Vinaya below.
[The text] explains: One who possesses the full precepts (*upasampadā*) has the various formal procedures (*karmavācanā*), whereas one with the ten precepts (*daśa-śīla*) does not.

Regarding the statement in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) that one must receive them in their entirety to obtain [the precepts], this refers to the first fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*.
The *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 124, is likewise. Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* asks: "For what reason does the Sūtra establish [the categories of] 'one part,' 'few parts,' 'many parts,' and 'complete'?"

[The text] distinguishes between the lay follower (*upāsaka*) and others. The answer states that this refers to the stage of observance (*dhāraṇa-avasthā*), not the stage of undertaking (*samādāna-avasthā*).

Regarding the one-day precepts (*upavāsa-śīla*), the *Śāriputrābhidharma* (Treatise on the Abhidharma of Śāriputra), fascicle 24, records that the Venerable Ghosaka said to the assembly: "One should say that the one-day fast may be observed with none at all, or with one, two, three, or even up to seven [limbs];
it is not necessary to possess all eight. Such a statement does not mean that there are no limbs at all, but rather that it may extend up to seven.

It is called "near-abiding" (*upavāsa*). As for "near-abiding," it must be complete with eight branches. Regarding the questions and answers concerning the eight precepts, they are as explained in the "Chapter on the Eight Precepts" in the twelfth fascicle [of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*].
Regarding the questions and answers concerning the five precepts, they are as explained in the "Chapter on the Five Precepts" in the eleventh fascicle [of the same work].
Concerning the time, it is as stated in the first fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the twelfth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
As seen by Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, the twenty-fifth section on Leather in that Vinaya states: Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa entered the ocean to gather jewels and returned;
he passed through a city of hungry ghosts (preta) and reached a tree at nightfall.

There he saw a man and a woman of handsome appearance, wearing celestial jewel crowns, enjoying themselves together. When the night had passed and the woman vanished, a dog immediately appeared and devoured the man.
The flesh of his own son. Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa questioned him about this, and he replied: "In a previous life, I was a butcher.

Kātyāyana transformed me, and I said, 'My ancestors have always practiced this trade; how can I stop? He then saved me by saying, 'Since you slaughter during the day, you should observe the precepts at night.
Because of this, my karmic retribution is now such as this. Remembering what he had previously encountered, he went further to another tree.
He saw a man who experienced pleasure during the day; the full explanation is as before. This was due to his fondness for sexual indulgence.
Kātyāyana instructed him, saying, "Since you are greedy for sexual indulgence at night, you should observe the precepts during the day," and so forth, as detailed therein.
If one follows the first volume of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Section 124), these passages may be reconciled. As for the *Vibhāṣā*, it asks: "How should such statements be interpreted?"

(That is to say: if one does not allow for the undertaking [of vows] by day and night divisions, how then should such scriptural passages be interpreted? Answer: They are subsumed under "excellent conduct" (*sucarita*) and do not constitute formal discipline (*saṃvara*); they refer to the fruit of undertaking excellent conduct.

It is not the fruit of non-restraint; therefore, there is no fault. Other masters say that this was a transformation created by the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of that Venerable One, and is not real, intended to cause Koṭikarṇa to become weary of the world; thus, it need not be explained away.

Some say that one may also obtain [it] (meaning one may obtain it partially). The critique says: the former explanation is superior, because it concerns the precepts for a day and night (*rātri-divasa-śīla*). Now, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is cited to prove the partial [attainment].
Regarding the "receiving" [of the precepts], this corresponds to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*’s explanation of what is not the correct principle.

However, according to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, chapter twelve, the "Chapter on the Sevenfold Good Restraints," it says: "Whether for only one day, or only one night, or for half a day, or half a night—one obtains them according to one's capacity to receive them."

"Free from adornments for a day and night. (The commentary states: One must receive this precept at dawn; it is because one must observe it for a full day and night. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 124, says:

As for the "defiled-path śramaṇa," this refers to the bhikṣu Mahallaka, who delighted in stealing the property of others and so forth. (Mahallaka means "one who is greatly dull-witted.")

[The term] formerly translated as *mahallaka* (an old man). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 29, states: "First, those who excel in the path; second, those who teach the path; third, those who live by the path; fourth, those who destroy the path.

One should know that the Sugatas are called 'śramaṇas who excel in the path' (this excludes the Pratyekabuddhas, which differs from the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*; however, the meaning is the same as 'Nirvāṇa,' which is the ultimate attainment of the path).

Those who expound the True Dharma are called 'śramaṇas who teach the path' (this includes both ordinary beings and Bodhisattvas, etc., which differs from the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*; in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is said they demonstrate the path)."

[The same applies to] those who have attained [the fruit]. Those who practice wholesome deeds are called "living śramaṇas" (jīvamārga-śramaṇa); they are termed "living" because they are capable of generating the Noble Path. This category includes ordinary persons (pṛthagjana), which differs from the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Nirvana is the realization of the Path; it may be understood in this same way. Those who engage in wrong practices are called "monks who destroy the Path" (the wrong practices consist of the three types of misconduct in body, speech, and mind;

this is as described in the aforementioned sutras and treatises regarding those who defile the Path). Furthermore, those in training and those beyond training are called "those who excel in the Path," because they have eradicated all afflictions of both the views and the meditative stages (this differs from the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*).
Those among the assembly of Śrāvakas who uphold the Tripiṭaka are called "monks who explain the Path" (referring exclusively to the Śrāvakas). As for other...

One who is born [into the path], for the sake of touching what has not yet been touched and realizing what has not yet been realized, diligently cultivates the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and is capable of touching and realizing it, is called a "Śramaṇa of the Living Path.
Because he currently possesses the warmth (*uṣmagata*) of various wholesome dharmas, which can give rise to the life-faculty of noble wisdom (*āryaprajñājīvita*), he is called "living" and not "dead.

(This reveals the practitioner who trains as a Śrāvaka. The destruction of the path should be understood as explained extensively therein. One who approaches a Dharma teacher practices through reflection and hearing.
The three types of wisdom correspond inversely to the first three kinds of śramaṇas; the fourth, who defiles the path, is as can be understood from the usual explanations.

Regarding the nineteenth [category], the forfeiture of the Dharma: the detailed explanation is found in the section on the precept against sexual misconduct below. For now, I shall provide a verse: Forfeiture of the Three Jewels and the two teachers;
Fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring, the precepts, and the study; Accepting a layperson, a *saimi*, or an outsider; A non-śramaṇa or non-śākya.
