As for the "one type of precept," it refers to that which is conferred by means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations). (End of the cited treatise. Regarding the phrase "prior to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one is fully endowed with the four abandonments (*upekṣā*)," this means:

Prior to the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), there are seven stages of preparation (prayoga): first, the contemplation of the five stabilizing practices (pañca-sthāpanīya-bhāvanā); second, the mindfulness of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna);

third, the mindfulness of general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna); fourth, the stage of Heat (uṣmagata); fifth, the stage of Summits (mūrdhan); sixth, the stage of Patience (kṣānti); and seventh, the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma). What is referred to here as "prior to the foundations of mindfulness" [refers to these stages].
This refers to the period prior to the third expedient means. Regarding the fulfillment of the four types of relinquishment (*tyāga*): the relinquishment at the end of life is evident.

As for the remaining three relinquishments—relinquishment through the power of regression, relinquishment through the ritual act of abandoning the precepts, and relinquishment through the two sexual organs—it is possible for them to occur when the power of contemplative practice is weak.

If that is so, when one enters the stages such as *uṣmagata* (Heat) and the rest, does one not also undergo retrogression, the severance of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), the appearance of both sexual organs (*dviliṅga*), or their loss?

For instance, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle seven, states: Question: When the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) have arisen, can one again receive the male organ (*śaṇḍha*), the hermaphrodite organ (*paṇḍaka*), the absence of organs (*aliṅga*), or both organs (*dviliṅga*)?

Answer: One may again receive them; however, this applies only to the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*), and not to the others. (This means that one may retrogress from Heat or Summits, or after death, again receive the two organs and so forth. However, [the various...]

The treatise explains that the first three roots of goodness are abandoned at the time of death, just as they are in the case of the prātimokṣa vows; furthermore, the first two roots of goodness may also be abandoned through falling away (whereas *kṣānti* is never subject to falling away). Moreover, the *Abhidharmakośa*, chapter twenty-three, states:

If one who has attained the stage of *uṣmagata* (heat) can fall away, sever the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), and commit an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*), then according to these passages, since it is admitted that they may sever the roots of goodness and undergo the arising of both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), it should also follow that they may likewise die or relinquish [the stages]. Why, then, do all [texts] state that prior to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one possesses all four types of relinquishment?
Answer: This is stated "prior" with respect to the gravity of the offense; however, in reality, it does not preclude [the possibility of falling away from] the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*.
There are also four types of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Regarding the statement that "the four present patiences (*kṣānti*) and those following them belong to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) because they lack two faculties": this refers to the observation of the Four Truths.
When one directly accepts [the truths] through patience, giving rise to the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, these are called the four present patiences.

Regarding the statement that "the dharmas of the form realm (rūpadhātu) lack two faculties": one asks whether this claim that they lack two faculties refers to the case where, even if there is regression, two faculties are still absent;
or if it refers to the case of non-regression, in which case—just as the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that [those stages] lack the four calamities—they should likewise lack all four, rather than just two.

If it refers to the case where, even upon regression, two faculties are absent, then it contradicts the seventh fascicle of the *Vibhāṣā*, which states that those at the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*) may regress and receive [them again].
Regarding the two sexual organs (*dvindriya-kāya*), how should this be interpreted? In the present chapter on "Exegesis," it is explained based on the state of non-retrogression.

As for the statement that there are "no two organs," the term "no" (*wu*) signifies "contrary. Why is this said? Because these are the dharmas of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), and they are contrary to the two organs.
This means that the arising of the two organs is fundamentally due to sensual desire; therefore, the dharmas of the Form Realm must necessarily be contrary to the two organs. If this is so...
The dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) likewise contradict and sever the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Why, then, are they not mentioned? Answer:

The two faculties and sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) are definitely contradicted by their specific adversaries within the form realm. However, the severance of the roots of goodness and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are contradicted merely upon their reconnection;

it is not necessary for them to be contradicted by dharmas of the form realm. Therefore, they are not mentioned. In the preceding chapters, this has been a general demonstration that the dharmas of the form realm contradict these two.
The "forms" (liṅga) should further be distinguished individually. For each root of goodness, there is nothing that is abandoned [simultaneously]. Therefore, the next chapter states:
"However, within the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, there is no duality of forms. This merely clarifies the oppositions and contradictions within those two stages.

Since this stage does not directly contradict the severance of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) or the performance of formal acts (*kriyā*), the abandonment [of these] is omitted and not mentioned as being severed, and so forth. If...

Furthermore, the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) does not directly contradict the severance of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Why, then, does the treatise state that upon reaching the stage of patience, one eliminates the severance of the roots of goodness?

As the treatise says: "The mind of patience is twofold; it excludes the two types of [persons who] sever the roots of goodness through the loss of sexual organs. (Regarding "the mind of patience is twofold," there are two explanations: first, the mind of patience has two kinds of relinquishment—relinquishment due to [the loss of] the organs and relinquishment at the end of life; second, "the mind of patience is twofold" refers to the two things being excluded: the loss of sexual organs and the severance of the roots of goodness). Answer: Regarding the elimination of the severance of the roots of goodness at the stage of patience:

[it is because] at the stage of patience, one abandons the state of being a hermaphrodite (*ubhayavyañjana*), and since the severance of the roots of goodness occurs only in those with such a constitution, it is said to be eliminated. Furthermore, at this stage, one attains the certainty of non-retrogression regarding the realization of the Truths (*satyābhisamaya*), and thus the possibility of severing the roots of goodness is permanently removed. Therefore, it is stated that the severance of the roots of goodness is excluded at the stage of patience.

The preceding stages of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summits) may involve the regression that severs the roots of goodness; however, at this present stage of *kṣānti* (Patience), there is definitively no such regression or severing of the roots of goodness.

Because it possesses this distinction, it must be explained separately. If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter 23, even though one may regress from the stage of *mūrdhan*, one does not sever the roots of goodness.
Thus, its verse states: "Heat necessarily leads to Nirvāṇa; Summits never sever the roots of goodness; Patience does not fall [into the evil realms]."
Regarding the "evil destinies" (*durgati*): the first entry is into the state of separation from birth (*vairāgya*). The prose commentary states:

"If one attains the stage of 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*), although there may be a regression of roots of goodness, the commission of immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*), or falling into evil destinies, one will not wander for long and will certainly reach Nirvana.

If one attains the stage of 'Summit' (*mūrdhan*), although there may be regression and the commission of immediate transgressions, one will ultimately never sever the roots of goodness. (From the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Chapter Seven).

The principle is the same here. Regarding the person [at this stage], it accords with the thirty-sixth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, which states that at the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), one is already able not to sever the roots of goodness.
The sixty-first fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* also says the same as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Based on these sūtras and śāstras, if it were stated in this present chapter that the roots of goodness are severed only upon reaching the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*), it would be far too late. However, the intention is to demonstrate that there is no retrogression from the severing of the roots of goodness... [until]... reaching [the stage of Patience].

It is only at the stage of *kṣānti* (patience) that one speaks [of such things], because in the two preceding stages, both [the possibility of] regression and [the possibility of] abandoning [the path] are admitted. Furthermore, according to the stage of *kṣānti*, there should be no wearying or abandoning;

yet, with respect to the desire for making offerings, abandonment is admitted, as in the case of the śrāmaṇera Cunda, who vowed to remain a śrāmaṇera in order to make offerings to his teacher—how much more so, then, regarding the stage of *kṣānti*.

Regarding the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) and those who do not abandon [the roots of goodness] upon seeing the Truths: while one is in the stage of contemplation (*darśana-mārga*), there is no abandonment through non-action (*avijñapti*), because one is necessarily entering the state of a Noble One (*ārya*).
There is no abandonment through the severance of the roots of goodness, because one does not take on an evil body; thus, there is no possession of both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*).

(In the preceding stage of Patience [*kṣānti*], there was already no severance of the roots of goodness or possession of both organs, much less so now at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas. There is no death [during this stage]. As previously explained, since it lasts for only a single moment, it is brief in duration and therefore [these abandonments] do not occur.
It is possible for one to pass away [at that stage]. If that were so, then during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there would have to be death.

Therefore, according to the current interpretation, by the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*), one must necessarily enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*); thus, one does not pass away. Furthermore, the highest degree of patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) also lasts for only a single moment;

this is based on the twenty-third fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, which states that once the highest patience has been attained, one possesses the quality of non-arising regarding the eighth existence. It is also...
This is due to the power of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); it is impossible for such a person to die, as they must necessarily enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*).

If, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, those who possess the four levels of patience (*kṣānti*) are also limited to dying [in that state], this was previously explained in terms of what is manifest;

therefore, the four types of equanimity (*upekṣā*) were individually assigned to them. Now, following the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and speaking according to the ultimate principle, if one does not fall back from the four kinds of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), [one cannot die].
It is determined that within this [state], there are no three types of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Regarding those who have already produced the goodness of ethical discipline (*śīla*): prior to its relinquishment, it possesses the functional activity (*kāritra*) of the category of ethical discipline. This consists of two aspects:

first, the dharma of ethical discipline (*śīladharma*), and second, the action of ethical discipline (*śīlakarman*). The dharma of ethical discipline is the very essence of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). The action of ethical discipline is the efficacy of grasping and bestowing fruits.

It is possible. This means that although subsequent non-manifest karma (*avijñapti*) does not continue once it has been severed, that which was previously produced and has entered the past still remains within the body;
thus, the fruit and the functional capacity for the fruit are not lost.
If one speaks of "abandoning karma without losing the dharma that constitutes its fruit," this refers to the *prātimokṣa*.

While it brings about results within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), once the fruit of *anāgāmin* or *arhat* is attained, one will certainly not be reborn in the desire realm; therefore, the *prātimokṣa* is abandoned.

Although its essential nature is not lost and thus it is called "non-loss" (*avipraṇāśa*), because its functional capacity to produce its result is definitely lost, it is termed "abandoning karma. However...

According to the Mahāyāna, those who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) and beyond do not create new karma. This refers to those in the first two fruits (*phala*) while still at the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
If they had previously obtained the precepts, they possess both the projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and the completing (*paripūraka*) karma that brings about birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

However, if they receive the precepts only after attaining the state of a noble one (*ārya*), they can only generate the substance of the completing karma; they lack projecting karma because they no longer create it. According to...
The minor lineage (kṣudra-gotra) is permitted to create new karma and likewise possesses both types of karma. Other ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) may be understood by analogy.

Therefore, regarding those who "obtain what is obtained" (prāpti-prāpta), this section briefly distinguishes the essence of obtaining (prāpti) and relinquishing (tyāga). This is presented in four sections: first, the explanation of the names.

Second, the essence; third, the distinctions; fourth, the mutual requirements. First, regarding the explanation of the names: when one first acquires a dharma within the continuum of a sentient being's body, it is called "acquisition" (*prāpti*);
when it is subsequently acquired in a continuous succession, it is called "possession" (*samanvāgama*).

Although acquisition, attainment, and possession are identical in their essential nature, they are explained in this way by distinguishing their characteristics. If a sentient being’s body has just lost [a dharma]...
The dharma is called "renunciation" (*prahāṇa*). When it subsequently continues as renunciation, it is called "non-accomplishment" (*asamanvāgama*).

Although non-possession (*aprāpti*) and non-accomplishment are distinct, their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is actually the same, whether it be loss or renunciation; yet they are provisionally distinguished in this way. Next, regarding the analysis of their essence:

according to the Sautrāntika and Mahāyāna schools, there is no separate entity apart from matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). For instance, in the case of the sense faculties, objects, matter, and so forth...

Dharmas, as well as mental factors (*caitta*) and other such phenomena, when they are comprised within one's own continuum, are termed "acquisition" (*prāpti*). Once they have been lost or abandoned, they are termed "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*).

Apart from form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), these do not possess any separate substantial entity. According to the Sarvāstivādins, apart from form and mind, there exists a distinct real entity which is neither form nor mind;
it is an unconditioned factor (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) among the five aggregates, specifically included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

[Included in the] aggregates. The inclusion within the Mahāyāna aggregates is likewise the same; however, these are merely conventional dharmas (*prajñaptidharma*). Next, to distinguish the differences:
the distinctions in the Mahāyāna are too numerous to analyze exhaustively here. For now, following the Sarvāstivāda, the *Vibhāṣā* (158) states:

"There are four types of acquisition (*prāpti*): first, acquisition prior to the dharma; second, acquisition simultaneous with the dharma; third, acquisition subsequent to the dharma; and fourth," [and so forth].

There is acquisition of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). However, since all unconditioned phenomena do not conform to the world, it cannot be said that they are acquired before, after, or simultaneously.
There are six types of acquired phenomena: first, there are acquired phenomena that can only be acquired simultaneously, such as those born of maturation (*vipākaja*);

second, there are acquired phenomena that can only be acquired prior to them, such as the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) at the conclusion of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and so forth; third, there are [acquired phenomena...]
1. Attainments of dharmas that exist only simultaneously and subsequently, such as the prātimokṣa vows and the like. 2.

Attainments of dharmas that exist only prior to and simultaneously with [the attainment], such as the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti) and the like. 3. Attainments of dharmas that possess all three—prior, simultaneous, and subsequent—as in the case of other wholesome or defiled dharmas and the like.
4. Attainments of dharmas for which it cannot be said whether they exist prior to, simultaneously with, or subsequently, yet which are nonetheless admitted [to exist].

There is acquisition (*prāpti*). For example, in the case of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), there is definitely no "subsequent acquisition" (*paścāt-prāpti*) that exists solely after the dharma itself.

Question: With what intention did the author of the treatise establish these six categories? Answer: Among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there are three degrees of potency (*bala*), namely: superior, middling, and inferior.

Now, as for a phenomenon of the superior grade, it stands to reason that it should possess all three types of acquisition—prior, subsequent, and simultaneous. However, this superior grade is now divided into three categories: first, those that possess only prior acquisition; [the others being those with only subsequent acquisition, and those with both].

It is attained. Because it is of the highest grade (*adhimātra*), there is the aforementioned attainment (*prāpti*). However, due to the deficiency of conditions (*pratyaya-vaikalya*), it never arises.

Since it neither flows into the present nor the past, there is no simultaneous attainment (*sahaprāpti*) nor subsequent attainment (*paścātprāpti*). If it were to flow [into those times], then all three would necessarily be present.
Second, there is only the prior and simultaneous attainment; this too is of the highest grade, but only because the subsequent moment is necessarily...
Because it has been relinquished, there is no subsequent acquisition (*prāpti*). If it were not relinquished, then logically there would also be [a subsequent acquisition].

Third, regarding those that possess both the aforementioned simultaneous and subsequent acquisitions, the meaning may be inferred accordingly. Next, for intermediate-grade dharmas, there are only simultaneous and subsequent acquisitions;

next, for inferior-grade dharmas, there is only the simultaneous acquisition, together with the acquisition of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, six categories are established. Next, to distinguish non-acquisition (*aprāpti*): in relation to conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena, there is one [category].
There are four types: first, there is non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) that exists only prior to the dharma, such as the final momentary aggregates at the time of entering *nirvāṇa*;
second, there is that which possesses both [non-acquisition] prior to and subsequent to the dharma; third, there is the non-acquisition of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*);

and fourth, as explained in detail in the *Vibhāṣā*, it is certain that there is never a case where there is only non-acquisition subsequent to the dharma, nor is it certain that there is non-acquisition simultaneous with the dharma. One should reflect upon this according to reason. 4.

Regarding the analysis of the characteristics [of acquisition]: it is asked, since one speaks of "acquisition" (prāpti) because of obtaining what is to be obtained, by whom is this acquisition itself obtained?
If there were an acquisition of the acquisition, it would lead to an infinite regress. In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, fascicle 158, the Master of the Evaluation (*Vibhajyavādin*) explains:
"According to this explanation, within a single moment there are only three factors: first, that dharma; second, its acquisition; and third, the acquisition of the acquisition. This is as follows:
Because [the acquisition] is attained, one accomplishes that dharma and accomplishes the acquisition itself. Furthermore, the acquisition is attained by means of another acquisition;

thus, it accomplishes the acquisition through mutual attainment, and so there is no infinite regress. Based on this, the acquisitions co-arising with dharmas (*dharmasahaja-prāpti*) and so forth have been briefly analyzed.

However, according to the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, their characteristics are distinguished by including both those co-arising with dharmas and those arising subsequently. Thus, it says: "Each individual entity first arises..."
At that time, these three factors arise together with their own intrinsic nature (as may be known by reference to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*). In the second moment, six factors arise together:

namely, the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the three factors and the acquisitions of those acquisitions (*prāptiprāpti*). In the third moment, there are nine acquisitions and nine acquisitions of acquisitions for all the factors produced.
In this manner, these acquisitions increase successively in later moments; because they are without resistance (*apratigha*), they mutually accommodate one another.

If it were not so, then if one sentient being were to attain [it], space would not be able to contain it, let alone a second and so forth. One should know that the *Samyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, chapter thirteen, also explains the meaning of "attainment" (*prāpti*).

The statement that, "apart from these, the three types of sensation cease within the intermediate state, and furthermore, this is restricted to Jambudvīpa," is based on the second section of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
If one relies on the principle established by myself previously, the aforementioned dharmas may extend to the final age and also pervade other directions.

Regarding their number: however, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, they are restricted to Jambudvīpa.
As for the precepts that serve as the cause for the substance of the undertaking, the teaching is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and the precepts are the objective cause (*ālambana-hetu*).
Regarding the "expedient means of body and speech" up to the "treatise on the mind," as for the "bodily movement of the agent's body" as an expedient means:
in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 113, it is asked, "For what reason is it called 'karma' (action)? One master explains, saying:

this is bodily karma (*kāyakarman*). Although there is in reality no movement, it is like proceeding toward another location.
That which acts is mental karma (*manaskarman*), which instigates the former two. For this reason, they are called "karma. (The above is the treatise. However, there is no deliberation.
Family. Now, regarding this *Cittaviparyāsa-śāstra*, taking this [point] explains that it relies on the conventional designation of a continuum (*saṃtati-prajñapti*).

Therefore, it speaks of "movement. According to reality, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) perish moment by moment; once arisen, they immediately cease. Thus, they possess no sense of moving or shifting.

Consequently, the thirteenth verse of the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Bodily intimation is admitted to be a distinct shape; movement is not its essence. In the prose commentary, it says: "The treatise states: By the power of volition (*cetanā*), a distinct..."
The arising of such and such bodily forms is called bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti-karman*).

Other schools state that movement is called bodily informative action, because when the body moves, it is moved by karma. To refute this, it is said that there is no movement, because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are momentary (*kṣaṇika*);
[they] arise in one place and perish in that very same place, with no possibility of transferring from here to there.

[It occurs] in other directions. Therefore, one cannot say that movement is what constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*). (Commentary: Since it is stated that other schools maintain that there is actual movement, this does not refute the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*’s [position] that movement is merely nominal.
If that is so, how could karma in many schools not be merely nominal? Answer: If one discusses its essential nature (*svabhāva*), [it is real].
Moment by moment, it has actual matter as its substance. Now, in discussing its characteristics, there is no error in citing movement and action.

However, regarding "action" (*vijñapti*) and "non-action" (*avijñapti*), or what are termed "informative" (*vijñapti*) and "non-informative" (*avijñapti*) in older translations, the newly translated sūtras and śāstras name them "manifest" (*vijñapti*) and "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*).
To explain these terms: wholesome volition and so forth initiate bodily and vocal actions that manifest good or evil; therefore, they are called "manifest. As for "unmanifest":

Regarding this, the first chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Although the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) has the nature of matter and action just like the manifest (*vijñapti*), it does not communicate [itself] so as to make it known to others;
therefore, it is called 'unmanifest'. (Commentary: Although the nature of unmanifest matter is the same as that of manifest action, it lacks any communication [of itself];

therefore, it is named "unmanifest. Regarding "instruction" (*vijñapti*): "instruction" has the meaning of "indicating. Following the explanation of the manifest and so forth, one should understand it as "informative" (*kriyā*) and "non-informative" (*akriyā*).

As for the term "that which acts," it refers to the activity of performing; this meaning is somewhat remote from the intended sense. The new translation has revised it to refer to both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).

Regarding the phrase "coexisting with other consciousnesses," "others" refers to indeterminate minds (*avyākṛta-citta*) and so forth. Although the names differ, the essence of "mind" (*citta*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is the same.
Regarding "defiled and indeterminate": first, we distinguish the defiled. In newly translated sūtras and śāstras, these are termed "contaminated" (*kliṣṭa*).

Contaminated states encompass both the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). Next, we distinguish the indeterminate: these refer exclusively to the unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
"Those who discipline the mind" refers to the scriptural passage [from] the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*, chapter seven. Furthermore, "precept" (*śīla*) is called "training" (*śikṣā*).
One trains to discipline the mind, wisdom, and the sense faculties; therefore, it is called "training. (The above constitutes the full scriptural passage.

This means that by disciplining the mind, one becomes free from craving; by disciplining wisdom, one becomes free from ignorance; and by disciplining the sense faculties, one guards them well. To guard [them]...
"Guarding" (ārakṣā) refers to the restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara).

Regarding its designation based on its meaning and function: to provide a general analysis, the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the dharma is the "meaning," while the activity of the dharma is the "function. This should be understood according to the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Therefore, as for establishing the name "precept" (śīla) based on its function: every sentence in that sutra states that "precept" is called "restraint" (saṃvara).

Furthermore, "precept" is called "superior" (uttara). This "precept" is a name established through its function; it is a specific name for the five [precepts] whose general meaning is applied universally, as assigned in the respective chapters.
Regarding the statement that "at that very moment, non-informative action (*avijñapti*) has seven names":
according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (112), both informative action (*vijñapti*) and non-informative action each have seven names. Thus, that text states:

"In this context, the seven fundamental paths of wholesome karma—whether they be informative or the non-informative [action] of that same moment—each possess seven meanings: first, morality (*śīla*); second, sublime conduct (*sucarita*); third, restraint (*saṃvara*)."
The four types of prātimokṣa restraint, the six actions, and the seven paths of action. The thirteenth verse of the *Cittaviveka* states:
"Restraint, excellent conduct, the paths of action, the initial liberation, karma, and śīla—these are the names for the seven kinds.

The commentary cited in this chapter explains that they are called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because they serve as the antidote to all immoral conduct; thus, it defines the term "restraint" precisely by its function as an antidote.

Because this discipline (*saṃvara*) has the meaning of "protection" (*saṃvaraṇa*). The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "It is called discipline because it can protect the body and speech. The *Chapters* (*Śāstra*) state:
"Because it protects against unwholesome precepts (*duḥśīla*), and because it is included within the seven classes of practitioners, it is called the Prātimokṣa discipline.

The text of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* does not contain the numbers "one," "two," and so forth; however, the Master of the Commentary [Yaśomitra] has added them based on the sense of the meaning. Since this is the case here...
It is called *vinaya* (discipline). Furthermore, it must be explained that "discipline" (*vinaya*) refers to protection and guarding.

Moreover, the passage beginning with "protecting against unwholesome discipline" is the commentary by the Master of the Subcommentary (*śāstrakāra*), not the original treatise (*śāstra*). Furthermore, regarding the statement "not being bound by the assembly of evil," [it is as follows].

Furthermore, let us consider one aspect. However, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Because the initial manifest and unmanifest [karma] involve the successive abandonment of various evils, the name 'Prātimokṣa' (Individual Liberation) is established based on this initial, distinct abandonment.

Thus, we know that when the treatise speaks of entering the seven classes of practitioners (*saptanikāya*), its intent is to clarify that it is precisely upon receiving the precepts that one first enters these seven classes;
at that very moment, one is able to abandon [evils] individually, and is therefore called "Prātimokṣa" (Individual Liberation). The *Chang* (Chapter/Commentary) says: "Third, regarding the one..."
Because it is attained by all sentient beings and because it is well-performed, it is called "sublime conduct" (*sucarita*).

This distinguishes it from the restraint obtained within a range of one hundred *yojanas* by non-Buddhists; in the present case, it is not so, and thus it constitutes sublime conduct. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"It is called sublime conduct because the wise praise it. Fourth, because it attains desirable fruits and because it is the path of volitional intention, it is called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*).

The term "path" (*mārga*) has the meaning of "passage. Because it leads to the production of the fruit of craving, it is called a "karmic path" (*karmapatha*). Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Because it leads to the production of diverse results of maturation—namely, suffering and pleasure—it is called a karmic path. Furthermore, "path" has the meaning of that which is traversed;

this refers to the physical and vocal forms, which are what volition (*cetanā*) traverses. Therefore, it is said: "because they are the paths of volitional aspiration. These five are the primary factors that accord with liberation.
It is called *prātimokṣa* because the term *mokṣa* (liberation) is established based on its initial abandonment [of transgressions].

It is called "action" (*karman*) because it arises from the six types of performance. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* raises an objection: "Is it not the case that the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is also called 'non-performance' (*akriyā*)?

How can you now say that its essential nature is 'performance'? The response is: It is called "non-performance" because one does not commit various evils; however, it is "performance" in the sense that it is produced by manifest action (*vijñapti*) and volition (*cetanā*).

It receives the name "that which is to be done" (this implies that it is called both "done" and "not done"). Seventh, regarding the term *śīla* (precept): it is because of the arising of a mind of purity, goodness, and non-harming.
The treatise states: "*Śīla* has the meaning of purity and goodness; it is so called because of the arising of a mind of non-harming.

(Commentary: The meaning of purity and goodness correctly explains *śīla*. It is because one practices purity and goodness, namely, by virtue of the arising of a mind of non-harming. (*Abhidharmakośa*)
It is said: Because it can level perilous karma, it is named *śīla*. The fourteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa* also lists seven names.

[The claim that] there are six names contradicts the one hundred and thirteenth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, which enumerates seven according to their number; it also contradicts the verse in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, which states:
"Thus are the seven kinds of names."
Regarding the "single moment of the third *karmavācanā*," this is cited from the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*.

Concerning the fundamental action (*mūlakarma*) and non-informative action (*avijñapti*), that treatise states: "The first seven courses of action (*karmapatha*) necessarily possess non-informative action.
Sexual misconduct necessarily possesses informative action (*vijñapti*), because it is completed by oneself. The remaining courses of action are not fixed; they may be performed by oneself, or..."

Because he had consistently omitted this [explanation], the verse says "or. Question: Now that you are explaining the meaning of the precepts (*śīla*), why do you cite the unwholesome paths of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*)?
That treatise further explains next: "Abandoning the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of unwholesome paths of action is itself the preparatory stage of wholesome paths of action;

abandoning the fundamental act (*maula*) and abandoning the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*) are likewise so. Question: How is this matter to be understood? Answer: It is as stated by the Venerable Śāriputra.
From the acceptance of the full ordination up to the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation), all are preparatory stages (*prayoga*).

At the third moment, the manifest action (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) constitute the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*), as cited in the commentary. This is likewise stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Chapter 16) and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Volume 113).
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, from the first moment [of thought] onwards, is the treatise in the first fascicle.
"By the power of the Path" refers to the power of the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

The "threefold classification of aggregates" consists of: first, the aggregate of form; second, the aggregate of mind; and third, the aggregate of non-associated factors that are neither form nor mind.

Furthermore, if one distinguishes the aggregate of mind into two, there should be four aggregates; the distinction of these two refers to the aggregate of mind and the aggregate of mental factors (*caitta*).

When the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is added to these, they constitute five aggregates. Regarding the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), the method for determining their nature is as explained in the commentary on the first fascicle.

Regarding "the mind and the four characteristics are non-associated," the mind is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), while the four characteristics are non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*);
this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Regarding "and unmanifest [form] and derived form," the first fascicle of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states in verse: "The ten types are the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*). And...
"Unconditioned derived matter (avijñapti-rūpa): this is the analytical [classification] of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), as taught by the Muni. (Commentary:

The intent of that treatise in analyzing the aggregate of form is that there are, in total, eleven kinds of matter. Among these, ten kinds—namely, the five faculties (indriya) and the five objects (viṣaya)—are all the substance of matter;
because they are what is apprehended by the ten bases (āyatana), they are called "ten kinds," which refers to the base of visible form (rūpāyatana). Together with unconditioned derived matter...
According to the Sarvāstivāda, non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) is real; that it is now said to be provisional is the specific doctrinal construction of those masters. How is this known?
For instance, in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, fascicle 127, the section on the "Derived Matter" (*bhautika-rūpa*), it says:

"The Venerable Dharmatrāta states that there is derived matter distinct from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). He speaks of mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*) as being not identical to the mind (*citta*). However, he says...

Among the categories of form (*rūpa*), two are not substantially existent (*dravyasat*): namely, derived tangible objects (*bhautika-spraṣṭavya*) and the form included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*).
Although the master of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* is not actually Dharmatrāta of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, he is nevertheless referred to as the teacher Dharmatrāta.

His treatise frequently follows the tradition of the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and Dharmatrāta; for instance, the twelfth chapter of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states: "The Venerable One says... (in the commentary).
It says: "This Dharmatrāta [is so named] because he was the Venerable Dharmatrāta of antiquity (Dharmatrāta means 'Dharma-Savior')."

One should understand this accordingly. The author of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* also establishes that the substance of unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) within the "factors" (*dharma-āyatana*) is conventional (*prajñapti*).

However, regarding the master Dharmatrāta mentioned in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, he is one of the four great masters of the Sarvāstivāda school, as noted in *Vibhāṣā* 77, *Nyāyānusāra* 52, and *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 20.

Furthermore, regarding the threefold classification within the third aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*), one should understand that all phenomena (*dharma*) are fully subsumed within the three categories:
first, the twelve bases (*āyatana*). These are: (1) the eye; (2) the ear; (3) the nose; (4) the tongue; and (5) the body (the aforementioned are called the five material sense-faculties).
Six mental objects (the aforementioned six kinds are the six internal sense bases). Seven visible forms. Eight sounds. Nine odors. Ten tastes. Eleven tangibles (the five kinds listed above).

[This refers to] the objects of the five [sensory] colors. Regarding the twelve dharmas (the six mentioned above are the six external objects): as for the term "twelve bases" (*āyatana*), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains that they are called "bases" in the sense of being the gateways through which the mind and mental factors arise and grow.

The older term "twelve entrances" (*āyadvāra*) signifies the meaning of the mind and mental factors entering into the faculties and their objects. However, within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), there are four kinds of phenomena: first, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*); second, the various mental factors (*caitta*); third, the dissociated [conditioned phenomena] (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*); and fourth, the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

The second [category] consists of the eighteen *dhātus*: 1. The eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*). 2. The ear-element (*śrotradhātu*). 3. The nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*). 4. The tongue-element (*jihvādhātu*). 5. The body-element (*kāyadhātu*) (the above five are the five material sense-faculties).
6. The mind-element (*manodhātu*) (this one has the essence of the mind as its nature; the above constitute the six internal sense-faculties). 7. The eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).

8. The ear-consciousness-element (*śrotravijñānadhātu*). 9. The nose-consciousness-element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*). 10. The tongue-consciousness-element (*jihvāvijñānadhātu*). 11. The body-consciousness-element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*). 12. The mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).

(The above six consciousnesses, together with the mind (*citta*), constitute the essence [of the mental element]. This is the extraction of [the *citta*] from within the previously mentioned "mental element" (*manodhātu*). These six elements, together with the aforementioned mental element, are collectively termed the seven mental elements).
Thirteen elements: fourteen, the sound element; fifteen, the odor element; sixteen, the taste element; seventeen, the tangible object element (these are the five external sense objects).

The eighteen *dhātus* (this *dhātu* also has four categories; it is explained according to the preceding explanation of the *dharmāyatana*. As for the term "realm" (*dhātu*), it means "lineage" (*gotra*); that is to say, all phenomena collectively comprise eighteen distinct lineages). Third, the five aggregates (*skandhas*):

first, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)—namely, the five sense organs, the five sense objects, and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) within the *dharmāyatana* and *dharmadhātu*. Second, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*).

3. The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)—these two [perception and feeling] are established as distinct aggregates within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the constituent of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), among the various mental factors (*caitta*). 4.

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)—this consists of all other mental factors and the dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), excluding feeling and perception, taken from within the sphere of phenomena and the constituent of phenomena. 5. The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)—this consists of the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) among the twelve spheres, and the seven constituents of mind (*cittadhātu*) among the eighteen constituents.

In the preceding three categories, within the framework of the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*), the five material sense-faculties and their five corresponding objects, as well as the unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) included within the element and base of phenomena (*dharmadhātu-dharmāyatana*), are established as the three types of matter.
Although there are differences among them, such as sound and odor, they are described here in terms of their common characteristics.
All of these are aggregates of matter (*rūpa-kalāpa*). As has already been explained above, these are likewise subsumed under the aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*).

Regarding the statement "three kinds of matter," the *Śāstra* says: "First, visible and resistant matter; this refers to the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) [in the new terminology, it is called 'possessing matter, possessing visibility, and possessing resistance'].

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā* briefly explains: It is called 'visible' because it can be demonstrated as having distinctions such as 'this' or 'that'; this corresponds to the old term 'visible. Because it is an aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*), and because it obstructs and is obstructed by others, it is called 'resistant. Its essence is matter, thus it is called 'possessing matter. The *Śāstra* calls it the 'sense-base of form. This refers to...
(Within the twelve bases, it is the base of form. Second, invisible and resistant form.

This refers to the five sense organs and four objects (formerly called the "five dusts"; in the new terminology, the "five spheres. Here, "four objects" means that from among the five, the object of visible form is excluded. These four objects, together with the five spheres and organs, are collectively termed invisible and resistant form.

In the new terminology, this is called "possessing form, invisible, and resistant. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: it is called "invisible" because its distinctions as "this" or "that" cannot be demonstrated; it is called "resistant" because it consists of atoms in aggregation and because they are mutually opposed). Third.

Invisible and non-obstructive form refers to that which is within the *dharmāyatana* (the sphere of mental objects), specifically the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). Within the *dharmāyatana*, four categories are taught; here, three are excluded, and only the unmanifest is taken as "invisible and non-obstructive form.

The new terminology for this is "form that exists, but is invisible and non-obstructive. Regarding "invisible": explain it according to the previous definition. Regarding "non-obstructive": it is not a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*) that obstructs one another; therefore, it is called non-obstructive. Nevertheless, its essence is still form.

Therefore, it is said to be "possessing form" (*rūpin*). If one speaks of the "precept of action" (*kriyā-śīla*), it is subsumed under the first two types of form (the *vijñapti* of body and speech); since its essence consists of visible form and sound, it is thus subsumed under those first two forms.

Because the "unmanifested dharma" (*avijñapti*) is included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is not among the three that possess resistance (*sapratigha*). Question: Although mental factors (*caitta*) are also subsumed within the sphere of mental objects, they possess resistance in terms of being objective referents (*ālambana-pratigha*);
therefore, one should know that it is not by virtue of being this [unmanifested] factor within the sphere of mental objects that it is so classified.

It is not "with resistance" (sapratigha). Answer: Although mental factors possess two senses of "resistance," they do not possess all three; therefore, they may also be termed "not [possessing] the three types of resistance.
Alternatively, one may follow the explanation in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, which states that what is not an aggregate of atoms (paramāṇu-saṃghāta) is called "without resistance" (apratigha).
As for the words of the commentaries (*śāstra*), why the trouble of laboriously defending them?

Regarding the statement that "the meaning of the three types of *pratigha* (resistance) should be explained in detail," the second chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Resistance (*pratigha*) has the sense of obstruction (*āvaraṇa*).

This is further of three kinds, distinguished by way of the object (*viṣaya*) and the focal point (*ālambana*): (1) resistance as obstruction (*āvaraṇa-pratigha*), (2) resistance as object (*viṣaya-pratigha*), and (3) resistance as focal point (*ālambana-pratigha*). There are two kinds of obstruction: first..."

This refers to resistance through obstruction (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*), as in the case of obstructive resistance (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*). Second is resistance through confinement (*ālambana-pratighāta*), as in the other two types.

Obstructive resistance refers to the ten bases of form (*daśa rūpāyatanāni*). When one occupies its own location, it is obstructed by another and cannot arise there; for example, a hand is obstructed by a hand, or a stone by a stone, or two [objects] are mutually obstructed. (These are the five sense faculties and the five objects of form.

Since they are aggregates of atoms, a single aggregate has no second aggregate occupying the same space, because they mutually obstruct one another. Thus, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states: "If that one exists, then a second atom does not exist, because of the occupation of space. [Commentary: Obstructive resistance...

This refers to "resistance by way of object" (*ālambana-pratighāta*), which is an *appositional compound* (*karmadhāraya*). It consists of the twelve [realms] and a portion of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), namely, all those phenomena that possess an objective sphere (*viṣayin*).

Regarding the objects such as form (*rūpa*), there are the six sense organs and the six consciousnesses, which constitute the twelve bases (*āyatana*). As for "a portion of the dharma-base" (*dharmadhātu-pradeśa*): among the four categories [of conditioned phenomena], it excludes the other three and consists solely of the collection of mental factors (*caitta*).

Therefore, it is called a "portion. Among these, the mental factors correspond respectively to the preceding six consciousnesses; subsequently, depending on the six organs, they are able to apprehend the six kinds of objects such as form. This is what is meant by "resistance of the object" (*viṣayapratighata*). It is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive compound) construction:

because each has its own specific object as that which is resisted, it is named "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*). The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: as the *Prajñapti-śāstra* says, "There are eyes that have resistance in water but not on land, such as the eyes of fish and the like. There are eyes that have resistance on land but not in water, for the most part like those of humans. There are eyes that have resistance in both, such as..."

Regarding the Piśācas and others: there are those whose eyes are neither obstructed nor limited by light, such as bats and owls; there are those whose eyes are not [obstructed] during the day but are during the night, for the most part like humans and others; there are those whose eyes are obstructed, such as dogs, jackals, cats, and wildcats;

and there are those who do not possess these characteristics (excluding the aforementioned cases). Regarding "resistance in terms of the object" (*ālambana-pratighāta*): this refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) with respect to their own respective objects. (The "mind" refers to the seven consciousness elements; the "mental factors" refer to the mental factors within the dharma-element.

These minds and mental factors, according to their respective natures, possess the sense of being constrained or obstructed with respect to their own objects; this is "resistance in terms of the object," interpreted according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound. Furthermore, regarding "the object as a sphere" (*viṣaya-ālambana*)...

What is the distinction [between these]? (The intent of this objection is as follows: the five types of material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are called "resistance with respect to the object" (*viṣayapratighāta*) because they can grasp objects; since they do not involve cognitive reflection (*ālambana*), they are not "resistance with respect to the focal object" (*ālambanapratighāta*). This meaning is easy to understand.

However, regarding the two categories of "resistance with respect to the object" and "resistance with respect to the focal object," both treat the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and their associated mental factors (*caitta*) as their essential nature. Thus, there should be no difference between resistance with respect to the object and resistance with respect to the focal object).

If a certain faculty possesses efficacy toward a particular phenomenon, that phenomenon is said to be the "object" (*viṣaya*) of that faculty. As for the mind and its mental factors, they grasp that [object]...

Arising. Regarding those [objects], such as the mind and so forth, they are called "objects of cognition" (*ālambana*). (If it says "those phenomena," these refer to objects such as form and so forth. If it says "this has the capacity," this refers to the fact that a portion of these twelve bases (*dhātu*) possesses the single capacity to grasp an object. To say "that is the objective sphere of these phenomena" means to say that those forms and so forth are the objective spheres of this portion of the twelve bases and the dharma-base [*dharmadhātu*].

The general meaning is as follows: the capacity to grasp an object is established as being named "resistance through the objective sphere" (*viṣayapratighata*). It is like the flame of a lamp, which possesses the capacity to burn the wick. As for "the mind and mental factors arise by grasping them," this means they arise by grasping those objective spheres such as form and so forth;

that is to say, the mind arises only by relying on the power of the object. In summary: [The Chinese text continues with a commentary on the nature of resistance. ...In total, the capacity to grasp an object is established as being named "resistance through the objective sphere. Then it can abide for a long time; if the mind is weak, it will not abide for long. For example, if one receives the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*), they abide for one day;

"Shield" (khaṭvāṅga) refers to a side-shield.

however, this is not a statement made in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*. First is "simultaneous with the manifest" (*kriyā-sahabhū*), which clarifies that non-manifest action occurs at the same time as the manifest action.
Thus, the *Cittabhūmi-śāstra* says: "When the third *karmavācanā* is completed, both the manifest and the non-manifest [arise]. Second is "the object remains," such as when one constructs...

"Whether one constructs an image of the Buddha, or even maintains a well, bridge, boat, staircase, resting place, or similar structures—the unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*) produced by these various manifest actions (*vijñapti*) possesses three conditions for its continuity to remain uninterrupted.
First, it is due to the intention (*āśaya*), namely, being directed toward those objects."

One gives rise to deep joy, and the mental disposition does not cease. Second, by way of the basis: that is, the body which serves as the basis, its homogeneous continuity, while the life-force has not yet ended.
Third, by way of the object: that is, the objects such as Buddha images that have been constructed, before they have entirely perished.
If any one of these three conditions is lacking, the non-informative (*avijñapti*) karma is severed. This is consistent with the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter 12, Section on Karma;
the *Cittaviparyaya-śāstra*, Chapter 4; and other such texts. Regarding the third point, "arising from function," the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Volume 11, Chapter on the Three Obstacles, states:
"One eats the food of a donor, wears the clothing of a donor, and enters an immeasurable meditative absorption; yet this donor obtains no [merit]."

Heterogeneous Object (*viṣaya-bhinna*): This is explained according to the opening and closing of the object of feeling (*vedanālambana*), as described above.

that is to say, although it is wholesome karma, it is not a formal restraint (*saṃvara*), or although it is unwholesome karma, it is not an evil vow (*dauḥśīlya*). Because it abides in moderation, it is called "the middle way. Master Tong states: "Wholesome..."

In the Sarvāstivāda school, the two types of restraint—the dhyāna-restraint and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) restraint—exist within the meditative and path-consciousnesses.

therefore, the precepts of absorption and the path, even when present within the *anuvartaka* (concomitant) state, lack the quality of being "prolonged.

Thus, the *Śāstra* says: "It is because the non-manifestation of the path is broad and long-lasting. This is correct. Therefore, [it is stated] in the seventeenth [chapter] of the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*.

The *Śīlasaṃvara-parivarta* states: Question: Some say that when one enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is the restraint of dhyāna (*dhyānasaṃvara*), but when one emerges from absorption, it no longer exists.

How is this matter to be understood? Answer: It exists constantly, both during entry and emergence, as explained at length therein. Since this is the case for that which is concomitant with concentration (*samādhisaṃprayukta*), it should be the same for that which is concomitant with the Path (*mārgasaṃprayukta*).

It may be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), but it is certainly not unwholesome (*akuśala*). Following this principle of "according with" (*anuvartana*), it is just as when one speaks of being "narrow.
