Twenty-three people, including Huìguǒ, Jìngyīn, Sēngyào, and Zhìjǐng, received the precepts. After this, it is impossible to record them all in detail.

From that time onward, these cases have been regarded as instances of properly receiving the precepts. Question: What evidence or verification is there to know that one has obtained the precepts? Answer: Master Nanshan’s records state:
Formerly, in the third year of Emperor Wén of the Wèi dynasty, an internal *wu zhè dà huì* (unrestricted great assembly) was held. Emperor Wén asked:
He asked, "How can one know the origins of how the monks and nuns of this land received the precepts? None of the great virtuous ones answered.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who requested to travel to the Western Regions to inquire about the source of receiving the precepts.
Upon arriving in Northern India, he encountered an arhat and inquired, saying, "Do the monks and nuns of China receive the precepts? The arhat replied, "In my small..."
“Venerable One, I do not know whether it can be obtained or not. He then said to the bhikṣu, “Stay here for a moment;
I shall now go on your behalf to ask Maitreya whether it can be obtained or not. Thereupon, he entered into meditative concentration and proceeded toward Tuṣita Heaven, asking:
“I am but a minor sage and do not know whether the precepts can be obtained in the borderlands. Therefore, I have come to ask your honor. Maitreya replied: “In the borderlands...”
She attained the precepts and subsequently requested a sign of verification. She immediately took a golden flower and made this vow:
"If the monks and nuns of the borderlands have truly received the precepts, may this golden flower enter the hand of the Arhat; if they have not, may the golden flower not enter.

Having finished her vow, the golden flower immediately entered the palm of his hand, appearing with a shadow one chi in length. Since such a marvelous sign had occurred, she harbored great joy within her heart. Maitreya said:
He said, "Go down to the place where the bhikṣu Zhendan is and you must also make a vow:

'If the precepts obtained by the monks and nuns of China are not in vain, I pray that this golden flower may enter the bhikṣu’s hand. Once you have made this vow according to the instructions, press the flower with your hand;
the flower shall enter the bhikṣu’s palm and appear there as a shadow one chi in length. When the auspicious response had thus occurred, he wished to return to his own country.
The deity Kāla manifested his form and spoke, saying: "The road is remote and fraught with many perils. Your disciple shall escort you, Master, so that you may reach that country.
Before he had yet arrived, golden flowers appeared as reflections in the air before the palace of Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty.
The Emperor asked the Grand Astrologer, "What strange omen is this? The Grand Astrologer replied, "In a western land, there is the Buddha-dharma."
He came here. Not even a month had passed when a golden flower appeared in the palm of the bhikṣu’s hand.
On the day he arrived, the golden flower in the sky vanished and was no longer seen. When they were about to set out from the territory of Han, there were more than eighty people in total;
some, their longing for the Sage so profound, remained in that region, while others met with calamities and lost their lives. There was only one person who followed him.
Daoyuan extensively sought out ancient traces and traveled to the land of Qin. Now, examining this in detail:

as for the Unrestricted Great Assembly (Mucade Mahāpariṣad) held during the third year of Emperor Wen of Wei, if it refers to the former Emperor Wen of Wei, it would be the year Renyin, the third year of Huangchu.
Calculating the years and months, they do not quite correspond. For instance, the *Tujiji* (Record of the Translation of Scriptures) by the Tang dynasty Dharma Master Jingmai states:
"The śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan was a native of Liangzhou. He left home to become a monk at the age of twenty. Wearing patched robes, he sat in quietude, supporting himself through alms-gathering.

At that time, in the thirteenth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty, after the Later Qin was extinguished, [he] returned from the reign of Yao Hong (Yao Hong was the son of Yao Chang)."

[He was] the grandson [of...]. In the eighth month, he was captured by Liu Yu of the Eastern Jin and executed in the marketplace of Jiankang. Wang Hui, the Duke of Shixing, while traveling with the imperial entourage to view the mountains, encountered Yan Chansi and immediately invited him back to the capital.
However, Yan had previously obtained scriptures from the Western Regions, but their Sanskrit originals had not yet been translated.

Later, at the end of the Jin dynasty and the rise of the Song (in the tenth month of the second year of Yuanxi of Emperor Gong of Jin, Liu Yu, the Grand Marshal of the Eastern Jin, received the abdication of the Jin and changed the era to the Song), this reached the time of Emperor Wen of the Song.

In the fourth year of the Jiā era (counting from the thirteenth year of Yìxī to the fourth year of Yuánjiā, totaling eleven years), the year being Dīngmǎo, he translated the *Puyào jīng* (Lalitavistara Sūtra) and other texts at Zhīyuán Monastery in the capital of Yáng, totaling thirty-six fascicles.
However, prior to his ordination, Fǎyán had received the five precepts and had committed some transgressions.
Later, when he received the full precepts (*mahāśramaṇa-saṃvara*), he doubted whether he had attained them. Consequently, he traveled by sea to India to seek counsel.
He questioned an Arhat, but the Arhat could not provide a definitive answer. He then requested Maitreya, who replied that he had indeed received the precepts. Fayian was greatly delighted.

Calculating from the third year of the Huangchu era of the Former Wei (the Renyin year) until the fourth year of the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty (the Dingmao year)—the time when Fayian performed the translation—it amounts to two hundred and six years. How could there have been [any discrepancy]?
A person [lives] over two hundred years. If one speaks of Emperor Daowu of the Later Wei, who first established the capital at Beida;

in the third year of Huangshi, when the year-cycle was Wuxu—at that time, they did not yet revere or believe in the Buddha-dharma. Who, then, could have questioned him regarding the origins of his receiving the precepts?
Moreover, there is a difference between the Huangshi era and the Huangchu era; the reigns of Emperors Wen and Wu were each distinct. How, then, can [the dates] be reconciled?
[This is] a verification. Thus we know that Nanshan’s record is erroneous. Now, examining this in detail: this refers to Yao Xing of the Later Qin, posthumously titled Emperor Wen-huan.

In the third year of Huangchu, the cyclical year being Jingshen (the title "Huangchu" is not the same as the "Huangchu" of the preceding Wei dynasty's Cao clan). This continued until the fourth year of Yuanjia.
This totals thirty-two years. According to this calculation, when Zhiyan first departed for the Western Regions, he must have still been a youth.

Considering the time spent traveling back and forth and his subsequent delays, another thirty-two years would have elapsed; thus, this aligns perfectly with the *Yijing tuji* (Record of the Translation of the Scriptures).

One should examine the historical records of the Qin and Wei dynasties and inquire of Dharma Master Zhiyan: if he was originally in the Qin court, how could he have performed translations during the Song dynasty? Now...
In detail: Later Qin was destroyed by Liu Yu of the Song dynasty. This is why Zhiyan left Qin and entered Song.

Furthermore, according to the Way of the renunciants, it is permissible to travel and propagate the teachings in various regions; thus, there is no harm in this. (During the Yuanjia era, when Yan was translating, there were six kingdoms in total: first, Western Qin; second, the Xia state;

third, Northern Liang; fourth, Northern Yan; fifth, Later Wei; and sixth, the Song state. Within this context, calculating from the time the Great Monks first received the precepts during the Wushen year of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty...
It has come down to the present, the third year of Chang’an of the Great Zhou, the cyclical year Gui-mao,
which marks five hundred and thirty-six years since the second formal reception of the full precepts by the great *saṃgha* began in the second year of Jiaping of Emperor Fang of the Wei dynasty,
the cyclical year Geng-wu. From that time until the present, the third year of Chang’an of the Great Zhou, the cyclical year Gui-mao, the total count is four hundred and fifty-four [years].

As for the years: from the first year of the Huangchu era of the Former Wei, the cyclical year Gengzi, when the bhikṣuṇīs first received the precepts, until the third year of the Chang’an era of the Great Zhou, the cyclical year Jiu-mao, four hundred and eighty-four years have already elapsed.

The second stage of the *bhikṣuṇī* ordination began from the year Guiyou (463 CE), the tenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, until the year Guimao (703 CE), the third year of the Chang’an era of the Great Zhou dynasty—a period spanning two hundred and seventy-one years.

(During this interval, following the suppression of the Buddha-dharma by Emperor Wu of the Zhou, eighteen masters of the Tripiṭaka, including Dharma Master Lingyu and others, remained at the residence of General Lemo Ti. When the great [revival] was first established, only nine people were obtained to confer full ordination upon others.)

Regarding the second period of translation: I have carefully examined the *Chizang-si Fanyi Tujì* (Illustrated Record of Translations at Cien Monastery) by Dharma Master Jingmai, as well as the preface to the Vinaya translated by Zhi Falin during the Qin dynasty, and verified the Vinaya text itself. It appears that this Vinaya underwent two translations in total.
The first was the initial translation by Jueming, and the latter was a re-translation by Falin. Thus, the *Fanyi Tujì* states: "During the Yao Qin..."
The world-renowned śramaṇa Buddhayaśas—here translated as "Awakened Name" (or "Awakened Sound")—was a native of Kaśmīra.

His conduct was pure and upright, his observance of the precepts firm and steadfast, and his demeanor auspicious and refined. His gaze was extraordinary. He had mastered the five sciences and the four Vedas, as well as the three piṭakas and twelve divisions of the scriptures;
he maintained a profound understanding and possessed an unhindered flow of eloquence. In the Hongshi era of the Yao Qin dynasty, he arrived [in China].
In Guzang, Dharma Master Kumārajīva had previously served him as his teacher. He subsequently urged Yao Xing, the ruler of Qin, to go and welcome him.

An imperial edict was immediately issued to receive him, along with various gifts; however, he declined and would not accept them. After messengers were sent repeatedly to urge him with earnest entreaties, he finally arrived in Chang’an.

The ruler of Qin went out to meet him and established a new monastery for him at the Xiaoyao Garden. Although offerings of the four requisites were provided to him throughout the four seasons, he accepted none of them.
He received alms; when the time came for his daily rounds, he would eat but a single meal. He had reddish-brown hair and was well-versed in the *Vibhāṣā*;
people of the time called him "Red-bearded Vibhāṣā. The Ruler of Qin provided him with offerings sufficient to fill three rooms, yet he did not set his mind on them.
He subsequently sold them to build a monastery. From the fifth year of Hongshi, the year of Renyin, he translated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* in forty-five fascicles.
[This volume], along with one scroll of the *Dharmaguptaka-śīla-sūtra* and various other miscellaneous sūtras, was transcribed by Zhu Fonian and others.
According to the preface to the Vinaya by Zhufa Ling: "In the year of Renchen, there was a śramaṇa of the Jin state named Zhufa Ling.

Moved by the deviation from the Sage in the frontier lands and lamenting that the True Teaching had declined among the barbarians, he traveled west across the shifting sands, passing through Khotan, where he encountered Dharmānanda..."
The Section on Virtue: The śramaṇa Buddhayaśas, who had mastered the Mahāyāna Tripiṭaka, possessed brilliant talent and vast learning;

he was well-versed in the Sūtras and Vinaya, and had thoroughly memorized and mastered the Vaipulya scriptures of the Tripiṭaka. While in that country, Fali had extensively collected various rare sūtras.

In the year Wushen, they first arrived in the state of Qin (it was because both [Fali and Buddhayaśas] were governing together that when the Jin returned to Qin, it was due to their joint administration). Immediately upon reaching that year, [he] once again...
I request that the Vinaya Piṭaka be brought forth. At that time, more than three hundred śramaṇas who upheld the Vinaya assembled at Zhong Temple in Chang’an to produce it.

Led by his disciple Huibian, they acted as translators and editors; they refined and polished the text repeatedly, striving to preserve its unadorned essence while ensuring that both the beginning and the end were precise and exhaustive, as if it were the original promulgation.
I respectfully note that this was the time when Juemeng translated it during the *renyin* year of the Yao Qin dynasty.

In the fifth year of Hongshi, during the year Wushen, when Faling was translating [the text], it corresponded to the eleventh year of Hongshi (which is the fourth year of the Jiayi era of the Jin dynasty;
calculating from Renyin back to Wushen, the interval is seven years). Furthermore, the Preface to the Vinaya states: "I requested again for the Vinaya-piṭaka to be brought forth.
Based on this, the chronological sequence is sufficiently clear. Question: Faling encountered Juemeng in the West; why did Juemeng arrive first?

Regarding the translation: The answer is that Dharmagupta traveled westward during the Jin dynasty. From the year *Renchen* until his return to Qin in the year *Wushen*, a total of seventeen years elapsed.
During this time, Dharmagupta extensively collected various sūtras from the Western Regions; it was for this reason that he arrived later, and thus there is no cause for doubt.
Furthermore, according to the Vinaya texts, at the beginning of the *Zhongjue* (Saṃghāvaśeṣa), there is a version of the Vinaya root text titled *Śikṣā-karman*.

Regarding the term *dharma* (the Chinese transcription is incorrect; it should be *śikṣākarani-dharma*). There are some who have continued the writing, and the text should correctly proceed from this point of the *śikṣākarani*. Since it is impossible to correct every single character according to the original text, I have thus classified and explained them here.
The above, including the annotations, are all recorded in the Vinaya. It was only known that Juemeng (覺鳴) was the original translator;
however, because the person who transcribed the words used incorrect phonetics, when it reached Faling (法領), who personally understood the local dialects, he subsequently corrected it.
Furthermore, Juemeng’s original version reads "like breaking an eranda leaf," while Faling’s version reads "like breaking an eranda leaf. Additionally, in the text of the Vinaya, it is listed...
Regarding the three items belonging to the Saṃgha, the first two or three items have their textual order inverted, and there are numerous other discrepancies throughout the various texts.

These are all due to differences between the two translations. The *Yijing tuji* (Record of the Illustrations of the Translation of the Scriptures) records only the initial translation and omits those produced later;

this is likely due to its brevity and negligence. Furthermore, upon close examination, there are three versions of the Vinaya: the first is the original version by Juemeng; the second is the [version by] Fa... [text fragmentary].

Regarding the revised edition: the character for "corpse" (尸) was ordered to be changed to "cross" (又), yet it remained unaltered; thus, these three instances have been changed to follow the "cross" (叉) version.

Furthermore, following the accession to the throne in the first year of the Yonglong era (the year of Yisi, 705 CE) of Emperor Shengtian of the Great Tang’s Zhongxing period, the monk Daolin of Chongxian Monastery in Luoyang (a native of Huzhou) took the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* compiled by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing...

Regarding these verses added to the Vinaya, they were falsely claimed to have been translated [from an original]. Initially, at Chongxian Monastery, the Vinaya manuscript was cut open and these were inserted therein.
Furthermore, two copies were made: one was placed in Chongxian Monastery and the other in Dasheng Shanshan Monastery.
Fearing that future generations might not understand the circumstances, I have recorded this here.
The relative gravity and urgency [of precepts] have already been analyzed in the preceding fascicle. That is to say, "light" is equivalent to "slow," and "heavy" is equivalent to "urgent";

however, because they differ in their conceptual categories (*arthamukha*), they are discussed separately. Nevertheless, when compared to the perspective of inherent evil (*prakṛti-duṣṭa*), what is called "light" restrains light offenses, and what is called "heavy" restrains heavy offenses;

thus, they are termed "light and heavy" rather than "slow and urgent. Therefore, one should explain it as follows: if something is slow or urgent, it is inherently light or heavy. There are indeed cases of the light...
This is a matter of gravity rather than urgency; this can be seen upon reflection.

Regarding the "four coins and three *kākaṇīs*": in the third fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus, "From now on, you should know that nineteen old coins are called one *kārṣāpaṇa*. Divide one *kārṣāpaṇa* into four parts. If one steals one..."
If it is worth one part, one commits a *pārājika* offense. For this reason, since ancient times, this has been calculated as four coins and three *koṭis*.
That is to say, nineteen is divided into four parts. Four times four is sixteen; there remain three coins, each of which is divided into four *koṭis*.
Three times four is twelve, which constitutes twelve *koṭis*. These twelve *koṭis* are then divided into four parts, each part being...
"Triangular. Thus it is said, "four *kārsāpaṇas* and a triangle. This is a mistaken tradition from antiquity; it shall be examined later in the section on the precept against stealing.
Regarding "both groups mutually": when members of the same group slander one another, it is called "mutual"; when members of different groups slander one another, it is called [the other].

Regarding the mutual distinction between what constitutes an offense and what does not: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one establishes a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*), it is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing);

according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one makes the three robes (*tricīvara*) without relinquishing the pure status, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). In this [present] Vinaya, there is no offense in either case.
The *Yijiao sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching), in the "Chapter on the Differentiation of Robes by the Fivefold Saṃgha," states:
When the Buddha was in the world, there was a bhikṣu named Rājuka who always returned empty-handed from his almsrounds.

The Buddha, knowing his past karma and wishing to manifest the retribution of his misdeeds while simultaneously clarifying the precepts, commanded the assembly of monks to divide themselves into five groups, each wearing robes of one of the five colors, and ordered Rājuka to follow one of these groups every day.
They beg for alms, following their respective ritual regulations until they attain liberation. Subsequently, they establish titles and designations, each honoring the color of the robes they wear.
Those of the Sarvāstivāda school are broad-minded, versatile, and sagacious; as they guide others through wisdom and transform them through the Dharma, they should wear saffron-colored *kāṣāyas*.
Those of the Mahīśāsaka school uphold the weighty precepts and adjudicate according to the laws and rules; they should wear black *kāṣāyas*.
The Kāśyapīya school is diligent, courageous, and decisive; they rescue and protect sentient beings and should wear saffron-colored (*mūlana*) *kāṣāyas*.
The Mahīśāsaka school contemplates deeply through meditation and thoroughly elucidates the profound and mysterious; they should wear blue *kāṣāyas*.

The Mahāsāṃghika school diligently studies the various sūtras and expounds their meanings and principles; they should wear yellow *kāṣāyas*. Thus did the Buddha [teach] because of the request of Rājagṛha.
They were unable to obtain food, so that the bhikṣus might know there is karmic retribution.
They returned and divided themselves into five groups, with each group going out to seek food on successive days; yet none obtained any. This continued until all five groups had done so.
The Buddha then ordered Rāhu to sweep and sprinkle water within the monastery, while others were invited for a meal. For one day, he did not perform his task. Śāriputra [acted] for him...
When he went to beg for food, he turned over his alms bowl on the road and ate it all; having nothing left to eat, he said, "Since my merit is so meager, what need is there for me to remain longer?

He then ate sand, drank water, and entered *nirvāṇa*. (This sutra is suspected of being apocryphal. The lower fascicle of the *Weiyijing* and the *Śāriputraparipṛcchāsūtra* describe five types of robe colors that are largely identical to this sutra.
The *Śāriputraparipṛcchāsūtra* is also suspected of being apocryphal). Question: Previously there were five intentions; why were they not distinguished? Answer: Because...
This is due to two meanings, as discussed in the chapter. If this is so, the three vehicles have three intentions, while the Tathāgata currently manifests five;

if these intentions correspond to five types of capacities, why is there no distinction among the Buddhas? Answer: The three vehicles are taught for the sake of gradual guidance, where distinct explanations facilitate practice.

The manifestation of the five intentions serves as a comprehensive prevention of error. Question: It is said that [the teachings] are harmonized and free from dispute. If this is so, for what purpose does the Buddha manifest without making distinctions? How is it then?

The *Deng jing* (Equal Sūtra) states: "Among the five groups of monks, what *vinaya* do they study? Furthermore, the *Fangguang jing* (Vaipulya Sūtra) states: "They use the property of the five groups of monks interchangeably.

Also, as in the case of Rāhuṇa, he followed the five groups of monks for alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*). These instances all seem to indicate a shared distribution; how then can one say there is no distinction? Answer:

This is likely because although the Saṃgha is divided into five groups, their training in the precepts remains the same. Furthermore, in the *Śatadharma-svapna-sūtra*, King Aśoka had ten dreams... [dream]... *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on monastic discipline and scriptural citations regarding the division of the Saṃgha.)*
He saw white cotton wool fly down from the sky and, upon reaching the ground, divide into five sections. The King was then distressed and came to question the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said: "This is not the King's business; it belongs to my Dharma. After my parinirvāṇa, my assembly of disciples will divide my Vinaya into five schools.
Since it is said to occur after my passing, it does not manifest as a division now. (The above is the dialogue between the Venerable and the Buddha.)

Regarding the "five kinds of sentient beings," this refers to the five distinct capacities of the [spiritual] faculties. Chong states: "Even one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was still but one school; the five sections had not yet arisen.

How could it be that in the time of [Kumārajīva], when only twelve years had passed, there were already said to be five types of faculties? Now, examining this closely: how could it be that the five types of faculties exist only because the schools have been divided?
Therefore, the existence of five types of faculties does not preclude their being students of the same [teaching].
If it were said that while the extensive benefit [of teaching] is not universal, how could the entrustment to disciples be universal?
Therefore, it should be explained further. The Vinaya itself states: "It is impossible for the Tathāgata to recite the Prātimokṣa within an impure assembly.
This is its intended meaning. See the fifth fascicle of the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* regarding the instruction on the Prātimokṣa.

Regarding the phrase "five years after [the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa]," the *Zhì* (祇) states in fascicle 23: "Five years after the World-Honored One attained enlightenment, the community of bhikṣus was pure.
From that time onward, they gradually began to act improperly; the World-Honored One established the precepts according to specific incidents and instituted the recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
The claim that "twenty years" refers to this is not correct. The *Jiàn lùn* (見論), fascicle 6, states: "Ten years after the Buddha attained enlightenment..."
Two years later, Sudinna went forth into homelessness. He practiced the Way in another country for eight years, after which he returned to the village of Kalandaka.
Since twenty years had passed since the Buddha attained enlightenment, it would not be correct to say that [Sudinna] "arrived" [at that time]. Therefore, let us now examine this in detail:

there are numerous instances where the textual accounts of various schools differ, such as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which states that the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the second month. Sa...

In the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other treatises, it is stated that the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa on the eighth day of the eighth month; how could this coincide [with other dates]? The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* places it in the fifth year [after his enlightenment];

this should likewise be adjusted accordingly. Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata’s correct teaching," the Venerable One says: "This refers to the cessation of teaching" (the word "correct" [zhèng] is used because he composed [the text]).
The *Poṣadha-khandhaka*. Ānanda requested the Buddha to recite the precepts, but the World-Honored One did not do so.
Maudgalyāyana perceived that there was one bhikṣu whose conduct was impure; Maudgalyāyana dragged him out, clearly knowing that this was indeed the second offense.
Regarding the five masters who maintained the tradition, the details are as found in the *Dharma-śarīra-piṭaka-avadāna* (Fu fazang zhuan) and the *Aśoka-rāja-avadāna* (Ayuwang zhuan).
Regarding those who enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) after making a vow, the Sarvāstivāda school states in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 135:
"Not long after Mahākāśyapa entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food and had finished eating, he ascended Mount Kukkuṭapāda.
This mountain has three peaks resembling the outstretched feet of a cock. The Venerable One entered into its center and sat cross-legged, making this solemn declaration: 'May this body of mine...'"
He also took up his alms bowl and staff, which remained undamaged for a long time, even until fifty-seven koṭis and six hundred thousand years had passed.
When the Tathāgata Maitreya appears in the world, they shall perform the work of a Buddha. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "He has entered parinirvāṇa;

it is not that he has entered meditative absorption. As for the manifestation of supernatural transformations when Maitreya appears in the world, this refers to the preservation of emanated forms (*nirmāṇakāya*). Other schools [hold this view].
Among these, there is permission granted that this is indeed entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Regarding one who entered cessation while on a boat in the Ganges River, it is as described in the first fascicle of the *Dharmatrāta-śāsana* (The Lineage of the Dharma):
King Ajātaśatru requested of Ānanda, "Since the Tathāgata and Kāśyapa have entered *parinirvāṇa*, my own transgressions are many; they cannot all be fully [expiated]."
"I have seen the Honored One. Whether he has entered parinirvāṇa, I only wish for him to grant me his instruction. Ānanda replied, "Very well.

Later, Ānanda went into a bamboo grove and heard a bhikṣu reciting a verse from the *Dharmapada*: "If one lives a hundred years and does not see the water-hen grow old, it is not as good as living for a single day and seeing it completely. Having heard this, Ānanda spoke to the bhikṣu: "This is not [the word] of the Buddha."
[The Buddha] said: "It cannot be practiced. You should now listen as I recite the verses of the Buddha:
'If a person lives for a hundred years without understanding the law of arising and ceasing, it is not as good as living for a single day and attaining such understanding.
At that time, the bhikṣu addressed his teacher, who told him: 'Ānanda is aged and decrepit; his wisdom has declined and his speech is full of errors. He is not to be trusted.'"
"Very well. You should now simply recite as before. Later, Ānanda heard this, yet he continued to recite the previous verse. He then asked for its meaning.
He replied, "Venerable One, my teacher told me that you, Ānanda, are old and your words are often false; therefore, I shall simply recite as before.
Ānanda reflected, "He disregards my words, or perhaps he has received other instructions," and he immediately entered into *samādhi* to investigate the superior [teaching].
The Venerable One saw that no one was able to turn his mind back, so he spoke these words: "The sufferings of the world are such that it is extremely difficult to dwell there for long;
today, it is fitting for me to enter parinirvāṇa. He further thought, "King Ajātaśatru has a prior engagement with me; I ought to speak to him.
He then proceeded to the royal palace and addressed the gatekeeper, saying, "Inform the King on my behalf. The gatekeeper replied:
He said, "The King is currently asleep; if he were to wake up, my offense would not be small. Ānanda said, "If the King wakes, you may convey my message.
King Ajātaśatru dreamed that the shaft of his parasol snapped (symbolizing the loss of protection), whereupon he was suddenly awakened.
His attendants delivered the full message, and upon hearing it, the King fainted. After a long while, he regained consciousness. A garden deity said to the King, "Ānanda has now already departed..."

In Vaiśālī, [King Ajātaśatru] immediately arrayed the fourfold army and went to the banks of the Ganges. Ānanda was traveling by boat in the middle of the river when the great earth shook in six ways.
At that time, five hundred rishis dwelling in the Snowy Mountains, having seen this portent, [were struck with wonder].

He flew through the air to visit them and sought their compassion for his renunciation. He immediately transformed the Ganges River into a field of golden earth and preached the Dharma to the sages according to their needs.
Their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, and they became arhats; all of them simultaneously entered parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda ascended into the air and performed the eighteen transformations. He entered the *vāyu-vega-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Swift Wind) and divided his body into four parts.
One part went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to be with Śakra Devendra; one part he gave to Sāgara, the Dragon King of the Great Ocean;
one part he gave to the King of Vaiśālī; and one part he bestowed upon King Ajātaśatru. Thus, in each of these four places, [the body] arose.

Regarding the Jewel Stūpa (where Ānanda entered nirvāṇa while flowing in the river): it was for the sake of protecting King Ajātaśatru and the noble-minded people of Vaiśālī that [the stūpa] neither advanced nor retreated. Some say:
It is not the case that one does not see the drying up of floods.
Regarding what is called the "Transmission of the Tripiṭaka," the Venerable One said, "This is the True Meaning (Paramārtha).
As for the "Śāstra" (Commentary), ancient scholars used the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to explain the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; therefore, it is titled the "Śāstra. However...
In that first hundred fascicles, it mentions only the Kāśmīra Vinaya; having excluded the Jātaka stories, it takes only the essential portions to form ten sections.
This is also the statement regarding what was upheld by the Mahāsāṃghika school.

Regarding the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*: within this treatise, I have cited passages from that sūtra, occasionally modifying the wording. Now, I have carefully recorded them and provided annotations. The seventh fascicle of that sūtra states:
"After my parinirvāṇa, my disciples shall receive, uphold, transcribe, read, and recite the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures.
Yet, they will misunderstand their meaning and propagate it erroneously. Because they teach it perversely, they will obscure and conceal the Dharma."
Because they conceal the Dharma, they are called Dharmagupta (this is the Dharmaguptaka school; the term "conceal" (*gupta*) in the sutras carries the meaning of "secret.

Alternatively, they are called Dharmakośa, where "kośa" also carries the meaning of "secret"). Furthermore, they study, recite, and transcribe non-Buddhist texts; they accept [teachings regarding] the three times as well as internal and external [doctrines];
they refute non-Buddhists and are skilled in explaining doctrinal arguments. They maintain that all natures may receive the precepts, and they are able to answer all questions and challenges.

Correct. For this reason, it is called Sarvāstivāda (the "Adherents of All-Existence"; this school maintains that the three time periods possess substantial reality; regarding "all natures," it means that within the three natures of mind, one fully attains the precepts).
It teaches that there is no self (*ātman*) nor a recipient (*vedaka*). It turns away all afflictions (*kleśa*) as if they were a corpse.

For this reason, it is called Kāśyapīya (The Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists maintain a real self that experiences sensory objects, which is termed the "recipient. Regarding "turning away all afflictions": "turning" means to abandon. The ocean does not harbor corpses, hence the use of this metaphor).
They do not conceptualize the characteristics of earth, nor the characteristics of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness; therefore, they are called the Mahīśāsakas.

Furthermore, these six elements are all taught to be empty, which is why it is said that they do not conceptualize characteristics. They all maintain the existence of a self (*ātman*) and do not speak of the characteristic of emptiness; they are like small children.
Therefore, they are called the Vātsīputrīyas (*Vātsa* is translated here as "calf" and *Pudra* as "son"; *Pula* is an abbreviation). This refers precisely to the Vātsīputrīya school.

Furthermore, this school maintains that the self is neither identical to the aggregates (*skandha*) nor distinct from them, yet there exists a real self. In Sanskrit it is called *bālapṛthagjana*; this is translated here as "foolish ordinary beings" (*yù yìshēng*). In older translations, it was rendered as "infantile worldlings. According to this sutra:

One should say it is "just like an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*). Since ordinary persons conceive of a real self, they are cited as the analogy. When the Sūtra speaks of "infants," it intends the meaning of "fools.
Having extensively and universally studied the five divisions of the scriptures, they are therefore called the Mahāsaṃghika.

Good son, although these five divisions are each distinct, none of them obstruct the Dharma-realm of the Buddhas or Great Nirvāṇa. (The above scriptural passage is easy to understand. The Chapter says: "Receiving [the fruit] afterwards..."
The "three periods" [of time] is an error. Regarding the question of why only five categories are listed when six divisions were mentioned:

among these, the two theories of twelve and eighteen divisions have never been seen in the original texts of the sūtras or śāstras, and the traditional records have also been lost; thus, they are difficult to rely upon with confidence.

Regarding the statement in the second fascicle of the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* concerning the twenty schools, as cited in the present chapter, it is largely consistent with the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*.
For now, I shall set forth the account from the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*, providing a commentary and interpretation as appropriate. The *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra* states: "Thus it has been heard."

More than a hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of the Bhagavat, when the time since the Sage had passed and he was like the sun long set, there was a king named Aśoka who ruled over Jambudvīpa from the city of Kusumapura in Magadha.
He received a miraculous white parasol, and his transformative influence harmonized both humans and spirits.
At that time, the Great Assembly of the Buddha’s Dharma was first divided, due to the fourfold assembly’s collective deliberation on the five [theses] of Mahādeva.
Because their practices differed, they split into two schools: first, the Mahāsāṃghika; second, the Sthavira (in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, *sthavira* is translated as "Elder").

Regarding the four assemblies: first, the "Noble Elephant" assembly (the assembly of Vinaya masters); second, the "Frontier" assembly (the assembly of Mahādeva); third, the "Learned" assembly (the assembly of Sūtra masters);
fourth, the "Virtuous" assembly (the assembly of Śāstra masters). Another interpretation states that the first refers to Mahādeva, who was difficult to restrain like an elephant.
The second were the disciples of Mahādeva; the third were ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who observed the precepts; and the fourth were the noble assembly (*āryasaṃgha*).

Regarding the dispute over the five points, there is an account of its origin in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vasubhāṣya), fascicle 99. However, it differs slightly from the explanation in the *Zhen-di bu-zhi shu* (Commentary on the Tenets of the Satyasiddhi School);
it cannot be related in full detail here. To discuss it briefly now: prior to his renunciation, this Mahādeva had a secret affair with his mother.
He became proficient [in archery] and subsequently killed his father. Ashamed that others might know of his deed, he fled with his mother and hid in the city of Pāṭaliputra.
There he encountered an arhat bhikṣu whom his own country had previously supported; fearing that his secret would be revealed, he then killed him as well.

Later, seeing his mother in private with another man, he killed her too. Having thus committed three of the heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), he was deeply stricken with grief and remorse, desiring to seek their extinction.

He committed an offense and consequently left the household life. Not long after, he was able to recite and uphold the Tripiṭaka. When the king heard of this, he repeatedly invited him to enter the palace for offerings.
Paramārtha further relates that the queen consort then had a secret affair with Mahādeva, yet he continued to claim, "I am an Arhat."
Later, while in the monastery, he dreamed that he had discharged impurity and ordered his disciple to wash the soiled garment.
The disciple said, "Master, your afflictions have been exhausted; how can you permit such a thing? He replied, "There are briefly two kinds of discharge: first, that of affliction."

Arhats no longer possess [the body]. Second, regarding impurity: Arhats have not yet escaped it. Although their afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted, how could they be without excrement, urine, tears, or saliva?
However, my discharge was caused by the harassment of Māra; you should not find this strange. This is what is meant.
There was impurity within his body, such as mucus and saliva; because he was being harassed by Māra, it was immediately discharged.
Zhen Di (Paramārtha) recorded: "This was because a māra-demoness, wishing to destroy me, defiled my robes with impurity. Furthermore, he composed a sūtra himself.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: "Because the celestial maidens of Māra sought to disparage those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), they defiled their robes with impurities.

Regarding the five matters in the *Sectarian Tenets Commentary* (*Buzhi shu*), it is stated that all were composed by the author himself; these will not be discussed again below. (This is the first matter.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] desired that his disciples attend upon him personally and memorize the four fruits of śrāmaṇya in succession. A disciple asked: "A..."
The Arhats and others ought to possess realized knowledge (*jñāna*). How is it that we do not know this at all?
He replied: "Arhats also have ignorance (*ajñāna*). There are two kinds of ignorance: first, the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), which Arhats no longer possess;

second, the non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*), which Arhats still possess. (The second matter. The disciple spoke again: "I have heard that the Noble One has already crossed beyond doubt regarding the Four Truths and the Three [Treasures]."
"O Jewel, I still harbor doubts. He said that even Arhats have doubt and hesitation. There are two kinds of doubt: first, the latent (anuśaya) doubt, which Arhats no longer possess;
second, the doubt regarding what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthāna), which Arhats still possess. (Commentary: That which accords with principle is called 'possible' (sthāna);
that which does not accord with principle is called 'impossible' (asthāna). One wavers regarding all matters, both those that accord with principle and those that do not."

[The Buddha] did not resolve it; this is called doubt regarding what is possible and what is impossible (this is the third matter). The disciple spoke again: "I am an arhat; I should be able to realize this for myself.
Why must I rely solely on the teacher’s deliverance? I possess no manifest wisdom by which I can realize it myself.
He claimed that even an arhat is delivered by another. Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were foremost in wisdom and supernormal powers; yet if the Buddha had not yet bestowed his prediction upon them...
They do not even know this themselves; how much less could you, of dull faculties, who require deliverance by others, understand it on your own? Zhen Di said:
"There are also sages who rely on others to sever their doubts"—this refers to the fourth matter. Now, although that Mahādeva had committed many evils, he had not yet severed his roots of goodness.
Later, in the middle of the night, he reflected upon his grave sins and pondered where he would have to undergo intense suffering, becoming filled with anxiety and dread.
Being thus oppressed, he cried out in a loud voice, "Alas! Alas! The disciple immediately asked, "Master, if you say that what was to be done has already been accomplished, why do you cry out 'Alas'?
He then replied, "I am calling for the Noble Path; that is to say, the five factors of the Noble Path."
And he spoke in verse: "The cause of outflows in those beyond training is the lure of Māra; Ignorance and doubt are overcome through others.
When the Noble Path manifests, it is merely called forth by sound— This is termed the Tathāgata’s truly pure teaching. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (Treatise on the Wheel of Tenets) states:

"Led astray by others and ignorant [referring to an Arhat being enticed by Māra], Hesitating and led into [the path] by another, The Path arises because of sound— This is named the True Buddha-teaching."

At that time, among the assembly were those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as those of great learning, observers of the precepts, and practitioners of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Upon hearing what he had said, they reversed his verses (the first three lines being the same as before; the fourth line being): "These are your deluded words, not the Buddha's teaching.
Thereupon, they engaged in a tumultuous dispute throughout the entire night until the end of the day. The city’s officials and commoners, even up to the king himself, came to mediate the conflict.

They applied the Vinaya texts in a biased manner and used the method of voting (śalākā) to suppress disputes by means of the "majority opinion" (yadbhūyasikīya). In the assembly of noble and holy ones, although the elders were numerous, the number of monks was small;
whereas among the followers of Mahādeva, although the elders were few, the number of the assembly was large. Consequently, they split into two factions.
First was the Sthavira school, and second was the Mahāsāṃghika school. Upon hearing this, the king became enraged and sent a multitude of virtuous monks down the Ganges River in a wrecked boat.
As they were sinking in midstream, the noble assembly ascended into the air; those who shared their same views but lacked supernatural powers were also gathered up along with them.
He departed toward the northwest and went to the kingdom of Kaśmīra. When the king heard this, he repented and apologized, as described in the treatises.
According to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, he invited [the monks] back to his country; however, Mahādeva had altered the scriptures so that they no longer accorded with the original.

The Arhats then reconvened for a council, which constitutes the Third Council. It is characterized by three points: first, the Saptaparṇa Cave; second, the ten unwholesome dharmas; and third, [the restoration of the canon].
At this time, it is further said that among these five matters, some are false and some are real. As for the real: first, celestial maidens can certainly not cause disturbance;
second, there is the presence of habitual tendencies and ignorance; third, regarding the three gates of liberation, there is none that is not personally realized;

fourth, those of dull faculties who have attained the first fruit do not necessarily know it themselves, and thus must inquire of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), who then explains to them that they possess the four kinds of unshakable confidence (*aveccappasāda*).
Furthermore, by observing and examining himself, he realized this for himself. Fifth, when Śāriputra recited a verse from memory, he immediately attained the Noble Path.
Because of this discernment, the school split into two branches; this was not as described in the *Vibhāṣā*, which states that the division occurred immediately. (The Treatise says:)

Subsequently, during this very second century, three schools emerged from within the Mahāsāṃghika. (Paramārtha states: "In the second century, the Mahāsāṃghikas resided in the kingdom of Aṅguttara, which lies to the north of Rājagṛha.

This school propagated such sūtras as the Avataṃsaka, the Nirvāṇa, the Śrīmālādevī, the Vimalakīrti, the Suvarṇaprabhāsa, and the Prajñāpāramitā. Within this school, there were both those who believed and those who did not. Those who did not believe said:

'These are sūtras composed by themselves, for they are not found among the four Āgamas. Because of this, the school subsequently split into divisions. Each of these schools [is called] a *Ekavyavahārika* (this school maintains that both mundane and supramundane phenomena lack reality).

Their essence is the same conventional designation (*prajñapti*). In the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, this is called "clinging to a single expression. The commentary on the sutra states, "That which is clung to is the same as [the term] 'only' (*kevala*). This is an interpretation made by those who translated the sutra at that time).

Second, the Lokottaravāda school (this school maintains that the mundane world arises from inversion and possesses only conventional designations, whereas the supramundane is non-inverted and entirely real. The commentary on the sutra calls this "laudatory terminology," which is likely erroneous. Furthermore, among the various schools listed below in the sutra, each subsequent school emerges from each preceding one;

this differs from the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*, so it will not be discussed further here). Third, the Kukkutika school (the original sound is *Kaukkuṭika*; Paramārtha translates it as "Ash-Emergence" [*Hui-chu*]. The rocks of this mountain are suitable for making [ash]).

"Ashes. Master Ji said: "Neither the original sound nor the meaning provides this explanation. It is correctly translated as 'Chicken-Descendant' (Kukkulika). In ancient times there was a seer who begot children by mating with a hen; they belong to this clan. The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "This is the surname of the Master of the Vinaya.

This school does not propagate the Sūtras and Vinaya [claiming] that the Sūtras and Vinaya are merely provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*), for the Buddha himself has refuted them in certain instances. They propagate only the Abhidharma, practicing seated meditation to sever delusions.

Subsequently, during the second century after the Buddha's passing, another school emerged from within the Mahāsāṃghika, named the Bahuśrutīya (True Meaning says: "During the Buddha's lifetime, there was an Arhat named Śivaka").

[The master] Cīvara was formerly a rishi who wore garments of tree bark to worship the gods. Later, after he had renounced the world, he followed the Buddha and preached the Dharma, being able to recite and uphold it all. Before the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa*, he went to dwell in the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*) to practice meditation, unaware that the Buddha had already passed away.

In the second century after the Buddha’s *parinirvāṇa*, he emerged from the Snowy Mountains and saw that the doctrines propagated by the Mahāsāṃghika school were shallow. He was greatly astonished and marveled at this; he then further perfected them, reciting out both the shallow meanings and the profound meanings. Within the profound meanings lay the Mahāyāna teachings.

Among those present, some did not believe, while those who did believe separated to form a distinct school named the Bahuśrutīya (the "Much-Hearing" School). The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* originated from this school, and thus it incorporates Mahāyāna doctrines. Subsequently, in this place...

In the second hundred years, another school emerged, called the Prajñaptivāda (the School of Designation). Master Ji said: "Both mundane and supramundane phenomena are understood to encompass both designations and reality."

This is not the same as the Ekavyāvahārikas or the Lokottaravādins. [The school] translated as the Vibhajyavādins by Paramārtha was founded by Mahākātyāyana. While the Buddha was still alive, he composed a treatise to provide detailed explanations. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he joined the Mahāsāṃghika community and analyzed the Tripiṭaka, distinguishing:

"This is a provisional teaching of the Buddha; this is a definitive teaching. This is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); this is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). This concerns cause and effect. There were those who did not believe him, so he established this separate school apart from them; it is this one school that is missing from the extant scriptures.
At the completion of the second century after the Buddha’s passing, there was a renunciant non-Buddhist who abandoned heterodoxy for the true path; he was also named Mahādeva. Great...
Among the various schools (*nikāya*), there were those who had left the household life and received full ordination (*upasampadā*), who were learned and diligent, and who resided on Mount Caitya.

They deliberated once more with the monks of that school regarding the five matters; because of this, they fell into dispute and split into three schools. (Regarding the phrase "left the household life and received full ordination": this differs from the tenets of other schools. The *Shu* [Commentary] states:

When the King of Magadha perceived that the Buddha-dharma was being propagated and the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) were losing their advantage, he subsequently shaved his own hair and lived as a "thief-resident" (*caura-vāsaka*) among the renunciants. When the King heard of this, he dispatched the Bhikṣu [named] Hui [to investigate], and after purging [the community], nearly everyone was removed. Yet several hundred [genuine] individuals remained, who could not be distinguished. The King again ordered his men to interrogate them repeatedly.)

There was a disciple who had gone forth among the assembly. When his teacher was questioned and investigated, it was found that he was a "thief-dweller" (a person who assumes the appearance of a monk without being ordained). Because of this, a dispute arose. Some said: "If the teacher has broken the precepts and lacks them, yet the other monks are pure, one naturally obtains the precepts.

The Sarvāstivādins and others all adopted this interpretation. Others said: "If the teacher has broken the precepts and lacks them, the disciple likewise lacks the precepts. The Mahāsāṃghikas adopted this principle. Mahādeva was the leader of these thief-dwellers; not being accepted by the assembly, he consequently caused a schism in the school. 1. The Caitīya School (*Caitīya* is translated as "spiritual shrine").

During a single lifetime of the Buddha, there were spiritual shrines at four locations—his birth, his attainment of enlightenment, his turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and his parinirvāṇa—which were all sites of offerings. This mountain was such a spiritual shrine.

[This refers to] their location. The name of the sutra is *Cetika*. The commentary states that this is the name of a mountain where the Master of the Vinaya resided; *Cetika* is synonymous with *caitya*). Second, the Western Mountain Dwelling School (*Aparaśaila*);

third, the Northern Mountain Dwelling School (*Uttaraśaila*)—the Western Mountain [School] is named for its location on the western mountains, and the Northern [School] is likewise so named. These three are all based on their locations. The name of the sutra is *Pūrvaśaila* (Eastern Mountain).

Thus, the Mahāsāṃghika school split into four or five branches; when the primary and secondary divisions are explained separately, they form nine schools: first, the Mahāsāṃghika; second, the Ekavyāvahārika; [and so forth].
3. Lokottaravāda; 4. Kaurukullaka; 5. Bahulika; 6. Prajñaptivāda; 7. Caitīya; 8. Aparaśaila; 9.
Uttaraśaila (including the Mūlasarvāstivāda, which constitutes five schisms; if the root school is excluded, there are four).

[This concludes] the section on the removal of provisional designations according to the sūtras). As for the Sthavira school, they remained in harmonious unity of a single flavor for that duration of time.
At the beginning of the third century, a slight disagreement arose, and they split into two schools: first, the Sarvāstivāda, also known as the Hetuvāda;

second, the original Sthavira school, which changed its name to the Haimavata. During this period, while the Sthaviras primarily propagated the Sūtra-piṭaka and less extensively the Vinaya and Abhidharma, there appeared Kātyāyanīputra...

He composed the *Abhidharmajñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and extensively propagated the Abhidharma; thus, there arose disputes. Regarding those who propound that "all exists" (*Sarvāstivāda*), "existence" is of two kinds: first, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) which exist as real entities throughout the three periods of time; second, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) which exist as real entities apart from the periods of time. This is the established tenet of this school concerning the explanation of causes.

This is because it extensively sets forth the causes [of such phenomena]. In the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, the title is given as "All Speech" (*sarvabhāṣita*). The commentary states that "all" refers to whatever speech can be employed; "speech" (*bhāṣita*) is synonymous with "discourse" (*pravacana*). As for the "Himalayas," this refers to the followers of the Sthavira school, who were subdued by means of the exposition of these causes.

They moved to the Snowy Mountains (Himavat). Furthermore, since the Śākyas had been subdued by others, their school became weak and cold, comparable to the snowy winds; thus, within the treatises (*śāstra*), they are the Sthavira-vāda, which was subsequently renamed the Himavat-vāda. It is an error [to claim] that in the sūtras, "Snow" is enumerated separately outside of Tāmraparṇī.
Subsequently, during this very third century, a school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda named the Vātsīputrīya (The School of the Son of the Cow).

[In ancient times there was a rishi who, having fallen in love with a cow, fathered a son; this is their lineage. Paramārtha says they are the "Vatsiputriya" (The School of the Son Who Can Dwell). Master Ji says this principle is difficult to understand and prays that it may be examined in detail.

Now, examining this: it is due to the length of the Sanskrit vowels. If pronounced with a long vowel, *Vāsiṣṭhīputra*, it means "Son of the One Who Can Dwell. If pronounced with a short sound, *Vāsiṣṭhīputra*, it means "Son of the Cow. Paramārtha says that Rāhula was the son of Śāriputra.

"Vātsīputrīya. His disciples may remain; they propagate the *Śāriputrābhidharma*. The second volume of the *Jñānaprasthāna* also states: "The Vātsīputrīya practitioners and others recite the *Śāriputrābhidharma*.

Subsequently, during this third century [after the Buddha’s passing], four schools branched out from the Vātsīputrīya: first, the Dharmottarīya (the scripture is titled *Dharmasreṣṭha*, being the first).

1. The Uttarīya school (so named because there is a doctrine that can be ascended). 2. The Bhadrayānīya school (the leader of this school was Bhadra; "yāna" refers to his followers. *Yāna* is synonymous with lineage). 3.

The Saṃmitīya school (so named because they correct [doctrines] so as to be free from error; their sūtras are called *Sarvāstivāda*, meaning "that which is honored by all"). 4. The Kṣudraka-vana-parvata school (there is a dense forest on a mountain where the leader of this school resided;

their sūtra is called *Śaṇḍa-parvata*. Paramārtha says: these four schools commented upon the Śāriputra-abhidharma; because some meanings were deficient, they supplemented them with the meaning of the sūtras, and thus they split into separate schools). Subsequently, during this third century, from...

From the Sarvāstivāda school, another sect emerged called the Mahīśāsaka (the name derived from the fact that its founder was formerly a king whose transformative influence [mahī-śāsa] reached across the earth; later, he renounced the world and entered the monastic life, taking his former title as the name of the school).

According to their tenets, they were called the Sāmmitīya (meaning "those who rectify the land," as Paramārtha explains: this refers to the king’s preceptor who corrected the boundaries of the realm). Their scripture is titled the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Irreversible), and its commentary is as set forth in the chapter. The commentary on the scripture states: "The name means 'one who can shoot' (*iṣu-kāra*)."
Subsequently, during this third century, a school emerged from the Mahīśāsaka school named the Dharmaguptaka.

They claimed their lineage derived from the Master Mūla-śālīya (alternatively named Dharmagupta). Master Ji stated that it is incorrect to identify this as the name of the founder; rather, because it was kept secret in the aforementioned *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, it is actually the name of the teaching.

"Śālī" means bean (*māṣa*). In ancient times, there was a rishi who gathered green beans for food; since Maudgalyāyana was born of that lineage, he was called the Master Mūla-śālīya. This school established five piṭakas. Three piṭakas are as usual; the fourth is the Mantra-piṭaka. The fifth...

This refers to the five types of action. Therefore, it is known that prostration consists of these five types of action. Furthermore, the *Vinaya* states: "One should prostrate by joining the palms, bowing the head, touching the ground with the five limbs, circumambulating, and reciting verses of praise. This is because the *Vinaya* also says: "One should prostrate by joining the palms, bowing the head, touching the ground with the five limbs, circumambulating, and reciting verses of praise. Therefore, it is known that prostration consists of these five types of action. Moreover, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Prostration is the act of bowing the head and joining the palms. This refers specifically to the physical aspect. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Prostration is the act of bowing the head, joining the palms, and touching the ground with the five limbs. This refers to both the physical and vocal aspects. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Prostration is the act of bowing the head, joining the palms, touching the ground with the five limbs, and making offerings of flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth. This refers to all three types of action. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Prostration is the act of bowing the head, joining the palms, touching the ground with the five limbs, circumambulating, and reciting verses of praise. This refers to the four types of action. The *Saṃyuktāgama* states: "One should prostrate by joining the palms, bowing the head, touching the ground with the five limbs, circumambulating, and reciting verses of praise. This refers to the five types of action. Therefore, it is known that prostration consists of these five types of action. Furthermore, the *Vinaya* states: "One should prostrate by joining the palms, bowing the head, touching the ground with the five limbs, circumambulating, and

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Bowing the head and touching the feet" is therefore called "paying homage" (*namas*). Alternatively, there is homage through speech alone, as in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, where it says, "Having led the assembly to stillness, I bow my head.
There is also homage through the mind alone, as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says, "By recollecting the Buddha with a profound mind and practicing the pure precepts.
One may observe that these may involve both body and speech, or only the actions of body and mind; some possess all three.

Regarding "homage" (*namas*): the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* by Vasubandhu states, "Therefore, with utmost sincerity, I repeatedly cultivate the practice of unerring homage through body, speech, and mind.
Since this Master of the Vinaya possesses the three karmas in their true sense, it is said here that he "bows his head" (*praṇipatya*).

Regarding the statement that one is called a Buddha because they possess all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), have thoroughly penetrated all phenomena, and have awakened themselves as well as others:

the masters of this school traditionally explain that "all-encompassing wisdom" refers to that which takes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as its object, while "wisdom of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) refers to that which takes the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as its object.

Paramārtha Tripiṭaka Master, however, states that "wisdom of all modes" refers to that which takes emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its object, while "all-encompassing wisdom" refers to that which takes existence (*bhāva*) as its object; this is Paramārtha’s own explanation.

It is said: The knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*). Because the wisdom of emptiness can give rise to the understanding of existence, the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) is the understanding of existence.
It is called "all" because it distinguishes the various aspects of existence. The intent of the chapter here adopts the explanation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*):

because the wisdom that takes emptiness as its object is the true severance of hindrances and constitutes the initial attainment of Buddhahood; whereas the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) penetrates all differentiated dharma-gates and establishes [them].

He establishes names and conventions to transform the classes of sentient beings; therefore, he must possess both the fundamental wisdom and the subsequent wisdom. Because he is able to realize [reality] for himself, he distinguishes himself from ordinary fools;
and because he is further able to awaken others, he distinguishes himself from those of the Two Vehicles. Thus, he is called a Buddha. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Possessing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he is free from the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Regarding all phenomena, in a single..."
One who can fully awaken to the characteristics of all seeds, and can likewise awaken all sentient beings—
like waking from a dream or like a lotus blooming— is therefore called a Buddha.

Regarding the understanding of phenomena (*dharma*) by way of their essence: they are called "phenomena" because they maintain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). For example, nirvāṇa maintains its own characteristic of being eternally abiding;
conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are to be understood accordingly.
Regarding that which functions through the method of resolution: it is called "Dharma" because it gives rise to the understanding of sentient beings.

This is just like *nirvāṇa*, which can be realized through realized wisdom (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*) to produce the constant understanding [of liberation] (other conditioned phenomena should be understood accordingly).
Regarding that which is cherished and esteemed by the world, this is a general explanation of the term "jewel" (*ratna*). As stated in the second fascicle of the *Ratnagotravibhāga*: Question:
For what reason are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha called "jewels"? Answer: A verse states: "True jewels are rare in the world..."
"Clarity, purity, and power can adorn the world; supreme, immutable, and so forth. The prose commentary explains:
"Based on these six kinds of analogous qualities (*sādharmya*), they are called 'jewels' (*ratna*). First is the quality of being difficult for the world to obtain:
because sentient beings who lack roots of goodness cannot obtain them even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas."

The verse states that it is a "True Jewel, a Dharma rare in the world," because it does not exist for sentient beings who lack roots of goodness even throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Second is the analogous dharma of being "stainless," because it is free from all out-flowing (āsrava) dharmas; the verse states this is because it is "luminous and pure.
Third is the analogous dharma of "majestic power," because it is fully endowed with the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), which cannot...

1. The analogy of being inconceivable, because of its sovereign majestic power; as the verse says, "because of its potency. 2. The analogy of being like a reflection, because it is the basis for the manifestation of all phenomena;

as the verse says, "because it is the support. 3. The analogy of being like a great ocean, because its majestic power is sovereign; as the verse says, "because of its force. 4. The analogy of being like an ornament, because it can adorn the supramundane;
as the verse says, "because it can adorn the world. 5. The analogy of being sublime and excellent, because it is a supramundane dharma; as the verse says, "because it is supreme. 6. [The sixth...]
This refers to the dharma of similarity and correspondence that cannot be altered; because one has attained the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas, the eight worldly dharmas cannot shake them.
Thus, the verse says: "Because it is unchanging."

Regarding the distinction between individual characteristics and the single essence: the single-essence Three Jewels have True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their essence, because all phenomena have Suchness as their nature.
Within this nature of Suchness, that which possesses the meaning of awakening is called the Buddha; that which possesses the meaning of guiding and upholding is called the Dharma;
and that which possesses the meaning of non-contention is called the Saṅgha. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The Buddha is the Dharma, and the Dharma..."
This is precisely the assembly. These Three Jewels all possess the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Furthermore, it is said: "All sentient beings are suchness (*tathatā*);
all phenomena are suchness; all noble sages are suchness; even Maitreya is suchness. The lower fascicle of the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) states:
"Because the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, and even all phenomena are suchness," as is fully detailed in the sūtras and śāstras. It is not [otherwise].
One may elaborate further. Regarding the distinct characteristics: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha are explained as three distinct entities.

The three bodies of the Tathāgata—namely, the svabhāvakāya, the saṃbhogakāya, and the nirmāṇakāya—are designated as the Buddha Jewel. The Mahāyāna teachings, as well as the principles, practices, and fruits, are designated as the Dharma Jewel.
The assembly of bodhisattvas, or alternatively including the śrāvakas of the four stages and four fruits, is designated as the Saṃgha Jewel. Question:

What is the difference between the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and its underlying principle (*dharma*), as well as all the bodhi within the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Jewel of the resultant Dharma?

Answer: Their essence is the same, but their aspects differ; thus they are established as two distinct Jewels of the Buddha-dharma. If one were to explain them according to the specific characteristics of the Hinayana school:
Among the four types of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*) mentioned above, that which constitutes their essential nature is the *dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena).
"True" (*tathā*) means truly real; "as-it-is" (*-tā*) means constant as it is. Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

"Because the true nature of selflessness is unchanging, it is called the *dharmadhātu*. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* further states: "The sublime [wisdom] of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas..."
Because it is the characteristic upon which phenomena depend (meaning that because it serves as the constituent nature (*dhātu*) for all phenomena, it is called the *dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the four stages of attaining Buddhahood, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the masters of the Kaśmīra country establish only four *pāramitās*:

namely, generosity, ethical discipline, diligence, and wisdom (ethical discipline subsumes patience, and wisdom subsumes meditative concentration). The masters of the Western regions [i.e., outside Kaśmīra] speak of six *pāramitās*.
"Madhu" (honey) refers to the addition of patience (*kṣānti*) and meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) to the preceding four. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Chapter 18) also expands them into six;
although there is this difference between expansion and contraction, their meaning is in fact no different.
Regarding the first of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* (the meaning of *kalpa* is as distinguished below in the *Bhikṣu-prakīrṇaka*):
the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 178, states that during the first *kalpa*, one encounters and serves seventy-five thousand Buddhas; the first is named Śākyamuni and the last is named Ratnaśikhin.
During the second *kalpa*, there are seventy-six thousand; the first is Ratnaśikhin and the last is Dīpaṃkara. During the third...

Within the kalpas, there were seventy-seven thousand. The kalpa immediately preceding Dīpaṃkara was Roca; the one immediately following it was Abhibhū. The eighteenth verse of the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"When the three incalculable kalpas are completed, one encounters, in reverse order, Abhibhū, Dīpaṃkara, and Ratnaśikhin;
[the first was] Śākyamuni" (this is easy to understand).
Regarding the cultivation of the four outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) perfections (*pāramitā*), the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:

"By giving universally out of compassion alone, Remaining free from anger even when one's body is mangled, And praising the Buddha Tiṣya— These lead next to unsurpassed enlightenment. [Commentary: These four lines herein fully encompass the six perfections.
The text states that "cultivating the four outflow-tainted [perfections]" refers to the first three lines; that is, by means of a compassionate mind...
To give all things, even one’s own body and life, without any attachment or change of heart, is called the fulfillment of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

If one’s body is broken until not even a portion the size of a mustard seed remains intact, yet the mind harbors not the slightest resentment, this is called the fulfillment of both the perfections of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*).
If one can, with single-minded sincerity, for seven days and nights, forget to set down a foot while praising the Tathāgata with sublime verses, [this is the fulfillment of diligence].

Śākyamuni is named "Perfected in Diligence. A praise says: "In heaven and earth, within this realm, and in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa, Throughout the palaces of the departed and the celestial realms of the ten directions, there is none.
The Great Śramaṇa, the Bull-King among men, Searching through the lands, mountains, and forests, finds no equal. (Because of this praise, Śākyamuni surpassed Maitreya by nine kalpas. [Commentary:

"In heaven and earth, within this realm" refers generally to heaven and earth within this Sahā world. "Vaiśravaṇa" means "Much-Hearing" (in Chinese). Among the Four Heavenly Kings, he is the victorious king of the north; citing his abode, it is called "Much-Hearing."

"Śravaṇa-śālā" (聞室) refers to the first heaven of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). "Gati-mandira" (逝宮) refers to the palace of Brahmā, the first heaven of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*); "gati" carries the meaning of "death. Because non-Buddhists falsely reckon Brahmā to be eternal, they call that place the "Palace of Death" (*gati-mandira*).

"Deva-sthāna" (天處) refers to the heavens of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The above clarifies that these do not exist within this Sahā world-system of three thousandfold worlds. Not only are they absent here, but they are likewise absent throughout the ten directions across all three thousandfold world-systems; therefore, it says "non-existent in the ten directions.

Next, it praises the Buddha for possessing the virtues of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), the virtues of a Bull King (*ṛṣabha*), and the virtues of a Śramaṇa—virtues that cannot be found even by seeking upon the earth.
The exclusion of *dhyāna* and *prajñā* [from the first three incalculable eons] explains the fourth line of the *Abhidharmakośa*.

These two types—meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*)—are only fully perfected at the subsequent Vajrāsana. Therefore, they are excluded and not included during the first three eons. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Abiding in the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), the perfections (*pāramitā*) of this concentration and wisdom reach completion through cultivation. Hence, the verse says: "Next..."

This refers to unsurpassed bodhi. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "All that has been explained here is said to be 'perfected' based on the predominance of a single moment or a single practice.
According to the true meaning, however, it is only upon attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that the four pāramitās (which are actually six) finally attain perfection."

Regarding "being the cause for the knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*): having excluded meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), the remaining four perfections serve as the causes for the knowledge of all modes.

As the commentary based on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states: "The knowledge of all modes is the wisdom of emptiness," as has already been established previously. Because this knowledge is what is first realized at the outset, it is singled out for mention.
Regarding the cultivation of the causes for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) during the second incalculable eon: [the thirty-two marks and eight...]
The ten secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*). These shall be analyzed in the *Śīlaskandhaka* (Chapter on Receiving the Precepts). The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 178, states:
"During ninety-one *kalpas* while performing the karma that ripens into the marks of a Buddha, he encountered and served six Buddhas; the first was Vipaśyin and the last was Kāśyapa.
One should know that this refers specifically to the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni; for other bodhisattvas, it is not necessarily so. [Fascicle] 17.

Seventeenth: It is said that [the Bodhisattva] generally requires one hundred great kalpas; however, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, through his supreme diligence, transcended nine great kalpas and completed his cultivation in only ninety-one kalpas.

Furthermore, by means of the highest-grade wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) within the desire realm, he focused upon the Buddha’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), gave rise to superior volitions and aspirations, and thereby accomplished this karma. This is the correct interpretation of the *Pūrvācāryas* (the masters of the past).
It is said: thirty-two volitions induce the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), each of which is further perfected by manifold karmas, as explained at length therein.
Regarding the third stage, that of the final body, when one cultivates the contaminated four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and so forth:

all Bodhisattvas must necessarily first become detached from the defilements of the lower eight stages; subsequently, they must necessarily rely upon the fourth *dhyāna* for thirty-four moments of mind.
One attains Buddhahood in a single sitting. As stated in the twenty-fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*:

"Among the various uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), one contemplates the impure phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the immediately lower stage through three aspects—coarseness (*audārika*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and being an obstacle (*ādīnava*)—adopting whichever one aspect is appropriate. As for the various paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*):"

In relation to the various contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) of the stage immediately above that [the present one], among the three aspects (*ākāra*) of "calm," "sublime," and "principle," one adopts whichever aspect is appropriate.
That which is called "gross" (*audārika*) is so designated because it is not tranquil; it is said to be gross because it can only be transcended through great exertion.
