Next, that which is called "suffering" (*duḥkha*) is so designated because it is not exquisite; it is said to be suffering because it is characterized by much heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and is capable of causing harm and opposition.

Therefore, that which is called an "obstruction" (āvaraṇa) is so designated because it is not conducive to renunciation (naiṣkramya). It is an obstruction because it hinders one from transcending its own level (bhūmi), just as thick prison walls obstruct escape.
The three qualities of tranquility (śamatha), excellence (praśrabdhi), and detachment (viveka) should be explained as the opposite of this. The rest is clarified in the [relevant] chapter.
Regarding the fourth case—attaining Buddhahood through the sequential cultivation of thirty-four moments of mind beneath the Bodhi tree:
even for a Pratyekabuddha, there may be one who first becomes detached from the defilements of the lower eight stages and realizes awakening in a single sitting;

yet, regarding the ninth stage, they must necessarily give rise to the two paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) in succession. Although they do not abandon the afflictions within the lower eight stages, this is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of their contemplative practice.
These must arise in successive order. Calculating the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and liberation (*vimukti*) paths across the nine stages, there are one hundred and sixty-two moments of mind;
adding the sixteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are a total of one hundred and seventy-eight moments of mind before one attains realization and awakening.

Now, based on the Bodhisattva, because their faculties are superior, after the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they bypass the intermediate stages and immediately give rise to the nine paths of non-interruption (*ānantaryamārga*) and the nine paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Thus, thirty-four moments of mind are established. This should be understood as it is explained in the *Nyāyānusāra*.

Regarding "subsequent patience" (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and "subsequent knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*): *anvaya* has the meaning of "category" or "type. This refers to the subsequent knowledge that arises after the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), which observes the two upper realms;
therefore, it is called "subsequent patience" and so forth. It does not mean that one infers (*anumāna*) that because the lower realm is suffering, the upper realm must likewise be suffering.

Because this wisdom is realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and is not a wisdom of inference (*anumāna*), it is what the new sūtras and śāstras refer to as "patience regarding categories" (*jāti-kṣānti*) and so forth.
The final type, the Buddha’s mind of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-citta*), is precisely the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*).

The fivefold dharma-body has already been analyzed above in the section on the establishment and rejection of conditions for sensation; it is explained in full in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
As for the "body born of parents," this refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
The "four aggregates born of retribution" refers to the remaining four aggregates; together they constitute the five aggregates.

Regarding the three Buddhas in the Mahāyāna: if categorized by their general characteristics, they are collectively termed the Dharmakāya; if according to their specific characteristics, there are three distinct types.

Within these, there are further the three Buddhas elucidated in the school of the five lineages (*pañca-gotra*), as well as those in the school of the single nature of Buddha-nature (*eka-gotra-buddhatva*).
Regarding the three Buddhas elucidated therein, according to the doctrine of the five lineages, as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*: "Thus, the Dharmakāya has three distinct aspects:
first, the Svabhāvakāya (Self-nature Body), which is the essence of the Dharmakāya and is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); second, the Saṃbhogakāya (Enjoyment Body)."

Within this, there are further two [types]. First is the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment body), which dwells solely in the land of retribution; it was formerly called the "retribution body" (*vipākakāya*).

Second is the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (other-enjoyment body), which dwells in the land of other-enjoyment and manifests the physical marks for the sake of bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages, performing deeds of benefit.
Third is the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), which dwells in the land of transformation and acts for the sake of those bodhisattvas who have not yet ascended to the stages.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas, as well as ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, manifest their bodies to dwell in both pure and impure lands, performing deeds for the benefit of others.

It should be understood that within this context, [the Buddha] is distinguished into four bodies—namely, the two types of *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment bodies), together with the *dharma-kāya* and the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body).

Alternatively, they are condensed into three bodies by combining the two *saṃbhoga-kāyas* under the single name of *saṃbhoga-kāya*, together with the *dharma-kāya* and the *nirmāṇa-kāya*. Among these, there are the *dharma-kāya* and the body for one's own use.

Both are without limit or measure. Their manifestations for the benefit of others and their transformations vary in size, superiority, and inferiority, appearing indeterminately according to circumstances; this is the doctrinal tenet of the Five Families (pañca-gotra).

The meaning of the present chapter, however, belongs to the School of One Nature (eka-gotra). As the chapter states: "After the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*), one suddenly attains the eternally abiding five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

This reveals the non-interruption of permanence and corresponds to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra*, specifically the Bodhi of the Reward Buddha (*vipākabuddha*) and the practices of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*).

It is fulfilled because one attains the realization of eternal nirvāṇa. As the sūtra says: "Since my actual attainment of Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas have passed.
The commentary states: "The ninth pure consciousness is the *dharmadhātu* of true suchness (*tathatā*)."
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha taught that there are nine consciousnesses. This corresponds to what is stated in the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*: "The mind consists of eight kinds, or alternatively, nine.
Paramārtha states: "The six consciousnesses are as usual; the seventh is the ādāna-vijñāna, which here is translated as 'appropriating consciousness' (*zhíshí*)."
Because this nature of delusion is always characterized by grasping, the Tripiṭaka Master from Tang said: "Ādāna" means "grasping and holding," because it grasps and holds the seeds of all phenomena;
it is also an alternative name for the eighth consciousness. This was a mistaken interpretation by Paramārtha.
The seventh consciousness should be named *manas*, which is translated here as "mind. Paramārtha further stated that the eighth is named "Ā... [the text is incomplete].
The *ālayavijñāna*. The ninth is named the *amala-vijñāna*. The Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty stated that this translates as "stainless" (*wugou*).
It is also an alternative name for the eighth consciousness. At the time of attaining Buddhahood, the eighth consciousness is transformed to become the stainless;

there is no separate ninth consciousness. This is explained in detail in works such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. Since the Tang dynasty, [scholars] have been biasedly attached to this view. This is truly because...
This is because it does not seek out the school of a single nature (*ekasvabhāva*). As for that seventh consciousness, it is likely a lapse in the text recited by Paramārtha;
it may be refuted as previously stated. Most of what was translated by Paramārtha was produced from oral recitation, as there were no Sanskrit manuscripts available.

Regarding the ninth consciousness, as the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* (Miyin jing), lower fascicle, states: "The Tathāgata’s pure storehouse is also called stainless wisdom (*vimalajñāna*). Thus, one knows it is not erroneous.
Furthermore, according to the Buddha-nature school, the seventh consciousness arises from the seeds of deluded attachment within the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
It is named after its respective objects. As the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* (Miyin jing) verse states:

"Just as the celestial palaces, the various stars, and the sun and moon depend upon Mount Sumeru and are moved by the power of the wind (taking the mountain as their support and the wind as their sustainer), so too are the seven consciousnesses (referring to the seven types collectively) supported [by the eighth]."
"Regarding the ālayavijñāna, it is sustained by the perfuming of habitual tendencies and constantly flows everywhere" (as stated in the sūtra). The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha said:
"The amala-vijñāna is of two kinds: first, that which is the object of cognition (*ālambana*), which is suchness (*tathatā*); second, original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*)."
This is the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness). That which takes it as its object is the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*; that which is the object itself is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.

According to the general exposition, both of these have *tathatā* as their essence; they correspond to what is described in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* as the "Dharma-tathatā" and the "Wisdom-tathatā.
These two *tathāgatagarbhas* were originally hidden within the *saṃkleśa* (defilements), shrouded by adventitious dust, but now they have emerged.

The *paryavasthāna* (entanglements) are the true *dharmakāya*. This corresponds to the *Dharmabuddhabodhi* discussed in the *Fa-hua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra), namely the *tathāgatagarbha*, the intrinsically pure *nirvāṇa*, because it is eternal, constant, cool, and unchanging. As the sutra says: "The Tathāgata knows and sees the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are.
Furthermore, according to that school, the *dharmakāya* may also be divided into two bodies: that which is called the *dharmakāya* and that which is called... [the *sambhogakāya*].
The Wisdom Body (jñānakāya) arises precisely because the two Tathāgatagarbhas emerge from their entanglements to become the two [Bodies].
Just as with the Reward and Transformation Bodies, there are likewise four bodies; however, these differ from the four bodies found in the Five-Family (pañcagotra) school.

The meaning of the Transformation Body is explained in the chapter [of this text], which corresponds to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*’s description of the Bodhi of the Responding and Transforming Buddha: it manifests according to what should be seen by sentient beings. As...
The Sūtra states: "Having departed from the palace of the Śākyas, not far from the city of Gayā, he sat at the site of enlightenment," and so forth.
The meaning of his three bodies is fully explained in the Commentary on the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra.
Regarding "prostrating with the head" (*jìshǒu*): the *Shàngshū* states that "prostrating with the head" means the head reaches the ground. Cáo Chōng says that "jì" means to examine;
one brings the head to examine the ground, hence it is called "prostrating with the head. Now, examining the first fascicle of the *Shàngshū*, "jì" (pronounced as *jī*) is glossed as "to examine."
This means that although Yao possessed sagely virtue and followed the ancient Way in his conduct, he did not reverently adopt the practice of bowing one's head to the Buddha.
Be careful not to rely on such [practices].
As for the treatise containing many meanings, it is the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding "those who look downward" and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle four, states: There are renunciants who compound medicines, sow grains, plant trees, and so on;
such impure means of livelihood are called "food from below. There are renunciants who observe the stars, the sun, the moon, wind, rain, thunder, lightning, and hail;
such impure means of livelihood are called "food from above. There are renunciants who... [are crooked]... [text continues].

To flatter those of power and influence, to act as a messenger to the four quarters, to employ clever speech for excessive requests, and to maintain one's life through impure means—this is called "food from the four directions" (*caturdiśa-bhakṣa*).
There are renunciants who study various incantations and spells, calculate auspicious and inauspicious omens, and practice minor arts that are not upright;

such practitioners who maintain their lives through impure means engage in "food from the four intermediate directions" (*vidiśā-bhakṣa*). The preface to these verses consists of forty-six and a half lines. [This is] the judgment.
This is explained according to the chapter. Chongsheshe’s *Yichao* contains extensive refutations; there is no leisure for further elaboration.

As for the cause of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is that which is brought about by the practice of the teaching. Cessation here refers to cessation through deliberation.
Regarding the explanation according to the meaning of the Tripiṭaka, there are five meanings of *tattva* used to explain the Vinaya, which are not fully detailed here in this chapter.
First, that which is capable of leading forth various kinds of benefits is the meaning of Vinaya; that is to say, it is capable of leading forth supramundane goodness.
Within this, there are two aspects: first, it can induce the production of forty-two thousand merits of the True Dharma;
second, it can induce a mind free from regret. Because of this absence of regret, the mind becomes joyful and attains concentration, leading even to liberation.

The second aspect is that which can teach the purity and correctness of body and speech; this is the meaning of *vinaya*. It is so named because it restrains the body and speech, preventing them from giving rise to evil.
As for its teaching: because it is not defiled by the turbidity of karma (*karmakāṣāya*) or the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśakāṣāya*), body and speech are pure;

because it is not defiled by the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭikāṣāya*—the five views being termed the turbidity of views), it is called "correct and true. By virtue of purity, one attains rebirth in the good realms;
by virtue of being correct and true, one is able to realize *nirvāṇa*. Thirdly, it can extinguish the obstacle of transgressions; this is the meaning of *vinaya*.

Within this, there are further two parts: first, the means for cessation; second, the actual cessation of offenses (actual cessation refers to attaining *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*, which is nirvāṇa; in this chapter, only the means for cessation is taken up).
[The reader] should understand this for themselves below. Because morality (*śīla*) can obstruct all sinful hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), it is called the "means of cessation.

Because hindrances do not arise, the destruction of sin is attained; since both of these are achieved, it is termed *vinaya*. The fourth [meaning], "that which can lead to excellence," is the sense of *vinaya*:
it can lead householders to go forth from the home, and lead those who have not yet abandoned desire to attain the Brahma-abodes (*brahmavihāra*). From these Brahma-abodes, one attains...
The noble abode (*āryavihāra*). From the noble abode, one attains *sa-upadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; from the state with remainder, one enters the state without remainder.

Because each subsequent stage is more excellent than the last, it is called "leading to excellence" (*viśeṣāvahana*). This fifth [category] is that which is practiced by superior persons; this is the meaning of *vinaya*.

The Buddha is the most superior, followed by the Pratyekabuddhas, and then the Śrāvakas, because these are the practices undertaken by such superior persons. Furthermore, even among ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), they are likewise superior.
Only by means of these can one practice. Among these five, the first two and the last two are explained in terms of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).

The middle one explains both the training rules and cessation (*nirodha*). If one speaks of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it includes the training rules; however, if one is speaking specifically in terms of the training rules, one cannot explain them by means of analytical cessation (for the training rules are the precepts).

Regarding these eight *vinayas* of this Vinaya, their actual substance consists of only seven: first, offense (*āpatti*); second, dispute (*adhikaraṇa*); third, transgression; fourth, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);

fifth, monks (*bhikṣu*); sixth, nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*); seventh, direction (*diś*); eighth, universal (*sarva*). A summary verse states: Offense, dispute, transgression, latent tendency, Monk, nun, direction, and universal—these are the grave offenses (*pārājika*).
Regarding the discussion of the five meanings of *vinaya*, the seventh fascicle states: "As for *vinaya*, there are generally five meanings. First, repentance (*deśanā*):
as in the Seven Chapters [of the Prātimokṣa], whatever has been transgressed should be repented; that repentance can extinguish [the offense] is called *vinaya*. Second, conformity (*anuvidhāna*):
the seven classes of the community follow what the Buddha has prescribed and taught, practicing it through their acceptance without any opposition. Third, extinction (*nirodha*): namely..."

The extinction of the seven types of disputes (*saptadhā vivāda*). Fourth is "severance" (*cheda*), which means being able to cause afflictions (*kleśa*) to be extinguished and not to arise again. Fifth is "renunciation" (*praṇidhāna*). There are two kinds of renunciation:

first, the renunciation of what has been done, which refers to the commission of the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. Regarding these thirteen matters, if nine matters are committed, the offense is established immediately and one may not be admonished;
that is, for the first nine *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, there is no formal admonition. For four matters, there are three admonitions, yet [the offense is still established].

Regarding the *pratideśanīya* (offenses requiring confession): if the Saṃgha performs the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the three subsequent proclamations (*karmavācanā*), the offense is established; if only the motion is performed and the three proclamations are not, the matter is not established.

These thirteen [rules] are called "abandoning what was done" (*kṛta-prahāṇa*). Second is "abandoning what was seen" (*dṛṣṭi-prahāṇa*); as in the case of Liṭha’s statement of desire, because one abandons this view, it is called "abandoning.

The verse says: "The seven categories are confessed according to the teaching; the seven confessions sever the afflictions. Abandoning the evil views that were formed follows the sequence of the five *vinayas*."
Regarding the nun:
concerning those produced by the eight conditions of origination, that treatise states: "There are eight causes for the arising of offenses.

First, there is an offense arising from the body, not from speech or mind, such as sleeping together with one who does not possess the great precepts (*mahāśramaṇa*) without closing the door, and so forth. Second, [an offense] arising from speech..."

1. Arising from body and mind, but not from speech: as when one with a virtuous mind preaches the Dharma to others for more than five or six words, and so forth. 2. Arising from mind, but not from body or speech:

as when one speaks of offenses and hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) from the perspective of the mental ground—meaning that by forming a firm resolve to kill, etc., one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). 3. Arising from body and speech, but not from mind: as when one with a virtuous mind acts as a matchmaker, and so forth.

4. Arising from body and speech, but not from mind: as when one with a virtuous mind acts as a matchmaker, and so forth. 5. Arising from body and mind, but not from speech: as in the case of [the aforementioned] intentional act.
1. Emission of semen and so forth. 2. Six [offenses] proceed from speech and mind, but not from body; for example, speaking lewd words to a woman with a defiled mind.
3. [Offenses] proceed from body, speech, and mind; for example, acting as a matchmaker with a defiled mind. 4. There are cases where none of the three proceed;

for example, if one first speaks a great lie to another person, but that person has not yet understood it, and this person has already confessed the three preparatory offenses (*prayoga-āpatti*). That person...
If, at a later time, the person understands the meaning of those words, this individual incurs the offense of *pārājika*. The *Miaomiao shu* (Clear Commentary) asks:

"If one first utters a great falsehood toward another person, but that person does not yet understand it, and the speaker has already performed the confession for the three preparatory offenses (*prayoga*), since this person has not yet committed a grave offense, can they still attain the state of an *ārya* through cultivation?
The answer is: "If that person understands [the words] later, this individual commits the offense immediately; there is no [attainment of the state of an *ārya*]."
Regarding the principle that a noble one (*ārya*) who commits a grave offense cannot repent and will inevitably enter the evil realms:

since a noble one has no possibility of being reborn in the evil realms, this person certainly cannot attain the fruit of sainthood before that [offender] dies; only after that person dies can it be attained.

Even if that person takes on a subsequent body, there is no obstruction to liberation, as the physical bodies are distinct (this point shall be further examined in the supplementary text below). The three realms...

The five classes of afflictions and the nine knowledges of permanent abandonment (*navātyanta-prahāṇa-jñāna*), as well as cessation (the above concludes the *Abhidharma-śāstra*). Regarding the "nine knowledges of permanent abandonment," these are the wisdoms that realize [the truth].
"And cessation" refers to the cessation that is realized. According to the new sūtras and śāstras, this refers exclusively to what is realized, up to the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).
Thorough knowledge is simply another name for the abandonment of the afflictions. If one were to provide a detailed analysis, it could not be exhausted here; however, it may be stated briefly:

It is merely a matter of classification. In terms of the exhaustion of the delusions (*kleśa*) of the three realms and five categories (*pañca-varga*), there are distinctions therein consisting of nine thorough knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).

The twenty-first verse of the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "There are nine thorough knowledges of abandonment: One for the first two abandonments of the desire realm; Two [more] for each [of the remaining two], totaling three;

The same applies to the three [abandonments] of the upper realms; The remaining five are for the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*); And three for the total abandonment of the form realm. [Commentary: This refers to abandonment...

When the afflictions of suffering and origin in the desire realm are exhausted, the dharma-knowledge-acceptance (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) ceases and the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudayadharmajñāna*) arises.

The abandonment attained at this time is called the first "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the desire realm (hence the verse says: "The first two abandonments constitute one").

Second is the complete knowledge of the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha*) in the desire realm. Third is the complete knowledge of the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga*) in the desire realm.
The fourth is the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin within the form and formless realms.

The fifth is the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the vision of cessation within the form and formless realms. The sixth is the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the vision of the path within the form and formless realms.
Attaining these thorough knowledges does not constitute the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*). (Thus the verse says: "Two names combined as one make three"; "the three of the upper realms").

[This concludes the] establishment [of the categories]. In the verse, it says "the remaining [abandonments] through the vision of the truths"; "the remaining" refers here to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Within that, there are further three distinctions:

namely, the seventh thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), which is the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*). One who attains this thorough knowledge is also called one who has attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
The five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīyāni*) are: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); second, the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*);

third, doubt (*vicikitsā*); fourth, sensual desire (*kāma-rāga*); and fifth, ill-will (*vyāpāda*). Due to the latter two, one does not transcend the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and cannot attain rebirth in the higher realms.
Even if one is able to sever sensual desire and ill-will and thus attains birth in the higher realms, due to the former three, one returns again to be born below. (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra)
The thirty-ninth [verse] provides an analogy: "The latter two kinds of fetters are like two jailers who guard a criminal, preventing them from leaving the prison.

The former three kinds of fetters are like three pursuers; even if a criminal, by the power of friends or by the power of wealth, harms the jailers and escapes far away, the three pursuers will still seize him and bring him back, confining him."
The "prison" is a metaphor for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The "criminals" are a metaphor for foolish worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*).

Even if such worldlings should, by means of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) or the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-bhāvanā*), suppress greed and hatred and even reach the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), their views of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) will still seize them and place them back within the desire realm; therefore, these are called the five fetters bound to the lower realm (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).

The complete exhaustion of these five [fetters] constitutes the seventh thorough knowledge (*parijñā*). (Therefore, the verse says: "The remaining five are for the sake of the subsequent [categories].

Regarding the eighth, it is the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of the fetter of craving for the form realm [the word "form" must be included here]. The ninth is the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters. Upon attaining this thorough knowledge, one is also called an Arhat fruit [the verse says:
"The exhaustion of all three is"]. Because four conditions are fulfilled, the first six thorough knowledges are established: first, the cessation of two causes.)

Second, the separation from both fetters; third, the attainment of the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*); and fourth, the deficiency of the various pervasive knowledges (*parijñā*) regarding the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Based on these five conditions, the latter three pervasive knowledges are established—namely, the aforementioned four plus the permanent transcendence of the realm—as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
The first six [types of non-acquisition] are established by three conditions; the latter three are established by four conditions.

Within the aforementioned four and five conditions, one respectively excludes the condition of dissociation (*visamyoga-pratyaya*) and the condition of co-existence (*sahabhū-pratyaya*), because the cessation of both causes necessarily involves dissociation. No distinction is made regarding the time periods (*adhvan*).
For a detailed analysis, see the *Vibhāṣā* (62) and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (21). Thus far, the discussion has been based on the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) that is realized.

Nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) are established; accordingly, there are also the cognitions that realize them which arise. In the Sarvāstivāda school, the nine thorough knowledges are established solely in reference to what is realized.
Now, the Saṃmitīya school clarifies both the realization and the means of realization; therefore, it says "nine knowledges of permanent abandonment (*atyantaprahāṇajñāna*) and cessations."
Regarding bathing: this is also clarified according to the specific regions; it refers to the borderlands.
This is as cited in the relevant chapter from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, specifically the seventh fascicle of that treatise.

One who is "equipped with the Vinaya" (vinayadhara) should, in meaning, master both treatises on the Vinaya. See the fourth chapter of the *Vinayavibhāṣā*. Regarding the five benefits of upholding the Vinaya, they are as cited in the relevant section.
Furthermore, the sixteenth chapter of that same treatise also lists five benefits; it modifies the fourth [benefit] to be "establishing the True Dharma."
This is for the purpose of subduing all enemies; thus, it shares the same meaning as the preceding text, though the phrasing differs.
As for those who say it is the same as this explanation, they are identical in that there are only five benefits, which should be assigned accordingly.

With Upāli at the head, the principles of the previous classification have already been briefly explained. I fear that what is explained in this chapter may not accord with reason. Chong states: "The Buddha originally established the precepts..."

The entire assembly of monks gathered; Upāli was among those assembled from the very beginning of the meeting, and thus he is called the "foremost. Those within the assembly who heard it together are termed "the others" (*anye*).
Alternatively, Upāli was at the start of the compilation, while the others were members of that same assembly.

Or again, Upāli is designated as the "foremost" because he inherited the Vinaya, while Kāśyapa and the others are called "the others" because they were *kāyasākṣins* (bodily witnesses). The *Shiyi* states: "The ancients were appropriate [in this regard]."

It is not that consciousness fails to discern right from wrong, nor is it the influence of celestial beings; yet one dies without awakening to this. Now, examining your veneration of Śākyamuni, it completely contradicts the meaning of the text.
Why do you utter such coarse and malicious words?

Regarding the phrase "one who has realized through the body" (*kāyasākṣin*): if an *anāgāmin* attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they are called one who has realized through the body.

In this Vinaya text, however, it clarifies that the person who transmits the Dharma is, by principle, not an *anāgāmin*. Therefore, as explained in the commentary: if an *arhat* attains the meditative absorption of cessation, they are called "liberated in mind" (*cetovimukta*) and also "one who has realized through the body.
When wisdom exhausts all outflows (*āsrava*), it is called "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*). Thus, it is said that [the Dharma-transmitter] is "complete" in both respects.
Regarding the second point on liberation:

it is not correct to say that among the five masters who transmitted the teachings, Upāli alone was given a name. This is because it was already stated in the previous section on the division of schools that there were those who transmitted the Vinaya by name.
As for the claim that Upāli had no name because he lacked a karmic connection with sentient beings, this is also incorrect.

Regarding the second point, "possessing the two practices to constitute being an elder": these are the two practices of benefiting oneself and benefiting others. As the *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), verse 25, states:
"That which is called the mark of an elder does not necessarily depend on advanced age; it is not merely having a thin body with white hair and beard."
"To grow old in vain while possessing no inner virtue" is precisely that meaning. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 17, states: "Mountains can support the earth, keeping it from tilting or shaking.

If one seeks the foremost and most supreme among those who practice the preliminary conduct (*pūrva-gamana*), the Venerable One said: 'Not so; for within the preliminary conduct, precepts (*śīla*) are [the foremost]."

"First and foremost. Now, this further states that it is not merely maintaining precepts, nor is it the diligent pursuit of precepts; yet it again speaks of "maintaining precepts," which would otherwise lack the distinction between subject and object.
It should rather be said that "first and foremost" refers to the Bodhi of the Three Vehicles, because maintaining the precepts is the remote cause for liberation.
"Throughout one's life, do not violate them" establishes a time limit. This can give rise to two [results].

"Wholesome" refers to the two types of wholesome discipline—restraint and engagement—pertaining respectively to body and speech, as explained in the section on observance and transgression (*śīla-āpatti*).

Regarding the statement that "the mind constitutes body and speech," this is further explained in the second commentary on the meaning of observance and transgression: the mind does not commit a transgression alone; rather, it has the sense of assisting the transgressions of body and speech.
Regarding the phrase "those who slight the Brahmin" (the character "yi" is an error; it should read "qingbo," meaning frivolous or contemptuous):

The *Rāhula-sūtra* states that when Śāriputra and Rāhula were on their almsround, there was a frivolous person who gave rise to a malicious intent. He took sand and soil, placed it in Śāriputra’s bowl, struck Rāhula on the head until blood flowed and smeared his face.
Śāriputra told Rāhula, "You should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness. Rāhula then went to wash at the water's edge.
[He] bled and said of himself: "My pain lasts but a moment; what is that [other] long suffering compared to it? He spoke at length, stating that which was spoken by the people who raised the matter.
They reported this transgression to the Buddha. The case of Śreṇika was the same. This does not accord with reason. "To raise" (*udāhṛta*) here has the sense of "to bring to mind" or "to inform.
In this context, "raising" the king has the sense of "to recommend" or "to nominate. Therefore, they do not correspond. Now, it should be explained further why this was established.

The King (a metaphor for the Dharma King appearing in the world) arises because of worldly disputes (a metaphor for seeing sentient beings give rise to tainted faults; thus the Buddha appears in the world).

He is the one exalted by the multitude, according to the constant law of antiquity ("exalted" means to be promoted or honored; this metaphorizes those who appear in the world to cultivate goodness, who respectfully follow the Buddha’s teachings, as the Way is the same throughout the three periods of time). Those who commit offenses know the law.

One who accords with the Dharma achieves [this] (a metaphor for the characteristics of one who practices virtue by following the path). The precepts are likewise. It is like a king governing according to the True Dharma (this is a general synthesis:

when a Dharma King appears in the world, he perceives faults and transgressions, causing practitioners to reverently accord with the Buddha’s teachings and clearly discern what is to be observed and what is to be avoided).
Regarding the four incurable offenses mentioned in the *Mātṛkā*, the third volume of that treatise states: "A *pārājika* offense does not give rise to wholesome roots;
it can never be expiated through repentance, nor is there any ritual (*karmavācanā*) by which the transgression may be removed.

For example, as in the case of Devadatta, who drew blood from the Buddha’s body—this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense that will never give rise to untainted (*anāsrava*) wholesome roots, and for which no ritual exists to remove the transgression."
There is a *pāyattika* offense that does not give rise to roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), nor is there a ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) by which the offense can be removed.

For example, if one, out of a mind of anger, intends to take the life of a Buddha, striking the Buddha incurs a *pāyattika* that cannot be expiated. There is a *duṣkṛta* offense that does not give rise to roots of goodness, nor is there a ritual procedure for removing the offense.
This applies, for instance, to a *śrāmaṇera*, *śrāmaṇerī*, or *śikṣamāṇā* regarding any of the four *pārājika* offenses. If...

If one commits a single offense, it cannot be expiated. (The Commentary states: "That is to say, *pārājika* and *sthūlātyaya*. This means that these four matters are designated as the four *pārājikas* based on the characteristics of the prescriptive teachings (*vidhi-śāsana*).

Among them, striking the Buddha is a *sthūlātyaya*, while the subsequent offenses for the assembly are *duṣkṛta*. Since these are identified as incurable within the category of natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), they are distinguished [and excluded] from the gate of the prescriptive teachings.
There is a version of the commentary that reads "that is to say, *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta*," which contains the superfluous character "lán" (*sthūla*).

This is so. With the exception of those who commit the two *ānantarya* offenses, because they have disrupted the *saṃgha*, their destiny for the next life is fixed, and they must undergo retribution for one *kalpa*. Among the five *ānantarya* offenses, disrupting the *saṃgha* is the most grave.
In the treatises, it is stated that one who sheds [a Buddha’s] blood is not cured; by this principle, it should be inferred that the case of disrupting the *saṃgha* is likewise fixed.
Therefore, it is said there are two immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*). In reality, however, the treatise states only that the single transgression of drawing blood is incurable.
This serves to exclude the case of [striking] a monk. Thus, we know that the character "Lan" (僧) was erroneously added previously.

Regarding the four fears of transgression, the following four passages are added: first, as if there were a man who had committed a crime punishable by decapitation, which is analogous to a *pārājika* offense;
second, as if there were a man who had committed a crime punishable by being struck with a blade, which is analogous to a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;

third, as if there were a man who had committed a crime punishable by being struck with a staff, which is analogous to a *pāyattika* offense; fourth, as if there were a man who had committed a crime punishable by censure.
Regarding the offenses: they are called the "fourfold transgressions to be feared," comparable to the *pratideśanīya* (offenses requiring confession).
It would be better to revise the phrase "among many, confronting an individual" to "having a simultaneous time limit."
Regarding the five meanings of a corpse, the *Vṛddhapañcavastuka* states: first, impurity; second, a foul odor; third, being fearful;
fourth, causing others to be fearful, whereby evil spirits find an opportunity; and fifth, being a dwelling place for wicked beasts and non-human beings.
A person who violates the precepts is likewise: first, their three karmas are impure, like the impurity of a corpse; second, a bad reputation spreads abroad, like the foul odor of a corpse.
1. One's aura is foul. 2. All virtuous bhikṣus will shrink away in fear. 3. When good people see such a person, they will conceive thoughts of impurity and aversion.
This is called associating with evil associates, which increases one's unwholesome karma; it is like a person seeing a corpse who fears that a ghost will find an opportunity to seize them.
4. Being personally impure oneself, one also dwells together with evil people. These points may be understood by correlating them respectively with the five preceding metaphors.

Regarding those who are like a fire driven by a whirlwind, there are four matters that must not be underestimated. As stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 24: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
When the elder Candraprabha (Moonlight) had a son born, the Nirgranthas examined his features and declared, "This child has little merit; you must take him and kill him.
The elder did not agree, desiring instead to consult the Tathāgata. On the way, he thought to himself: "Gautama is young; I fear he may not [be able to answer]."
"Please dispel my doubt. At that time, a celestial deity announced from the air: "There are four things that must not be treated with contempt:
a king, though small, must never be treated with contempt; fire, though small, must also never be treated with contempt; a nāga, though small, must likewise never be treated with contempt;
and a person who studies the Way, though they may be young in years, must also never be treated with contempt. He then spoke this verse: "Though the lord of the land be small,"

"By means of this method, one may inflict harm. Though a small fire has not yet blazed, it burns away the grasses and trees of the mountain. Though a divine dragon appears small, it sends down rain according to the needs of the season.
A student, though young in years, can deliver beings without limit. Having heard this, the elder was filled with joy and went to the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, like a split *elā* leaf. [This occurred] in the presence of Kāśyapa.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had this thought: "If plucking a leaf from a sandalwood tree incurs the fault of destroying its beauty, what harm is done by plucking a leaf from the stinking *elā* tree?
Due to the retribution of this karma, he was born among the nāgas; atop his head grew an *elāpattra* tree whose roots entered the dragon's head.
When it was buffeted by the wind, thick blood flowed forth from all sides, causing him great suffering and distress. [He then approached] Maitreya.

When the man emerged, he was just shedding his dragon body; this refers to the Dragon King Elāpattra mentioned below. Question: Since killing a living being constitutes a *pāyattika* offense, it should not be used as an analogy for a minor transgression (*dukkaṭa*).

Answer: This is merely based on the fact that he acted with a light mind and did not follow the Buddha’s teachings; it does not necessarily mean that the gravity of the offense must correspond exactly to the nature of the object.
Regarding the ninety-eight *anuśayas* (latent defilements), this is according to the Sarvāstivāda school. There are ten root *anuśayas*:

namely, greed (*rāga*), hostility (*pratigha*), ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Based on their abandonment through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), there are ninety-eight. Specifically, those abandoned by the path of seeing number eighty-eight. As the verse in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states: "If..."

Possessing all [factors]—(the "lower" refers to the suffering of the desire realm; it is called "lower" because it belongs to the lower realm; "possessing all" means possessing the ten underlying tendencies). Regarding the truths of origin, cessation, and dispassion, three views are excluded (among the five views, this means excluding the first three).

Regarding the truth of the path, two views are excluded (among the five views, this means excluding the first two). Thus far, based on the four truths of the desire realm, there are thirty-two *anuśayas* in total.

In the higher realms, anger does not function (this means that for each of the four truths in the two higher realms, anger is excluded; since anger is necessarily absent in the higher realms, this results in twenty-eight for those two realms combined with the previous thirty-two of the desire realm, totaling eighty-eight).

Greed, hostility, ignorance, and pride—these four latent dispositions (anuśaya) are to be abandoned through both seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*). As previously discussed, those to be abandoned by seeing [are as explained above];

next are those to be abandoned by cultivation. In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all four are present. In each of the two upper realms, anger is excluded. When the three realms are considered together, they constitute ten types;
combined with the previous eighty-eight, this totals ninety-eight.

Regarding "the pure heaven of nirvāṇa" (*nirvāṇa-śuddha-deva*): nirvāṇa itself is the pure heaven; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Thus, the treatise says: "Beyond the realm of birth and death. "Beyond" (*biao*) means "external.

If one follows the commentary on the *Sūtra-samuccaya*, it should not be so. For instance, when one speaks of "seeking heaven," if "heaven" refers to nirvāṇa, then the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are what is truly sought.
As for the heavens of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*), it is through ethical discipline (*śīla*) that one can proceed toward them.

The phrase "never at last" (終不) does not govern the following two sentences. This means that one will never finally turn back toward the flow of error; this corresponds to the preceding [line], "Though deep, there is no sorrow of drowning.
It means that one will never finally sink into the sea of birth and death; this corresponds to the preceding [line], "One is thus able to reach the other shore."
Regarding the thirty-seven factors: four, three, two, five, seven alone, and eight; combined, they total thirty-seven. These are called the four foundations of mindfulness:
first, contemplating the body as impure; second, contemplating feelings as suffering; third, contemplating the mind as impermanent; and fourth, contemplating phenomena as selfless.
Because these four objects are observed through wisdom, they are named the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 141.

Question: This essence is wisdom (*prajñā*). For what reason did the Blessed One call it the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)? Answer: Wisdom abides upon its object by means of the power of mindfulness;

therefore, it is called a foundation of mindfulness (this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the abiding of mindfulness"). Alternatively, it is because the power of this wisdom causes mindfulness to abide upon its object.

Therefore, they are called the foundations of mindfulness (this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "foundations established upon wisdom"). The four right efforts are also called the four right abandonments and the four right strivings:
(1) for the purpose of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies the mind, and sustains the mind;
(2) for the purpose of preventing evil and unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising, one generates desire, exerts effort, and so forth.
As previously stated: third, regarding wholesome dharmas not yet arisen, in order to cause them to arise, one generates desire and so forth, as previously described;

fourth, regarding wholesome dharmas already arisen, in order to cause them to remain stable, not to be lost, and to further cultivate, increase, and expand them, one generates desire, exerts effort, and so forth, as previously described.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The essence of diligence is established based on its differing functions within a single moment."

There are four kinds, just as a lamp has four distinct functions in a single moment: namely, consuming the wick, exhausting the oil, heating the vessel, and dispelling darkness. Regarding "right abandonment" (*samyak-prahāṇa*):

it refers to that which, through the power of diligence, is able to abandon laziness. Regarding "right exertion" (*samyak-saṃskāra*): because this is the most excellent among the activities of body, speech, and mind that are correctly maintained.

The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are: first, the base of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of concentration through the application of desire (*chanda-samādhi-prahāṇasaṃskāra-samanvāgata-ṛddhipāda*).

The bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) accomplished through the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi*) and the formations of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*): first, the base of psychic power accomplished through the cultivation of concentration and the formations of abandonment based on desire; second, the base of psychic power accomplished through the cultivation of concentration and the formations of abandonment based on effort; third, the base of psychic power accomplished through the cultivation of concentration and the formations of abandonment based on mind; and fourth, the base of psychic power accomplished through the cultivation of concentration and the formations of abandonment based on investigation.

This refers to the time of preparatory application (*prayoga*), when one may, by the power of desire, induce meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and so forth, up to inducing meditative absorption by the power of investigation. Thus, through such preparatory application, there are four...

The dharmas increase accordingly, causing meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to arise; thus, one attains the state of stability. Within a single meditative concentration, four types are established. One explanation in the *Vibhāṣā* states:

"The name 'samādhi' refers to the 'divine' (*deva*), while the four factors such as desire refer to the 'bases' (*pāda*). Another explanation states: "Samādhi is both the 'divine' and the 'base'; the four factors such as desire are only the 'bases,' not the 'divine'.

(The intent of the former explanation is to show that because the divine has four bases, they are called the "four bases of divine power" [*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*]. The intent of the latter explanation is to show that...)

The feet have four bases; hence they are called "supernormal powers" (*ṛddhipāda*). The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-five, refutes this by stating: "In that case, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) would consist of thirteen entities, because desire and mind are added.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 196) states: "The factors of enlightenment number thirty-seven, but in terms of substantial entities (*dravya*), there are only eleven. That is to say, among the seven limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), there are seven substantial entities: first, mindfulness; second, wisdom; third, energy; fourth, joy; fifth, tranquility; sixth, concentration..."

The seven factors of abandonment (*prahāṇa*), together with faith among the faculties and powers, constitute eight. Furthermore, adding right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) from the Eightfold Path makes nine; right speech (*samyag-vāc*) makes ten; and right action (*samyak-karmānta*) constitutes the essence of right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*), which is not mentioned separately because it is not distinct from speech and action.

Next, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*), along with wisdom (*prajñā*) among the faculties and powers, and right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) from the Eightfold Path, as well as the factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) among the seven factors of enlightenment, are subsumed under these. Next, the four right efforts (*samyak-pradhāna*), along with diligence (*vīrya*) among the faculties and powers, and right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*) from the Eightfold Path, as well as the factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) among the seven factors of enlightenment, are subsumed under these.

Next, the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhi-pāda*), along with concentration (*samādhi*) among the faculties and powers, right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) from the Eightfold Path, and the factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) among the seven factors of enlightenment, are subsumed under these. Finally, mindfulness (*smṛti*) among the faculties and powers, along with right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) from the Eightfold Path, and the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) among the seven factors of enlightenment, are subsumed under these.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* establishes that there are only ten substantial entities (*dravya*), because the three—vocal action, livelihood, and [the others]—are subsumed within the category of morality (*śīla*). Since this is the logical conclusion, if one were to add "desire" and "mind," it would become thirteen, which would contradict the correct tenet of its own school.

Consequently, the master of the *Abhidharmakośa* provides the following formal explanation: "That which is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is called 'supernormal power' (*ṛddhi*); that which sustains the karma produced by desire and so forth is called 'basis' (*pāda*). [Commentary:

"The fruit of meditative concentration" refers to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth. These fruits of concentration are the "supernormal power," which arises from the "bases. The bases are themselves the meditative concentrations; they are the foundation of the supernormal power.
Because they are "feet," they are called *ṛddhipāda* (bases of supernatural power). These feet arise from four causes, such as desire (*chanda*), and are therefore further designated as "four.

This name is established based on the cause, the fruit, and the essential nature and function [of these powers]. (Now, examining the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, it states that because there are four feet of the supernormal, they are called *ṛddhipāda*.

What was Vasubandhu’s intention in falsely refuting this and causing [the text] to be augmented? The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are: first, the faculty of faith; second, the faculty of diligence; third, the faculty of mindfulness; fourth, the faculty of concentration; fifth, the faculty of wisdom.
The faculties (*indriya*). The powers (*bala*) are likewise. These five are each one among the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) as their essential nature.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Because they can produce roots of goodness, they are called 'faculties' (*indriya*); because they can destroy unwholesome dharmas, they are called 'powers' (*bala*). Others say: "That which has increased functional efficacy is a faculty;

that which cannot be overcome is power. The seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*): first, the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*); second, the factor of investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

The factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are: (3) the enlightenment factor of energy, (4) the enlightenment factor of joy, (5) the enlightenment factor of tranquility, (6) the enlightenment factor of concentration, and (7) the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
Among these, the investigation of phenomena has wisdom as its essence; "wholesome" refers to the faculty of joy; and "equanimity" refers to the equanimity of formation (saṃskāra-upekṣā).

The remaining four are as [explained] for the names. Among the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), each one constitutes its own essence. The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) constitute ultimate awakening;

because they take seven factors as their divisions, they are called "factors of awakening" (*bodhyaṅga*). Alternatively, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that accords with reality takes seven factors as its divisions, and is thus called the "seven factors of awakening.
Among these, the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is both awakening itself and a factor of awakening; the other six are factors of awakening but not awakening itself. (8)
The factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are: first, right view; second, right intention; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right effort;
seventh, right mindfulness; and eighth, right concentration. Among these, the essence of right view is wisdom (*prajñā*). Right intention is applied thought (*vitarka*).

The three—speech, action, and livelihood—are concomitants that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*). The remaining three are as their names imply. Within the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), these three factors constitute...

The essence [of the path] is that which traverses and penetrates; therefore, it is called the "path" (*mārga*). Because it consists of eight divisions, it is named the "eightfold path" (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*).
Right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is both the path and a limb of the path; the remaining seven are limbs of the path but not the path itself. Question:

It was previously stated that *samādhi* is both the "divine" (*deva*) and the "foot" (*pāda*), whereas desire and the others are only "feet" and not the "divine. To this, the following defense is offered: The divine has four feet; therefore, [desire and the others] are not included among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

Regarding the mind of desire: among the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), it should also be understood that the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*) is both enlightenment itself and a factor; whereas the remaining six, such as mindfulness (*smṛti*), are factors but not enlightenment itself.

Consequently, mindfulness and the others should likewise not be subsumed under the category of enlightenment-factors. This same principle should be understood to apply to the refutation regarding the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

Answer: The discernment of dharmas is already included within the enumeration of mindfulness and the other factors. When their characteristics are combined, they constitute seven. However, the essence of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is not included among the four, such as desire (*chanda*), and so forth. Therefore, [the objection does not hold].

This is not an exception. *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 96, asks: "For what reason are the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) taught first, and so on, up to the eightfold path factors (*mārgāṅga*) taught last?

It answers: "Because they follow the sequence of elegant literary composition. Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness possess a consistently superior power and function from the stage of a beginner (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*) up to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*); therefore, they are taught first. [Next are] the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*)."

From the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) up to the "Knowledge of Exhaustion and Non-arising" (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*), their functional power is always superior; therefore, they are explained next. The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are superior from the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) up to the Knowledge of Exhaustion and Non-arising.

The five faculties (*indriya*) are superior from the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*) up to the Knowledge of Exhaustion and Non-arising. The five powers (*bala*) are superior from the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) up to the Knowledge of Exhaustion and Non-arising.

Among the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), those of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) are superior. Among the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), those of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are superior. Question: Why?

Therefore, among the eight factors of the path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*), the path-factors are preeminent within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); and among the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), the enlightenment-factors are preeminent within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Answer: The meaning of "path-factor" (*mārgāṅga*) is the sense of seeking and proceeding. Because the path of seeing is swift and does not transgress the intended goal, it accords with the sense of seeking and proceeding;

therefore, the eight path-factors are preeminent within the path of seeing. The meaning of "enlightenment-factor" (*bodhyaṅga*) is the sense of awakening. Because the path of cultivation consists of nine grades and involves repeated awakening, it accords [with this sense].

Because it has the meaning of awakening, the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are preeminent within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). According to the Mahāyāna, the factors of enlightenment pertain to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) pertain to the path of cultivation.
For now, however, we rely on the Hīnayāna; as for why the Vinaya text mentions only the seven factors of enlightenment, it cites the preeminent to reveal the subordinate.

Since it is clearly known that there are also the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), the treatise summarizes them as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

Regarding the distinction between "reaching" in the first half [of the verse], this means that the second phrase is combined with the first phrase, and the first phrase is combined with what precedes it.
This is the second phrase.
Regarding the "five warriors" in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, it is the twenty-fifth discourse.
As for "dying without regard for one's life," the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 119) states: "Having already received the prātimokṣa vows..."
One should engage in correct mental attention and discernment, such that one would not intentionally commit an offense even for the sake of one's life.

This is illustrated by the account of a bhikṣu who went for alms at the house of a jeweler in the past. The bhikṣu’s robes were red, and their reflection made the jewels appear like pieces of meat. A goose, thinking them to be meat, swallowed the jewels.

When the jeweler found his food missing, he gave the jewels to the bhikṣu. After the two had exchanged thanks and the bhikṣu had departed, the jeweler later realized some jewels were missing and set out in pursuit.
Upon examining the site, blood flowed everywhere. A goose came to feed on the blood; the man, filled with rage, struck the goose and killed it.
The bhikṣu then requested to see whether the goose was dead or alive. The man immediately rebuked him, saying, "First attend to recovering the pearls;

what business is it of yours regarding the goose? The bhikṣu insisted, but the man said it was already dead. The bhikṣu told him, "The goose has swallowed your pearls. The man then took up a knife and cut [the goose open].
Inside the belly of the goose, he found the lost pearl. Filled with shame and remorse, he said to the Bhikṣu, "Venerable One, why did you not show me this sooner?
The Bhikṣu replied, "I have received the prohibitive precepts; rather than give up my own life, I would never harm an ant's egg.
Had I shown it to you earlier, I certainly would have harmed the goose. How can one who does not protect living beings be called a keeper of the precepts?"

It is just like the case of Aṅgulimāla. Chongyun (崇雲) states: "Various masters collectively cite the verse beginning with 'The Great Śramaṇa remains stationed,' yet they do so because they fail to understand the meaning of the text.
This matter is found in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle thirty-one. Now, examining this closely, the location where it is taught is not a single passage;
one should carefully guard one's speech so as not to wound the feelings of others. For instance, in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*... [text continues].
Third, it is said: Aṅgulimāla wished to kill his mother. The Buddha, knowing he was ready for deliverance, manifested as a bhikṣu and walked along beside him.
When Aṅgulimāla saw the Buddha, he abandoned his mother and rushed toward him, intending to kill the Buddha. Seeing him approaching, the Buddha walked slowly away.
Although Aṅgulimāla ran with all his might, he could not catch up. He then called out from afar, "Bhikṣu, wait a moment! The Buddha replied from a distance, "I..."
"I always abide in myself, yet you do not abide; therefore I ask: how is it that you abide while I do not?

The Buddha said, "My faculties are tranquil and stilled, and I have attained mastery. You, however, have followed an evil teacher and received instructions that lead to the transformation and fluctuation of your mind."
He was not permitted to remain stationary; consequently, he conceived faith. The Buddha immediately ordained him, and he attained the state of an Arhat.
At that time, when the people of the country heard the sound of Aṅgulimāla, they were all struck with terror. Humans and animals who were pregnant were so terrified that they could not give birth.
At that time, there was a bird that was unable to hatch its young. The Buddha commanded Aṅgulimāla to go and speak these truthful words:
"Since my birth, I have not killed a single person. Aṅgulimāla said to the Buddha, "I have killed many; how can you say I have not killed? The Buddha told him: [The rest of the discourse follows.]
Within the Noble Dharma, this constitutes being "newly born. Aṅgulimāla, having received these instructions, went and spoke; as soon as he did so, they were all established in peace and security.
Regarding the lack of shame (*ahrīkya*), it is explained at length in the *Vibhāṣā* (Treatise on the Great Exposition), fascicle 34, in the section on the "Absence of Shame" (*Anapatrāpya-nirdeśa*).
Regarding the conclusion of the third section, which may be understood: the Master of the Vinaya says that the elicitation of the supreme fruit takes precepts as its cause.

To open the way and guide [practitioners], he has entrusted these words with full detail. Although his virtue transcends all worldly calculation, it cannot be discussed extensively in its peripheral aspects.
Since the brief exposition has already served its purpose, he says, "it has been explained. Now, about to provide a formal exposition, he again pays homage to the Great Master.

From here on follows the prose section (*gadya*). Master Śīla initially judged this to still be an exhortation to faith. His explanation ranges from the beginning up to the phrase "How [will it be] in future ages?
In this, the Master of Vinaya expresses reverence and praise, exhorting faithful practice. Within this, the preceding verses clarify that which is the medicine suited to the capacity of the listener;
the subsequent prose clarifies the capacity of the listener for whom the medicine is intended. That is to say, his intention was that the verses contain only the Vinaya itself.
The Master [Buddhabhadra] directly exhorts by citing the Buddha’s words regarding the future; this is the Vinaya Master’s citation of evidence for the purpose of exhortation.

If he did not cite such evidence, the bhikṣus of the final age might think: "When the Buddha was in the world, his superior faculties were in resonance with those of his time, so the teaching could be practiced.
Now that it is the final age, it need not necessarily be practiced. Therefore, the Buddha spoke of the future, saying: "What will be in the future? This means:
This is the Master of the Vinaya. He cites the origin story (*nidāna*) of the subsequent rule regarding the "sudden gift of robes" (*akālacīvara*) as evidence for this. Someone might say:

"If this were not part of the 'Exhortation to Believe' (*śraddhā-deśanā*) section, then since the Buddha had already established the first rule during the five years [following his enlightenment], and Ānanda was born on the day he attained the Path, he would have been only five years old at the time the rule was established. How then could the name of Ānanda appear in the origin story? Therefore, it is..."

To cite scriptural evidence, there is no such contradiction. Deng says: "If Ānanda were not present during the occasion for the establishment of the prohibitions, then since Ānanda was also present at the origin of the precept against killing, how would you explain his presence during the winter of the six-year period? Now, examining these various explanations, there is no need to labor over disputes.
When comparing different schools, how can the dates be fixed? For instance, regarding the day of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there are already two [different accounts].

The difference between the eighth month and the [lunar] month is a matter of divergent theories among various schools that cannot be reconciled at once. We shall instead rely on the preceding chapter;
it is established as the "Introductory Chapter on the Arousing [of Resolve]."
Regarding the greatness of the merit of this treatise: its fourth fascicle states, "Greatness means that from small causes there arise great results;
therefore, the merit of the Bhikṣu-saṃgha is exceedingly great. Regarding the greatness of the fruit: the treatise states, "Even the least among them attains the stage of Srotāpanna.
Regarding the greatness of the assembly: the treatise states, "Because a great multitude of five hundred has gathered. Since these are the words of the treatise, some people...
Refutation. One must examine this carefully (the following sections concerning citations from the *Abhidharmadīpa* are mostly from its fourth fascicle).
Regarding the multiple meanings in the *Dīpa*, among these four meanings, the first two appear to accord with the treatise (*śāstra*), whereas the latter two do not.
This is not the main text of the treatise. If one were to speak of it in general terms, neither would be the main text.
As for the claim that "Bimbi" refers to the water's edge and so forth, this interpretation is incorrect; the treatise states directly: "The continent of Bimbi-mandala."
"This is the *liàn-mù* tree. Therefore, one should not provide a separate explanation for the character 'bīn' (賓).

However, upon consulting the Sanskrit manuscript, it says *bīn-zhōu-mán-tuó-luó*; this is indeed a Sanskrit term, and thus it cannot be explained using Chinese characters. Thus said the Tripiṭaka Master Jing."
As for the statement in the *Saddarśana-śāstra* (Shan jian lun) that it is a *liàn* tree, this is also not the case. It resembles a *liàn* tree, but it is not actually a *liàn*.

As for the term *śramaṇa*, the fourth fascicle of the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Seeing) states: "A *śramaṇa* is one who subdues the afflictions (*kleśa*); it is also said that he repels the afflictions;
and it is further called 'one who has stilled the mind' (*xi xin*). (This is easily understood.)
"The first five [attributes] benefit oneself, while the latter five benefit others. This claim by Chong (Cheng) is a hasty interpretation that fails to understand the essential meaning of the school;

what significance does it have? It is not the case that the former do not benefit others, nor that the latter do not benefit oneself. Furthermore, regarding those who cite the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* as proof, this interpretation is also incorrect.
That treatise explains each of the ten titles one by one, and only after concluding does it state in general: "Benefiting oneself and benefiting others. This is the meaning.

Now, examining that treatise, specifically within the tenth chapter on the Ten Titles in its first fascicle, it explains the five titles of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, and Sugata in succession.

Regarding the statement "Nāgārjuna’s Treatise says": the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 27, states, "Because he has come by way of the path of reality, he is called the Tathāgata.

"One who does not abide in the path" means that because they practice the six perfections, they do not abide in the extreme of emptiness; because they have realized the nature of emptiness, they do not abide in the extreme of existence.
Therefore, it is said that they "do not abide."

Regarding the eleven kinds of emptiness, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle sixteen, states: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, beginningless emptiness, essential emptiness, non-existence emptiness, ultimate truth emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, and great emptiness.
These are explained in sequence according to that sūtra; they are not recorded here.

Therefore, when it is said that "extinction is ultimate," the intended meaning is as follows: since the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that one "attains all meanings," this is precisely the meaning of "ultimate extinction.
Why is it called "ultimate extinction"? Because it is the Great Parinirvāṇa; hence, it is called "ultimate extinction. According to the third fascicle of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*:
"Because one attains all meanings; because it is the unsurpassed field of merit; because it is worthy of offerings."

Therefore, he is named "Arhat" (the Worthy One). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 38, states: "Having already attained all meanings that ought to be attained, he is worthy of being the unsurpassed field of merit for the world;

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* further states: "Because [this state] is supreme, most excellent, and ultimate, and never regresses, it is called Sugata."

Those who advance to exhaust the ultimate source proceed through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), severing the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) as they progress, until they reach the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*),

That is to say, all wholesome phenomena lead to what is beneficial; if they are unwholesome...

Dharmas that lead away from what is beneficial are "non-meaningful. If they are neutral (avyākṛta) dharmas, they lead away from neither. The term "present obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) refers to meaning, while "subsequent obscuration" refers to benefit.
The original sound is *Bhagavān*; here, it is translated according to its meaning as "World-Honored One" (*Shizun*). It is also called *Bhagavat*, which is a phonetic variation of the same term.

The three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*)—which in the new sūtras and śāstras are termed the "three demonstrations" (*tripradarśana*)—are so called because "demonstration" (*pradarśana*) carries the meaning of a "wheel" (*cakra*), as they are capable of crushing and destroying the obstacles of affliction.
First is the demonstration of miraculous power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), which is the supernormal knowledge of the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*) among the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Second is the demonstration of mind-reading (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*), which is the supernormal knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*). Third is the demonstration of instruction (*anuśāsana-prātihārya*), which is the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*).
Regarding the three wheels: the attainment of supernormal powers and their realization constitutes the demonstration through miraculous power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*).

The constant preaching of the true Dharma and so forth constitutes the demonstration through instruction (*anuśāsanīprātihārya*). In preaching the Dharma, one must necessarily observe the faculties and dispositions of those [listeners].

This also reveals the presence of the "instruction by mind" (*cetokhila*) among the supernormal powers; this will be further explained in the *Upasampadā-khandhaka* below. The *Dṛṣṭi-śāstra* offers many interpretations:

This refers to a mind that grasps at signs). It should also be paid homage to.
