This differs from the ancient interpretation: according to the ancient masters, when one acquires the dharma, the act of building a dwelling constitutes "observance through action" (*kriyā-saṃvara*), whereas the complete cessation of such action constitutes "restraint" (*saṃvara*).

It is maintained that when one makes a formal commitment to abandon evil, there is no agent within the intermediate state; thus, the wholesome manifest and unmanifest form (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*) not subsumed under the vows is termed "intermediate" (*madhyama*).
For example, if one has committed to prostrating to the Buddha for a hundred days but remains indolent during the process, there is no fault in the absence of the unmanifest form.

Because it is destroyed, it is also called "cessation-maintenance" (*śīla-dhāraṇa*). This cessation-maintenance can enter into the other three [categories]. Regarding the two types of maintenance, there are two transgressions;
where there are two transgressions, there are not two types of maintenance. These two types of maintenance serve to block the two transgressions.

As for what is called "pervasive," it means that a transgression possesses the quality of persisting over a long duration; therefore, it can enter into the midst of the other three positions. This is what is meant by naming the essence of the transgression.

This constitutes its sense of "pervasion" (tong). The meaning of "pervasion" in this context differs from that in other gates. In other gates, "pervasion" means being able to encompass others; thus it is called pervasion.
In this gate, the meaning of "pervasion" is being able to enter into others; thus it is called pervasion.

Regarding the five benefits of the *kaṣāya* (robe) of virtue that are free from transgression: staying overnight apart from one's robe, accepting invitations separately, eating in a group apart from others, entering a village without having made an announcement, and not declaring the surplus robe as pure (*pariśuddhi*).

Among these, the single precept concerning eating in a group apart from others constitutes the essence of "restraint through cessation" (*saṃvara-śīla*). The remaining [benefits] are all "dual-restraint" (*ubhaya-śīla*).

Because one has received the robe, during the five months [of the rainy season], there are five benefits and two types of restraint; since their essence is constantly pure, each and every restraint is included.

The remaining three cases also fall under the category of "intermediate" (madhya). Regarding the separation from one's robes, staff, and water-strainer: having obtained the necessary authorization (*dharmaprāpti*), one may act; this constitutes "dual maintenance" (*ubhayadhāraṇa*).

It is generally said that within this section on the gates of individual karma, there are likewise four sets of four, totaling sixteen cases. For instance, when wishing to fetch water, first placing the water-strainer [in its position] constitutes the "expedient means for abiding in observance" (*sthiti-dhāraṇopāya*).

On the day of the *poṣadha* ceremony, one does not wish to attend the assembly and remains hidden in one's room, manifesting the appearance of being absent (this is the preparatory act for an offense of abstention).

Knowing that music will be performed, one should come and lock the doors of the *śrāmaṇeras* (this is the preparatory act for maintaining discipline). Nowadays, as in the case of forest hermitages (*araṇya*), one first instructs the donors not to come and deliver food. One sets out implements for killing (this is the preparatory act for an offense of commission).
Subsequently, among the four types of conduct, one performs any one of these acts; whichever of those four is ultimately carried out constitutes the full offense.
Question: Within this section on the gates of penetration and obstruction, the third part clarifies the establishment of the characteristics of one's own karma.
Regarding the advancement toward [the goal] and the disciplinary teachings concerning that advancement, it cites the *Dīrgha-āgama* and other texts to explain their meaning.

Within the *vinaya* (teachings of restraint), there is also the citation of "long-term departure" (*dīrgha-viveka*). What is the distinction between these two teachings? Answer: They differ in their conceptual meaning and also in the breadth or narrowness of their essence (*svabhāva*).

That is to say, in relation to the *vinaya*, that which pertains to the side of exertion and progress is termed "advancement" (*abhyudgama*), while that which pertains to the side of preventing transgressions is termed "teaching of restraint.

Regarding the breadth or narrowness of their essence: if it is a teaching of restraint, it is necessarily an instance of advancement; such is the case with the sphere of training in the precepts (*śīla-śikṣā*). However, there are...
Advancement (*abhyudgama*) is not the teaching of restraint; rather, it is the sphere of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Therefore, one should know that within the context of the "gate of accomplishment" (*siddhi-dvāra*), although the teaching of advancement is not explicitly mentioned, with respect to the aspect of exhortation and progress, it nonetheless possesses the meaning of advancement. This is another interpretation.
It cannot be recorded [as such].
This is because, although the four modes of conduct beginning with "stopping" (sthāpana) are distinct, each possesses both manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*).

At the time of preparatory effort (*prayoga*), one necessarily possesses manifest action. Regarding non-manifest action, it is not yet finalized; however, once it reaches its own final completion, it then possesses both.

As for the types [of precepts], teaching others to reach ultimate completion involves only non-action (*avijñapti*). Therefore, it does not hinder teaching others to act; this is called "stopping action" (*nirodha-karma*).
Regarding the fact that the prohibitive teachings (*pratiṣedha-śikṣā*) are likewise: the meaning of stopping oneself from acting is easy to understand.

Teaching others to stop acting means teaching others to abstain from killing, which is precisely teaching others to practice "stopping and maintaining" (*nirodha-dhāraṇa*). Teaching others not to engage in disputes means teaching others to observe the rules of decorum (*śayanāsana-vinaya*).

"Complete. Reciting the precepts and so forth constitutes teaching others to practice observance (*dhāraṇa*). Teaching others to take life constitutes teaching others to commit transgression (*āpatti*).

As for the ability to repent of both types of conduct within a single article of the code, it is because both the abstention and the action are extinguished by means of the same remedy; therefore, it is said to be "universal" (*sāmānya*).
Furthermore, among these [two categories], the "observance and maintenance" (asamādāna-śīla) also generally encompasses the other three; this refers to their inclusion within it.

Moreover, within the "prescriptive teachings" (vidhi-śāsana), there are also those that pertain to "progressive advancement," such as the recitation of the precepts (*prātimokṣa*) and the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts); although these are prescriptive teachings, they are also...
There is the sense of active engagement (*pravṛtti*).

Regarding the statement that "abstinence (*nivṛtti*) applies to all thirteen [categories], while performance (*pravṛtti*) is restricted to a small portion of the first category": this means that when one remains in a state of dignified composure without acting, one maintains all thirteen [rules] through abstinence.

Even if one were to perform an action, such as requesting the formal procedure (*jñapti*) for the first category, although it is nominally "performance through maintenance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*), because it does not exceed the prescribed measure, it is still considered "abstinence through maintenance" (*nivṛtti-dhāraṇa*). Half.
Since only half [of the training] is practiced, it is called "partial. The remainder may be understood by analogy.
However, the phrase "excluding the ear-tying precept" refers to those above this point, spoken in relation to the Great Monks (bhikṣus).

Regarding the eighteen [cases] such as "keeping a retinue" (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), they are analyzed in detail below in the sixth commentary. In the *Bhikṣuṇī-Prāyaścittika*, it says: there is one case where the precepts are identical, which is "not listening.
There are seventeen cases where they are not identical. Regarding the five ways of receiving ordination, these are: taking the robe but not granting the ordination; not granting the precepts;

furthermore, receiving [the precepts] but not granting the two years [of training]; not granting the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*) and the fundamental rule (*mūla-dharma*); and [granting them] after an overnight stay.

There are five ways of violating respect: namely, not requesting [instruction], not listening, not allowing [others] to act as they please, not relying on the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), and not performing prostrations (these five aforementioned types).

Not resolving disputes for others, not entering the *varṣā*, not departing when expelled, not receiving others through the two methods [of instruction and exhortation], not attending to the illnesses of those living with one, not departing at the conclusion of the *varṣā*, and not escorting a courtesan for five or six *yojanas* (these latter items, combined, total eighteen). In summary:
The verse says: Taking the year, the six, receiving, receiving; invitation, listening, prostration, at-will, peace; peace, peace, extinction, expulsion, inclusion;
ear-disease, sixty *yojanas*.

Even if a nun commits [an offense] that may be categorized under the first category [of the *pārājika*], she must nonetheless confess it if she has concealed another’s grave offense; therefore, this is the practice.
"Hold fast.
Furthermore, regarding the fourth 'not having': begging for ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, milk, curd, and so forth—one must strictly refrain from these."

Regarding the point that [the classification] based on the existence of the offense is also to be understood as narrow: this means that within the category of "existence," there are only eighteen factors such as "hearing" and so forth.

As for the former interpretation that the object of the transgression is broad while its substance is narrow: the locus where an offense arises is termed the "object" (ālambana), namely the three [types of objects].
This refers to the study [of the precepts]. The offense produced by this is termed the "substance" (the essence), which is precisely ignorance due to a lack of study.
As for those who commit only the fifth [offense], in reality, within the fifth category of offenses, there is no such *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
This is also its narrow aspect. It is the same as in the previous section on the gates of prohibitive precepts (*śikṣāpada*): the scope of the transgression of abstaining (*virati*) is narrow.

Regarding the statement that "the sphere of the transgression and the substance of the transgression are both broad," the locus where an offense arises is called the "sphere" (*viṣaya*), which refers to the training in the precepts (*śīla-śikṣā*).
That which is the offense arising there is called the "substance" (*bhāva*), which refers to all acts of commission and transgression, such as sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth. Now...
The Master’s intention is as follows: the nature of the object (*ālambana*) is also explained as before.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that one must not listen with one ear while distracted, if one fails to listen attentively, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;

on top of that, if there is additionally ignorance (*ajñāna*), one incurs a *duṣkṛta*. Jue says: "Because of not listening previously, one subsequently fails to comprehend the conditions; this is termed 'ignorance'."
This very lack of knowledge constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. The Master of the South Mountain (Nanshan) explains that there are two types of lack of knowledge:

first, a fundamental lack of knowledge resulting from not having studied at all, for which one incurs a *pāyattika* offense; second, a lack of knowledge resulting from having previously recited [the precepts] but now being unable to recall them, for which one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
Now, examining this in detail, it is best to follow the explanation provided in the present chapter (*to that point where it is not subsumed under the prohibitions, one should analyze*).

This is like the case of one who is ignorant. That is to say, it is as if there were a person who studies diligently, yet because his capacity is insufficient to understand, he does not comprehend despite his application;
in such a case, he incurs no offense.

Regarding the two *duṣkṛta* offenses of "not learning" and "lack of knowledge": these refer to the two *duṣkṛtas* of not having studied and being ignorant. [The opponent argues: "One is ignorant because one does not understand the object;

thus, ignorance is further established. Now, we examine this and find it is not so. If one were to never direct the mind toward an object for the rest of one's life, could one truly avoid committing an offense for the rest of one's life?
Our explanation is as follows: within a state of mind that does not understand, one incurs ignorance for each and every precept one violates. Therefore, the text below states: [insert citation].

I say that such a person is deluded regarding the offenses from *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* down to *durbhāṣita*. Furthermore, to revere one’s teacher while failing to understand the limits [of the teachings] based on specific conditions is unreasonable.

The phrase "remaining silent while falsely concealing" means that, for example, one might pass through the appearance of dawn, or pass through questioning regarding conditions, yet fail to comprehend them as they truly are;
this is the meaning of the text.
Regarding the term "cessation of offenses," this refers to the *pratiṣedha-dharma* (prohibitory rule). Regarding "performing an action," this refers to such acts as constructing a dwelling.
There are also cases of a single prohibitory rule, such as ceasing the recitation of the precepts; or a single action, such as sitting down to receive food.
Regarding the method of cessation according to the object (*vastu-vasthāpana*): it is as in the case of keeping an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*).

If, with respect to the objects, there are both simultaneous and non-simultaneous cases—for instance, when the extra robe has reached ten days and the plastering of the dwelling is completed at the same time—one incurs the offense simultaneously;
therefore, this is called "simultaneous. The "non-simultaneous" case can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the delimitation of the categories of the formulated teachings (prajñapti-śāsana) based on preceding matters, this refers to instances such as the accumulation of extra robes until the end of the period.

As for distinguishing them by way of their doctrinal principles (artha-mūla), those within the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma that correspond to the fundamental intent of the Vinaya discipline are all termed "doctrinal principles."
The "precept of guarding the sense faculties" (indriya-saṃvara-śīla) is precisely the restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara).

Regarding the next two types of inner-worldly ordinary persons (antarapudgala), these refer to the inner-worldly ordinary persons who must give rise to the skillful means of the wholesome roots such as "heat" (uṣmagata) and so forth.

However, the present precept of guarding the sense faculties begins with the stage of initial practice (ādikarmika) and culminates in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa); it is not restricted solely to the inner-worldly ordinary persons. If that concentration and that precept give rise to "heat" and the other stages, it may be so.
Regarding the term "inner ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*): if one lacks the stages such as *uṣmagata*, even if one attains the four *dhyānas*, one is still not an inner ordinary person.
As for the first two fruits being based on the *anāgamya-dhyāna*: this refers to the first and second fruits, because they definitely cannot attain the fundamental four *dhyānas*;
therefore, they must rely on the *anāgamya-dhyāna* to give rise to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). The old name for this is *anāgamya-dhyāna*; the new name is *anāgāmya*.

"Reaching concentration" refers to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the first dhyāna. It is generally termed "future dhyāna" (*anāgamyadhyāna*), which refers to the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
This is truly laughable (as recorded above in the first fascicle; one should understand this characteristic).

"There are four virtuous deeds that result in evil fruits. First, reciting and chanting the sūtras for the sake of surpassing others. Second, upholding the prohibitive precepts for the sake of gain and offerings.

Third, practicing giving for the sake of making others one's subordinates (meaning to cause others to become dependent upon oneself). Fourth, [practicing] the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception..."

Because one dwells [in these states], one fixes the mind in contemplation (meaning that one seeks only the ultimate rewards of the mundane world). These four wholesome deeds result in evil retributions. Among these four matters:
This is the meaning of the second proof cited in the commentary).
Regarding the first path: the three types of karmic activity that lead to enlightenment are all the first path, because they transcend the world.

As for the statement that "upholding [the Dharma] differs in a thousand ways," this should be distinguished according to the time period, as explained in the second fascicle of the *Dharmatrāta-śāsana* (The Storehouse of the Transmission of the Dharma).
Śāṇakavāsin, having ordained Upagupta and conferred the precepts upon him, saw that he had attained the path of an Arhat. He then thought to himself:
"At this moment, I have beheld the Dharma-body, yet I have not yet seen the body of the Tathāgata with its marks and signs. Having reflected thus, a deep [aspiration] arose within him.
On the occasion of the funeral rites, there was an elderly bhikṣuṇī who was one hundred and twenty years old and had once seen the Tathāgata.
Upagupta, knowing that she had seen the Buddha, wished to go to her dwelling. When the bhikṣuṇī heard that he was coming, she immediately filled a bowl with oil and placed it behind a door-panel.
As Upagupta entered, he spilled several drops of the oil; they then exchanged greetings and comforted one another. Afterward—
She sat down and asked, "Sister, when the World-Honored One was alive, what was the conduct and deportment of the bhikṣus?

The bhikṣuṇī replied, "In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks were coarse and violent; though they entered this room, they never left me so much as a single drop of oil.
Yet you, Virtuous One, are noble and eminent, whom the people of the world call the 'Buddha without the marks' (animitta-buddha). Nevertheless, you have entered..."
"In my room, I have discarded several drops of oil. Judging by this, those who lived during the Buddha's time must certainly have been extraordinary.
Upon hearing this, Kātyāyanīputra felt profound shame. The nun said, "Venerable sir, you should not feel ashamed of yourself. As the Buddha said:
'After my parinirvāṇa, the beings of the first day will be superior to those of the second day; after the third day, they will indeed become inferior. Thus it is."

As time passed, wholesome dharmas gradually declined. How much more so now, O Great Virtuous One, when one is a hundred years removed from the Buddha; though it may not conform to the formal deportment, why should it be considered strange?

Next, one should consider the location: among the three continents of the human realm, there is the Prātimokṣa precept, and the southern continent is the most excellent because the intensity of its aversion to worldly passions is greatest;
the other continents may be understood by analogy.
If a student of the Dharma intentionally violates the precepts, they will certainly not commit the five transgressions of sexual misconduct, theft, killing, lying, or drinking alcohol;
as for the remaining precepts, violations may occur. Nevertheless, such a person will certainly not fall into the three evil realms.
Regarding those who commit grave offenses, as stated in the sixty-fifth verse of the *Nyāyānusāra*: "The fool who commits even a small transgression follows after evil;

"The two types of cessation are both such" refers to the two cessations of the prohibitive teachings (*vinaya*) and of spiritual cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

For the text states: "If one acts intentionally, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). Answer: It says "not intentional," meaning that [the fault applies] only when there is no intention. It does not apply to those who act unintentionally.
Regarding "acting in deliberate violation of the holy teaching" and so forth, these are explained as in the chapter.

As for "the remainderless" and "the remainder": the *pārājika* (defeat) is "remainderless" according to the teaching; the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) and so forth are "with remainder" according to the teaching.

The four types of incorrigible natures are "remainderless," while the remaining natures are "with remainder. Whether an offense is subject to confession or not is explained according to this principle. To call it "different" is to mean "altered."

Regarding the "Increment by Two" (Dvika-vardhana) section consisting of twenty-one items: taking the *pārājika* (defeat) as the first term and proceeding through the remaining six categories (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*, etc.), this forms six phrases.

The eighth verse says: "The five offenses can be confessed," etc. Three lines are as explained in the chapter. The fourth line says:
"The Tathāgata distinguishes the fetters" (this is Śāriputra’s question; Upāli answers this verse).

Regarding the phrase "understanding the minor, the non-minor that follows the minor, and so forth," this refers to the [following] point. That treatise states: The verse says: "Understanding the minor, the non-minor that follows the minor, and the non-minor precepts.
The commentary explains: The Buddha, the World-Honored One, established the precepts in three categories. The "minor precepts" refer to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and so forth.
The "precepts that follow the minor" refer to those incomplete offenses (*aniyata* or *sthūlātyaya*). The "non-minor precepts" refer to the four *pārājika* offenses. Furthermore...
Regarding "the minor precepts" (*kṣudrā-śikṣā*): among all the precepts, these are those that are natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) which are minor. Regarding "those that are not minor precepts":

among all the precepts, these are the proscribed offenses (*prajñapti-sāvadya*), such as the four *pārājika* rules (as stated in the treatise). In the *Mingliao shu* (Commentary on the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*), the preceding phrase "furthermore" (*punar-aparam*) is explained as follows:

there are offenses with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*) that are not extremely grave; therefore, they are called "minor. Within the category of the five classes of offenses (*pañca-varga-āpatti*), the three preliminary efforts (*prayoga*) are all accomplished as the fundamental [offenses].

Furthermore, because they accord with the root [offenses], yet are minor in nature, they are called "minor" (āpatti-dukkaṭa); because pārājika is extremely grave, it is called "not minor. The subsequent commentary explains:

"In this context, we do not discuss the preliminary or the consummation; rather, among the various precepts, if there is a remainder or a middling offense that constitutes a natural transgression (prakṛti-sāvadya), it is all termed 'minor.
If it is a proscribed transgression (prajñapti-sāvadya), it is termed 'minor-concomitant' (anvaya-dukaṭa). Pārājika is 'not minor.'"

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the treatise: it includes [the acts of] shedding blood and causing a schism in the Saṃgha. These too are extremely grave and are not minor matters; therefore, the term "and so forth" is used.
Regarding the four [offenses] among the prohibited dharmas, the *Pratiṣedha-kaṇḍa* states: breaking the precepts, breaking the view, breaking proper conduct, and breaking right livelihood—these four.
Regarding false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*): as stated in the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, the *Vinayottaragrantha*, and the *Vinayavibhaṅga*.
The commentary on the tenth fascicle explains: "The *Vinayavibhaṅga* refers to a light state of mind; it concerns fragmented, frivolous, and joking untruths (the source for this is unknown).

Regarding the mind: while the other two [offenses] are committed without a specific mental state, killing, stealing, and lying constitute offenses when one possesses a conscious mind—meaning that one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy or self-congratulation.

Alternatively, regarding the distinct entities such as *śīla* (restraint) and *dhāraṇa* (observance): if one were to rely on the sequential gradation of the grammatical formulation, they would be identical to the "trainable" (*śikṣamāṇā*) forms of observance (*dhāraṇa*), and logically there would be no need to establish nine distinct categories.
However, because they involve the general engagement with the activity of constructing a dwelling for others, their characteristics are distinct.
Therefore, it is discussed separately again. Since there are these two paths of meaning, the word "or" is used.

If one does not fundamentally recognize [the object], then there is no minor grade (*mṛdu-pakṣa*); this refers to, for example, killing someone while fundamentally mistaking them for a tree stump, or perhaps performing an excessive act while conceiving the thought that it is not excessive.
Because of this fundamental delusion, there is no minor grade. Regarding the third point, "not recognizing the matter," it is even more subtle.

The commentator says: If a person who is deluded perceives a human being as a non-human being and so forth, there is still the auspiciousness of the subsequent mind, which likewise constitutes nine cases.

Even if one takes a member of the same realm of existence (*gati*) as an object of a different category, although this is a case of not recognizing the actual entity, it is equivalent in meaning to recognizing the entity because the perception of a "human" is not deficient.
Regarding the fact that the minds of persons vary in their duration: when a state of doubt repeatedly takes the original object as its focus, it is termed "long," and this is judged to be grave.
When the conceptualizing mind exclusively abandons the original object to take up another, it is termed "short," and this is judged to be light.

If one were to further add twelve *duṣkṛta* offenses for the two full sets of three phrases—such as "doubting" or "not recognizing" regarding a matter that ought to be learned—this would be logically untenable.

If the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) establishes his position based on the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), then when one doubts the nature of the object or fails to recognize it due to mental confusion and error, the transgression is not under one's own control;
how, then, could one be charged with the offense of "lack of training" or "ignorance"? Consider, for example, a person who has lost their way.

Regarding the case of mistaking a person for a tree stump, or forming the notion that something is not excessive when it actually exceeds the limit, how could such delusions be eliminated merely through study?

For what reason, then, is "lack of learning and ignorance" established as a fault? Furthermore, the Commentary itself states: "The three doubts and three non-recognitions regarding the matter are called 'expedient means.'"
How could one incur the offense of violating the rules of conduct through lack of training and ignorance? Therefore, this is illogical.

Regarding the three doubts and three forms of non-recognition concerning offenses, these are considered ultimate [offenses]; that is to say, both lack of training and ignorance constitute resultant offenses.
Regarding the twelve types of delusion that likewise reach their ultimate limit: there are twelve kinds of objects that can be learned;
ignorance regarding them constitutes one offense, while knowledge regarding them likewise constitutes two offenses when directed toward the same object. This is the ultimate limit.

If one suspects that an action exceeds the prescribed measure but does not recognize it as such, this is called a "concordant offense of *duṣkṛta*. This clarifies the principle of "abstaining from what should be maintained" (*śīla-virati*).

How could there be an exceeding of the measure? Because exceeding the measure constitutes an active transgression (*āpatti*). Answer: It is because in reality there was no exceeding, yet the mind suspected an exceeding; therefore, there is no fault.
However, upon examining the context, it appears the character "not" (*pu*) has been omitted. One should instead say, "an action that does not exceed the measure."

This is double the measure of the previous two. In the former case, regarding the transgression of what should not be learned—the cessation of what is prohibited—one only incurs the two *duṣkṛta* offenses based on the side of the fault (*āpatti-pakṣa*), namely those of "not having learned" and "ignorance.
Now, in this present case, which concerns what should be learned, one does not merely incur these two *duṣkṛta* offenses based on the fault;

rather, one also incurs them based on the objective matter (*vastu*). Thus, by doubling the two types of *duṣkṛta* offenses from the previous category—namely "not having learned" and "ignorance"—it totals twenty-four.

Regarding "those not explicitly stated in the categories of objects and perceptions": this refers to the fact that in the Vinaya texts, the categories of objects and perceptions for all the precepts comprise six permutations;
however, the sixth permutation is omitted from the text for brevity.

Regarding the success or failure of distributing lower robes according to the rules: In the *Cīvaravastu*, if there is a monk and one perceives him as such, the distribution of the robe is invalid, and one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If there is a monk but one has doubt regarding him, the distribution of the robe is invalid, and one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If there is a monk but one does not perceive him as such, the distribution of the robe is invalid, but there is no offense.
If there is no monk and one does not perceive a monk, the distribution of the robe is valid, and one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is none [further].

If there is a monk, but he has doubts [regarding the distribution], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense when the distribution is completed. If there is no monk, yet one perceives there is a monk, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense when the distribution is completed.

If there is no monk and one perceives there is no monk, the distribution is completed without fault. The six cases regarding the acceptance of robes (*cīvara*) are also like this (accepting the robe from another is called "receiving"; the formal ritual procedure is called "distributing").

Regarding those who perform ritual procedures (*vidhi*), they directly take the seven *vitasti* (spans) and so forth as their object. Even if there is doubt as to whether the object is recognized or unrecognized, it constitutes the three mental states directed toward the object.

Regarding the explanation of "accomplishment" and "non-accomplishment," this is explained in relation to the mind; for example, perceiving what has not been designated as designated—this [perception] does not originally exist.

Regarding the Dharma, one says that the Dharma is accomplished. Furthermore, one does not resolve the doubt as to whether the Dharma is originally non-existent while the mind suspects whether the Dharma is accomplished or not.
Whether it be its cessation or its activity, this present "activity-and-maintenance" (作持) serves as a formal grammatical structure; in principle, they are identical.
Regarding the stages of *śīla* (observance) and *dhāraṇa* (maintaining), both rely upon the nine modes of conduct (*navavidha-vṛtti*). However, when one examines the texts, their application differs.

As previously established for the correspondence between *śīla-dhāraṇa* and its contraries (*āpatti*), each phrase is equivalent. Yet, regarding the contraries of *kriyā-dhāraṇa* (active observance), one takes the sixth mode of the "object and perception" (*ālambana-saṃjñā*) as the basis for the transgression.
If one does not make such a distinction, it remains unclear whether this constitutes *śīla-dhāraṇa* or [its contrary].
Since it must be analyzed in this way, it differs from what preceded.

Furthermore, the distinction made regarding the commission of an offense (*āpatti*) also does not resemble the former case. That is to say, previously one analyzed whether the commission and the offense were established or not, and whether there was doubt regarding the cause, the fruit, or the transgression;
whereas here, one analyzes whether there is doubt regarding the measurement of the object (*pramāṇa*) in relation to the performance of the observance (*dhāraṇā*). Therefore, they differ.

They are not the same. For instance, regarding those who frequently assert what is incorrect, this has been extensively analyzed in the *Kuangpi shu* (Commentary on the Expansion). To briefly cite examples:

as in the *Cengzheng jiandu* (Section on Disputes over Cities), there are forty-nine permutations based on the seven classes of offenses (*sapta-varga*) when one makes an illegal self-accusation. For example, claiming "I have not committed a *pārājika*" [when one has].

The transgressions of the seven classes (*saptāpatti*) constitute seven propositions. This continues up to the case where one who has not committed an offense falsely claims to have committed the seven classes;

this results in forty-nine propositions (seven times seven). If one acts according to the Dharma, and having actually committed the seven classes, explains each accordingly, these constitute the seven propositions;
conversely, there are forty-nine propositions.
Regarding the statement that "the essential characteristics [of the precepts] are hidden beneath the text concerning offenses":

this refers to the fact that within the explanation of the characteristics of each individual precept, one first clarifies how the five classes of practitioners incur an offense, and only then states the conditions for non-offense, such as being asleep and lacking awareness. This passage now points to those specific texts.

The general explanation is now concluded. Now, to examine it in detail: there were no lack of objections and difficulties in what preceded; however, following the sequence of the commentaries, I have not had the leisure for extensive discussion.
Nevertheless, as for the establishment and refutation [of views], they have already been analyzed at length in the "Refutation of Deluded Records" (*Pomiji*), so I shall cease here for now.

Regarding the formation of the three poisons through the ten categories of meaning: in various sūtras and śāstras, the arising and formation [of offenses] are all analyzed in relation to the ten unwholesome courses of action (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*).

However, in this Vinaya, one cannot fully encompass [the analysis] by directly analyzing only four precepts; rather, it analyzes the reality [of offenses] by relying upon the ten unwholesome courses of action.

Regarding their establishment: in this Vinaya, the four precepts are directly distinguished in accordance with what is taught in the Sūtras and Śāstras. Killing refers strictly to the intentional taking of life; stealing is fulfilled only when the value reaches five *māṣakas*;

sexual misconduct is prohibited in all its forms; and lying refers only to a grave falsehood. Therefore, they are not entirely identical [to the Sūtra and Śāstra formulations]. The texts of the Sūtras and Śāstras are numerous.

It cannot be recounted in full; let us briefly indicate the texts. As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (116), the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra* (6), the *Abhidharma-samaya-pradīpikā-śāstra* (10, Chapter on the Ten Unwholesome Paths of Action), the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (4), and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (16)—all of these provide extensive explanations.
To state the general principle: the preparatory acts (*prayoga*) all arise from the three poisons, while their completion (*niṣṭhā*) is not fixed. As the verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
It is said: Killing, harsh speech, and malice are all ultimately rooted in hatred (*dveṣa*). Theft, sexual misconduct, and covetousness are all ultimately rooted in greed (*lobha*).

False view is ultimately rooted in delusion (*moha*). This is accepted as being derived from the [remaining] three [roots]. (This is the same in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* as in the *Abhidharmakośa*). Regarding the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there are two explanations.
The former explanation is the same as the *Kośa*. The latter explanation states: "There are those who say that sexual misconduct is not fixed; that is to say, if one intends..."

Regarding the statement that "only when emission occurs and impurity is discharged is the path of action (karmapatha) fully established," the three [unwholesome roots] serve as the preliminary application (*prayoga*), and by means of these three, it reaches completion.

For all remaining paths of action, the three likewise serve as the preliminary application, and through them they reach completion (as stated in the treatise). The extensive explanations in various texts concerning these three preliminary applications need not be recorded here in detail.

However, when comparing the offenses defined by the Vinaya rules with the offenses of the paths of action, they may be either broader or narrower, as in the case of the "breaking of delusion" (*mohabhañjana*).
Commentary: That has already been explained in brief, so it will not be recounted here at length.

Regarding the statement that "to understand through the words of another that one has not yet committed [an offense] necessarily relies upon the person of another," although the various masters of antiquity shared the same teacher’s interpretation, upon examining their underlying intent, it appears they did not fully grasp the meaning.
For instance, the fourth fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (*Cittaviveka*) states: "The autonomous one..."

To kill a *ṛṣi* because one dislikes his speech is said to be [an instance of] verbal and mental karma; however, this is not so regarding its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because the intrinsic natures of the various types of karma differ.
Thus, the matter is not ultimately established (as stated in the treatise). Ancient commentators have explained that this refutes the position of an external opponent.

This refers to the assertion of the *Tattvasiddhi* masters that bodily and vocal actions are distinct karmas, each capable of producing the other. The master of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* then refutes this, stating:
"Because their natures as karma differ. That is to say, the three branches of the body and the four transgressions of speech have distinct natures.

Furthermore, the phrase "the matter is not ultimate" is an explanation intended to resolve the objection of the *Tattvasiddhi* master. The objection states: "If the natures of the karmas are distinct..."
Regarding the claim that taking life is exclusively a physical action (*kāyakarman*): for example, when a powerful lord speaks words that a *ṛṣi* finds detestable, is this not killing by speech?
Answer: At the time when the verbal action and the mental aversion occur, the person has not yet died; therefore, it is said that the act is not consummated.
This refers to cases such as when one employs protective spirits or deities to strike and kill an entire nation, or when one employs others to strike and kill.

The preceding scholar (in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, fascicle 12, states: "When a non-Buddhist seer gives rise to a single thought of anger, he immediately incurs the karma of *ayoguru*"). If that is so, when a lion kills an animal, yet when one utters a roar to kill a person, how can there be bodily karma?
Answer: Because his physical strength is great, the person dies only after the roar is uttered. If that is so, when a deep river is falsely claimed to be shallow, how can there be bodily karma?
Answer: At the time of the deception, the person has not yet died; it requires the person's body to actually enter the water [for the karma to be established].
[Question: It is also bodily action (*kāyakarman*). If that is so, when there is the transgression of enchanting an object, how can there be bodily action? [Answer:

According to the judgment of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is because it is sustained by the power of the incantation. [Question: If that is so, when one utters a false speech accompanied by gestures, would this not constitute bodily action?

[Answer: It is merely a vocal action (*vākkarman*) dependent on another; since one utters words such as "sit" or "stand," it is not bodily action. Master Tong says: "If that is so, what about writing a letter and placing it for another?"

Upon seeing [the truth], one is immediately liberated; how, then, could there be any vocal karma? Thus we know that logical reasoning leads to this conclusion, which constitutes one school of thought. Now, examining this closely:
because the masters hold that the bodily karma of the protective deity (yakṣa) is thus, they consequently judge it to be the bodily karma of the immortal (ṛṣi).

If this were so, the immortal would incur the sin of taking life committed by another. How could it be permissible for one to receive the fruit of an action performed by another? False speech manifests...

[The opponent’s] argument based on analogy—that judging my verbal karma by another’s oral recitation is likewise refuted—is now to be further explained according to the intention of the Sarvāstivādins:
they maintain that mental karma cannot kill a living being, and one does not judge one’s own bodily karma by means of another’s body. This is what is meant by "bodily karma."
It certainly does not depend on anything else to be able to sever life. Now, the seer’s mind was filled with rage, and thus he merely made use of another's body;
therefore, we know that mental action (*manas-karman*) cannot directly commit killing. If this were so, the seer would incur the transgression of taking life.

Since it was not a mental action, and you do not allow for the determination of karma through another's body, by what means would he receive the retribution for killing? Answer: Since mental action is not directly accomplished as killing...

Because it is a matter of fact, one must rely on another’s body; by taking the killing of that other as a condition, the non-informative (*avijñapti*) within the body of the seer is produced, which constitutes bodily action (*kāyakarman*).

Similarly, when a deep river is misrepresented as shallow, one relies on the previous person entering [the water] and dying as a condition to produce the non-informative of bodily action within my own body.

Even down to the case of creating a written document and placing it with another, since this does not immediately enable the other to hear it with their ears, we know that [it does not exist] within the body.
One personally utters the words, yet relies on another’s recitation as a condition for understanding; thereby, an unmanifest vocal karma (*vāg-avijñapti*) arises within one’s own continuum.

Thus, it is said that the nature of the karma is distinct. This differs from the Mahāyāna, the Sautrāntika, and the *Tattvasiddhi*, all of which maintain that mental indignation alone can directly constitute the act of killing, without requiring a separate manifest or unmanifest expression within the body.
Therefore, they are not the same. Consequently, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* refutes [this view].
The Lesser Commentary (Xiǎozōng) says: "If places such as Daṇḍaka are empty [of sentient beings], how can it be that through the anger of a seer, mental punishment constitutes a great sin?
How, then, could this [emptiness] come to be? [Commentary: The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha states: "Daṇḍaka is the name of a king. At that time, there was a seer."
Before he had attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), he already had a wife whose countenance was so upright and beautiful that she was peerless in the world.
Later, when that seer had finally attained the five supernormal powers, he practiced meditation in the mountains and would always have his wife prepare food and drink for him.
King Tālajaṅgha entered the mountains for recreation and encountered the seer’s wife. He asked, “Who is this? A courtier replied, “This is the seer’s wife. The king—
The seer remarked, "Since I have already abandoned desire, what use have I for a wife? He then entered the palace.
When it was time for the seer to eat, he looked for food but could not find any; when he asked where it had gone, someone replied, "The king has taken her away.
The seer went before the king and demanded his wife back, but the king refused to return her, saying, "What use do you have for keeping a wife? The seer said, "I have her to provide for me."
Regarding food and drink, [the king] did not return it for two or three times. The rishi then became enraged. During that very night, he caused sand and stones to rain down.
The king and all the people of the country died completely; in an instant, this land became a forest and mountains. In such places as these, there is emptiness and stillness with no people.
Since this resulted from the rishi’s anger, is it not the case that mental karma constitutes the act of taking life? Therefore, the Sarvāstivādins say: "One must guard..."

The sages, ghosts, and spirits revere the sages. Knowing that [the killing] was done out of resentment, they immediately refuted it, saying: "If the intention constitutes a great sin, how then can this [act] be established as such?
This means to say: Formerly, there was an elder named Upāli who came to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha asked him: "Have you ever heard that the Daṇḍaka Forest is entirely empty and silent? The elder replied: [He did not.]
The Buddha said, "This was due to the resentment of the rishi. The Buddha further said, "Elder, you should know that among the three types of punishment, mental punishment is the greatest;
by a single thought, one may kill an entire nation. How could physical action possibly involve such a great sin?

Since the Buddha cited this case of the *Taṇḍaka* grove to establish that mental punishment is primary, how can you, a Sarvāstivādin, insist on saying that the rishi was killed by a protective deity or spirit?

Question: Since the Mahāyāna and other schools admit that killing can be accomplished through the mental faculty (*manas*), why does the Sūtra state that the karmic path of killing is always categorized as bodily action (*kāyakarman*)?
Answer: This is determined based on the majority of cases; it means that most killings are carried out by the body, not that mental action (*manaskarman*) is incapable of killing.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "Vocal action or bodily movement... (up to)... because the natures of the actions differ [they are distinct], yet they are also [driven by] the mind" (this is the answer in the fourth fascicle of the *Cittaviveka*). It continues further: "Adhering to the body..."

Regarding verbal action (meaning that each case is individually attached and there is no room for confusion): if a nun instructs a monk regarding a seminal emission, the nun incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if a nun herself causes a seminal emission, the nun incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the fourfold set of offenses and non-offenses: one’s own offense while another’s is not (such as instructing another to buy or sell);

another’s offense while one’s own is not (such as having a *bhikṣuṇī* wash an old garment); both are in offense (such as killing or stealing); and neither is in offense (such as performing the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhakti* rite and commanding another). Regarding the two sets of fourfold cases:

the agent is grave while the object is light (when admonishing Devadatta, if one has performed the formal motion (*jñapti*) but the view has not yet arisen, and one instructs him not to abandon it, Devadatta incurs a *duṣkṛta*, while the instructor incurs a *sthūlātyaya*); the object is grave while the agent is light (instructing another to commit sexual misconduct); and both are grave (both possess...).

Regarding the intent to steal (and stealing an amount reaching five *māṣakas*): both may be light offenses. There are cases where the one who strikes the ground commits an offense while the one being instructed does not (the instructor has the intent to steal, while the instructed person lacks the intent).

The second case (the opposite of the above, where the one acting on their own is the subject) involves both committing the offense (both possess the intent to steal) or both not committing the offense (both lack the intent to steal).
Furthermore, regarding the fact that celestial objects would be useless for humans: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 38, states:

"The robes of the Four Heavenly Kings weigh two *liang*; those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven weigh one *liang*; those of the Yāma Heaven weigh eighteen *zhu*; those of the Tuṣita Heaven weigh twelve *zhu*;

those of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven weigh six *zhu*; and those of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven weigh three *zhu*. As for the robes of the gods in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), they possess no quality of weight. (Commentary: Since...
It is entirely trivial; therefore, it is of no use.
Regarding "one who, over time, gives rise to anger," this refers to the passage below concerning Nāgapāla’s intimidation of the World-Honored One.

Regarding "stealing from or deceiving animals both incurs a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅)," according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (鼻奈耶), stealing from an animal constitutes a *pārājika* (夷); this [present] *vinaya* does not contain such a rule.

The scriptural text also states that one should be able to transform [oneself]. To steal [a transformed object] constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense; not transforming it is auspicious. Regarding the deception of animals, there is explicit clarity in the Vinaya:

transforming oneself constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense; not transforming oneself is auspicious. Since the meaning of the text is thus established, there is no need for further inquiry or response within this chapter.

Regarding the "two superior [offenses] for those with much wisdom," these refer to humans and non-humans. "Cutting off life" and "seizing property" correspond respectively to *pārājika* and *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the four stages of offenses for animals: *pārājika* refers to sexual misconduct; *sthūlātyaya* refers to killing;
and *duṣkṛta* refers to theft and deception (according to the *Tattvārtha*, theft and deception constitute *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta*).

Regarding the objection that self-generosity and self-avarice are mutually contradictory: one might raise a difficult question, saying, "If there is no such thing as 'self-stealing,' then there should likewise be no such thing as 'self-avarice.

Why, then, does the Sūtra state: 'Furthermore, there are people in the world who do not provide for themselves with food or clothing; when their lives end, they shall fall [into evil realms]'? Answer: The fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) or stealing (*steya*) is defined in terms of harming others.
If that is so, since there is indeed "self-avarice," there should also be "self-generosity" (*ātma-dāna*). Answer: Generosity (*dāna*) is based on the relinquishing of wealth.
It is permissible to subsume these under a single category.
However, if one discusses distinct objects (*visaya*), everything below is restricted to offenses committed based on distinct objects.

Regarding cases where both specific (*niyata*) and general (*aniyata*) [intentions] result in a light offense, "specific" and "general" refer to a single substance; this has already been distinguished above. As for the meaning of "error," it is distinct.
This is also as explained above.
Regarding the "Dharma" mentioned in the context of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) and error, it is as explained in the relevant chapter. However, [the author] respectfully cites *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* 51:
"Question: Is there any case where a bhikṣu falsely claims to have attained the noble Dharma (*āryadharma*) and incurs the offense of pārājika? Answer: Yes. A bhikṣu..."
Regarding the *Śrāmaṇera-śikṣāpada-vibhaṅga* (or *Vinaya-saṃgraha*), the eighth fascicle: when intending to speak of a *srotāpanna*, one mistakenly speaks of a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Now, it is granted that if one intends to refer to this noble one but erroneously refers to that noble one, it logically constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
How could such an error possibly constitute a *pārājika*? Furthermore, examining the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, it differs from the ten recensions; thus, in the *Sudarsana*, [this case is] the twelfth.
It is said: "Intending to speak of the first dhyāna, one utters the words, 'I enter the second dhyāna. This is an error of speech. The same applies to the third and fourth dhyānas;

in all such cases, one commits a grave offense (and the relinquishing of the precepts is likewise). Regarding the ten types of sevenfold cases concerning those who have not received full ordination leaving their place:
this refers to relinquishing the precepts and thereby becoming one who is no longer fully ordained.
Although the objects of anger are twofold—namely, sentient and non-sentient beings—the offenses incurred are not equal.
If one kills a non-sentient being, one does not commit a *pārājika* offense; however, regarding the path of sentient beings, one must further explain it as a *sthūlātyaya*.

Deception must involve a conscious mind; if the object lacks consciousness, it does not constitute a false deception. Chong says: "This interpretation was made because [the author] did not understand the textual basis.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that each of the three [unwholesome paths of action] constitutes the preliminary application (*prayoga*).

How, then, can it be said that a covetous mind arises prior to the first two? Now, examining this closely: this [text] refers to the four precepts, while that [treatise] relies on the paths of action (*karmapatha*). Furthermore, it is based on what is most prominent. What inconsistency is there?
Regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*), this has already been extensively refuted in the "Record on Dispelling Delusions.

As for the phrase "the winter portion of the fifth year" and so forth, this follows the lunar system of the Western Regions (India), in which the dark fortnight comes first and the bright fortnight follows.
Calculated according to this, it is only after the middle of the first month that it truly constitutes the first month.

This differs from the fifty-two precepts, which permit one to remain in secular life without severing ties with one’s own wife and do not prohibit sexual misconduct entirely; therefore, it is placed third.

If that were so, the śrāmaṇera should be subject to the first prohibition since he must completely abstain from sexual misconduct. Answer: The śrāmaṇera is young and sexual desire has not yet arisen in him generally.

Just as a small child lacks compassion and thus killing is the primary offense for them, this [rule] is stated according to the initial circumstances, as in the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya* regarding Rāhula.
One leaves the household life; at the age of nine, one receives the precepts—this is the way of a śrāmaṇera.

To this day, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, various śrāmaṇeras in the Western Regions gather flowers to make offerings to Rāhula. Now, examining the *Adbhutadharma-paryāya Sūtra*, it is indeed a sūtra.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the sequential order, it may be explained further: the successive precepts were established to prevent the transgressions of those preceding them.

Regarding killing and sexual misconduct, both share the same primary meaning. The initial [definitions] for sexual misconduct, killing, slander, and strife are identical to the previous explanation regarding "seizing"; this can be understood through reflection.

The śramaṇa Bin of the State-Protecting Practice Hall at Mount Song composed this treatise on the Six Gates of the Meaning of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā.
Regarding śamatha and vipaśyanā: śamatha is concentration (samādhi), and vipaśyanā is wisdom (prajñā).

According to the Satyasiddhi school, the two dharmas of śamatha and vipaśyanā do not occur simultaneously. However, according to the Sarvāstivāda and the Mahāyāna schools, they exist within a single moment of mind.
Within this, the two dharmas of śamatha and vipaśyanā are in simultaneous correspondence. Although they are permitted to occur simultaneously, there are times when the power of śamatha is stronger;
it is then designated as "vipaśyanā," such as in the formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti). Alternatively, there are times when the power of vipaśyanā is stronger at that same moment;

it is then called "vipaśyanā," such as in the preparatory stage (anāgamya-dhyāna). Or, there are times when śamatha and vipaśyanā proceed in equal balance, such as in the four fundamental dhyānas (maula-dhyāna).

Regarding the allocation [of these categories] now: that which is "to be recollected" corresponds to the gate of *śamatha* (calm abiding); that which is "to be contemplated" and "to be abandoned" corresponds to the gate of *vipaśyanā* (insight).
