Regarding the phrase "the five [coins] are reduced because the subject and object have already been distinguished": this refers to the four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) such as when, according to the aforementioned preparatory instruction, one seeks to reduce the amount to less than five coins but obtains more than five coins, and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "according to the *Dṛṣṭiparyāya*, there are four types of bhikṣus," this is explained in the tenth fascicle of that treatise.

If a person has a separate agent, one might say that the karma of instructing another is not established as being identical to one's own action. If, however, they share the same agent, it is logically necessary to investigate and discern the matter.
Regarding the point that "the principles of the fundamental precepts are exhausted": this refers to the fundamental precept against stealing clarifying the offense of *mī* (stealing).

As for the three types of direct doubt (*zhíyí*): these are when one actually perceives a human being, yet toward another who is a non-human or an animal without an owner, one gives rise to three kinds of direct doubt—doubting whether it is a human or a non-human, doubting whether it is a human or an animal, and doubting whether it is a human or ownerless.

There are three types of "transverse doubts" (*hengyi*). When an object is actually a person or a thing, one gives rise to three transverse doubts: first, doubting that it is not a person but an animal;
second, doubting that it is not a person but ownerless; third, doubting that it is an animal but ownerless (this is the interpretation of Master Yun).

The Master of the Commentary (Sūzhǔ) does not maintain this position, as there is no textual authority for it. If that were so, the statement in the *Chapters* (Zhāng) that "only three [categories] would also be unreasonable" would follow.
That is to say, within this text, the "with owner" and "without owner" cases stand in direct opposition, forming only two pairs;
if one were to open them into three sentences, one would have to admit they are a pairing of heavy and light offenses, which would also contradict this text.

Regarding the statement: "The gates of 'with-owner' and 'without-owner' offenses, and the gates of the five degrees of gravity and lightness—how can these be explained together? Now, upon careful examination:

even within the category of "with-owner," the distinction between persons and non-persons constitutes a gate of gravity and lightness; likewise, the "five" and "exceeding five" are also gates of gravity and lightness. These must certainly not be combined.
For instance, if it is said that one perceives a person as the owner and steals five coins—or exceeds that—how could this be [treated as a single case]?

This is termed "valuable object with the perception of a valuable object. Having finished explaining this combined case, if one were to compose a text stating: "a human being with the perception of a non-human being;

a valuable object with the perception of a non-valuable object—this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*," then this would indeed be a correct combination. Therefore, I shall now directly refute [your position].

Within the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), the Vinaya texts consistently state "five transgressions" and "five coins. How can you then claim, "a valuable object with the perception of a valuable object"?
The combined explanation has already been concluded. However, Chong also states that the claim "the combined explanation has already been concluded" is unreasonable.

Regarding the sections on transgression and non-transgression, as well as the sections on gravity and lightness, these correspond to the meaning of the "perception of the object" (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*) as found in the third commentary below.

Regarding the Master’s question concerning the conditions [for an offense] where one must distinguish between "single" and "double" based on the presence of a mental error (*cittāntara*) regarding heavy objects:

I now examine this. Why is it that one need only distinguish between "single" and "double" when the conditions are deficient? One should also state the full conditions as: "a heavy object with the perception of it being a heavy object.

If one asks about the conditions, I now examine this further: why is it that one need only distinguish them when the conditions are deficient? To say "a heavy object with the perception of it not being a heavy object," or "doubt," is precisely what constitutes a mental error. It is not otherwise.
The thought of multiple layers refers to the single omission; the absence of doubt regarding the multiple layers refers to the double omission.
However, as for why the aforementioned conditions do not establish the thought of a heavy object, the meaning has been explained above.
Regarding the general phrase of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*: the *Prātimokṣa* states, "Not to give," which is the first phrase.

Therefore, within the explanation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), this general phrase is expanded into the three [categories], specifically the latter three sets of three phrases. Since these are spoken together in the *Prātimokṣa*, it is referred to as "objects" (*vastu*).
*Shizongyi Ji*, Fascicle Four, Part One;
*Shizongyi Ji*, Fascicle Four, Part Two.

From below, in the third section of the commentary on the conclusion of the establishment of the precepts (*zhijie jing zhong*), regarding "the superior retribution of the human realm" (*renqu bao sheng*), Cheng (Chong) says: "The retribution of the human realm..."
"Superior. It should be the same for devas as well.
This applies even to those whose physical form and mind are both vessels for receiving the Path. Chong says: "Devas possess the Noble Path; killing them does not constitute a pārājika offense.

In the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), one may incur a pārājika offense, but this is not due to being a vessel for the Path. Hermaphrodites and those with dual sexual organs are difficult cases to classify, similar to those in the Northern Continent. Now, let us examine this chapter in detail.

First, among these, non-animals are excluded. Therefore, it is said that "the retribution of the human realm is superior" (this reveals the superiority of the fruit). It is "invoked by wholesome causes" (this reveals the superiority of the cause).

If that were so, one would incur the offense of *pārājika* by killing a superior being such as a deva; to eliminate this doubt, it is specified that both physical form and mind must be the vessels for receiving the Path.

First, there are those whose physical form belongs to the category of beings capable of being vessels for the Path, such as those in Uttarakuru, yet the minds of the people in that continent [are not].
First, because they are excessively heedless, their minds are not suitable vessels. Second, their minds are of the class that are vessels for the Path, like eunuchs and others;

they exist only in Jambudvīpa. Although those in Jambudvīpa possess a mind that is a vessel for the Path due to their intense weariness with existence, because their physical form is deficient, their bodies are not vessels.

Third, both [mind and body] are of the class that are vessels for the Path, such as those possessing complete faculties within the three continents. Regarding these three propositions, [the verse says] "killing."
They are all likewise excluded from the category of those fit for the Path (*mārga-bhājana*). Thus, one selects the various devas; they are all alike unfit vessels for the Path.
Their forms are not human, and their minds lack both revulsion and aspiration. Therefore, both their form and mind render them unfit vessels for the Path.

By this same principle, it is further clarified that those in the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) as well as eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and others are all included within the category of those fit for the Path. Thus, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha-śāstra*, fascicle three, asks: "For what reason..."
If one kills a human being, one incurs a *pārājika* offense. The answer is that humans possess the three refuges and the five precepts;

it is among humans that the *prātimokṣa* is attained and the four fruits of the śramaṇa are realized. Furthermore, it is among humans that Buddhas and *pratyekabuddhas* exhaust their outflows (*āsrava*). For these reasons, killing a human being [constitutes a grave offense].

One incurs a *pārājika* offense; it cannot be committed through other paths. According to this treatise, it is thus revealed that the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) and those such as eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) belong to the category of those who possess the "vessel" (*bhājanatva*) for the path.

Question: Since gods are capable of entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*), why are they not considered to possess the vessel for the path? Answer: Because gods lack the *prātimokṣa* vows, and because they attain the path with little frequency.
Therefore, the treatise states that the fruits of the śramaṇa are mostly attained among human beings. Furthermore, the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) reside in humans.

[This applies] to the three continents; it is absent in the northern continent because [killing] is difficult there. Since the definition is established by subsuming the characteristics of its category, the proposed thesis is not improperly formed (though the inhabitants of the northern continent have a fixed lifespan of one thousand years and cannot be killed, as they do not suffer untimely death).
Regarding "one should destroy the four equanimities" (*catasraḥ samatāḥ*): the old name was "four equanimities," while the new name is "four immeasurables" (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).

This refers to practicing the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] by taking all sentient beings as an equal object; thus they are called the "four equanimities. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, fascicle 29, states:
"They are called 'immeasurable' because they take immeasurable sentient beings as their object, they draw forth immeasurable merit, and they produce immeasurable fruits. Chong says:
These four immeasurables are accomplished because one is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); they are not attained by those still in training (*śaikṣa*) or by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

How, then, can it be said that one "should destroy the fourfold equanimity"? Furthermore, regarding the accomplishment of the fourfold equanimity: a person who commits killing certainly does not possess the fourfold equanimity.

Now, upon careful examination, it is logically consistent that one who possesses the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) certainly does not commit killing; yet, to say that only those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) can destroy these four immeasurables contradicts both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.
To begin with, regarding the contradiction with the Hīnayāna teachings: the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 81, states:

"All noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within our own Dharma possess both types [of attainment]—namely, those previously attained and those not yet attained. Ordinary beings outside our Dharma possess only those previously attained."

(External dharmas refer to ordinary beings; that is, non-Buddhists). Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 44, states: "Briefly, there are three kinds of bodhisattvas who cultivate the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

The first is the immeasurable with sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambana-apramāṇa*), which universally takes the ten directions as its object and abides in unerring resolve regarding sentient beings."

One cultivates a mind accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in two ways: first, the immeasurable with phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana-apramāṇa*), wherein one dwells in the superior and most excellent intention (*adhyāśaya*) of the mere perception of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñāmātra*), correctly contemplating that sentient beings exist only as conventional designations of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*).
Second, the objectless immeasurable (*anālambana-apramāṇa*), wherein one further distances oneself from conceptualization regarding phenomena and cultivates a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.

It should be understood that the three—compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—are likewise [of these two types]. Regarding the object of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*):
That which is shared with non-Buddhists is called "having dharmas as its object" (*dharmālambana*); this is shared with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, but not with non-Buddhists.

That which is "without an object" (*anālambana*) is not shared with anyone at all. Based on these passages, since even non-Buddhists can attain it, how could it be said that only those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) achieve it?

Regarding the explanation of the name: in Sanskrit it is called *manuṣyavadha*, which is translated as "killing a human. Chong says: "The old interpretation is not correct. My current interpretation is as follows:
'life' (*sheng*) refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*); to sever it so that it does not continue is called 'killing life. Alternatively, furthermore, 'life'..."

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is called "birth," and its interruption is called "killing. Now, examining the twentieth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is explained for King Ajātaśatru that the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) is called "birth.
Since King Ajātaśatru was a layman, [the Buddha] did not contradict conventional designations (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), referring to the vital breath as "birth."
The Blessed One, following the principle of conventional discourse (*anuvartana-yukti*), spoke thus:

"If one were to rely on ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), since the vital winds do not circulate while the sense faculties (*indriya*) of the *kalala* and other stages are not yet fully developed, would these not be called 'born'? If they are not called 'born,' then killing them would entail no fault."
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (Vol. 26) states that when the sense faculties (*indriya*) of the *kalala* and other stages are not yet fully developed, the vital winds (*prāṇavāyu*) do not circulate.

Furthermore, it states that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is what is called "a living being. This contradicts the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (Vol. 118), in the section on the taking of life (*vadha-nirdeśa*), which says: Question:
Since there are only phenomena (*dharma*) and no sentient beings (*sattva*), how can there be the offense of killing? Venerable Vasumitra replied:
Just as there are no sentient beings yet one has the perception of sentient beings, so too, although there are no sentient beings, there is the offense of killing a living being.

(The commentary states: The meaning of the question is: Since there are only the five aggregates—form and so forth—which are real dharmas, and no separate sentient being exists, why is there the offense of killing?
Vasumitra’s answer means: Although there is no sentient being, foolish worldlings [perceive] the five...

Within the aggregates (skandhas), there is the notion of a "sentient being" (sattva). Now, by mistakenly claiming that one has killed a living being when one has merely severed the five aggregates, one incurs the sin of killing.

Since the treatise explicitly states that no sentient being exists, for what reason do you dogmatically insist that a real sentient being exists? Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools agree that there is no sentient being.

If you insist that such a being exists, you are identical to the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika); how could this conform to correct reasoning? Therefore, one should follow the commentary and sever [the aggregates].

Regarding the objective sphere of the aggregates (*skandha-viṣaya*), this is taken as the correct view. Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 118, states: "Question: Among the various aggregates, which aggregate can be killed?
Some say it is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), because the aggregate of form can be struck by weapons or clubs.

Others say it is all five aggregates, because when the aggregate of form is destroyed, the remaining four aggregates also cease to function; just as when a jar is broken, the milk and other contents are also lost. Thus...
The fifth fascicle of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* cited in the Commentary (*Śū*) is also clear evidence.

However, according to the Sarvāstivāda and Mahāyāna schools, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are fully present within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). As for the Satyasiddhi school, the "Chapter on the Ten Unwholesome Paths of Action" states:

"Within the continuity of the five aggregates, there is that which is called a 'sentient being. To destroy this continuity is what is termed 'killing'" (the above is the scriptural passage). This refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Perception, feeling, and formations arise in succession. By destroying the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), one causes consciousness, perception, and the others not to arise in continuity;
this is called "killing.
Regarding the use of the object as the name [of the action], the Vinaya Master Tong said: "Killing" is the action (*prayoga*), while "living being" is the object (*viṣaya*).

Regarding the statement "if according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*," there is no such text in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. This is actually stated in the fifth chapter of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* and in the section on "Taking Life" (*prāṇātipāta*) within the *Vibhāṣā*.

As for the phrase "the four aggregates and the life-faculty" (*catur-skandha-jīvitendriya*), in reality, the life-faculty is subsumed within the four aggregates; what purpose, then, does the word "and" (*ca*) serve? Now...

The intended meaning is that life-force (*jīvitendriya*) is the sovereign of the retribution; therefore, it is mentioned separately (the life-faculty is included within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind).
Regarding the point that present suffering caused by weapons and staves prevents future continuity, this accords with the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.

The two explanations are one and the same. One interpretation in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "One kills future aggregates. Question: Since the future has not yet arrived, how can it be killed?
Answer: That [future state] abides in the present; by obstructing the various conditions for its conjunction in the future, it is called "killing.

Because one obstructs the causes and conditions for the arising of the conjunction of other aggregates, one incurs the sin of killing. Another says: "One kills present and future aggregates. Question: Regarding the future...
It may be so. [The present] does not abide; even if one were not to kill it, it would naturally cease. How, then, can there be killing? The answer is:
to sever its power and function is what is called "killing. Although the preceding present aggregates cease without abiding, they cannot prevent the subsequent aggregates from continuing.
However, when the present aggregates cease without abiding, they are able to cause the subsequent aggregates not to continue.
Therefore, one also incurs the offense of killing in the present life (the above is from the treatise). The two explanations in the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* are likewise the same;

however, regarding the statement that the retribution for killing consists only of matter (*rūpa*) and not the other three [aggregates], this is a general discussion of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

In total, there are four types of the indeterminate: first, maturation (*vipāka*, formerly called "retribution"); second, the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*); third, craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*); and fourth, transformation (*nairmāṇika*, also called "supernormal transformation"). These four are... [incomplete source].
The *vijñapti* (informative action) pertains to both the aggregate of matter (*rūpa*) and the aggregate of mind (*citta*). It does not induce one another; rather, each arises independently.

This differs from the other three [non-informative actions], which produce the matter of body and speech. For instance, when an internal mind of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*) arises and induces bodily action, one walks along a path;

therefore, it is named after its function as "deportment" (*airyāpathika*). Furthermore, a mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*) induces bodily and vocal actions, such as carving or painting on walls and other surfaces.
Craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*). Therefore, craftsmanship is named after its basis. Furthermore, the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) gives rise to bodily and vocal karma;

it ascends into the air, undergoes transformations, and transforms metals and stones, etc., and is thus called "transformation. All four [types of neutral mind] are exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

They give rise only to manifest action (*vijñapti-karma*) and do not produce non-manifest action (*avijñapti-karma*). (In the Mahāyāna, maturation [karma] is exclusively indeterminate; deportment and craftsmanship are common to all three natures; transformation is common to both wholesome and indeterminate. This differs from the Hīnayāna school.)

Regarding the statement that "only the tangible object (spraṣṭavya) is karmically acquired (aupacayika), while the other eight are not": among the twelve bases (āyatana), ten types of form-bases (rūpāyatana)—with sound excluded—are all derived from retribution (vipākaja).
It has already been clarified above that sound is not a dharma of retribution. However, as the verse in the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states:
This refers to the fact that only the four external elements (dhātus) can act as the instrument of cutting (*chettṛ*) and the object of cutting (*chedya*).

Therefore, one should know that among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), the four external objects—visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility—are all subject to being killed (*vadhyamāna*), not merely the object of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*).

This is because the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and other texts state that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) can be touched by swords and clubs; thus, they identify tangibility itself as the object of killing. However, that which is touched by swords and clubs refers to their [respective] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

The obstruction [of the senses] against [objects] is called "contact" (sparśa); it does not necessarily refer to the objective field of contact (spraṣṭavya). (Alternatively, because the objective field of contact can give rise to cognition, it may be designated specifically as the objective field of contact.)
Regarding the severance of the two locations—the head and the waist—the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 27, states: Question:

Why is it that death occurs immediately upon severing the head or the waist, whereas death does not occur when the hands, feet, and other limbs are severed? Answer: The head and the waist are the primary vital joints (*mahā-maraṇa-parvan*); therefore, death occurs as soon as they are severed. This is not the case for the hands and other limbs.
Furthermore, sentient beings of the desire realm subsist on edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). It is through the throat that this edible food passes.
The abdomen is the support for food; therefore, when these two locations are severed, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is immediately cut off.

Furthermore, the head is the locus of the various sense-faculties such as the eye (as it is said in the chapter that "many people dwell" therein—meaning that within the head, the five material sense-faculties are complete; these five sense-faculties are the five bases [āyatana] among the twelve bases). If it is severed and destroyed, the eye and other sense-faculties are impaired.
The abdomen is the place where the vital breath (*śvāsa-vāyu*) resides; if the waist and abdomen are severed and destroyed, the breath has no place to abide.

Because it is the basis, when the two locations are severed, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is then severed. (The Chapter states: "The waist is the place where inhalation and exhalation abide," which is what the Treatise means by the "basis of the wind of breath.")

In a single moment of thought, there is no real dharma that constitutes a "sentient being" who kills. According to this school, a single moment of thought does not possess the five aggregates (*skandhas*).

Rather, it arises sequentially through the four mental factors of consciousness, perception, feeling, and formations; together with their basis, which is form (*rūpa*), they constitute the five aggregates.

It is upon these five aggregates that the designation "sentient being" is conventionally established. Apart from the aggregates, there is no separate essence, just as a forest has no essence apart from the trees. This is also...
Thus it is. Therefore, the aggregates (*skandhas*) are the actual sentient beings, not merely provisional designations.
As for karma and afflictions being the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*): because one summons the retribution of a single lifetime through karma and afflictions, they are established as the faculty.

However, this life-faculty (jīvitendriya) has no separate essence apart from matter and mind; it is not like the Sarvāstivāda school’s position that there exists a distinct, real entity apart from matter and mind which serves as the essence of the life-faculty.

Regarding "being deluded about the perception of dharmas and lacking the appropriate perception of dharmas": others all say this refers to committing an offense against the Dharma due to being deluded regarding the five conditions.

Now, examining this closely, it refers to the five aggregates themselves as real dharmas; these are designated as "dharmas. If one's conceptualizing mind is deluded regarding the perception of these dharmas, or if the mind of doubt lacks [certainty], this constitutes a lack of the appropriate perception of dharmas.
Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "It is a lack of the mind that determines and corrects."

Regarding the statement that "there is no prior mind [of intent] when one perceives a non-human as a human," the ancient masters merely saw the scriptural passage concerning non-humans occurring before the perception of a human;
they did not understand the sequence of the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and the mental state of killing (*vadhacitta*).
"Comparing it to the transformation of perception (*saṃjñā-parāvṛtti*) and so forth" is an illustration.

For example, as in the case of "transforming the perception of a human into the perception of a non-human," this refers to the subsequent perception of a non-human to conclude the *sthūlātyaya* offense regarding the prior human.

Now, "the perception of a non-human regarding a human" likewise refers to the subsequent object of a non-human to conclude the *sthūlātyaya* offense regarding the prior human. Both the subsequent characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the subsequent object (*viṣaya*) function through these two gates.
There are different versions with two distinct readings. Both are cases where the subsequent [text] cites the preceding cause of an offense.
If this passage is indeed the one in question, it is not the passage concerning the perception of a person as a non-person.
"Lacking definitive resolution" means being in a state of hesitation.
Next, regarding "the double deficiency" (*ubhayāpatti*): because a different object replaces the original person as the object, the first of the five conditions is deficient.

Furthermore, one entertains doubt and hesitation regarding this different object; this constitutes the second [deficiency]. Therefore, it is called "the double deficiency. The subsequent categories of precepts should be understood by analogy.

Regarding the difference in the deficiency of the first condition: if the first condition is deficient, one must give rise to the perception of the original object toward an object belonging to a different realm of existence (*gati*).

This distinguishes it from the previous case of the deficiency of the second condition; in the former, there was doubt regarding the original object, whereas now this is not so—therefore, there is a distinction.

Regarding the cases where both the single and the double are absent—namely, the first and the sixth [categories]: this means that within the "double absence," there is contained the sense of both the absence of the object (*ālambana*) and the absence of the mind (*citta*).
Therefore, with respect to the absence of the mind, it must be assigned to the absence of the second condition and explained within the analysis of the absence of the mind.

With respect to the absence of the object, it must further be assigned to the absence of the first condition and clarified within the analysis of the absence of the object. However, within the absence of the object, the single and the double each...
The "six" includes [the perception of] a person; it does not take a stump of wood as a distinct object, and thus there are six.
Regarding the simultaneous absence of both perception and doubt, the "one-six" refers to the original person-object:

the perception shifts outward, taking as its object that which is neither a person nor a stump of wood; the doubting mind is likewise. Thus, there are six. These are merely two types of expressions regarding the "one-six."

The "intention" excludes the human realm, treating it as a distinct object (*viṣaya*). Because killing a human being—a distinct object—does not exempt one from the offense of *pārājika*, it is therefore excluded for the time being.

Regarding the two categories of "single" and "double" exclusions, each having nineteen [instances], these collectively refer to the four objects, such as humans and so forth, distinguished by their relative magnitude.

Regarding the objects (*viṣaya*): since there are nineteen cases involving doubt regarding the original object, there are likewise nineteen cases involving doubt regarding a different original object. As for the "nineteen":

this refers to the three distinct objects—human, non-human, and animal—each of which contains the conditions of being mistaken about the object, having a distracted mind, and the absence of a strong intention, yet proceeding to kill.

This results in fifteen [offenses]. Excluding the "stump" (sthāṇu), there remain four types, which then become nineteen. The same applies to "perception" (saṃjñā) and "doubt" (vicikitsā); these constitute the thirty-eight variations of the object (*viṣaya*).
All subsequent sections on the heads of the precepts should be understood according to this principle; there is no need for further elaboration. (The *Chapter* states:
"These two omissions" refers to the omission of both the single and double [categories]; this is what is meant by "there is no need for further elaboration" below.)

Regarding the offense of *tīkṣṇa-garha* (striking): if one strikes without killing, a *mahābhikṣu* incurs the offense of *pārājika*, while other members of the assembly incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the two types of *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses)—the light and the heavy—the distinction is based on the proximity [of the victim].
Regarding one who possesses the seven preparatory stages (*saptaprayoga*): if one lacks the first two of the three general conditions, one lacks the preparatory stage itself.
Among the specific conditions, if the first condition is lacking, it is a discrepancy in the object; if the second is lacking, it is a mistaken perception or doubt;

if the fifth is lacking, it is a discrepancy in the intensity of the object such that the intention ceases. Because these three [conditions] are absent, killing cannot occur; this should be understood as applying to all subsequent categories of precepts.

Regarding the other two categories, although they differ in terms of gravity, one must in all cases determine the intent, explain the name, and establish whether the requisite conditions are complete or lacking.

When a non-human transforms into an animal, it is classified as a "non-human" for the purpose of this rule; killing such a being incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If it does not transform into an animal, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Both cases are detailed below in the text.
The *Ratnakaraṇḍa-vyūha-sūtra* provides the narrative concerning King Udayana, as described in its tenth fascicle.

Regarding the statement that there are no two distinct immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*), the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter eighteen, states: "If one harms one's father who is also an Arhat, one incurs only a single immediate transgression, because the basis [of the act] is one.
If this is so, how should one reconcile this with the illustrative parable? [The answer is: It refers to the case where [the father] has already lost his status as an Arhat.
"Upāli, you have already committed two heinous crimes (*ānantarya*): namely, harming your father and killing an Arhat. This demonstrates that one heinous crime is established through two conditions;
thus, his offense is rebuked by way of these two aspects. (This refers to a *dṛṣṭānta-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, a sūtra containing parables. *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 119.)

The same applies here. *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Chapter One. Question: Is it possible for one to kill a bhikṣuṇī who is neither one’s mother nor an arhat, yet commit a pārājika offense and incur the crime of a heinous act (ānantarya)?

Answer: Yes. If a father has left the household life and received full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), and his precepts have transformed so that he becomes a bhikṣuṇī—if one strikes this bhikṣuṇī, one incurs a duṣkṛta;
if one strikes the father who possesses full ordination, one incurs a sthūlātyaya. All other texts state that it is merely a duṣkṛta.

Regarding the phrase "the father’s actual self has truly undergone transformation," this refers to one who, upon the completion of his life, immediately receives the retribution of an animal within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) during that very moment.
The intent of the commentary is as follows: the father’s provisional form has actually transformed into the body of an animal;

that is to say, at the moment the father’s life ends, he receives an intermediate body for but a single *kṣaṇa*, and immediately thereafter receives the retribution of an animal. Because this process occurs with such extreme rapidity, it is not perceived. This is the actual principle.
In the interim, they have already undergone birth and death. Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 70, states: "At the beginning of the kalpa, humans suddenly transformed into snakes.

Regarding this, one commentator says: "Other masters maintain that they underwent death and rebirth. If this were so, they would necessarily undergo the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) during those deaths and births;
why then do people not perceive any interruption? The answer is: "The intermediate state is so rapid that people of that time did not know it was there, just as in that [other] case."

This is explained at length. Although the *Vibhāṣā* provides a detailed exposition of this view of other masters (*paravādin*), it is incorrect. Why would these other masters necessarily submit to the *Vibhāṣā*?

There is another interpretation, as in the *Pomiji* (Breaking Delusions Regarding Records). The reason it is not recounted here is that [the author] wishes, for the time being, to clarify the high arrogance of his revered master;
yet he does not take this to be the actual truth. However, [the author] refutes these sixteen points of the old interpretation, stating:
The transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) is the fundamental nature of birth and death. Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* explains regarding humans at the beginning of the eon:

"Suddenly there were those who moved by crawling on their bellies; they were collectively called 'snakes'. When asked, "How can it be that the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*) itself becomes an animal (*tiryagyoni*)?", the answer is:

"It is not that the human realm itself transforms into an animal; rather, it is only that the physical form of those beings differs before and after [the transformation]. Among these, some say that they are always humans, yet due to past...
The conditions of karma are such that prosperity and decline are uncertain. Initially, when meritorious karma was predominant, they took human form.

Later, as evil, deceit, and crookedness increased, their human features vanished and they transformed into something resembling animals. It is like a person who, through another's incantations or spells, is transformed into a donkey or the like, yet remains a human in reality.
Furthermore, some say that they are indeed animals; however, they have universally descended from the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Upon death, he passes away in purity; yet, driven by past evil karma, he undergoes rebirth in the realm of animals.
Due to the residual power of his former merit, he initially resembles a human, but later, as his wickedness and deceit increase, his human features vanish and he assumes the form of an animal.

Thus one may know that the old interpretation contains four errors. It is heard that Master Chongshi used this [text] to inquire about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) with Dharma Master Bao (this Dharma Master was later...).

The Dharma Master resided at Foshouji Monastery in the eastern region for several years, yet he was unable to reach a definitive conclusion. Later, while examining the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, he encountered this passage and finally reached a resolution, deeming [the previous view] incorrect.
Now, upon careful examination, it appears that the Dharma Master likewise did not understand the essential intent of the *Vibhāṣā* school.

According to this *Vibhāṣā* school, a single moment of volition (*cetanā*) produces the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), whereas multiple moments of volition produce the completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*).

Regarding the performance of complete karma (*paripūrṇa-karman*): since it is a collective retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*) produced from a single undifferentiated volition (*cetanā*), it cannot be altered for the duration of one's entire life.
As for complete karma, because it is a distinct retribution (*viśeṣa-vipāka*) produced by multiple volitions, it is possible for it to be transformed.

Therefore, the intention behind the two explanations in the *Vibhāṣā* is as follows: either one creates a single volition (*cetanā*) that brings about the retribution of an animal, yet this karma is fulfilled through many volitions;
thus, at first it resembles a human, and later it returns to its original form. Or, one creates a single volition that brings about the general retribution of a human.
Furthermore, this karma is brought to completion through repeated volition; thus, one is initially a human being, but later receives the retribution of an animal.
According to the Mahāyāna, it is through repeated volition that [karma] projects and through repeated volition that it completes.

Therefore, while the total retribution projected by repeated volition can indeed be altered, it is because the seeds of specific designations for "human" and "animal" within the *ālayavijñāna* serve as the immediate causal conditions, due to the actions one has performed.
Due to the dominant power of karma at the time of its maturation, it causes the seeds of humans and animals to arise and manifest in mutual confusion.

How could this be the same as the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, which states that five hundred arhats, despite being free from ignorance (*ajñāna*), were unable to sever [the latencies] and thus falsely explained a single volition (*cetanā*) as a projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), claiming that one who appears as an animal is actually a human, or that one who appears as a human is actually an animal? How could it be so?
To say that this is truly a human being is profoundly erroneous. If that were so, when a Mahāyāna practitioner transforms into an animal, would there be an intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
Answer: Because they are traveling to another location, there is an intermediate state. If they were to be born in their original place, what need would there be for an intermediate state?

This is truly because the myriad categories of karma created differ; thus, it is difficult to conceive. The distinctions in form and retribution are such that only a Buddha possesses the power of knowledge regarding the specific nature of one's own karma.

Only then can it be fully understood. How could Arhats and others possibly provide a comprehensive explanation? Therefore, in this present commentary, we rely on the views of other masters to discuss the actual principle;
one should follow the Mahāyāna. Question: The later explanation in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Originally an animal, appearing as a human at first—if one kills this person, what offense does one incur? Now, examining this closely, although the *Vibhāṣā* provides a mistaken interpretation, for the time being, one should [proceed as follows]:

Commentary: One incurs the offense of *pārājika* because the intent to harm is grave and the human characteristics remain; thus, although it is a real person, it resembles an animal. The opposite case should be explained accordingly.

Regarding those whose labor is not fulfilled, others all explain that while there is the debt of gratitude for giving birth to one's body, there is no thought of nurturing that body; therefore, the labor is not fulfilled.

Now, to examine this in detail: the debt of gratitude toward the one who gives birth is weightier than the debt of gratitude toward the one who nurtures. Thus, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 119, states:
"Suppose there is a woman with a *kalala* [embryo], and another woman receives it and places it within her own body; when the child is later born, whom should he consider his mother?"

Regarding the question of which [mother] must be killed for one to incur the immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*): the answer is that of the two—the biological mother and the foster mother—it is only by killing the biological mother that one incurs the immediate retribution.
This is because the *kalala* (embryonic stage) depends upon the biological mother for its birth. All matters concerning the child should be consulted with the foster mother.

As there are four passages in the eighteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* that accord with this treatise, according to this textual authority, it is the biological mother, not the foster mother, whose killing constitutes the offense.
This is contrary [to reason]. Therefore, one cannot say that there is birth but no nurturing; this is termed "labor not being fulfilled.

One should rather say that "labor is not fulfilled" because the parents' affection and love for their child are slight, as they raise a being lacking in wisdom; this is termed "labor not being fulfilled. As for the child toward the parents...
The malicious intent was not grave because the retribution was inferior; thus the chapter says, "Furthermore, because the retribution is inferior.
Regarding the initial four *pārājikas*: if one were to rely on different objects, there would be one instance of a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding the "four phrases on changing thoughts": this refers to the transformation of divergent thoughts; that is, the transformation of perception (*saṃjñā*).
"Those below this level" refers to other persons in training (*śaikṣa*). As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 119: Question:
Just as killing an Arhat incurs the immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*), does killing various persons in training also incur this same transgression? Answer: No.

It is so. Why is this? It was previously stated that [the offense] is incurred through two conditions: first, ingratitude toward those who provide sustenance; second, the destruction of a field of merit (*guṇakṣetra*).

Killing those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) does not constitute the destruction of a field of merit, because they possess both virtues and faults, and because they engage in both sublime conduct and evil conduct, and possess both roots of goodness and roots of unwholesomeness. Question: Regarding the falling away from the state of an Arhat...
"Would there not be an immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) for harming him? Answer: "No, because he is still one in training (*śaikṣa*). As previously stated. Question:
"Since he will necessarily abide in the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) at the moment his final life is about to end, why is there no immediate retribution? Answer:

"Because within the body of one beyond training, there is neither evil nor [afflicted] mind. That is to say, the intention to kill and the application [of the act] arise only within the body of one in training."

It applies to those in training (*śaikṣa*), but not to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because there is no cause for immediate succession [of rebirth]. Thus, one does not incur an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*). (The "ungrateful person" refers to one who commits the parricide or matricide of the *ānantarya* offenses.
The *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra* is the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha Sūtra*.
Regarding those who commit an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) through a thoughtless mind: the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 118, also says: Question:
Since that person does not recognize [the victim] as an Arhat, for what reason does he incur the immediate transgression? Answer: One does not incur the offense because of recognition;

rather, one incurs the offense because of destroying a field of merit (*guṇakṣetra*). Because he gave rise to an intention to kill—characterized by a lack of discernment—toward the community of bhikṣus, by this...

Because an extremely evil mind caused harm even to an Arhat, it constitutes a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense. Regarding this, the intention of the ancient masters was that the following passage refers to a person who offered food to the Buddha with a distracted mind;

however, the present master refutes this, stating that since the tree deity informed [the Buddha], there is no need to cite such a passage to judge whether an act is intentional (*krta*) or unintentional (*amata*).

Regarding those who commit an offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*): this refers to one who does not intend to kill, but acts with the intent to strike the Buddha; such cases belong to the category of offenses similar to immediate retribution, but are not actual immediate retribution itself.

Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa*, chapter eighteen, states: "It requires the intent to kill for an offense of immediate retribution to be established. If one strikes [the Buddha] with the intent to hit him and blood flows, there is no immediate retribution.
However, the third fascicle of the *Mātṛkā-vinaya* states: "There is a *pāyattika* [offense]; one does not produce roots of goodness, nor is there a formal ritual (*karma*)."

By rubbing [the image], one may eliminate the offense. Why is this? For instance, if a bhikṣu, with a mind of hatred, intends to take the Buddha’s life and strikes the Buddha, he incurs a *pārājika* offense that cannot be expiated (as stated in the treatise).
If he strikes with the intent to kill, he would otherwise incur only a *sthūlātyaya*; however, because it was the causal condition for killing, [the full offense applies].
If one does not intend to kill or strike, it can then be termed a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

If the Buddha were to lack two factors—namely, the principle (*li*) and the teaching (*jiao*)—and another person were substituted for him, it would not constitute a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense; this is a deficiency in the principle.
What was originally intended to result in a *pārājika* (defeat) now results only in a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense); this is a deficiency in the teaching.
Regarding the phrase "original *duṣkṛta*, present *duṣkṛta*": the Buddha certainly does not impose the act of killing based on external conditions. Nevertheless, one should only incur a *duṣkṛta*.

Although the current matter differs from the time [of the initial intent], and even if a different object replaces it, one still incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. Therefore, it is said: "original *duṣkṛta*, present *duṣkṛta*.
"Original" refers to the preparatory effort (*prayoga*); "present" refers to the cessation of the action.
Regarding the phrase "the father and so forth as being one": this refers to the previous case where the Buddha was harmed and another came to take his place. Herein there are two perspectives:

first, from the perspective of what was originally intended, it is merely a deficiency in the realm, principle, and teaching of the Buddha; second, from the perspective of the indestructible, it is a deficiency in the principle of the original Buddha’s realm but not a deficiency in his teaching.
Now, regarding the harming of the father and another coming to take his place, there is only one perspective: namely, with respect to the father.

"Superior. This means that both the secular and the rebellious are absent; this is what is meant by being devoid of both principle and teaching. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "father and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes the mother and Arhats.

As for the doubt concerning the perception of [the Buddha] as such—whether it be two or one regardless of whether the realms of rebirth are the same or different—the former, "or two," is explained first.
Since he is in fact a Buddha, and for a Buddha there is no sense of malice, one certainly cannot be executed; this constitutes a failure in the teaching.

Because of external conditions, there may be doubts regarding the characteristics of different realms of existence. Due to a light-mindedness of heart, there is furthermore a deficiency in principle. Next, the phrase "or one" is explained.

The principle regarding the omission [of the precepts] is the same as before. However, in cases where there is no omission of the teaching—namely, when one was originally a *rāṇaka* (a novice) and remains a *rāṇaka* now—the reason for the single omission of the principle but not the omission of the teaching, even though the father and others belong to the same category and suspect one another, is that one was originally a *mleccha* (barbarian) and remains a *mleccha* now.
This is the single definitive meaning. As for the statement that "one was originally a barbarian and is now a barbarian," this may have some basis in reasoning, yet it is not absolute.

For instance, according to the scriptural text, if one harbors the thought of another person or entertains doubt, one first incurs the offense based on these two causes—thought and doubt—and only then, if one does not take their life, it is not necessarily the case that one becomes a barbarian in this present life.

Regarding the teaching that the name [of the offense] applies to three persons: if one strikes the Buddha, an Arhat, and one's father without killing them, these three instances of striking are all *pāyattika* (offenses of expiation).

For a layperson, striking one’s father constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Therefore, it is said that striking a lay father is entirely different [from the other cases]. Furthermore, since striking either a lay father or a monastic father does not constitute a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense, it is said that in all such cases there is no violation of principle.
"Regarding the conditions for the formation [of the precepts]: this person refers to the very circumstances that led to the establishment of the Vinaya rules.
Regarding the impurity meditation as an antidote because desire predominates among the five *smṛtyupasthānas*:

the afflictions of all sentient beings increase disproportionately, yet they do not exceed five types. To remedy these five, one cultivates the five *smṛtyupasthānas*. [This is] the thirty-sixth item in the *Nirvāṇa*."
The five applications of mindfulness (*pañca-smṛtyupasthāna*) are also fully explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, within the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi* (the twenty-sixth stage).
As that treatise quotes from a sūtra, it says: "How does a bhikṣu diligently cultivate the practice of contemplation? This yoga practitioner, with respect to a corresponding object..."
He should settle his mind. That is to say, a bhikṣu whose mind is characterized solely by greed should settle his mind upon the object of impurity (aśubhālambana).

If it is characterized solely by hatred, he should settle his mind upon loving-kindness (maitrī). If it is characterized solely by delusion, he should settle his mind upon the nature of conditions and dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
If it is characterized solely by pride, he should settle his mind upon the analysis of the elements (dhātuprabheda).
One should settle the mind. If there is only the mode of discursive thought (*vitarka*), one should settle the mind upon mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
This is called settling the mind upon a corresponding object (*anurūpa-ālambana*). (Commentary: That is to say, there may be someone for whom desire is particularly predominant;
because of this mode of predominance of desire, they are called "one of desirous temperament" (*rāga-carita*). Such a person of desirous temperament must...
Taking an object as one's focus, one forms the perception of impurity; when the mind’s craving is thus stilled and increased [in its cessation], one is then able to enter the Path.

This is what was formerly called "stopping the mind" (*tingxin*), which carries the meaning of "stopping and stilling. For those with a temperament prone to aversion, one should cultivate loving-kindness and compassion.

For those with a temperament prone to delusion who are confused about the nature of objects—thereby falsely clinging to such things as the "Dark Principle" (*tattva*) or Brahmā as the origin of dependent origination—one should investigate the twelve links of dependent arising.

This is the nature of correct dependent origination. To eliminate conduct characterized by delusion, or for those who give rise to the conceit of "I am," one should contemplate the distinctions between the six elements within the body to realize selflessness, thereby eliminating conduct characterized by conceit (the four great elements, space, and consciousness constitute the six elements).

Or, for those whose conduct is dominated by discursive thought and whose minds are excessively agitated, one should take the breath as the object of focus to still such restless activity. These are all medicines prescribed by the Blessed One according to the specific capacities of his disciples.

Yet Chong says: "However, even the five *sthāpanā-cittas* (stabilizing practices) are not practiced universally; among them, the essentials consist of only two gates, namely, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*).
Now, considering the principles of desire and discursive thought, these two are indeed necessary. But as for those whose natures are dull or deluded, how could they be the same?
This [argument] originates from the biased teachings within the Lesser Vehicle’s *Abhidharmakośa*; how could it possibly provide universal understanding?

Regarding the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, it is further said that there are four types of desire (*rāga*): first, desire for color (*varṇa-rāga*), which takes as its object a livid corpse (*vinīlaka*) and so forth;

second, desire for shape (*saṃsthāna-rāga*), which takes as its object a corpse being devoured (*vikhādita*) and so forth; third, desire for exquisite touch (*sparśa-rāga*), which takes as its object a worm-infested corpse (*vipūyaka*) and so forth;

fourth, desire for service (*paricaryā-rāga*), which takes as its object an immobile corpse (*avilambika*) and so forth. Although these desires can be eliminated by means of the skeleton (*asthi-saṃkalā*), this is because within the skeleton, the objects of these four types of desire do not exist. Thus [it is taught].
When a bhikṣu cultivates the contemplation of the skeleton (aṭṭhika-saṅkhalikā), he is immediately able to eliminate those four types of craving so that they do not arise.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "For one afflicted by the disease of sensual desire, teach the contemplation of the skeletal form.

If one performs this contemplation of the skeleton, it not only accords with this specific passage, but also does not contradict the sequential stages of entering the Path (*mārga*). If one takes the five kinds of impurity from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, [the following applies]:
As for this "explanation" (śeṣa): it is not merely that it is not a gateway for entry; it also contradicts the characteristics of all the sacred teachings.
The various masters, failing to understand the underlying intent, simply see that the name "impurity" is the same and cite it as an explanation, thereby creating a great obstacle.

Since this [the skeleton] is already subsumed within the stage of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), how could one subsequently practice the mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) therein? Now, upon careful examination, the chain of bones is the object of focus.

Regarding the "external body": this refers to those who possess desire, who crave the manifest forms and features of another's body; therefore, they practice the meditation on bones (*asthi-saṃjñā*) in order to eliminate the four types of craving.
Now, examining the Vinaya text, it concerns one’s own internal body as an object of impurity; once the meditation is perfected, one becomes self-disgusted. How can you falsely judge [otherwise]?
If one performs the meditation on bones, it accords with the Vinaya. Question: According to which scriptural authority does one practice the meditation on impurity by taking another as the object?
Is there a distinction regarding the objects of focus? The answer is found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the twenty-sixth section, the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.

There are six types of the gateway of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) for the purpose of eliminating the five kinds of greed; these have already been explained in detail within the refutation of delusions regarding mental objects (*nimitta*). They will not be presented here in full.
To state the essentials: craving is twofold. First, regarding one's own internal body, there is the craving for sensual desires and the craving for form.
Second, regarding external persons, there is lustful desire and lustful craving. Impurity is also twofold.

First, impurity based on internal defilement, referring to the thirty-six items within the internal body, such as hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and so forth. Second, impurity based on external defilement, referring to...
Whether it be livid discoloration, or putrefaction and festering, and so forth in detail up to the skeletal chain or excrement and filth—
among these two types [of objects], by means of the internal impurity as an object of focus, one brings about purification of the mind regarding desire and lust for the internal body (that is,
by focusing on the thirty-six impure substances filling one's own internal body, one uses this as an antidote to the lustful desire for external objects). By means of the external...
By taking impurity as the object of focus, one brings about purification of the mind regarding lust and sensual desire for the external body.

There are four further types of craving associated with lust: first, craving for visible color, such as the sight of a bloated corpse; second, craving for shape, such as the sight of a discolored corpse;
third, craving for exquisite touch, such as the sight of a skeleton; and fourth, craving for service, such as the sight of a mangled corpse. This should be understood accordingly.
The critical analysis sufficiently demonstrates the distinction between the internal and external;

thus, we know that the five kinds of impurity cited therein pertain to the internal body, which accords with the Vinaya, as the Vinaya texts express revulsion toward internal retribution. Having established the correct principle, the following describes the intent of this veneration:

The five kinds of impurity constitute the stage of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). In general, when practicing the methods of contemplation, one must first proceed through the five cessations (*pañca-viśrāma*) before entering the foundations of mindfulness.

Now, since these five impurities already pertain to the foundation of mindfulness regarding the body, why does the subsequent text instead instruct one to practice breath-holding? This is because breath-holding belongs to the category of the five cessations.

If one were to revert from the foundations of mindfulness to practice the five cessations, it would be known that this contradicts the principle. Now, examining the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhìdù lùn) in detail...

21. Commentary: Within the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), these five kinds of impurity are clarified. That intention seeks to distinguish the stage of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad bodhipakṣadharmāḥ*).

Whether it be the initial stage of training, the five stages of settling the mind (*pañca cittasthāpanāḥ*), or mindfulness in its general and specific aspects, all are subsumed within the four foundations of mindfulness among the factors of enlightenment.
How could one simply see that the names of the four foundations of mindfulness are identical and [conclude that they are the same]?
You arbitrarily judge this to be the stage of abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness among the seven preparatory practices (*saptaprayoga*).

Furthermore, you teach that holding the breath is for those whose conduct is characterized by discursive thought (*vitarka*), while teaching the cultivation of the foul (*aśubha*) is for those whose conduct is characterized by greed (*rāga*). These objectives are entirely different; how can they be called a sequential progression? Moreover, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:

Mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) is likewise subsumed under the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); how could it be restrictedly judged as belonging only to the stage of the five cessations (*pañca-vyupaśama*)?

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 53, states: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when one cultivates the contemplation of the body within the internal body, with single-minded mindfulness, one knows the inhalation when inhaling, and one knows the exhalation when exhaling," as explained at length therein. All such [passages] are based on...

The general name is "four applications of mindfulness" (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). When one takes only material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) as an object, it is called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). Taking feeling, mind, and so forth as objects follows the same principle.
Therefore, there is no contemplative gate—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—that is not subsumed within the four applications of mindfulness.
How can the five *sthāpanā* (cessations) not be included within the *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness)? The dharma-characteristics of the sūtras and śāstras are exceedingly profound;
they may be combined or separated, and their application may be general or specific. I pray that you eliminate your stagnant attachments and carefully examine the true exegesis.
Regarding the five types of craving for the body (*kāya-tṛṣṇā*): these were established by the ancient masters as a summary of the sūtras and śāstras.

First, craving for wealth is countered by the cultivation of few desires (*alpeccha*). All treatises state that "few desires" and "contentment" (*saṃtuṣṭi*)—formerly translated as "few desires and contentment"—are synonymous.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-two, states: "Contentment means the absence of discontent; few desires means the absence of great [desires]."

Regarding desire (*kāmacchanda*): if one asks how the two types of distinction between them are defined, it is said that to seek more than what one has already obtained, such as fine clothing and so forth, is called "lack of contentment" (*asantuṣṭi*).
To intensely long for fine clothing and so forth that one has not yet obtained is called "great desire" (*mahecchatā*).

Vasubandhu refutes this, saying: "Is it not the case that seeking more also takes what is not yet obtained as its object? If so, the distinction between these two would consequently [be non-existent]."

This is not established. Therefore, it should be stated as follows: if one is dissatisfied and lacks joy regarding what one has already obtained—whether it be of poor quality or insufficient—it is called "lack of contentment" (*asamtuṣṭi*).
If, regarding what one has not yet obtained, one seeks for that which is of superior quality or in greater quantity, it is called "great desire" (*mahecchatā*).

The remedial dharmas that are the opposite of these are called "contentment" (*saṃtuṣṭi*) and "fewness of desires" (*alpecchatā*). Furthermore, regarding the two types of greed for form (*rūparāga*), the practice of impurity (*aśubhābhāvanā*) is taught. Thirdly...

The immeasurable [meditation on] equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the antidote for sensual greed (*kāmarāga*). The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, fascicle 29, states: "The *Vibhāṣā* says that there are two types of sensual greed:

first, [greed for] form (*rūpa*), and second, [greed for] sexual intercourse (*maithuna*). Impurity (*aśubha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) serve as their respective antidotes. (Form refers to agreeable visible forms, shapes, and so forth; sexual intercourse refers to lustful desire.

Some claim it does not refer to lustful desire, but this is an error. The ninth fascicle of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* is likewise. Vasubandhu further provides a distinct interpretation in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "In reality, however..."

Purity (*śuddhi*) serves as the antidote to lustful greed (*kāmarāga*), while equanimity (*upekṣā*) serves as the antidote to greed for other relatives and friends. This is *upekṣā*, which is one of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

Both of these have non-attachment (*alobha*) and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as their essential nature. The fourth is called "greed that conceives of sentient beings" (*sattvagrāha-rāga*). According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), one provisionally designates a "sentient being.
Clinging to this provisional designation as a real birth, one gives rise to craving; this is termed "greed for names" (*nāmagraha-rāga*).
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, Chapter Thirteen, "The Causes of Greed," states: "When one becomes attached to provisional names, craving arises.

Chapter Twenty-three, "The Characteristics of Wisdom," states: "Just as a bottle that contains nothing outside is called an 'empty bottle,' so too, because there is no self (*ātman*) within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they are called empty.

Regarding the fifth point, the antidote for craving for phenomena (*dharma-tṛṣṇā*) through emptiness: having realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), one further contemplates the five...

Because the aggregates (*skandhas*) are truly empty. The fourteenth chapter, "On the View of a Self" (*Satkāyadṛṣṭi-varga*), states: "Furthermore, by means of the characteristic of emptiness, one extinguishes the characteristics of the five aggregates.
It further says: "The dispersal and extinction of the five aggregates is what constitutes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). The detailed exposition is as found therein.

Regarding the ability to transform and eliminate impurities, that treatise states in its long prose: "Even the finest delicacies and various flavors of food, within the interval of a single night, all become impure.
Even if one were clothed in celestial garments and fed with celestial food, because of the nature of the body itself, it would still become impure;
how much more so for the food and clothing of humans. (The Commentary says: This physical form is a composite of the four great elements; it is called [the body].
Regarding the nature of the body: the nature of the body is such that it transforms food into excrement. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 26, states:
"Or one may be born as a pig or a dog, constantly eating excrement. Thus we know that "excrement" (*chú*) refers precisely to feces.
Regarding the phrase "first, citing the second [section] above, etc.": as in the preceding outline, there are four parts: (1) administering medicine according to the illness;

(2) the bhikṣu’s silent contemplation; (3) attaining success by following the instruction; and (4) seeking to relinquish life through external means. Now, this second major section also has four parts.
The first contains three textual passages, which are respectively a reiteration of the latter three sections from the previous major division.
Regarding the observation that the Śramaṇa Mṛgāra assumes the outward appearance of a śramaṇa: the tenth fascicle of the *Jianlun* states:

"He assumes the form of a śramaṇa by shaving his head while leaving a small tuft of hair (*cūḍā*) at the crown, and wearing robes of dyed color (*kasāya*). He covers his body with one garment, which he places over his shoulder."
"Entering the monastery to rely [on the community], the bhikṣus would gather up their leftover food for their own livelihood" (as stated in the treatise).
This is from the tenth fascicle of the *Jñānaprasthāna*. Regarding the Vārakā River: there are people in the world who say, "This river can wash away a person's sins.
The śramaṇa Mṛgaśiras thought to himself, "I shall go to the Vārakā River to wash away my sins" (as stated in the treatise). This is the tenet held by these non-Buddhists.

Regarding the statement that "the staff is like [the rules for] the cemetery," etc., the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Daolun), fascicle three, poses the question: "The Buddha possesses all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajña*).
For what reason did he instruct the bhikṣus in such a way as to cause them distress? If he were unaware [of this], he would not possess all-encompassing wisdom.

The answer states: "At that time, he was not instructing only these sixty people. The Buddha’s teaching is without partiality; however, there are those who receive much benefit and those who receive little. Therefore, there is no fault."

Furthermore, the Buddha knew that according to the beginning and end of the faculties and karma of the assembly, they would surely obtain great benefit through this condition later on. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, fascicle 10, states:
"He said to the bhikṣus: 'I shall enter into a state of joyful seclusion and dwell alone for half a month; do not allow anyone to come to my place. Only...
"Allow one person to deliver food. Why did the Tathāgata issue such an injunction? It was because he observed that in the past, five hundred hunters killed many deer;
consequently, they fell into the evil realms. After a long time, they were able to emerge and were born among humans, where they left the household life to practice the Way as bhikṣus.
Yet, because the karmic retribution for their past misdeeds was not yet exhausted, within half a month they continued to kill and harm one another due to this evil karma."
There are those whom even the Buddha cannot save; therefore, the Tathāgata enters seclusion for half a month. Among the five hundred [monks], there were ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).

For this reason, the Tathāgata taught them the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). By contemplating impurity, they became weary of and detached from sensual desire, thereby attaining rebirth in the heavens.

Had they not been free from craving, they would have been born in an unwholesome realm. Therefore, he taught them so that they might be born in a wholesome realm. The Buddha spoke thus for their sake.

Having done so, he further thought: "If a bhikṣu were to die and come to me saying, 'A bhikṣu has died,' or 'Two, three, four, or even seven have died,' it would not be possible for me to rescue and protect them through my supernormal powers. Therefore, I shall enter seclusion to silence all such criticisms, so that people may say:
'The Buddha is omniscient, yet he could not prevent his disciples from killing one another. Among them, there was a person..."
He replied: "The World-Honored One has entered meditative concentration; therefore, he was unaware. Had the Buddha known, he would certainly have prohibited it.
Regarding the two points within the text of the Dharma discourse: the first concerns the wording of the preceding section, and the second is the request below for a change in the contemplation.
The present statement, "further explaining the Dharma," serves as the topical outline (*uddāna*).

"Those afflicted by craving" reveals the afflictions (*kleśa*). From afflictions, karma is produced; thus, both karma and afflictions constitute the essence of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

This section sequentially refutes the four propositions concerning the causal conditions for killing mentioned previously. In the previous discussion on the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), there were four points:

first, administering medicine according to the illness (the present text is likewise); second, the bhikṣu’s silent contemplation (this is likewise); third, attaining success in accordance with the teaching (this text is likewise);

and fourth, seeking death through various means (this is the fourth point here, which constitutes the attainment of the fruit). Thus, we know that the first three [points] are the attainment of the fruit, and are therefore different from the preceding text, which concerns the cause and effect of killing.
Thus it is said that they are opposites.
Regarding the naming [of this meditation] after its attendant factor: in reality, the essence of this contemplation is wisdom (*prajñā*).

That it is now called "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is because mindfulness can cause the mind to dwell single-pointedly on one object; since mindfulness and wisdom are both mental factors (*caitta*), they are associated as attendants. *Abhidharmakośa* 2.33.
12. It is said: In the sūtras, *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) is taught. "Āna" refers to the inhalation of breath;
it means drawing external wind into the body. "Apāna" refers to the exhalation of breath; it means drawing internal wind out of the body.
Because wisdom takes this as its object through the power of mindfulness—where "object" refers to the breath—the practice is called *ānāpāna*.
Mindfulness has wisdom as its intrinsic nature; yet it is called "mindfulness" because it is sustained by the power of mindfulness, whereby the object is perceived with clarity.
(Up to: This characteristic becomes perfected through the possession of six causes: first, counting; second, following; third, settling; fourth, observing; fifth, transforming; and sixth, purifying.

Counting means binding the mind to the object of inhalation and exhalation, proceeding from one to ten, neither decreasing nor increasing, for fear that the mind might become overly concentrated on the object.

Because it is distracted, [one] subtracts ten from the mental aggregate (i.e., ten mental states are lost). However, within this process, three errors may occur: first, the error of undercounting, which is to say one for two;
second, the error of overcounting, which is to say two for one; and third, the error of confusion, which is to say "emerging" when it is "entering," or "entering" when it is "emerging.
To be free from these three errors is called correct counting. If the mind becomes distracted during the interval between the tenth [count], one should again begin from the beginning.
Count them in sequence. Having passed through [the cycle], begin again. Continue until concentration is attained (initially counting from the entry: five entries and five exits constitute ten).

"Following" means binding the mind to the object of the inhalation and exhalation; without applying effort, follow the breath as it moves. As the breath moves, inquire how far it reaches during its entry and exit:
that is, when mindful of the inhalation, does it travel throughout the entire body, or does it travel only a portion? Follow accordingly.
As that breath enters, it travels through the throat, heart, navel, hips, thighs, shins, and even to the toes; mindfulness constantly follows it.

If one is mindful of the breath as it goes out, leaving the body, it extends for the distance of one span (*vitasti*) or one fathom (*vyāma*); mindfulness constantly follows it in whatever direction it reaches.
Other masters say that the breath extends as far as the wind turns, or even to the Vairambha winds. This is not reasonable. (Regarding the Vairambha winds...)

[This refers to] the "swift wind. This mindfulness is conjoined with true attention (*tattvamanasikāra*); if it is conceptual, it is called "resolute attention" (*adhimokṣamanasikāra*), such as when one visualizes one's own body as white bones;

if it accords with the actual object, it is called "true attention. "Calm abiding" (*śamatha*) means binding the mindfulness solely to the tip of the nose, or between the eyebrows, or even down to the toes—settling the mind wherever one prefers—and observing the breath dwelling in the body like a thread through a pearl, whether cold or warm.

"Damage becomes benefit" means that after observing the wind of the breath, one simultaneously observes the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) that coexist with the breath, as well as the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*) that abide in dependence upon that matter, taking all five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as the object of observation (according to this observation of the five aggregates, this is the stage of the four applications of mindfulness, since the four applications of mindfulness subsume the five aggregates).
"Transformation" means shifting; it refers to redirecting the awareness that was focused on the wind of the breath toward increasingly superior and wholesome roots.

[The section on] the "Middle" extends up to the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)—that is, from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one initiates the contemplation conditioned by the Four Noble Truths, progressing gradually from "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) up to the Supreme Mundane Dharma and so forth.
