these constitute right speech, right action, and right livelihood. From this point onward, he further gives rise to hearing and reflection, and through right view, he develops right diligence and right mindfulness, entering the state of meditative concentration with a concentrated mind.

Regarding the term "noble right samādhi": it is called "noble" because it is wholesome; it is called "noble" because it is untainted (*anāsrava*). Thus, it encompasses both tainted and untainted concentrations.
A detailed explanation is as found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and it is fully set forth in the *Yogācāra-bhāṣya*. The chapter states:

"The eight liberations and entries" refers to what the treatise calls the "superior entries" (*abhibhv-āyatana*) of the eight liberations; that is to say, the liberations and the spheres of mastery (*abhibhu-āyatana*).
These are two dharma-gates.

Regarding the nine cessations: if one enters the first dhyāna, verbal expression ceases. Since vitarka and vicāra can give rise to verbal expression—and verbal expression is termed "verbal formation"—in the first meditative absorption, there is both vitarka and vicāra.

This refers to the wholesome vitarka and vicāra associated with a concentrated mind that is free from desire, ill-will, and so forth—namely, the wholesome vitarka and vicāra of renunciation (*naiṣkramya*). Because these wholesome vitarka and vicāra can extinguish the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as well as ill-will, harm, and so on, they are said to be "extinguished.

Upon entering the second dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are judged to be extinguished (because in the second dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are entirely absent). Upon entering the third dhyāna, joy (*prīti*) is judged to be extinguished (because in the third dhyāna, one is detached from joy and possesses sublime bliss).

Upon entering the fourth dhyāna, inhalation and exhalation are judged to be extinguished. If one enters the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the signs of form (*rūpanimitta*) are judged to be extinguished. If one enters...
In the sphere of consciousness, the sphere of infinite space is determined as ceasing. If one enters the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of consciousness is determined as ceasing.

If one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the sphere of nothingness is determined as ceasing. If one enters the attainment of cessation, feeling and perception are determined as ceasing.
These are called the nine cessations.
The nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) consist of the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

The nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) consist of the seven aforementioned perceptions, with the addition of the perception of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃjñā*) and the perception of detachment (*virāgasaṃjñā*). The explanation of these terms follows the previous [section]. However, the terms "abandonment" and "detachment" are intended to manifest the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

Detachment from the fetters of the desire realm is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*). Detachment from the fetters of the form realm is called "separation" (*viveka*). Detachment from the fetters of the formless realm is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).

Now, because one realizes the cessation explained for the two lower realms at the time of the path of detachment through the cultivation of the aforementioned perception of impurity and so forth, the two perceptions of abandonment and separation are added.
Question: If one cultivates the perception of death, does one become detached from the formless realm?

[Question: Regarding defilement (*saṃkleśa*), why does one only realize the cessation (*nirodha*) of the two lower realms? [Answer: Because the perception of death (*maraṇasaṃjñā*) is either complete with its preparatory application (*prayoga*) and its culmination (*niṣṭhā*), or not yet complete;

therefore, one is unable to realize the cessation of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). (If following the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 27: the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena attained through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is called the "realm of abandonment" (*prahāṇadhātu*);

the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is called the "realm of detachment" (*vairāgyadhātu*); and the cessation of all bases is the "realm of cessation" (*nirodhadhātu*). These should be understood accordingly as the two types of nirvāṇa.)
The ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*) consist of the nine perceptions with the addition of the perception of cessation (*nirodha-saṃjñā*). Their meaning may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 20) and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Volumes 166 and 167) provide extensive explanations of these ten perceptions. Thus far, they have been explained according to the general interpretation.

Following this are the perceptions of universal impermanence, suffering, non-self, and death; these are intended to reveal that the perception of death is the ultimate [realization] of the Noble Path.

This refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). The phrase "impure food, weary of the world, and not finding delight" reveals the noble path (*āryamārga*). The "application, abandonment, detachment, and cessation" reveal the fruit of the path (*mārgaphala*).

Furthermore, with respect to all [factors], one distinguishes between the primary turning (*pravartana*) and the secondary following-turning (*anuvartana*); that is to say, among the ten aspects, three perceptions (*saṃjñā*) constitute the primary turning.
The seventh is that which follows along (anuvartaka). For instance, when the perception of impurity (aśubha-saṃjñā) arises, four perceptions follow along:
namely, the perception of world-weariness (anabhirati), renunciation (vairāgya), cessation (nirodha), and extinction (nirvāṇa). What is their meaning? It is as follows:

the practitioner first goes to a cemetery and contemplates the appearance of a corpse, from its livid discoloration (vinīlaka) up to the interconnected chain of bones. Having grasped this sign, he goes to a nearby place and, with eyes closed, reflects with focused attention.
If one does not clearly perceive it, one should go and observe it. Having properly grasped the characteristics, one should quickly return to one's dwelling.
One should harmonize and lubricate the body and mind to free them from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Taking the previously observed external signs, one compares them with one's own body, thinking:

"This body of mine possesses all these aforementioned impure characteristics. Starting from the bones of the feet, using the ankle bones as a pillar, and proceeding up to the skull, one subsequently fixes the mindfulness thereon.

At the space between the eyebrows, one enters the application of mindfulness of the body from that very point; proceeding in sequence, one eventually enters the application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Alternatively, for one who prefers extensive observation, one recedes from the space between the eyebrows and proceeds in sequence back to observing the bones of the feet.
In this manner, one may observe one set, two sets, or three sets [of skeletons], extending sequentially from a single bed and a single room until reaching the ocean.
The entire perimeter is completely filled with white bones. Gradually narrowing the scope from there, one returns to observe the space between the eyebrows.
Having completed this contemplation of the perception of impurity, one reflects: "How can the various formations of birth and death be a source of delight?
At that moment, one feels no desire or pleasure whatsoever for the formations within the three realms. By means of this, one first cultivates the worldly [unattractiveness]...

Joy is also attained in its full perfection. Because of this lack of attachment, one delights in *nirvāṇa*; thus, the previously cultivated perceptions of abandonment, detachment, and cessation all attain full perfection.

Next, regarding the transformation of the perception of revulsion toward food (*āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñā*), there are likewise four corresponding mental concomitants (*anuvartaka*), their number being the same as before.

That is to say, when a practitioner gives rise to revulsion toward food, they observe the food in their hand and recognize that it originates from grains and the like; [they further recognize] those grains and the like...
Furthermore, seeds arise from the soil, and the soil arises from mud and filth;
since they are produced through such successive stages of impurity, what wise person would feel attachment toward them?

Moreover, when begging for food, at the time of morning ablutions and chewing the tooth-stick, one should regard the water as urine and the tooth-stick as a finger bone. When putting on robes and entering a village, one should regard the robes as...
One should perceive moisture as human excrement; the waistband as human intestines; the alms bowl as a skull; and the mendicant’s staff as a shin bone.

Seeing pebbles and stones on the road, one should perceive them as bones. Upon reaching a village, one should perceive the city walls as a cemetery. Seeing men and women, one should perceive them as skeletons.
When entering for alms and receiving *saktuka* (flour cakes), one should perceive it as a human stomach; if it is *pāṃśu* (powdered flour), [one should perceive it likewise].

Contemplate rice flakes as bones; when obtaining salt, contemplate it as human teeth; when obtaining rice, contemplate it as maggots; when obtaining rice and vegetables, contemplate them as human hair;
when obtaining soup or broth, contemplate it as excrement; when obtaining milk, contemplate it as human brain; when obtaining ghee and honey, contemplate them as human fat;
when obtaining fish and meat, contemplate them as human flesh; when obtaining rice, contemplate it as human blood; and when obtaining *modaka* (joy-balls), contemplate them as [human organs].
One should conceive of [the food] as dry excrement. If eating in the midst of the Saṃgha, one should regard the pure grass as the hair of a dead person and the sitting mat as a heap of bones.
Regarding the leftover food obtained, it is as explained extensively above. Question: Why must one conceive of food, drink, and so forth as impure?
Answer: One should reflect thus: there is nothing like birth and death. It is because of conceiving the impure as pure that one wanders in saṃsāra.

The five destinies. Now, because one wishes to depart from those destinies in order to attain the bliss of nirvāṇa, and furthermore, so as not to give rise to pure perceptions that increase craving and obstruct the Noble Path, one must cultivate revulsion.
Once revulsion has arisen, how could one take delight in the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of birth and death?
The detailed explanation is as before. Next, regarding the stage when perception transforms, seven perceptions follow along; that is to say, the practitioner—

He observes that all phenomena arise and perish from moment to moment. In the springtime, he sees various plants and trees producing flowers and leaves, vibrant and lustrous in colors like crimson and deep blue, resembling the hue of exquisite jewels;
he also sees the rivers, ponds, and marshes overflowing with moisture, where fish and birds frolic and play. Thereupon, he reflects thus:
Now, as external objects arose, he entered a village and saw men and women singing, dancing, leaping about, eating, drinking, and celebrating.
He immediately approached them and asked, "For what reason is this? They replied, "A son or a daughter has been born here; therefore, we have formed this thought."

Now internal phenomena arise: during the latter part of summer, he sees flowers and leaves flourishing and rivers and ponds overflowing. He further reflects that external phenomena have now become prosperous.
Having entered a village, he sees men and women beating drums and blowing conch shells, amidst a tumultuous clamor of laughter and merriment.
He immediately questioned those before him and learned that there was a settlement for married women. He then thought, "In this place, the internal Dharma flourishes.

Later, in autumn, when the leaves had all turned yellow and withered and the rivers and ponds were gradually drying up, he thought, "Now the external things have already decayed. He then entered the village.
Seeing those with white hair walking with staffs, their bodies bent and hunched, he reflected on internal phenomena: "Now I have already grown old.
Then, during the winter season, when the frosty winds blew and struck, and all the leaves lay upon the ground while the rivers and ponds were parched, he reflected on external phenomena:
"Now they have already perished and vanished. He entered a village and saw men and women with disheveled hair beating their breasts; having asked, he learned of this place.
Upon the death of his parents, he thought, "Now the internal dharma has also perished.

Having correctly grasped the signs regarding both the internal and external, he returned to his dwelling to harmonize and refine his body and mind, practicing the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñā*) based on the various marks of impermanence as he had perceived them.
He observes the internal body: that throughout the course of a single lifetime, the various aggregates (skandhas) pass through such-and-such stages, each aggregate being distinct.
He sets aside the other stages and contemplates the aggregates of any single stage—how they arise earlier and perish later—whether it be for a year, a season, a month, or a day and night.
Proceeding in this manner until the final two moments arise and those two moments cease, at that time it is called the "perfection of the preparatory application" (*prayoga-paripūri*).
Immediately thereafter, one is able to contemplate the various aggregates as arising in one moment and ceasing in one moment;

at that time, it is called the "perfection of the perception of death" (*maraṇa-saṃjñā-paripūri*), because the cessation of all states is itself death. Having contemplated this, he then forms this thought:
"What the Blessed One has taught—that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent—is truly well-spoken. At that time, one first cultivates the perception of impermanence until it is fully perfected.
Then, observing how one is oppressed by momentary change, one reflects upon the perception of suffering as taught by the Blessed One."
This is indeed well-spoken; for when the perception of suffering is fulfilled, there is no self-mastery. To recollect what the World-Honored One taught regarding non-self is indeed well-spoken;
for when non-self is fulfilled, since there is no self-mastery, one does not give rise to craving or delight toward the collection of empty formations.
Consequently, one does not give rise to attachment or delight toward the three realms; thus, the previously cultivated world-as-unpleasantness is brought to fulfillment.

Since one does not take pleasure in nirvāṇa, it is explained at length in this manner. The above has been a brief account of the *Vibhāṣā*’s interpretation; those who desire a detailed understanding should seek it for themselves by consulting the original text.

The ten *ṛjuka-dharmas* (straightforward dharmas) refer to the ten untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas within the bodies of the ten types of *aśaikṣa* (those beyond training), which are subsumed under the five aggregates (*skandha*).

As previously established in the section on the conditions for feeling (*vedanā-pratyaya*), this has already been briefly explained. Among these ten categories, that treatise explains the various ten universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*).

Regarding the eleven liberative entrances (*vimokṣāyatana*): this refers to relying upon the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the first three formless states (*ārūpya*) of mind, whereby one attains liberation from what was previously unliberated, up until the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Now, to examine this in detail: the four dhyānas manifest the meditative concentrations that serve as the basis;
the four immeasurables manifest the capacity for detachment from desire; and the first three formless states manifest the final limit of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).

Regarding the statement that the fivefold Dharma-body is like the "knowledge of equanimity" (*samatājñāna*) conditioned by feeling: in the new sūtras and śāstras, this is termed "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).

This is because conventional wisdom universally takes all phenomena as its object; thus, it is established under the name "equanimity. However, these four wisdoms open up the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) into the wisdoms of the Four Truths.

They are established as the knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge by virtue of their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), and they are established as the wisdoms of the Four Truths by virtue of their objects (*ālambana*). These two categories are mutually inclusive.

When analyzed, these constitute six knowledges (*jñāna*). These six, according to their respective applications, fully encompass the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*);
thus, they comprise the ten knowledges.

Regarding the statement that "each has four dharmas": it is easy to understand [the four] consisting of one's own person, sending a messenger, and so forth. Within the act of sending a messenger, because one may send another messenger on behalf of the first, there are likewise four.
Alternatively, there may be five dharmas, wherein the primary agent includes the four beginning with the messenger.

Regarding the comparison between what is called "similar" and "dissimilar": having concluded the discussion on the roots, powers, and factors of enlightenment as applied to those who have truly attained the Path versus those who speak of them falsely, although the words may appear similar, the resulting offenses are dissimilar; this can be understood from the text itself.
Regarding the "notion of phenomena" (*dharmasaṃjñā*): it should be stated as "the superior phenomenon," "the notion of the superior phenomenon," and so forth.

As for the phrase "speaking of oneself as having the causes and conditions of karmic retribution," it is as described in the subsequent passages: [the account of] Yaśas (Yan hao) correctly recollecting events from five hundred *kalpas*.
In the second fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says: "This person, in a previous life, passed away from the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*) and was reborn here."
[Interval. One who has received [the fruit] in the Heaven of No-Thought for five hundred kalpas may speak according to their mental conceptions without committing an offense;

this was already explained above in the first section. However, regarding the statement in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*: "One must not dwell together," and so forth, including "as before and after," Bao says:
This refers to the period prior to the commission of the offense; because the person is pure, one is permitted to participate in the two types of rituals.
Regarding "dwelling": if one commits an offense even once, one may no longer dwell with the bhikṣus as before; hence it says, "as previously.

If one commits it again, one likewise does not participate in the previous examples of communal dwelling; hence it says, "the latter is also equal. It further states: "formerly, when he was not yet in the stage of full ordination..."

He was not included among the ranks of the Sangha. Now, having committed an offense, he is as he was before; thus it says "as previously. Furthermore, to prohibit a repeated offense, it says "also later.

The interpretation of Master Chongyi is the same as this. Now, examining this in detail: if one has never committed an offense, the principle of co-residence is established with respect to both the past and the future.

However, if one commits an offense now, the prior sense of communal life is severed, and there is no longer any communal life for the future; therefore, it says "it is not permitted. As it was before, so it is also after.

This is so. According to the first volume of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, a grave offense (*pārājika*) is committed through repeated transgression, for there is no further vessel of the Path that can be destroyed.

Since ancient times, this has been commonly cited as a case of a grave offense within the Vinaya where the offense is committed repeatedly; for example, regarding the nun’s rule on physical contact, each instance of contact constitutes a separate grave offense.

Now, upon careful examination, the nun’s discipline is a profound safeguard; since the offense is extinguished when one changes gender (*vyañjana-parivṛtti*), how could it be analogous? If one commits the latter four offenses among those of the nuns, the principle may indeed apply.
However, if one commits the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*), one should judge the case according to the treatise.

● From here on, the second section concerns the two types of false accusation regarding teaching others with a sense of self-agency. In these cases, both the teacher and the student commit the offense together; thus, it should also be asked whether the act of teaching others constitutes a shared or non-shared offense.
Why is this so? If a specific name is designated—such as "you slandered so-and-so"—then one may say that both have committed the same offense.

However, if it is merely a general instruction—"you should slander someone"—then they should not be considered to have committed the same offense. This principle should also apply to cases such as matchmaking and the like.
Regarding the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for which there is no specific time or occasion: Devadatta committed the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* of causing a schism in the Saṃgha, yet it was not finalized.
As with the two cases of "contact" and so forth: first, contact; second, emission.

Regarding the "completeness of conditions": this refers to instructing another person to slander someone else so that the act of harming the object is accomplished; this constitutes the eight conditions of completeness.

As for the confession of offenses, it must necessarily be performed by oneself to dispel the karmic burden; if one were to rely on another as the causal agent, the requirements of the Vinaya texts would not be fulfilled.
The essential method for repentance is to cultivate proper deportment (*īryāpatha*).
Regarding the precepts on defiling families and the category of killing: these refer to acts such as irrigating and thereby damaging the ground, as described in the specific contexts (*nidāna*).
Regarding the remaining four precepts and the category of false speech: within this fourth position, there are the three admonitions and the two instances of slander.
Regarding the "distinctions of categories and stages" already explained above, this refers to the Vinaya Master Fu’s exposition on the observance and transgression of the precepts.
As for "relying on many conditions and much strength," it means depending upon numerous conditions and great effort.
One who destroys the factors of practice has already violated their conduct; regarding the utilization of the Saṃgha, such a person is not a complete cause of purity.

As for "harmony of the matter" (*vastu-sāmagrī*), the term *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is called "harmony of the matter. Harmony of the matter serves as the gateway; by means of it, one distinguishes what constitutes an obstruction. "Harmony of sentiment" (*citta-sāmagrī*) may be understood by analogy with this explanation.
Regarding "the time of destruction": it refers to the period when people abide in a state of respectful mind.

Regarding "the loss of precepts and the slandering of the correct [Dharma]": the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*), fascicle three, states: "Worldly people and non-Buddhists shall say: 'The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, act..."
Impure conduct is no different from that of the laity.
Those among the devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits who possess faith often say: "If one performs this act, even though it be in private, the devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits will all see it."
Regarding "lacking this objective condition": if one employs the right path while lacking this objective condition of what is not the path, it constitutes an offense.
Regarding "the three conditions as usual in the text": first, the Buddha’s dwelling place; second, the circumstance of having traveled until one becomes emaciated and thus violates the rule;
and third, the proximate condition.
That which is called "non-cause" is not the cause of pleasure.
The phrase "in this True Dharma, that which is to be abandoned through desire is taught" refers to the abandonment of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

"That which is taught regarding pride" refers to the conceit of grasping at a self within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). "The eradication of craving and the severance of all fetters" reveals the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Craving...
"Exhaustion and equality" refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Regarding the five faults of the distracted mind and eye, the *Pañcavargika* (Wufen lü), fascicle 2, states: "If one falls asleep with a distracted mind, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Jianlun* (Jianzong lun), fascicle 12, states: The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "If, after bathing, you desire to sleep, you should form this thought: 'I..."

One should rise before one's hair has even dried. If it is at night, one should likewise know the time, thinking: "When the moon reaches such-and-such a position, I shall rise," or "When the stars reach such-and-such a position.
Taking mindfulness of the Buddha as the foremost, one should focus on whichever of the ten wholesome paths of action accords with one's inclination.

Regarding the twelve types of dreams cited from the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, there are four kinds of dreams; however, within this context, they are entirely useless and are therefore not recorded here.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on the Establishment of Knowledge), fascicle five, states: "Dreams are false and unreal.

If dreams were real, then those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) within my Dharma would not attain liberation. Because all dreams are unreal, those who practice the holy life within my Dharma are able to exhaust suffering and achieve its removal."
Regarding the statement that "the others may also be understood in the same way": the *Mahīśāsaka* school recognizes seven colors: ghee, oil, milk, blue, yellow, red, and white.

The *Pañcavargika* school recognizes ten colors; these are the seven from the *Mahīśāsaka* plus vermilion, black, and honey. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* recognizes five colors: blue, yellow, red, white, and thin (or pale).
As for blue, it refers to the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) and the crown prince who has received his office, and so forth.
"That which is taught in that sutra" refers to the calculations of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
"Brahmins who have left the household life" and so forth refers to those who have faith in the non-Buddhists.

Regarding the statement that "the mind and mental factors experience suffering and pleasure," this means that based upon form (rūpa), there exist the mind and mental factors that experience suffering.
Joy (*sukha*). This is because safety and danger are shared in common.

Regarding the sixth [point], if one refers to the fourth and fifth sections below the section on internal form (*adhyātma-rūpa*), this means referring to the two preceding passages, the fourth and fifth.
Jue (Jue) says: "It would be better to say that the third and fourth are being referred to; to say 'fourth and fifth' is an error. The subsequent sections should be understood accordingly.
It should be understood that the *Jueyun* commentary states that "three thousand three hundred" is an error. The previous third [point] was an error; it was an error.

[The text] establishes fifty phrases through mutual combination, rather than explaining them based on the eleven matters of the external objects. It simply takes the sixth [category], internal form, and multiplies five by six to reach thirty;
adding another three hundred phrases, there would be a total of three thousand six hundred. Now, upon careful examination, this is not the case; such a thing does not exist.

The emission of semen without sexual desire is termed "expectation" (*kṣaṇa*). If it is for the sake of pleasure, how could that not be an expectation of desire? Therefore, the commentary is already sufficient;

there is no need to labor further. Regarding the three types of instruction: first, a bhikṣu instructing a bhikṣuṇī; second, instructing two [bhikṣuṇīs]; third, instructing other persons. This is according to the *Jianlun* (Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 10.

The second opinion states: For any part of the body that is sentient—excluding hair, nails, dry skin, and the non-vital essence (asman)—if the vital essence leaves its original location, whether it reaches the [sexual] organ or not, or even if it comes out and lands on another object such as a single fly, one incurs the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Regarding "for a long time, within dreams": the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Seeing) states: "If a bhikṣu sleeps with mental intention (*saṃjñā*), having first employed a preparatory means—namely, narrowing his legs and clenching his hands—and sleeps while maintaining that intention, and seminal emission occurs during the night in a dream, he incurs a *śeṣa* offense. (Based on this, it is understood that emission in a dream is not exempted unless there was no prior preparation and no such intention;
otherwise, it may be as stated in the text). If one emits impurity through the thought of desire, the *Jian lun* says: 'When a bhikṣu is about to rise from desire, he grasps [the organ]...'"
If semen is emitted by a woman, there is no offense. Why? Because it results in auspiciousness due to the act of sexual desire. If one reaches the [sexual] organ, there is a *pārājika* offense;

however, if the semen is emitted upon touching the woman’s body—whether by embracing or stroking—it is not an offense for the emission itself. Yet, because of the act of stroking and touching, one incurs a *thullaccaya* (residual) offense.

Regarding the phrase "if one sees a beautiful form," the *Śīlaparivarta* (or *Shanjian*) states: "Or if one sees the female organ and the organ becomes erect, even if one watches the emission of semen, it does not constitute a *thullaccaya* offense."
If one obtains [semen] after seeing it, and the seminal essence is discharged through the movement of the organ, one incurs a *śeṣa* offense (the same applies to sitting together with a woman).
In the text concerning expulsion (*pārājika*), since it is stated that "in all cases there is no intention to discharge," it is sufficient to know whether an offense has been committed or not.

Regarding the precept on touching and the cessation of lustful doubt, many say: "When people see it, they do not think it is merely a direct grasping," and so forth. As for "the woman being different from the man," etc.:
This distinguishes them from men.

Furthermore, regarding the broad explanation that applies to both monastics and laypeople, as well as to those who are close or distant, it may be understood from the *Cīvara-vastu* (The Fifth [Book]), which states: "As for women:
mothers, sisters, relatives and non-relatives, whether old or young, whether lay or ordained. It is also seen in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (The Twelfth [Book]), which says: "By means of mindfulness..."
Therefore, to touch the body of one's mother is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). It is the same for female sisters. Why is this?
Because women are enemies to those who have left the household life. If one’s mother were drowning in water, one must not laboriously take her up with one's hands.
If there is a wise bhikṣu, he should rescue her using a boat, or by means of bamboo, wood, rope, a staff, or even a *kāṣāya* robe. If the mother grasps the *kāṣāya*, [the bhikṣu should pull her up].
The Bhikṣu should merely hold her by the hem of her *kāṣāya* robe. If they reach the shore and the mother is terrified, he should say to her:
"Donor, do not fear. All things are impermanent; now that you have been saved from death, why should you continue to be afraid?

If the mother dies as a result of drowning while in his grasp, the Bhikṣu may take hold of her with his hands to perform the funeral rites; there is no offense. However, he must not abandon her or cast her away. If the mother [is still in] the mud...

It is the same with a well. The *Jì* (祇) states in the fifth fascicle: If a woman falls into the water and makes a cry of distress, seeking rescue from a bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu, perceiving her to be a snake, seizes her and pulls her out, he commits no offense. If he uses bamboo, wood, or rope to pull her out, it is likewise.
There is no offense. If a bhikṣu says, "Though you suffer, you must accept it as your past karma," there is no fault.

(Furthermore, it is stated that) the text regarding mothers, sisters, female relatives, and so forth is distinct: if they meet with joy and embrace the bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should remain established in right mindfulness.
If there is a different mind, it is a *śeṣa* offense.

Regarding "each four for non-humans and animals": [if one] transforms into a female animal and comes to take the place of a male, and so forth—these three cases should be explained according to the preceding [rules].
Fifty-fourth: when we reach the subsequent explanation of the text, its meaning will become self-evident. The same applies to the ninety *laṅ* [offenses].

If a touch constitutes a *śeṣa* (residual) offense, it is not called "neighboring" (*pārājika-anantarya*), nor is it called "grave. This is because it is not the cause of gravity; whereas stealing five [measures] results in four neighboring grave offenses.

Thus, there is a distinction between being a cause and not being a cause, and a difference between being neighboring and not being neighboring. Therefore, this question and answer are irrational. In reality, this is intended only for the case of touching in sexual misconduct.

Regarding the offense of *laṇ* (a type of theft): it was originally suspected that stealing four [units] would result in the attainment of the four fruits; however, this is not the case for the preparatory stage (*upāya*).
As for the distinction between internal and external objects: defilement arises within the body, whereas that which is outside the body is different.

Regarding the claim that multiple thefts not reaching the full measure constitute a continuous act of stealing: although this is so according to the subsequent text, it is not a statement that exhausts the principle.

If there is a single owner and the intent to steal has not ceased, one may speak of continuity. However, if there is a single owner and the intent to steal ceases after each instance—even if one performs a hundred thousand such acts—there is no continuity.
Nor does one commit a grave offense; thus, it is also indeterminate.

Regarding the three types of reprimands in the text: first, a secular woman; second, the Saṃgha; third, the Buddha. As for the secular woman: the first [reprimand] is appropriate as a general censure; the second clarifies the intention behind the reprimand;

the third, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, concerns those in whom lustful desire is particularly prevalent. Question: If lustful desire is so predominant, why does one not act [upon it]?
[Question: "Why did he not perform the Great Deed (mahākārya) [of passing away]? [Answer: "This person’s faculties were mature; he was destined to attain the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya).

Furthermore, he was to deliver the inhabitants of this city of Śrāvastī, numbering a full thousand households, yet was short by only one person. For this reason, he did not perform the Great Deed. Why have these women come to see him?
First, because worldly affairs are many and there are many pressing duties. Moreover, the dwelling place of those who have left the household life is one of tranquility."
1. Because it is peaceful and pleasant. 2. Because they wish to approach spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and hear the Dharma. 3.
Within the monastic quarters, there are various ornaments, painted beds, mats, and bedding that are delightful to the eye; for this reason, they come to look. Why do they come after the main meal?
Furthermore, it is said that it is not necessary to resolve all doubts at once. It is also said that laypeople have many affairs before their meals.

There are many circumstances. Sometimes they prepare food and drink or assign tasks to their servants; having attended to each of these matters according to the occasion, they subsequently accompany one another to climb mountains, wander through marshes, or visit monastic dwellings.
It is also said that they may go for the sake of hearing the Dharma. If they come before the meal, the bhikṣus will beg for alms.
Because they were not in the monastic quarters, why did the women enter the rooms? The answer is: because the renunciants have severed desire and are pure, the women entered out of faith.
Question: Why are there some who remain silent and others who do not? Some say that those with much lustful intent remain silent, while those with little lustful intent do not.
Others say that if she is an acquaintance, one remains silent; if she is not an acquaintance, one does not.

[The one who] does not remain silent. Furthermore, it is said that human natures differ: there are those who delight in concealing their transgressions and thus remain silent, and those who do not delight in hiding their faults and thus do not remain silent.
Others say: there are those who remain silent because they have no parents, brothers, husbands, sons, or daughters, and thus have nothing to fear or dread;
and those who do not remain silent because they do have things to fear and dread. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle three, states: "One who does not rejoice shall immediately go outside the room."
He said to the bhikṣus, "Venerable sirs, is it the nature of the Dharma that one may preach the Dharma to women for various reasons?
Having preached the Dharma to the many women through various causes and conditions, they paid their respects and departed. Maudgalyāyana said, 'As for those who preach the Dharma, they should say:
"The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are a field of merit that is excellent and auspicious; they are worthy of trust and reverence. Do not destroy yourselves on account of a minor matter. "
"Roots of goodness. Furthermore, it says: "By praising the various merits of Kālodāyin, one shall attain the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya).
To deliver a thousand families constitutes a great benefit; do not, seeing only minor circumstances, lose your own respect."

Regarding what was stated above in the section on the precept against sexual misconduct—namely, cases such as with one who is asleep, one recently deceased, or one whose body is partially decomposed—the present explanation is likewise based on the text of the Vinaya-vibhaṅga (Tiao-bu). The subsequent passage states:

"If a bhikṣu has physical contact with the body of a dead woman whose body is not yet decomposed, or with one that is mostly not decomposed, the Buddha declared this a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. If the body is half-decomposed or mostly decomposed, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
Regarding the phrase "not [applying] to those who possess discernment but have not yet died," the *Kṣudraka-vinaya* (Exposition on Sitting in the Open) states:

"A human female" refers to one who possesses discernment and whose life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not severed; [in such cases], this [rule] does not apply. As for "the hair touching hair" and so forth, according to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, if the body touches the hair, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Since these two have already been clarified by the pair of five and six [cases], how could there be another such pair?

This refers to the six cases of the *duṣkṛta* (吉羅) mentioned in the subsequent text, which serves as a counter-argument against the ancient masters who, despite lacking textual authority, falsely established the first case as a "pair. Specifically, the former Master Fuli said:
"If a woman comes to touch [the monk], there are four cases: first, moving the body and experiencing pleasure (this is the 'pair'); second, not moving the body and experiencing..."

"Delight. These two phrases constitute a *śeṣa* offense. Furthermore, there are two other cases: first, moving the body without experiencing delight; second, not moving the body without experiencing delight.
Because these two do not involve delight, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If a bhikṣu, with a defiled mind, makes a conscious effort to touch a woman...

All four permutations result in a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The Vinaya text, however, only specifies two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses for the woman coming [to meet him]; the other two permutations are *sthūlātyaya*, as are the four permutations involving a bhikṣu going [to meet her].
These six cases are all omitted [in the text]. The Master’s intention here is that within the section on minor infractions (*duṣkṛta*), there are six permutations in the Vinaya text.
1. Experiencing pleasure; 2. not experiencing pleasure (these are termed the "five-position phrases"). 3. Not receiving pleasure while moving the body; 4.

not moving the body while receiving pleasure (these two are termed "interlaced phrases"). 5. Not receiving pleasure and not moving the body; 6. receiving pleasure and moving the body (these two are termed "double-headed," also called "double-clarifying phrases").
Within the chapter, the interlacing of the third and fourth and the double-headed nature of the fifth and sixth are first described, followed by the presentation of the first and second.
[The opponent] objects: "Since the text already clarifies both [aspects] through the five and six [syllables], how can these first two phrases also constitute a pair?
The intent of this objection is as follows: if the first phrase among the 'residues' (śeṣa) is permitted to be a pair, then the first two of the 'auspicious' (śubha) should also be a pair.
If the first two of the auspicious are permitted to be a pair, then the five and six are also a pair; how then could the initial [phrase] be otherwise?"

"Secondly, one also obtains this pair. This is a counter-objection (*pratyavasthāna*). Next, the text establishes it in accordance [with the established doctrine], stating: "Therefore, it is known that the first two establish the positions," as explained at length in the *Śāstra*.
The intent of this establishment is as follows: based on the six cases of the *Auspicious* (*śubha*), one explains this section; hence it says, "Now, in explaining this, etc.
That is to say, regarding the passage where a woman touches a bhikṣu, the first sentence corresponds in meaning to the first of the *Auspicious* cases.

Regarding the "established position" (*sthiti*), it refers directly to the experience of pleasure. In the second phrase of the text, the meaning corresponds to the sixth couplet within the "Auspicious" (*śubha*) category:
the movement of the body experiences pleasure. According to principle, this should correspond to the fourth "crossing" phrase of the "Auspicious" category, which states:

"the non-movement of the body experiences pleasure. This [phrase] should likewise exist here within the "Residue" (*śeṣa*). Consequently, this residue consists of three phrases, as explained in detail in the relevant chapter, up to the calculation.

This constitutes eighteen phrases. Regarding the six phrases within the "Auspicious" category, for what reason does [the text] only rely on the three phrases concerning the experience of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) and fail to clarify the three phrases concerning the non-experience of pleasure (*asukha-vedanā*)?
The commentary explains: "This is a residual position; it is not necessary to establish the 'neither-painful-nor-pleasant' (*aduḥkhāsukha*) category."

Regarding the statement that "the same applies to the lower eight," a careful examination reveals this is not so. While acts such as *titana* might allow for the body to remain unmoved, how could this be the case for acts such as *pratikūla-maithuna*?
Therefore, one must further exclude these cases according to what is appropriate.
Regarding the four distinct positions: there are two phrases for the woman coming and two phrases for the bhikṣu going; thus, there are four. The others are all to be understood accordingly.
As for the statement that these three positions constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense (or even cases such as the three positions of a matchmaker), this refers to the original act itself.

Regarding one who intends to commit the offense of sexual misconduct and touches a woman: depending on whether she is clothed or otherwise, and before the act is completed, it constitutes a single class of *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
It is not divided into the three offenses of *pārājika*, *saṅghādisesa*, or *dukkaṭa*. Just as with matchmaking (*sañcaritta*), there is a distinction between *dukkaṭa* and *saṅghādisesa*;

likewise, if one intends to commit the fault of sexual desire by acting as a physical intermediary, these are all *thullaccaya* offenses and are not divided into *dukkaṭa* or *saṅghādisesa*. They are not divided.
This refers to the distinction between auspicious and inauspicious [conditions].
It is said that if a woman should grasp one’s feet in salutation, one should tell her to stand back a short distance;

or, at times, one should show her one's teeth and tongue so as to cause her pain, rather than allowing her to perceive the smoothness of a woman’s body. (It is further stated: To share a bed with a woman is contrary to the rules of decorum and gives rise to lustful thoughts.

[If] crossing [a stream], they should not touch the bed-frame (as all [other materials] such as wood or stone are treated accordingly). If a woman carries a heavy load and cannot lift it onto her shoulder, she may ask a bhikṣu for assistance;
he should not assist her. He should instruct other men or women to help support her.

If there are no others, the bhikṣu should lift the load to a higher place so that she can carry it. (It is also said: When traveling together through water, the bhikṣu should stay behind; [if she slips,] her foot—

To splash water on a woman is not dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*). If one acts out of lustful intent, it constitutes a *vyatikrama* (transgression). If one kicks water at a person with a lustful mind, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

(It is further stated: When begging for food, if a beautiful woman gives food to a bhikṣu and he perceives a lustful thought upon seeing her, he should set down his bowl on the ground and have another person hand it to him. (It is further stated: If a bhikṣu happens to encounter a woman in a narrow alleyway, he should...

Regarding "dwelling": if one acts competitively in a manner contrary to dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*), or if, with a lustful mind, one even touches a woman down to her feet—such as when a woman grasps one's feet—if there is a question as to whether the objective condition (*viṣaya*) and the mental state (*citta*) are present:
if a woman grasps one's feet, the objective condition exists but the mental state does not; this refers to the absence of the preliminary intention (*pūrvaprayoga-citta*).

If one touches robes, bowls, and so forth, the mental state exists but the objective condition does not, because such items as robes are not objects of defiled contact. As for touching one another in jest: [this constitutes a transgression].
It is when one touches [the object] by mistake while laughing in jest, with a mind free from defilement.
Regarding the "Deer Speech Precept," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "May all devas bear witness to my heart. This means that one intends for the devas to know one's heart.

"I beg a boon from you. This rule concerns instructing another to make a vow; its principle should be interpreted according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, for it is not identical [to other rules].
Regarding "like consuming ghee," the following text mentions a woman consuming ghee whose body was exposed; when a bhikṣu saw her, he said: "You..."
[The monk] said, "I have digested the ghee. He replied, "Venerable sir, I have digested the ghee. The Buddha said, "An *anavajja-pācittiya* (an offense of expiation for not being clear).

[He] further said: At that time, there was one wearing red garments who appeared in the form of a woman. Having seen her, he spoke, saying, "You are wearing red clothes," and so forth, until: "An *anavajja-pācittiya*. [Commentary:
The bhikṣu intended to refer to the woman's form by the name "ghee" (*ghṛta*) and so on. However, because it was not clear, it is an *anavajja*. If he had been clear...

If one knows [the situation], one incurs the *śeṣa* (residual) offense. However, the current *Tripiṭaka-saṃgraha-dharma* states that "thin leaves" refers precisely to the act of sexual intercourse between a man and a woman;
this is an extremely indecorous expression. Traditionally, it has been translated as the "precept against lewd speech," "evil cursing," and so forth, yet these are also merely "lewd.
Upon investigating the underlying principle, one does not violate this precept unless one actually utters such indecorous words.

Regarding the phrase "improper speech": one is only violating this precept when the words actually express sexual intercourse. Although such speech is not categorized as vulgar or evil, in the Sanskrit original, the term for "sexual intercourse" (*śayana*) was avoided;
thus, it was rendered as *yava-bandha*. *Yava-bandha* translates here as "barley chaff. Although the word used is *yava-bandha*, the intended meaning is *śayana*.

This was done so that those listening would not feel shame or embarrassment. Now, upon careful examination, it is certain that this school [the Vinaya tradition] does not agree with that [Sanskrit usage], as seen in the text.
He said: "If one manifests the aspect of suchness, how could one possibly utter disrespectful words?
'Regarding the leaves' means that for each individual leaf of speech, a formal act (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) is incurred.
[The Precept on Brokering Marriages]
Regarding the "Conditions" (*pratyaya*): according to the calculation of principles, it does not require the manifestation of objects to be fully clear.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, seventeen or twenty moments (*kṣaṇa*) constitute one instant (*tatkṣaṇa*). If it is as stated in the *Saṃyuktāgama*, fascicle 36:
One hundred and twenty kṣaṇas constitute one tatkṣaṇa. Sixty tatkṣaṇas constitute one lava, which contains seven thousand two hundred kṣaṇas.
Thirty lavas constitute one muhūrta, which contains two hundred and sixteen kṣaṇas.
Thirty muhūrtas constitute one day and night, which contains twenty small [muhūrtas].
Six thousand five hundred and ten *kṣaṇas* constitute one day and night for this body composed of the five aggregates;
such is the number of births and cessations that occur within its impermanence. (It is further stated: The increase and decrease of the day and night each last for one *lava*.
One month consists of one *muhūrta*, and thirty *muhūrtas* make up one full day and night. Within this period, there are four categories of variation regarding the length of the day and night.
The same applies to the increase: its maximum duration is eighteen [muhūrtas], while its minimum duration is twelve. There are fifteen positions where day and night are equal;
that is, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, day and night are equal.
From this point onward, the days decrease and the nights increase by one lava each, until the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, when the night [is equal].
There are sixteen *muhūrtas*. During the day there are fourteen [the remainder may be inferred accordingly]. As for the month of *Kārttika*, it is the eighth month according to Western reckoning;

since the dark fortnight precedes the bright fortnight, one knows that the white half of *Kārttika* corresponds to the fifteenth day of the ninth month. *Mṛgaśīrṣa* refers to the period after the middle of the ninth month. The sequence of black and white [fortnights] follows the previous rule.
A *muhūrta* is translated as "a brief moment" (*xūyú*). Regarding the four different categories: from the eighth day of the ninth month throughout the year, one night increases by one [unit].

From the eighth day of the third month onward, the day increases continuously; that is, on the eighth day of the third month and the eighth day of the ninth month, the day and night are equal, thus forming four categories.
As the *Abhidharmakośa* states in verse twelve: "One hundred and twenty kṣaṇas constitute one tatkṣaṇa.
Ten of these are a lava (translated here as 'ten'). Thirty of these are a muhūrta. Thirty of these are a day and night. Three...
Ten days and nights constitute a month; twelve months constitute a year. Within that [year], the nights are reduced by half. (Commentary: This is the tenet of the Sarvāstivāda school;
it cannot be reconciled with the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.
Regarding the statement that there are twenty types of women, although only nineteen are listed by name, according to the commentary, one of them—the maidservant—is omitted from the middle.

Regarding the phrase "accomplishing the first four matters," the supplementary explanation states: "In principle, it should be said that they are accomplished within a single thought-moment or a brief interval."
There are two matters. Now, examining the meaning of the commentary (*śāstra*), it says: the first two refer to the act of being husband and wife over a long period of time;
the latter two concern the act of being husband and wife for a temporary duration. Thus, they constitute four matters.

Regarding these various fourfold sets (*catuṣkoṭi*): in the first set, all [factors] are self-originated across all three times; in the second, all are self-originated in the first two times and driven by the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in the third time;

in the third, all are driven by the latent dispositions in the middle time and self-originated at both ends; and in the fourth, all are self-originated in the first time and driven by the latent dispositions in the latter two times.
Regarding the four middle lines where speech and writing are combined, these are all the first speech and the latter two writings (the remaining lines follow this pattern).
As for the sixty-four lines formed by combining one or two dharmas, this means that speech and writing, as well as their respective characteristics, each constitute sixteen;
thus, there are sixty-four. Now, wishing to explain and interpret this, I shall elaborate upon the text according to the meaning of the commentary.
This is to clarify what is right and what is wrong. Furthermore, regarding the extensive exposition: among the sixteen [categories], the first four are composed of a single dharma alone;
the remaining three sets of four are composed of two dharmas. Therefore, it is said that they are "either one dharma or two dharmas intermingled."

Furthermore, regarding the sixteen items headed by "speech" (*vāc*): there are four sets of four for pure speech; four sets of four for speech and writing; [the details of] the text have already been extensively set forth. There are four sets of four for speech alone;
four sets of four for the characteristics of speech. The text abbreviates both. "Fingers" (*aṅguli*) refers to manifest signs; it is also like this.
Next, regarding the sixteen phrases headed by "writing" (*lipi*): there are four sets of four for pure writing; four sets of four for writing and seals. The text is extensive therein.

[The text] emerges. Regarding the fourteen [sections on] written signs and the fourteen [sections on] spoken words, the wording is abbreviated and extracted. The remaining two sets of sixteen are likewise abbreviated and extracted;
they are set forth in detail within the chapters. The first sixteen are concluded. As for the remaining three sets of sixteen, it is merely stated that "the other three are each likewise."
Next, the interrelation of the three types of dharmas is explained. The chapter states: "As for the forty-eight phrases, this means that speech, writing, and seals each constitute twelve;
thus there are forty-eight. However, the extant text currently contains only sixteen phrases. Regarding the first twelve:

speech, writing, and seals constitute one set of four (the text provides these in full). Speech and signs constitute another set of four (one phrase is provided in full within the text, while the remaining three are abbreviated).
...). The above completes the twelve phrases of the first position. Next, regarding the twelve phrases of the second position:
"Writing" and "seal" constitute one tetrad (the text is extensive for this one phrase; the remaining three phrases are abbreviated and not set forth).

"Writing," "seal," and "speech" constitute one tetrad (the text is abbreviated and not present). "Writing," "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), and "speech" constitute one tetrad (the text is abbreviated and not present). Next, the third position has twelve [phrases].
Regarding the "phrases" (*pada*): the texts are all largely absent. First, the phrase of mutual speech; second, the phrase of mutual writing;
third, the phrase of both speech and writing. As for the twelve phrases of the fourth position, these are likewise entirely missing from the texts.
Regarding the latter three sets of twelve within the chapter, the commentary states: "The text is simply one."
Fourth: Regarding the omission of the final two sets of four and the remaining two heads, they are all briefly not analyzed; as was extensively analyzed above, they may be found by looking there.
Next, to analyze right and wrong: it is asked whether these various phrases of the Dharma are composed based on the mutual intermingling of their own respective characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Is it performed by relying on the three periods [of time] and combining whichever methods are appropriate for each? Or is it performed by relying on the three periods and determining which specific methods to combine?
Or is it performed by relying collectively on the meanings of the preceding three? If that were so, what would be the fault? There would be faults in all four cases.
First, if one relies on the mutual correlation of the individual characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the [four] conditions themselves, there should be only one set of four, and no more.

Second, if one relies on the application of whichever method is appropriate among the three times (*adhvan*) to correlate the factors, this refers to the explanation in the text of the latter two sets of four.
Furthermore, it is unreasonable to omit the remaining two heads [of the argument]. For instance, if one were to deliberate with a messenger, saying:

"We shall simply employ these three methods universally; there is no need to fix upon using 'speech' at the initial stage, 'writing' at the intermediate stage, and 'immediate action' at the final stage," then the sixteen [categories] would already be sufficient when integrated with the three methods according to the text. Why then must one further distinguish the latter two?

Regarding the four [categories] and the other two heads: if one were to further analyze them, consider for instance the second "four" within the second position, which states that "writing is three, and speech is one," making four.
How does this differ from the first "four" in the first position, where "all writings are three, and speech is four"?
There is no difference, because those three factors are not restricted to their time of application. One should understand it accordingly. The second...
The third and fourth tetrads of the second stage are identical to the second tetrad of the first stage.
The first tetrad of the third stage is identical to the first tetrad of all stages [subsequent to it], and the third tetrad of the first stage.
The second tetrad of the third stage is identical to the first tetrad of the second stage. The third tetrad of the third stage...

The second and fourth phrases of the third position are identical to those of the second position; the second and fourth phrases of the fourth position are identical to the first and fourth phrases of the third position;
and the third and fourth phrases of the fourth position are identical to the second and fourth phrases of the third position.
Therefore, this is not logical. Thirdly, regarding the three periods of time, which specific method is to be applied?
Regarding the "various phrases": this means that within the initial set of terms, one must necessarily employ "day and night," while in the subsequent fixed application, one employs "immediately.
Proceeding thus by successive extension, there are forty-eight [phrases]. Although there is no logical contradiction [in this], for what reason are one dharma and two dharmas interspersed therein?

Why is it not distinguished that speaking of all three times together constitutes the first phrase; that the first two terms followed by one written character constitute the second phrase; and that the intermediate terms [constitute the third]?
A preceding word and two subsequent characters form the third phrase; a preceding single character and two subsequent phrases form the fourth phrase.
The same applies to other words and their combinations. Is it not so? Yet, in this text, there are four instances where the phrasing is consistently pure prose.

Furthermore, when the initial prose is combined with two subsequent verses, this constitutes the second set of four, and so on, even when prose and verse are intermingled. As for these four: [The text continues with the enumeration of the four categories.]

As for those who claim that three categories constitute the method of the *pada* (phrases): within the systems of one category and two categories, they lack the fourfold *pada* method previously analyzed;
when three categories are combined with the middle category, they further lack the sixteenfold meanings according to their respective applications across the three times previously explained.

How could it be otherwise? Not only are the latter two sets of four and the latter two headings omitted, but based on this principle, it appears that the translators of the Vinaya [failed to preserve the full structure].
The translation of the text is excellent, yet it is insufficient in conveying the full meaning.

Regarding the numerous instances where the beginning and end correspond to one another, Zongchong stated that they exceed forty thousand. Now, upon careful examination, these are merely calculated by counting phrases to manifest the virtues;

however, if one were to actually investigate them in detail, one must proceed as previously analyzed in order to exhaustively grasp the underlying principle. As for the number of such phrases: this...
These are minor matters, left to the discretion of those who study them.
Regarding the three types of *laṅgi* and three types of *dvaya*, they are: first, receiving speech; second, hearing speech; and third, not receiving speech.
Regarding those who each lack one of these [three factors]: the original intention was for one, two, or all three factors to combine to act as a mediator;
yet when the time comes, they are deficient according to the circumstances of the three periods.

Regarding "up to the extensive phrases": this refers to a case where, using a single woman as the starting point and the end, one intends to act as a matchmaker from beginning to end, yet at the actual time of the act, the necessary conditions are lacking.
Regarding the "perception of matchmaking": when a man and woman have not yet had contact, one perceives them as having already done so, and thus brings them together.
Some say that it is like a husband and wife who, having already received a document of divorce, now reconcile; they claim this constitutes no offense.

Now, upon careful examination, this is actually a transgression born of delusion regarding the teachings. According to principle, in addition to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one should further incur the fault of ignorance (*ajñāna*). For what reason would one dare to sever all hope [of repentance]?

The four supports for the precept against constructing an oversized dwelling are: relying on living under a tree, relying on rag-robes, relying on alms-food, and relying on decomposed medicine. If one violates the first by constructing a dwelling, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If one violates any of the remaining three supports, it is as in the case of [keeping] extra robes, eating in a separate group, traveling together, or consuming food at an improper time without having formally accepted it.

And so forth. As for medicines kept beyond seven days, these are all *pāyattika* offenses. Since the facts and characteristics differ—whether they have an owner or no owner, whether they are measured or unmeasured—they may not be combined into a single formal act (*karmavācanā*).
[In the case of] first speaking discordantly and later vexing the Saṃgha, or first harboring resentment and later reviling.
They are both the same precept.

The Venerable Sūtra Master (Shou Lüshi) of old said that failing to inform those in the preceding room constitutes the second [offense]. He asked himself: "If that is so, why is it listed first in the text? He answered:
"In the section on the precept against killing, it states: 'Killing an animal is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense),' placing it at the beginning; whereas the [other] ninety offenses are listed below."
In the middle [section], since that [text] begins with the first [offense], this is likewise.

Regarding the cases of three, two, or one offenses: although one may have committed a subsequent precept, within that subsequent precept there may also be the two types of offenses—*aniyata* (undetermined) and *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense)—depending on whether the specific circumstances are present or not;
thus, there may be three, two, or one. However, upon examining the commentary (*śāstra*), it is stated as follows:
The commentator explains: regarding the white-robed [layperson] who begs for an excessive amount, none of it may be retained. Why is this called "only lacking the first condition"?
If the fifth were lacking, there would have to be six *pārājika* offenses; however, when both are lacking, they are subsumed within the fifth, and their distinction is clarified within the mind.
Therefore, there are six.
The "last two lumps" refers to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Tàolùn).
Regarding "the offense of *thullaccaya* for destroying a village of spirits": this refers to the subsequent precept concerning the felling of trees, which incurs a *thullaccaya*.

As for "admonishing the deity to be patient," according to the *Samantapāsādikā* (Jiàn-lùn), chapter fifteen, because of the felling of the tree, the arm of a spirit-child was injured; thus, the tree deity spoke.
The Buddha. The Buddha spoke a verse for him: "If a person gives rise to a mind of anger, it is like a runaway chariot;
that a charioteer can restrain it is not to be considered difficult. That a person can subdue their own mind of anger—this is truly difficult.

Upon hearing this Dharma, the tree deity attained the stage of Srotāpanna (the deity’s attainment of the Way means that he has achieved necessary penetration and realization). *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Chapter Ten. The tree deity said: "My children are still young."
During the eight nights of winter, the cold wind pierced through the bamboo and the freezing frost was extreme. "In what place shall I find safety for my children? he thought.
The Buddha commanded the other spirits, "You must provide them with a dwelling. Because of the Buddha’s words, the spirits immediately granted them a residence.
In the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle three, the name Kāśyapa is explained by his great discernment and because he was born into a family of great wealth and status. Second...

1. Because they are able to renounce great wealth, high status, and noble lineage to leave the household life; 2. Because they are able to practice the great dharma of *dhūta* asceticism, having few desires and being content; 3.
Because they are honored and supported by kings, emperors, nāgas, spirits, and those of great knowledge and renown; 4.
Because they renounce the great worldly gains and offerings, possessing few desires and practicing contentment while begging for alms—just as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana achieved [these qualities].
Because he possesses great wisdom and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and because he has accomplished great merit, he is named Mahākāśyapa.
Regarding the phrase "one who built many rooms," the *Jī* (祇) states in the sixth fascicle that he constructed five hundred private chambers.

Regarding the request from the birds, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle six, states: When the birds gathered at dusk, the bhikṣu said, "O Śakuntaka birds, each of you must give me one feather;

However, having no other choice, they each plucked a feather and placed it on the ground. In the morning, he requested them again; at that time, the birds immediately departed. This is a different account.

They then deliberated together, saying: "We must depart; it is no longer fitting for us to return. Fortunately...
In the second verse of the *Pañcavargika*, it says: "The wise do not speak of begging; one who speaks of begging is certainly not wise.

Regarding the five *yā* and four *yā*: the five *yā* are as explained in the twenty-second fascicle of the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, which has already been cited above in the section on the precept against sexual misconduct.

As for the four *yā*, they are as explained in the second fascicle of the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, as was already analyzed above in the commentary on the first fascicle in the explanation of the meaning of a *bhikṣu*.
Regarding the sixth [section], which speaks of the measurements for the height and width of a hut: the walls are one zhang and two chi high;
