There are forty-nine such permutations (seven times seven), none of which constitute a valid formal motion (*jñapti*). As for the nine general categories, the first is...
First, those who love my enemies; second, those who hate my good friends; third, those who hate my own body in the past, will hate it in the future, and are hating it in the present.
Since there are three for each of the three time periods, they constitute nine.
Regarding the arising of anger toward insentient objects: as secular texts say, during the severe cold of winter, even commoners speak of resentment, indignation, and lamentation.
This is a general explanation. There are ten causal conditions; what is now discussed regarding slandering others pertains to nine in total, though it may also apply to all ten.
This can be understood through reflection.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "eye-consciousness arises following seeing," the verse in the second fascicle of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* says:

"If the eye arises following seeing, the ear-element arises following hearing. To state in the commentary that "eye-consciousness arises following seeing" is incorrect; for the twentieth fascicle states: "The eye itself sees form;
it is not that eye-consciousness sees, nor is it wisdom, nor is it the aggregate [of the sense-faculties]. It is not seen by the [unconditioned] group."
"Because it obstructs visible form. (Commentary: "One's own eye" (*svāṃśacakṣus*) refers to the eye-faculty that is presently producing consciousness; this is called "one's own eye.

Because it performs its own specific function together with the eye-consciousness, it is termed "one's own" (*svāṃśa*). In the new sūtras and śāstras, it is called the "homogeneous eye" (*sabhāgacakṣus*).

As for the phrase "it is not that eye-consciousness sees," this is the established tenet of the Sautrāntika school, because they maintain that it is not the eye, but consciousness, that sees. Furthermore, there is... [text continues].
Other schools maintain that the wisdom associated with visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna-saṃprayukta-prajñā*) is able to see visible forms.

Furthermore, there is a teacher of the Sautrāntika school who holds a distinct view, asserting that the conjunction of the eye and visual consciousness is called "seeing. Now, the Sarvāstivādins refute both of these positions, stating: "Because obstructed forms are not seen.

This means that when the mind and mental factors apprehend an object, there is no obstruction or separation; if it were consciousness and so forth that sees, it should also see what lies beyond obstructions. Therefore, [the eye alone] sees.

The view that consciousness sees is not consistent with correct reasoning. In this chapter, although the cited scriptural passage resembles the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, its statement that "consciousness sees" accords with the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
Thus, the fifth fascicle, in the "Great Chapter on the Faculties and so forth," states: "Only consciousness is able to see."
The eye receives its name; the detailed explanation is as in that [text].
Regarding "the divine eye is not a physical faculty": the divine eye is a supernormal power (*abhijñā*), and thus differs from the physical eye.
As for "the explanation is clear": when sound is apprehended through hearing, it is logically inconsistent for doubt to arise subsequent to seeing; rather, form is apprehended through seeing.
Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): in principle, [the four types of wrong view] do not arise subsequent to hearing or doubt.
As for "doubt regarding self and others," these four each combine with three faculties (*indriya*).
Although it is possible for these four to be false, this implies they may possess the quality of falsity; it does not mean they are definitively false.
Regarding the phrase "because seeing and hearing are not certain": this does not mean that one has definitively and clearly seen the person entering or leaving the grove;

nor does it refer to hearing the sound of their moving the bed and so forth. However, since one does not know for certain that they have actually committed an offense, it cannot constitute the faculty of seeing (*darśana-indriya*) or the faculty of hearing (*śravaṇa-indriya*).
Rather, it is categorized as being subsumed under the faculty of doubt (*vicikitsā-indriya*).
If there were a third [type of perception], then there would be no remaining three types of perception. According to reason, one must admit that the root of perception arises spontaneously.
Furthermore, others say that when a person commits an offense, that very act constitutes the root of perception; thus, it coexists with other roots. The same applies to the category of doubt.
Therefore, the explanation provided in the *Śāstra* does not fully capture the underlying principle.

Regarding the statement that "from another, there should be only two": since the self, the other, and doubt each contain three roots, while from another there are only two, does this not contradict the established rule?

As for the phrase "citing slander as an established case," this explains the meaning of these roots. Previously, four gates were set forth; in the second gate, it was stated: "The determined roots are many."

The few cases where the "empty" (vitaṇḍā) and "substantial" (vastu) are not simultaneous are equal [in number]. Here, in order to explain this, the word "middle" (sama) is indicated. Therefore, it says: "Regarding the accusation, whether it is established or not.

As for the two types—self and other—if they exist, the accusation is established; however, if one is necessarily lacking in virtue, the accusation is also not established. Yet, it is not established... [text ends].
This is slander.
One who has realized the true meaning but is weak in strength, because of their distorted thoughts, will be unable to provide a coherent response to each question when the Sangha interrogates them.

If there is no [actual fault], one may incur the offense of groundless accusation (*ābhyākhyāna*). When a real basis (*mūla*) replaces the basis of perception (*saṃjñāmūla*), this is also termed "non-existence.

However, because the person possesses virtuous qualities, it constitutes a formal act of suspension (*utkṣepa*). On the other hand, if there is simply no basis of perception and one falsely alleges another's transgression, this constitutes an accusation.
Thus it is said, "one may incur the offense of groundless accusation. Because the real basis has been replaced and the five virtues are lacking, it does not constitute a formal act of suspension.

However, because the *indriya* (faculty) exists, it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense of "slandering one who has been formally accused" (*uddiṣṭa*). Some commentators explain: "To 'constitute' means to accuse;

'not to constitute' means to slander. Regarding "not constituting an accusation by slandering": since the previous case constituted an accusation, the current case does not constitute a slander; since the previous case was a slander, the current case does not constitute an accusation.
Now, upon careful examination, this explanation does not accord with the original intent; therefore, the previous explanation is superior.
"Non-identity with perception" means being identical to a prior perception, or being within a prior perception;

even when a real faculty replaces it, this is called "non-existent," and when it is simply absent, this is also called "non-existent. For this reason, there may also be cases where an accusation is raised that does not constitute a valid accusation.

Regarding the statement that "seeing and hearing are not called the roots of doubt," this is the underlying intention [of the author]: Why does he not here speak of the root of doubt as the "root of doubt through seeing" or the "root of doubt through hearing"?

Regarding the statement that "the matter exists and is real": although the act of entering the forest and moving the bed exists, and though it is seen with the eyes and heard with the ears—thus not being false—it is nevertheless said to exist and be real.
However, doubt pertains to both what is seen and heard, and furthermore, it pertains to both existence and non-existence.

"Those cases where seeing or hearing is not yet established" means that doubt arises by taking both the instances of seeing and hearing as its object, and it also arises regarding instances where there is both an offense and no offense;
therefore, at the time of seeing or hearing, one has not yet definitively known whether an offense has been committed.

Regarding the fact that the categories of doubt are not exhaustive: if one says "doubt regarding what is seen," this only reveals doubt conditioned by what is seen (*darśana*), but does not reveal doubt conditioned by what is heard (*śruta*) or by existence and non-existence (*sadasat*);
therefore, it is not exhaustive. If one says "doubt regarding what is heard," the same should be stated for this case as well.
This principle applies to all four cases; that is, doubt arises regarding the four possibilities of seeing, hearing, existence, and non-existence.

Specifically, "doubt regarding whether an accusation is established or not" refers to the doubt that one has falsely accused someone who is innocent, as well as the doubt that one has failed to accuse someone who is guilty.

That is to say, if one suspects without cause that someone is concealing [a fault] and thus accuses them, it constitutes a false accusation. Conversely, if there is a suspicion based on valid grounds (*mūla*), this constitutes a legitimate basis for bringing forth the charge, and the concealment is thereby established.
This is a denial.

Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the broad and the narrow: examining the intent of the *Shu* (Commentary) now, doubt concerning the sense bases (*indriya*) is broad, because it arises in all four instances—seeing, hearing, existence, and non-existence.
Doubt concerning the horizontal [objects] is narrow, because it doubts only three of the sense bases. Yao says: "Doubt concerning the sense bases is broad..."
Regarding the five offenses, "doubt concerning the object" (heng-yi) is narrow because it concerns the three roots [of greed, hatred, and delusion].

Other commentators explain that "doubt concerning the object" is broad because it applies to all three roots, whereas "doubt concerning the root" (gen-yi) is narrow because it arises only from what is seen or heard. We adopt the former explanation as it accords with the intent of the *Shu* (Commentary).
Thus, the *Shu* explains below: "Doubt concerning the root arises from the matter of what is seen or heard. This refers to the matter that is seen, such as entering...
Regarding forests and the like, as well as objects of service such as moving beds and so forth, one may have doubts within these matters as to whether there is an offense or no offense.

Furthermore, it is said that [cognition] does not arise from the two preceding faculties; rather, there is a distinct arising of visual and auditory cognition, yet one does not doubt that which is seen or heard.
Regarding "doubting matters that do not constitute an offense," this means: it does not arise from the two preceding faculties [of sight and hearing].

It refers to cases where one has a distinct lack of clarity regarding what was seen or heard—such as entering a forest—and yet does not doubt the capacity for seeing or hearing itself, but instead wonders, "Did I see it? Did I not see it? and so forth.
Regarding the case where a perception (*saṃjñā*) and a factual basis (*mūla*) share the same object and both arise in relation to an offense:

this refers to a mistaken perception that, together with the factual basis, regards a point of transgression as an actual offense. Thus, one perception is assigned to each of the three bases to demonstrate their mutual similarity.
Although they are shown to be similar, since the names of the perception and the basis are different, there is no fear of confusion between them. If...
The doubt is horizontal; its characteristics are not analogous. Therefore, the three faculties are not individually assigned to doubt.

Furthermore, were they to be so assigned—if seeing were assigned to doubt, it would conflate the faculty with the doubt; one should know that the same applies to assigning hearing to doubt. Thus, by speaking of doubt in general, the horizontality is revealed.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "one may also consider it analogous to the first two faculties (*indriya*)": the previous explanation treated the actual faculties (*bhūta-indriya*) of seeing and hearing according to their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), whereas the designation "faculty of doubt" was established according to their general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Now, in this treatise, horizontal conceptualization (*tiryag-vikalpa*) is a specific characteristic; therefore, it is analogous to the first two faculties.
However, horizontal doubt is a general characteristic; therefore, it is analogous to the third faculty, which is doubt.
Question: Regarding the eight phrases of minor falsehood (*mṛṣāvāda*), why is it that these [four] lack six of those phrases? Within minor falsehood, there are four phrases:

claiming to have seen what was not seen, claiming to have heard what was not heard, claiming to have touched what was not touched, and claiming to have known what was not known. Furthermore, there are another four phrases which should be understood as the opposites of these.
Why is it that among the [types of] slander (*paiśunya*) there are only the first two phrases of minor falsehood, while the remaining six are absent?
Regarding the transgression of objects that are not perceived through direct contact: according to the commentary on the *Mingliao shu*, the root of doubt arises from all five sense-objects.
For example, seeing a woman’s garment on a bhikṣu’s bed, one immediately suspects a transgression; or hearing a woman speaking with a bhikṣu;
or smelling the scent of a woman on her clothing; or seeing her give only a small portion of alms when begging for food.
Or [if one] gives alcohol and so forth; or if a bhikṣu touches another person; it should be known that the same applies here.
Based on this, it should also be understood that doubt may arise after such contact. The rest can be inferred.

Regarding the phrase "doubt arising from doubt regarding the two": this refers to doubt arising from what has been seen or heard. According to tradition handed down until now, it is universally said that Dharmagupta inverted the interpretation of the meaning;
he intended to speak of non-existence (*asat*) but first explained existence (*sat*). Now, upon careful examination, this is not necessarily so.
It is not on the basis of this specific meaning that one should explain his inversion.
It should be said that the third and fourth [categories] involve doubt and falsehood, while the fifth and sixth are free from doubt and free from falsehood.
In this chapter, the order has been inverted for the sake of making the phrasing more convenient.

Regarding the second mind being verified by the third and fourth minds: since the second [mind] in the text is already characterized by "having thought" (*sa-saṃjñā*) and "not forgetting," this verifies that the first [mind] has "thought" and does not forget.

Since the third and fourth [minds] in the text are characterized by "having doubt" (*sa-vicikitsā*), "forgetting," and "not forgetting," this proves that the first two [minds] possess "characteristics" (*nimitta*) and involve "not forgetting" and "forgetting.
Thus, the ancient masters spoke of the mind as "having thought" and "not forgetting."

Regarding the term "one who has attained [the basis]": this refers to the underlying intention, namely that while the object before him is actually pure, he maintains a coarse and unrestrained perception regarding external appearances.
When that slanderer sees, hears, or suspects those coarse signs, he forms the thought: "Based on these coarse signs, he must certainly have committed an offense.
This is the "perception" (saṃjñā). Yet, when the time comes for the actual slander, he says: "I have no such perception; I..."

Regarding "actually seeing" and so forth: the Master’s intention here is to explain that one gives rise to a retrospective mind, thinking, "I saw," "I heard," or "I suspected" that they committed an offense;

this constitutes the root of perception (*saṃjñā*). Since it is described as being based on perception, how could it constitute a false accusation? Therefore, [the opponent's position] is known to be unreasonable.

Regarding the contradiction between the preceding and the subsequent: the former statement says there are no characteristics of seeing, hearing, or doubting, while the latter states, "I have seen, heard, or doubted you.
If there are no internal mental characteristics of seeing and so forth, how can one verbally claim to have seen them? This is a direct contradiction.
To name it thus would be redundant.
As for the statement, "The single [term] is the same as the latter six; that which manifests the six is yours," this is logically tenable based on what is currently manifesting.
However, the two additional phrases added [therein] do not accord with reason.
Regarding the second thought of minor lying, which involves the desire to speak such words as "I did not see" and so forth:

that second thought of minor lying states, "If a bhikṣu has not seen, heard, touched, or known, yet there is within him a semblance of having seen and so forth, and he says 'I did not see' and so on—knowing [the truth] but speaking falsely, it is a *pāyattika*.
Although this too is a case of having the perception [of what one claims], it is not a lie; nevertheless, he utters those words.
Not seeing constitutes falsehood, which is contrary to one's mind; conversely, manifesting that one sees means it does not constitute falsehood.

Therefore, within this category of slander, if one speaks of having seen, it likewise does not constitute slander. Thus, the treatise states: "It is like the second thought-moment of minor falsehood," and so forth.

The former judgment [of the Vinaya masters] classified five instances of lying as *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), while the second instance of lying was taken to apply only to those whose hearts were insincere. If this refers to the ancient interpretation, it would result in self-contradiction;
if it refers to the present interpretation, there is no room for such a self-proclamation.

Regarding the statement that "the absence of thought is not false, whereas the presence of thought is": when one originally perceives a preceding object and forms a pure understanding, each such perception constitutes "no-thought.
Later, when perceiving that same object, one suddenly claims there was an offense; this is precisely the falsity of what was previously considered non-offensive.
This principle for resolving doubts regarding the mind of falsity should be applied accordingly.
Regarding "to prevent [the use of] such artifice": if I had originally harbored doubt without falsehood, it could be said that I have committed slander;
however, since I was entirely without doubt at first and only later developed doubt, it should not constitute slander. To prevent such artifice, both cases are judged to constitute slander.

If one previously held a perception, even if it were false, it could be said that slander has been committed; however, since I was entirely without doubt at first and only later developed doubt, it should not constitute slander. To prevent [this], [both are judged as slander].

Because of this skillfulness, it constitutes a denial (and so forth). Therefore, one does not say "there is no perception" with reference to what exists; rather, it refers to the meaning of the second clause in the text.
If there were first a perception, then even at the time of that denial, one would still have to falsely negate it before the denial could be established—how much more so now at the outset?

Since the prior mention of "non-perception" (asaṃjñin) is sufficient to constitute the charge of denial, why is it necessary to state that there is a separate phrase for the denial of "perception" (saṃjñin)?
It is said to be "non-perception" only in contrast to that phrase; therefore, the subsequent commentary concludes: "Thus, one does not speak of 'non-existence' in opposition to 'existence'."

The question regarding whether "hearing" and "doubt" exist or not, etc., is a response to the words [of the opponent]. This describes the meaning of the ancient master's objection. The ancient master’s objection states:

"If 'hearing' and 'doubt' exist, it conforms to what precedes while obstructing what follows. (To "conform to what precedes" means to conform to the preceding text which says "did not see"; to "obstruct what follows" means to obstruct the subsequent statement made at the time of the slander that he "heard and doubted.")

[If one] commits [an offense] and yet succeeds in establishing a ground for slander (abhyākhyāna). "Hearing and doubting" (*śruta-vicikitsā*) are likewise non-existent; "following the latter" obstructs the former. ("Following the latter" means following the subsequent fault. Regarding "the body and time succeeding in slander": it is non-existent within the text.
"Obstructing the former" means obstructing the previous case where it was stated simply as "not seeing. Now, examining this in detail, one should also speak of "hearing and doubting.

If these exist, they follow the former and act as an obstruction to "hearing and doubting"; if these are non-existent, they follow and thus obstruct the former. The intent of the present chapter is to recount this ancient objection; therefore, it says "if... [and so forth].
If this "existence" can be spoken of as being "only not seen," then this accords with what preceded. Furthermore, one should also say that the Way is neither heard nor doubted;
why then is "only not seen" singled out? This contradicts what preceded.

Regarding those who have found it difficult to understand and have criticized [this work] since ancient times: various people have remarked that the explanations of the ancients are difficult to comprehend and their expressions are so disordered as to be hard to grasp.
Now, taking the essential meaning of the ancients, I have composed this elegant prose to manifest its significance. As for what was said to be difficult by the ancients:
This refers to the objection that [the text] follows the preceding [case] while obstructing the subsequent one, and so forth. Regarding what is called the "ancient interpretation":

first, it provides a general discussion on seeing, hearing, and suspecting, each of which has three types. [The author] himself and others maintain that there are three roots for these, though this master does not establish a third root for "suspecting" (doubt).

Next, regarding the correlation with the Vinaya text: since all three types of "seeing" are absent, the preceding passage merely specifies "not seeing. As for "hearing" and "suspecting," although they lack the two categories of "self" and "other," [they are still accounted for].

Regarding "hearing and doubting": because the mental state of conceptualization (*saṃjñā-citta*) still exists, and the faculties of hearing and doubting remain present, one cannot say that there is neither hearing nor doubting.

This is the intention of the ancient masters. Since the mental state of conceptualization exists and hearing and doubting are present, it does not obstruct what precedes; and since those respective acts of hearing and doubting by oneself or others are absent, it does not obstruct what follows.
If this is so, and since the mental state of conceptualization, along with hearing and doubting, is already present, how can slander be possible? It was precisely as before.
The commentary explains: By concealing the conceptual mind (*vikalpa-citta*) and raising only the actual hearing of doubt, one incurs the offense of slander (*paiśunya*).
Furthermore, Master Yun says: For instance, in the fourth section of the second chapter [of the *Vinaya*], regarding the third mental state, one should say:

"If one does not doubt that he has committed a *pārājika*, yet there is doubt therein, one should simply say: 'I have seen or heard that he has committed a *pārājika* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. However, this case..."
"Doubt" refers here to horizontal doubt (*tiṅ-yí*). Since there is this horizontal doubt, the text may also state [the position] as such;

this would contradict your claim that all three views are absent and that only "not seeing" (*bù jiàn*) is singled out. This is because, by not doubting, one does not possess the absence of all three, yet the text singles out "not doubting.
Furthermore, there are others who take this Master Yun to be in accord with the principle and thus assist in refuting [the opponent], saying: "This exists..."
There are two types of cross-objections (*paryanuyoga*). First, the upper objection: since there is already a cross-objection in the fourth chapter, one may say "there is no doubt.
How then can you say that all three views are absent and specifically designate only "not seeing"? Second, the lower objection:

since the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the [third] chapter contains a cross-objection, one may say "there is no doubt. Likewise, even if there are perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*), one should hear [the same].

[Objection: One might ask, "Can it be said that there is no hearing and no doubt? For this reason, the initial explanation is not reasonable. Now, upon closer examination, Master Yun (Yun-shi) does not contradict reason.
On what basis do you falsely claim that Master Yun accords with reason? Take, for instance, what Master Yun says regarding those who have "transverse doubt" (*heng-yi*):
he bases it on the conceptualization of doubt, naming the essence of this conceptualization "transverse doubt. Thus, that which is transverse doubt is the conceptualization of transverse doubt.
In that case, there would be no distinction between the fourth phrase, which involves a mind of doubt and forgetfulness, and the second phrase, which involves a mind of perception and forgetfulness.

That is to say, regarding the second mental state, the formulation should state: "If one does not doubt that a *pārājika* offense was committed, yet within this there is a perception of it, and later one forgets this characteristic, one then says, 'I saw or heard that a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense was committed. Therefore, [the second] should not be distinct from the fourth. If...
Regarding the essence of doubt, it refers to horizontal doubt (*yōgi*). Suppose an ancient master were to offer this defense:
"I merely stated that the three views are all absent; I never said that horizontal doubt is absent. What fault is there in my position? Would this not constitute a valid objection?

Therefore, the present commentary completely discards the ancient interpretation, stating: "Those who have hitherto formulated these objections and explanations are mistaken. It then proceeds directly to refute [the opponent] by saying: "Because..."
The initial mind is non-existent. Being without thought, it does not forget. From where could a mind with thought, hearing, or doubt arise?

If one were to allow for a mind with thought, hearing, and doubt, then the commentary’s reference to "thoughtful exposition" would constitute slander. This is precisely what has been extensively refuted through the five points above. Now, examining this closely:
by using the second mind to refute [the first], it is clearly shown that [the opponent's position] is irrational. What further use is there [in further argument]?
Furthermore, this refers back to the third mind within the fourth section of the gates. This is the second mind. The Vinaya text states:
"If one does not see that person's offense, yet has the perception of seeing it therein, and later forgets this perception, one then says, 'I heard of a doubtful offense.

If you maintain that all three types of seeing are absent, and thus it is designated as 'not seeing,' for what reason is there the perception of seeing in the text concerning the subsequent mind, and why is it also so designated?"

"Is not seen. Regarding the phrase "the same applies from the section below": since this chapter contains neither the denial of mind nor the denial of hearing and doubt, the subsequent chapters likewise contain neither the denial of seeing nor the denial of doubt and so forth.
This means that all [denials] are based on the disposition of the slanderer—specifically, what they wish to cite as a root for their denial and what they do not wish to cite.
They are cited alternately; it is not the case that they are absent in the same way as the mind of perception and the three views.

Regarding the question on the second phrase, "not seeing his offense," etc.: the intent of this objection is to say that while this phrase intends to cite cases of hearing, doubting, or slandering another, the text does not mention the perception of hearing or doubting.
Since the perception of hearing or doubting is omitted, for what reason was it intended to be cited in the preceding chapter?
Regarding the three types of slander, the text itself states that there are three perceptions; does this mean that three perceptions are forgotten?

The commentary explains that, according to the principle within this section, although all three faculties are absent, one is established as "not seeing" (because, according to a certain commentary, it says:).

"Based on faith, one establishes 'one non-perception' (ekādarśana). Furthermore, there is a commentary text which says: 'In the stage [of the path], one establishes one non-perception'. This means that according to the ultimate principle (*tattva*), all three faculties are absent;

yet, out of a desire for others to have faith, one establishes "one non-perception. The general intent here is this: while the ultimate principle is fixed such that all three are forgotten, what prevents one from establishing "one forgetfulness" within that context?
Another interpretation states: even if one is in the stage of non-perception, it does not preclude the possibility of also having the three perceptions (*saṃjñā*).
Both [cases] involve the forgetting of the three perceptions; the latter is easier to understand.
The answer—that because transverse perceptions do not arise, there is "non-existence" (asat), etc.—has this general meaning: originally, the non-seeing is established and termed "non-existence.
Because one establishes the perception of seeing based on this, and furthermore establishes the perception of forgetting the seeing in contrast to the perception of seeing, this is the Vinaya.

This is the intended meaning of the text. Originally, it was established that there is neither hearing nor doubt; therefore, it is not the case that all [instances] involve this absence of hearing and doubt.

Rather, the notions of "hearing" and "doubt" are established precisely because such notions do not exist, yet this does not mean they are forgotten. As for those who speak according to the principle, in all categories (*dharmaparyāya*), in reality there are not three [aspects].

However, the reason the first category alone states that there are not three is that it explains the matter exhaustively according to the principle. Now, as for citing the sentiment of slander: *Note: The original text contains a complex discussion regarding the ontological status of "hearing" and "doubt" within a specific philosophical framework (likely Madhyamaka or Yogācāra), where the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is devoid of these conceptual constructs, even while conventional discourse (*saṃvṛti*) employs them.*
This refers to the discussion of the chapters from the second onwards.

Regarding the establishment of their number: it means that when a slanderer, either in his own mind or by his own mouth, says, "I did not see [it], yet I have the perception of having seen it," or "I forgot the perception of having seen it," the compilers of the canon established these as chapter headings based on those verbal statements. The other phrases are of the same nature; thus they alternate.
To a certain extent, there is no need to compose many phrases. Master Yuàn Lǜshī said: "Furthermore, among the three [categories], there is none superior to the first, 'the mind.
If one were to expand this by adding six phrases, the total number would be seven. In the original text, the first phrase already contains the three instances of 'raising' (jǔ); the second has none."

The third [case] involves the three types of accusation (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) for slandering based on what was seen and heard; the third [of these] lacks the three types of accusation for slandering based on doubt;

the fourth lacks the three types of accusation for questioning based on doubt; the fifth lacks the three types of accusation for a single instance of seeing; the sixth lacks the three types of accusation for slandering based on what was heard; and the seventh phrase lacks the three types of accusation for slandering based on doubt.

(Up to this point, there is only the first phrase; adding six further phrases results in seven phrases in total. For each of the five subsequent phrases, one should understand that six phrases are added accordingly, as before. (That is to say...)
Regarding the phrase "no three" (*amūlaka*) within the three [categories]: there are sixty-four sentences (six times seven). Now, the Master’s intention is as follows:

if you add six sentences to each of the six original sentences to make seven, then among all those added six sentences, the second, third, and fourth are "accusations based on two faculties without three grounds.
What difference is there between these and the second, third, and fourth [sentences] in the current text, which are "without three grounds and two views"? There is none at all.
Otherwise, furthermore, regarding all the added phrases, the fifth, sixth, and seventh are "three [grounds] lacking, one root slandered.
Within the current Vinaya text, amidst its voluminous wording, it says "three [grounds] lacking, one view. How then can these two be different?
Therefore, neither is reasonable.

Second, regarding the distinction between similarity and difference based on minor omissions: wishing to distinguish their similarities and differences, I shall first set forth the two sets of six propositions concerning these minor omissions.
However, while those [texts] fully treat them in terms of seeing, hearing, touching, and cognizing, I shall here restrict myself to "seeing" alone for the sake of brevity.
Regarding the first six: first, not having seen, one has the perception that one has seen and says "I have not seen"; second, having doubt, one says "there is no doubt";

third, not having seen, one has doubt and says "there is no doubt"; fourth, not having seen, one has no doubt and says "there is doubt"; fifth, not having seen, one has no doubt and says "there is doubt";
sixth, not having seen, one has no doubt and simply says "I doubt."

Regarding the latter six: the subsequent text merely states that "this should be explained in detail. As for what should be explained in detail, there should be another six points: first, seeing yet saying one did not see;
second, seeing something yet having the perception that one did not see it, and then saying one saw it; third, seeing something with doubt yet saying there is no doubt and that one did not see it;
fourth, seeing something with doubt yet saying there is no doubt and that one saw it; fifth, seeing something without doubt yet saying there is doubt and that one did not see it; sixth...

"Seeing without doubt" and "doubting views"—these two sets of six phrases are both explained in terms of actual objective conditions. Therefore, in the first, third, and fifth [phrases], both the mind and the object are contrary;
in the second, fourth, and sixth, the object accords with the mind while the mind is contrary.
Regarding the "object of reality" (*vastu-viṣaya*): its characteristics were already explained above in the section on "forgetting the great.

Here, among the remaining six phrases, the Vinaya text states that the other person is impure while one regards oneself as being free from the three [impurities]; this constitutes a pure object. To then think of it as pure is a purity of mind.
Now, to contradict these two purities and yet insist upon them is called "both mind and object being empty" (*ubhaya-śūnya*). This is explained according to the actual facts.
This is an explanation regarding the objects of the marks (*nimitta*). The six phrases are all likewise [to be explained] (next, they shall be assigned and interpreted).
Regarding "entering the three states of non-forgetfulness by means of the three states of forgetting the mind": this refers to entering the state of no-thought (*asaṃjñā*) by forgetting thought;

entering the state of no-doubt by not forgetting; entering the state of doubt by forgetting; and entering the state of no-doubt by not forgetting. The meaning of "not forgetting" is as explained above. That is to say:
The second is subsumed within the first; the sixth is subsumed within the third; and the fourth is subsumed within the fifth.
Thus, the six are condensed into three. This is identical to the minor omission [noted] elsewhere: namely, the first, third, and fifth.
All of these are cases of turning [the truth] upside down. Among those latter six, the term "seeing" refers to the six instances of not seeing; this constitutes a denial of the six propositions.
All of these are cases of claiming to see what was not seen—a first instance of doubling over.

Regarding the "two places, two, four, and six": this refers to the second, fourth, and sixth phrases within the two sets of six [of the *Abhidharmakośa*]. In those cases, the object is favorable while the mind is adverse;
therefore, they are not the same as this case where both the object and the mind are adverse.

Regarding the statement in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* that the two types of parricide and slander incur *sthūlātyaya*, while other offenses incur *duṣkṛta*: this is not so. In the fifty-first [chapter] of that Vinaya, the three [offenses] such as killing one's mother result in *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the "four clear methods": these refer to hand gestures (*mudrā*), signs, writing, and sending a messenger—these four.

If one adds "doing it oneself," it would be better to say there are five methods. Alternatively, the four methods may refer to the four barbarian tribes. Generally speaking, they are: first, slander; second, hand gestures; third, signs;
and fourth, writing—which corresponds to the omission of the messenger in the formal list.
There are seven things by which one may disparage another: first, caste; second, family lineage; third, occupation; fourth, craft or skill; fifth, transgressions; sixth, fetters and afflictions;
and seventh, physical characteristics, such as being blind or squint-eyed.

Regarding "the principle of having the perception of an object": one should speak of [cases such as] perceiving a great monk (*bhikṣu*) as a great monk, or perceiving a *bhikṣuṇī* as a *bhikṣuṇī*, and so forth.
Regarding the statement in the opening text that "one speaks of reality," Nanshan says: "There are five kinds of reality: first, true reality; second, reality through perception."
The three matters are factual. For example, if one kills a king and yet says, "I killed the king," it is factual. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fascicle 51, states:

"If one says of oneself, 'I killed my father,' while falsely accusing another by saying, 'He killed my mother,' this is a case where the matter is not factual. Fourth, the three bases (*tri-vidyā*) do not interchange [as cited above from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 4].

Fifth, the four precepts do not interchange as factual [according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 51: "If a bhikṣu says, 'I have committed sexual misconduct,' and another bhikṣu falsely accuses him, saying, 'You have committed killing or stealing,' he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense"]. Now...

It is detailed that the four [categories] are indeed possible. As for what is called "truth" (*tattva*), it should be subsumed under the others as appropriate; it should not be established separately.

○ Regarding the "false accusation based on a semblance of evidence" (*mūlāpatti-viṣaṃvādana*), the Sanskrit is *liśyaka-anudgama* (or *liśyaka-anudgama-śa*). This is translated here as "semblance-evidence false accusation. In the *Guangshi* (Extensive Explanation), Chong states:

It was not understood that "rootless phrases" (mūlāpagata-pada) refers to the fact that the *śīla-vibhaṅga* clarifies the "distinctive roots" (*visabhāga-mūla*), which is precisely what is meant by "rootless. Therefore, it is stated in this chapter:
"In the commentary, the third [section] concerns the superior roots of the distinct category (*visabhāga-uttara-mūla*)."
Regarding the term "distinct category" (*visabhāga*): observing this Vinaya text, it is consistent with the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* and differs from the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*.
For instance, the fourth precept in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* of the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya* states: "Taking even a fragment or something resembling a fragment from within a distinct category.

The extensive commentary (*vibhāṣā*) therein states: "The 'distinct category' refers to the four *pārājika* offenses. Why? Because among these four *pārājikas*, if one commits even a single offense, [it is not...]"
A śramaṇa who is not a son of the Śākyas and has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu is called "one of a different category" (*nānābhāga*).

There are thirteen matters [of defeat], two indeterminate matters, thirty-nine and ten *pārājika* offenses, and the seven rules for settling disputes; these are called "not of a different category" (*anānābhāga*).

Why? Because even if one commits such matters, one is still called a bhikṣu, called a son of the Śākyas, and does not lose the dharma of a bhikṣu; therefore, this is called "not of a different category."
"A single moment (kṣaṇa)" refers to matters within the various modes of conduct (īryāpatha); this is called "a fragment" (khaṇḍa), and it is also called "a fragment of a moment. (Commentary states:

According to the intent of the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā*, because they are distinct from the portion of Nirvāṇa, they are termed "distinct portions" (bhinnabhāga). Now, in this *Daśādhyāya-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), if one commits the four pārājika offenses...
Because he is not a śramaṇa; the intention [of this] is the same as that [previous case]. If that were so, then the preceding precept should also be called "partially different" (*anyabhāga*).
Therefore, it is further explained: "A fragment, for even a brief moment. This is the correct explanation of the "provisional root" (*prajñaptimūla*).

As for the word "fragment" (*khaṇḍa*) in that text, it refers to various matters of deportment (*īryāpatha*). The intention is to say that one resorts to other four modes of deportment to perform unrighteous acts. Thus it says "for a moment" (*muhūrta*).
Regarding the term *yupian* (a small fragment): *xuyu* means "a small portion. This refers to taking a small portion and making it similar to *ḍhapa*.
It is as stated in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*: "resembling a fragment. According to the *Samantapāsādikā*, chapter thirteen, regarding "another portion":
*ḍhapa* is a human being, while the sheep is a non-human (*amanusya*). Using the sheep in place of *ḍhapa* is called "another portion. Thus it is said.
A ewe is equivalent to a nun; it is also called "another portion" (*anyabhāga*). Why? Because the circumstances are similar. Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states:
"If even a fragment resembles [the offense]" (as cited above in the treatise). Based on this, as seen in the Śāstra, one may directly employ a false basis to explain "another portion."
"Distinct category" (*aññabhāgiya*) means a fragment that resembles a fragment. Regarding the subsequent text concerning these four categories:
when an impure person, resembling an impure person, slanders another on account of this matter, and by means of a groundless charge based on a distinct category, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
This appears to be similar to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*.

Regarding the first four pairs of phrases, which refer to those who have committed the six [offenses] below [the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*], the Venerable One said: "If one examines the Vinaya text closely, the first phrase is the head of the fourth phrase.
This is because the first phrase says, 'namely, having committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense,' while the fourth phrase says, 'namely, having committed a *pāyattika* offense.'"
Thus, one should know that the fourth phrase is precisely the point where it connects to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
Combining these two phrases constitutes what is called "the six [offenses] below" regarding transgressions. Examining the third line, it is the beginning of the second phrase;
combining these two beginnings of phrases and combining these two phrases constitutes what is seen as "the six [offenses] below" regarding transgressions.
Regarding the summary of the four and six [categories]: first, seeing an offense; second, being accused of an offense; third, hearing of an offense; fourth, suspecting an offense.
○ The precept concerning schism in the Saṃgha and the refusal of admonition.
There are seven [offenses] for bhikṣus. Among the *śeṣa* (saṃghāvaśeṣa) offenses, there are four involving formal admonition;

among the *pratyantika* (pāyattika) offenses, there is one: first, refusing admonition in private; second, Liṭha’s defiance of the Saṃgha’s admonition; third, treating others with contempt and refusing instruction.
Together with the previous [three], they total seven.
There are six specific [offenses] for bhikṣuṇīs; that is to say, they differ from the precepts [of the bhikṣus].

First, complying with a bhikṣu who has been suspended and violating the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha’s three admonitions (this is the first item in the first section). Second, the saṃghāvaśeṣa offense of practicing independently and violating the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha’s three admonitions.

Third, slandering the Saṃgha and associating with [laypeople], which constitutes a *niḥsargika-pācattika* after three admonitions. Fourth, abandoning the Triple Gem out of a mind of malice, which constitutes a *niḥsargika-pācattika* after three admonitions.
Fifth, instigating the four types of disputes, which constitutes a *niḥsargika-pācattika* after admonition (this refers to the four items in the second section above).
Sixth, associating with the sons of householders, which constitutes a *pācattika* after three admonitions (this is the first item in the third section; the total count thus far is six).
Regarding the statement that "the dharma consists of only one stage": it is called "one" because it does not involve the successive distinctions found among human beings.

The meaning can be understood by analogy: those who oppose the admonitions of the Saṃgha are restricted to the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), whereas those who engage in private admonitions apply to all boundaries.
There is only the *tīkṣṇa-dukkaṭa* (sharp offense). "Dukkaṭa" refers to a *dukkaṭa* within which one does not accept admonition or restraint. That text states:

"If another person prevents you by saying, 'Do not do this,' and you respond, 'It should not be so,' yet you proceed to act intentionally, you commit a root offense (*mūlāpatti*). It is not a *dukkaṭa* arising from speech.

(This means that because the mind is deluded and one thinks to oneself, "I am doing this," and this thought is real, it is a *dukkaṭa*). If one knows for oneself that what one is doing is wrong, yet one still commits the root offense intentionally, it is not [a *dukkaṭa*].

Regarding the two *pāyattikas* for speaking [falsely] (this refers to the *pāyattika* for knowing one has committed an offense oneself while being aware that others are admonishing one; this is a grave transgression, hence it is a *pāyattika*):
as for the two *pāyattikas* where each is not fully established, the previous section has already excluded those who are light-minded and do not accept instruction.
Therefore, these two *pāyattikas* apply only to cases of *tittira* (insolence) and refusing a private admonition.
Regarding "one who violates the Six Groups": it refers to Devadatta and others violating the admonitions of the lower six groups;

this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). Furthermore, "one who violates an admonition once or twice" means: violating one heavy rule among those subject to admonition, such as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;

or violating two heavy rules, such as a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits a *pārājika*. This consists of two parts: first, violating the formal procedure of admonition before the assembly; second, violating the formal act of censure by the Great Saṃgha.
This is because it is the Dharma; thus, it is *yi* (even/equal).
Regarding the eleven detailed subdivisions of the six aforementioned categories: this refers to the six preceding sections, which, when subdivided, constitute eleven sections.
Among these six, the first section is divided into four, the second section has only one, the third section has two, and the fourth section has one.
The fifth section has two [subsections], and the sixth section has one (if one returns to the previous commentary, the text will be clear of itself).
These correspond to the two types of schism; because those who assist in a schism commit a grave transgression, there are the first three sections.

1. Regarding "one of evil lineage," this excludes the procuress and those with two households. 2. Regarding "manifest," this excludes secret transgressions. 3. Regarding "disturbing the Saṃgha," this excludes the two types of coarse offenses involving physical contact.

Generally, it is said that these exclude the two types of slander, because the two types of slander do not constitute disturbing the Saṃgha. 4. Regarding "relying upon [others]," this generally excludes the preceding nine categories.

Dengyun says: "The two types of *pāyattika* offenses are also 'relying' (*yi-bang*) because they rely upon the opening [of the formal act] by the Buddha; therefore it is said that the two types of slander are also 'relying.

Because they rely upon the formal accusation (*juei-zui*), he immediately explains: although they also rely [upon the opening], they do not possess the four conditions; therefore, there is no admonition."

Regarding the confusion between what is similar in expression and the two teachings of principle and practice: for instance, Devadatta’s five wrongs are confused with both the teaching of principle and the teaching of practice;

other instances, such as his evil nature and defiance of admonitions, are merely cases of similarity in expression, meaning they rely upon the Buddha’s teachings [without embodying their true intent].
It is simply because they observe only their own bodies that they possess an evil nature and defy admonition; all cases should be understood accordingly.
In hoping for them to reform their delusion, "delusion" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), meaning they do not fear cause and effect; it does not refer to the delusion of thought or mind.
Because the mind is empty due to the contradiction of conceptualization. Some say it would be better to state: "One should hope that they will reform their deviance and follow the correct path.
As for what "should be explained in detail" refers to, it shall be explained in detail within each of the subsequent precepts concerning admonition.

The reason why the existence or non-existence [of the four offenses] is questioned here, while the nine residual offenses (*śeṣa*) are not questioned and not subject to formal admonition, is that they are difficult to treat as being of the same category.

Why is it that when one establishes the admonition regarding the four [root offenses], there are four instances of existence and nine of non-existence? This is precisely because one uses non-existence to overturn existence, and uses existence to challenge non-existence.

As for the reason why the nine residuals are not questioned and not subject to admonition, it is not because one wishes to question the nine residuals alone and exclude them from admonition; rather, it is because one does not wish to apply the same difficulty to the remaining four.
This refers to admonishing.
Regarding those who admonish others, there may be both those who are deluded and those who have attained awakening. As in the four propositions concerning the schism of the Saṃgha:

that which is characterized as non-Dharma is awakening; that which is perceived as Dharma is delusion. Even if one’s words are deluded, one must still offer admonition. Furthermore, regarding benefit...
"Ṭa" refers to delusion; the others refer to awakening.
Regarding the matters for which admonition is given, there are those that have occurred and those that have not. "Not yet" refers to the schism of the Saṃgha; the rest are "already" [occurred].

Regarding the statement that slander and a malicious nature do not require further elaboration, this refers to the expulsion for slandering and so forth; even in the subsequent text, he speaks of himself in this way.

As for the claim, "I shall be known by name after my body has perished, therefore know this to be false," I have now examined this in detail: how could one who speaks with the notion of a "dharma" [be so]?
There is no need for three admonitions. Thus, one should know that this refers to the interpretation that [the offender] cannot overcome those who were already established.

Regarding the statement that "the formal act (*karma*) is difficult to accomplish according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*," this is the opinion of the ancient masters. The seventh fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"At that time, the bhikṣus performed the formal act of suspension (*utkṣepa-karman*) against Devadatta. During the first two proclamations of the formal act, there was no one who offered an objection."
During the third *karmavācanā*, Devadatta, facing the group of six, spoke these words: "The Saṃgha is now performing the *utkṣepaṇīya-karman* against me;
it has already been recited twice, yet you all remain silent. You now hold me over to the crowd like curd smeared on roasted flour given to a bird;
like ghee smeared on a cake given to a *nākulī*; like oil mixed with rice given to a jackal."
While those practicing the holy life were being observed by others as they sat [in assembly], the group of six monks immediately rose and said:
"Just so, just so, Elder! This is a statement of Dharma, a statement of Vinaya; many people have obstructed the *karmavācanā* so that it was not accomplished."

Regarding whether one should or should not act as stated in the "Increase by Two" (Dvaya-vardhana) section: the text of the "Increase by Two" below states, "Furthermore, there are two dharmas for which a bhikṣu should undergo the karma of censure (tarjanīya-karman):
speaking what is non-Dharma as Dharma, up to speaking what should not be spoken as what should be spoken.

The same applies to the karmas of banishment (pravāsanīya), dependence (niśraya), prohibition (pratisedha), and suspension (utksepa). If one relies on the formal procedure itself, the Tarjanīya-khandhaka contains its own clear exposition.
This is the textual [explanation]. As for the case of Līḷha, why is he cited? Among the ninety rules concerning formal accusations (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*), there is a procedure for accusing Līḷha;
however, there is no mention of Līḷha’s refusal to accept admonition within those specific precepts.

Regarding the provisional explanation that "only those who follow [the first two] are auspicious": this means that among the four cases mentioned previously, only those following the first two obtain auspicious results.

Regarding "the latter two are not heterodox": this refers to those who corrupt the household through their evil nature; they are not like Liṭa, who preached desire as being heterodox (*mithyā*). According to the former explanation, since there is no "raising" [of the issue], one infers that a third case does not exist.

According to the latter explanation, since there is no "raising," both [the third and fourth] do not exist. Furthermore, within the latter explanation, the latter two are not heterodox; that is to say:
There is no illness to be remedied by the three formal acts (*tri-utkṣepa*).

One who speaks in accordance with the Dharma is "like" (如) [the Dharma]; "like" (如) is equivalent to "thus" (而). (It should be understood that in ancient times, the character 而 was frequently written as 如; one should know this according to the context.)
Regarding the statement that "conditions are the seeds" and so forth, the meaning follows the third fascicle of the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

As for the explanation of the name: in Sanskrit it is called *saṃghabheda*, which is translated as "schism in the Saṃgha. Following the rules of literary inversion, it should be rendered as "breaking the Saṃgha" (*bhedasaṃgha*).
"Can be known by analogy with what precedes" refers to the fourth *pratyaya* (condition).

This major section is divided into two parts: from the beginning up to "the division of the True Dharma remains," which clarifies the characteristics of the formal enactment of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*); second, from "desiring to recite the precepts" onwards, which clarifies the characteristics of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).

Within the first part, there are three further divisions: from the beginning up to the "fourfold motion and proclamation" (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) for reprimand and admonition, which correctly elucidates [the prohibition of] non-...

The first [section] concerns the causes for the abridgment of the rules due to the corruption of fame and profit. The second, from this time forward, establishes the precepts for the bhikṣus as a detailed supplement to the abridged version.
The third collects the ten points of meaning and subsequently brings forth the ten benefits.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "The Father King sent two brothers from among the Śākyas to leave the household life. The *Lalitavistara Sūtra* (*Puyao jing*) states:
"He delivered five hundred Śākya youths across [to liberation]. Regarding the father’s words that "human life is impermanent," the thirteenth verse of the *Śāriputra-abhidharma* says:
"Day and night, it is constantly decaying, like a fish in hot water; there is no birth without suffering."
[The King] pressed him again. In the third fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, King Bimbisāra addressed [Ānanda] with these words: "I pray that you do not violate your vow.

The King said, "I shall grant your wish; let me have seven more years. Ānanda replied, "After seven years, the Buddha may no longer be present, and furthermore, my life is precarious and my very existence difficult to preserve. How can Your Majesty now set this as a deadline?"
To compare the past with the present: formerly, when he was in the pleasure groves, it was as if the sun were rising.
Regarding the cessation of slander: had he ordained Devadatta, Devadatta would later have caused a schism in the Saṅgha and would have slandered the Buddha, claiming he lacked omniscience.
Had he ordained Ānanda, Ānanda would later have served the Buddha and would have slandered the Buddha for being greedy for offerings, seeking his own salvation.
Regarding the attendants who realized the higher stages: since Upāli and others were already liberated by the Buddha, it is clear that they had previously attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).

Their current realization of the "higher stage" refers to their attainment of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Thus, the third fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The six persons attained the exhaustion of outflows."
The Arhats and Ānanda, who attended upon the Buddha, had not yet exhausted all outflows (āsrava), while Devadatta alone was empty-handed and attained nothing.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation of the Dragon King Anavatapta; however, because Devadatta had not yet attained supernatural powers (abhijñā), he was unable to go.
Feeling both envy and shame, he went at once to inform the Buddha, saying, "I pray that the Buddha will teach me the method for cultivating supernatural powers.
The Buddha immediately taught it for him; Devadatta received the instruction and, during the summer retreat, attained supernormal powers.

Within the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is established that while Devadatta was dispelling his doubts and manifesting transformations, Vāṣpa addressed the Buddha, saying, "In the past, when I lived as a householder, I resided within seven layers of city walls and moats, where there were seven rows of elephants."
There were seven rows of horses, seven rows of chariots, and seven rows of infantry surrounding him on all sides. Suddenly, he heard strange sounds; his heart was startled and his hair stood on end.
Now, standing beneath a tree on an open road, he is at ease and free from anxiety; therefore, he exclaims, "How joyful!"
Regarding the two points that can be understood from the text: first, transforming others to inspire faith; second, being mindful of maintaining a retinue of disciples.
Regarding the five points that should be understood as not being the actual text: first, Kāśyapa pays his respects and comes to inform Maudgalyāyana;

second, because he received these words, he goes to consult [the Buddha]; third, the Buddha returns to question him and answers that it is false; fourth, [the Buddha] stops [him], and the true words are expressed.

The Buddha is without error. His five admonitions revealed five matters that showed my lack of compliance. In the *Pañcavargika*, it is stated that Kāśyapa attained the stage of *anāgāmin* and was reborn in the Brahma Heaven;

according to this principle, he was reborn in the Heaven of Mastery over Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati*), and was not immediately a *anāgāmin*. Question: Why do you not believe that Devadatta split the Saṃgha? Answer:
The fourth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "I observe among humans and devas that there is no one capable of splitting the harmonious Saṃgha."
This is merely a demonstration; therefore, the Buddha could not heed Maudgalyāyana’s words.
Regarding the combination of the metaphor and its meaning: in the metaphor, Devadatta’s greedy mind is like the wicked, solitary nose;

King Ajātaśatru’s circumambulation and offering of the *vaḍavāmukha* (fire-pit) and his striking with a club only increased that fool’s delusion, just as the metaphor illustrates the increase of cruelty.
Regarding the establishment of the two topical headings: first, the section on harming the Buddha; second, the section on killing the king.

As for distinguishing the provisional and the ultimate based on the cause: the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) to harm the Buddha is termed the "cause. This refers to what is recorded below in the *Śīlaskandhaka* (The Chapter on Receiving the Precepts):
in the past, when the Buddha was the young Brahmin Mṛṣāvādin, he gathered twelve ugly Brahmins known as the "Twelve Uglies. These Twelve Uglies are [the subject of] the present...
This was Devadatta.
As for the two who were without cause, it means they had no enmity in the past.
"Discerning through skillful means" refers to manifestation; it is not the ultimate reality.
The *Śāstra* states: Regarding the reason why the Buddha engaged in fishing, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says:

Eight hundred devaputras attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*) and saw that the Buddha had performed such acts as fishing in the past, which would have prevented him from attaining Buddhahood. Because these devaputras did not believe in cause and effect (*hetu-phala*), he manifested those events for them.
The chapter states: The fifth section, "Establishing Deviant Views and Dividing the Saṃgha," consists of three parts. First, the initial mental application and preparatory means.
Second, from "Devadatta immediately departed" onwards, his collaboration with companions to establish deviant versions of the Triple Gem.

Third, from "At that time, Devadatta employed the five dharmas" onwards, his use of those deviant teachings to seduce and deceive new learners. The first segment of the text is explained and analyzed as set forth in the chapter.

Regarding the second section of the text: although the topical divisions (*koḍa*) therein are somewhat extensive and complex, I shall not alter the silent commentary (*śūci*) within the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), but shall instead provide an extended topical outline divided into ten sections:
(1) attracting companions by means of their names; (2) the fear that the companions will not succeed; (3) citing the gates of the orthodox teaching;

Fifty-nine. *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 181, explains the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). Their meanings differ slightly. To begin with, the *Vibhāṣā* states: As the Sūtra says, there are:
first, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever food one obtains; second, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever clothing one obtains;
third, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever bedding one obtains; fourth, the noble lineage of delighting in non-existence and existence.
"Delighting in the cultivation of the noble lineages. Question: Why are they not the same? Answer:

According to the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the ancient masters established the four noble lineages as being identical to the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*). Therefore, the present *Vibhāṣā* reveals the position of the new masters, who—among the four reliances—exclude the reliance on medicine and add a fourth:
delighting in the new cultivation of existence and non-existence. These constitute the four; that is, the Sūtra says:
In the Vinaya, there are these two passages; thus, while combining the ancient and the modern, the wording differs. Question: For what reason are these two passages so different? Answer:
The Buddha spoke differently because he taught according to what was appropriate for his listeners and in order to eliminate their attachments. Regarding that which was appropriate for his listeners:
This refers to a certain class of individuals whose minds are free from perverse attachments and who delight only in practicing in accordance with the Dharma;

therefore, for their sake, one should directly proclaim the requisites of the path and the essential nature of the path itself—namely, that the first three [aggregates] serve as the equipment for the path, while the fourth serves as the essential nature of the path.
If there is a certain class of people whose minds are possessed by perverse attachments— whether they cling to self-starvation as the "noble lineage," or cling to nakedness,
or cling to standing on tiptoe, or cling to such things as the "cow-vow" or "dog-vow"— consuming grass or dung, thereby afflicting their bodies and minds with suffering.
There is no benefit to the Path [if one does not apply this]. Therefore, as an antidote to that, the four stages are taught. Only after practicing the Middle Way can one advance in cultivation;
thus, the Four Reliances are established as the noble lineage. Now, because of Devadatta’s perverse attachment to the literal text of the teachings, these Four Reliances are presented.
They are established as the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). Next, regarding the explanation of their names: the explanation of their ancient name has already been clarified in the preceding chapter.
As for the explanation of the new name, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Some say they are called 'noble lineages' because they are both noble (*ārya*) and lineages (*vaṃśa*).

That is to say, they are called 'noble' because they are wholesome (*kuśala*), and they are called 'noble' because they are untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, these are able to give rise to all dharmas of merit."
Because it continues in an uninterrupted succession, it is called a "seed" (*bīja*). There are many other explanations, which should be understood as they appear in those [other texts].

The meaning of this explanation is that the path of all wholesome dharmas is called "noble" (*ārya*); these very wholesome dharmas, because they can produce subsequent states, are further called "seeds."
This has been a preliminary explanation of the names of the "noble lineages" (*āryavaṃśa*). Their fourfold nature has not yet been explained. Now, to examine them in detail:

the first three serve as conditions that are able to produce the noble lineages, while the fourth one is itself the noble lineage; therefore, they are called the "four noble lineages. Furthermore, regarding the fourth:

"existence" refers to craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), and "non-existence" refers to craving for non-existence (*vibhavarāga*); it is toward these two types of craving [that the fourth lineage acts as an antidote].
One delights in abandoning [defilements] and cultivates the Noble Path. Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* says: "Delighting in the abandonment of afflictions and delighting in the cultivation of the Noble Path.
Furthermore, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is called "delighting in abandonment," while the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is called "delighting in cultivation.

Alternatively, the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is called "delighting in abandonment," and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is called "delighting in cultivation," as explained at length therein. Those who possess craving for existence (*bhavarāgin*) are those who, regarding all conditions for future existence, aspire to its permanence.
There is never any cessation or annihilation; these are mostly sentient beings who possess happiness.
Those who lack craving are those who, by means of the subsequent existence (*punarbhava*), aspire for its cessation so that nothing remains; these are mostly sentient beings who possess suffering.

Since one gives rise to perverted craving toward these two objects, it is necessary to apply an antidote; therefore, it is said: "One cultivates [the perception of] happiness in both existence and non-existence."

Next, regarding the essential nature [of the noble lineages]: within this section, the conditions for the arising of the noble ones—namely, the essential nature of robes, food, and so forth—are first presented, followed by a systematic exposition of the actual nature of the noble lineages themselves.
To briefly explain the conditions, the text states: "If distinguished according to phenomena, they consist of the four sense objects (*viṣaya*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and so on."
The four objects (viṣaya) are form, odor, taste, and tangibility. The four great elements (mahābhūta) are the primary productive causes of these four objects.

However, form, odor, and taste are exclusively derivative (upādāya-rūpa). Within the object of tangibility, there are both [the primary elements and the derivatives]; that is to say, it includes the four great elements as well as smoothness and roughness.

Lightness, heaviness, cold, hunger, and thirst [are the secondary elements]. Among these, the four great elements (mahābhūta) are the creators (upādāna), while the remaining seven kinds are the created (upādāya).

If discussed restrictively, the two categories of clothing and dwelling each possess the four sense objects (viṣaya) as well as the four great elements. As for the two categories of food and medicine, they are of the nature of edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra);

Regarding desire: those who possess an increase in desire lack desire for what is real, yet they are called "those with few desires" (since having few desires has non-greed as its essential nature, it should be called "desirelessness";
why then is it termed "few desires"?). Within contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*), such a thing does not exist; therefore, the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are established.
Some say that "few desires" operates toward things not yet obtained in the future, whereas "contentment" operates toward things already obtained in the present; it does not grasp at the present.

Although possessing even a single *kāliṃśapaṇa* coin is established as a form of contentment, it is not established as such because of the difficulty of being satisfied with the future status of a Wheel-Turning King.
Furthermore, in order to distinguish [the Buddha's teaching] from that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), "fewness of desires" (*alpecchatā*) is not taught as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).
For if "fewness of desires" were taught as a noble lineage, the various non-Buddhist sects would say: "We, too, are truly those who abide in the noble lineages. This is why [it is not so taught].
Why is this? You still wear rag-robes, whereas we go naked and without clothing.
You still sustain yourselves by begging for alms, whereas we mostly starve ourselves and do not eat.

Because we mostly starve ourselves and do not eat, and you still sit beneath trees, whereas we often remain with our hands raised and our feet thrust upward—it is for these reasons that we are truly called "those who dwell."

Regarding the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), in order to exclude those [faults], it is taught that one should simply be content. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Chapter 22), the masters of the Abhidharma all maintain this view:
"To seek more than what one has already obtained, such as excellent robes and so forth, is called 'lack of contentment' (*asaṃtuṣṭi*);

to desire what one has not yet obtained, such as excellent robes and so forth, is called 'great desire' (*mahecchatā*). [This concludes the exposition of the Sarvāstivāda position. Below, Vasubandhu does not accept this, saying: "Is it not the case that seeking more..."
Furthermore, if it were based on what has not yet been obtained, the distinction between these two would be untenable. Therefore, it should be stated here as follows:
regarding what has already been obtained, to feel regretful and dissatisfied because it is not excellent or sufficient is called "lack of contentment" (*asamtuṣṭi*).

Regarding things such as clothing that have not yet been obtained, to seek excellence and seek abundance is called "great desire" (*mahēcchā*). Contentment and fewness of desires are able to counteract these two.
The distinctions [of the opposite] should be understood accordingly (end of treatise).

All the holy assemblies of Jambudvīpa are not equal to sitting in quietude and purely maintaining the precepts;
this is the pure offering to all the holy ones (as the precept against killing was already cited above).

Regarding the formal statement (*vāc*): If it has not yet been formally declared that the Saṃgha possesses affection and so forth—which would constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense—the *Cīvara-vastu* states that once a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* has arisen, with the exception of the four *sthūlātyaya* offenses arising from irrational assertions against the Saṃgha, all other instances such as private admonition, admonition before a group, and admonition before the full Saṃgha collectively constitute a single *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

According to that Vinaya text, stating that the Saṃgha possesses affection and so forth constitutes a separate *sthūlātyaya* offense; in addition to incurring the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, one still [incurs the *sthūlātyaya*].
A separate confession is required.
Regarding the opening of the text: parents must nourish the sick to relieve their suffering; small children may be left unattended for fear of injury;

and it is permitted to give them things, such as allowing them to plant flowers and the like, for the purpose of making offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle 14, states that this is not permitted.
If digging the ground damages seeds, one must use "pure speech" (kappiya-vācā). If there is water free of insects, one may personally irrigate [the fields] and so forth.

Regarding the case where crossing a river by leaping does not constitute an offense: this is permissible in the case of large ditches and canals; however, it is not allowed for small ones. In the *Pañcaśata-praśna*, it is asked:
"May a bhikṣu leap over a small stream or a small embankment? The answer is: "He commits a *pāyattika* offense. Formerly, there was an upāsaka.
He invited a bhikṣu, saying, "Make me a fine robe; I wish to give it to you. The bhikṣu followed him along the road, where there was a small stream.
The bhikṣu leaped across it. The donor thought to himself, "I considered this man to be a person of noble character and wished to give him a robe, yet he leaps over the water."
"I should give him half a robe. This bhikṣu was one who was free from attachment; knowing his thought, he stepped forward and saw water, so he again leaped across.
He thought again, "I should give him a single coarse cotton cloth," and as he stepped forward, he leaped again.

He thought of giving coarse linen, and his thoughts regarding the sudden meal were likewise. Then, seeing water once more, he lifted his robe and waded across. The worthy one asked, "Why did you not [cross]?"
The bhikṣu replied, "At first he gave me one robe; next, half a robe; and so on, until finally he gave me a single meal.
That he does not now hesitate is because he fears that I might lose my meal again. Thereupon, the worthy man repented and made a grand offering. By this one may verify [the truth].

"Do not leap over ditches or water. Regarding "shouting out," the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Duo lun), fascicle 4, states that the five groups of monastics must not shout; to utter confused speech would destroy one’s dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
Regarding "reading books and carrying them along," the *Samantapāsādikā* (Jian lun), fascicle 14, says: laypeople may employ bhikṣus to prostrate to the Buddha, recite sūtras, or offer prayers;
or they may employ bhikṣus to strike the sounding-block clearly to assemble the community for various Dharma activities. Thus, laypeople may direct and employ [monastics].

There is no offense. If one is sent on an errand by a layperson (*avadātavasana*), it is an offense of *duṣkṛta* for each step taken upon departing; if one receives food or drink, it is an offense of *duṣkṛta* for every swallow.
There is no offense if one does not go so far as to act as a messenger for the layperson, though all questions and answers [in such a case] incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.

This does not apply if one is sent on an errand by members of the fivefold assembly of renunciants (*pañca-vargīya pravrajita*). The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (*Duolun*) further states: "If one gives out of compassion for those who are solitary, destitute, or begging, it is permissible for all outsiders..."
