The Path constantly acts as a great adversary to the Buddha-dharma, seeking out its flaws and shortcomings. For this reason, one should provide incense-scented robes; this brings auspiciousness to the fourfold assembly.
If a nun receives such a robe, she commits a *pāyattika* offense. Furthermore, none of the five types of perfumes may be used to sprinkle upon the ground, except for the sake of the Triple Gem.
One who wears flower garlands hinders and obstructs the practice of the Way; for the sake of the Triple Gem, one must not do so either.
Furthermore, one must not place flowers, incense, necklaces, or other ornaments upon the body of a Buddha; they may only be scattered on the ground as an offering.
One must not scatter flowers upon the bodies of the Sangha. If flowers are placed upon a drink, it is not permitted to drink it. If one causes elephants to fight...
Even down to the fighting of roosters, the five assemblies are strictly forbidden from doing so. Crying out—down to the death of one's parents—is entirely forbidden for the four assemblies;
for bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *pāyattika* offense. Because their hearts are deeply attached, the *Wǔbǎiwèn* (Five Hundred Questions) asks:
"If a teacher, disciple, parent, or sibling dies, may one weep? The answer is: to raise one's voice even once constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; one may only weep and sob slightly."

Regarding the two types of observance of the precept against being ill-natured, rejecting the Sangha, and defying admonition: these consist of the two categories of abstention (*virati*) and performance (*karaṇa*).
As for the scriptural passage stating, "My Holy Lord has attained Perfect Enlightenment," the *Jīvitasthiti-sūtra* (The Seventh) says: "In the past, he already maintained my light..."
In the past, there was a great Brahmin teacher who constantly instructed five hundred youths in the Brahmanical laws; those of lower castes were not permitted to hear them.

However, a slave born into his household heard them because of his association with the youths and was able to retain them. Later, he fled to another country where he studied the non-Brahmanical laws.
Because he had already mastered the former teachings, he was able to retain everything he heard. His master was greatly pleased and gave him his daughter in marriage.

The wife prepared food for him, but he was constantly dissatisfied and prone to anger. When the master went to seize him, the slave spoke secretly, saying, "I declare that you, my lord, are my father;
please do not obstruct me, and I shall pay the price of a slave. The master replied, "You are indeed my son."
He was sent off early. At that time, his wife came secretly and prostrated at the feet of the brahmin, asking, "My husband always complains about the food and drink;
I pray you, teach him what to eat from our own home. The master of the slave thought, "He is tormenting my children," and as he was about to depart...
He taught him a verse, saying: "Wandering to other lands without kin, you deceive the people of the world. Coarse food is your constant fare; why do you begrudge eating it?
He gave this verse to him, instructing that whenever he begrudged the food, he should recite it softly with his face turned toward it. Later, the wife tested him.
After hearing this, the slave constantly spoke with servility. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "I was that master, and the slave was Chanda.
At that time, he relied upon me to insult others; now he does the same again. The tenth chapter on Nirvāṇa contains a verse which says:
Regarding the words of others, he follows them without opposition and does not observe whether they act or do not act. At that time, he spoke these verses solely for Ajātaśatru:

"Good son, it is also said that one who guards and upholds the precepts without violating them, who achieves dignified deportment, and who sees the faults of others—[for such a person] these verses were spoken" (the above is the scriptural passage). This chapter cites the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, though the text is incomplete. That...
The fourth fascicle of the *Śāstra* states: Question: The sūtras say, "One should simply observe one's own bodily conduct and clearly discern what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.

How is this not in contradiction with the statement that [monastics] should "instruct one another"? Answer: The Buddha established his teachings according to the specific circumstances; thus, while the words may differ, their intent is the same.
This is not contradictory. Because the minds of others may harbor love and hatred, their speech can be harmful; therefore, [the Buddha] causes them to observe their own physical conduct.
If it is for the sake of a compassionate mind that brings benefit, he thus exhorts them to instruct one another even with harsh words.
However, if one is of dull faculties and lacks wisdom such that one’s speech brings no benefit, one should observe oneself. This applies to those who are intelligent and of sharp faculties.

If one’s words are beneficial, one should instruct and exhort others accordingly. If one has heard little and seen but a small measure, yet speaks without providing benefit, one should reflect upon oneself.

If, however, one has heard extensively and possesses broad vision such that one can propagate and benefit others, then one should instruct and exhort others in turn. Furthermore, it is said: if one acts for the sake of fame or profit...
When there is something to be spoken, one should observe one's own body. If it is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings and proclaiming the Buddha-dharma, one should teach others in turn.

It is further said: For the sake of happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha*), one should observe one's own body (speaking in general terms, attaining the Noble Path is called "happiness of the Dharma"; if explained according to specific characteristics, the four fundamental [dhyānas] are called "dwelling in happiness in the present life").
If one wishes to transform and benefit sentient beings through the Dharma, causing them to realize what one has realized oneself, one should transmit it from one to another.

"Teaching" (meaning that having attained the noble state oneself, one causes others to do the same). Furthermore, when newly ordained, one may feel attachment to parents, siblings, wives, and children;
for this reason, one should be made to contemplate only one's own body. If one has practiced and studied for a long time, one possesses the power to assist others;

for this reason, one should be made to teach others in turn. (The above constitutes six successive explanations. The *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra* states: "If one possesses even a small amount of goodness and wishes to disparage or treat others with contempt..."
One should know that such a person deeply obstructs the Buddha-dharma. In the detailed commentary (*vibhaṅga*), following the topical outline (*kośa*) of the *Prātimokṣa*, it says:
"There are three matters regarding the act of admonishing. Now, in the detailed commentary, the meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above; this explains the first [point], the person who can resist.
From "of evil character and not accepting [admonition]" onwards, it explains the second [point]: how various virtuous bhikṣus should admonish according to the Dharma. First, for now...

First, the individual explanations; second, the combined explanation. The text for the individual explanations has three parts: first, the explanation of having a wicked nature and not accepting instruction;

second, the explanation of being "in accordance with the scriptural text" regarding the precepts and the Dharma—this refers to the section beginning with "having proceeded by means of the precepts" and so forth; third, the explanation of being "in accordance with the Dharma," which constitutes the combined explanation.
"From 'If a bhikṣu has already [committed an offense]' below, this explains how various virtuous bhikṣus should offer admonition according to the Dharma.

From 'He himself commits what is improper' below, this explains the third [point]: refusing instruction and guidance while hoping for respect from others as a teacher. The preceding explanation of the matters to be admonished is concluded; the remainder may be understood accordingly."
Regarding the phrase "the text does not itself [mention] *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) and so forth," some have cited the fourth fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* to explain this passage.
However, upon careful examination, that text differs from the present Vinaya; therefore, there is no need to cite it. That text states: "In this regard, as for the offense:
if a bhikṣu says, 'Do not tell me of a *duṣkṛta*, do not tell me of a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), do not tell me of a *pārājika* (defeat); I likewise shall not tell you of a *sthūlātyaya*.'"
Ānanda, I do not speak of your minor offenses (dukkaṭa). If you say, "I shall abandon these teachings of yours," because you have reviled the assembly, you incur a *thullaccaya*.
If you first speak gently and persuade him to abandon this matter, he should be made to perform four *dukkaṭas*, two *pācittiyas*, and one *thullaccaya* for his transgression.
If he does not abandon it, a formal motion (*ñatti*) and the rest [of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*] should be performed. The second section above is concluded.

In the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* it says: "Regarding the nine [offenses] where the first is an immediate offense (*pārājika*) and up to those involving three admonitions. Sengyao states: This is introduced to resolve a doubt.
While it may be appropriate for the first nine offenses committed in private to be concealed, the latter four, which are committed in the presence of the Saṃgha, should not require concealment;

therefore, he immediately explains: "If one commits any one of them," and so forth, as explained at length. [The text] asks: Among the eight *pārājika* offenses of the nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), should it also be stated that seven are immediate offenses and one is not?
"Up to three admonitions. Why is this so? Answer: That [offense] cannot be remedied, as there is no doubt to be resolved. Now, examining the text: "One should forcibly grant *parivāsa*.
This means that if one confesses from one's own heart, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is not required for its completion.

If, however, one repents—or perhaps does not repent—the Sangha should formally charge him; hence it is called "forcibly. In the following passage, it is stated that purity, lightness, heaviness, and indeterminacy are not permitted.
Compelling one to repent is entirely different from this; it serves as an obstacle and renders [the act] unreasonable.
Regarding the "additional" [penance] of six nights and so forth: since the previous offense had already been punished for concealment, this is now an additional penalty. Question:

Since the first two categories (pārājika and saṃghāvaśeṣa) both have methods of punishment, why is it not the same for the last three categories? Answer: Upon detailed examination of their meaning, there is no restoration of purity [for them]; therefore, it is so stated.
One must distinguish [the two]. The lower fascicle is easy to repent; its text is entirely missing. Only at the end of this fascicle is the method for repentance explained.
By citing what is difficult, the ease [of the latter] is revealed; thus, the lower fascicle is abbreviated. Other explanations involve redundant words, and therefore they are not recorded here.
II. The Section on the Purpose of the Unclassified [Topics]. Others all say: "The chapters herein merely establish the locations; they do not reveal the purpose of their inclusion."

He then cited the former Master Guangtong, who said: "The sacred prohibitions follow conditions and meander through myriad threads; offenses arise according to individuals, and the regulations for subduing them are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Since it is difficult to fully prepare for and maintain these practices, if we do not mutually examine one another, there will likely be no sense of self-discipline.
For this reason, the Sages permitted trustworthy women to point out offenses in both private and public settings, thereby preserving the path of mutual benefit."

Now, examining this in detail: the statement in the *Zhang* that "for the sake of obstructing what is credible, one may cite the seven [categories] such as the five [aggregates] and so forth" does not differ in meaning from the passage concerning "mutual examination between [the author] and Guangtong. Thus, its purpose is explained by its placement; there is no need for a separate exposition.
In the *Śènmíng* (Explanation of Terms), it quotes a verse from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, stating: "...therefore they are said to be indeterminate" (the above is the text of the treatise).
This treatise states that these two are indeterminate; they may be called "three corners" (*trikoṇa*) or "three paths" (*trimārga*). These two types—corners and paths—are both indeterminate.

Regarding the phrase "all sins are the three corners because they are the three paths": the verse does not explicitly mention the three paths because their meaning is identical to that of the three corners.
Now, in this commentary, they are explained fully and extensively because they do not necessarily coincide with the three corners, or because they may proceed along the three paths.
For example, regarding those of the indeterminate group: all sentient beings are comprised within three groups in total.

First, the group of those fixed in the right nature (referring to those who have entered the stage of the aids to penetration, from the level of *kṣānti* [patience] onwards). Second, the group of those fixed in the wrong nature (those who commit the five deeds of immediate retribution and are certain to fall into the evil destinies).

Third, the group of those of an indeterminate nature (those other than the two aforementioned categories; namely, ordinary worldlings who are not fixed because they follow various conditions, whether wholesome or unwholesome). Here, we take this third group of the indeterminate nature as a metaphor for the two.
It is indeterminate.
As for the "Tripiṭaka Commentary," this refers to the commentary by Paramārtha.
"Corner" (*koṇa*) means "accumulation," because three vertices gather together to form a single corner. This triangular accumulation is as previously [described].

The three categories of sentient beings (*sattva-rāśi*) are taught with differing meanings; however, their interpretation is not fixed. Among the three points [of the triangle], the first point is not taken because it is fixed;
only the latter two are taken to explain that which is not fixed. The three paths should be understood accordingly.

Regarding those who should not sit: the *Miaoliao shu* (Clear Explanation) states that if one sits with a defiled mind, it is a *pāyattika*; if one sits without a defiled mind, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one sits because they did not realize they had arrived there, it constitutes an offense against the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).

Regarding the twenty-eight offenses: within each of the four modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*), seven categories of offenses may occur; the twenty-four [remaining cases] should be understood accordingly.

This is analogous to those within the three categories who belong to the indeterminate category (*aniyata-rāśi*); it serves as a metaphor for sentient beings whose spiritual disposition (*gotra*) is indeterminate.
Regarding the five ways of reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, according to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*), the recitation of the precepts should be summarized into five types:

first, reciting the introduction (*nidāna*); second, reciting up to the four *pārājika* offenses; third, reciting up to the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; fourth, reciting up to the *aniyata* offenses; and fifth, reciting the full text in detail.

Regarding the eight conditions for origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are explained as follows in the *Zēngliù shū* (Commentary on the Sixfold Increase). This means that by taking the body and speech as conditions, one commits various offenses.

Other masters state that these two indeterminate categories resemble the original meaning of the Vinaya; however, because their number is small, they are not [included here]. (The above is the treatise.)
"Obtaining the meaning according to the original Vinaya text" refers to the word "seemingly" (*sì*) in the Master’s commentary on the treatise; that is, this is concise while that is extensive.
All that follows consists of explanations derived from the intended meaning of the treatise's text.
Regarding the three places for seeking [the precepts]: first, the *nidāna* (origins); second, the *śīla-mūla* (root precepts); and third, the extensive commentary (*vibhaṅga*).

The statement that the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* is also like this refers to the fourth fascicle of the *Mahā-vibhāṣā*, which says: "As for the 'undetermined' [offenses], the Buddha, while sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), immediately determined the five categories of offenses and so forth.
This is as cited later in the commentary (*śāstra*). This is the intention of the ancient masters: that one should seek [the precepts] in these three places, and it is also based upon...

Regarding the characteristics of the various treatises, there are only three categories: *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and *pāyattika*. Thus, we know that the offenses being prevented are definitely fixed at either three or two.

As for the points where this agrees with the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it was previously cited from the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations): "A trustworthy woman does not know whether an offense has been committed or not."
One knows where the offense was committed; it is simply that a woman came and went to that place. This is also consistent with the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya* (Many-Text Vinaya). An ancient said:
"The three offenses and two offenses are what is to be prevented (*pratiṣedhya*); freedom from defilement and purity are what serve as the remedy (*pratipakṣa*).

A non-Dharmic self-accusation is what is to be clarified; a Dharmic self-accusation is what serves as the remedy. Furthermore, when the punishment for an offense is not applied correctly, this constitutes what is to be prevented."

It is capable [of determining guilt] by punishing according to the Dharma. The traditional interpretation refutes this, stating that "non-Dharmic self-accusation" is what is clarified [by the *aniyata* rules].

Since a nun may also engage in self-accusation, there ought to be an *aniyata* offense for her as well. Furthermore, how could it be permissible to require that one must wait for a self-accusation before committing an *aniyata* offense?

If the punishment of those who commit offenses is not carried out as it should be, the fault lies with the Saṃgha. How could this precept be intended to govern the monks who administer the punishment?
Master Shou stated that its essence consists of "suspicion and semblance. This was refuted by the argument: since the suspicion resides in the woman, how can it constitute the essence of the offense?

The commentator further argued that both concealed and exposed places must be investigated and examined as the objects to be guarded against. Now, having already explained the meaning and significance of these points:

This is the general explanation. Fearing that people might still be confused, I shall now provide a specific explanation. That is to say, the two *aniyata* (undetermined offenses) occur in secluded or exposed places where suspicion may arise;
walking, standing, sitting, or lying down are what must be guarded against. It is like a parent restraining a wayward child to prevent them from committing transgressions;
thus, one does not permit them to go to places that are questionable. Even if they should go there, the parents must inevitably interrogate them upon their return.

It is the same in this case as well. Chong says: "When one has not yet verified [the reality], one is included within the indeterminate category; once the verification is complete and the reality is established, one belongs to the fixed category.

Why then must the nature of that which is prevented be clarified here? Now, we grant that the restraint of the *saṃvara* is under discussion; the essence of the two hundred and fifty precepts must be maintained.
How could it be permitted that there is no nature of that which is prevented within this? Therefore, because of these doubts..."

"Place" refers to that which is to be guarded against. Question: Since one may commit any offense while in a situation of suspicion, why should it not be restricted solely to those precepts concerning lustful attachment?

Answer: In principle, although it applies to the commission of all precepts, because the fault of lustful attachment is particularly grave, this indeterminate category was established to guard against it by means of that specific [precept].
Furthermore, this also demonstrates that for a nun, if she has a companion, she remains concealed and thus the offense is not established.

This refers to the *niyata-śikṣāpada* (fixed precepts). If one considers only the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it appears that the *aniyata-śikṣāpada* (undetermined precepts) were established because they generally prevent violations of all other precepts.

Thus, the fourth fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Regarding the three matters: among the four *pārājika*, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and the ninety [other] offenses, one may speak of any single instance."
It is taught that for a single matter, two factors [must be present]. The same applies to the *pārājika* offenses. Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"One merely sees [the person] coming and going, sitting and standing; one does not see [them] committing sexual misconduct, theft, killing, cutting grass, or eating past noon.

Since that text speaks of a single matter in a general sense and further specifies that one does not see the acts of cutting grass or eating past noon, it is known that these prohibitions apply universally to prevent all defiled actions, yet they are not fixed as specific categories.

Therefore, regarding the statement that "within self-assertion of right and wrong there are no two indefinite [cases]," this clarifies the matter of self-assertion of right and wrong at the end of the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Section on the Settlement of Disputes) in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

Regarding "and not the three aforementioned [locations], but a place secluded from seeing and hearing": this means being far removed and devoid of people, which is what is meant by "secluded from seeing and hearing.
Thus, it is known that this is not a place where monks, nuns, or laypeople reside. However, in the extensive explanation in the subsequent text, it says:
To see it in a secluded place is precisely this.
As for the statement that there is also uncertainty regarding the degree [of the offense], such that it may either exist or not exist—this is the intention of the ancient masters.
They mean that if one commits many offenses, there is indeed uncertainty, because one does not know for certain which specific precept has been violated. However, if one commits few offenses, then...
There is no uncertainty; this may be understood by analogy.

As for the case where nuns or laymen might also be indeterminate: according to Paramārtha, female lay followers (*upāsikā*) who have attained the three fruits are all permitted to censure [a transgressor], with the sole exception of those who have attained the fourth fruit.
If one has attained the fourth fruit, they must necessarily be ordained; thus, it refers to the community of ordained nuns.
This is because the Buddha prohibited the formal accusation of offenses.
Now, regarding the explanation that the first two [points] differ from the ancient interpretation: the Vinaya Master Yun previously had two interpretations.

One interpretation stated: "This is the second [point]. I have verified this through the text; the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* allows for the treatment of offenses, whereas the other chapters do not. Therefore, we know there is no "first" [point]. If...
Question: Regarding your source, what is the "first offense" (*ādyāpatti*)? Answer: In the various sections (*varga*), it refers to the first [offense] in general;
here, it refers to the first [offense] in detail. Although the names are identical, their meanings differ, and thus there is no contradiction. Question:

Since the *pārājika* offenses in this [text] appear before the *bhikṣuṇī-vibhaṅga*, and because the text explicitly states they are the "first offenses," one might ask: if the *aniyata* rules concerning secluded places were the first *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rule, [would that not contradict the sequence?]

The middle section is incomplete; it should be the second. The answer concerns the discussion of offenses according to their locations. While the offenses themselves are indeed fixed, they are clarified here according to location, as both possess an initial stage.
This refers to the "screened" and "exposed" locations, which constitute the initial detailed offenses; that is, the initial abbreviated offenses for each category [of the Vinaya].

The broad [rules] are established to supplement the abbreviated ones. Regarding the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules, because the first offense is broadly defined in its totality, the total breadth is established as a regulation to supplement the specific breadth.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: since the two *aniyata* rules are established collectively based on the location, there is a "separate first" [rule], which is precisely the first one;
it is established in relation to the collective location to rectify the abbreviation. Now, the Master’s prior establishment of the meaning of what is to be guarded against differs from the ancients.
The Master [Daoxuan] therefore explains the first two [cases], which also differs from the ancient masters. As the meaning explained in the chapter states:

"If one considers the three or two offenses to be examined, although this is the second [case], now, in accordance with what must be investigated and verified to ascertain the reality, it refers to a secluded or exposed place where there is suspicion or obstruction; this is the first [case]."
The fourth section concludes by stating: "In this context, the meaning of 'the white statement' (*śuklavāda*) and so forth is called *vinaya*.

In reality, however, it is not the *adhikaraṇa-śamatha-vinaya* (the *vinaya* for settling disputes). This can be understood from the chapter, as the intent of this *vinaya* is consistent with that of the *Adhikaraṇa-śamatha-khaṇḍaka*."
"In the case of the *pratijñā* (self-accusation) cited above, it refers to this specific text on the precepts.
Regarding the *pratijñā* cited below, it refers to the *pratijñā-vinaya* for settling disputes found in the section where the medicine and the ailment are paired."

Regarding the statement in the lower section that "the five categories (*pañcāpatti*) are fully cited within the *madhyama*," one should say that "the seven groups (*saptasaṃghāvaśeṣa*) are fully cited.

This refers to the subsequent passage at the end of the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (or *Adhikaraṇa-śamatha-vastu*). As for the phrase "all are similar," in principle, the seven groups may indeed be cited in all three locations.
"Seeking the reality" means seeking out the transgression so as to reach the actual facts; that is, the locus of the offense.

The *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (vinaya before one's eyes) is subsumed under these two categories. All *vinaya* procedures necessarily depend upon being present before [the assembly], and thus they are subsumed within these two—either through one’s own confession (*pratijñā*) or the locus of the offense—and cannot be discussed separately.
The fifth section on the settlement of disputes should be understood accordingly. Some say: "If a monk sits with a woman, the husband may dismiss his wife;
therefore, the text states that if the husband sees it, he should reprimand his wife, lest she develop a lack of faith. If a nun sits with a man, the wife has no grounds to dismiss her husband;
therefore, there is no indeterminate offense. Now, examining this closely: this was intended to prevent such calamities, not to provide protection.
This was the fault of sending away his wife.
Regarding "two [offenses] for the nun beforehand and one afterwards," this excludes the two coarse words and the act of touching from among the residual offenses.
As for the text stating that she went immediately to listen while leaning against a wall, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Duo-lun), fascicle four, asks: "Vaiśākha was intelligent..."
He was of sharp faculties and highly esteemed by the virtuous. When he learned that a bhikṣu was sitting in a secluded place with a woman, he asked why [the other] had gone there. He replied:
"This man has already entered the path of the noble ones and deeply delights in the Buddha-dharma; he often says himself that there are five personal benefits in listening to the Dharma."
First, they hear what has never been heard before; second, their purity becomes firm and steadfast; third, they eliminate wrong views; fourth, they attain right view;
fifth, they touch the profound Dharma. For these reasons, Viśākhā delights in the purity of the Dharma and does not allow herself to be falsely constrained by suspicion.
Regarding the fourteen points of debate, this upāsikā had ten sons and ten daughters, and each of her sons and daughters had twenty grandchildren.

There were four hundred and twenty people in total. When the people of the country saw that Viśākhā had many grandchildren, both sons and daughters, they all discussed it together, saying, "This is excellent.
Each came forward to welcome and take them [as their own], establishing this as a precedent. In the extensive commentary (*vibhaṅga*), the first passage consists of six points:

first, the meaning of *bhikṣu*; second, the woman; third, the explanation of "alone" (*ekākinī*); fourth, the explanation of "a secluded or covered place" (*raho 'vacchanna-sthāna*); fifth, the explanation...
It may serve as a place for sexual misconduct; this is the sixth instance of improper speech.

Regarding the phrase "a laywoman who has faith and devotion" (*śraddhopāsikā*), which refers to one who has faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, the *Cīvaravastu* (or *Jīvaka-vastu*) states that one who accomplishes sixteen qualities is called a "credible laywoman" (*śraddhopāsikā*).
That is to say, she relies upon the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and her reputation is such that it can cause others to be known [as credible].
[It is] so. [The Sangha] has an ill reputation; it can cause it to be quickly extinguished (this is the fourth). It does not follow after desire, hatred, fear, or delusion (this is another four).

It is free from desire and directed toward the attainment of the noble (this is another two). This is the wording of the Vinaya text. To have faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is precisely the "three undestroyed [jewels]" of that Vinaya, because the three undestroyed faiths constitute its essence.
To take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is identical to taking refuge in the Three Jewels according to that Vinaya.
The "jewels" (ratna) and so forth—namely, the five [precepts] beginning with non-killing—are identical to the noble precepts (ārya-śīla) established in that Vinaya.
The four [qualities] beginning with "gaining benefit" and the four beginning with "not being fond of" constitute the distinctions within the first six [categories].

The "candidate for the state of freedom from desire" (*vītarāga-pratipannaka*) refers to those who are directed toward the [first] three fruits. This means that because their craving within the three realms has not yet been completely severed, they are directed toward its exhaustion;
hence, they are called "candidates. Within this category, there are four divisions: first, the six who are fully endowed with faith and shame;
second, the four who provide offerings and offer praise; third, the four who dwell well in equanimity; and last, the two consisting of the path and the precepts of the path.
Regarding the statement that words are true and not false, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 4, states: "This refers to one who has accomplished untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*).
Such a person will never intentionally utter a falsehood. Even if someone were to say to them: 'If you speak falsely, it shall not harm your life.'"
"If you do not speak falsely, I shall take your life. He then reflected to himself: "If I do not speak falsely, I shall lose this single body;
but if I speak falsely, I shall lose immeasurable bodies and, moreover, harm my Dharma-body. I vow not to speak falsely. The man spoke again, saying:
"If you speak falsely, your father, mother, brothers, sisters, and all your kinsmen shall live; but if you do not speak falsely, [they shall all perish]."

He killed them all. Then he reflected again: "I have not spoken falsely; yet by harming these kinsmen of this single lifetime’s birth and death, if I had spoken falsely, I would have been reborn in the three evil realms, forever losing my kin of successive human and celestial lives, and losing the noble and holy companions of the supramundane.
Another person then said to him: "If you speak falsely, I will give you precious jewels and various kinds of wealth and profit; if you do not, [I shall not]."
"If I do not give it to you, I shall not lie; yet by this, I would lose these worldly riches. If I were to lie, I would lose the wealth of the noble Dharma. He then reflected thus.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'If a bhikṣu' and so forth, which explains the third [offense], the Undetermined Confession (*aniyata*)...

Now, upon examining the text, there are six sentences in total beginning with "If a bhikṣu. Among these, the first sentence fully cites the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), as well as the five matters of self-confession (*svavacana*);
from among these, they are cited in full according to what is appropriate. Therefore, within this chapter, the third [offense], the Undetermined Confession, is analyzed and explained accordingly.

This refers to the "determined" (niyata) category. As for the remaining five phrases, regarding the five matters, starting from the first matter, the latter one, two, three, and even up to five matters are all "undetermined" (aniyata).
These are combined to form five phrases; all of these must be treated as offenses at the place where they were committed.
Therefore, in the commentary, the fourth [category] of treating offenses as undetermined is assigned and explained, and this classification is established in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*).

This concludes the section. To provide a general explanation: these two undetermined offenses (*aniyata*) should be understood in relation to whether or not one of the seven or six offenses committed while sitting is mutually cited.

The same applies to the other three postures (*īryāpatha*). However, because the offense is raised based on a credible report regarding the posture of sitting, it is here summarized by reference to that alone;
yet, for each individual posture, one must likewise consider whether the offenses are mutually cited or not.

Regarding the statement that "the principle applies to both seven offenses and six offenses," the intended meaning is that, within the context of the four modes of deportment, one must carefully distinguish between the seven and the six offenses.
This is to clarify whether to cite or not cite [the specific rule] when resolving the disciplinary offense.

However, due to the circumstances of the origin story (*nidāna*), a trustworthy woman reported the general posture of sitting to the assembly of monks, rather than distinguishing the differences between the seven offenses and so forth. Consequently, taking advantage of this momentum, [the rule was established] in summary.

The four modes of conduct generally clarify whether offenses are mutually cited or not cited; however, in reality, within these four modes of conduct, if the seven or six offenses are not mutually cited, they must all be dealt with according to the specific location of the offense.
In the "Explanation of Punishments," regarding the initial phrase of the former interpretation, it states that the preceding four waves do not cite the previous four [categories].

This refers to the explanation within the fourth section on "Indeterminate Punishments for Offenses. According to Master Yun’s intention, he says: "One who confesses their own action commits a *pārājika* offense;

one who lies down commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; one who sits commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense; and 'reaching the destination' or 'tending toward' refers to the preparatory offenses (*prayoga*) of *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and so forth. There is...

People say: The ancient masters stated that "speaking for oneself" is auspicious. Furthermore, it is erroneous to exhaustively assign [the offenses] in sequence according to the five categories (*pañcāpatti*).
Regarding the first phrase, the four preceding [offenses] are not raised; rather, the four preceding [terms] are cited. This refers to citing two causes and two effects.

Regarding the second phrase, the three preceding [offenses] are not raised; rather, the three preceding [terms] are cited. This refers to raising the four preceding [terms] and citing the three preceding [terms].
The fourth [case] refers to the two causes and two fruits drawn out by the waves. In the second phrase, the upper three are not raised;

the upper three drawn out by the waves refer to the two causes and one fruit. The remaining phrases should be understood accordingly. Now, the Master refutes this, saying: "This is not necessarily so. (And so forth...
As for the statement that "all contain seven [factors] in their explanation," this reveals the correct principle and thereby refutes the ancient interpretation.

Regarding the phrase "although [the text] lists and quotes [the offenses]" and so forth, the intended meaning is as follows: although the text itself mentions "speaking" (*vāda*) or "lying down" (*śayana*) and so on, "speaking" (*vāda*) encompasses all seven offenses;

however, it does not necessarily correspond exactly to what is stated in the text, because the specific wording may not be equivalent. If one examines this closely, there are instances where they do not correspond at all.
This does not yet constitute a formal determination.
It merely concerns the points regarding whether one incurs more or fewer offenses and the specific dharmas subject to discipline;

as for the statement in the text that "the agent performs [the act]," this does not necessarily refer only to the commission of a *pārājika* offense or similar acts. This term "agent" applies generally across all four postures (*īryāpatha*), each involving the commission of seven types of offenses. Now...

To speak generally of the "author" (the commentator), this refers to the commentary on the fourth line of the Vinaya text concerning the indeterminate punishment for offenses, specifically the passage on the fifth line that deals with the application of legal rules (*dharma*) regarding whether or not an offense is established based on the presence or absence of witnesses and the quantity of evidence. This refers to the section within these five lines.
Regarding the first four phrases, there are citations of one's own words; as for the fifth phrase alone, there are no such words at all.

Since there are varying degrees of presence or absence among the citations within the preceding four, it is said that "the citations vary in number and presence. All of these must be dealt with according to the specific offense and location;

therefore, they are further called the "Procedures for Dealing with Offenses and Locations" (āpattiyathādharman). Within this text, there are other sections concerning the "approach" (upasampad) and so forth.

The meaning of this is easy to understand. However, within this text, it is stated that the one who commits the act incurs all seven offenses; this should be understood as explained in the commentary (*śāstra*).

Regarding the statement below that there is no *pārājika* (defeat) for the subsequent precepts—that is, excluding the one who commits the act—it is said "this principle applies to all seven" while discussing the *pārājikas* specifically. This is an explanation intended to resolve a potential objection. The objection is as follows:

Previously, it was stated that one incurs all seven [offenses], yet the root text (*mūla*) of the subsequent precepts does not mention the commission of an offense, or at most, it only mentions it when explaining the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the offense.

[The text] subsequently omits [the mention of] *pārājika* (defeat). Thus we know that the mention of "committing" (*karoti*) serves only to clarify the commissioning of a *pārājika*. Now, the explanation is as follows:

the subsequent precepts omit *pārājika*; this is stated provisionally based on one predominant characteristic. In reality, there should also be mentions of committing and performing *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) offenses and so forth.

Regarding those who should not receive dependence (*niśraya*) and so forth, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten-Recitation Vinaya), fascicle 4, explains the matter in detail. Its meaning is the same as the forfeiture of thirty-five matters in this [Mūlasarvāstivāda] Vinaya.

In the third fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it states that a śrāmaṇera commits a *duṣkṛta* offense, while other assemblies are not mentioned. According to the *Samantapāsādikā* (Jianlun), fascicle 14, those who are insane and so forth are also exempted.
Regarding the phrase "once the matter has been relinquished" in the fourth section of the *Śū-ben* (Commentary): "matter" (*shi*) refers to wealth.
As for the three kinds of relinquishment, Chong states that the ancient masters, relying on the explanation in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, maintain that relinquishment has three meanings. Now...

[The author] explains: The *Śāstra* does not contain a formal text establishing these three meanings. According to principle, it is simply because one relinquishes material wealth that it is termed "relinquishment" (*tyāga*).

If one were to define "relinquishment" solely by the mental state of renunciation, then even a *pāyattika* offense would have to be called "relinquishment. Now, examining the fourth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, it says:

"Based on having already relinquished the offense and already repented, while the subsequent continuity of mind has not yet been severed, if one further obtains a robe, this is a 'subsequent robe' (*paścāt-cīvara*). Regarding this...

One incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense regarding the edge of the previous robe. Furthermore, it says: "The robe has already been relinquished; subsequently, the continuity of intention is severed, yet the offense has not been confessed.

Even if one obtains another robe on that very day, one must confess the *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) for its relinquishment" (this passage is cited later in the commentary itself). Since this accords with the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, if the intention has not yet been severed, one commits an offense by dyeing the subsequent robe;
likewise, if the offense has not been confessed, one also commits an offense by dyeing the subsequent robe. This differs from a *pāyattika* where the mental offense (*citta-dosa*) has not yet ceased.

Regarding "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*): since there is no sense of defilement (*saṃkliṣṭārtha*) in this case, we shall follow the commentary once more. There are three kinds of abandonment; these are taken as the correct [interpretation]. Question:

If one has not yet abandoned the offense of staying overnight with those who have not received full ordination (*anupasampanna*), and there is no allowance for two nights, is this not a case of mutual defilement? Answer: Even if the offense of mind (*cittāpatti*) is defiled, there is no material object (*dravya*) that can be abandoned.

Regarding the statement that "all [cases] possess the three meanings," Chong says: "The old interpretation held that whenever one enters into the state of relinquishment (*utsarga*), all three meanings are necessarily present. My current explanation is not so;
it is simply because if one uses [the object] without having relinquished it, there is an offense, whereas once the ritual of relinquishment has been completed, there is no fault in using it.

Based on this single meaning, entering into relinquishment does not require the other two. Now, examining this closely: the three meanings must indeed be complete, for it is not as if one were using it with one's own property.

Because there is no possibility of relinquishing it; because the substance of the wealth does not exist [with oneself]; and because there is no possibility of using it. "Relinquishing it incurs no fault" is because both he and I have permitted it.

Regarding that which "must be understood through the mind," this refers to the three points previously explained—such as the impossibility of relinquishing what is not one's own wealth—and these three meanings are mutually required.
According to the tradition handed down from former times, two further conditions are added beyond these three meanings: fourth, that it is light enough to be carried on the person.

This refers to excluding cases such as covering a roof with more than three layers. The fifth [category] is an offense involving the entire body; this refers to excluding robes that exceed the prescribed measurements.

There is an offense for what is outside the measurement, but none for what is within it. Furthermore, some say that the three meanings and five meanings are both unreasonable, and that only two meanings should be taken as correct:
first, when greed is particularly heavy, one takes objects in a manner that violates the proper method; second, [when greed is particularly heavy, one takes objects] beyond the proper measure.

This would obstruct and ruin one's correct cultivation; the gravity of such censure for transgression is great. Now, upon careful examination, twenty-four of the ninety minor precepts possess these characteristics;
therefore, [the current classification] is not logical.
The chapter states: Regarding the twenty-four precepts, they are summarized in verse as follows:

"Praise, one [meal], separate, sufficient, non-remainder, receiving, fine food, medicine, insects, water, bowl, true liberation, covering, white, high bed—seven; adding 'using insects' makes twenty-five. (Commentary:
First, accepting food praised by a *bhikṣuṇī*. Second, exceeding the limit of one meal. Third, eating from house to house (*paryāya-bhojana*). Fourth, eating separately (*pratyekabhojana*).
1. Eating in a group; 2. Eating after having finished one's meal; 3. Eating at an improper time; 4. Eating food kept overnight; 5.
Eating food not formally offered; 6. Soliciting choice foods; 7. Accepting an invitation for medicine for more than four months;
8. Drinking alcohol; 9. Drinking water containing insects; 10. Taking more than three bowls of food; 11. Receiving a gift of pure food without asking; 12. Sitting [inappropriately].
16. A bed with detachable legs; 17. Looking over the three robes; 18.
A high-legged bed (the following seven items in this section on the chapter on years are termed "high beds"); 19. A bed stuffed with cotton or fine silk; 20. A needle case made of ivory or horn;
21. An oversized sitting mat (*niṣīdana*); 22. An oversized wound-covering cloth; 23. An oversized rain-bathing garment.
Regarding robes: there are twenty-four types, such as the robes equal in measure to a Tathāgata. Now, upon close examination, one should also distinguish between the use of water containing insects;
therefore, this is added to make twenty-five.

The thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules are subdivided into thirty-two precepts. Within the various sections [of this chapter], one should understand that they are presented either according to the thirty or according to the thirty-two, as appropriate.
Regarding the thirty: (1) keeping extra robes; (2) being separated from robes; (3) keeping extra robes for more than one month;
(4) taking robes from a nun who is not a relative (also known as the "acceptance" rule); (5) having a nun who is not a relative wash robes; (6) from...
A non-relative householder begging for robes (the sixth acceptance). Accepting robes beyond what is sufficient (the seventh acceptance).

A single householder providing the price for robes (the eighth acceptance). Two householders providing the price for robes (the ninth acceptance). A royal minister sending precious materials (the tenth acceptance).
Wild silkworm bedding, also known as a cotton mattress (the eleventh). Black wool bedding (the twelfth). White wool bedding (the thirteenth). [Deficient]...
(14) For six years, [one] relies on the three robes; (15) one does not record the sitting mat. (16) Carrying wool. (17) Having an unrelated nun card wool.
(18) Possessing precious objects (receiving them). (19) Trading precious objects (receiving them). (20) Engaging in buying and selling (receiving them).
(21) An extra bowl. (22) Begging for a bowl (receiving it). (23) Begging for thread. Having an unrelated person weave it. Also...

24. Encouraging Weaving (receiving); 25. Taking Away Robes; 26. Medicines Stored for More Than Seven Days; 27. Seeking Rain-Cloths Before the Proper Time and Using Them Before the Proper Time (these two precepts are combined;

the act of seeking them before the time is termed the "receiving" offense); 28. Receiving Emergency Offerings Before the Proper Time and Keeping Them for More Than the Prescribed Period (these two precepts are also combined;
the act of receiving them before the time is termed the "receiving" offense); 29. Separating from One’s Robes While in a Forest Hermitage; 30. Diverting Property Belonging to the Sangha.
Regarding the objects (thirty in number, concerning receiving), the summary verse says (in seven-character lines): Long robes, separation from robes, the month-long robe;

Nuns washing robes, begging beyond the limit, one residence, two residences, kings, ministers, spreading [seats], carrying, sheep, the two jewels, trading, long bowls, thread, urging, seizing, medicine, rain, haste, separation, and returning communal property.
Regarding the pure gift of external wealth (*bāhya-vitta-śuddha-dāna*), it is the truly pure gift (*tattvika-śuddha-dāna*).

Now, upon careful examination, it may also be said that among the thirty [rules], one possesses three meanings; or, regarding those that come as five, it means that the property must truly belong to oneself.
It does not become "belonging to another" merely through the act of a pure gift. From this, one should understand that among the ninety [rules], the truly pure gift lacks the second meaning. Why?
However, this means that one incurs a *pāyattika* offense by the mere act of taking [the item], not by wearing or using it; for there is no offense in the act of wearing itself.

How could this be the same as the thirty [offenses]? Since one commits a *duṣkṛta* for every use of an object already transgressed, we know that this offense lacks a specific counterpart (*pratipakṣa*) and thus carries a fault even when currently being used.
This "True Precept" (*bhūta-śīla*) is the most significant obstacle among the thirty precepts; now that it has been explained and resolved, all [other matters] are settled.

Regarding the difficulty concerning the cessation [of the offense]: there is also a difficult objection stating that if one gathers more than three bowls of food and it is not one's own property, but someone else steals it, with whom is the offense incurred?
This objection is irrational. It is like the case of damaging the protector; how could that be due to one's own property?

Regarding the fact that the taste of food is common property: first, it accords with human sentiment; in all instances of eating and consuming, it is logically necessary that the food be shared among people. Second, it is verified by scriptural evidence;
for example, when a bhikṣu has completed the ritual of setting aside leftovers (*kṛtapiṇḍapāta*), everyone may eat together without incurring any offense.

Based on these two principles, we know that this [taste] is common property. However, if we discuss the alms bowl and robes, they must necessarily belong individually; for instance, if one person performs the ritual of pure giving (*śuddhadeya*).

[The procedure] is concluded. If it is given to another person, the ritual must be performed again; thus we know that [the object] belongs separately [to each recipient]. This principle occurs frequently in the subsequent chapters;
this alone should be understood, and no further analysis will be provided.
The two *nissaggiya* (rules involving forfeiture) are the rule concerning robes and the twenty-ninth rule concerning the six-night separation from one's robe.

The five beginning with "excess" (*atireka*) are the rules concerning excess; that is, the ten-day rule for robes, the excess bowl, the excess medicine, and the medicine received after the time of urgent offering.
These correspond to the first, third, twenty-first, twenty-sixth, and twentieth rules listed previously.
These are the eight precepts.
As for the five items of bedding, they are the eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth,
and fifteenth precepts listed above.
As for the remaining types of experience, they consist of fourteen experiences; namely, those previously listed as the fourth,
sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, eighteenth, nineteenth, twentieth, twenty-second, twenty-fourth, twenty-seventh, twenty-eighth, and thirtieth.

Regarding the bowl, there is no such thing as "shared use. This explains that an extra bowl is not subject to the offense of "excess" through shared use. That is to say, if one uses it for oneself, one incurs the offense of excess for oneself;

logically, there can be no shared offense. Even if it were used in common, one would not incur the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (forfeiture and confession), because since it was requested collectively, one does not even incur the offense of forfeiture.
How much more so when one knows that it is being kept in common? In such a case, one does not commit an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

Therefore, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* is cited as proof, stating that if two people beg for a single bowl together, they incur only a *duṣkṛta* offense. Since they do not share in the same offense, it is permitted to perform the ritual of *viśuddhi* (purification) with respect to a fellow resident while keeping an extra bowl;
thus, the accomplishment [of the ritual] is achieved. This is explained in the commentary (*śūtra*) itself.
As for the remaining items that can be explained: those such as the one-month supply, the six-year allowance, food, medicine, rain-cloths, and bathing garments—all these may be kept for oneself.
Since each has its own distinct purpose, there is no sense of a common offense [if they are used separately].

If one is traveling far away and has a householder declare the *śuddhi* (purity), [and so forth], such that there is no offense. Question: Previously, one kept an extra robe (*dīrgha*) in common with others;
one had a householder apply the *śuddhi*-method to it, yet now, because the householder does not apply it, an offense is incurred.

Since it was kept in common, how can it be relinquished? Answer: This is based on causing it to be relinquished. Since they were living together as a single unit, each was individually the master; there was no division of ownership.
Because of this principle, one may relinquish [the robe] in its entirety.

Regarding the single long robe that has not yet been formally purified (*adhiṣṭhita*) and is shared with others: the intention here is to say that if it is given as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*) to another, the three conditions are not fulfilled;
even if a nun washes it, it does not enter into the category of what must be relinquished. Now, upon careful examination, it is not by virtue of being a pure gift that it belongs [to another].
He has already been explained previously.

Regarding the passage in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun) stating that "two people share one robe," this is the text from the fifth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*. It is cited here for the purpose of distinguishing [the specific case] from others.

If it is said that there are six precepts with different modes of transgression when speaking in this way, that is not so; one should say there are seven precepts with different modes of transgression.

This refers to adding the "extra robe" (*atireka-cīvara*) to the outside [of the previous list], as its unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) has already been distinguished previously within this chapter.

Regarding the "other fifteen shared offenses," a detailed examination reveals that this too does not fully accord with reason. Among those fifteen, there are cases where one does not incur an offense, such as keeping an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) or traveling a long distance;

logically, these must be excluded. Furthermore, in cases such as taking a nun’s robe, begging for a robe from a non-relative, or carrying wool, if one takes them face-to-face together, they may be said to be shared offenses.
However, if one does not take them together, nor beg for them together, nor carry them together, how can they be considered shared?
Regarding the offenses, one should therefore reflect and discern them. First, concerning robes, fifteen verses state: Taking an extra robe; taking a nun’s robe; begging for a robe;
the first and second [cases of] staying; the king’s carrying; the two types of splitting; the two kinds of jewels; wealth and thread; urging; and turning back urgently.
As stated in the accounts of the councils: during the Council of Seven Hundred, ten practices were improperly adopted.

On the day of the *poṣadha*, when a donor offered gold and silver, they divided it among themselves. When asked whether it was permissible to accept such things, they replied that it was not. Where was this prohibited? They replied:
"It was established as a rule because of Upananda."
Regarding the shared and individual aspects of the five types of beneficial [robes]: among these five, the *atireka-cīvara* (extra robe) may be shared;

however, the remaining four—namely, the *nissaggiya-pācittiya* for keeping a robe apart from one's person, the *pācittiya* for exchanging robes with others, the *pācittiya* for a group not belonging to oneself, and so forth—do not have the sense of being shared. As in the case of instructing another to beg for a robe when one already has enough, or having someone act on one's behalf, all such instances allow for the fulfillment of one's intentions; this should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, according to the chapters, excluding the eleven [offenses] and grouping the remaining nineteen, they are summarized in verse (in seven-character lines):

The two on extra robes, the month-long separation, the robe for nuns, begging for robes, and exceeding the proper amount; one and two on kings, carrying wealth, two on bowls; encouraging weaving, long robes, rain, and haste—four;
bodily and verbal cessation of activity, and those shared with the body are classified as bodily offenses. Regarding "bodily cessation," it refers to the physical restraint [of activity].

[The practitioner] consents. The mouth ceases [the recitation] without relinquishing it; the body performs the act of departing. Although the vocal action (*vākkarman*) is absent, it can still be described as the cessation and performance of both body and speech, for the actual performance belongs solely to the body.

Furthermore, when the body remains overnight, it is called "shared with the body" (*sahakāya*). Other [details] have been explained extensively elsewhere. Specifically, the initial undertaking is called vocal action;
the joining of palms by the body and so forth is called bodily action; and keeping the mouth closed without relinquishing it is called... [omitted].
Cessation of speech refers to not joining the palms and so forth; this is called cessation of body.

That [the offense] occurs when the body and the robe are in mutual proximity is an interpretation that is likely incorrect, because it does not speak in terms of the time of the offense, and furthermore, it lacks the meaning of "the body departing," and thus is incomplete.
Regarding the "other twelve instances of receiving" (*dvādaśa pratigraha*)—which involve the body and speech receiving [objects] while depending on another's body—the meaning is as follows:

one personally requests with one's own mouth, personally receives with one's own body, and is granted by another's body; hence the name. These twelve instances of receiving are precisely the fourteen instances of receiving mentioned in the subsequent section, excluding two actual [instances].
Regarding "the six cases of using [an item]": "using" refers to using it beyond the previously permitted period.

"If one commits an offense by washing, dyeing, or beating, and likewise by beating, dyeing, or washing," means that if one commits an offense by washing or beating an item that has already been dyed, or commits an offense by dyeing or washing an item that has already been beaten.

The "five faults" refers to the five types of long [robes]. The "six acts" refers to the five types of spreading [the robe] and begging for thread (the Venerable says it should be called the "six accomplishments," because one does not commit an offense at the time of performing them).

Therefore, there are two clauses. Regarding the precept on taking back a robe, it says: "If one takes it back oneself or instructs another to take it back, and then conceals or stores it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one takes it back but does not conceal it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If it is hung upon a tree, placed upon a shelf, or even spread upon the ground, taking it away from its place constitutes the offense."

Regarding the *niḥsargika* [offenses]: it is a transgression (*duṣkṛta*) if one does not remove [the object] from its place. The ancient masters say: "According to this text, if one places [an object] upon a tree or similar location, there is a repeated offense.

The intention of the sub-commentary (*śāstra*) is as follows: In the preceding cases such as "seizing for oneself," an offense occurs only when one seizes what is present before one's eyes and removes it from its place.

Regarding the subsequent phrase, "if one places it upon a tree or similar location," this refers to an offense occurring immediately upon removal from the place even if not seized while present before one's eyes; it does not mean that a double offense is committed.

The cited passage makes this clear: the text states that "this *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* robe must be relinquished" (which refers to the relinquishing of the material object). "Having relinquished it, one must confess" (which refers to the relinquishing of the offense).

"The Saṃgha shall then return this robe to the bhikṣu" (which refers to the returning of the robe). "If they do not return it, it is transformed into a *śuddha-dāna* [pure gift] and so forth, which constitutes an offense" (which refers to the incurring of guilt for failing to return it).
Furthermore, regarding the three items beginning with "jewels": these refer to two types of jewels and a cotton mattress;

the subsequent items are all to be understood accordingly. Regarding the sixteen staffs: one must maintain them as external pure gifts (*pariśuddha-dakṣiṇā*). If they are not pure gifts, one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
As the following text states: large cauldrons and their lids, large jars and their ladles; small cauldrons and their lids, small basins and their ladles; and washing bottles and their [lids].
"Covering jars, water jars, and ladles. (The Commentary states: Within this, there are in total two cauldrons, two jars, four covers, four water jars, and four ladles.
Regarding the distinctions between the Middle Way, the worldly path, and their respective differences that can be known, these refer to the various ritual procedures, phrases, and sentences;
they differ for each case—whether directed toward the laity, the Path, the Sangha, or individuals—and within each individual precept, there are explicit clarifications.

Alternatively, there are four factors for those facing three persons or more, such as a *saṃgha*: first, the gathering of requisites; second, the gathering of the object of the procedure; third, the cultivation of dignified deportment;
and fourth, the utterance of the formula of relinquishment. As explained below in the commentary on the text, their meaning will become self-evident.
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "the absence of dharma," the Venerable One said: "This possesses two dharmas: first, the accumulation of wealth; second, its destruction.

In the section on the objects for repenting offenses within the *Śīlaparivarta*, it says: "Regarding the three precepts beginning with the Jewel [refuge], they apply exclusively to individuals. Question:

Since these apply only to individuals, can one perform the repentance before a separate assembly (*pṛthag-jana*)? Answer: These three, as well as the other precepts, all permit repentance before a separate assembly. Some people...
It is said: "If there are no monks within the boundary, one may confess before an individual. If there are monks, one must assemble the Sangha before performing the confession.

If it were not so, what would be the use of the formal motion (*jñapti*) for receiving confession? Now, examining this in detail: if one wishes to seek confession within the Sangha, one must formally announce the reception of the confession.

If one does not wish to confess within the Sangha, it is also permissible to do so before a separate group (*pṛthag-jana*). There is no textual authority regarding whether one should be superior or inferior; thus, it is called "confession face-to-face" (*pratyekamukha*).

[Regarding] confession (*pratideśanā*): it is not accomplished if performed apart from the assembly. In the Western practice [of India], it is likewise permitted to perform individual confession (*pratyekapratideśanā*) in the presence of another.

Furthermore, observing this Vinaya, in the *Poṣadha-vastu*, it is stated that if the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense and does not recognize its name or characteristics, and a visiting bhikṣu arrives who is easy to instruct, one should take him to a secluded place where other bhikṣus can see him but cannot hear what is said.
Standing, he instructs [the offender] to perform the confession according to the Dharma. Having done so, he returns to the place where that bhikṣu is and says these words:

"The offense committed by this bhikṣu has now been confessed. (Commentary states: Since it is said that one stands in a place where it is seen with the eyes but not heard with the ears, this appears to be a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*).

It is asked: for what reason is the offense relinquished and the robe returned? There is a *karmavācanā* procedure for relinquishing the offense, but there is none among the rules for relinquishing property. This shall be explained below.

As for the "discrimination," according to the meaning below, one should answer: "The repentance and removal of past karma is not a formal ritual act (*dharmakarma*). Furthermore, because it is performed before an individual, it is appropriate that a formal announcement (*jñapti*) be made."

Regarding the method for returning robes: when the Saṃgha returns robes, it is logically improper to give them to oneself. If one does not perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), the matter cannot be brought into alignment with that [proper procedure].
As for the relinquishing of property, the act of relinquishing property is a manifest event; it does not exclude prior karma. Furthermore, the performance of the ritual is not permanent.

Moreover, because it is conducted collectively before the Saṃgha, there is no need for a formal announcement (*jñapti*). Finally, since this is the personal gift of another, it originates from their own mind and cannot be determined by mere knowledge.
What need is there for formal ritual procedures?

Regarding the sixfold procedure performed before the Saṃgha: first, the request for confession; second, the invitation of a presiding master of confession; third, the formal announcement of receiving the confession; fourth, the actual relinquishment of the offense.
Fifth is the treatment by reprimand; sixth is the acceptance and establishment of the essential precepts.

For those of the three lower grades, five [procedures] apply, namely excluding the request for confession. Furthermore, when receiving the role of the presiding monk (kṣamāpaka), one must inform the neighboring monks to replace oneself; the person receiving the confession must then announce this.
Thus there are five. One person has four [requirements]. Furthermore, the "white-bound person" (śuklāntika) is excluded. Regarding the "four":

among the six requirements for a *saṃgha*, one excludes the begging bowl and the formal announcement (*jñapti*); the remainder are all included. As for the remaining [cases]: among the six [requirements], one excludes the begging and the formal announcement; the rest are as before.
The four dharmas apply universally to all precepts (*śīla*). (Note: Some commentaries state that "the others apply universally," but this is an error.

As for the fifth category—excluding the three [precepts] regarding jewels and so forth, as well as the begging bowl, there are twenty-eight other precepts and so on—it is such that the [precepts regarding] jewels and so forth are restricted to the four [assemblies], while the bowl is restricted solely to the six;
the remaining twenty-eight apply universally to both the Saṃgha and individuals. Within these, those directed toward a single person have already been excluded.
Externally, the others all possess the five [factors].

Regarding the three cases such as the forfeiture of precious objects (*ratna*), which are restricted to only four factors: now, upon careful examination, although the forfeiture of precious objects is not performed before the Saṃgha, once it has been forfeited, one must confess the offense.

What prevents one from confessing before the Saṃgha? If it is permitted to confess before the Saṃgha, it would not be limited to only four dharmas. Therefore, the fifth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duolun), regarding the precept on possessing precious objects, states:
"Once the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*) has been performed, one may then enter the assembly to repent."

Regarding the "six phrases" in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, this refers to its fourth fascicle. As for the fifth and sixth phrases, both constitute the offense of *sāpattika-thūl'-accaya* (offense involving forfeiture), which must be confessed.

Furthermore, it says: "The term 'continuous' (*anubandha*) does not mean merely being sequential; rather, because the mind repeatedly seeks [the object] such that the sequence is uninterrupted, it is called 'continuous'.
Question: What is the distinction between the meanings of the third and fifth [phrases]? Answer: The third is based on the confession of the offense (*āpatti*).

It is said that one obtains a robe; however, since the robe has already been relinquished long ago, the fifth case—where one obtains another robe precisely at the time of relinquishing the previous one—is therefore different.

Regarding the statement, "If the rain-cloak exceeds the period for its acceptance, it may be so," this means that if it exceeds the period for acceptance, even if one has not yet formally undertaken its observance, there is still room for the offense of *rañjana* (staining/attachment).
Because it is long [in duration], one returns after having stayed overnight.

Regarding other precepts and so forth, if they are relinquished, they are immediately returned; this may be considered as being subject to "long-term defilement. In this chapter, the discussion is based solely on robes for the time being.
If one obtains food through trade, seven-day medicines, and so forth, one should understand them accordingly.

"Long-term medicine," "together with the remainder," "the remainder is discarded," "the remainder is combined," and "that which is returned immediately. If one acquires seven-day medicine or other such items through trade, these should also be understood accordingly as the case may be.
The distinctions made above are based on repeated offenses; this explains the position of the ancient masters. The intent of the ancient masters is that [this applies to] selling.

Regarding robes of equal measure: having already committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) due to possessing an extra robe, one further commits another offense involving forfeiture by using that surplus wealth to purchase this [robe].

Even before the purchased wealth has been forfeited, one is still subject to defilement [by the offense]. If the extra wealth is given to him and he is made to forfeit it, and he returns immediately upon sitting down, he is clearly still subject to defilement;
therefore, he must remain with the goods overnight before returning.
If one were to provide an explanation based on the premise that the offense is not repeated, the Master of the Commentary (Sū-zhǔ) refutes that doctrine of repeated offenses in the following passage.
Regarding the statement, "If one causes [the object] to be abandoned with Chang and others, it must also pass through the night," the Master’s intent is as follows:

although one is not defiled prior to the abandonment, this differs from the ancient interpretation; once the abandonment has occurred, since the substance of the property is pure, if it should return to one's hand, then—
They may become defiled by one another.
Regarding the fact that their property cannot be entirely separated: although there are differences in the extent of their trade, these items do not differ in nature like the bowl and the robe;
since the robes, when compared with one another, are not entirely distinct, they thus become mutually defiled. Other interpretations are irrational.
"There is no need to labor over remembering this.

'Following what one's own inclination honors' means that regarding wealth obtained through trade and the like, whether one discards it at the beginning or at the end, neither case is subject to defilement;

therefore, only the five types of surplus goods must be kept overnight before being returned. Now, upon detailed examination, we take the former [view] as the primary standard, and it is better that all [items] be kept overnight. [End of] Former [Commentary].

The text below states: "Regarding all medicines kept for more than seven days—such as ghee for anointing the door-latch, honey, and rock-honey—one gives them to the garden-keeper on the first day they were obtained (as the ancients called this).
If it reaches the seventh day, one relinquishes them to a bhikṣu; the bhikṣu should then take and eat them (as the ancients called this 'obtained on the seventh day').
If it is less than seven days, one should return it to this bhikṣu; one should grant it through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (as the ancients called this 'the second day')."

"Go. On the sixth day, you will obtain it. Regarding the phrase "less than seven days," this refers to the five intermediate days). Now the Master says: the phrase "less than seven days" means from the third day onwards until the seventh day;
the medicine obtained during that time must also necessarily remain overnight before being returned. Furthermore, the text states that "on the seventh day, it is relinquished to a bhikṣu";
this refers to the medicine [obtained] on the second day. When it reaches [the seventh day], it is relinquished.
On the eighth day, the seven days are completed.

If it appears that no error has occurred, the Sangha relinquishes what was relinquished by the Sangha, and the individual relinquishes what was relinquished by the individual; it is not necessary for the person who originally performed the legal act to return it.

Regarding the methods of returning [items], there are two types, one of which is twofold. To discuss this generally, there are several kinds of "twos": first, returning on the same day versus returning after an overnight stay;
second, returning directly on the same day versus returning after a circuitous route; third, regarding the overnight stay, returning the bowl and returning the robes;
or returning the bowl and returning the medicine and the robes. The intent of the present commentary is to discuss the first two [categories].
Regarding what is called "one": it may refer to one night spent together, or it may refer to both being on the same day.

If it refers to that which is subsumed under the category of theft through ultimate depletion, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* (Shanxian lü piposha), fascicle 14, states: "If one does not return [the object], it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense."
If one has accepted something and already knows it is not one's own property, yet employs skillful means to conceal and hide it, one incurs an offense according to the value of that object.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, there are five kinds of relinquishment (*pratyāpanna*); among these, two concern precious objects. This is explained in the tenth fascicle of that Vinaya.
Regarding the misappropriation of property belonging to the Saṃgha, this is explained in the eleventh fascicle of that Vinaya.
Regarding "black wool and *koseyya*," this is explained in the ninth fascicle of that Vinaya. "Black wool" refers to pure black sheep's wool as defined in this Vinaya;
"*Koseyya*" refers to bedding made from wild silkworms as defined in this Vinaya.
Regarding "bedding with black and white wool": this refers to the bedding consisting of two parts black and three parts white as specified in this Vinaya.
The term "against sheep" (*dui yang*) is an error; it should be "to raise" (*yang*).
The inclusion of "sheep" (*eḍaka*) is an error; it refers simply to a large flock of sheep.

Regarding the other three types of relinquishment (*pratyāśraya*), they are the same as this: first, the relinquishment of extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) and so forth. Among these, the rules for extra robes are as explained in the eighth fascicle [of that text].
