Regarding the necessity of holding one's robe with the hand due to the presence of various boundaries: this refers to places such as beneath trees where men and women may come;

it is only by holding [the robe] with the hand that the "meeting-robe" (*saṃvāsaka-cīvara*) is established. If no laymen or women come, merely reaching a stone-paved area does not constitute an offense.
In the eighth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, there is another description of the characteristics of the meeting-robe, which states: "A bhikṣu puts on his upper and lower robes and enters..."
In a village, there was a woman who said to a bhikṣu, "I wish to make offerings to the images tonight; please assist me in preparing them.
The bhikṣu then assisted her. When the sun had set and he wished to return, she earnestly requested him to stay the night. [If] that bhikṣu’s residence was there...
If any bhikṣus possess extra robes (*atirekacīvara*), they should temporarily borrow them for the purpose of formal possession (*dhāraṇa*).
If they have none, they should likewise borrow from those nearby. If there are no bhikṣus, they may borrow from bhikṣuṇīs. If there are none of these, they should borrow clothing from laypeople.
Having had it purified by a woman with a needle and thread, they may then take formal possession. If none of this is possible, [then later...]
If the city gates open during the night, you should return quickly to the monastery; do not attempt to pass through the city walls.
If you arrive at the gate of the vihāra and it has not yet opened, you should request that it be opened. If you cannot get it opened, you should stay beneath the gateway.

If there is no gateway, you should insert your hand into the opening. There are two kinds of openings: the drainage channel and the [door] hole. Regarding the drainage channel, do not insert [your hand] first.
If there are snakes or vipers on one’s hands or feet, one should first startle them with a staff, and only then insert the hand into the garment.

If there are no openings, one should climb over the wall or fence to enter. One should make a sign so that those inside recognize it, ensuring that the people inside do not suspect one is a thief and cause a commotion.
If one cannot gain entry, one should quickly discard the garment; it would be better to be without the garment than to commit an offense of transgression (vayatikrama).

Regarding the Vinaya: because the light is treated as heavy, [the rule for] receiving and maintaining the monastic robes (saṃghāṭī) logically requires that one first relinquishes them and then receives them again.
As for why there are only nine categories in this section: the single phrase "staying overnight in another monastery while lacking a single robe" is omitted; therefore, there are only nine cases.
The same applies to the category of staying overnight under a tree.
One *zhǒu* equals one foot eight inches (referring to the cubit of a person of average build). The *Zhi* [Vinaya] further states:

"If a bhikṣu lies down on the road and uses his three robes as a pillow, if he leaves them [within reach], it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*; because they cannot be cut [to shorten them], all must be relinquished" (the above is from the Vinaya text).

Some say: based on this, it is known that the twenty-five cubits in the *Zhi* Vinaya refer to the actual measurement of the boundary under a tree (*vṛkṣamūla-sīmā*) and so forth, and not [to the robe measurements].

This refers to the "sphere of influence" (*pradeśa*). If it were merely a matter of the sphere of influence, then the path would also have to be included; for what reason, then, is it said that one commits an offense simply by leaving the head [of the bed]? Now, considering this carefully:

even when a monk travels on a road carrying his robes, it is permitted for them to extend beyond the path by twenty-five *cubits* (*hasta*). How much more so in the present case, where he is merely resting his head [on the bed] and yet is said to commit an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*)?
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter five, states: "There was a bhikṣu who lay down within two boundaries (*sīmā*). His robe was separated from his body... [and so forth].
Half an inch [outside]. If it falls into another territory (*parakṣetra*), one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If even a corner of the robe remains on one's person, there is no offense.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this should also be due to falling into another territory; if it does not fall [beyond], there is still the extent of twenty-five cubits (*hasta*). The *Mahāsāṃghika* says:
If, out of fear of bandits, one hides a robe halfway down a well and stays overnight above it, one commits an offense when the dawn light appears.
However, if one stays overnight with the robe still attached to one's body, there is no offense regarding the forfeiture of the robe.
Regarding the formula: "I, bhikṣu so-and-so, have committed the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* by staying overnight separated from my robe;

I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha," one should specify whether it was the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, or whichever robe it was, naming it accordingly. This must likewise apply to all procedures such as the confession (*pratideśanā*).
One must not simply recite the text literally as "staying overnight separated from my robe"; all cases should be understood according to this principle.
Regarding non-offenses: first, specific exemptions; second, general exemptions.
As for the four perceptions, there are five perceptions in the text, as the perception of destruction has been added.
○ The Precept on the One-Month Robe.

If the materials of the robes differ— whether it be silk and cotton cloth that differ, or those that vary in coarseness or fineness— then what is called "identical" should be understood as the opposite of this.

Regarding the statement "without asking whether there is knowledge, one cuts based on the expectation of non-expectation," as in the *Pañcavargika* [Vinaya] and the fortieth chapter of the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, it is thus.

In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, chapter eight, and the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, chapter fourteen, it is stated that one may obtain cloth and wealth intended to supplement the three robes (*tricīvara*), yet the funds remain insufficient.
If one expects to receive more within a month in order to complete the full amount, the Buddha permitted [the storage] while waiting for the funds to be sufficient to make the robes.
If, within ten days, one expects that [the expectation] will cease, from that point on it is always permissible; this does not yet constitute an offense of "excess" (*dīrgha*).

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if more than ten days have passed and the expectation ceases on that very day, one must immediately perform a "pure gift" (*viśuddha-dāna*) to make it into a robe, or give it to others.

If one does not dispose of it within that night, one immediately incurs the offense of *dīrgha* (excess). This should be understood by analogy for the period from the eleventh day up to the thirtieth day.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is similar to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*; however, the intent of the chapter is that if the robe has not yet been obtained in full, one may keep it for one month even if there is no prospect of obtaining more, which differs from other Vinayas.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the tenth day [of the month], he..."

If one makes [the robe] during the first ten days and obtains it during the middle ten days, one should make it on that very day of the middle ten. If one makes it during the last ten days and obtains it during the middle ten days, one should make it during those last ten days.

If, during the first ten days, five days have already passed and one obtains the expected robe, one should take the remaining five days of the first ten days and combine them with the first five days of the middle ten days; within these ten days, one should make the robe. If, during the middle ten days...

The first five days of the [latter] ten have already passed, and one has obtained the robes as desired. One should then take the final five days of that [latter] ten and the first five days of the subsequent ten;
within these ten days, one should make the robes. If the first five days of the [subsequent] ten have already passed...

Having obtained the robe as expected, one should immediately make the robe within these five days (in this manner, it should be understood that making the robe within four, three, two, or one day follows the same principle).
According to this, it differs from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states:

"Regarding 'expecting to obtain,' one may expect to obtain it from within the Saṃgha, or expect to obtain it from within a group, or expect to obtain it from a relative or friend, or expect it from a place where there are many discarded rags (*pāṃsukūla*)."

It is obtained. Or it is obtained by expectation of one's own property. If on the twenty-ninth day one obtains the expected garment and it is fine while the previous garment was coarse, the previously coarse garment should be formally declared as pure (*śuddha-vyavahāra*), for the newly obtained garment may be expected for another month. If the expected garment is coarse...
Furthermore, one may stay for another month. In this manner, they may proceed by turns as long as they please;

however, for the sake of conformity, it must not exceed one month (according to this treatise, this is the maximum limit). It is further stated that "conformity" is insufficient: even if one conforms with those who have already obtained the cloth, it is still considered insufficient if the robes have not yet been made.
Regarding the insufficiency [of robes] due to their arising: it may be so that one has sufficient cloth of the same quality, yet does not make a robe.

Among the two aforementioned types, although each individually is insufficient, if both are taken together—whether of the same fineness or the same coarseness—the principle dictates that they should indeed suffice.

Why then do you not make a robe? The Venerable One said: "This may also be an allowance for those who practice superior conduct; it is not intended to be subject to the formal declaration of purity (*śuddhi-ārocana*), but rather to praise the three [types of robes]."

Regarding robes, it was originally permitted to wait until one’s needs were met. The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks, however, did not follow this superior practice; they imitated others in waiting for their needs to be met and thereby gave rise to transgressions.

Examining the intent of the text now, the original allowance for "waiting until sufficient" was not restricted by a time limit. It was because the group of six used this scriptural passage as a pretext for luxury and arrogance that the rule of one month was subsequently established.

In principle, this applies to all three grades of practitioners; it serves as a substitute for the three robes and is not limited to those of superior conduct. Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun) states:
The fourth [section] states: "One must certainly spend one month diligently seeking to complete the robe, ensuring that mindfulness does not cease.

The text says: "On the eleventh day, one should cut, sew, and make the robe. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (*Ji*) states: "Others should assist with washing, dyeing, and even the replacement of threads and the stitching.
Once it has been purified, one should accept and maintain it. If one fears it will not be finished in a single day, [one may use] coarse [materials]."

One should hide it and cause it to be kept; later, one may again remove the fine thorns. According to this, the essential requirement is likewise that it be kept on that very day. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle 4, states:

"If within ten days one does not perform the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*), nor gives it away, nor keeps it [as a finished robe], then upon reaching the eleventh day, one commits an offense," and so forth.

Now, the commentary in this treatise states: "The offense is incurred only when the characteristics of a finished robe are established. This does not distinguish the necessity of performing the ritual of keeping (*dhāraṇa*).

The chapter states: "Clothing that is not [permissible] *cīvara* refers to surplus materials for which there is no thirty-day allowance; therefore, one must perform the forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

The formal declaration (*pratijñā*) should be stated as follows: 'I, bhikṣu So-and-so, have possessed several pieces of untimely clothing (*akālacīvara*) for more than [X] days; I have committed an offense requiring forfeiture'—this should be understood."

Regarding the precept on taking a nun’s robe, [the claim that] it is not an offense when taking robes from two groups of persons—namely, when a śrāmaṇerikā is a relative and a bhikṣuṇī is a non-relative, or when a śrāmaṇerikā is a non-relative and a bhikṣuṇī is a relative—is incorrect. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Qishi), fascicle 8, states:
"If a śrāmaṇerikā is a relative and a bhikṣuṇī is a non-relative; or if a śrāmaṇerikā is a non-relative and a bhikṣuṇī is a relative—in these cases, one may obtain the robe."
[This constitutes] an offense. Apart from these two groups, there is no offense. Regarding "giving with a hollow mind": this refers to giving with excessive joy.

Some say that "hollow mind" means a lack of sincerity; this is incorrect. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle 5, taking a bowl of proper measure [exceeding the limit] constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 8, it is not an offense.
The chapter states: "As for those who were able to give their robes to others, leave the household life, and attain the Way, there are four sections within it:
first, [the nun] shared a husband with her mother; she reviled and loathed her female body, abandoned it, and departed. Second, at a later time, she shared a husband with her daughter;
she again reviled and loathed it, abandoned it, and departed. Third, from 'she went' onwards, she approached the Buddha and attained the fruit. Fourth, from 'the Buddha said' onwards."
"Leaving the household life to exhaust the outflows. The fourth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "As for the woman who was terrified: formerly she shared a husband with her mother;

now she shares a son-in-law with her daughter. Confused by the cycle of birth and death, she has reached this state. Without severing her pursuit of sensual desires, she leaves the household life to study the Way."

"How can such delusion and confusion be brought to rest? Thinking thus, she departed and went to the Jetavana. There she realized the Truth and exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), as described at length in that [text].
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle five, states: "The Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā was of upright appearance, with the complexion of an *utpala* lotus.
In a past life, many kalpas ago, this person was the daughter of a Brahmin. Her father..."

The mother’s family had gone to sea to gather treasures, leaving this daughter behind. Unable to support herself, she lived together with several courtesans, selling her beauty to provide for her needs.
This woman’s appearance was not particularly striking, so no one came to visit her;
she constantly reproached herself, wondering why she alone was in such a state. At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha whom everyone revered and admired. Someone said to her: “You—”
"Whoever is able to make offerings to a Pratyekabuddha shall have their every wish fulfilled according to their heart's desire in birth after birth.
At that time, the woman followed his words; she prepared exquisite food and drink, covered it with *utpala* flowers, and presented it to the Pratyekabuddha.
She then made this vow: "May I, in birth after birth, always be born as a woman, peerlessly beautiful, honored by all people, and beyond reproach."
Furthermore, she made this vow: "May I obtain the merits attained by śramaṇas; may I myself attain them.

For this reason, even in this life she remains a woman, yet her countenance is foremost among all. It is because of her original vow that she has now attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
(The above is from the treatise. Question: Suppose there were someone who took this cloth and flesh. From whom would one incur the offense? From the thief, or from the nun? Answer: From the nun.
Regarding the phrase "it is an offense of the limits;

Regarding the phrase "because she dwells in a separate room, she gives [the gift]": the nun acts as the patron (*dānapati*) and constructs a separate monastic dwelling (*vihāra*), inviting a bhikṣu to reside there. At that point—
In this room, various provisions are supplied; because of this, there is no offense. In the West, many such gifts are given. (From the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle 5.

If a bhikṣu obtains clothing suitable for a bhikṣuṇī, or a bhikṣuṇī obtains clothing suitable for a bhikṣu, [there is likewise no offense].

Merchants, for the sake of clothing and other necessities, travel about in various directions seeking them, thereby obstructing and abandoning their practice of the Path and incurring all manner of afflictions and harms;
for this reason, [the Buddha] permitted it.
Regarding "parents and kinsmen up to the seventh generation," the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views), fascicle 14, states:
"Parents and kinsmen of the seventh generation" refers to the father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather, continuing in this manner up to the seventh generation.

The same applies to the mother’s seven generations (this is calculated by taking the great-great-grandmother as one, the great-grandmother as two, the grandmother as three, the father as four, oneself as five, the son as six, and the grandson as seven; hence the phrase "up to"). As for "paternal relatives," it includes uncles, brothers, and so forth.

Regarding "children and grandchildren" (when referring to the father, this includes the father’s paternal uncles as belonging to the father’s generation; the brothers belong to one’s own generation; children and grandchildren may be known accordingly). Regarding the "mother":

maternal uncles, maternal aunts, and even children and grandchildren—through seven generations, all are the mother’s kin (this explains the mother’s kin: maternal uncles and maternal aunts belong to the mother’s generation; by calculating according to principle, there are additionally [one's] brothers, who belong to one’s own generation;

and children and grandchildren belong to their own generation of children and grandchildren). If they are one's own daughters and sons, or even grandchildren, they are all kin (this explains one’s own children, daughters, and grandchildren). *Liao lun* (Treatise on Clarification).

The verse says: "The four relatives should take [the precepts]. The prose commentary explains: "There are four types of relatives. The rest of the text is as in the chapter. The *Mingliao shu* states:
"The paternal relative (*fùzǔ qīn*) refers to the grandfather; the maternal relative (*mǔzǔ qīn*) refers to the grandmother. The maternal relatives (*wàimǔ*) are to be understood by analogy.
Although only 'four relatives' are mentioned, this encompasses all kinship relations, such as the maternal grandmother, parents, uncles, and brothers."
Disciples, nephews, and cousins are considered one’s own kin through their connection to one’s maternal grandmother; the same principle applies to other mutual relationships.
This Vinaya states that even trading a single pill of medicine for a robe constitutes a formal inquiry (or transaction). This differs from the eighth section of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, which says:
"If one has obtained a full robe from another and gives them a smaller robe, this is not called 'giving'; one should give a complete and sufficient robe. It further says to take... [text ends].

The written text states that for a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. The commentary says: "Regarding the question of a bhikṣuṇī taking robes belonging to the Saṃgha," etc.; this explains the present passage.

(Commentary: This refers to following the established practice of the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha by observing the Eight Rules of Respect (*gurudharma*).

If one follows this Vinaya, then the instance where Mahāprajāpatī committed an offense by having wool carded by a subordinate would necessarily differ from the view presented in the *Samayabhedoparacanacakra*. Mahāprajāpatī is... [text fragment].
Because one does not receive the precepts from the great Saṃgha.

[This concludes] the Precept on Begging for Robes, found in the fourteenth fascicle of the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*. There were eighty thousand sons of the Śākya who had left the household life; among them, Upānanda was the most frivolous.

As for those who could not perceive both her words and her appearance, whether they were told she must be given or that she need not be given, in either case, they could not give her away.

"If a bhikṣu traveling on a road encounters bandits, he should take his robes and bowl and give them to a junior monk, instructing him to run and hide. If the bandits seize the junior monk and lose the robes, the senior monk [is not at fault]."

If one is of low status, one may, upon obtaining even a single person, have them pluck grass or tree leaves and hand them to others so that they may cover their bodies while heading toward the monastery.
If a layperson sees a bhikṣu who is naked and offers a lay garment, or if one obtains a garment of the five primary colors, there is no offense.
Therefore, it is stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "There was a bhikṣu wearing a white garment or a garment of superior color [without having cut it]."

A thread-garment: there is no offense. This refers to a bhikṣu who has lost his robes due to encountering bandits. If he obtains a garment made of bird feathers or a wooden-board garment from a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), he may wear it;
there is no offense. However, he must not adopt the false views of those [non-Buddhists]. As for wearing monastic robes and the like, if they are destroyed, there is no need to compensate.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Chapter Nine: If traveling on a road with merchants, and if bandits come from one direction or two directions...
If [the thieves] come from three directions, one may flee at will to escape them. If they come from all four directions, one should not run away;

rather, one should remain standing with the body upright and must not abandon the thieves. If the thieves say, "Bring us the saṃghāṭī," one should reply, "For your long life," and give it to them one by one as they request.
One must not shout loudly, call out, or revile the thieves. Once it has been given, one should remove it and enter the forest thickets.
[In the] midst [of the journey]. If, after the bandits have departed, there remain robes that have not been formally accepted (parigṛhīta), they should be accepted.

If there are none [to cover them], even down to using leaves from trees to shield the front and back while walking. If even this is unavailable, one must not walk with arms flailing like the Nirgranthas;

rather, one should walk on the road shielding the body with one's hands. One must not enter a thicket of *zhen* trees (*zhōngmǔ*, according to the *Shuowen*: "a cluster of trees"; according to the *Guangya*: "trees growing in a clump").
One should cause the bandits to believe that one is a pursuer. One should walk along the roadside through shallow grass.
If one encounters people coming, one should walk through the shallow grass and sit slightly exposed. When passersby see this, if someone asks, "Who is this naked person?
one should answer, "A son of the Śākyas who has been robbed by bandits. If they do not beg but give much clothing of their own accord, there is no offense in taking it. If...
One should not accept [robes] from those who do not offer them; when they do offer them, one should take two or three pieces.
Regarding robes of three or five cubits (*hasta*), the text says "householder" and "householder’s wife" as mentioned above. The Venerable One said:

"It should be stated as in the 'Six Silences' (*ṣaḍ-ārya-vastu*)," because the preceding section provides an explanation for seeking [robes]. In the sixth fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, regarding "one whose robe has been seized": if the authorities seize it...
If it is stolen by thieves, or by enemies, or by the enemy's faction; if it is lost and its whereabouts are unknown; if it has rotted away; if it has been gnawed by insects;
if it is burnt—whether consumed by fire or boiled by the sun; or if it is carried away—whether swept by water or blown by the wind.
Regarding the precept against receiving more robes than necessary:
if one receives them on behalf of another, one need only perform the *pratideśanīya* confession, as there is nothing to relinquish.
In the ninth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, Upānanda says to the monk who has lost his robe: "If you are unable to beg for one, I shall do so for you."

"Go and beg. He immediately took up paper and pen and said to the lay devotees (upāsakas), "Help me to beg, for there is a bhikṣu who has come from the north and lost his robes while passing through bandits.
He then went to the marketplace and begged, obtaining many garments. Nanda spoke again:
Still not satisfied, the upāsaka asked, "How many people are there? He replied, "Many. He asked again, "Exactly how many?
Drawing out his voice, he said, "There are as many as sixty. The upāsaka said, "This robe could suffice for five hundred bhikṣus;
how much more so for sixty? Do you wish to fold it and sell it? He immediately threw down the paper and brush in a fit of anger and said:
Where does this person who is "insatiable" arise? The text speaks of "contentment," which means knowing that the three robes are sufficient.
Even if one loses one, two, or even all three, receiving a fourth is still considered sufficient. To receive more than that is what is meant here.

According to this Vinaya, if one loses two, receiving [more] is not permitted at all; if one loses three, receiving three is called "knowing contentment. If one receives four, it is likewise [not permitted].
This is not permissible. According to the *Ji lü* (Sectarian Vinaya), section nine, if one loses three [robes], one is permitted to receive only two.

According to the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Views), section fifteen, if one loses the three robes, one may receive the upper and lower robes; the remaining one robe must be sought elsewhere. If one loses two robes, one may receive one; if one loses only one, one may not receive any.
For a nun, if she loses five robes, she may receive two; if she loses four, she may receive one; if she loses three, she may not receive any.

[The section on] Receiving. ○ Regarding the exhortation to a layperson concerning "raw" and "worked" [gems]: one should say "raw color. There are two kinds of jewels: first, raw color; second, that which can be dyed. Now...
Just as gold cannot change its color, for it is naturally so by birth; whereas silver and other such substances can have their colors changed, which is termed "dyeable.
"Image" (*xiàng*) has the meaning of "color" (*sè*); therefore, it is called "born-image" (*shēngxiàng*).
Regarding the statement that "one coin is one-sixteenth [of a unit]": this refers to sixteen *māṣas* constituting one *kārsāpaṇa*.
One sixteenth part is thus four *māṣas*. To refer to this as a "coin" (*qián*) is an error.
Regarding the "request for one robe": the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle five, states, "In this context, 'robe' refers to a robe of standard measure.
Based on this, the ancients consequently referred to it as "a single strip."

Regarding "Exhorting the two lay devotees to observe the precepts" and "Exhorting the third to not disturb those who are minor": Jue says that the text increases [the number] by one, so it should also be "disturbing those who are minor. Thus we know that exhorting the two is established as the rule;
by analogy, we know that the third and fourth are likewise limits for offenses. This may also be understood through the meaning within the chapter. In reality, it is disturbing.
This is because it is subtle. To increase the number of strands by one is merely a matter of dyeing and prevention; how could it be that when giving encouragement, one increases only by one strand?
Now, upon careful examination, if one were to increase by one strand, what transgression would one wish to incur? Therefore, the previous interpretation is preferable.
○ [The character] 忩 (chuāng) is pronounced as *jiè*. Regarding the rule that if one does not ask for a bowl there is no offense: "asking many times" (*duō*) refers to requesting it repeatedly.
If one requests it once and commits the offense of begging for a bowl, that is not so. That [bowl] is a pure gift; the person is not the owner of the bowl. Why?

The acquisition of a begging bowl is now explained. According to the explanatory passage below, if one gives it for the purpose of a *pārihārika* (extra) item and receives it with timely and gentle speech, there is no offense.
Thus, it is known that requesting a bowl is the same as [requesting] a *pārihārika*. This applies unless it is done at an improper time.

One should simply incur a *duṣkṛta* offense; this differs from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Duo lun). According to the *Kāśyapīya-vinaya* (Jian lun), fifteen [instances] constitute [the offense]: if one solicits once with speech, it constitutes two [offenses], and twice by remaining silent.

This explanation in the present Vinaya is identical to the *Kāśyapīya-vinaya*. However, the fifth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The essence of this precept lies precisely in three solicitations and three silences."
There is no fault. If one obtains a robe after seven returns, it constitutes an offense; failing to obtain it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

Regarding the phrase "according to the explanation of the first two, etc.," this refers to explaining only the first two and the last two of the six phrases within the preceding root precept (*śikṣāpada*).
The written text states that there are those who are "born" Brahmins; this refers to those born into the lineage of pure conduct (*śuddha-ācāra*).
Alternatively, there may be those born into other lower castes who study the dharma of pure conduct; these are not "born" Brahmins.
Regarding "immediate giving": the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Ji-lü), fascicle nine, states that one may request three times with six instances of silence. This present *vinaya* likely differs;
it simply says to request at the proper time, and does not necessarily restrict one to only six instances of silence and so forth.
○ Regarding the precept on bedding made of wild silkworm silk:
in Sanskrit, this is called *kauśeya-saṃskṛta*, which is translated as "bedding of wild silkworm silk. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Ji-lü), fascicle nine:
A bhikṣu requested *kauśeya* [silk] from a host. The host said, "Wait a moment. The bhikṣu sat down while waiting; he then rose again and thrust his finger into the cauldron.
[He] checks whether the bath water is hot, and immediately says, "The water is already hot," and so forth. Now, the Tripitaka Master says:

*Goseya* is the name for wild silkworms. These insects are not raised; they live naturally in the mountains and marshes. In the Western Regions there are no mulberry trees, so [the worms] mostly feed on the leaves of the *kṣīrikā* fruit tree.
Their form is brilliant white, as thick as a thumb, and two or three inches long. [Month...]
The remainder simply grow old; they wrap themselves with leaves and form cocoons inside, about the size of a toe, which are extremely hard.
Butchers harvest them and process them into silk. This silk is exceptionally firm, its texture neither fine nor smooth.
If these insects were not collected, after about a month, moths would emerge from within the cocoons, their two wings spread wide like an outstretched hand. (From the *Wénzhāng*)
They are brilliantly radiant, like the color of crimson silk. Whenever midnight arrives, the males and females pair together;
they then return to their feeding trees and lay their eggs. These insects are collectively called *goseya*. In the Western Regions, only those who are professional butchers engage in this occupation;
even those of superior lineage and noble clans utterly defile their own lineages. Consequently, the Buddha prohibited monks and nuns from entering such dwellings when seeking alms.

Regarding those who are making robes: according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, fascicle nine, if one makes a *saṃghāṭī* from *koseyya* (silk) and an *uttarāsaṅga* from wool, or if one makes a *saṃghāṭī* from wool and an *uttarāsaṅga* from *koseyya*.
As for the phrase "and the borders," the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "If the center is wool, the borders are *koseyya* (or the reverse)."
Regarding the difficulty of identifying the characteristics: the Tripiṭaka Master states that what is called a "reclining mat" (*śayanāsana*) consists of two distinct types.
The first is woven; the second is stitched. The woven type refers to items such as *kūrpa* (woolen carpets), while the stitched type belongs to the category of felt mats.
This means that one takes *kauśeya* silk and weaves it to form the reclining mat. Or [it may be] *gauṣa*...
In the world, silk is used to sew together what is called a *paryaṅka* (a bedding mat). Inside, it is filled with wool or tree-flower cotton to serve as a bedding material;

originally, this was a lying-mat (*śayanāsana*), not one of the three robes (*tricīvara*). For those who would take such a thing to serve as one of the three robes, it is indeed entirely inadequate and negligent.
I shall now examine this in detail and distinguish it later in the section on the precepts. The *Aṅgulimāla Sūtra* states: "Cotton, silk, brocade, leather..."

And so forth. To refuse to accept [an offering] from the hand of one who has engaged in successive acts of killing is the law of a bhikṣu. One who accepts it is not called "Greatly Compassionate," yet this does not constitute a violation of the precepts.
The wording for the renunciation and confession is as follows: "This bedding has already been cut and destroyed. The remainder should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the prohibition on black wool originating from the four great kingdoms, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, chapter nine, states: "Furthermore, wool is very precious;
one may obtain one *liang* for a single coin, or even two, three, or four coins for one *liang*. Moreover, this wool is extremely fine and soft, such that it can touch the pupil of the eye."

Those who do not shed tears are exceedingly rare. From among the four great kingdoms—the kingdom of Vaiśālī, the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, and the kingdom of Nandivardhana—they seek this wool; thus, sometimes they return, and sometimes they die without returning.
Regarding the phrase "layered" in the text: the meaning is that if other robes are fine or thin, one should fold this woolen *kaṭhina* [blanket] over them.
There are two layers. At the time they are completed, there is no offense, because the original intention was not to use them alone.

The text states that making a mattress or a bedding mat involves no offense; this, however, contradicts the bedding rules for the three types of *piṭaka* (Tripitaka) practitioners. Now, let us examine this in detail.

According to this, it is not a woolen rug (*śāṭī*). Furthermore, according to the subsequent precept, it is also not one of the three robes (*tricīvara*); it is precisely a sleeping shawl (*śayanapracchādana*).

Regarding the precept on white hair, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that this is not "pure white. Its seventh fascicle says: "The group of six [monks] (*ṣaḍvargika*) thought: 'The Buddha has established a precept and does not permit [this].'"
"An underlay made of pure black wool: I shall instead make an underlay by mixing a small amount of white goat-wool with black goat-wool.
Because of this, [the Buddha] prohibited it, decreeing that two parts must be black and the third part white, and so forth; these are the two sets of requisite conditions.
This is according to the traditions of our own and other schools. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Daolun), fascicle 5, states that four *liang* constitute one *bala*.

The *Lokasthāna-abhidharma* says that one *liang* in the south is called one *bala*. It appears that the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* refers to the smaller measure, while the *Abhidharma* speaks according to the larger measure.
My current interpretation is that *bala* is translated as "portion" (*fen*). For example, *prasākhā* is translated as "limb" (*zhi*); how could a limb possibly be four *liang*?
...as well.

Regarding the phrase "the five [rules] for the sixth year of ordination are as above": this refers to the rule concerning being separated from one's robes (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*), wherein if one is ill and the robe is heavy, one must have it with one when traveling.
1. From "He thought within himself" onwards is the section on the opening of mindfulness. 2. From "He spoke to the monks" onwards is the section on entrusting the staff and expressing doubts. 3.
From "When the monks had heard this" onwards is the section on requesting a formal decision. 4. From "The World-Honored One" onwards is the section on the formal procedure for the opening.
The scriptural text states that if one discards an old [robe] and makes a new one within six years, there is no offense.

How could this apply to the precept regarding the "one-month robe," which requires discarding the three robes before making a new one? Since the old robe is not discarded, it would constitute an offense; therefore, we know that this does not refer to the three robes.

Treatise on the Many, Chapter Five: An offense is committed if one makes [a robe] by begging for materials; however, there is no offense if someone gives them of their own accord without being asked, or if one uses one's own clothing or wealth, or if one purchases clothing or wealth to make it.

Regarding the point that the precepts are not recited one by one, but rather explained as two offenses, this is merely a restatement of the intent behind the *Shushu* (Commentary on the Vinaya), which seeks not to show undue respect [for the literal form]. Nanshan’s view is likewise the same.

The ancient commentators established four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding this: first, making something new that does not exceed the prescribed measure (one commits only this precept); second, making something old that exceeds the measure (one commits only the offense of exceeding the measure);

by analogy, one should understand the cases where one commits both or commits neither. Now, upon careful examination, just as one might commit the offense of exceeding the measure and subsequently commit the offense of failing to mark it, the same principle applies here as well.
The five conditions for not accepting an invitation are explained in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun), fascicle 5.
Regarding the Buddha’s span (*vitasti*) being two feet, this is from fascicle 5 of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.

According to the opening text, if one has no place to obtain [the measurement] oneself, then according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 9, "one hand of the Samyaksaṃbuddha" refers to a length of... [two feet].

Two chi and four cun. When taking an old rug, one must not [rely on] those who have heard little, those who have violated the precepts, those who lack learning, those who dwell in ruined rooms and do not repair them, those of ill repute, those who have severed their right view, those who distance themselves from their *upādhyāya* and *ācārya*, those who do not consult or inquire, those who cannot destroy Māra, and those who do not discern the works of Māra. Such persons as these—
One should not accept [it] from such a person. One should accept it from one who is learned, up to and including one who discerns the works of Māra (based on this principle:
if one lacks it oneself, one must seek it from another; this differs from this Vinaya, which permits making new [robes] for oneself).
Regarding the precept on carrying wool:

"Wool" (*kṣauma*) refers to fine sheep’s wool according to the *Zilin* (Lexicon of Characters). The *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) states: "Birds and beasts all produce soft wool, that is, fine hair. This is what is meant.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, Chapter Nine, it constitutes an offense even if one carries it while circumambulating a stūpa for a distance of three *yojanas*, and even if the amount is as small as what would fill a needle-eye.
Using bamboo hair [for a broom] also constitutes an offense. If one carries camel hair or wool, there is no fault provided it is made into a vessel.

Regarding the precept against storing precious objects (*ratna-śikṣāpada*) as cited from the *Śaṅgharakṣitāvadāna* (or *Sūtra on the Origin of Goodness*), there is no explicit canonical text for it; it appears only in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-vyākhyā* by the two Dharma Masters Yan and Yuan.
It is thus transmitted. There is a single fascicle of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* which enumerates eight kinds of impure things;
however, upon examining that sūtra, it appears to be a spurious scripture and cannot be relied upon. The *Samantapāsādikā*, fascicle 15, states:
"If someone offers a slave to the Sangha, it may not be accepted. If, however, they say they are offering a 'pure person' (*śucika-purisa*) or an 'attendant' (*parikarmaka*), it may be accepted."
(If it is so even for the Saṃgha, then it is logically improper to accept it for an individual).

Regarding the practice of designating an item as pure (*śuddha*) by entrusting it to a layperson to act as a custodian, the fourth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Duo-lun), in the section on the precept concerning extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), states:

"As for the method of pure donation: in the case of money or any kind of precious object, one should first seek out a layperson (*avadātavasana*) who knows the Dharma to act as a pure attendant (*śuddha-puruṣa*). The meaning of the instruction is as follows..."
Please understand this: it is the law of us bhikṣus not to keep money or precious objects. Now, you, the donor, shall serve as the *viśuddhidāyaka* (purifier).

Whatever money or precious objects we subsequently obtain, we shall give entirely to you, the donor. Once you have been appointed as the purifier, whatever money or precious objects we later obtain, we shall declare them as pure (*viśuddhi*) before the bhikṣus.

It is not necessary to state the name of the *śuddhikara* (the one for whom the purification is made) [as this excludes the case of long-term extra robes, for which the name of the *śuddhikara* must be stated].

After the purification has been performed, if one obtains money or precious objects, one may keep them for as long as is appropriate. If the *śuddhikara* has gone far away to another country, one should seek another *śuddhikara*.
The text says: "There are two kinds of purification. If a layperson brings money or precious objects and gives them to a bhikṣu, he should simply say: 'This is an impure object; I..."
It should be kept. If it is pure, one may accept it; this constitutes the *śuddhi-dharma* (the rule of purification).

If a layperson says, "I am giving this treasure to the bhikṣu," and the bhikṣu says, "I should not keep it," and the attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) says, "I shall purify it and then keep it," the bhikṣu must not himself perform the declaration of purity (*śuddhi-vācana*).

He should simply set it aside on the ground. If there is a bhikṣu present, he should follow that bhikṣu’s declaration of purity and keep it for as long as necessary. If no bhikṣu is available, he must not [keep it].
"Taking. Having taken [it], one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense requiring forfeiture). (The above is all from the treatise.

Regarding the fourth section, where one exchanges eight kinds of impure items for ten kinds of robes and incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this refers to the potential commission of the offense of "buying and selling.
(Exchanging with sentient beings does not constitute buying and selling; exchanging with the Buddha constitutes the tenth [category] and may involve the commission of an offense.)
Regarding the two types of offenses involving forfeiture in the sixth and seventh [categories]: the sixth offense is the keeping of precious objects;
within the seventh, gold and silver are treated likewise, as is the offense regarding long woolen rugs.

Regarding the fact that the remaining six types of impurity result only in a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing): if one possesses other items that are not permitted, one must speak of them; because of the fault of failing to speak of them, it is merely a *duṣkṛta*.
(These are all coarse distinctions; if one were to distinguish them finely, they should be understood according to the principle.)

Question: Regarding the three categories of precious objects, robes, and medicine—each has both "keeping" (*āstha*) and "trading" (*parivartana*), whereas for alms-bowls there is "keeping" but no "trading," and for food there is "trading" but no "keeping.

This question and answer are formulated here based on the underlying principles (*artha*), not based on the literal wording of the precepts (*śīla-pada*). For instance, within the category of "keeping," there are six precepts in total;

that is, within the text of the precepts, precious objects constitute one instance of "keeping," and robes constitute three instances of "keeping" (namely: the ten-day limit, the one-month limit, and exceeding the period for urgent gifts).

Medicine is one possession; the bowl is another possession. In this present inquiry, although only "precious items," "robes," and "medicine" are mentioned together as possessions, the bowl is included to make four possessions in total.
Regarding the exchange of requisites, there are generally two types of exchange:

namely, within the *Prātimokṣa* text, precious items constitute one exchange, while robes, medicine, and food are combined into a single exchange (as seen later in the twentieth precept concerning buying and selling, where the four types of medicine, such as those for the time, etc., are treated accordingly).

"Discerning" means trading. That *pāṭikāra* (a patched robe) is precisely a robe made of rags (*paṃsukūla*), for it is obtained through trading. In this present inquiry, precious robes, medicine, and food are permitted to be traded, and thus they are raised as questions.
From this opening and closing [of categories], we know that this is based on the underlying principle (*artha*) and not on the literal wording of the precepts (*śīla-pada*).
Regarding the further division into seven types: according to the subsequent precepts, there are three each for gold and silver, plus money, making seven.

Those that are "treasures" (ratna) include such things as copper, stone, conch shells, and cowries; these are not [the primary] true treasures. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duōlùn), fascicle five, states:

"The essence of this precept is established by the prohibition against possessing treasures. To grasp a treasure or to take up a treasure constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; this is one of the ninety matters."
This refers to the precept on taking precious objects.
Regarding the "seven treasures" in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, that text’s seventh [chapter] mentions "precious objects" (*ratna*) alone, which refers to gold and silver;
taking them constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. As for taking iron, copper coins, or even wooden coins, [that text] does not mention the term "seven treasures."
Regarding the fifth "many" [category] of treasures in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*: precious items include gold, silver, maṇi-jewels, pearls, coral, musāragalva, and aśmagarbha.

To keep such treasures constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; to take money constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Since this treatise is a commentary on the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the present sub-commentary states that the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* enumerates seven types of treasures.
"This is the essential provision for those who receive [offerings] without fault. The meaning of the *Shu* (Commentary) is as follows:

"In order to construct a dwelling, one is permitted to accept precious objects. This interpretation is made because the Vinaya text below opens the allowance for accepting money for dwellings and money for medicine.
Master Nanshan’s intention is that since the text says "seeking timber and so forth," one may accept timber.

"One should not do so for one's own sake" means that one should not accept precious objects. Now, observing the textual evidence, the interpretation as "forming the intention to receive pure objects" is superior.
This differs from the case during the Council of Seven Hundred, where they directly accepted [valuables] because there was no prior offense.
In the text concerning the Council of Seven Hundred, the acceptance of precious objects was permitted for the sake of building monasteries; that passage is explicit.

Regarding the "four afflictions of the sun and moon," although five afflictions are listed in the current text, they are logically combined into four, as these correspond to the four afflictions of the śramaṇa.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 27) states: "The disks of the sun and moon are obscured by five veils;
they are not bright, do not illuminate, are not expansive, and are not pure. What are these five? First, clouds; second, smoke; third, dust; fourth, mist; and fifth, *halāhala* [fog]."

The hands of the asuras. Herein, "clouds" refers to when, during the height of summer, a few clouds arise and in an instant increase until they completely cover the void, obscuring the disks of the sun and moon so that both are made to disappear.

"Smoke" refers to when, in a forest or wild, grasses and trees are set ablaze and suddenly smoke arises, completely covering the void and obscuring the disks of the sun and moon so that both are made to disappear. "Dust" refers to...

It is like during a drought, when a great wind swirls and strikes, causing a tumultuous cloud of dust to suddenly arise and completely cover the void, obscuring the disks of the sun and moon so that neither appears.
As for mist (*nīhāra*): it is like when autumn or winter arrives and mountain rivers are shrouded in mist;

or as in foreign lands, when rain has first cleared and the sun shines upon the valleys and plains, the vapors of the earth surge upward and disperse in fine spray, completely covering the void (the rest is as previously described).
Regarding the hand of the asura Ghalaha: when the asuras fought with the devas, the devas used the sun and moon as their banners.
By the power of the sun and moon, the devas were constantly victorious over them; at that time, the asura Ghalaha [acted].

His mind was filled with wrath toward the sun and moon, and he desired to destroy them. However, due to the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, he was unable to destroy them despite exhausting all his skillful arts.
He then used his hand to block them, causing them to temporarily vanish. As it is said in the Sūtra: "O Bhikṣus, you should know this."
There is no large physical form, such as that of an asura; this refers to a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) and not to an actual body.
Regarding the statement that those with wrong views destroy the roots of goodness: looking into the Vinaya texts, it is "wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*) that is the fourth affliction.
To say "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is an error; one should rather say that "wrong livelihood" obstructs the roots of goodness.

Regarding the four items that should be relinquished for a major offense (*mahāsthāna*): first, the relinquishment of wealth; second, the confession of transgressions; third, the returning of wealth; and fourth, the non-returning of wealth, which refers to the pursuit of what was not returned.
This is because one fears the confusion with the method of relinquishment (*tyāga-dharma*).

As for the distinction between the "method of relinquishment" mentioned in the text and *viśuddhi* (purification through declaration), if one committed the offense of hoarding precious objects after performing this rite at the time of the original acceptance, performing this rite now constitutes the "method of relinquishment. This is to be understood according to the preceding citation.
The fourth volume of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* sufficiently clarifies this principle. Furthermore, according to the explanatory text (*kai-wen*), these words are also present there.

To claim that "this is a restatement of the relinquishment (*śikṣāpada*) to clarify the allowance" is incorrect; rather, this is the fundamental method for declaring purity (*śuddhi*). Once this relinquishment has been performed, one must next perform confession (*pratideśanā*).

This excludes only the act of wearing and using [the item]; there remain six categories, which are further divided into three stages: first, the confession of the offense (*āpatti*), followed by silence.

The four categories of minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*) are each concealed by intentional concealment. Next, repent for silent falsehoods. Next, repent for *thullaccaya* offenses. The formal recitation states:
"I, bhikṣu [Name], intentionally committed the offense of possessing such-and-such precious object; I have thus incurred such-and-such *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses."

Regarding the phrases "this treasure has already been relinquished" (if it has already been used up, one should say "this treasure has already been used up"), and the terms for relinquishment and so forth which follow the procedure for acknowledging the fault of loss:
this means that at all times when there is something taken or given, one should always say "I acknowledge this," and so on.
The opening text states: "To give back to the original donor" refers to the previous passage: "You should take it back and not let it be lost.
Regarding the "Precept on Trading Valuables" (the *Prātimokṣa* says:

"Various kinds of buying and selling"), the term "trading" (*mào*) below refers to the subsequent precept. This subsequent precept refers to trading with other wealth; this specific trading involves only valuables (*ratna*).

The *Shi shu yao lü piposha* (Commentary on the Essentials of the Vinaya), fascicle five, states: "Regarding the essence of this precept, it should be said that one must not engage in various uses of precious objects;
it should not be said that one may not buy or sell. This precept constitutes an offense immediately upon its commission; it differs from the precept against trading.

The precept against trading constitutes an offense because one buys for profit and then sells again" (the above is the text of the treatise). This [offense] is committed by both oneself and others. As for the precept against trading, which is committed by oneself alone: if, regarding the subsequent precept, one [acts] oneself...

Regarding the agent: whether seeking profit or not seeking profit, it is invariably an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If one employs a lay attendant (*karmadāna*) who does not seek profit, there is invariably no offense.

Even if that attendant seeks profit, according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is also an offense. Now, following this Vinaya, it is not stated that the offense occurs specifically because of seeking profit;
even if a lay attendant is made to seek profit, it is simply improper for an ordained person to do so, as such an act is not permitted.
Therefore, one merely incurs an auspicious outcome; it is also not a forfeiture offense (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

Regarding the distinctions among the objects of wealth, the sphere, and the ritual of relinquishment: "wealth" refers to precious items; the "sphere" applies only to laypeople; and the "ritual of relinquishment" is as stated in the text.
Regarding the separate confession (*pṛthak-deśanā*), this has already been explained in detail above. It is also permitted to perform it before the Saṃgha;

thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), fascicle seven, states: "One should enter among the monks and say: 'Venerable Sirs, I have committed a *pāyattika* offense by misappropriating various articles. I now openly confess and repent this transgression.
The Saṃgha shall ask: 'Do you see your fault? Hereafter, do not commit it again,' and so forth."

Regarding the differences in the objects and dharmas of the precepts: whereas later precepts have objects and dharmas that involve formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*), these precepts are entirely devoid of such dharmas, because they pertain to laypeople.
Regarding the opening of what was previously prohibited: it is permitted for use such as anointing the feet, as should be understood from the following passages.

The other three Vinayas and the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* all state that "that which is made is exchanged for that which is not made, and that which is not made is exchanged for that which is made. The *Samantapāsādikā* (Jianlun), fascicle 15, states:
"The 'made' may be either a finished vessel or an unfinished vessel. A finished vessel is exchanged for an unfinished vessel, and an unfinished vessel is exchanged for a finished vessel."
"This *vinaya* has already become gold, etc. This refers to the fact that it has already become vessels and so forth.
○ Regarding the precept on buying and selling (the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* says: "various kinds of trading"; here, the title of the preceding *vinaya* rule is taken as the name for this precept).
As for the detailed explanation, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle five, states: "Even if one provides food for the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should not eat it," and so forth.

One should not prostrate toward an image. Furthermore, it is said that one should simply prostrate with the intention that it is the Buddha. In general, one should not use these items for an ordinary bhikṣu who maintains the precepts.

If such a bhikṣu dies, the Saṃgha should perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual); because after death the continuity [of the individual] has been severed, he is no longer the same as when he was alive.
The *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) states: "Question: If a bhikṣu earns a living and gives food and clothing to others, may they accept them?"

"No. [The Buddha] replied: "If one takes the robe, one commits an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). In a place of extreme distress where there is no food, one may have a layperson (avadātavasana) prepare food for oneself and eat it.
If a practitioner who makes a living says to the community, 'This object is not mine; it belongs to that person,' then if it is so, one may eat it."
If the host does not provide food for the assembly, one commits a *pāyattika* offense. Two or three people may also make a formal announcement (*jñapti*).

If a layperson who is acting on behalf of a monastic says, "This is my property," it may be eaten (this refers to when a layperson acting for a monastic says, "This is my property," and the bhikṣu may then eat it). *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika*, fascicle five: If one uses goods obtained through trade to make food, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for every mouthful;
if used to make clothing, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for every garment worn; if used for beds or bedding, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for every time one lies upon them.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, chapter fifteen, states: When a merchant brings cloth that already has a fixed price and a bhikṣu comes with money to purchase it, placing the cloth on the ground, he should say to the owner, "I know this price for this cloth. If he does not speak thus but silently takes it away, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
There is a custom in certain kingdoms regarding market transactions: when someone brings money to the side of a commodity, the owner nods his head; one should know [this as consent].
[They] consult with one another. A bhikṣu should also speak thus: "I know only this. If the person ahead understands, he must make such a statement;
otherwise, there is an offense of transgression (*vyatikrama*). (And so on... Regarding taking by means of pure speech after distinguishing the price through impure speech:

[the bhikṣu] asks the person ahead, "For how much is this object being sold? I wish to know the value of this object. This is taking by means of pure speech after distinguishing the price through impure speech. As for... [it is] as follows.
This is the classification of objects. [In the case of] one who classifies the price with impure speech and takes it with impure speech:
they classify thus, "He asks for so much; I shall buy it at such a price. [In the case of] one who classifies the price with pure speech and takes it with pure speech:

they know the price thus, and knowing it thus, they take it. (The first two phrases constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense; the third phrase constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; the fourth is without fault.)
The fifth volume of the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, in the section on the precept against buying and selling, states: "Having purchased something and then reselling it constitutes an offense.

Alternatively, there may be an offense in the preliminary means (*upāya*) while there is no offense in the final result (*phala*). For example, if one buys grain or stores salt for the sake of profit, but later develops a virtuous mind and immediately gives it to the Sangha as a meritorious act, this is an auspicious offense in the means, but there is no offense in the result. Or, there may be no offense in the means while there is an offense in the result. As for example...
To purchase rice for the sake of livestock, and later, seeing a profit, to sell it for one's own gain—this expedient means is without fault, and the result is auspicious.

Offenses of this kind may be understood by analogy (the preceding treatise refers to knowing the remaining two cases by analogy). This is precisely what the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fascicle seven, states:
"To buy for the sake of profit and not sell is auspicious; to sell for the sake of profit and not buy is likewise auspicious."

For the sake of profit, having bought [an item], one sells it back—this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense (the fourth phrase is excluded). The intention of the commentary (*śū*) is that it is also a *pāyattika* at the time of purchase;

this differs from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Regarding the text’s mention of "repeatedly buying and selling," the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Treatise on the Great [School], *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*), fascicle five, states:

Regarding the robes of the Saṃgha: before the three proclamations have been made, one may pay the price; once the three proclamations have been completed, one should not pay the price, nor should the Saṃgha give the robe, for it has already become the property of another.
Having obtained the robe after the three proclamations, one should not regret the transaction; even if one regrets it, the Saṃgha must not return it. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Chapter Ten:
When selling items within the Saṃgha, the highest price offered shall be accepted. If the Upādhyāya or Ācārya wishes to take [the item], they may not do so.
[Excerpt].

Regarding the statement that "the same applies to buying": the seventh fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there was a person selling clothes, and the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks sought expensive clothes at a high price.
The Buddha said: "If one seeks another's expensive clothes by reducing the price [to force a sale], it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. If you require such an item, you must deliberate carefully."

Regarding the statement of the price: "I have purchased this for such an amount. If the other party does not give it, one should speak a second time. If they still do not give it, one should speak a third time.
If they do not give it after the third speaking, and one urgently requires this item, one should seek out a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) and have them purchase it.

If the *kappiya-kāraka* does not know how to bargain at the market, one should first instruct them. According to the tenth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, if the price should be fifty coins but one demands a hundred, the bhikṣu says:
I [shall] take fifty [coins]. Knowing this, one does not commit an offense. One must not snatch from the market; rather, one should ask, "Are you coming?
If he says, "I am indeed coming," and one snatches [the goods], it is an offense of *vyatikrama*. If he says, "It is my bed," one may take it. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Chapter Five).
One should instruct a *karmadāna* (attendant), saying, "For my sake, exchange this item for that item. One should think in one's mind: "May he rather obtain my profit."

I did not obtain that benefit. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Chapter Ten: Hiring someone to repair leather sandals, to repair the walking path (*caṅkrama*), and so forth, while using impure speech, constitutes an offense of transgression (*sātisāra*).
Regarding the statement that "the three phrases for purchasing should also be applied," the Venerable One says: "Following the previous [explanation] for selling, one should simply say:

'purchasing at a reduced price,' 'purchasing at a heavy price,' and 'purchasing at a further reduced price. The explanation of these three names is no different from that in the chapter. Now, examining the meaning of the text, the three cases regarding selling are as follows:

"selling" refers to when the seller initially asks for one *kārsāpaṇa*, but then repeatedly increases or decreases the price. For example, suppose a person sells an object and originally demands one *kārsāpaṇa*. The buyer...
The person returned one [coin]. The seller again demanded three coins. The buyer then said, "I will not buy it anymore. The seller said, "If you will not buy it, you may take back one coin.
This is called "repeatedly going up and down" (in price). Regarding "increased selling": originally he demanded one coin;
once one coin was returned, he immediately demanded three coins and sold it for three. This is called "increased selling. To increase further—
Regarding "selling at an increased price": originally one demanded one *qián*, and upon receiving one *qián*, one immediately demanded three *qián*.

Upon receiving three *qián*, one again demanded five *qián* and sold it for five *qián*; this is called "selling with successive increases. Regarding the three types of buyers: first, the buyer returns five *qián* as the original principal;
second, when they are about to give [the price], they instead return three *qián*; the owner then says, "I will not sell now," and so forth.
To return five coins and then take [the goods] back is called "repeatedly going up and down. Second is "buying at a reduced price":

one originally returns five coins, but when it comes time to give them back, one returns only three coins and obtains [the goods] for those three; this is called buying at a reduced price. Third is "successive reduction in purchase":
one originally returns five coins, but when it comes time to give them back, one returns only three coins; having given those three, one returns [them] again.
"One coin; obtained for one coin—this is called purchasing at a reduced price.
Regarding the opening text which says "using oil instead of *sū* (ghee)," and the commentary in the chapter which explains this as being for external use:

since the previous explanation of the characteristics states "for seven days," we know that the former refers to internal use. Internal use provides physical strength and increases craving; therefore, it constitutes an offense.

External applications are the opposite of the above; they are permitted because there is no fault. Furthermore, that which was previously for one's own use—where seven days were exchanged for another seven days—is what constitutes "personal reception. Now, exchanging ghee for oil and so forth is an act of offering.
The fifteenth section, the *Dīrgha-pātra-śikṣā-dṛṣṭi-vāda*, states: "One bowl and two burnings; it does not mention three. The twenty-ninth [section] of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
Three types of color were encountered: first, the color of a peacock’s throat (a green luster);

second, the color of a *pulinga* bird (traditionally said to be unknown, but upon detailed examination, it appears to be red); third, the color of a pigeon (that is, a grayish-blue). The Buddha said, "When fumigating, have them made in these colors.
The Venerable One replied, "Add a fourth characteristic as well," because since the characteristics did not match, the bowl was not fit for use.
This refers to maintaining [the bowl].

Regarding "obtaining the bowl for five days," etc., this is the text from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun), fascicle 5; it is also found in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* (Jian-lun), fascicle 15.

If it is cracked or perforated like a grain of millet, the maintenance [of the bowl] is lost. If one repairs it with iron filings, one may maintain it. (It further states: "Nissaggiya" means that the bowl has not been relinquished.
Confession: If it is a *duṣkṛta* offense, (it is further stated that) if one buys another's bowl, one must not accept or possess it even if the price has been repaid.
If the price for the bowl has already been paid and the owner of the bowl has finished fumigating it, he informs the bhikṣu; yet if the bhikṣu does not take it within ten days, [an offense occurs].

Regarding the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (this refers to a specific school; one need not rely upon the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, for according to that treatise, even if the three robes are not maintained, it is still said to be an offense of "excess," yet in the present case where the robes are lacking, how could it logically constitute an offense of excess?).

Regarding the precept on begging for a bowl with five patches: the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, fascicle 4, states that if a bowl is broken into five pieces, the method for patching it is to place each patch at an interval of two finger-widths (*aṅgula*).
The intent of the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* is the same. Now, the Tripiṭaka Master says that "five patches" refers to... [text continues]
It is joined by five kinds of fastenings; it is not joined at five locations. Now, examining this closely, it contradicts the Vinaya-vibhaṅga itself.

Regarding the "four dharmas being the same as above," this refers to the precepts concerning extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) and so forth, which correspond to the section of the text immediately following.
Regarding the second part, the confession of offenses (*pāpadeśanā*): first, one requests the method for confession; next, one invites the presiding confessor (*deśaka*);

next, one receives the formal announcement of the confession; and finally, one performs the actual confession. There are also eight categories of *duṣkṛta* (minor) offenses. Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Jìzhī lù), fascicle 10, states:

"In this context, using an impure bowl incurs immeasurable *vinayātikrama* (transgressions of the discipline). The formal declaration should state: 'By using a *niḥsargika-pātra* (bowl subject to forfeiture), one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.'"
Regarding the offense (or the recollection of the count, etc.), other terms may be understood by analogy.

Since it is mandatory that one must return the extra bowl from another person after it has been kept overnight, it is required that one relinquish it. If one were to return it immediately, there is a fear that the intention to keep the extra bowl (*atireka-pātra*) might not yet have ceased;
thus, even if one were to receive this bowl through such a request, it would constitute an offense for keeping an extra bowl. Therefore, one must return it after having kept it overnight.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, chapter ten: This bowl is of great value; one should sell it to obtain the price of ten bowls. The remainder is as explained in the chapter [if the bowl is not of high value, the matter is easily understood].

As stated in the *Vinaya* texts: once the inferior bowl has been returned and the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal motion with one proclamation) is completed, one takes this bowl and exchanges it starting from the senior monk (*sthavira*) down to the junior monk (*navaka*).

If following the three *vinayas* (the eighth chapter of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the tenth chapter of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, and the fifth chapter of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*), if eight persons are present...
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu, so-and-so, whose alms bowl has not yet reached five mends, has requested a new bowl;
he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the distributor of bowls. If the time is right for the Saṃgha..."
"May the Sangha listen with patience. The motion is thus announced. The formal ritual (karmavācanā) may be understood by following this announcement.

The Master of the Commentary intends for the appointment of the bowl-distributor to follow the other three Vinayas, rather than this Vinaya, where no such formal procedure for appointment is required. Why is this so? Because in the other three Vinayas...

Once the *śuddhika-prāyaścitta* (confession of abandonment) has been completed, one immediately appoints a person to distribute the bowls (*pātra-cāraṇa*). According to principle, this distribution of bowls is itself the method of returning them;

for in the three Vinayas, there is no separate *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal motion with one announcement) specifically for returning bowls, and thus they merely appoint someone to distribute them. Since this Vinaya does include a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for returning bowls, it is therefore necessary that the presiding *karman*-master perform the announcement and then distribute the bowls.

Regarding "the absence of five matters," the *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya) states: "If it is too large, if it is too small, if it is perforated or defective, or if one chants incorrectly, it should not be given;
if these five matters are absent, it should be given" (the commentary notes that the citation "if it exceeds the measure" is an error).

The statement that "the *Sīla* [Vinaya] monks all filled their bowls with water and passed them around" is an error; there is no such text in the *Sīla-vinaya*. The eighth fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Regarding this bowl which should be relinquished in the midst of the assembly, one should fill this bowl with water and pass it around among the Saṃgha. (And so forth... It continues:
"The bhikṣus should immediately each take the bowl they previously used and gather them in one place. This should be followed accordingly.
The Vinaya text states: "One walks with water held in one's own bowl; this signifies that the assembly is neither leaking nor impure.

Regarding the phrase "or it may also be given," this is likely not the case. According to the text, it appears that one must first exchange it for the bowl of the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) before it can be given.
If one follows the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle five, which says: "If, when the water is being distributed among the monks, no one takes any, it should be returned to him."
For the bhikṣu, the five parts are likewise the same.

As for the statement that one should not take [the robe] because it is improper to protect the Saṃgha, this explains the meaning of "should take" mentioned above; this should be understood according to the commentary (śāstra).
Regarding the statement in the text, "One should also not accept or hold an inferior bowl (*hīna-pātra*) and so forth," the commentary explains this in terms of the owner of the bowl.
This interpretation is likely incorrect. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The bhikṣus should each bring their own bowls that they have been authorized to hold.
If a bhikṣu discards the bowl he previously received and brings another, inferior bowl, he commits a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline)."

Regarding the two types of cases mentioned previously for returning the bowl: first, returning the bowl after it has been exchanged; second, returning the bowl directly. These may be understood from the text.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, fascicle eight, states: "If a bowl has been repaired more than five times and one seeks a new bowl to accept and maintain..."

Among four persons, one must undergo the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the motion followed by one proclamation) to receive and maintain [the bowl]; with three or fewer persons, it is not permitted. (The above is from the *Śāstra*).

This refers to the practice of "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*) as the name for the act of holding. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle five, states: "Regarding the bowl previously received and maintained according to the Dharma, one continues to maintain it;

the subsequent bowl is not formally received, but is simply kept in constant possession. The rest is as explained in the chapter. This refers to the method of adding the rite of formal reception and maintenance, where the name "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*) is applied to that Dharma.
Thus it was said. Jīvaka said: "When a bhikṣu repairs his bowl while begging for food, he should repair it after he has finished eating.

He should wash it clean with either ash or earth, but he must not use hard objects to pierce holes through it and break it open; he should use a bird's quill to pierce it. He must not use sand or ash to remove the glaze;
he should use *gomaya* (cow dung) that is free of sand. He may use the juices of roots or leaves [as adhesives], but he must not stand on the edge of a pit or a precipice."
One must not stand on a high or precarious place, nor beneath a tree with ripe fruit, nor upon a stone or a brick. One should wash on level ground.
If there is no place to sit, one should lean the body away from the ground by the distance of one span (*vitasti*). Having washed, dry it in the sun and re-sew it.

Place it in one spot and cover its opening with an object (one must not use a food cloth or similar items to cover the opening). If one is pressed for time by urgent business, one need not wash it thoroughly.
One should smear it with root-juice and the like. When finished, one should wash it. After washing it the following day, one should carry it for alms;
even if it is difficult to mend, one should use it until it is finally worn out. It must be washed clean. If it should nonetheless break, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
