One says: "Other teachers state that if it is an object currently being perceived by the five sense faculties..."

That which is called "the seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) refers to the objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by the five consciousnesses. That which is called "the heard" (*śruta*) refers to what is transmitted by others;

it is the object of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) conveyed through the ear, and this constitutes authoritative scripture (*āgama*). That which is called "the sensed" (*mata*) refers to what is inferred through various reasonings by one's own mind according to what is accepted;

this is inference (*anumāna*) on the mental ground. That which is called "the known" (*vijñāta*) refers to what is directly realized by the mind; this is direct perception on the mental ground, namely the state of the mind following the five consciousnesses as well as the objects of meditative concentration. Among these five objects:

Each [of these] can give rise to four kinds of verbal expression: seeing, hearing, cognizing, and knowing. Regarding the sixth object (the mental), with the exception of "seeing," there are three [other types].
Another explanation states: The former masters have reported that it was said thus:

what is directly perceived by the eye is called "the seen" (this refers to the objective domain of direct perception by visual consciousness); what is heard from others is called "the heard" (as before); and what is conceived through the movement of one's own mind is called "the thought."

That which is called "the object of cognition" (as previously stated) refers to what is internally experienced and what is personally realized; this is termed "the object of knowledge" (referring to the objects of direct perception by the four consciousnesses, such as the ear-consciousness, and the objects of direct perception on the level of the mental consciousness).
According to the Mahāyāna Yogācāra school, for instance, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states in its first chapter:

That which is experienced by the eye has the meaning of "seeing. That which is experienced by the ear has the meaning of "hearing. To naturally contemplate and construct [the understanding] that one should know in this way has the meaning of "cognition" (*vijñāna*).
That which is internally experienced within oneself has the meaning of "knowledge" (*jñāna*). (Commentary: The general purport is the same as previously explained by the Master.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (second), the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (ninety-second), and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (eighteenth) all explain its meaning;
these cannot be recounted in detail here, as they are fully contained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-bhāṣya* (which follows the commentary below).
Regarding the claim that the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) can produce consciousness through five conditions and thus perceive—that is, discern—objects: this is based on the Sarvāstivāda school.

According to this school, the visual faculty perceives visible forms only by means of the arising of consciousness; it is only when the faculty is present that it receives the designation "seeing" (where "consciousness" carries the sense of "discerning").

Regarding the statement that "auditory consciousness can hear," it is the auditory faculty (*śrotrendriya*) that hears. To say that it is "consciousness" [that hears] is because it is only when consciousness resides in the faculty that it is designated as "hearing";
thus, there is no error in this meaning. The same principle applies to all other cases. Treatises such as the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* all accept this interpretation.

However, according to the tenet of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it is consciousness that sees and hears; this has already been clarified above in the refutation of the [wrong] view regarding the precepts.

This is because the mental faculty (*manas*) is capable of cognizing all [objects] simultaneously. Furthermore, another commentary states: "The mental faculty is capable of cognizing all things simultaneously because it gives rise to consciousnesses. (Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "capable of cognizing all simultaneously," the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), in its own primary function, cognizes only the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); however, when it performs the functions of others, it is also able to cognize them.
Regarding the phrase "because the other seventeen realms give rise to consciousnesses," the intent of the commentary is that the visual consciousness and the other [sensory consciousnesses]—
Since it is induced by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), we know that the mental consciousness also shares the same objects of perception as the visual consciousness and the others.

Now, examining this in detail, various treatises of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools state that consciousness arises from three conditions: first, the sense organ is unimpaired; second, the object is present before one;

and third, the attention (*manasikāra*) capable of producing [consciousness] is correctly activated. Examining this attention in detail, it is a mental factor (*caitta-dharma*) whose intrinsic nature is to alert the mind; it is of two kinds.

There are two types: first, that which is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which can cause the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the mental consciousness to induce the visual consciousness and the other sense-consciousnesses;

second, the visual consciousness itself, which possesses its own attention (*manaskāra*). Although it arises simultaneously with the visual consciousness, it is nonetheless called "that which causes the visual consciousness to arise.
This is because there is no logical contradiction in the principle of simultaneous cause and effect. The intent of the preceding commentary was merely to distinguish the former.
Regarding the meaning: one may explain both [theories] together, and neither is contradictory (for this reason, the mental consciousness also possesses all three conditions).

As for those sense organs whose nature is dull and whose functional capacity is limited—namely, the nose and so forth—they can only specifically apprehend the three objects of fragrance, flavor, and tangibility, which are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) realms; therefore, it is said that their function is limited.

The second verse of the *Cittaviveka* states: "The two objects are not received when not proximate. The prose commentary explains: "The two realms are not received when not proximate" refers to visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*).
They do not perceive objects that are too close; for example, one does not see a color that is pressed against the eye. The same applies to the ear.

"If pressed, one does not hear" (this explains the first phrase). As for "mental consciousness," it perceives all objects, whether distant or near, with the exception of its own substance and those factors that are associated or co-existent with it;
everything else it perceives (this explains the second phrase).

As for the others, they invariably experience [their objects] through proximity; that is, the consciousnesses of the tongue, nose, and body must have their objects in close proximity, because the basis and the object are without interval.

(The "basis" refers to the sense organ upon which consciousness relies; the "object" refers to the sphere perceived by consciousness. Only when there is no separation between the organ and the object can there be experience.)

Regarding the nature of the three faculties as supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the *Sañcetanīya-sūtra* states: "The two faculties of eye and ear constitute the supernormal powers of the eye and the ear;
the faculty of mind (*manas*) fully constitutes the remaining four supernormal powers."
Regarding the statement that "the four [cases] such as 'not seeing' take non-existence as their object," the meaning of the commentary (*śū*) is as follows:

One gives rise to the intention to speak falsely, taking those matters of "not seeing" or "not hearing" as the object; one then utters false words in contradiction to that object. Furthermore, to briefly summarize the intent of the commentary:
when one says they "saw" what they did not see, the object contradicted is broad, while the substance designated by the claim is narrow; this refers to the object that is contradicted.
In total there are four kinds: first, seeing; second, hearing; third, touching; and fourth, cognizing. Therefore, it is said that [the scope of] "seeing" is broad.
Yet, when one speaks of "seeing," the substance [of the act] is narrow. The other three—such as hearing and so forth—should be understood by analogy with this.

In explaining the following passage, regarding the statement "seeing yet not seeing": the object contradicted is narrow, while the substance referred to is broad; that is to say, it refers solely to what is seen by the eye.

Because it refers only to the specific object that was violated, it is said to be "narrow. However, when speech is uttered from the mouth, there are four types: first, not seeing; second, hearing; third, touching;
and fourth, knowing. Therefore, it is said to be "broad. The remaining three [cases] are to be understood accordingly.

In the section below that specifically clarifies the delusion, the text mentions "seeing" in contrast to "not seeing," and "not seeing" in contrast to "seeing," rather than providing a detailed analysis.
This refers to the passage concerning the subsequent six mental states (*ṣaḍ-citta*), which simply state that one does not see, hear, or know.
As for the mention of "seeing, hearing, touching, and knowing," the text does not provide an extensive analysis thereof. Had it been extensively analyzed, it would be as in the chapter;
had it followed the preceding passage, it would be a case of citing what is not seen in contrast to what is seen—this too should be understood as not being an extensive analysis.
Had it been extensively analyzed, it would be as in the chapter; had it cited what is seen... [the text continues].
"Speaking while not seeing," and so forth, should also include "hearing," and so on, as follows.

Among these, the first, third, and fifth cases involve a contradiction with both the object and the mind; the second, fourth, and sixth cases involve a contradiction with the mind alone (the second, fourth, and sixth are also termed "object-conforming, mind-contradicting").

Regarding the "object" (*viṣaya*) herein, it is as distinguished in the three types of objects within the precept against great falsehood; in these instances of falsehood, it refers exclusively to actual facts.
This is the analysis of the objective realm (*viṣaya*). It means that this actual reality, when compared with the limits of verbal expression, constitutes either contradiction or conformity.

However, when compared with the objects manifested within one's own mind, all six propositions are entirely contradictory. For instance, as in the second mental state, it says: "One does not see the perception of seeing.
Within this perception-mind, there is also a manifested form (*rūpa*) appearing before the mind; now, [the proposition] contradicts this object and gives rise to...
To say "not seeing" is it not the case that both mind and object are in contradiction? The remaining phrases should be understood accordingly.

Regarding the statement, "When there is doubt and delusion, there is immediately no doubt": Question: Previously it was said, "referring to the three types of deluded minds," yet their meaning did not follow [from the context].
Why is it now stated that "having doubt and delusion" refers to the two minds of "minor delusion" and "no doubt"? Answer: This refers to the meaning...

"Come. This does not mean that the text itself comes. Nevertheless, students must clearly memorize the six mental states (*citta*) regarding both the offenses of slandering the Dharma and minor falsehoods;
only then can they consult the commentary to examine and weigh their distinctions.
Regarding the second point, "by means of perception, feeling, and formations (*saṃjñā-vedanā-saṃskāra*)," the term "etc. includes the mind (*citta*).

This refers to the arrangement [of the five consciousnesses] into the four mental factors of real consciousness, perception, feeling, and formations, according to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*. According to the *Satyasiddhi* school, the five consciousnesses are neither defiled nor free from defilement.

Consequently, the five consciousnesses possess no wholesome or unwholesome formations. How, then, could there be a mind of formation within them that perceives a tiger or experiences a cold tactile sensation? For these two objects are...

This is because they are the objects of the eye and the body. The commentary explains: "By means of the eye, the body, and their objects, one flows into the mind of formation (*saṃskāra*), deliberating upon benefit and harm, and so forth.

The intent of the sub-commentary (*śū*) is that the three—view (*dṛṣṭi*), desire (*chanda*), and contact (*sparśa*)—are all assigned to formations; acceptance (*kṣānti*) is assigned to feeling (*vedanā*); perception (*saṃjñā*) is assigned to perception;
and thought (*citta*) is assigned to consciousness (*vijñāna*). Now, examining the meaning of the text: "view" has the sense of discernment through wisdom (*prajñā*); "acceptance" is superior...
"Understanding" (*vijñāna*) has the meaning of "discerning. These two [mental factors] are among the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*) within the Mahāyāna system.

"Desire" (*chanda*) means aspiration; "contact" (*sparśa*) means the conjunction of the three; "perception" (*saṃjñā*) means grasping an image. These three are among the five omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga*) within the Mahāyāna system.
They have the meaning of the mind-king (*cittarāja*) discerning its objects. Herein, the five mental concomitants (*caitta*) are distinguished.

Regarding this mind-king (*citta-rāja*): according to the Sarvāstivāda school, it is included within the category of universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), which in total comprise ten dharmas.
These five [mental factors] are precisely part of those ten; thus, one knows that the fundamental [system] includes these five numbers among the universal mental factors.

Together with the mind-king, they form six. Because they are universal mental factors, they pervade all states of mind; for this reason, they are singled out for mention. This interpretation is definitive; do not [doubt it] further.

One doubts this. Regarding the enumeration of the five types of false speech, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten-Recitation Vinaya), chapter nine, states: "There are five kinds of false speech: some result in a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), some result in a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), some result in a *pārājika* (defeat), some result in a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the community), and some result in a *pāyattika* (expiation).

The *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* are as can be known. That which results in a *sthūlātyaya* refers to cases that do not fully constitute a *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. That which results in a *pāyattika*... [text continues].

This refers to the offense of groundless slander (*anuvādaka*). Regarding "entering into a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing)": with the exception of the four types of false speech, all other instances of false speech constitute a *dukkaṭa* offense (excluding the aforementioned four).
As for the essence (*bhāva*) of false speech: generally, the essence of false speech consists of saying one has seen what was not seen, or saying one has not seen what was seen, and so forth;

its essence is non-noble speech (*anariya-vācā*). Among these, the first, third, fifth, and so on, are this very essence, whereas the second, fourth, sixth, and so on—such as saying one has not seen what was not seen—are likewise included.
Because [the marks] appear as if they were real within the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are for the time being not called "substance" (*tattva*).
Furthermore, it should be stated that when there is doubt, one explains by opening up four or three phrases from each of the two preceding sets of six;

and it should also be stated that when there is no doubt, one explains by opening up five or six phrases from each of the two preceding sets of six. Jue says: "This interpretation is incorrect. Regarding the preceding...

Since it has already been stated that the three [precepts], the first, the third, and the fifth are permitted, one should not now further state that the three are permitted, nor that the fifth is permitted.

○ Regarding "slandering the precepts" (*śīla-avamāna*): in the Sanskrit language, this is called *uṇāmanuṣyavāda*, which here means "reducing speech. This refers to disparaging or diminishing another.
This refers to the person; it carries the meaning of disparagement.

Regarding the "one hundred carts" mentioned in the *Nidāna*: during the rise of the laws of the Ji Zhou dynasty, three *sheng* of that period were equivalent to one *sheng* of the present day; calculating this in total amounts to slightly more than thirty *shi*.

Regarding the "five hundred fetters" (*pañca-śata-saṃyojana*), the traditional commentary explains that the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) are divided into five categories, totaling four hundred and ninety.

When combined with the ten root proclivities, they total five hundred. Alternatively, one may exclude the ten root proclivities and add the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*)—as the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states:

"The eight envelopments are shamelessness, lack of dread, envy, stinginess, regret, torpor, restlessness, and lethargy; or ten by adding anger and concealment"). Now, examining this in detail, the eighth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Kātyāyanīputra... [text continues].

In the *Abhidharma* of Kātyāyanīputra, ninety-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) and ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are taught as the one hundred and eight afflictions (Kātyāyanīputra composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* approximately two hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
he was the patriarch of the Sarvāstivāda school). In the *Abhidharma* of the Vātsīputrīyas, the fetters and proclivities (*anuśaya*) are likewise the same.

There are five hundred *paryavasthāna* (entanglements). (Furthermore, it is said: Regarding these entanglements, some say there are ten entanglements, while others say there are five hundred entanglements;

this is based solely on that treatise (*śāstra*). As for the statement in the present Vinaya regarding "five hundred fetters" (*saṃyojana*), this is a translation error; it should read "entanglements.
However, since the Dharmaguptaka and Vātsīputrīya schools arose in the world at the same time, the doctrines they uphold may well be identical (referring to both having three hundred...).
If one says that this Vinaya belongs to Dharmottara, it then emerged from the Vātsīputrīya school; therefore, its tenets remain identical to the original system.
Since there is no extensive commentary on this school in the treatises, one cannot say that the ninety-eight [defilements] are divided into five categories and so forth;
one simply knows its distinct tenets.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, Chapter Twelve: Regarding those of low caste, one says, "You are a *caṇḍāla*, a barber, or the like. Regarding those of middling caste, one says, "You are of intermediate [caste].
Regarding those of high caste, one says, "You are of the *kṣatriya* or *brāhmaṇa* lineage. One speaks these words with the intent to cause them shame.

Regarding those of low occupation, one says, "You are a butcher, a seller of meat, a bird-catcher, or the like. Regarding those of middling occupation, one says, "You are a seller of incense or a shopkeeper."
Regarding those who work in shops, fields, and so forth: the superior type among you are those who dwell in shops dealing with gold, silver, mani-jewels, and copper vessels;
the inferior type among you have blind eyes, hunched backs, crippled feet, shaved heads, and saw-like teeth;

the middling type among you are too dark, too pale, too yellow, or too red. As for the superior type among you, you possess the thirty-two marks, a halo, and golden skin. [The inferior type] are afflicted by disease.
All such as these are entirely categorized as "low. You who suffer from scabies and ringworm, even up to madness—all such transgressors are entirely categorized as low.

This includes those who commit *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, *prāyaścittika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *vinayātikrama* offenses. Those who revile others are all categorized as low; they are lewd, dissolute, and impure.
All evil abuse and the fetters are collectively termed "inferior. You are foolish, dull-witted, and ignorant, like a lump of clay;
you are like a sheep, a white crane, a horned bird, or an owl.
In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, there is a class of *sthūlātyaya* offenses that are lighter than *pāyattika* offenses.

Regarding "repentance in one's mind," this refers to repentance through self-reproach; it differs from a simple *vyatikrama* (transgression), which requires a face-to-face encounter with another person.

Regarding the discussion on the precept against divisive speech (*paiśunya*) concerning the instigation of strife among great *bhikṣus* and others: this is cited in the sixth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Daolun), as was done in the aforementioned topical analysis.

The same applies to the ninth fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* (Shisong). Furthermore, the second fascicle of the *Vinayavibhaṅga* (Jia) also states: "Divisive speech directed toward a *bhikṣu* constitutes a *pāyattika*; [the same applies to] the fourfold assembly including *bhikṣuṇīs*."

Regarding the term "bianji" (邊吉): when a nun [speaks] toward a monk as "bianji" (or perhaps these are distinct categories, because the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* states that minor falsehoods, disparagement, slander, and so forth, as well as the interpretation of physiognomy and the like, constitute "ji" [faults]), this is indeed empty speech.
This is not so; for even transmitting what is true constitutes an offense.

The eighth [precept] of the Five-Part Vinaya concerning sleeping with a woman: from the time a woman is first born, the text states "possessing both" (*ubhayato-vyañjanā*); "possessing both" is the wording from the Five-Part Vinaya.

Regarding the three cases of the *tri-gati* (the three realms of rebirth): the nineteenth [chapter] states, "If oxen, donkeys, and the like hold their heads up, there is no offense; when they lay their heads down to sleep, it is a *thullaccaya*.
A female dog has no offense when she extends her head; when she curls her head to sleep, it is a *thullaccaya*. A goose or a chicken has no offense when they curl their heads under their wings;

when an elephant stands upright, there is no offense; when it leans over to sleep, it is a *thullaccaya*. Since these offenses apply to animals, one should understand that they apply to non-humans (*amanusya*) by analogy."

Regarding the offense of a young girl while sleeping: the *Jì* (Zhìlù) states that if many bhikṣus are sleeping together in a room and a woman enters carrying her daughter, all the sleeping bhikṣus commit a *thullaccaya*.
The *vīnā* (steward) or administrative official should say to her: "You must stand the child upright before entering.

According to this rule, a small child should not constitute an offense. In the subsequent explanation of the characteristics [of the act], it specifies that the human female must possess discernment (*vijñā*).
This is because the life-faculty has not been severed.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter sixteen, states: "As for 'a woman,' it refers to a human female, a non-human female, or a female animal. Whether a man is sitting or lying down [with her]..."

This is termed "staying overnight. According to this Vinaya, as indicated in the opening text, sitting [through the night] does not constitute an offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* further states that staying up all night sitting and not lying down does not constitute an offense.

However, if one stays overnight in another's house where there is a woman, it is an offense if there is space sufficient for a kitten to enter. *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣikā*, fascicle 8, states: "If one keeps a woman capable of [sexual intercourse]..."

Sexual intercourse constitutes a *thullaccaya*. If one is unable to engage in sexual intercourse—such as with a barren woman, one whose organs are impaired, a female spirit, a celestial maiden (*devī*), or a female sparrow—it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (or *pācittiya*).
[These specific categories need not be strictly adhered to.]
Regarding those who commit offenses through similarity: although they commit the offense of "staying overnight," because they were actually sitting upright, they do not incur the full offense.
Regarding "those without delusion": according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, although Ānanda had attained arhatship, he should not have stayed overnight with a woman.
Just as warm food and drink are desired by people, so too is it with women toward men (this refers to ordinary persons, not Arhats).
Ji said: "On great assemblies such as the Buddha's birthday or the day he attained enlightenment, if the Dharma is preached throughout the night, one should stay in the open air.
If there is wind, snow, or cold, one should enter a building and sit with the body upright. If one is elderly or ill and unable to sit [in this manner], [one may remain indoors]."

One must provide a screen. The screen must not be made of coarse materials; it should be as high as the shoulders and armpits. When traveling on the road and entering a village to stay overnight, one should occupy a separate room.
If there is no building, one should stay in the open air. If it is windy or cold, one may enter a house and sit with the body upright.
If one is old or ill, one should make a screen. If there is none, and if the woman is trustworthy, one should say to her: "You sleep first; I shall sit here for a while."
When the Buddha wished to sleep, he would say, "Rise! I wish to sleep; you must not sleep. For one who sleeps, there is no merit.

Regarding the rule against staying overnight with those who have not yet received full ordination, the *Karmavācanā* states that there is no fault in being with a woman, provided the three offenses do not occur; however, there is no textual authority for this.
Regarding "if she has already stayed two nights with a man," there is a textual passage in the second volume of the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*.
As for "the bhikṣuṇī precepts," this refers to the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya-mūla*.

Regarding the phrase "reciting the prohibitions and subsequently granting exceptions," the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Daolun), fascicle eight, states: "If [the Buddha] had not permitted it at all, there might be circumstances where one’s life would be lost."
(Up to: Out of compassion, they are permitted to stay together for two nights; however, to protect the Buddha-dharma, they are not allowed to stay for three nights.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), fascicle 15, states: "For two reasons of benefit: first, for the sake of the śrāmaṇeras; second, for the sake of laypeople who have come to the monastic quarters."

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is recorded that there was a lay follower of pure faith who built a latrine for the Buddha. Although the Buddha had no need for it, he accepted it in accordance with worldly custom.

Once, while Rāhula was sleeping in the open air, a wind and rain arose during the night; he went to the World-Honored One’s latrine and lay down, using a wooden board from the latrine as a pillow. During the night, a black snake appeared.
He was also afraid of the wind and rain and wished to enter the latrine. The Buddha, who constantly observes sentient beings, saw the snake and feared it would distress Rāhula.
He immediately emitted a radiance and went to the latrine himself. With his golden, smooth hands, he helped him up, brushed the dust from his body, and led him into his own room.
Pointing to a bed, he said, "Dwell here; the Tathāgata has [already provided for you]."
He established the precepts for his disciples; therefore, one should practice these precepts accordingly. Thus, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged until the ground was reached.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the Buddha feared being stung by insects while staying overnight in a latrine; he came and spoke this verse: "It is not because of poverty that you have left home, nor is it because you have lost wealth and status;
it is solely for the sake of seeking the Way that you should endure suffering as a renunciant. He then led him into the dwelling and arrived at the ground.
Having finished [his meal], he said to the bhikṣus: "This śrāmaṇera is pitiable; he has no parents. If we do not show him compassion, by what means shall he survive?
If he encounters a predatory beast, he will suffer great distress. His kinsmen will surely resent this, saying:

'The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, are able to keep a śrāmaṇera, yet they cannot protect him. Having rebuked them, he established the precept. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle 15, states: "The reason why..."
Regarding entering a Buddha’s latrine: it is because it is clean and pure, and many people offer incense and flowers there; for this reason, one enters within.

As for the offense of staying overnight with those who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*): the allowance for two or three nights after the initial prohibition was granted because the previous restriction was too strict.

Thus, while there is no offense for staying for a single night, the allowance extends up to three nights. This is understood through observation within the military, which later served as a precedent.
For this reason, [the Buddha] permitted staying for two or three nights and established a separate precept against exceeding that limit.

However, regarding the cases of "viewing an army" and "staying because of a prior cause or condition," which permit seeing an army without offense: at the time of viewing an army, the offense is incurred upon seeing it during the day;

one does not have to wait for the appearance of the dawn-light (*āloka*). Therefore, the subsequent commentary states: "However, viewing an army is not 'staying' (overnight). If that is so, then regarding the viewing of an army...
Is there also an exception? Therefore, the subsequent explanation states: "Due to the circumstance of three nights, one may incidentally see an army; this is not a formal exception. ... up to ...
"Therefore, it is not analogous" means it is not analogous to the exception for staying together, because the category of "staying" is the same; thus, it is a formal exception.
While spreading the bedding in the screened area, the original intention was merely to depart for a short time; however, having stayed for three nights, the original resolve was to leave permanently.
At the moment of exiting the door, the offense is incurred. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle 15, states: "Even if one constructs a hut using cloth as the covering, it is an offense.

If there are many rooms sharing a single door, it is also an offense, provided they have separate doors [otherwise it is not]. It further states: 'If the four sides each have doors opening inward toward a central space, and there is one large common door through which one exits, [it is an offense]."*

Entering [the dwelling] also constitutes an offense. If there is a separate entrance, there is no offense. (It is further stated: If houses are connected and large, even up to one *yojana* in extent, they constitute a single entrance and entering them is an offense.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣikā*, fascicle 8, states: "If one has stayed together for two nights and then moves elsewhere, having stayed overnight in that other place, there is no fault in returning to stay together again.
The seventeenth rule of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* regarding cold and snow is the same as the preceding precept.
One should know its characteristics.
(From the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle 6): "In order to distinguish the speech so that it may be clearly understood" (the character "令" is omitted in the chapter).

Regarding the passage on reciting Buddhist scriptures with laypeople: *The Five-Part Vinaya*, Chapter Six. At the outset, there was an occasion concerning the instruction of laypeople (*avadātavasana*) in reciting scriptures.
At that time, various bhikṣus who had gone forth from different countries [of India] were incorrect in their pronunciation and phrasing. The householders (*gṛhapati*) criticized them, saying:

"How is it that you have attended upon [the Buddha] day and night, yet do not know the speech of men, women, eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*), or those with dual sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*)? The Buddha rebuked the householders.

Consequently, he was prohibited from teaching. Later, when [the student] came again to request instruction, he was permitted to recite [the texts] concurrently. (In the Western tradition of *śabda-vidyā*, there are three types of voice: first, the masculine voice; second, the feminine voice; [and third, the neuter voice].)

(3. A voice that is neither male nor female). *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, chapter thirteen: There was a Brahmin who spoke with disdain, saying, "In the midst [of this], there is a chirping sound like that of children in a schoolhouse reciting their lessons;
one does not even know who is the teacher and who are the disciples."
Having seen this, that person does not give rise to faith.

Regarding the statement that "the principle of the three practices is complete," the first three lines— “Commit no evil,” and so forth— correspond respectively to the three practices of ethical discipline (*śīla*),
meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) (as analyzed above in the six sections on the establishment of the precepts).
The *Śāstra* states: "Regarding 'identical sounds but different phrases,' this refers to the sixth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* (多論).
Regarding 'the manifestation of cessation and conduct being incomplete,' 'cessation' (*śīla*) is precisely the precepts.

Regarding 'this alone constitutes the substance of the transgression,' within the preceding section on the intent of the regulation, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* states: 'In order to distinguish speech, so that one may understand it clearly.'"
Therefore, because it is not currently distinguished, this constitutes an error.
As for the statement that "the benefit of nourishing the spirit is called *pada* and *vyañjana*," I have now examined the Sanskrit original, which reads *pradeśana*;

this is translated here as "text" (*wen*). The old translation of "taste" (*wei*) has lost its correct meaning. In the Western lands [India], one calls it "text" (*wen*), "fan" (*xian*), "salt" (*yan*), or "man and woman" (*nan-nü*).

The *indriya* (faculties) are also called *vyañjana* (manifestations). This refers to the syllable (*vyañjana*) as the basis, which is able to manifest the name (*nāman*) and the phrase (*pada*). A fan is able to manifest [the movement of] wind; salt manifests the flavor of food;
the two faculties of male and female manifest the distinction between their retributions (*vipāka*). Because the meanings are confused, this is a mistranslation.
Since the translation itself contains errors, the commentary (*śāstra*) that explains it is likewise incorrect.
To claim that the name "body" (*tǐ*) refers to the principle of completeness (*yuán*) and thus constitutes the meaning of the term "syllable" (*zì*) is also incorrect. Now, examining this in detail:
the *Lü* (Vinaya) briefly cites the five syllables from the "Chapter on All-Talk" (*Xītán zhāng*). However, these forty-nine syllables of the "Chapter on All-Talk" are the root of all syllables.
For the most part, these do not yet constitute "meaning" (*artha*). It is only when they combine in pairs or groups of three that they come to have a cause [of expression];
therefore, one should not say that the essence of the *vyañjana* (phoneme) is complete [in isolation]. Furthermore, in the *Siddhaṃ* script, there are fourteen phonemes (or twelve, or sixteen):
*ka*, *a*, *i* (pronounced with an oblique tone), *ī* (pronounced with a level tone), *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *lṛ*, *l̥*, *o*, *aṃ*, *aḥ*. (These are the fourteen above.)

*Śabda* (Sound). These consist of pairs of two. Within the first eight characters, arranged in pairs, each preceding character is a short vowel and each succeeding one is a long vowel. Within the subsequent six characters, arranged in pairs, each preceding character is a long vowel and each succeeding one is a short vowel.
Next, there are twenty-five characters in groups of five, which are called *pratibhāṣa* (Corresponding Sounds). The first group of five is:

*ka* (pronounced as in "ku-ǝ"), *kha*, *ga* (a sound produced between the root of the tongue and being light), *gha* (a sound produced from the throat and being heavy), and *ṅa* (pronounced as in "yu-ǝ," still to be called with a rising tone). The second group of five is: *ca*, *cha*, *ja* (the tip of the tongue [producing the sound]).

*Śa* (a sound from the throat, light); *ṣa* (a sound from the throat, heavy). Third group of five: *ṭa-ṭha* (the *ṭa* is a sound from the upper palate, light; the *ṭha* is a sound from the throat, heavy);
*ṇa* (pronounced with an elevated tone). Fourth group of five: *ta-tha-da* (the *ta* is a sound from the tip of the tongue, light;

the *tha* is a sound from the throat, heavy); *na* (pronounced with an elevated tone). Fifth group of five: *pa-pha-bha* (the *pa* is a sound from the lips, light; the *pha* is a sound from the throat, heavy); *ma*.
(Pronounced with the third tone). Next are eight characters called *chāoshēng* (transcending sounds):

*yà* (lǐjiǎ fǎn), *luó* (lǔwǒ fǎn), *pó* (púwǒ fǎn), *shē* (third tone), *shā* (third tone), *sāhā* (these two combined as one character), *qǐchā* (chǔhè fǎn; these should still be pronounced together as one character).

Now, in the Vinaya texts: *hē* is the first of the fourteen vowels; *luó* is the third character among the *chāoshēng*; *pó* is the fifth character among the *bǐshēng*; *zhē* is the [first] among the *bǐshēng*... [text continues].
(The second five is the middle character. "Na" (is the fourth five, the middle character). Take, for example, the character *pa*.
Compared to the preceding fourteen sounds, excluding the sounds *li* and *li*, it forms twelve characters when compared to the remaining twelve. That is to say, one should state:

*po*, *pa*, *bi* (pronounced *bǔ yǐ*), *bi* (*bǔ yí*), *bǔ*, *bǔ*, *bì* (*bǔ mǐ*), *pèi* (*bǔ dú*), *pù*, *bǎo*, *fàn* (*bù hàn*), *bó* (*bái yú*). [The remaining twenty-four characters each form twelve; follow this principle.]

It should be understood that these characters have been temporarily replaced by Chinese equivalents; in reality, they are difficult to equate. As for the term *siddham*, this is translated here as "accomplishment" (*chengjiu*).

Formerly, at Dafuxian Monastery in Luoyang, I personally met Tripitaka Master Jingtai and examined the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Caturvarga-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) contained within this *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

In that Sanskrit text, it reads *pada* (translated here as "phrase"; the current Vinaya text says "phrase-meaning") and *anupada* (translated here as "following phrase"; the current Vinaya text says "non-phrase-meaning").

*Padasaṃhitā* (here translated as "text"; the current Vinaya text calls it "phrase-flavor"); *anupadasaṃhitā* (here translated as "following the text"; the current Vinaya calls it "non-phrase-flavor"); *vyañjana* (here translated as "syllable";

the current Vinaya text calls it "syllable-meaning"); *anuvyañjana* (here translated as "following the syllable"; the current Vinaya calls it "non-syllable-meaning"). The meaning here is as follows: reciting with a uniform tone is called a "phrase" (*pada*);
chanting by following the continuous flow of the sound is called "following the phrase" (*anupada*).
The same principle applies to syllables (*vyañjana*), which should be understood accordingly; the underlying meaning of the Vinaya is the same.
In the sense of the Sūtras and Śāstras, that which fully and perfectly reveals the meaning is called a phrase (*pada*). Therefore, the Vinaya says, "Commit no evil," and so forth.

Furthermore, there must also be names (*nāman*) and designations corresponding to names (*anuvyañjana*) that express the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena; these are termed "names. For example, the term "all conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra*) refers to that which has the nature of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, by stating "impermanent," it is revealed that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are certainly not eternal. Since this also distinguishes them from the eternal, it manifests the meaning of differentiation.
When the meaning is thus fully complete, it is called a "phrase" (*pada*). Therefore, the treatise states: "Names (*nāman*) express intrinsic nature; phrases express differentiation.

"Phonemes" (*vyañjana*) are simply the syllables (*akṣara*), serving as the basis for these two. Question: Why does [the treatise] not mention "names and what follows names"? Answer: Because of the phrase.

Because it is included within the middle [category], the Vinaya does not mention it. Question: Since a *vyañjana* (phrase) is identical to a *akṣara* (syllable), there should be no distinction between them.
Answer: Although a *vyañjana* is indeed a *akṣara*, their meanings differ. That which manifests a name (*nāman*) or a phrase (*pada*) is designated as a *vyañjana*.

Therefore, when this Vinaya says "the eye is impermanent," it is clarifying the substance of the *vyañjana*, which is capable of manifesting the name "eye" and the term "impermanence" and so forth. If one discusses the *akṣara*, in the West...
This is explained as being without any variation in its circulation. For instance, the letter *A* does not change at all within any speech, whether virtuous, non-virtuous, or otherwise;
therefore, it is called a "letter" (the primary meaning, with a secondary discussion following the commentary).
Regarding the passage beginning with "If the śrāvakas and devas, having been empowered by the Buddha's power... (the thirteenth text):
as for the phrase "writing and bestowing," it means writing with the hand while reciting aloud; it does not mean merely writing and handing over.
Therefore, there are distinctions such as whether the written words are clear or unclear, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "opening the text to chant together," the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Duo-lun), fascicle six, states: "If two people both possess mastery of the scriptures and chant together, there is no offense;
however, they must not chant in unison (*saṃbhāṣya*). If a bhikṣu has no one from whom to receive the recitation, he may even receive the dharma from a śrāmaṇerī;
he need only seek out someone who upholds the precepts well and possesses great virtue to serve as a companion and witness. He may also receive it from a layperson (*avadātavasana*)."

The Dharma may be received; however, one must not address the recipient as "Ācārya. In this manner, one may successively receive the Dharma from others, provided that one carefully observes the situation so as not to lose one's dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
The *Cīvaravastu*, chapter thirteen, states: "When a verse is being recited within the Saṃgha, one must not recite the same verse as another;
rather, one may simultaneously recite other verses individually."

Regarding the passage in the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* on the "Coarse Precepts" concerning the group of six monks speaking with laypeople and others: according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, chapter fourteen, there was a householder who invited many bhikṣus.
There was an elder who, while performing the *mānatva* penance, sat in the lower row. A laywoman said, "Venerable sir, you were previously seated at the head;
why do you now sit here in the middle? Upāli said, "Your preceptor’s childhood games have not yet been abandoned.
Upon hearing this, she thought, "My preceptor must still be violating minor rules of discipline (*duṣkṛta*)."
He sat down below [the monk], seized a ball of rice, threw it on the ground, and departed, saying: "Venerable sir, take this food.
Having spoken, he entered his room, closed one leaf of the door, and recited this verse: "Long has he been ordained, And long has he practiced the holy life (brahmacarya).
Yet he does not cease from childish play; How can he accept the offerings of the faithful?"

Regarding the wording of the formal proclamation and subsequent allowance: if one does not know whether an act is grave or not grave, and internally does not know what offense has been committed, one simply tells a layperson, "So-and-so has committed an offense. Only later does one realize that he has actually committed a grave offense.

Causing blood to flow and causing a schism in the Saṃgha—these are the offenses committed by Devadatta. Since Śāriputra was already fearful [of this], it is clear that these are subsumed under grave offenses (sthūlātyaya).

As for the discrepancy with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, that text lacks an explicit statement; however, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 51, states: "If one slanders [another] so as to cause blood to flow..."

Causing a schism in the Saṃgha constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense in all cases. According to that text, since the two types of ānantarya offenses are distinct from the pārājika offense of slandering [the Dharma], it is known that the three other ānantaryas are not subsumed under the category of "grave offenses" (sthūlātyaya).

Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun), fascicle six, states: "If one speaks of shedding blood, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, or [other such acts], one incurs a duṣkṛta offense" (this is the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* commenting on the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*).
Furthermore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, fascicle six, states: "A person who has been subjected to a formal act (*karman*) by the Saṃgha..."

One must follow the instructions of the Saṃgha. If one is instructed to speak to person A, yet speaks to person B; or if one is instructed to speak of this offense, yet speaks of that offense—in all such cases, it is a *pāyattika*.

Regarding the statement that "if the words are clear, it is a *pāyattika*," the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* says: "This is for the sake of great protection of the Buddha-dharma. If one speaks to a layperson...
Regarding the offense of a bhikṣu: if one lacks faith and reverence toward the Buddha-dharma, it would be better to destroy stūpas and images than to speak of a bhikṣu’s faults to others.
To speak of them is to destroy the Dharma-body. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fascicle 52, states: [text follows].

If one is within the boundary (*sīmā*) and speaks to someone outside the boundary (or vice versa), one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding the case where one is within the boundary, the explanatory text states:
"If a layperson has heard [of the offense] first," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (T. 1425) XIV states:

"If someone asks, 'That bhikṣu has committed an offense of sexual misconduct or drinking alcohol,' the bhikṣu should ask him, 'Where did you hear this? He should answer, 'I heard it from such-and-such a place.'"

[Question: "Have you heard it? [Answer: A bhikṣu should answer, "I have also heard it in such a place. If he has not yet been formally interrogated (*karmavācanā*), he should answer, "You shall know this for yourself later. [Topic:
The Precepts of Attaining the Path.
Regarding the term "the treatise": it refers to the sixth fascicle of the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

As for "supernormal powers (abhijñā) and noble capacities," this is stated provisionally from the perspective of the noble ones (*ārya*); in reality, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) may also attain the five supernormal powers (excluding the power of the exhaustion of outflows).
Because there are variations in the degree of their excellence or subtlety, [the rule] must be established for the Saṃgha; however, if they are subtle, they may not be discussed.
The phrase "skillful reflection" refers to the aforementioned "right mindfulness. "Right concentration" is equivalent to that "right reception" (samāpatti).
(Detailed explanations for both are as provided in the section on the grave precept against false claims of attainment.)

Regarding "those who are not of the same class and do not share the same intent": in this text, the offense of not sharing the same intent is explained first, followed by the explanation of the faculties and powers.

To speak [of these] to one who has not yet received full ordination is termed "not being of the same class. Furthermore, it is interpreted that "not being of the same class" is precisely "not sharing the same intent.

This is because the object of not sharing the same intent is not of the same category as the object for committing a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). This may be verified by examining the meaning of the commentary on the precept against false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).
This is understood. Hereafter, the interpretation is superior.

Regarding the statement in the opening text that "one who has overweening pride (adhimāna) does not commit an offense": if this were so, then even one who truthfully declares what they have actually attained would still incur a *thullaccaya* offense;

how then could one who speaks with pride to deceive others be without offense? The answer is: it was prescribed that one must speak the truth in order to protect others, as will be explained in the text below.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "Stop, stop; there is no need to speak further. These bhikṣus will not believe your words, and because of their lack of faith, they will incur much sin and suffering.
Let these bhikṣus not give rise to disbelief, lest they suffer for a long night. If you were to speak of pride,"

Since these are not real, there is no offense in not believing them. However, because the mind is actually free from the fault of untruth, this allows both [cases] to be opened as non-offenses (according to the cited passage above, this refers to the *nidāna* concerning Maudgalyāyana’s disagreement).

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-saṃgraha-śāstra* (Shuōfǎjì duōlùn), fascicle 6, states: "The five phrases refer to the five kinds of phrases: 'the aggregate of form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent'—the six phrases may be understood accordingly.
The *Jiàn lùn* (Treatise on Views), fascicle 15, states: "One sentence of the sūtra text and five sentences of the commentary (yìshù) together constitute six sentences."
There is no offense. It is generally said that if there is a wise man, or if the species [of being] is different, it is not permitted in any case.
The man must be a layperson (*avadātavasana*); no monastic may do so, for the circumstances are identical.

*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Chapter 13: "Whether seven years old or older than seven; even if over seven years old, if one does not understand the meaning of speech, they are still called 'unwise'. (It is also said: "The community..."
If there are many women who wish to hear the Dharma, he may preach six phrases to each of them individually. He should say to the first woman, "I shall preach six phrases for you.
Having finished speaking, he should again say to the second woman, "I shall preach six phrases for you. In this manner, it is not an offense even if he does so for a great multitude.
Once the bhikṣu has departed, he should bid the women farewell as they escort him out; if he offers a blessing, he should say, "May it be so for you..."

If one reaches the end of suffering, one incurs a *pāyattika*. If one says, "May you be free from illness, at ease, and without fault," and then goes to another house, and the woman who was there first arrives later, if the bhikṣu sees her and says, "Listen," he incurs a *pāyattika*.
Even if he sees her but does not speak with her, yet directly preaches the Dharma to the other women, although the woman who arrived first hears it, she incurs no offense.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) states that in this case, one incurs an offense against the woman who was there first. If...
If one does not know that a woman is inside, there is no offense. (It is also said: For those who recite the sutras, every such instance constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense.

Regarding the two precepts concerning digging the earth—namely, first, digging the earth, and second, killing grass—the treatise states: "The third [offense] is added as 'not being permitted to carry [loads]."
(Carrying wool is as already cited in the section on the categories of meaning above).
"Either two or three" refers to: first, having been [carried] for four months as it was originally; second, having been soaked by rain as it was originally;
and furthermore, third, having been carried for four months, second, having been rained upon, and third, being as it was originally.
Regarding the phrase "not asking about covered or exposed [ground]," this is not so. The opening text states: "If one removes soil from within a room, there is no offense.

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, chapter ten, within the precept concerning the possession of precious objects, when gold and silver are being handled: if it is native soil, one instructs a lay attendant (*karmadāna*) to know [the procedure];
if it is dead soil in a covered place, one may dig it up oneself or have a junior bhikṣu dig it up. (The commentator says: Therefore, we know that this refers to dry ground beneath a roof.
Digging [the earth] does not constitute an offense. If it is beneath a new building and the ground is still damp and moist, one must not dig there.

Regarding the phrase "burning fire" (*aggi-uddharaṇa*) mentioned in the text, the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle 15, states: "If the ground has been burned, it is no longer 'true earth' (meaning that which has already been burnt and ruined does not constitute an offense).
It is further stated: if one’s hand is burned by fire, throwing [an object] onto the ground does not constitute an offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 19, states: "If [it is] rained upon..."

[Regarding] the ground: it should be leveled like the footprint of a mosquito. (Furthermore, it is said: If one wishes to demolish a wall, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) remove the mud first;

afterwards, one may personally dismantle it down to the foundation. If the wall has not been plastered, or if it has already been rained upon, one should have the *kappiya-kāraka* remove two or three courses [of bricks].
If one digs from the surface down to the ground level, once the dead earth has been soaked by the rain, one must not take it oneself; one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) take it.
One may take it oneself only after reaching the limit of what was saturated by the rain; there is no offense in this. After new rain, one must not draw water from a well oneself.

If a *kappiya-kāraka* is too small [in stature] or incapable, one should first lower the *kappiya-kāraka* into the well to stir it up and make it turbid, and only then draw the water oneself (the same applies to pond water). If the mud is...

After rain has fallen, one must not take [water] oneself. Regarding water used for the needs of defecation and urination: if one uses it by rubbing the ground with the hands, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a jar or vessel containing water is in an open space—or if various objects are on covered ground—after the rain has ceased, a bhikṣu must not take them himself.
The conditions for violating the precept against destroying living beings are also the same as those for the preceding precept; they are identical except for the change in name.
Regarding the brief explanation of the four phrases at the beginning, it means that the fifth phrase is explained in detail within the subsequent section.

Regarding "ghost villages" (*bhūtagrāma*): according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, these include both ghosts and animals, and are collectively termed "ghosts. The tenth fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"A ghost village refers to the dwelling places of sentient beings born from grass and trees. These sentient beings are:
tree spirits, spring spirits, river spirits, house spirits, crossroads spirits, market spirits, highway spirits, mosquitoes, gadflies, dung beetles, butterflies, and hemp-eating insects."
Scorpions, insects, and moths—these sentient beings take grasses and trees as their dwellings, and likewise as their villages, hamlets, cities, and towns.
According to the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Views), Chapter Fifteen, regarding *uśīra* (the fragrance of the root): the commentary states that this is an error for "scallion" (*xīng cài*).

The *Jian* [lun] says that the two types of trees mentioned here, namely *tṛṇa* and *jāti*, are found only in Jiaozhou and Guangzhou; they are not seen in other regions. The *Jian* [lun] further mentions *sumana*.
The fragrance of its flowers is similar to that of the *mallikā*. As for the *mallikā*, it is found in Guangzhou; its flowers grow by climbing.

Regarding the phrase "whether touching the ground or rising above it," this means that because the species of the plant possesses the nature of growth, even if the roots are detached from the ground, destroying it constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense.
This is like grains and the like; how could they possibly depend upon having roots?

Regarding the "provisional designation of a life-principle" (*jīva-prajñapti*): according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, within the real dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one provisionally establishes the name "sentient being.

This sentient being has a name but lacks an intrinsic essence; this is called a "provisional designation. Within this, the essence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is likewise provisional, for apart from the aggregates, it has no essence.
Regarding the phrase "to look at this" and "to know this," the sixth chapter of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu requires anything, he says to the *kappiya-kāraka* (the attendant):
'You know this. If [the attendant] does not understand, he speaks again, saying: 'You look at this. If [the attendant] still does not understand, he speaks again, saying: 'I require this.
If [the attendant] still does not understand, he speaks again, saying: 'Give this to me.'"
Regarding the fourteen types of seeds in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: they are like the seventeen kinds of grain; these must be purified by fire or by removing the husks.
For example, in the country of Kukkutavatī, when a heap of grain was gathered for fear that non-humans (*amanuṣya*) might steal it, one would mark it by circling it with ash;
this constituted purification. Likewise, when Māmadattika had unrefined grain in his granary and feared that young bhikṣus who did not know the Dharma [would take it], he...

From the time the *kappiya-kāraka* (lay attendant) performs the fire-purification (*aggiparidhamma*) until the food is consumed, the bhikṣu may always say, "Pound it," and there is no offense. (It is also said:

Regarding seeds that have a hard shell, such as those of the jujube (*āmalaka*), one should remove the kernel by scratching it with the fingernails after performing the purification; if one wishes to eat the kernel along with the fruit, it must be purified by fire.
The sixth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (*Shan-chi lü pi-po-sha*) states the same.
Regarding the three remaining verbal transgressions under the precept against false speech: first, lying; second, slander; and third, divisive speech.
Regarding the bodily karma of frivolous speech termed "provocative contact," the Venerable One said: "This is not so."
Regarding "causing provocation as described in the text": this refers to not coming when summoned, up to and including speaking when one should not speak.

Thus, we know that causing provocation also extends to vocal karma. Therefore, it should be explained as follows: asking a question and answering with something else is called *anuvāda* (irrelevant speech). *Anuvāda* is exclusively vocal karma.
Consequently, violating the rules of decorum is termed "causing provocation" (*upaghātana*); thus, causing provocation extends to both types of karma (vocal and physical).

Regarding the rule that if one utters irrelevant speech before the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been made, it constitutes a transgression for the practitioner; thus, the Vinaya establishes this as an offense.

However, there is also a principle of leniency if it serves a beneficial purpose. Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 14, states: "If someone asks a bhikṣu, 'From where have you come?
and he answers, 'I come from the past,' or asks, 'Where are you going? and he answers, 'I am going to the future'... [The text continues with further examples.]
"Sleeping. "Sleeping on eight pieces of wood" (the bed has four wooden planks; together with the four legs, they make eight). "Where do you eat? He replies, "I eat with five fingers.
One who answers incorrectly in this manner commits a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline).

If bandits enter the monastery and ask the bhikṣus, "Show us the property of the Saṃgha," the bhikṣus must not show it, nor must they speak falsely. They should instead point out the rooms, beds, seats, and so forth. If they are asked...
Regarding "objects belonging to the stūpa": one should point out the various vessels and implements used for offerings at the side of the stūpa.

If [the thief] says, "Show me the clean kitchen," one should point out the cauldrons, pots, basins, and other such utensils. If a domestic animal from a butcher's house should escape, one must not reveal its location;

rather, one should say, "Look at my fingernails, look at my fingernails" (in the local dialect, this is pronounced similarly to "I do not see"). If a prisoner escapes from an *āraṇyaka* (forest-dweller) settlement and questions a bhikṣu... [as above].
The answer regarding animals is as follows: If one answers differently when questioned within the Saṃgha, it is a *pāyattika* offense;

before many people, or in the presence of elders such as the *upādhyāya*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Now, the Tripiṭaka-master says: Suppose a hunter, pursuing a deer, enters a monastery and asks a *bhikṣu*, "Have you seen [the deer]?
One should employ a skillful means, contemplating emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or examining one's fingernails, and reply to the hunter, "Nava-paśyāmi" (I have not seen it). Or...
It is said: *nākha-paśyāmi*. Here, *nava* refers to space; *paśya* means "to see"; and *mi* means "I.
Thus, it signifies "I see space. Furthermore, *nākha* means "nail" (or "claw"), while *paśya* is the same as before.
Although the words are thus, their meaning differs. For instance, although *nava* refers to the great void, [the compound implies a different sense].

It also expresses the meaning of "non-existence. Based on this, it is also a case of the view of self (ātman-dṛṣṭi) being meaningless. Since he actually saw the deer, one cannot say it did not exist; yet, by looking toward the vast void, he indirectly conveys the meaning of non-existence, wishing to cause the hunter to return with a mistaken understanding. Furthermore, as for *nirgha*: [The text continues: ...it is like a person who, having been struck by a poisoned arrow, is told by a physician that there is no poison in the wound. Because of this, the patient develops a false notion, thinking, "There is truly no poison," and thus does not take the antidote. Consequently, his life comes to an end. This is called the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*). It is also like a person who, having seen a deer, says, "There is no deer here"; because of this, he develops a false notion, thinking, "There truly is no deer," and consequently does not pursue it. This is called the view of non-existence. It is also like a person who, having seen a snake, says, "There is no snake here"; because of this, he develops a false notion, thinking, "There truly is no snake," and consequently does not kill it. This is called the view of non-existence. It is also like a person who, having seen a thief, says, "There is no thief here"; because of this, he develops a false notion, thinking, "There truly is no thief," and consequently does not seize him. This is called the view of non-existence. It is also like a person who, having seen a fire, says, "There is no fire here"; because of this, he develops a false notion, thinking, "There truly is no fire," and consequently does not extinguish it. This is called the view of non-existence. It is also like a person who, having seen a disease, says, "There is no disease here"; because of this, he develops a false notion, thinking, "There truly is no disease," and consequently does not seek treatment. This is called the view of non-existence. It is also like a person who, having seen a weapon, says, "There is no weapon here"; because of this, he develops a false notion, thinking, "There truly is no weapon," and consequently does not avoid it. This is called the view of non-existence. It is also like a person who, having seen a precipice, says, "There is no precipice here"; because of this, he develops a false notion, thinking, "There truly is no precipice," and consequently does not retreat. This is called the view of non-existence. It is also like a person who, having seen a river, says, "There is no river here"; because of this, he develops a false notion, thinking, "There truly is no river," and consequently does not cross it. This is called the view of non-existence. It is also like a person who, having seen a pit, says, "There is no pit here"; because of this, he develops a false notion, thinking, "There truly is no pit," and consequently does not avoid it. This is called the view of non-existence. It is also like a person who, having seen a thorn, says, "There is no thorn here"; because of this, he develops a false notion, thinking, "There truly is no thorn," and consequently does not remove it. This is called the view of non-existence.
