Although the term "nail" (nakha) is also included among those that lack meaning [in this context], the other explanations are the same as before.
Regarding the phrase "the Elder calls," it must be for a matter that is in accordance with the Dharma. [This concludes] the precept on reviling out of resentment.
Regarding "face-to-face reproach" (*mianxian*): the *Shichang* (Exposition of Characteristics) states that it refers to being seen face-to-face and subjected to derision.
○ Regarding "spreading out [the bedding] in the open":
the *Ji* (Sects) volume 14 states, "abandoning [it] at twenty-five *zhū* [is the rule]" (this does not mean departing from the gate for twenty-five *zhū*).
Regarding the phrase "resembling [the category of] monastic property": this refers to property that has not yet been relinquished to the Saṃgha (the gist of the *Shu* [Commentary] is:

this is property entrusted to the Saṃgha but not yet definitively assigned to it; one does not incur a minor offense for failing to report it. This is the analysis of the ancient masters. As for the third case, when the property arrives, it is similar to the first type of property. Examining the meaning of the text now: a person gives such-and-such an amount, and if it is insufficient, more is added).

Regarding "for the sake of the Saṃgha": it is prepared for the Saṃgha, but not yet relinquished to the Saṃgha (examining the meaning of the text now: such-and-such property is relinquished, but it is not yet determined to which specific group it belongs. The gist of the *Shu* is likewise [it belongs to the Saṃgha]). "That which has already entered the Saṃgha" means it has already been assigned.
"Given to the Saṃgha" (meaning: having used such an amount of goods, they have already entered this assembly; the intent of the commentary is likewise). An ancient version of the Vinaya text states:

"Property of the Saṃgha" refers to that which has already been given to the Saṃgha (this corresponds to the third category of objects mentioned above). "For the sake of the Saṃgha" refers to that which has not yet been given to the Saṃgha (this corresponds to the second category).

"Belonging to the Saṃgha" refers to that which has already entered the Saṃgha, yet has not yet been relinquished (this corresponds to the first category). Now, upon careful examination, it appears the ancient masters relied upon this latter version.

Therefore, this differs from the Master of the Commentary (Suzhu) by exactly one point. The Master of the Commentary was unaware that such a version of the Vinaya existed; thus, he stated, "it arrives at what seems [to be correct].
However, upon examining the version of the Vinaya relied upon by the ancient masters, it was precisely the original translation of the Vinaya by the Tripitaka Master Buddhayaśas of Ayuwang Monastery.
Later, the Śramaṇa Zhi Falin of the Jin dynasty returned from the Western Regions and subsequently re-examined and verified it once more.
It was revised from time to time; this is the original text upon which the commentator relied.
○ Regarding the statement, "If I possess [something], it belongs to him," because we are close, what I possess is what he possesses. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Chapter Eleven.

It is said: If a bhikṣu, for the purpose of annoying others, closes a door or opens a door, closes a window or opens a window, lights a fire or extinguishes a fire, lights a lamp or extinguishes a lamp;

or if he performs recitations, incantations, blessings, reading of scriptures, preaching the Dharma, or posing difficult questions—whichever such acts they find unpleasant—he commits one *pāyattika* offense for each.

Regarding "driving out [a monk] from the spring or winter quarters": since these quarters are not specifically allotted [to individuals], there is a sense of common ownership; therefore, the offense for driving him out is grave, and one commits a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If, however, it is during the summer and the quarters have been allotted as one's own property, the gravity of the intention when driving him out is light, and one merely commits [the minor offense].

These are minor offenses (*dukkaṭa*). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi), there are fourteen: if one embraces a pillar, or seizes a door, or leans against a wall and pulls it away—each instance constitutes a *pāyattika*.

If one drives them away by shouting at them verbally, each time they move away upon hearing the words, it is a *pāyattika*. If a bhikṣu, out of anger, drives snakes or rats out of a dwelling, it is a transgression;
however, if he says, "These are useless things," and drives them out for that reason, there is no offense.

Regarding the rule on water containing insects, the explanation in the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) states that there is no offense for one who does not know [the presence of insects]. This refers specifically to cases where there is intentional action (*vijñapti*) but no perception (*saṃjñā*), which is a state of total fundamental ignorance.

According to the sixth fascicle of the *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya), even if one suspects the presence of insects, it constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). However, if one examines the water carefully and sees nothing, and it has been strained through a filter... [text continues]
It is obtained; there is no offense. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter eleven, regarding the six permutations of the perception of the object:

perceiving water with insects as having insects, acting while perceiving it as having insects when it actually has none, and perceiving it as having insects when one suspects it does (these three cases constitute a *pārājika* offense); two cases constitute a *duṣkṛta*; and one case is understood to be without offense.
As cited in the sixth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā*, and as stated again in the eighth [fascicle]: "Once, Śāriputra, with his pure divine eye, saw in the sky..."
Insects were as numerous as the sand by a riverbank or as the grains of millet in a vessel—boundless and immeasurable. Having seen this, [the monks] abstained from food for two or three days.
The Buddha commanded them to eat. Regarding the prohibition against water containing insects, it applies to what is visible to the physical eye and what is caught by a strainer;
it does not apply to what is seen by the divine eye. As for the method of using water: one should take a high-quality fine cloth, one cubit in length and breadth, and make a strainer.

[The Buddha] instructed: "Let a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts, is learned, has deep faith in the consequences of sin and merit, is composed and discerning, and possesses pure physical vision, be made to examine the water.
Having strained the water according to the Dharma, place it in a vessel sufficient for one day’s use.
On the following day, examine it again; if there are insects, one must strain it thoroughly once more. Place the water in a clean vessel and observe it closely toward the light."
If there are still insects, one should construct it with two layers. If there are still insects, one should construct it with three layers.
If there are still insects, one should not remain in this place; one must move away immediately. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Chapter 15.

When a builder requires water—whether from a pond, a river, or a well—he must strain it until a vessel is full; only when there are no insects may he use it. If there are still insects, he must [filter it] again.
One should strain the water and examine it closely. If there are still insects after three layers of straining, one should dig another well and observe it as before.
If there are still insects, one should abandon the current site and go elsewhere. Regarding the method of straining water:

one should set up three wooden stakes and tie the straining bag to them, placing a vessel beneath to catch the water. Water should always remain in the straining bag, which must be emptied back into the well frequently.
In the midst [of the water], insects arise through impermanence; they may have been absent before and now exist, or they may exist now and later cease to be.

For this reason, monks should examine it daily with mindfulness and use it only when no insects are present. The above is a discussion on the Vinaya text. Regarding the term "hóngjiǎn" (宏墎) in the subsequent section of this Vinaya:

It should be written as the character *héng* (墎). Regarding "horizontal" (*héng*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to the wooden crossbars of a gate. Guo [Puzi] says it means "vast and expansive.
It is a term for that which is broad and open on the outside; it signifies being grand and magnificent. The character *hóng* (宏) does not carry this meaning.
"Fifty are likewise" means that the aforementioned characteristics are for the most part identical. Master Jing (Jing Sanzang) said: "Every morning, one must necessarily observe the water.
As for the method of filtering water: in the Western Regions, fine white cotton cloth (*dukūla*) is used; in the Eastern Land (China), it is appropriate to use fine silk.
Its threads must be thin and even, with the warp and woof closely and evenly woven. One may either rinse it with rice-water or slightly boil it; raw silk [is not suitable]."
When insects pass through, one may verify this for oneself. One may take a piece of silk four feet in length from the Zhou dynasty as a measure.
Fold it in half at the waist and sew one side closed. Pull apart the two corners; at the tips of these two pulled-apart corners, attach a strap to each.
Place buttons on both sides. Stretch it open with a horizontal rod; this is the pattern for a *śarāva* (strainer). As for the method of sewing the strainer: use fine thread and backstitch. Both...
When drawing water with a ladle, strive to take it without holes so that insects do not escape. Hang a strainer between two pillars and place a basin beneath it to catch what falls from the strainer.
If you pour water from above, ensure the vessel enters the strainer; pour slowly and steadily.
If you do not do this, insects will fall with the water, dropping onto the ground or into the basin, which would harm them. When finished drawing the water, first use pure water...
Cleanse the bottom of the water jar thoroughly two or three times, rinsing it with water until all insects are removed;
only then may you place the jar in a clean location. While drawing water has not yet been completed, do not set the jar on the ground, for fear that insects might fall out onto the floor.
Thereupon, take the water already filtered and place it in a new lacquered vessel, setting it upright upon bricks; alternatively, one may construct a separate stand for viewing the water.

Cover the mouth with one's hand. After a long while, look into it (if one looks as if into a copper vessel, the insects are white and resemble the vessel; they cannot be seen). If insects are seen, pour them upside down into water.
Rinse the vessel used for observation with other pure water until the insects are completely cleared away. Furthermore, turn over the insect-strainer and rinse it thoroughly with water.
According to the Śāstras and Vinaya, one should strain [the water] two or three times. The Tripiṭaka Master further says: "If six or seven..."
The *candra* insect is even finer; it can pass straight through ten layers of raw silk. One who delights in protecting life should observe this and take measures to ensure its avoidance.
Once the water has been strained, one may turn the filter over. It is essential that two people each grasp a corner of the filter and turn it so that it enters the vessel containing the raw water.
Then, pour water thoroughly over the filter three times, and finally rinse the outside of the filter completely with clean water.
One must strive to ensure that all insects are removed. The vessel for releasing them should be made as a small water-jar with a mouth that opens straight out, shaped like a bucket.
Furthermore, a handle should be attached to the bottom; a long rope is tied to this handle, and a hook is fixed to its side. This jar is lowered into the well by means of the rope.

Once the net has been released from the hook, it is submerged two or three times, and only then is it drawn up. If one does not do so, the net will turn over upon the surface of the well, and it will certainly [fail].
[The bowl] is placed upon a *kaṣāya* (filtering cloth). Even if one reaches the water, there is still fear that life will be harmed; therefore, one must maintain mindfulness.

At times, people make small round filters, barely large enough to hold one or two handfuls, made of coarse, thin silk. They do not actually strain the water at all, but merely hang them by the side of their bowls so that others may see them.

Having no intention to protect living beings, they incur transgressions day after day. Master and disciple pass this down from generation to generation, treating it as the transmission of the Dharma. This is truly [lamentable].

How lamentable! Truly it is enough to evoke sorrow and sighs. Regarding the water-viewing vessel: every person should possess one for themselves, and these vessels for releasing living beings must be present everywhere.

The water within the jar is sufficient to evoke sorrow and sighs; as for the water-viewing vessel, everyone should possess one for themselves, and these vessels for releasing living beings must be present everywhere.
The water within the jar should be inspected again after the night has passed (having first filtered it through the night, all subsequent cases should follow this rule).
Regarding the conditions for concealing a violation of the precepts, if one causes another person to conceal it, the precept may be concealed by oneself, yet it remains an offense.

As for the phrase "the house collapsed immediately," according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun), fascicle 7, when Channa was building a dwelling, it collapsed on that very same day. He then built another.

This great hall cost three hundred thousand coins; its construction was of immense scale. Although the monks preached the Dharma for the sake of the donor, the hall collapsed, yet his merit was fully accomplished.
Even before the hall had fallen into ruin, the Buddha had already arrived within it and made use of it.
The Buddha is the unsurpassed field of merit; since the Buddha has utilized it, the resulting merit is profound and vast, beyond measure.
It is further said: When a room is first completed, if there is a newly ordained bhikṣu of pure preceptual virtue who enters this room, the merit of the gift is fulfilled.

Even if one were to construct hundreds of millions of various types of rooms and pavilions, if there is a bhikṣu of pure precepts who uses them for even a brief moment, the grace of the gift is fulfilled.
Why is this? Because the Buddha practiced for immeasurable kalpas to achieve the Way; it is only now that he has realized his original nature.
The Prātimokṣa is bestowed upon sentient beings. The Prātimokṣa is that which turns one's back on the mundane world and faces toward the gate of Nirvāṇa.
Since ordinary dwellings and such things belong to the worldly dharmas, once a monk of pure precepts has even temporarily made use of them, the donor’s act of giving has fulfilled its purpose.
The Tripiṭaka Master now says: "This refers to the construction of a monastery, not a large dwelling. Examining this closely, it concerns different schools.

Regarding the precept on not appointing [a monk] to instruct nuns, if one possesses even a small amount of virtuous conduct, the Venerable One says: "Even if one lacks virtue, it is reckoned that one must necessarily commit [the offense]. (From the *Upāli-vinaya*, Chapter 5).

It is said: (1) if one fully upholds the Prātimokṣa; (2) if one is widely learned; (3) if one is eloquent, possesses a compassionate mind, and explains things with perfect clarity so that listeners may attain understanding;

(4) if one has committed a grave offense despite not having left the household life for the sake of the Buddha; and (5) if one has twenty years of seniority, or has exceeded twenty years of seniority.
"First, violating the teaching of the Eight Respectful Precepts; second, violating the original resolve of mind when receiving the precepts.

Regarding the distinction between these two cases—granting [the precepts] according to conduct versus according to formal reception—the reason for doing so is to clarify that the teacher of the teachings and the teacher of the precepts are difficult to encounter. The intent of this question is to state why it is necessary to cite [these points].
This passage provides the answer.

As stated in the chapter, these are the verses concerning Bandhula’s attainment of the Way. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle 16, states: "Bandhula means 'born by the roadside' in the Han language.
His mother was originally the daughter of a wealthy elder; she had an illicit affair with a slave and fled to another country."
Thereafter, she conceived. As her time of delivery approached, she remembered her mother and wished to return home.
Having traveled halfway, she gave birth to a son; feeling ashamed before her parents, she returned home. Later, she conceived again and, as before, gave birth to a son halfway home and returned.
Subsequently, she sent the two boys to be raised by their maternal grandparents. When the maternal grandparents were nearing death, they entrusted their entire household estate to them.
He entrusted his two sons to him. Later, upon hearing the Dharma, the elder brother left the household life and attained arhatship.
After a long time, the younger brother thought to himself: "My elder brother abandoned his family estate for me; it was no different than someone vomiting up what they had eaten.

He immediately went to where his brother was and requested to leave the household life. His brother ordained him and taught him a single verse, yet he could not master it after four months. His brother, perceiving his dull faculties, then...
He was pulled by his *kāṣāya* robe and led outside the gate. Paṇḍaka wept and did not wish to return home. The Buddha, observing that he was ready for deliverance, comforted his mind;
seeing that he would attain the Way, he spoke a verse on entering *śamatha*. Upon hearing this verse, Paṇḍaka immediately attained the state of an Arhat.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 180, states: In Śrāvastī there was a Brahmin whose wife repeatedly gave birth to sons, but as soon as they were born...

After his death, a son was born; he was abandoned on the great road (*mahāpatha*), yet after a long time he did not die, and thus he was named Mahāpatha. Later, another son was born; he was abandoned on the small road (*kṣudrapatha*).
The Venerable Mahāpatha possessed sharp faculties and was of the insight-type (*dṛṣṭicarita*); he left the household life and attained the Way.

The Venerable Kṣudrapatha possessed dull faculties and was of the craving-type (*tṛṣṇācarita*). Not long thereafter, his parents passed away and his wealth and treasures were lost. Mahāpatha felt compassion for him...
He ordained him as a monk and bestowed upon him a single verse: "Commit no evil with body, speech, or mind; abandon worldly desires and maintain right mindfulness.
Thus one shall not experience suffering or what is meaningless. During the four months of the rainy season, he practiced and recited this diligently.

Cowherds and shepherds on the road heard him and mastered the recitation. He himself, however, had not yet attained it. When the four months of the rains had passed, monks were [gathering] everywhere.

Tṛṇa came to pay his respects to the World-Honored One. Every morning at dawn, novice bhikṣus would go to their *upādhyāya* or *ācārya* to receive the texts and inquire about the meanings they had forgotten.
Kṣullaka, imitating them, was about to leave his room when his elder brother asked him where he was going.
He replied, "I wish to go to my *upādhyāya* to receive the texts and inquire about the meanings I have neglected and forgotten."
His elder brother said, "I am your *upādhyāya*. Where else would you go? Furthermore, that narrow path is for those who are to be censured and expelled.
He seized him by the crown of his head, dragged him out of the room, and rebuked him, saying, "Fool!
During these four months, I have taught you a single verse; even cowherds and shepherds have mastered it thoroughly, yet you still have not attained it."
Now he said that he wished to go elsewhere. Cūḍapanthaka was expelled and stood weeping at the gate of the Jeta Grove.
When the Buddha entered from outside, he saw him and asked, "Poor Cūḍapanthaka, why are you weeping? He reported the preceding events in detail to the World-Honored One.
By means of his supernormal power, the Buddha removed all obstacles to his recitation of the gāthās; immediately, he was able to recite them. Furthermore—
He gave him a verse for the removal of impurities and said, "Today a bhikṣu will come from outside; you should wipe the dust from his straw sandals.
Kṣullaka respectfully agreed and carried out the instruction. When evening arrived, there was a bhikṣu whose straw sandals were extremely dirty.
Kṣullaka wiped them, and one became perfectly clean, but he could not make the other clean despite wiping it with great effort. Then—

He thought to himself: "If external objects, which are but temporary stains, cannot be purified even when they momentarily adhere to one, how much less so the internal stains of greed, hatred, and delusion that have defiled the mind throughout the long night?

By what means can these be purified? While he was reflecting thus, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) appeared before him, and he immediately attained the fruit of Arhatship.
[The interlocutor] asked: "By what cause did the Lesser Path (Kṣullaka-mārga) [attain this]?"
Thus being dull-witted, he replied to the Venerable Kṣudrapanthaka: "In the past, during the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa, within that Buddha's Dharma, I fully received and upheld his Tripiṭaka.
However, because my mind was shrouded by the defilement of stinginess regarding the Dharma, I never bestowed either the words or their meaning upon others.
Consequently, I forgot the principles; due to that karma, I have now obtained such a fruit of extreme dullness. There is [a sūtra] on this.
It is said that in the past, while residing in the city of Vārāṇasī, that venerable one was a pork butcher.

He bound the mouths of five hundred pigs, loaded them onto a boat, and transported them to the opposite shore. When they were disembarked from the boat, because their breath had been stifled, all the pigs had already died.

Due to the power of that karma, he was thus dull-witted. Some say that in a previous life, the Venerable One once blocked the entrance of a *gotra* animal’s cave, preventing it from escaping so that it died inside; because of that karma, he was thus dull-witted.
The half-verse above, which correctly elucidates concentration and wisdom, reveals the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya).
The one and a half verses below, which correctly elucidate that which is to be remedied, reveal the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
It may also be understood as "possessing" [them]. Since concentration and wisdom exist, they must necessarily arise from precepts.
"Relieving the affliction of greed" means removing the bonds of greed.
Because one eradicates the eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of ignorance and deluded mind, it is called "subduing the conceit of self. Among the ten underlying tendencies, the former...

The explanation of greed and hatred has already been concluded. Now, the remaining eight are clarified; these are the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, all afflictions (*kleśa*) are merely specific manifestations of delusion (*moha*); apart from delusion, they possess no separate essence.

Therefore, it is said that "the eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the mind of delusion" (whereas in the Sarvāstivāda and Mahāyāna traditions, the eight latent tendencies each have their own distinct essence). The intent of this commentary is that, for the time being, within the text...
Regarding the statement "subduing the conceit of self," in principle this actually entails the complete severance of the eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Although this was already addressed previously, if we now examine the meaning of the text, these two verses reveal the six realms of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa-dhātu*). The meaning of the six realms of transcendence has already been briefly set forth above in the section on great delusion.
Now, let us correlate them with the text: "entering into tranquility" refers to seeing the Dharma with joy; "attaining peace and happiness" refers to doing so with a signless mind (*animitta-citta*).

The element of renunciation is also [the immeasurable]. That which is "supremely blissful through the absence of ill-will" refers to the immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī*); it has the nature of wishing to bestow happiness upon sentient beings, and its essence is non-hatred (*adveṣa*).
It is the renunciation of the element of ill-will. That which is "non-harming toward sentient beings" refers to the immeasurable compassion (*karuṇā*);

it has the nature of extracting suffering from sentient beings, and its essence is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*). It is the renunciation of the element of harming. That which is "worldly joy free from desire" refers to the immeasurable sympathetic joy (*muditā*).

It brings consolation and joy to sentient beings. In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), it takes the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as its essential nature; in the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), it takes the absence of envy (*anīrṣyā*) as its essential nature.
Regarding the prosperity and flourishing of others in the world, one has no desire for them oneself, nor does one feel displeasure; thus, the mind remains peaceful and blissful.
Bringing joy and consolation to others is precisely the renunciation of the realm of non-delight. Renunciation of sensual desire refers to the immeasurable state of equanimity (*upekṣā*);
it has non-attachment as its intrinsic nature and serves as the antidote to craving for sense-desires; it is the renunciation of the desire realm. As for "subduing the conceit of 'I' and so forth":

The liberation door of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) can counteract the *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") regarding the four aggregates of non-perception; it is the renunciation of the realm of *asmimāna*.

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (14), six realms of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*) are established because the transcendence of the three realms is difficult to achieve. That is to say: the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) transcend the lower desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
the mind of the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) transcends all signs; and by severing *asmimāna*, one transcends the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This...

This clearly demonstrates that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms have been completely severed. Furthermore, the meaning of this verse is as follows: by means of the signless mind (*animitta-citta*), one first enters the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and severs the afflictions of the path of seeing;

next, by means of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), one severs the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); and finally, by means of the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*), one severs the afflictions of the higher realms.
(This interpretation is definitive; do not harbor further doubts.)
Regarding "planting the causes and conditions for śrāvakas," this refers to planting the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) within the three vehicles.
Regarding the "three categories of dharma-gates," this refers to three types of dharma-gate divisions: first, the fivefold dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*);

second, the eight great awakenings; and third, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). As for the "eight awakenings of a great person" (*aṣṭau mahāpuruṣavitarkāḥ*), these belong to a great person.

That which is awakened to is called the awakening of a great person (*mahāpuruṣa*). Therefore, in the fifty-ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, after the cessation of afflictions has been analyzed, it states that there are many kinds of characteristics, namely the eight awakenings of a great person and so forth:
1. Fewness of desires (*alpeccha*); 2. Contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*); 3. The essential departure (*naiṣkramya*), which refers to the essence of the Path, namely wisdom (*prajñā*);

4. The undertaking of exertion (*vīrya-karma*), which refers to diligence (*vīrya*); 5. Abandoning the manifold (*vyapakarṣa*), which refers to seclusion (*praviveka*). (There are two types of seclusion.)

First, physical seclusion: dwelling alone in a quiet and secluded place. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that one should stay at least three li away [from others]; the further one stays, the more it increases the joy of the two types of seclusion. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter 22, speaks of being free from unwholesome discursive thoughts (*akuśala-vitarka*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, chapter 72, speaks of being free from the five desires and the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).

The wholesome [states] of the six destinies include two types within them: first, momentary concentration; second, meditative absorption. One does not dwell in clamor, which means being free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
(Consult *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 59 and the first fascicle of the *Ārya-vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*).

Regarding these three virtues—the first [the precepts], the ninety [sub-parajikas], and the [remaining] dharmas—those whose substance is the matter of bodily and vocal karma are all, by virtue of being maintained through practice, characterized by the substance of bodily and vocal intimation and non-intimation;
therefore, they are called "karmic matter" (*karma-rūpa*).
Regarding the "other nine [precepts] for the benefit of others," Jueyun says: "This is also not fixed. If one has not heard much of the teachings, there may be faults such as failing to study;

yet once these faults are abandoned, that itself constitutes self-benefit. Now, examining this from the perspective of avoiding faults, they are subsumed within the 'possession of the precepts' (*śīla-saṃvara*);
therefore, the commentary’s explanation is correct."
"Experiencing the acquisition of the pure four great elements" refers to the acquisition of the four great elements that produce sound.
This fragment concerns the nature of retribution (*vipāka-dharma*) and serves to clarify the tenets of other schools. Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 111, states:
"The Vātsīputrīya and Vibhajyavāda schools maintain that sound is a fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*). However, according to the Sarvāstivāda, sound is not a fruit of maturation."
The clarification of the distinct meanings regarding "that which can be known" is as explained below in the section on defining terms.

The statement that the *Mātṛkā* says "one who well understands the Sūtras, etc. is an error; it should rather say that the fifteenth [chapter] of the *Śāstra* (Jian lun) states: "One who is learned (*bahuśruta*)..."
"One who understands one Āgama, or perhaps two Āgamas, is called a Dharma-master of great learning.
Question: Why does it not say that he "knows the Abhidharma"? Answer: It is best if he can know the Abhidharma;

however, for those of inferior faculties, knowing the Vinaya and the Sūtras also qualifies them to provide instruction. (The above is from the treatise. Question: Why is it said that his "voice and diction are fluent"? Answer:
Women are generally more attached to sounds before they listen to the Dharma.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "those who defile the three groups of nuns," this refers to the fifteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

As for those who have committed other offenses but have not yet repented and thus do not possess [the precepts] from the beginning, the intent is to clarify that although they are equally "defilers of nuns" because they have not repented, they are nonetheless distinct [from those who have already repented].

The first [point] is established. Regarding the meaning of "having already repented," there is indeed a distinction; therefore, the subsequent explanation states: "Thus, the ninth [consciousness] and so forth are required.
That "the youth was frivolous and impetuous" is also an interpretation from the *Śāstra*.
Regarding the "instructor," this refers to the eight rules that must not be transgressed.

As for the formal text below, it states: "If one goes and explains these eight rules that must not be transgressed when the Saṃgha has not appointed [an instructor], or on a day other than the designated instruction day, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Based on this, the author of the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "Explaining the eight respects constitutes a *dukkaṭa*. The Venerable One says: "I fear..."

This is not so. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* clearly states that one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense) for failing to receive instruction. Furthermore, the commentary (*vibhaṅga*) states: "One must not transgress the eight [rules] regarding instruction.

It explicitly says that even failing to observe the Eight Respectful Rules (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) constitutes a *pāyattika*. If this is the case, how should the following passage be interpreted? Answer:

Since it says, "Or, on a day other than the day of instruction, she goes," we know that the mention of the [Eight] Respects is intended to exclude the specific day [of instruction]. Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle seven...

It says: "The instructor shall preach the Eight Rules of Respect (aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ). If one who has not been appointed as an instructor of nuns [preaches], for every word [spoken], there is a *pāyattika* offense.

If so, why is it that preaching the Dharma is not also cited? It is because the day of the formal assembly (*saṃghakarma*) is improper. The answer in the text merely clarifies that citing the day of respect is improper; it clarifies that the day of the Dharma is improper.
Citing the Dharma results in a *pāyattika* offense, and citing respect also results in a *pāyattika* offense.
"That all these matters are appropriate" means that this reverent practice is appropriate for all circumstances, not merely restricted to the eight [rules].
In the seventh fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Bhadanta asks a nun, "Have you ever heard of the Eight Rules of Reverence? She replies, "I have heard of them.
He then says to her, "Sister, listen further" (and thereupon enumerates the eight).

Regarding the prohibition against receiving food or clothing first: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 30, states: "If someone invites a bhikṣuṇī to a meal, she should say, 'Please invite the most senior [monks] first.
If the person says, 'I have no intention of showing respect to them; I specifically wish to invite the bhikṣuṇīs,' she should say, 'In that case, I will not accept either.
If the person says, 'I have already invited them,' then she may accept. This applies even down to those who were invited first.

If one invites the Saṃgha for a single portion of food, and a bhikṣuṇī subsequently receives various kinds of excellent food, there is no offense. (Regarding invitations to build a room for a bhikṣuṇī:

if one first gives the Saṃgha even a small kitchen, and later receives a large room, there is no offense. If one invites them for a bed, and previously gave a small bed, but later receives an excellent bed and bedding, there is no offense. The detailed explanation follows the above.)
Regarding the *Liaolun* (Treatise on Clarification), its commentary states: "There are three meanings of 'venerable' (*zun*). First, the Buddha is the World-Honored One (*shizun*);

because this is what he has spoken, it is called the 'Venerable Dharma' (*zunfa*). Second, one respects the World-Honored One. Third, if one receives these eight dharmas, they can cause this person to become venerable.
The old translation "Eight Respects" (*bajing*) is not actually the name for this.

Regarding the phrase "within the two assemblies of monks," the *Míngliǎo shū* (Commentary on Clarification) states: Among the eight rules of respect (*gurudharma*), if one violates any one of them, it is termed "conforming to the assembly" (*sui-bu-zhu*).

One repents according to the gravity of the offense; this is called *mānatta*, which means to offer an apology to the community of monks. It is not a disciplinary rite for those who have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, because the term *mānatta* is used universally [for other offenses as well].
Regarding "questioning and challenging a bhikṣu," the *Lun shu* (Commentary on the Treatise) states: "This refers to the formal accusation of an offense.
Regarding "teaching and instructing": even if a bhikṣuṇī knows [the rule] while the bhikṣu does not, she must not instruct him by saying, "You should do this," and so forth.

Regarding the *Āryābhikṣuṇī-śāsana-sūtra*: that scripture is an ancient translation whose textual structure is difficult to discern. I shall now extract its essential meaning and provide a brief exposition.
First, one must maintain a mind of reverence and receive the Dharma from the Saṃgha (corresponding here to receiving the precepts).

Second, if there is a newly ordained bhikṣu, one must not treat him with a contemptuous mind, but should instead comfort him by asking: "Is the new student weary from his diligent practice? (corresponding here to [the prohibition against] reviling). Third, regarding bhikṣus...

1. Bhikṣuṇīs must not reside together in the same dwelling. 2. They must observe the rains retreat (varṣā) in dependence upon the bhikṣusaṃgha, maintaining mutual supervision and restraint (the character *jiǎ* here means "to restrain" or "to bind," ensuring that they do not commit transgressions;
this corresponds to the *pravarana*). 3. They must not accuse a bhikṣu of an offense. 4.
When inquiring about matters concerning the Sūtras and Vinaya, they must not discuss worldly affairs. 5. If they violate the precepts, they must confess them before the Saṃgha every half-month.
Confessing one's transgressions. Eighth, a bhikṣuṇī who has been ordained for a hundred years must sit on a lower seat than a newly ordained bhikṣu, paying homage with humility and respect.

Now, examining this in detail: within the fourth section on "Respect" in that sūtra, the two practices of *ānanda* (inviting instruction) and *pravāraṇā* (the invitation to point out faults) are included;
by adding a third form of respect, these are made eight. Thus, that [sūtra] is broad while this [text] is narrow.

Regarding these eight items of this Vinaya, they are summarized in verse as follows: "The hundred [rules], censuring, raising [a case], receiving, repentance, requesting, settling, and the *pravāraṇā*.

Although there are many [topics] such as reverence for the Dharma, they do not exceed [the categories of] "receiving" (*pratigraha*) and "following" (*anuvartana*). Specifically, the fourth is "receiving," and the fifth, "repentance," is "following" (it may also be said that the fourth generates goodness and the fifth eliminates evil).
"First, those who give rise to understanding" refers to the sixth [category]. First is the production of good (the *an-gu*); second is the cessation of evil (the *tsz-tzu*).

It may also be appropriate to allow two [options] at will. The previous discussion regarding the arising of wholesome states and so forth was spoken in terms of the performance of practice; what is now called "allowing at will" is discussed in terms of the dharma itself.

Regarding these three auspicious cases—the third, fourth, and fifth—the fourth case, wherein one does not go before the Sangha to receive the precepts, definitely results in not obtaining the precepts.

Even if one conceives a slight mind of contempt and disparages this Dharma, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅); however, for the *bhikṣuṇī* vinaya, if one does not confer the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (提).
Furthermore, regarding taking robes without [the donor] giving them, or the *mūla-dharma* (本法) remaining overnight, these faults arise only within the *bhikṣuṇī* rules themselves;
they do not constitute a case of disparaging the Sangha or the received Dharma.

Regarding the second point, "one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense" which includes the meaning of a *pāyattika*: reviling the Saṃgha incurs a *pāyattika*; slandering [the Saṃgha] while containing a principle of truth incurs both a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and a *duṣkṛta*.
This is because, for example, slandering a *pāyattika* offense and so forth incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

Regarding the absence of superiority or inferiority in the attainment of the precepts: since both superior and inferior conditions serve as the causes for generating the precepts, other forms of receiving them differ from this.

As for the Venerable One’s statement that it may also be a violation of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure), this means that if one does not confer the precepts [properly], it constitutes an offense.

If one considers the fundamental path of craving (*tṛṣṇā-mārga*), there are eight factors for its possession. Here, the intended meaning is that the path of craving acquires the precepts; it is possessed through eight causes.

For other persons, however, it is acquired solely through the fourth cause, respect (*gaurava*). This is the subsequent distinction. Although it is based on the fourth cause, it is actually obtained from the Saṃgha.

Furthermore, with respect to the precepts themselves, it refers exclusively to their possession. If one considers the objective, the fourth cause pertains to those who are not yet fully ordained (*asaṃvṛta*), while the remaining seven pertain to those who are.
(The details are available in the commentary.

Because there were those who committed the offense together, she was accused of mediation after the four-fold admonition had been given. Since the Saṃgha had already previously committed the offense, if a Bhikṣuṇī were to commit it as well, it would constitute the second [offense];
therefore, confession must be performed before the dual Saṃgha (the monks and nuns). The Venerable One said: "Neither paying homage nor receiving [instruction] was also not yet regulated."
Why must one alone be reproached for repenting what has not yet been codified? Now, examining this in detail: the codification of precepts necessarily requires their observance.

Therefore, it was essential that the rules for maintaining or violating them be established first, before the Eight Respectful Precepts were granted, leaving it to the individual whether or not to proceed.

Thus, there is no fault of contradiction in establishing these rules beforehand (meaning that if one is capable of practicing them, one is permitted to go forth; if one cannot practice them, one is not permitted). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the codification applies to the entire dispensation, as discussed from the perspective of its fulfillment at the time of the First Council.

Regarding the term "hundred *la*": in secular texts, "*la*" refers to hunting birds and beasts to sacrifice to one's ancestors; this is the name for the ritual performed at the end of the year to worship the deities.
When the *sūtras* and *vinayas* speak of "*la*," it carries the meaning of the end of the year. Whether it is called "summer" (*xia*) or "year" (*sui*), they all refer to the same thing.

Regarding the first case, when the community of nuns appoints a person [to go for instruction]: as prescribed in the 141st rule of the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya, it is permitted to appoint one nun by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) so that she may go to the community of monks every half-month to receive instruction.
Since she would travel alone and lack protection, two or three people should be appointed as her companions (the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* is as follows in the text below).
Second, regarding the time of the formal entrustment (*anuśāsti*): the following text states:

"She shall go before the community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*), prostrate at the feet of the monks, and with her body upright and her head bowed, join her palms and speak as follows: 'Venerable sirs, please attend to me. The community of bhikṣuṇīs is harmonious;

we pay homage to the community of bhikṣus; this is our request for instruction. Thus she speaks three times [saying, 'I request a person to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs,' which is preferable]. These two..."

At that time, [the formal act] must be performed before the Great Sangha recites the Prātimokṣa. Regarding the third generation of invitations and the subsequent three periods for the appointment [of officials], these are fully contained within this section of the precepts and may be understood from there.
Regarding what is stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: in the thirtieth section on the instruction of nuns, there are eight matters:

first, at an improper time; second, in an improper place; third, after the time has passed; fourth, before the time has arrived; fifth, when the assembly is not in harmony; sixth, in the presence of [the nun’s] kinsmen; seventh, preaching the Dharma using long sentences.
Eighth, regarding the reception of the instruction (*ovāda*): as for "the improper time," it is from sunset until the appearance of the dawn light;

[if one gives] the instruction during this time, one incurs a *pāyattika* (as with each of the following seven cases, one incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya*). As for "the improper place," it is not in a narrow or confined space, nor in an exposed place;
it should be in a place that is neither deep nor exposed, such as a lecture hall or beneath a tree. Regarding the "three times," they are the fourteenth day and the fifteenth day.
Regarding "the four times not having arrived": on the first, second, or third day of the month, one should go to instruct [the nuns] starting from the fourth day until the thirteenth day.
Regarding "the five non-concordances": once concordance has been achieved, one should then admonish them; after they have settled, one should ask, "Has the community of nuns reached concordance?
If they have not reached concordance, they should be summoned. If there are circumstances such as old age or illness, it is permitted to grant their *chanda* (consent). Sixth, the retinue...
Regarding this matter: one must not provide instruction unilaterally; rather, one should instruct only after all the bhikṣuṇīs have assembled in harmony.
As for the seven long utterances, they are like those spoken by the Venerable Nanda when instructing the bhikṣuṇīs with long speech. One should speak thus: "Commit no evil;

practice all that is good; restrain the mind from all wrongdoing; this is the teaching of all Buddhas. Sisters, this is the exhortation. Those who wish to listen may do so; those who wish to leave may depart.

This refers to abiding in mindfulness. Regarding the eight ways of welcoming: if one hears that a bhikṣu is coming on a certain day and there is no one to provide offerings, one should invite some junior bhikṣus to carry flowers, incense, banners, and canopies to go out and welcome him.

If none are available, at the very least one should join the palms in reverence, show respect, and take up his robes and bowl for him, whether the distance is one yojana or half a yojana, or one krośa or half a krośa.

One should go as far as outside the city or village to welcome them, and should encourage others to provide morning meals and non-timely drinks, making offerings with all one's heart so that they and their retinue have no lack for seven days;
if there is nothing available, one should give from the surplus of one’s own robes and bowl.
One should use these to make offerings. If even these are lacking, one should at least join the palms in respectful salutation.
When a nun arrives, one must not remain with the head bowed; rather, one should observe her appearance and deportment.

If she is seen with oil applied to her hair, her eyes adorned, wearing high-quality dyed garments pressed to a glossy shine, and a white sash tied around her waist, one should admonish any laypeople present and must not allow them to instruct her.
If a person gives rise to unwholesome thoughts, saying, "The śramaṇa is instructing his wife," one should ask other nuns, "Whose disciple is she?
and tell her teacher to reprimand her so that she may act in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding this matter of the formal entrustment (*niśraya*) being applicable across five periods, the Venerable One says: "This is not fixed.

For instance, in the case of entrusting one's bowl and robes, asking whether [the Sangha] is available, and welcoming [a visitor], how could these not apply to the universal boundary (*sarvāstika-sīmā*)? (When a nun comes to a monastery, even before entering the formal ritual boundary, if she encounters someone within the area, she may entrust her bowl and ask for permission;

thus, it should be permissible. Furthermore, in the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, it is stated that one must not entrust them to four types of persons: those who are not guests, those who are not traveling from afar, and so forth."
It is not that there is no wisdom regarding illness.
As for what is said within the rules for bhikṣuṇīs, it refers to the 141st precept among the *pāyantika* offenses for bhikṣuṇīs, which has already been cited previously.
Among the five periods mentioned above, the third and the three subsequent periods are explained here. Within the third period, it is further divided.

There are two [methods]: first, by invitation; second, by appointment. The formal text for the invitation in this Vinaya is incomplete; according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-four, it says:
"When the bhikṣus who were unable to attend have declared their purity, one should rise from one's seat, stand before the Saṃgha, and announce:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen! The harmonious community of bhikṣuṇīs at such-and-such a vihāra prostrates at the feet of the harmonious community of bhikṣus.'"
Regarding the person requesting instruction: the text omits the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation) without error, as seen in the subsequent text.
Fourth: the community of bhikṣus should set a specific time to go [to the instructor]. One should ask whether it is appropriate to go at that time or not. The text states:

"Once he has been entrusted with the matter, if the bhikṣu does not go the following day to inquire, the Buddha said: 'He should go to inquire whether it is appropriate. The bhikṣu should go at the appointed time" (the remainder of this precept is as follows). Fifth.
The manner of reception may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the point that "the types [of persons] are not exempted," this ancient master also permitted that the merit of showing respect is not exempted from being taught; however, the Venerable One did not permit this, as has already been discussed above.
If "day" does not refer to two things—first, respect, and second, the Dharma—it is because both of these days are auspicious.
Regarding the phrase "the fault arises from the subtlety of the meaning," the arising of the fault is due to the subtle meaning of the Saṃgha.
It is clear that there is no case where the formal appointment (*jñapti*) does not fail.

"No failure" implies that there is indeed failure. For example, if one stays overnight with a woman, the offense is incurred immediately; it is not restricted by exceeding three nights. It is the same regarding the failure of the appointment. To say that an offense is committed immediately means that no specific limit of days is prescribed.

Regarding the boundary (*sīmā*), the restriction of exceeding three nights applies; however, this requires the presence of someone other than a woman. At dusk, the offense is restricted; this requires the formal appointment by the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the day is not [fixed] by the act of speaking, nor is it established through error," this means: there is no failure to err;

rather, it clarifies that there is indeed error. The intended meaning here is that the act of speaking constitutes the establishment [of the boundary], and this does not depend upon the presence of error.

It is not the case that [the conjunction] occurs only at the end of each day; it must necessarily depend on a difference. Since the day itself is not [the cause], it cannot be due to a difference, nor can it be due to an absence of difference.
According to the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Observation), there are sixteen instances where the day ends without a difference; these cannot be recorded in full here.

According to other Vinaya texts, such as the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (24th Khandhaka): Once the senior monk (*sthavira*) has finished delivering the formal exhortation on behalf of the nuns, he should respond:
"Receive it from so-and-so. If there is no one appointed by the Saṃgha who is capable of preaching the Dharma, he should respond:
"Go to the side of the bhikṣu so-and-so and receive it. If there is still no one, the senior monk should respond: "There is no one here appointed to provide instruction."
Furthermore, there is no one capable of preaching the Dharma. You all must not be negligent. Tomorrow, the nuns should come and ask the person to whom they were entrusted, saying:
"Have you reported this to the Saṃgha on my behalf? This bhikṣu should then convey the words of the Elder to them. (The Commentary states:

In principle, after the nuns have received the instructions of the Elder, they should return to the nunnery, assemble the Saṃgha, and solicit their consent (*chanda*). Once the *brahmaghoṣa* (sacred chanting) has been completed, he should...
The nun announced: "Elders of the Great Assembly, there is now a brief instruction. Upon hearing these words, the assembly of nuns rose together, straightening their bodies and standing upright.
Having stood, they fully proclaimed the brief instruction of the Elder. Once it was proclaimed, they chanted in unison, "We receive and uphold this," prostrated before the Buddha, and dispersed.
The opening text states: "On the day of the assembly, one should go in succession to explain the eight dharmas not to be transgressed. One should proceed accordingly.

Regarding the teacher of the Dharma, the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle 15, states: "If one does not preach the Eight Respectful Rules (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), it is auspicious to first preach other teachings.

If one has already preached the Eight Respectful Rules, it is not an offense to subsequently preach other teachings. This does not constitute an offense when answering questions (provided that if a nun first asks about other teachings, answering them is not an offense)."

The *Samantapāsādikā* (Commentary on the Vinaya), fascicle seven, states: "It was not the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda. In the past, when the Buddha Vipaśyin appeared in the world, he preached the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
After that Buddha had passed into parinirvāṇa, a king erected a tower made of gośīrṣa-candana sandalwood, adorned with various ornaments. This...
The king had five hundred consorts who made offerings to this stūpa, each making a vow, saying:
"May we, in the future, attain liberation from this king. The king at that time was none other than Nanda;
the five hundred consorts at that time were these five hundred nuns. Due to the causal conditions of this original vow, they should now attain [liberation] through Nanda.
Regarding "liberation" and "the place for ferrying by boat": this refers to a boat used by many people to cross when evening falls.
It means that if one is dispatched [to preach] because of a great assembly and expounds the Dharma extensively, it is logically a violation of the rule against evening hours.
In the past, nunneries were not established; now that nunneries are established, it is clear this is not a deviation from the rules.

Furthermore, because the Great Assembly (the *dàhuì*) also does not involve unauthorized transgressions—since during the time of the Great [Assembly], monastics and laypeople gather together without censure—it is permitted.

There is no offense. If one skips ahead in the sequence and eats at the third house first, there is as yet no offense; it is only when one reaches the second house and eats that an offense occurs.

To swallow even a single grain constitutes a *pāyattika*. (Based on this principle, where there are no monks, if one accepts many invitations during a single day out of compassion for laypeople, it is logically without offense.)

One should follow the proper sequence: guarding against over-eating and remaining free from greed. There are three causes and conditions under which one may proceed without being hindered by the rule of sequential order:

first, the gift of robes; that is, if the third household has both robes and food, there is no fault in eating there first. Second, when one is ill, it is necessary to eat the food of that third household first.
Third, regarding the first inviting household, if they have previously invited the bhikṣu to eat on two previous occasions. First...
Eating the third [portion] first and setting aside the first is without fault, because it is established as the traditional custom of the first family.
Out of compassion, the Tathāgata stated that if there are three conditions, eating in reverse order is without fault. (Commentary: This likely accords with the intent of the *Gāthā-śāstra*.

Regarding the two meanings of the intent behind the precept against eating separately from the community (*pṛthag-bhaktika-śikṣāpada*): these correspond to the sections on "breaking the Saṃgha" and "defying admonition" mentioned above.
The first meaning permits those numbering three or fewer to eat in separate locations without offense; the second meaning requires that four or more must assemble together to avoid offense.

When the loss is heavy and the benefit shallow, people generally give rise to vexation; this is what is meant by "the loss is heavy. Although one obtains the merit of giving, because the mind is not joyful, the benefit is shallow.

Regarding those who commit offenses through indiscriminate differentiation: both the subject and the object are members of the Saṃgha. If an offense were established based on the name of the object, then even when the subject and the object are both individuals, the offense should likewise be established based on that act of taking.

Regarding the statement that "the name *saṃgha* is restrictive while the name 'assembly' (*jù*) is universal," the intention of the ancient masters was as follows: within both the [distribution of] Dharma and the distribution of food, the term "gathering the assembly" is used.

A detailed explanation is provided in the section on "Breaking the Saṃgha and Contravening Admonition. The commentary on that passage explains: "The term 'assembly' (*jù*) is used as a translation for *saṃgha*, signifying harmony."

As for this, the monastic community’s conventional usage does not emphasize individual virtue; rather, it generally employs the term "saṃgha" (the assembly) as a collective to denote the Sangha and so forth.
The *Śāstra* states: "The Dharma-food is limitless; the more there is, the more sublime it becomes, and all should gather together.

If this is so, then gathering together for the sake of food would surely be even more sublime. In reality, one should indeed gather together in full; thus, both the ritual and the food become sublime. For now, let us distinguish the matter of the food.
Regarding the opening [of the *kaṭhina*] by three persons at separate locations: within the Dharma, there is no allowance for three persons to each uphold it individually.

However, if one fails to uphold the ritual (*dharma*) and merely commits a *duṣkṛta* offense, yet upholds it in the presence of another, this too is but a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is the intended meaning of the *Śāstra*:

in the places where the object to be distinguished is not upheld through the ritual and so forth, the subject that distinguishes it does not arise, resulting in all *duṣkṛta* offenses. Now, let us examine this more closely.

Commentary: Regarding the distinction between holding [the rite] and not holding it, when both the agent and the object reach [the conclusion], all three phrases are auspicious; this applies to both the *saṃgha* and the individual (*pudgala*). Fourth, regarding "both hold":

if one holds [the rite] in the presence of another, one also incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (light offense); this refers only to the individual. If one performs the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), one commits a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);

in this case, both the agent and the recipient are exclusively members of the *saṃgha*. If we consider the presence of another, there are likewise five or three phrases; in all three phrases, they are equally [auspicious].
Auspicious. There is no fourth phrase stating that both [the giver and the receiver] do not hold [the food], because this has already been explained previously.
That is to say, for one whose mental state is generally grave—meaning they intentionally cause distress to others—they shall not receive food or sustenance.

Regarding "the Dharma is correct or incorrect": "correct" refers to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure); "incorrect" refers to [procedures] such as those performed before a single witness (*pratimukha*).

"That which can be known through reflection" refers to the subject and object within the act of eating: the four people from the eastern house are the subjects who perform the discernment, while the one person from the western house is the object of that discernment; this constitutes the fixed rule.
If both houses have four members each, then with respect to the five [factors], they function as both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), and thus it is indeterminate.

Within the legal proceedings, that which holds the office is called the agent; that which does not hold the office is called the object. This is determinate. If both hold the office, it is clear that it is indeterminate.

Regarding those who both remove the boundary markers: if they belong to the same natural realm and together perform the ritual for establishing a boundary, this also constitutes a schism in the Saṃgha.
Someone says: "In the Council of Seven Hundred, worthy persons were selected and went to the place where the dispute was to be settled; was this not the proper order of the Saṃgha? The answer is:
since they took the consent (*chanda*) of others, how could it constitute the formal order of the Saṃgha?
"Stolen from the *saṃghika*" is translated as "possessed by the community.

Regarding the *Bao'en jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness), in its third chapter, it describes how an administrator, out of anger and resentment, felt displeased by the large number of visiting monks and consequently concealed the ghee and oil.
He hesitated and did not give it. According to the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish* (Xianyu jing), chapter fifteen, it also says:

When the Buddha was near the city of Rājagṛha, there was a large beast by the Wāng River. Its form resembled a snake, yet it had four legs; it ran back and forth, suffering immeasurable pain. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, during the Dharma of Vipaśyin Buddha, there were some merchants who collected various exquisite jewels."

He gave it to the community of monks, intending to receive food and drink in return. The monks entrusted it to the *karmadāna*. Later, when the monks' food was exhausted, they went to him to demand it.
He said, "You lot are eating excrement! This treasure is my own; for what reason do you demand it?

Because he had thus deceived the monks and reviled them with foul language, he fell into the Avīci Hell. For ninety-one kalpas (the chapter says ninety billion), his body constantly wallowed amidst boiling excrement.

[This is the same as the original scripture. Having emerged from hell, you have now fallen back into this state. The six Buddhas of the past all led their disciples here to explain the causes and conditions for them.
I, the seventh Buddha, now show it to you; likewise, all the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa will each show it to you.
Regarding the "Mṛgāramātṛ-vastu" in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, section fifty-nine states: "The Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta. Mṛgāramātṛ invited him separately.
(Omitted) Each [of the monks] entered through the window by means of their supernatural powers; some descended from the sky, some emerged from the ground, and some appeared from within their seats."
"One should immediately take a portion of this food and distribute it in sequence to those who are eating. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun), fascicle seven, states:
"If there is a meal provided by a donor within the boundaries of the Saṃgha, one should first form the intention to invite one person from among the monks;

yet if one falsely fails to invite them and has already finished eating, one should set aside a portion of the food and place it at the head of the seat for the senior monk to send to the community of monks. Those who are far away should take it."
Regarding this meal, it is to be served in sequence.
As for those who chant the *laba* (the ritual invocation), it is often said:

if there is a donor who prepares a long-term meal—whether for one month or ninety days—they first invite people according to their wishes and have each person fixed upon their place. On the first day of the meal, everyone assembles together at dawn.
Strike the *gandi*. Once the assembly of monks has gathered, the *karmadāna* bhikṣu should stand in one place and raise his voice to proclaim loudly:
"Those with sixty years of seniority (*varṣa*) should enter; if there are none, call out in order those with fifty-nine years of seniority, down to the novices (*śrāmaṇera*)."
If there is no śrāmaṇera, one may likewise attain purity (the remainder is as explained in the chapter). Furthermore, it says:
When the ninety days have concluded, if a donor continues to provide food for one month or half a month, one simply performs the previous ritual proclamation; it need not be proclaimed again.
Regarding those who should strike the *ghanṭā* (bell): it is generally said that when eating from the communal storehouse (*saṃghika*) food, one should perform four signs:

first, striking the *ghanṭā*; second, blowing the conch; third, beating the drum; and fourth, proclaiming the announcement so that all within the boundary may hear and know. These four kinds of signs must be maintained as a constant practice; one must not, for instance, beat only the drum or blow only the conch.
To fail to perform these four signs is termed "stealing from the Saṃgha's food. (The character "steal" [盜] is placed at the top.)

The precepts have already been explained). Regarding the three benefits: the text of the *Saṃghabheda-avavāda-śikṣāpada* states: "From this day forward, you must not eat separately from the community;
eating in groups of up to three is permitted. The reason for this is that there are two benefits: it is for the sake of gathering those who are difficult to discipline.

Therefore, out of compassion for the householders, and for what reason? Fearing those who are difficult to discipline, he intentionally formed a separate assembly to exclude himself from the general community of monks.
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there is no offense when four people each beg for alms and eat together in one place; the commentary explains that this is because they are distinct donors.
This differs from the present Vinaya, which describes five people begging for alms together from house to house, clarifying that they share a single donor.
Regarding the two sets of four propositions concerning the *pṛthag-bhaktika* (separate meal), that treatise, chapter sixteen, states: "There are two kinds of separate meals:
first, those by invitation; second, those by begging. How does one constitute a separate meal? There was a lay follower who went to four bhikṣus."
"Venerable Sir, please accept this. This is called "requesting to form a separate group for a meal" (this refers to the introductory formal motion).
Accepting the invitation at one time—whether tomorrow, the day after, or a later day—and accepting a meal at one location at one time constitutes forming a separate group for a meal.

All four persons incur an offense (this is the first case). Within each individual case, there are four factors to consider: first, the invitation; second, the departure; third, the acceptance; and fourth, the location. As for the expressions "tomorrow" or "the day after," these refer to the time of departure, which occurs all at once.

[This is] the section on the precept). Having accepted the invitations at one time, they each went to the houses of the donors; having accepted the food at one time, they returned and ate at their respective places.
As for the offense incurred, the Dharma Master said: "For what reason? Because they accepted the food at one time" (this corresponds to the second clause).

If one accepts invitations at different times and eats separately, there is no offense (this is the third phrase). If one goes to the donor’s house having been invited separately, and accepts [the food] all at once, there is an offense.

This is called "accepting an invitation and incurring an offense" (this is the fourth phrase, which also serves as a summary; this phrase likely refers to eating in a single location, though it is omitted from the text).
Now, these are summarized in verse: "The request to depart and the place of acceptance" (each of these four points is condensed here).

"The fourfold sameness of the request and the sameness of the acceptance" (the "fourfold sameness" refers to the first line; "the sameness of the acceptance" refers to the second line. Having already clarified the two types of sameness, one clearly understands the two types of distinction. The interpretation of the remaining lines follows this principle).

"The sameness of the request and the sameness of the acceptance" (the "samenesses" refer to the third line; "the sameness of the acceptance" refers to the fourth line). "Only the third [case] is without offense" (as stated by those who follow the *Śāstra*). Why is it that one incurs an offense through begging?

There are four bhikṣus who beg for alms. Whether sitting or standing, they see a lay follower (upāsaka) and say to him, "Give us four portions of rice," or they each beg individually, saying, "Give me rice.

It is the same for each case (the phrase "it is the same" means that the fourfold formula is identical to the previous one, with the only difference being that instead of a formal invitation, they beg at once).
Whether they go together or separately, they receive the food all at once; this is called "incurring an offense by begging."

(“Both go” refers to the first phrase; “each goes” refers to the three subsequent phrases. Regarding “receiving at once,” it means that within these various phrases, one incurs an offense by receiving [the food] all at once).
As for “there is no need to discuss the meaning,” this refers to not considering the act of swallowing; thus, it does not accord with this Vinaya school, and therefore it is not discussed. Question:

Within the Dharma, since detailed assemblies may be transformed into what is non-prohibited, should food also, through detailed assembly, constitute a transformation into pure food? Answer: The transformation of the Dharma yields greater benefit, whereas the exchange of food yields less benefit.
Therefore, they are not the same. Regarding "the fault of the matter": it refers to an inadequacy within the action being performed.

Although the first "fault" among the seven also contains the element of the matter, this commentary’s intent is to distinguish them based on the increase or decrease of the textual phrasing, as well as their application in procedures such as the *karmavācanā*. Question: Originally, for what purpose was separate food [established]?

Regarding the difficulty of taming those who are difficult to discipline and the compassion for worldly people, the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) describes the overturning of the alms bowl (*pātra*). This Vinaya provides seven exceptions; how can one avoid the two faults? Answer:
Following these exceptions to perform the ritual clearly demonstrates that one is not difficult to discipline; therefore, it does not contradict the principle. The *Jianlun*, fascicle 16, states:

"If four people are invited to eat together and there is one among them who understands the Vinaya, and they wish to eat together but fear committing an offense, he employs a skillful means to overturn his bowl and refuse the food. When the donor asks..."

[The questioner] asked, "Why do you not accept it? [He] replied, "I am giving food to only three people so that I may offer a blessing. After the three have finished eating, I shall then accept the food; this will not be an offense."
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* presents four propositions; these have been formulated here according to their underlying meaning rather than as a strict adherence to the text of that treatise.
Regarding the two divisions of long and short: first is the long, and second is the short.

The four [conditions] consisting of illness, the distribution of robes, traveling on a journey, and so forth—meaning traveling by land or by boat—and the offering of food to the *saṃgha* (taking "traveling" as the primary example).
The phrase "and so forth" refers to the other three [categories], thus making four with the preceding term. These six categories are expanded;

specifically, "illness and travel, etc. constitutes five, wherein illness is combined with the four categories of travel and so forth (among these six types, these five are first distinguished because, in terms of their meaning, they both rely on the aforementioned conditions and lack independent criteria).
Regarding the "two types of retribution," these are clothing and food.
As for the first interpretation [extending to] "a single stitch on a horse's tooth" and so forth, this prior interpretation directly addresses the period of one month or five months.
One must actually make the robe in order to receive the benefit; because this does not fully accord with the principle, it is further explained later.
Why must one make the robe within the month and so forth? It is therefore explained: "There is no receiving of the *kaṭhina* robe" means that the intention is for the purpose of making the robe.

If one definitely does not make it, or if one has already finished making it, then the *kaṭhina* robe is lost. Thus, the subsequent text speaks of "losing it when finished" and "losing it when not finished," and so on. This is [the meaning].
Furthermore, there is one person who simply accepts the robe without specifically designating it for the purpose of making robes;

this is limited to the five months and is called the "robe season," not the "robe-making season. It may be reasonable to distinguish these for the five months, but how is it for the [remaining] month?
The answer is that this also lacks intentional meaning. This person has no thought: "If I make a robe, I shall receive the five privileges; if I do not make a robe, I shall stop."

[The first case] is not accepted. Furthermore, there is another person who does not distinguish between these two by designating them as "the former" and "the latter. The former is named at the time of making the robe, while the latter is named at the time [of wearing] the robe.
Regarding gain and loss, although it does not depend on such a designation, there is still a difference based on the distinctions of the mind.

Regarding the statement that "the gift of robes to the assembly of śramaṇas" refers to those three being held in common: it may be accepted that the "assembly" and the "one" share them together. However, the other cases are not fixed.

When there is a joint invitation for the gift of robes to both the [monastic] community and the śramaṇas, they share them; if one comes of their own accord without being invited, they do not share them.
(The criteria for breadth and narrowness, etc., should be understood accordingly.)
Regarding the statement that "the other five indeterminate [factors] are not without the meaning of being shared": if both [persons] travel by boat, this is called "shared";
if one travels while the other does not, it is "unshared. Other similar cases should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the two modes of travel—by water and by land—as they relate to bathing, there are points of agreement and disagreement.

It is traditionally explained that, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the permissions and prohibitions regarding traveling in a group versus traveling separately, as well as bathing, are identical. However, according to the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, the meaning differs. To first distinguish the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:

if one intends to travel and has finished traveling, eating separately and bathing both incur a *pāyattika* offense. If, while actually traveling, one eats separately and bathes... [the text continues].
[The text] opens [the discussion], thus it is said they are the same. If one follows the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), eating separately is the same as before;

however, washing after the formal practice (*prātimokṣa*) and after the practice is finished constitutes separate washing, which is not the same. Now, searching the *Shisong* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), there appears to be a textual basis for this. If one searches the *Jianlun*, [it says]:

This passage does not exist [in that text]. Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), volume 13, states: "If one arrives yesterday and eats today, it is a *pācittiya*. If one departs tomorrow and eats today, it is a *pācittiya*.

If one departs on the same day and eats separately, there is no offense. The same applies to traveling by boat. Moreover, the text regarding the precept on bathing in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, volume 16, is also identical.

The seventh fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Commentary on the Mahīśāsaka Vinaya) is likewise the same. Upon examining the *Samantapāsādikā* (Sifen lü shanfan buque xingshi chao), this [passage] is indeed absent.
Commentary: If explained according to the underlying principle, it is logically permissible. That is to say, if based on a day’s interval, it is as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*;
