If those who have left the household life possess these marks, they will surely become Dharma-kings, transforming and guiding all beings.
Second is the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel: this refers to the pattern on the soles of the Buddha’s feet that resembles a wheel with a thousand spokes.
It is complete; its hub and rim are perfect, distinct, and exquisite. Even though the Devaputra Subhakarmā applies his utmost attention, he cannot emulate it, for he must create it anew.
Why is this? Because the things created by the Devaputra Subhakarmā are induced by what is non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*);
these characteristics are induced by purely pure karma (induced by innate knowledge or induced by applied knowledge).

(These are further established in two additional sequences: 3. The mark of long, slender fingers: this refers to fingers that are long and slender, tapering gradually to a fine point, with joints that do not protrude, which are set without gaps, arranged in perfect proportion, and endowed with full luster.
4. The mark of round and long heels: this refers to the Buddha’s heels being round and long, dignified, broad, and straight. The *Dichi* (Daśabhūmika) Sūtra, Chapter Ten, states:
Fourth is the mark of full heels. Fifth is the mark of soft and delicate hands and feet; this means that the Buddha’s hands and feet are as soft and delicate as *tūla* cotton.
Sixth is the mark of webbed fingers and toes; this means that between all of the Buddha’s fingers and toes there are webs, just like those of a king of geese.
When the fingers are joined, the webs do not appear, yet they are neither wrinkled nor lax; when they are spread apart, the webs immediately become visible.
There is no haste. Seventh is the mark of the well-proportioned and thick insteps. This means that the Buddha’s insteps are rounded and thick;
they slope toward the toes, being straight and rounded on both sides, in proportion with the heels. When he steps, they do not broaden out. The soles of his feet are the color of a red lotus flower.

The inner edges of the webbing between his toes are like the patterns of variegated trees, deep blue and lustrous. His toenails are the color of red copper leaves. The outer edges of the webbing are made of *tṛṇa* [grass-like] material.
8. His body is golden in color. 9. His webbed hair is deep blue and glossy like vaidūrya. 10. He has the *niyāṅku* [deer-like] calves;
that is to say, the Buddha’s calves are rounded and straight, tapering gradually toward the ankles like those of the king of *niyāṅku* deer. 11. He possesses the mark of the concealed secret organ.
This refers to the Buddha’s secret organ being concealed within a sheath, just like that of a horse king. If this is so, how is it that those to be converted are able to see it?

Some say that out of compassion for those to be converted, the Blessed One employs skillful means to reveal it. Others say that the Blessed One creates through transformation an elephant or horse with a most exquisite concealed organ, and tells those to be converted:
"As it is with them, so it is with me. Tenth is the mark of the perfection of the body's proportions; this refers to the Buddha’s body...

The proportions are perfectly symmetrical, like a *nyagrodha* tree; from the navel to the crown of the head, it is just as it is from the navel to the feet—upper and lower parts are in perfect proportion.
Eleventh, the mark of body hairs that point upward. Twelfth, the mark of a single hair growing from each pore.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "From every single pore of the body, a single hair grows; they are deep blue-black in color, with spirals turning to the right. Thirteenth.
This is the mark of body hairs curling to the right. On every pore of the Buddhas' bodies, a single hair grows;
it is like vaidūrya, deep blue and lustrous, curling gracefully to the right. The tips of these hairs point upward and touch one another.

The reason there is only a single hair in each pore is that, during his time as a bodhisattva, he taught the Dharma without confusion. Fourteenth is the mark of the body being the color of pure gold, which outshines...

It eclipses all the golden light of the world so that it no longer appears. Just as iron today cannot manifest its brilliance when compared to gold of the present day, so too the gold used today cannot manifest its brilliance when compared to the gold used during the time the Buddha was in the world.

Furthermore, the gold used during the time the Buddha was in the world cannot manifest its brilliance when compared to the gold found on the path of the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) at the edge of the great ocean, which is like broken sand.

The golden rim of the Mount Nimindhara does not manifest its brilliance when compared to the gold of the seven mountain ranges; nor does it manifest its brilliance when compared to the gold of the ornaments of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.

This should be understood in detail as it proceeds further, even to the gold of the ornaments of the Nirmāṇarati heaven, which does not manifest its brilliance when compared to the gold of the ornaments of the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven.

When this gold of the ornaments of the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven reaches the presence of the Buddha’s body, its brilliance does not manifest. Therefore, the golden color of the Buddha’s body is supreme, outshining all others.

Fifteenth, the mark of a fathom-wide constant radiance: a halo of light, one fathom in circumference, constantly surrounds him, illuminating day and night on all sides for a fathom each. Sixteenth, the mark of fine skin: dust and water do not adhere to it;
it is like vaidūrya or a lotus leaf. Even if a Buddha were to tread upon a mountain of dust with this [skin], the Vairambha...
Wind blows within it, yet it is impossible for even a single speck of dust to cling to the Buddha’s body or beneath his feet.
Seventeenth is the mark of the seven parts being full: the two hands, the two feet, the two shoulders, and the nape of the neck—these are the seven parts.
Eighteenth is the mark of the body being broad, majestic, and straight: the bodies of all Buddhas are broad, majestic, and straight; they are neither hunched nor stooped.
Not leaning to either side; upright, elegant, and full. Nineteenth is the mark of the lion’s upper body:
this refers to the Buddha’s chest being well-proportioned, broad, majestic, and solemn, like the upper half of the body of a lion king. Twentieth is the mark of the fullness of the shoulders.
This refers to the Buddha’s collarbones being perfectly rounded, a feature that cannot be matched by any of the powerful *malla* wrestlers.
Twenty-first is the mark of standing with hands reaching the knees: this means that when the Buddha stands upright with his arms extended, his hands touch his kneecaps.

Twenty-second is the mark of the lion’s jaw (*siṃhahanu*): [the character for "jaw" is pronounced *han* (hú gǎn fǎn)]. This means that the Buddha’s jaw is broad and well-formed, like a wheel. Thus it is called the "wheel-jaw. This means that the Buddha’s jaw is broad and excellent, like...
The Lion King: Twenty-third, he possesses the mark of forty teeth; twenty-fourth, his teeth are even, level, and closely set;
twenty-fifth, his teeth are brilliant white and radiant. This means that the Buddha possesses forty teeth, all of which are perfectly even with not so much as a hair’s breadth of space between them.
Their color is pure white, and their radiance is so bright and clear as to resemble snow.
World-Honored One, as for other people, they have only thirty-two teeth, yet it is said that within their bodies there are one hundred and three bones.
Since the Buddha possesses forty teeth, why is it also said that there are one hundred and three bones within his body, without any increase?
Answer: The skulls of other people are composed of nine parts, whereas the skull of the World-Honored One consists of only a single piece;
therefore, both possess one hundred and three bones. Twenty-sixth is the mark of obtaining the supreme flavor (*rasāgra-lakṣaṇa*).

This means that because the tongue-mark is pure, whatever food or drink is consumed is transformed into a supreme flavor. Some say that within the Buddha’s throat there are two milk-springs; if he consumes food or drink...

At that time, his milk flowed forth; even apart from all other food and drink, it became a supreme flavor. Furthermore, because the faculty of the tongue within this [body] is pure, it causes flavors to be exceptionally sublime.
This principle ought to be so. (27) The mark of the broad and long tongue: it is thin, soft, broad, and long.
When emerging, it covers the face up to the ears and hairline; even if it returns to enter the mouth, it causes no obstruction within the mouth.
Twenty-eighth is the mark of deep blue eyes: the eyes are long and wide, their color is a pure deep blue, like the petals of a *sujāta* blue lotus.
Twenty-ninth is the mark of eyelashes like those of a bull king: this refers to the Buddha’s eyelashes being beautifully and perfectly arranged.
30. Like a bull-king: the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa*. This refers to the hair on the Buddha’s crown, formed from both bone and flesh;
the bone is like a covered coil, blue, circular, and exquisitely wonderful. 31. The mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā*).
It is half a fathom in length, curls to the right, and its radiance is pure and penetrating. 32. The mark of attaining the Brahma-voice. This refers to the Buddha’s...

Within the treasury of the mind, there exists a sublime great element capable of producing delightful sounds that blend with the Brahma-voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird, and emitting deep, far-reaching peals like the drum of Śakra. Such vocal qualities possess eight virtues:
first, profundity; second, harmony; third, clarity; fourth, ear-pleasingness; fifth, heart-penetratingness; and sixth, joy-inducingness.
The seventh is easy to understand. Regarding the eighth, the mark of being tireless (*an-udvigna*), [the text] is condensed into a verse:

The feet are well-placed and marked with wheels; the toes are joined by webs, and the heels are rounded. The hands and feet are soft like those of the king of geese; the insteps are high like those of the king of deer.
The private parts are concealed within a sheath; the body is perfectly proportioned; and from the upper part of the body grows a single hair.
The hair curls to the right and is golden; his constant radiance makes his skin fine and smooth. Seven parts of his body are large and straight;
his upper body and shoulders are broad and rounded. His hands reach his knees and his jaw is like that of a lion.
He has forty teeth, even, dense, fresh white, and possesses the supreme sense of taste. His tongue is long, his eyes are deep blue, his eyelashes are well-formed, and he has the *uṣṇīṣa*.

The mark of the white tuft and the Brahma-voice (this differs slightly from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* regarding its inclusion and exclusion of certain features; it is largely identical to it: the hands, feet, shoulders, and neck constitute the seven places of fullness).

The Venerable Pārśva said: "Whether increased or decreased, both would give rise to doubt; only thirty [features] do not contradict the characteristics of the Dharma.
Some say that thirty-two is a number universally recognized in the world as auspicious, and for this reason it is neither increased nor decreased. Others say:
The thirty-two marks adorn the Buddha’s body, making him the most supreme and peerless in the world. If there were fewer than these, they would be deficient;
if there were more, they would be redundant and confused, neither of which would be excellent. Therefore, there are only this many.
Just as the Buddha’s teaching cannot be increased or diminished, so too is the Buddha’s mark: there is nothing to be added that could diminish it, and nothing to be removed that could increase it.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 30, states: "It is like an ornament for the body; though one may be wealthy and possess many pearls and gems, they cannot be worn in excessive measure.

Because they accord with what is favored in India, he manifests the thirty-two major marks and the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) [the eighty secondary characteristics will be explained below]. What is the difference between [the marks] of a Bodhisattva and those of a Wheel-turning King? Answer: Those obtained by a Bodhisattva are superior in four respects: first, they are blazing; second, they are distinct;

third, they are complete; fourth, they are attained in the proper place. Furthermore, there are five respects in which they are superior: first, the place of attainment; second, extreme majesty and beauty;

The explanation of the names of the seven treasures is found in the fifty-seventh chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. As described in the section on medicinal methods below, when Maudgalyāyana took the lotus root, there were seven great naga-elephant kings in that pond;

yet the sword has no intent to harm. When those sentient beings see the sword bound [to the king's side], they naturally submit and come under his sway.
Having submitted and taken refuge, they returned and stood before the king. Second is the hide treasure: merchants obtained the hide of a sea dragon king from the ocean and presented it;
it was not scorched by fire nor rotted when soaked in water, and it was exceedingly lustrous. It was five yojanas in height;
whenever the king traveled, the military host stayed beneath it, each obtaining their own separate dwelling. Third is the garment treasure: it was more exquisite, fine, and soft than ordinary ones.
Sixth, the jewel of dwellings: it can ward off cold, heat, hunger, and thirst. Within it, the sun, moon, stars, and other celestial bodies all appear.
Furthermore, the music of the devas is heard; the jewel of groves: all things such as the sun, moon, stars, and rare wonders appear within it.
When the devas perform their music, it manifests therein for the king to enjoy. Sixth.
These are the jewels used for his feet. When he walks upon them, he is not burned by fire nor drowned by water;

even if he travels as far as hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, he never experiences fatigue. These are the seven precious beds. Because the king’s mind is pure, these jewels are constantly manifest;
yet when he becomes negligent, they immediately sink and disappear. They are neither high nor low, neither stiff nor soft, always spontaneously conforming to his wishes.

The passage beginning with "Having preached the Dharma to sentient beings" and following explains the Wheel of Dharma (the meaning of the three wheels will be analyzed below).

According to the *Fobuxingzan* (Praise of the Buddha’s Past Deeds), he left home on the eighth day of the third month. According to the *Taizi wumeng jing* (Sutra of the Five Dreams of the Prince), the Buddha [left home on the eighth day of the fourth month].
He was born on the eighth day; Devadatta was born on the seventh day of the fourth month; Nanda was born on the ninth day; and Ānanda was born on the tenth day.
These were not only different days, but their years of birth were also different. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle 14) states that [the Buddha] went toward the Aṭaṇḍa forest.
Not far from the city, he dismounted from his horse and removed his precious garments. He said to Channa, "You may lead the horse and take these precious garments back to the palace.
I wish to pay my respects to my parents and bid them farewell as I depart to study the Path. I shall return before long;
I pray you do not grieve for me."
Regarding "fearing harm to others," the *Mahāyānopāya-sūtra* states: "There are three causes and conditions for shaving one's own hair:
first, the Prince’s majestic countenance was so awe-inspiring that none among humans, devas, or the eight classes of beings dared to approach him;

second, because the Prince was sincerely renouncing the world, he shaved himself to distinguish himself from worldly people; third, for the sake of protecting others, his father the King had issued a decree: 'If..."

There was one who would have shaved [the hair], but his five clans would have been executed; the present statement that "fearing it might be damaged" refers to this third meaning. The *Pañcavargika* states that he was then shaved.

He exchanged [his fine robes] for a coarse *saṃghāṭī* and, by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, remained for six years.
Regarding asceticism: The *Buddhabhūmi-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (The Buddha’s Original Deeds), chapter eighteen, states:
At that time, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven manifested in the form of a hunter, wearing robes dyed the color of *kāṣāya*. The Prince exchanged his own garments for these and put them on.

Regarding the passage "not listed among those who obtained the bowl," according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (五分律), chapter fourteen: when [the Buddha] entered the city to beg for food, his deportment was dignified and orderly;

he walked while keeping his eyes fixed upon the ground. At that time, as bowls had not yet been made, he held a lotus leaf. As he traveled along the road, the leaf did not detach from its root. The King...
On a high tower, together with his ministers, he saw the Bodhisattva from afar and, struck by his extraordinary elegance, turned to address the assembly:

"I have never before seen or heard of anyone like this person. They all said in unison, "In the past, we heard that the prince of Śuddhodana was examined by physiognomists, who prophesied that he would become either a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) or attain the path of Buddhahood;
this man must surely be him. The *Jian lun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle 16, states that he first received [the prophecy].
When the milk-rice was being offered, his alms-bowl sank into the waters of the Nairañjanā River. The Dragon King of the Sea took it to make offerings;
yet [the Buddha] did not speak of where he had obtained it, nor did he cast a sidelong glance (the *Shuowen* defines this as a slanted or oblique look).

Regarding the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*): the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 24, states that the reason one further cultivates the eighty secondary marks is because there are sentient beings in the world who serve eighty deities. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 49, states:

"The Tathāgata’s eighty secondary marks refer to the twenty fingers on both hands and feet, as well as the joints, all of which are exceptionally sublime; these are what are called the two [sets of ten]."

The ten secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*). The eight locations consisting of the two hands, the two feet, and the inner and outer surfaces [of the four limbs]—the four hands and four feet being all exceptionally exquisite—are termed the eight secondary marks.
The six locations consisting of the two ankles, the two knees, and the two thighs are exceptionally exquisite; these are termed the six secondary marks.
The six locations consisting of the two upper arms, the two elbows, and the two wrists are exceptionally exquisite; these are termed the six secondary marks. The waist...
The suture is exquisite; this constitutes one minor mark (*anuvyañjana*). The two testicles are exquisite; these constitute two minor marks (*testicle* here refers to the ovary).

The male organ is concealed and exquisite; this constitutes one minor mark. The two buttocks are exquisite; these constitute two minor marks. The hips, the abdomen, and the navel—these three are all exquisite; each constitutes one minor mark.
Both sides of the torso, the armpits, and the breasts are all exquisite; these constitute six [minor marks].
The secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*). There is one secondary mark each on the abdomen, chest, neck, and spine; these are as described above.

Excluding the area above the neck, there are sixty secondary marks on the lower part of the body. The upper and lower rows of teeth are both exceptionally exquisite, constituting two secondary marks (because the teeth are prominent and arranged in rows like a flower garland, they are so named).
The palate is exceptionally exquisite, constituting one secondary mark (*tālu*; *tā* pronounced as in *qu*, *lū* pronounced as in *wǔ*). The two lips [are also included].
The accompanying features of the two eyes are both exquisite; this constitutes two secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*). The chin is well-rounded and perfect; this constitutes one secondary mark.
Both cheeks are full and well-situated; these constitute two secondary marks. The accompanying features of the two eyes are both exquisite;
these constitute two secondary marks. The two eyebrows are exquisite; these constitute two secondary marks. Both nostrils of the nose are both exquisite; these constitute two [secondary marks].
The secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*). His forehead is exquisite; this constitutes one secondary mark. His temples, sideburns, and both ears are all exquisite;
these constitute four secondary marks. His hair is exquisite; this constitutes one secondary mark. As thus described, from the neck upward there are twenty secondary marks.
Together with the sixty previously mentioned, they total eighty secondary marks. *Bhūmivastu*.

the two temples and the two ears; and the hair.
"If the son is solemn," explains the external scholar, "the lord presides over the high station while the son loves the people below;

This refers to citing two of the three or four phrases from the section on praise. These are the passages stating that the person in question was not of low birth, as well as those concerning his gazing intently and moving forward, and so forth.
Regarding the names of his parents, some versions of the Vinaya state that his father’s name was Śuklodana (White Food), because he was the son of Prince Śuklodana.
If that is so, one might object that the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* cited previously refers to the son of King Śuddhodana. To this we reply:
the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* states that he was "the son of King Śuklodana, who dwells as a great śramaṇa. Therefore, one cannot rely on a single source as definitive.
It is also possible that they share the same clan name. According to some Vinaya texts, the father’s clan name was *Sūrya* (the Sun), meaning the "Sun-Burnt" lineage;
this indicates that the Solar Clan (*Sūryavaṃśa*) was the ancestral clan, while the name Śākya refers to the later clan.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* (Chapter 5) states: according to Western tradition, the Kṣatriya lineage was once oppressed by Muwei, and his son fled.
Outside, there was a seer who took him in and raised him until he grew up, wishing to ensure that the royal lineage would continue without interruption.
An astrologer informed the enemy king that the constellation of a Kṣatriya had appeared. The enemy king ordered his men to capture and bring the boy before him;
having abandoned him, they impaled him upon a sharp stake. The seer arrived and exhorted the child, commanding him to arouse desire so that the royal lineage might [be sustained].

The lineage was thus not cut off. The young boy suffered; his passions did not arise. The rishi transformed himself into a dense cloud to provide cover, and a fine rain moistened him, causing his suffering to cease for a time.
He then further transformed into a woman and united with the boy; the essence of the pool fell upon the ground.
The rishi then wrapped his semen in cow dung and took it back home, placing it within a sugarcane grove.
As the sun scorched the dung ball, a boy was born, handsome and well-proportioned in appearance. Later, when he grew up, he succeeded to the royal throne; thus the tradition was passed down.
Those who disparage it are called the "cow-dung lineage" (*gomaya-gotra*); those who praise it are called the "sun lineage" (*sūrya-gotra*).

Regarding the meaning: although the Mahāyāna may suppress it, the principle remains the same.

Regarding the claim that self-starvation is the path and so forth: it is now explained that this is not so.

It was simply because he sought the supreme Dharma that, encountering circumstances midway, he remained for six years without attaining the holy Dharma. That method of rest was precisely what led to his subsequent attainment of Buddhahood;
the asceticism of his father was not the method of rest. Now, to examine this in detail: as for "encountering circumstances and remaining for six years," how could this be [consistent with] Bodhi?

Sakyamuni abandoned [his body] for six years. If you further attempt to rescue this by saying that the Buddha is the "Buddha-trace" (the enlightened one) and thus not one who abandoned himself, then the "Transformation-trace" (the manifested one) should likewise be held to have starved himself to death; why then do you falsely refute this?

Next, regarding the one who approached the Great General (*mahāsenāpati*) during his ascetic practices: as stated in the preceding commentary, his conduct was identical to that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and his essence was one and the same.
As for the reference to "other sutras," the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya* states: "In the past, when the Buddha was a king, there was a man who inadvertently drank water from the royal pond.

He went before the king and bowed his head in submission. The king said: 'Now, he who buys a house possesses its well; he who occupies a field cherishes its... [The text continues with the principle that ownership extends to what is naturally associated with the property.]
Drawing water and cutting grass—these things one does not take without being told. You took them without being told; is this not theft? The rest is as explained in the chapter.
Regarding "those who are not [realized in] the two emptinesses," an ancient master said: "The preceding text is identical to the *Yājñavalkya* [Smṛti]; from here onwards, it is called..."

Returning to our own school, the text states that one "abandons desires and unwholesome states. This refers to the comparative evaluation of the two types of concentration—false and correct—in terms of their capacity to eliminate afflictions or their incapacity to do so;
this is the intention of the ancient masters. By comparing the two types of emptiness, one knows that [the former] is false concentration, which is then termed "desire" (kāma).

"Evil" means unwholesome. Now, according to the Master’s intention, it is said that desire, evil, and the unwholesome are obstacles to the first dhyāna, not to the two emptinesses; therefore, they are abandoned.
As for the statement that "in principle, one should say that one abandons [them] and attains [them]," if this phrase were added, it would constitute ten phrases.
There is no need to labor over an extensive [explanation] of these sixteen points; I shall now set them forth in detail. Regarding the first triad:

at that time, the Bodhisattva further thought, "Is it possible that through unwholesome states of desire one may obtain the Dharma of bliss? (This is the first sentence; the text currently contains it).
He further thought, "It is not by means of unwholesome states of desire that one obtains the Dharma of bliss" (This is the second sentence; the text also currently contains it). He further thought:

"I would now rather abandon sensual desires, evil, and unwholesome states" (this is the third phrase; it lacks the literal wording but possesses the underlying meaning). Second, regarding the third [stage], he further reflects:

"Is there perhaps the cultivation of desirelessness, the relinquishing of unwholesome states, and the attainment of the state of happiness? (this is the first phrase; it is explicitly present in the text).
Again, he thinks: "Indeed, it is by practicing desirelessness and abandoning unwholesome states that I have attained the state of happiness" (this is the second phrase;
the phrasing lacks logical sequence). Again, he thinks: "I should now practice desirelessness, abandon unwholesome states, and attain the state of happiness" (this is the third phrase;
the phrasing lacks logical sequence). Regarding the third triad, he again thinks: "Could it be that by this [practice] I am merely tormenting my own body?"

"One attains the Dharma of happiness" (this is the first phrase; while there is no [explicit] principle in the text, the meaning exists). Again, one reflects: "However, I do not attain the Dharma of happiness by thus afflicting my own body" (this is the second phrase;
it is explicitly present in the text). Again, one reflects: "I would rather now relinquish this body that afflicts itself in order to attain the Dharma of happiness" (this is the third phrase;
while there is no [explicit] principle in the text, the meaning exists). Regarding the fourth triad: again, one reflects: "Could it be that through food..."
"Could a small amount of rice and parched grain suffice to sustain my strength? (This is the first sentence; it exists in meaning but not in the text. He further thought:

"Indeed, it is certainly by eating a small amount of rice and parched grain that I have obtained sustenance for my strength. (This is the first sentence; it exists in meaning but not in the text. He further thought:
"Should I now eat a small amount of rice and parched grain to obtain sustenance for my strength? (This is the third sentence; it is found within the text.)

Regarding the *Kāraṇaprajñapti* and other sūtras which state that he consumed cow’s milk gruel, and other sūtras where he is seen wearing celestial robes (*divyavastra*) and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 38, says: “The Sūtra states:
‘I shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree; from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, [the gods] shall provide me with celestial robes as a seat.’”
"One should study the Prajñāpāramitā. The commentary says: Question: As stated in the sūtras, the Buddha sat beneath a tree on spread grass and attained the Way of Buddhahood;
why now do you say he sat upon celestial robes? Answer: In the Śrāvaka sūtras, it is said that he spread grass.
In the Mahāyāna sūtras, it is according to what sentient beings perceive: some see him spreading grass beneath a tree, while others see him spreading celestial [robes].
The *ruǎnrǎn* (fringed and embroidered) [robes] vary according to the amount of one's merit; thus, what is seen differs. (And so forth...

Such precious robes are spread out as seats, and when a Bodhisattva sits upon these seats, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. (Commentary: Regarding the phrase "I shall [sit] beneath the Bodhi tree," etc.:
This reveals the bodhisattva’s generation of the vow.

Regarding the phrase "seated upon the great precious lotus-king throne" and so forth: it means that within the Mahāyāna, the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) dwells upon the great precious lotus-king throne and attains perfect enlightenment.
Thus, the tenth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The self-enjoyment body, in turn, relies upon..."

"His own land" (this refers to the body itself, manifesting the land in which he dwells) means the pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (this identifies the transforming consciousness).
Through the maturation of the causes and conditions for his own self-benefiting, untainted cultivation in the past (this reveals the seeds of the pure land within the pure consciousness),

from the moment of his initial attainment of Buddhahood until the end of the future, it continuously transforms into a purely immaculate Buddha-land (this reveals that by the power of the pure consciousness and the aforementioned causal seeds, from the very beginning...).

Having attained Buddhahood, he will continue to manifest transformed pure lands in succession until the end of the future. Regarding these pure lands, as explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and other texts, they are collectively subsumed under eighteen types of perfection.
However, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* provides three interpretations: first, that this [pure land] is subsumed within the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) realm;
second, that it is subsumed within the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) realm; and third, that according to the true meaning, it belongs to Śākyamuni...
When the Bhikṣuṇī preached this sūtra, the great assembly prior to the stages (bhūmi) saw the *nirmāṇakāya* residing in this defiled land preaching the Dharma to them;

the great assembly of those who have reached the stages (bhūmi) saw the *saṃbhogakāya* residing in the Buddha’s pure land preaching the Dharma to them. Although what they heard was the same, what they saw differed for each.
According to the interpretation of the orthodox school (*siddhāntavādin*) in that treatise, those prior to the stages do not see the pure [land] at all.

The Land. When the great assembly on the earth beholds this pure land, it should be understood that, according to that treatise, this refers generally to both the self-enjoyment and other-enjoyment lands.
It is logical that the self-enjoyment land must also necessarily possess the eighteen perfections.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* explains the self-enjoyment land as follows: "It is circular and boundless, adorned with various jewels; the self-enjoyment body constantly relies upon it."
[The Buddha] dwells. (Commentary: This briefly demonstrates two of the eighteen perfections (*aṣṭādaśa-sampad*), namely, the perfection of measure and the perfection of support.
Since his own land already possesses these two perfections, what prevents there being the remaining sixteen, making eighteen in total?
The eighteen perfections are: first, the perfection of color; second, the perfection of shape; third, the perfection of measure.
1. The four directions; 2. Causes; 3. Effects; 4. The principal; 5. Aids; 6. Retinue; 7.
Sustenance; 8. Activities; 9. Encompassment; 10. Non-differentiation; 11. Abode; 12. Path; 13. Vehicle.
Seventeen topics and eighteen bases; summarized in verse: Manifestation, form, dimensions, and shape;
Cause, fruit, master, retinue, and attendants; Sustenance, activity, parasols, fearlessness, Abodes, paths, vehicles, gates, and bases.

The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "The Bhagavān dwells in a most supreme, radiant palace, adorned with the seven treasures, emitting great light that illuminates all boundless worlds—this refers to the perfection of color (the manifestation of hue).

That is to say, the great palace is adorned with the seven treasures of most supreme radiance; alternatively, because the great palace itself is adorned with the seven treasures, it is 'most supreme and radiant.
It is situated in immeasurable locations, with exquisite decorations arranged in rows—this refers to the perfection of form (color and shape). It is like the countless cities within our own country."

The city is arranged in its proper place. The Dharma Master Ximing said: "As for 'place' (fangsu), it refers to things such as the ornamental coffer ceilings (*qijing*). [Now, examining this, I find he has lost the intended meaning. It is circular and boundless; its measure is difficult to fathom (this refers to the perfection of its dimensions.

Alternatively, it means the circumference is difficult to fathom, or the extent of the sūtras is difficult to fathom). It transcends the spheres traversed by the three realms (this refers to the perfection of its location.

For instance, the three realms are the spheres traversed by the craving of their respective levels, and they are also where objective conditions and associated fetters increase in strength. Furthermore, they are the two types of resultant dharmas—maturation and dominant results. This Pure Land, however, is not..."

Because it is the sphere of activity for those three types [of beings], it is said to be "transcendent. It arises from supramundane roots of goodness (this is the perfection of the cause). According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the attainment of wisdom constitutes this pure land; it is the cause for the manifestation and arising of the land.

According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is established by means of both fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). It has the most supreme mastery of pure consciousness as its characteristic (this is the perfection of the fruit);

that is to say, while all phenomena have consciousness as their essential nature, this pure land has the Buddha’s untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) as its essential nature. It is the capital where the Tathāgata resides (this is the perfection of the lord). This land...
Because he is the Lord [it is so]. The great assembly of Bodhisattvas has gathered like clouds (this is the perfection of the retinue of attendants).

Immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth, up to humans and non-humans, constantly follow and serve him (this is the perfection of the entourage). According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, these manifestations are not real. Inferring from the underlying meaning:

if one considers his own land, the bodhisattvas and others are also the Buddha’s manifestations. This is because they adorn the land; as for that land itself, only a Buddha and a Buddha can truly know it. It is filled with the joy and bliss of the flavor of the vast Dharma.

Maintaining [this is the perfection of abiding; it is the "food of the joy of Dharma and the delight of dhyāna" from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*]. Manifesting all benefit and welfare for sentient beings [this is the perfection of activity;

it refers to the Buddha’s activity of transforming beings. "Manifest benefit" is called "benefit," while "future benefit" is called "welfare"]. Extinguishing the crosswise entanglements of all afflictions [this is the perfection of gathering and benefiting. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Furthermore, because one manifests the attainment of liberation from afflictions and entanglements, as well as superior merit and wisdom, it is called 'gathering and benefiting'"]. Remaining far removed from all māras [this is fearlessness].

It is also complete. That is to say, it is free from the four māras as adversaries. It is the locus of the Tathāgata’s adornments, surpassing all other adornments; this is the perfection of the dwelling place.

It transcends the abodes adorned by bodhisattvas; it is an abode adorned solely by the wondrous ornaments of the Tathāgata. Great mindfulness, wisdom, and conduct constitute its pathways (this refers to the perfection of the path).

"Great mindfulness" is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); "great wisdom" is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Both of these possess the dominant karmic activity of fashioning the pure land, and thus are both termed "conduct. It is through these two wisdoms that one universally takes birth in the pure land.

Therefore, it is called the "path of travel. Great tranquility (*śamatha*) and sublime insight (*vipaśyanā*) serve as the vehicle (the perfection of the vehicle; by mounting this tranquility and insight, one traverses the aforementioned path).

The liberations of great emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness serve as the gate of entry (the perfection of the gate; the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "One enters the Pure Land by relying on this gate," and further states:

"Within this Pure Land, there must also be paths, vehicles, and gates, which are taught in terms of practice so that sentient beings may delight in its true virtues"). It is a great jewel flower adorned with an immeasurable multitude of merits.

Within the great palace established by the assembly of kings (this refers to the perfection of the support: it has as its support a great precious red lotus king produced from immeasurable merits and various virtues, just as the great earth rests upon the wind-circle and so forth.

Regarding the "great precious lotus king": among all flowers, this is the most excellent, thus it is called the "flower king. Alternatively, because the Tathāgata is named the "King," and this great precious lotus king possesses such a king, it is named after that king.

Regarding "established by the assembly": these flowers are not singular; because there are many petals, they are called an "assembly. Because one relies upon this lotus king continuously for a long time, it is called "established"). These eighteen.
The sūtra text is complete, as found in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
A detailed explanation of its characteristics is set forth in the first and second volumes of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and the tenth volume of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*.

Regarding the statement that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* rely on the eight meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and so forth: the three stages of worthiness prior to the [ten] grounds constitute the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.

As for what are called the "three worthies," the first consists of the ten abodes (*vihāra*): (1) the abode of generating the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda-vihāra*), (2) the abode of purifying the ground (*viśuddhi-bhūmi-vihāra*), (3) the abode of cultivation (*caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*), (4) the abode of noble birth (*janma-udāra-vihāra*), (5) the abode of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-vihāra*), and (6) the abode of correct mind (*samyak-citta-vihāra*).

The seventh is the stage of non-retrogression (*avivartika-vihāra*). The eighth is the stage of youthful truth (*kumārabhūta-vihāra*). The ninth is the stage of the Dharma-Prince (*dharmarāja-putra-vihāra*). The tenth is the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*). The second decas [of practices] consists of: (1) the practice of joy (*pramuditā-caryā*); (2) the practice of benefit through circumambulation (*vicitrārtha-caryā*); (3) the practice free from malice and resentment (*avyāpāda-caryā*); (4) the inexhaustible practice (*akṣaya-caryā*);

(5) the practice free from delusion and confusion (*vigata-moha-saṃmoha-caryā*); (6) the practice of excellent manifestation (*sudarśana-caryā*); (7) the practice of non-attachment (*asaṅga-caryā*); (8) the noble and honorable practice (*ārya-vaṃśa-caryā*); (9) the practice of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-caryā*); and (10) the practice of reality (*tattva-caryā*). The third decas [of dedications] consist of:

(1) the dedication characterized by the protection and rescue of all sentient beings; (2) the indestructible dedication (*avināśana-pariṇāmanā*); (3) the dedication equal to all Buddhas; (4) the dedication reaching all places; (5) the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit; (6) the dedication of roots of goodness that are equal according to needs; (7) the dedication according to... [text truncated]

(8) dedication by observing all sentient beings in accordance with [their needs]; 9) dedication of the mark of suchness; 10) dedication of liberation without bondage or attachment; and 10) dedication to the immeasurable dharma-realm).

Next, from the first stage through the end of the seventh stage constitutes the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa. From the eighth stage through the end of the tenth stage constitutes the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
Regarding the "eight concentrations," there are four cultivated prior to the stages and four on the stages themselves, totaling eight.

Regarding the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), first to distinguish the stages: as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), Chapter Nine, one cultivates the four types of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*) and the four types of knowledge of reality-as-it-is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*) during the four stages beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

The four thorough investigations are: 1. Thorough investigation of names (*nāma-paryeṣaṇā*); 2. Thorough investigation of objects (*artha-paryeṣaṇā*); 3. Thorough investigation of the intrinsic nature of names and objects (*svabhāva-paryeṣaṇā*);

4. Thorough investigation of the distinctions between names and objects (*viśeṣa-paryeṣaṇā*). Contemplating these four objects as being conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent is called the four thorough investigations.

Contemplation: Contemplating the absence of an object of apprehension through inferior investigation is established as the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). Contemplating the absence of an object of apprehension through superior investigation is established as the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).
Regarding the four kinds of knowledge of reality (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*), these also take names and objects, as well as their intrinsic nature and distinctions, as their objects;

they consist in the thorough knowledge that both the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*) are empty. This is knowledge of reality. Among these, the inferior level is established as the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*). If it is superior...
Regarding the "stages" (*pakṣa*): the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) is established. These four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), in their respective order, are designated as follows:

first, based on the *ālokalabdha-samādhi*, because one initially attains the precursor to the sun of wisdom, it is named "Attainment of Light. Next, based on the *vṛddhāloka-samādhi*, because the signs of light become increasingly intense, it is named "Increase of Light.

Next, based on the *tattvārtha-ekadeśapraviṣṭānusāri-samādhi*, because one definitively confirms and maintains the absence of the grasped (*grāhya*) and within the absence of the grasper (*grāhaka*), [it is named "Entry into One Part of Reality"].

It is also in accordance with "patience" (*kṣānti*). It seals what precedes and accords with what follows; thus it is established as "seal" (*mudrā*) and "accordance" (*anuloma*). Next, based on the "uninterrupted concentration" (*ānantarya-samādhi*), it doubly seals the emptiness of both the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*).
Because one necessarily enters the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) immediately following this, it is called "uninterrupted.

That is to say, in the preceding stage of patience, there are three grades in total. At the time of "lower patience," one seals the aspect of the emptiness of the object. At the time of "middle patience," regarding the emptiness of the apprehending subject—
One accords with and accepts [the truth] through the patience of pleasure (*sukha-kṣānti*). At the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one seals the absence of a grasper (*grāhaka*);

now, at the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), one seals both types of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) simultaneously. Therefore, they are not the same. Regarding these four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*), the masters of former generations have provided approximately four interpretations. Master Chang said:
These four roots of goodness are assigned, in their respective order, to the forty mental stages prior to the [ten] bhūmis.

That is to say, according to the *Bunyue Yingluo Jing* (Sutra of the Necklace of the Original Vow), ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*)—namely: (1) faith, (2) mindfulness, (3) diligence, (4) wisdom, (5) concentration, (6) non-retrogression, (7) dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), (8) protection of the Dharma, (9) precept, and (10) vow—are added before the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).
Master Xiu states that the ten abidings constitute "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) constitute "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), and the ninth dedication constitutes...

This constitutes the perfection of patience. The tenth dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is the foremost. The Master Shi (Śīla) states that within the final stage of the tenth dedication, the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*) are opened.
The intention of the Tripitaka Master of the Tang [Dynasty] is to adopt the Master Shi’s view as the correct interpretation;

this refers to the end of the tenth dedication during the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, which is the "subsequent mind" (*anuparivartin-citta*). To distinguish the stages of the *bhūmis*, there are again four fixed positions, which are also as described in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle nine, explains: first, the Samādhi of the Great Vehicle’s Radiance (*mahāyāna-prabhāsvara-samādhi*), so called because it can produce the light of wisdom that illuminates and realizes the principles, teachings, practices, and fruits of the Great Vehicle;
second, the Samādhi of the King Who Accumulates Merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra-rāja-samādhi*), so called because it sovereignly accumulates boundless merit.

First is the concentration of royal power, because its sovereign force is without equal. Second is the concentration of guarding the virtuous, because it can guard both mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas.
Third is the concentration of heroic conduct, because it is the practice of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and other great heroic beings.
The Dharma Master Ximing said: Regarding these four concentrations (*samādhi*), if one were to distinguish their stages (*bhūmi*), no explicit textual evidence has been seen.

The various masters of old have taught that the first four stages are called the "Light of the Mahāyāna" (*Mahāyānaprabhāsa*); the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages are called the "King of Accumulated Merit" (*Puṇyasambhararāja*);

the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages are called the "Worthy Protector" (*Bhadrapāla*); and the Vajra stage, as well as those of the Tathāgatas, are called the "Courageous Progression" (*Vikrāntagāmin*) concentration. Now, examining this in detail... [text continues].

However, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* explains that within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one gradually cultivates the ten perfections (*pāramitā*). It further distinguishes the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) as a means of subsuming these ten perfections.

Among these, the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) constitute the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), and this training in concentration is itself subsumed under the perfection of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).

Since meditative absorption occurs in the fifth stage, that treatise analyzes its inclusion through four gates: first, inclusion by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-saṃgraha*), which refers to the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).

First, by way of inclusion: the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) includes only itself; meditative concentration (*samādhi*) includes the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna*); and wisdom (*prajñā*) includes the final five (namely, skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge). Second, by way of including both [the primary and its attendants]:

the three perfections [of giving, discipline, and patience] together with their attendants include all ten perfections. Third, by way of inclusion according to function: the first three [perfections] include the perfection of ethical discipline; meditative concentration includes the perfection of meditation.

Wisdom (*prajñā*) subsumes the latter five [perfections]. All three [of the first three] subsume diligence (*vīrya*). The fourth [perfection, patience] is subsumed according to its manifest expression. Ethical discipline (*śīla*) subsumes the former four;

meditative concentration (*samādhi*) subsumes dhyāna; and wisdom subsumes the latter five. According to their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the door of manifest expression, these four concentrations are restricted to the five stages (*bhūmi*).

If categorized according to the gate of function, it extends through the fourth and fifth stages; if categorized according to the gate of companions, it extends through all ten stages. This is very clear in the treatise, so why is it not seen?
It is truly because the fifth stage is called "Extremely Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*); therein, the aspects of the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—are mutually contradictory.
Because a single wisdom simultaneously realizes both [aspects] and is thus extremely difficult to overcome, these four dhyānas serve as the basis for this wisdom.
Regarding the two pāramitās of dhyāna and prajñā as the third stage: this refers to the sixfold contemplation (ṣaḍvidhābhāvanā) that is still with outflows (sāsrava). Question:

Since it was previously established at the site of Rājagṛha that he had already entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), it is clear that he had already abandoned the afflictions of the lower eight stages; why, then, does this begin here?
Regarding the statement "cultivating dhyāna": Furthermore, for those bodhisattvas of immovable lineage (*akopya-gotra*), there must first be a falling away (*parihāṇi*).

For what reason is this so? The answer is: In reality, they had already attained the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) at a prior time; however, for bodhisattvas, there is a specific sense of falling away. Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 61, states: "There are three kinds:

first, falling away from what has been attained (*prāptaparihāṇi*); second, falling away from what has not yet been attained (*aprāptaparihāṇi*); and third, falling away from enjoyment (*upabhogaparihāṇi*). It continues: "First..."

Regarding "those who fall back": this refers to those who have previously attained various superior virtues but subsequently regress due to encountering adverse conditions. Regarding "those who have not yet attained [regression]":
all sentient beings, if they were to apply themselves to the skillful means, would all be able to obtain the noble eye of wisdom;

however, because they do not diligently cultivate the correct skillful means, they have not attained clear realization regarding the Four Noble Truths, and thus there is a regression from the non-attainment of the noble eye of wisdom. This is what is meant by "receiving [the state of non-attainment]."
Regarding "regression" (*parihāṇi*): it refers to the non-manifestation of various superior qualities already attained. Thus, there are three types of regression.
For a Buddha, there is only one type, namely "regression from enjoyment" (*upabhogaparihāṇi*), because the qualities he has attained may fail to manifest. For a Pratyekabuddha, there are two types:

first, "regression from non-attainment" (*aprāptaparihāṇi*), and second, "regression from enjoyment. Among Śrāvakas, those who are "liberated at any time" (*asamayavimukta*) have two types [just as the Pratyekabuddhas].
[The Master] Buddhadatta says: At that time, liberation possesses all three [types]. Some say: "The Buddha never regresses at all" (and so forth). The critique states:

The first explanation is correct, because it is certain that all Buddhas experience a regression from the enjoyment [of meditative attainments]. According to this, although he had previously attained dhyāna, he now wishes to bring it into manifest enjoyment;
thus he practices it again to cause it to arise. This is because the concentration of all Bodhisattvas necessarily relies upon the fundamental fourth *dhyāna*.

One arouses the path of outflowlessness through the dhyānas; by means of thirty-four moments of mind, one attains Buddhahood in a single sitting. Therefore, it is necessary to cause those dhyānas to manifest before one, and thus there is no contradiction with reason.
This "actual sound dhyāna" (mauladhyāna) is called "cultivation through reflection" (*cintābhāvanā*); it refers to the meaning of the factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*).
For details, see the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicles 33 and 11; the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, fascicle 19; the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle 9; the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle 18;
the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicles 80 and 81; the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, fascicle 28; the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 77; and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 100.

From fifty-seven onwards is the *Samādhi-skandha* (Aggregate of Concentration). While its various distinctions were explained extensively above, they shall now be briefly analyzed through a threefold classification:

first, the explanation of names; second, the essential nature and characteristics; third, the establishment and exclusion [of categories]. Regarding the explanation of names, I shall first list them and then explain them.
To list the names, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "In the first *dhyāna*, there are five factors: vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and samādhi. The second...

The second [dhyāna] has four factors: internal clarity, joy, bliss, and concentration. The third possesses five factors: equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, bliss, and concentration. The fourth has four factors:
equanimity, mindfulness, neutral sensation, and concentration. The *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "Regarding the establishment of the factors: the first dhyāna has five factors.
What are the five? First, vitarka; second, vicāra; third, prīti; fourth, sukha; fifth, one-pointedness of mind. The second...
The second dhyāna has four factors: first, internal serenity; second, joy; third, bliss; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind. The third dhyāna has five factors:
first, equanimity; second, mindfulness; third, clear comprehension; fourth, bliss; and fifth, one-pointedness of mind. The fourth dhyāna has four factors:
first, purity of equanimity; second, purity of mindfulness; and third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The one-pointedness of the four minds. The enumeration of names in the *Vibhāṣā* (vol. 80) is identical [to this].

Although there are slight differences between the tenets of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools, the names and the number of factors are both exactly eighteen. Next, regarding the explanation of the name:

in Sanskrit it is called *dhyāna*, which here is translated as "meditative concentration" (*jinglü*). The old term "chan-na" is an error. It is translated as "contemplative cultivation" (*sīwéi xiū*), or alternatively as "grove of the accumulation of merit."

These are all translations based on meaning. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 80, states: "Question: For what reason are they called 'limbs of dhyāna' (*dhyānāṅga*)? What is the meaning of 'limbs of dhyāna'? Answer:
Because one calmly contemplates (*praśānta-cintana*), it is called 'dhyāna. Because they accord with this dhyāna, they are called 'limbs of dhyāna.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* asks: "Based on what meaning is the name 'dhyāna' established? It answers: "Because by means of this [state], one is able to be calm..."

"Because it is investigative (*vicāra*). 'Investigative' means that which truly understands. [The commentary] states: The essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is tranquility, while wisdom (*prajñā*) further investigates.
Because of both concentration and wisdom, it is called "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*). In the Sanskrit original, it is *dhyāna*; here it is translated as "investigative.
This refers to the etymological root (*dhātu*) of the word. In the Sanskrit, it is *dhyai*; this refers to the verbal root (*prakṛti*). Within this etymological root of the word *dhyai*...
The term *dhyāna* is established as a boundary for the assistance of the syllables; it is translated here as "meditative concentration" (*ting zhu*).
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* raises an objection: "If that were so, all states of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) should be called 'meditative concentration'.

The intent of this objection is that if "tranquil wisdom" is what constitutes meditative concentration, then since the various concentrations of the eight stages are also all accompanied by wisdom, they should all be designated as "meditative concentration. The explanation says: "As for all these absorptions..."

Regarding the middle [dhyāna]: it is established as having five factors and four factors. Because calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) proceed in equal measure, it alone is designated by the name "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*) based on its preeminence.
This is like the worldly expression that the sun is called "the light-emitter," whereas fireflies and candles do not receive the name "sun."

Regarding the second [topic], the essential nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*): first, having briefly defined the characteristics by citing the titles of new sūtras and śāstras, one subsequently defines the essential nature.

To begin with, regarding the citation of sūtras, the second chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* cites a sūtra for its explanation. Furthermore, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicles 80 and 81, it says:
"As stated in the Sūtra: 'O Bhikṣus, you should know that there are four paths to heaven which can cause those who are not yet purified to become pure.'"

This becomes further clarified: namely, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and possessing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, one dwells having fully attained the first *dhyāna*.

This is called the first heavenly path. Furthermore, with the subsiding of directed and sustained thought, with internal clarity and mental unification, without directed or sustained thought, and possessing the joy and happiness born of concentration, one dwells having fully attained the second *dhyāna*. This is called the second [heavenly path].
The Celestial Path. Furthermore, being detached from joy, one dwells in equanimity, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body;
this is what the Noble Ones describe as dwelling in the perfection of the third dhyāna. This is called the third celestial path. The *Xianyang lun* (Manifestation of the Teachings) states:

"Detached from joy, one dwells in equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, and experiences happiness with the body through right reception. The Noble Ones proclaim this as the attainment of dwelling in happiness through equanimity and mindfulness. The third [dhyāna].
He dwells having fully attained the fourth dhyāna, wherein pleasure and pain have been abandoned, and previous joy and sorrow have vanished;
it is neither painful nor pleasant, but is the purity of equanimity and mindfulness. This is called the fourth path to heaven. If one wishes to explain the Vinaya:

He then took the *Vinaya* text and, reproducing it here as it stands, provided an explanation. Taking this scriptural passage as his basis, he established the definitive interpretation according to the tenets of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools.
The intended meaning of the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "First, regarding 'separation from sensual desires and unwholesome states' within the first dhyāna:
'sensual desires' refers to the desire for objects and the desire for their possession; the remaining afflictions are termed 'unwholesome.'"

Furthermore, "desire" refers to the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). "Evil and unwholesome" refers to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). Furthermore, "desire" refers to sensual craving (*kāmarāga*).

"Evil and unwholesome" refers to the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*) within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). A detailed explanation is as found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 33. The intent is that there are two kinds of desire:
first, the desire of affliction (*kleśa-kāma*); second, the desire for objects (*vastu-kāma*). This [classification] comprehensively subsumes the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
First, the explanation: Furthermore, it is said that "detachment" (viveka) is twofold: first, detachment from association; second, detachment from objects.
These correspond respectively to severing the bond of association and severing the bond of conditions. Regarding "detachment from evil and unwholesome [actions]":

those unwholesome bodily and vocal actions produced by the desire of the afflictions—such as bearing clubs, bearing swords, feigning, and speaking falsehoods—are called "unwholesome. This, together with...

The minor schools differ on this point. Regarding the statement that there are "with vitarka and with vicāra," the *Vibhāṣā* explains that dharmas which coexist with vitarka and coexist with vicāra are termed "with vitarka and vicāra.
However, in the minor schools, vitarka and vicāra are distinct mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) with their own separate essential natures (*svabhāva*).
In the Mahāyāna school, vitarka and vicāra are provisionally established upon volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); apart from volition and wisdom, they have no separate existence.
Regarding vitarka and vicāra: according to the tenets of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, there are no separate vitarka and vicāra apart from the mind.

For this reason, the Sarvāstivādins maintain that they arise simultaneously with the mind within a single moment of consciousness. The fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains it as follows: "It is like [the sensation of] coldness upon water."
It floats upon clarified butter (*sarpis*). When struck by the intense rays of the sun above, the butter—due to both the water and the sun—is neither melted nor solidified.
In this same way, the mind that possesses vitarka and vicāra does not transcend coarseness and subtlety because of those very vitarka and vicāra. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Yoga-bhāṣya) states:

Regarding "with vitarka and vicāra": because one has not yet perceived the faults of vitarka and vicāra, and because that stage still possesses wholesome vitarka and vicāra that serve as antidotes to those of the desire realm, it is called "with vitarka and vicāra.
As for the term "born of seclusion" (*vivekaja*), one explanation in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

within the stage of the first dhyāna, one is able to become free from all faculties of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), as well as the faculties of [gender]—male, female, and the faculty of life.
Because shame (*hrī*) and so forth are free from the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the five desires (*kāmaguṇa*), and the like, they alone are termed "detachment" (*viveka*).

Although the stages of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bhūmi*) mentioned above also arise from detachment, because this [first stage] stands at the beginning, it alone receives the name. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains that "detachment" refers to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*);
because the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises immediately after it as its cause, it is called "arising. This meaning is the same as in the *Abhidharma-kośa*.

"Sha" is an abbreviation for "Śākyamuni. Regarding the terms "joy" (*prīti*) and "bliss" (*sukha*): according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, because one has already attained pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), the body and mind are harmonized and become functional;
therefore, they are termed "joy and bliss. According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, that which delights the side of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) is called "joy."
That which delights the ālayavijñāna is called "pleasure" (*sukha*), because the material body is sustained by the ālaya.

As for the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that "one who has attained pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*) manifests the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) and the harmonious adjustment of body and mind, this is as explained in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.

The Sarvāstivāda school, however, differs from this; according to that Lesser Vehicle school, pleasure is pliancy, whereas joy (*prīti*) is a category of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), and thus they do not agree with the Mahāyāna.
The essence of joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) is one; however, when it refers to the physical body, it is called bliss, and when it refers to the mental side, it is called joy.

According to the intent of the *Tattvasiddhi* school, this is largely the same as in the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains: "Initial" (*ādi*) means first obtaining it at the very beginning;
it is named "initial" according to its numerical sequence. As for "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*), it means fixing the mind in silent stillness upon a single object of focus.
Regarding "endowed": it means that because one has attained the path of liberation, one is so equipped. Regarding "abiding":
it means that because one has accomplished [the practice], one attains ease, such that one can remain correctly settled for up to seven days. Next, the second dhyāna is explained.
Regarding "the cessation of vitarka and vicāra and internal serenity": the meaning of yoga is that one is able to correctly distance oneself from agitated objects and abides in unagitated objects.

That mind is of a single flavor and tranquil; this is called "inner serenity through the cessation of applied and sustained thought. Regarding the term "busyness," it means that applied and sustained thought cause the mind to be busy.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: Question: Upon attaining the second dhyāna, are all dharmas of the first dhyāna completely severed?
Why is it said that only vitarka and vicāra are extinguished? Answer: Because these are the primary factors; by their total extinction, the remaining dharmas are also extinguished.
Furthermore, vitarka and vicāra are difficult to sever, difficult to destroy, and difficult to transcend; therefore, they are mentioned specifically. This is explained at length in that [text].

Regarding the *vibhāṣā*’s explanation of "internal serenity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*): "internal" refers to the mind; "serenity" refers to faith (*śraddhā*). Because faith brings about equilibrium, it causes the internal mind to be serene; thus it is so named.

Regarding "inner serenity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*): according to the Mahāyāna, inner serenity has three factors as its essence. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (63) and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (19) state:
Question: What factors constitute the essence of inner serenity? Answer: It has mindfulness (*smṛti*), clear comprehension (*samprajanya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) as its essence.
Based on what was previously stated, one causes the mind to abide in a state that is not agitated by objects, [experiencing] a single flavor (*ekarasa*).

"Tranquility" is termed "inner serenity. Regarding "one-pointedness of mind," the *Yogācārabhūmi* explains: having transcended applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and the state of interruption, one is able to correctly attain the state of non-interruption;
therefore, it is called "one-pointedness of mind. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:

it refers to dwelling in a continuous succession for the most part at the time of entry, such that various phenomena of applied and sustained thought do not constantly manifest. This is the "one-pointedness of mind" according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

This refers to "turning through a single gate. For example, while the mind of the desire realm turns through six gates, and the mind of the first dhyāna turns through four gates, the mind of the second dhyāna now turns through only one gate;
therefore, it is called "one-pointed" (*ekāyana*). According to the Mahāyāna interpretation, it is called "one-pointed" because it is free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*);
this carries the meaning of being focused and serene. Now, in the Hīnayāna, it is simply stated as "one gate," [referring to] the *araṇa* [samādhi].

The [defilements] are not exhausted by mere suppression; for although they may be transformed within a single door, they can still persist as more than one stream. As for "without investigation" (*avitarka*), it is because both have been severed.

Regarding the term "born of concentration" (*samādhija*), the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that "concentration" refers to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), while "born" refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks: "Since the first dhyāna also possesses concentration, why is the second alone called 'born of concentration'? The intended answer is that this [second dhyāna] is equal to...
Because it maintains and increases [the meditative state] beyond the first dhyāna, it is specifically mentioned.

Furthermore, because it manifests immediately after the first dhyāna, it is not the same as the initial state that is not induced by concentration, and so forth, as explained at length therein. Regarding "joy, bliss," and so on, they should be understood according to the preceding explanation.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Joy" (*prīti*) refers to the faculty of joy (*prītīndriya*), which is subsumed under the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). "Bliss" (*sukha*) refers to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), which is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
This differs from the Mahāyāna, as has already been explained above. Next, regarding the explanation of the third dhyāna, the term "detached from joy" (*prīti-viveka*) is used.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because he perceives deep faults in the characteristics of joy, it is said that he is 'detached from joy. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "With joy as the primary factor, [he] is detached from it in its entirety."

Regarding the remaining factors, it is further stated that joy (*prīti*) is difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend; these points should be understood as previously explained.

As for "abiding in equanimity" (*upekṣā*), the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: at that time, having abandoned the two types of disturbances of the mind—namely, applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and joy—one is able to maintain the mind within the second dhyāna;
therefore, it is called "abiding in equanimity. Because of this equanimity, one dwells securely in right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).

One does not practice joy. If it is not well-cultivated, or if mindfulness is occasionally lost, one immediately and swiftly recognizes this; thus, there is correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Equanimity" refers to equanimity as a mental formation (*upekṣā-saṃskāra*); "mindfulness" refers to wholesome mindfulness; and "wisdom" refers to wholesome wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "the body experiences bliss," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "Free from joy and tranquil—extremely tranquil—the experience of feeling arises in the mind. At that time, both the physical body and the mental body [experience it]."
Because one experiences the pleasure of sensation (*vedanā*) as well as the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), it is said that "the body experiences pleasure. The commentary states:

Both the satisfaction of the physical body (*rūpakāya*) and the mental body (*manaskāya*) are termed "pleasure" (*sukha*). This differs from the lower stages, where satisfaction of the mind is called "joy" (*prīti*).

Because that [joy] involves agitation and leaping, which are defects, it is not an ultimate satisfaction of the mind and thus cannot be termed "pleasure. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* shares this intent; therefore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* says: "Free from goodness, free from..."

"Courageously and at ease one experiences [it]; because it is subsumed under feeling (*vedanā*), it is called 'pleasure' (*sukha*). Regarding "The Noble Ones should speak of equanimity (*upekṣā*)," the intention of the Mahāyāna is that the Noble Ones should proclaim it;
the word "equanimity" is drawn down to connect with the subsequent explanation. The intention of the *Yogācārabhūmi* is that what follows explains the stages (*bhūmi*).

There is no such pleasure, nor is there uninterrupted equanimity (*sāntara-vairāgya*—that which flows constantly is called "uninterrupted"; this does not preclude the existence of interrupted equanimity belonging to lower stages).
Although the third dhyāna and those above it possess uninterrupted equanimity, they lack pleasure.
Therefore, regarding this stage, the Buddha and his disciples—the various noble ones (*ārya*)—should proclaim [its excellence]. The intention of the *Vibhāṣā* is that "noble" refers to all...
The Buddha and his disciples should explain this to others, while they themselves should abide in equanimity (*upekṣā*). Question: All stages (*bhūmi*) should be explained;
why is only the third stage mentioned? Answer: Within the third dhyāna, there are obstacles pertaining to both one’s own stage and other stages;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned. Regarding the obstacles of other stages: in the second dhyāna, one is swept away by joy (*prīti*), like a *rākṣasa* (masculine).

They are called *rākṣasa*; now, calling them with a feminine voice refers to *rākṣasī*. Within the great ocean, they manifest seductive forms and request men as husbands; the foolish are enticed and are then devoured.
Because this can cause a yoga practitioner to fall away from detachment in the second dhyāna, it should be described as "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).

As for what is called "the obstacle of its own stage," it is the bliss of the third dhyāna. Among the pleasures of saṃsāra, this bliss is the most supreme; thus, all yoga practitioners become attached to it.

Regarding this bliss, one does not seek a higher or superior state; it should also be described as equanimity (*upekṣā*). However, the intention of the *Yogācāra* is to explain its specific distinctions, and thus the Noble One proclaimed it as such.

The intention of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is to eliminate obstacles, and thus the Noble One spoke of "equanimity. These are not the same. In the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), the cited sūtra contains only the word "equanimity," which is still construed with what precedes it.
In the Mahāyāna, the cited sūtra says, "dwelling in bliss with equanimity and mindfulness" (*upekṣā-smṛti-sukha-vihāra*), which construes [the term] with that which follows.
The following is the explanation. The *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Manifestation of the Dharma) clarifies the meaning as follows: "In the higher stages there is no such bliss;

in the lower stages there is no such superior bliss, nor is there the equanimity and mindfulness that serve as remedial factors. Therefore, this stage is called 'dwelling in bliss through equanimity and mindfulness.
The third dhyāna, being fully established, should be understood by analogy with what precedes it. Next, the fourth dhyāna is explained: one abandons pleasure (*sukha*).
Regarding the phrase "having abandoned suffering, and with prior joy and sorrow extinguished," the intent of the *Yogācārabhūmi* is as follows:

If one were to follow the standard description of the third dhyāna, it should state that "one abandons pleasure, dwells in equanimity (*upekṣā*), and possesses right mindfulness (*smṛti*) and right clear comprehension (*samprajanya*). However, instead of making such a statement, it directly says "abandoning pleasure, abandoning suffering," and so forth.
This is because the equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension are capable of abandoning the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), and thus their nature is similar to that of the third dhyāna.
Therefore, it is not mentioned in detail; rather, one speaks directly of the pleasure that is abandoned, hence the expression "abandoning pleasure.
