At that very moment, all suffering and pleasure—sorrow being subsumed under suffering and joy under pleasure—are entirely transcended. Thus, it is stated collectively as "abandoning pleasure and abandoning suffering," wherein prior joy and sorrow have already subsided.
This refers to the time of entering the fourth dhyāna, when pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is abandoned; [likewise,] upon entering the second dhyāna, suffering...
Because the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) has been abandoned, one enters the third dhyāna. Because the feeling of joy (*prīti-vedanā*) has subsided, one enters the first dhyāna;

because the feeling of grief (*daurmanasya-vedanā*) has subsided, it is further described as "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (*aduḥkhāsukha*). This is stated provisionally with reference to the abandonment of the four feelings;

in reality, however, all factors (*dharma*) of the lower stages are abandoned, not merely these four feelings. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "purity of equanimity and mindfulness" (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi*), it means that all calamities and afflictions of the lower stages have already been severed, namely, applied thought (*vitarka*).
[One] attends to joy and bliss. Because inhalation and exhalation (i.e., the six kinds of disturbances) [are present], it is said that "equanimity and mindfulness are purified.

If one follows the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the statement "abandoning pleasure" means that, taking pleasure as the primary factor, all [defilements] of the lower stages are abandoned in total;

furthermore, because the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is difficult to destroy, it should be understood according to the preceding [explanation]. Thus, pleasure is specifically abandoned. As for the statement "abandoning pain," this is said with respect to what has already been abandoned. Furthermore, based on...
Because the pair of dharmas is exhausted, both are said to be "abandoned. Regarding the "pair of dharmas," this refers to suffering and pleasure.

At the time of becoming free from the defilement of desire, although suffering has already been exhausted, pleasure has not yet been exhausted. Now, by becoming free from the defilement of the third dhyāna, both suffering and pleasure are exhausted;

therefore, they are spoken of as a pair. The detailed explanation is as in that [text]. As for the prior disappearance of sorrow and joy: at the time of becoming free from the defilement of desire, the faculty of sorrow has already disappeared.

Having become detached from the second defilement, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) has already subsided; therefore, it is said that "first, sorrow and joy subside. Regarding "purity of equanimity and mindfulness, neither-painful-nor-pleasant":

it is called "pure" because one is free from the eight disturbances. The eight disturbances are: pain, pleasure, sorrow, joy, inhalation, exhalation, applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
The phrases "dwelling fully endowed" and so forth should be understood according to the previous [explanation]. Although the general meaning is the same, [the details differ].
However, the statement that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is severed upon the departure from desire does not accord with the Mahāyāna.

According to the tenet of the Mahāyāna school, since the faculty of suffering exists within the stage of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*), although there is in fact no suffering in the first *dhyāna*, there are still three consciousnesses that serve as the basis for suffering.
There is also that which is called "incapacity" (*asamarthatā*). According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is extinguished only in the second dhyāna.

However, this differs slightly from the Mahāyāna; thus, the eighteenth chapter of that treatise, the "Chapter on the Second Dhyāna," states: "In the first dhyāna, joy (*prīti*) arises because sorrow (*daurmanasya*) has already been extinguished;

in the second dhyāna, joy arises because suffering has been extinguished. That same chapter further states: "The first dhyāna is proximate to the unconcentrated mind (*avyavasthita-citta*); it is not..."

One whose mind is concentrated can give rise to the various consciousnesses of the desire realm, within which suffering arises; therefore, it is not said that suffering is extinguished in the first dhyāna.
The commentary states: The intention of that school is to say that the first dhyāna and the distracted states of the desire realm are extremely close to one another.
Therefore, it enters into and emerges from the minds of the desire realm; thus it is said to be "proximate to the indeterminate mind.
Since suffering can arise within the indeterminate mind, the mind of the first dhyāna also possesses a state of insensitivity (akṣamatā), and is therefore also called "suffering. Thus it is said:
"It is only in the dhyānas that the faculty of suffering is severed. The above citation of the sūtra and brief explanation of its characteristics is concluded.

Next, to distinguish their essential natures (*svabhāva*): first, the one hundred dharmas of the Mahāyāna and the seventy-five dharmas of the Sarvāstivāda are enumerated, after which their natures are set forth.
Regarding the one hundred dharmas of the Mahāyāna: there are eight mental states (*citta-dharma*) and fifty-one associated mental factors (*caitta*), which are divided into six categories.

First, the five omnipresent factors (*sarvatraga*): contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). Second, the five object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyata*): desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), discernment (*mati*), and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Third...

The eleven universal wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*): faith, diligence, shame, embarrassment, the three roots beginning with non-attachment, pliancy, heedfulness, equanimity, and non-harming. The six universal defiled mental factors (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*):

attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, doubt, and incorrect views (which comprise the five views). The secondary defiled mental factors (*upakleśa-mahābhūmika*): anger, resentment, concealment, vexation, envy, parsimony, deceit, guile, harmfulness, lethargy, lack of shame, lack of embarrassment, and restlessness.

Lethargy, lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, loss of mindfulness, distraction, and lack of correct awareness. The sixth category consists of the four indeterminate factors: drowsiness, sleep, regret, and vitarka-vicāra (applied and sustained thought). There are eleven material phenomena:

the five sense faculties, the five objects, and matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). There are twenty-four formations dissociated from mind: acquisition, life-faculty, homogeneity, the state of being an ordinary person, the two meditative attainments, and the maturation of non-conception.

Name-bodies (*nāmakāya*), phrase-bodies (*padakāya*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), flux (*pravṛtti*), distinctness (*anyathātva*), association (*samyoga*), rapidity (*java*), sequence (*anukrama*), direction (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), number (*saṃkhyā*), conjunction (*sāmagrī*), and non-conjunction (*asāmagrī*). The six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are: space (*ākāśa*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the immovable (*āniñjya*), the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*), and suchness (*tathatā*).
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, there are seventy-five dharmas: eleven material phenomena (*rūpa*)—the five faculties, the five objects, and non-informative matter (*avijñapti*);

one mental phenomenon (*citta*)—the six consciousnesses treated as a single category; and forty-six mental concomitants (*caitasika*) comprising the five categories and the indeterminate stage. This constitutes the first [section].

1. The ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*)—that is, those that are pervasive in the Mahāyāna, as well as the object-specific factors (formerly termed "universal to the ground"). 2. The ten factors of the great wholesome ground (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*)—among the eleven [factors] in the Mahāyāna, this excludes "absence of doubt" (*anirvicikitsā*).

3. The six great afflictive factors (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*): ignorance (*avidyā*), negligence (*pramāda*), laziness (*kausīdya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).

4. The two great unwholesome factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*): shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). 5. The ten minor afflictions (*parītta-kleśabhūmika*)—these are the first ten among the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) in the Mahāyāna. 6. The indeterminate ground (*aniyata-bhūmi*).

Eight [factors] (the four external factors of the Mahāyāna, plus greed, hatred, pride, and doubt). Fourteen dissociated [factors] (acquisition, non-acquisition, homogeneity, the state of non-conception, the two meditative attainments, the life-faculty, the four characteristics, and the three—namely, the group of names and so forth).

The unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are three (namely, space and the two types of cessation). The above is a brief listing of their names; if one were to provide a brief explanation, it would be as recorded in the first fascicle.
Next, regarding the presentation of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), the treatise states: "The essence consists of nine [dharmas]; according to specific instances, there are eleven;
including the branches, there are eighteen. This is based, for the time being, on the Sarvāstivāda school. Among the seventy-five dharmas, nine dharmas constitute the essence, namely the universal...

1. The Universal Ground (*mahābhūmika*; specifically, the four factors taken from among the ten universal mental factors). "Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to the clear recollection of an object without forgetting it. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "It is the cause for not losing track of an object;

it consists of clearly recording the object as its condition, serving as the cause for non-forgetfulness in the future. 2. Concentration (*samādhi*). In the new [Tibetan] scriptures and treatises, this is called *samādhi*, which is translated here as "equipoise" (*samādhāna*). It is also termed "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*), or simply "concentration" (*dhyāna*);

these all refer to the same essence. Regarding "equipoise": by the power of concentration, the mind is held evenly and abides upon a single object. 3. Wisdom (*prajñā*). Wisdom is the capacity for discernment (*viveka*). The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The discernment of the characteristics of objects—whether they are erroneous or correct—is designated as wisdom. Discernment...
[This concludes the selection of the final determination (also including those associated with doubt). IV. The Universal Wholesome Factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*) consist of three dharmas:

1. Faith (*śraddhā*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Faith causes the mind to become clear and pure. Some say: "It is called faith because one directly accepts the truths, the reality, and the results of karma.

The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "It possesses the power to remove the turbidities and impurities of the mind; it is like a water-clearing jewel placed within water, which causes all the turbid water to immediately become clear and pure."

In this way, the wish-fulfilling jewel of faith resides within the ground of the mind (whereby all mental impurities are entirely dispelled). Second is *praśrabdhi* (*praśrabdhi* refers to the bliss of lightness and ease; it is *praśrabdhi*. This means the mind is capable and fit. The *Nyāya-pravēśa* states:

"When correct attention (*manasikāra*) functions, body and mind become light, sharp, and pliant; it is the cause of such ease. The state of the mind being capable and fit is termed *praśrabdhi*. The commentary states: "That which has already functioned through attention" refers to attention that accords with reality (*yoniśo-manasikāra*). This attention, conjoined with *praśrabdhi*, can serve as the cause for the ease of body and mind.

"The state of the mind being capable and fit" points to its essential nature. Third is *upekṣā* (the state of mental equanimity, the state of non-arousal. The commentary states: "The state of mental equanimity" indicates its essential nature. That is to say, it is able to...)

It is so named because it counteracts the imbalance of lethargy (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*). "Alertness" (*apramāda*) is itself agitation; however, within this nature (*dhātu*), there is no alertness. (The above concludes the explanation of the three factors of the wholesome universal ground). Regarding the two factors outside the universal ground, namely vitarka and vicāra:
these exist beyond the five stages (*bhūmi*). Thus, the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Having thus explained the five classes of mental factors, there remain others, which are the indeterminate (*aniyata*) mental factors. According to the correct principle, one should simply call them the "indeterminate stage" (*aniyata-bhūmi*).
This is excellent. If one says it is outside the *mahābhūmi* (great ground), then it would not be the *parīttakleśabhūmi* (small affliction ground).

As for "vitarka" and "vicāra," these refer to *vitarka* and *vicāra* as defined in this sūtra and śāstra. The fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Vitarka and vicāra refer to the coarseness and subtlety of the mind.
The coarse nature of the mind is called vitarka; the subtle nature of the mind is called vicāra. Master Kuang said: "Vitarka means seeking; vicāra..."
Regarding this, Master Baoshan said: "Examination (vicāra) means 'to investigate. If examination is coarse, it is precisely vitarka; if seeking (vitarka) is subtle, it should be vicāra.

There is no need for separate designations. (Now, examining this closely: vicāra is certainly not coarse, and vitarka is certainly not subtle. Such is the distinction between the gross and the subtle; there are texts to this effect throughout the treatises. For what reason do you falsely refute this?)

The chapter states: "Eleven according to the categories of phenomena. If one relies on the numerical categories of dharmas as previously discussed, there are eleven when the category of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is divided according to the distinctions of the stages (*bhūmi*).

This is because the feelings of joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), when viewed from the perspective of their subtle limits of experience, are all of the same category of feeling;
however, since their essential natures and names differ, they are divided into three. Thus, the total becomes eleven. Among these eleven, the fourth...

The character "pleasure" (*sukha*) refers to the pleasure of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-sukha*). The tenth "pleasure" is a member of the category of feeling (*vedanā*). The rest may be understood accordingly.

This corresponds to what is stated in the *Vibhāṣā* (Treatise on the Great Abhidharma), Chapter 80: "Regarding the members of the four dhyānas, although there are eighteen names, how many are there in actual substance? Answer: There are eleven."
That is to say, the factors (*aṅga*) of the first dhyāna consist of five types, both in name and in substance (namely: vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and samādhi). The second dhyāna has four factors;

three in substance are the same as before, with the addition of internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) (meaning that prīti, sukha, and samādhi are the same as before, with the addition of one type, faith). The third dhyāna has five factors;

the fifth is the same as before, but with the addition of the preceding four (meaning that samādhi is the same as before, but with the addition of upekṣā, smṛti, prajñā, and sukha). The fourth [dhyāna] has four factors... [the latter...]

The three [factors] are as before; however, the first [factor] is added (that is, equanimity, mindfulness, and meditative concentration remain the same as before, but with the addition of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling). Thus, the actual entities of the dhyāna factors are eleven.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the actual entities of feeling are only ten, because the bliss of the first three dhyānas is combined into one.
The critique states: "He should not abide therein. This explains that the bliss of the first two dhyānas is *praśrabdhi* (pliancy); therefore, the previous explanation is superior.

This is identical to the critique in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-eight. Regarding the statement in the *Chapters* (*Zhàng*) that "there are eighteen factors," it refers to what follows immediately below:

"four factors are not differentiated": *vitarka* and *vicāra* (these two are restricted to the first dhyāna), faith (restricted to the second dhyāna), wisdom (restricted to the third dhyāna), and the remaining five.

Regarding the formation of fourteen by excluding the divisions: each of the concentrations consists of four (to specify the four concentrations: each of the four dhyānas has its own concentration, which constitutes the four; these are the single minds).

Regarding the four [types of] feeling (*vedanā*): in the first two dhyānas there is joy (*prīti*), in the third dhyāna there is pleasure (*sukha*), and in the fourth dhyāna there is neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*).

(These four feelings belong to the category of feeling. Regarding the remaining three [factors], each has two [occurrences]: pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) occurs throughout the first two dhyānas (thus it is of two kinds), while equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) are restricted to the third and fourth dhyānas (thus they are of four kinds).

Altogether, these constitute the eighteen factors (*aṣṭādaśa-dharma*). If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi*, pleasure is the feeling of pleasure; this is identical to the non-standard interpretation in the *Vibhāṣā*. 10.

Dharma is its essence. Therefore, the treatise states: "Their meanings are distinct. Thus, in the eighth fascicle of that school’s work, in the Chapter on the Five Feeling Faculties (*Pañca-vedanendriya-varga*), it says:

"The pleasure of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) is not different from the feeling of pleasure (*vedanā-sukha*). Furthermore, the eighteenth fascicle states: "Moreover, there is no separate dharma of tranquility."

However, at the time of its arising, one simply experiences joy; because the body and mind are free from coarse and heavy states (*dauṣṭhulya*) and are supple, pliant, and well-adjusted, it is called "tranquility" (*praśrabdhi*).

The commentary states: This is identical to the intent of the Mahāyāna. The exposition of the Mahāyāna meaning has been completed above. Based on this, the categories of dharmas are further established. Regarding the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*):

according to that school, there are no distinct mental factors (*caitta*) apart from the mind, nor are there eighteen separate branches of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*). If one considers them in terms of ultimate reality, they are all one.
Its essence consists of the Dharma-factors. That is to say, it is the mind-king itself. If one speaks figuratively, its essence consists of seven factors;

that is to say, among the aforementioned nine factors, excluding the two—tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) and faith (*śraddhā*)—the remainder are all the same as before, because inner clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is likewise the same in the Mahāyāna.
If these seven are expanded, they become eighteen. Therefore, the treatise says: "That is to say, vitarka and vicāra exist in the first dhyāna" (i.e., the second...).

[The first dhyāna] consists of five factors. Inner serenity (*adhyātmasamprasāda*) exists only in the second [dhyāna] (counting it together with the preceding, there are three). Tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) is restricted to the third [dhyāna] (counting it together with the preceding, there are four). It is called "tranquility" because wisdom is conjoined with bliss.

Neither-pain-nor-pleasure exists only in the fourth [dhyāna] (adding this to the previous, there are five). The factor of joy (*prīti*) is present in the first two [dhyānas] (adding these to the previous, there are seven).

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) are common to the third and fourth [dhyānas] (adding these to the previous, there are eleven). The factor of pleasure (*sukha*) pervades the first three [dhyānas] (adding these to the previous, there are fourteen). One-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is present in all stages (adding this to the previous, there are eighteen).

If one establishes their essential nature according to the numerical categories of the Mahāyāna, considering both the provisional and the substantial, there are seven factors. However, if one considers only the substantial entities, there are only six factors.
This is because vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) both have volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential nature.

Although they constitute two distinct types, from the perspective of their aspect as wisdom, they do not differ from the factor of wisdom within the third dhyāna; therefore, they are not added [as separate factors]. They are counted only from the perspective of volition.
If these are considered as a single category, they constitute one number. If one discards the discussion of actualities and treats them as provisional designations, they also constitute two numbers;

namely, *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought), which are the two [mental factors] of the non-concentrated stages (*asamāhita-bhūmi*). In the first and second dhyānas, there is joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*); in the third dhyāna, there is pleasure; and in the fourth dhyāna, there is neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*).

These six are the category of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*). [This constitutes one category of feeling; when added to the preceding *vitarka* and *vicāra*, it becomes three. In the third dhyāna, there is mindfulness (*smṛti*).

Wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as the mindfulness (*smṛti*) of the fourth dhyāna, and the respective samādhis of each of the four dhyānas—these seven are three of the specific mental objects (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*), namely mindfulness, wisdom, and concentration (adding these to the previous six makes seven).
The equanimity (*upekṣā*) of the third and fourth dhyānas—these two are one among the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*) (adding these to the previous makes seven).
Within the second dhyāna, internal clarity (*adhyātma-saṃprasāda*) has the three factors of mindfulness, equanimity, and wisdom as its essence. Therefore...

They are not discussed separately. Even if they were distinguished according to their respective functions, there would still be only ten; the principles are for the most part identical to those in the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra).
However, there is a slight difference. According to the Mahāyāna, within a single moment of mind, vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) do not coexist.

Because it moves toward the object in a coarse manner with a sense of urgency, it is called vitarka. That which moves in a subtle manner is called vicāra. There is no single moment of mind that is both coarse and subtle.

Furthermore, the two factors of vitarka and vicāra do not possess separate substantial entities. As for the remaining factors—prīti, sukha, ekāgratā, and so forth—they all arise simultaneously in a single moment.
If one were to maintain that [the factors] are substantially real, then it would be impossible for multiple factors to arise together within a single moment of mind.

For instance, regarding the claim that the first dhyāna possesses five factors: these are established as "factors" simply because there are that many dharmas in the first dhyāna which are conducive to the concentrated mind. However...
When they actually arise, each arises individually. This is because that school maintains that mental factors (*caitta*) are merely specific states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the mind;
they are designated by different names such as "joy" (*prīti*) or "bliss" (*sukha*) based on their functions. Since multiple functions cannot occur simultaneously, they arise one by one.
Alternatively, the factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*) is called "joy" from the perspective of gladdening the mind, whereas from the perspective of gladdening the body...
This is called "pleasure. This single category can arise together with two others; it is explained as being two for the sake of its meaning.
Next, regarding the establishment and exclusion of the third major section, there are four parts: first, clarifying the increase and decrease in the number of factors (*aṅga*);

second, establishing and excluding them in relation to the hundred dharmas and so forth; third, the analysis through questions and answers regarding the mutual relationship of the various factors; and fourth, the differentiation of the factors.
[This is] correct. Now, to distinguish the increase and decrease in the number of factors (*aṅga*):

The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks, "For what reason are five factors established for both the first and third dhyānas, while four factors are established for both the second and fourth? The answer is: "The meaning of 'conducive' is the meaning of 'factor.

That is to say, each of the four dhyānas possesses such qualities that are conducive [to its state], neither more nor less. Furthermore, [this is because] the various evils and difficulties of the realms..."
Because they are difficult to sever and difficult to transcend, the first dhyāna is established with five factors as a firm antidote.

Because the intense joy (*prīti*) of the second dhyāna is heavy and extremely difficult to sever, and even more so to transcend, the third dhyāna is established with five factors as a powerful antidote.
In both the first and third dhyānas, there are no such factors that are difficult to sever.

Therefore, only four factors are established. Furthermore, in order to counteract the craving for the five objects of desire in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), five factors are established in the first [dhyāna].
In order to counteract the heavy-grade attachment and delight belonging to the five categories within the second dhyāna, five factors are established in the third.

Because these dharmas are not known in the first and third [dhyānas], only four factors are established. The detailed explanation is as in that [text]. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 11, states: "All..."

Within the dhyānas, although there are other factors, these [five] are established as the specific limbs because they are preeminent and serve as the primary objects of reflection for one practicing concentration.
This is the same intention as that found in the *Vibhāṣā* regarding the first dhyāna. Next, regarding the establishment and exclusion based on the hundred dharmas and so forth:
Briefly, there are five levels by which to distinguish them: first, the gate of defilement; second, the gate of the three natures; third, the gate of concentration and distraction;

fourth, the gate of having an object of cognition versus having no object of cognition; and fifth, the gate of the mental king (citta) and mental factors (caitta). Regarding, for instance, the distinction between the defiled and the non-defiled:

Now, the factors of dhyāna (dhyānāṅga) are analyzed. Based on the establishment of the factors through the attainment of pure concentration (*viśuddha-vicāra*), those that are afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are excluded.

Specifically, according to the Minor School (*Hīnayāna*), this excludes the great afflictions (*mahā-kleśa*), the great unwholesome states (*akuśala*), the minor afflictions (*parītta-kleśa*), and among the indeterminate states (*aniyata*), greed, anger, pride, and doubt.

Second, regarding their nature (*svabhāva*), only those of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*) are taken; within the wholesome nature, those that are merely innate (*upapatti-labdha*) are excluded.

The wisdoms of hearing and reflection are excluded; it is exclusively the wisdom of cultivation. Precisely for this reason, within the categories of concentration and distraction, all three natures of the desire realm are simultaneously excluded, as they are all distracted.
Regarding the fourth [category], that which has an object and that which lacks an object: these are the essential natures of dhyāna.

All of these are aggregates of mind and all possess an object of cognition (*ālambana*). This excludes material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (80) asks: "For what reason are right speech, right action, and right livelihood not branches of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*)?"

That is to say, it is associated with dhyāna (the essence of which consists of concentration and wisdom); it necessarily has an object of focus (the sense bases being its objects); and it possesses both an object of focus and mental alertness.
Only that which is associated with [the mind] is called a "limb" (aṅga). Since right speech, action, and livelihood do not possess this characteristic, they are not limbs of that [dhyāna].

For this reason, these four characteristics as well as the acquisitions (prāpti) and so forth should not be established as limbs of dhyāna, because they do not assist meditative concentration (samādhi) in abiding on a single object.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Vibhāṣā) provisionally excludes [the factors] by means of vocal karma and life-force (*jīvita*), as well as through the corresponding lower categories;

in principle, it also excludes matter (*rūpa*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, among the one hundred dharmas, these four gates have already excluded sixty-seven dharmas. Only thirty-three dharmas remain unexcluded:

namely, the eight mental factors (*caitasika*), including the five universal (*sarvatraga*), the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*), the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*), and the four indeterminate (*aniyata*).

If, among the seventy-five dharmas, fifty have already been excluded, leaving only one category of mental factors (citta-dharma)—namely, ten from the universal ground (mahābhūmika), ten from the wholesome ground (kuśala-bhūmika), and four from the indeterminate ground (aniyata-bhūmika)—these twenty-five remaining dharmas shall all be excluded within the fifth section on the primary mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta).
Question: Regarding the eight consciousnesses of the Mahāyāna and the six consciousnesses of the Hīnayāna, why are they not considered meditative absorptions (dhyāna)?

[The term] *śākhā* (branch). The minor categories (*kṣudra-vidhi*) are not explained; they are made to rely upon the major category (*mahā-vidhi*). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter nine, states: Question:
Since dharmas are immeasurable, why are only the factors such as investigation (*vitarka*) established as branches? Answer:

Because they serve as the antidotal branches (*pratipakṣa-aṅga*), because they serve as the beneficial branches (*anuśaṃsa-aṅga*), and because they constitute the self-nature of the basis for those two (namely, the basis for both the antidote and the benefit, which is concentration itself). Through these three types [of factors], the branches are complete; nothing else is required.
Therefore, based on those three meanings, these various consciousnesses lack those three meanings and are thus not factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*). Question:

Among the five omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga*), why are the four types—contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)—not established as factors?

In order to analyze the remaining mental factors (*caitasika*), one first clarifies the conditions they possess. That is, the aforementioned *Abhidharmasamuccaya* establishes three conditions, to which a fourth—the differentiation of the factors of the stage (*bhūmi*)—is added.

They are distinct. For instance, the *vitarka* (applied thought), *vicāra* (sustained thought), and *prīti* (joy) of the first dhyāna; the *prīti* of the second dhyāna; the *sukha* (bliss) of the third dhyāna;

and the *upekṣā* (equanimity) of the fourth dhyāna—these six, according to their respective applications, ought to exist naturally within the four dhyānas. However, although these universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) pervade all minds, they consist solely of the single category of feeling (*vedanā*).
While they possess distinct characteristics across the upper and lower stages, the other four [mental factors] lack any such distinction whatsoever.

Because they are merely characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are not established as branches (*aṅga*). Among the five specific object-conditions (*viśeṣālambana*), concentration (*samādhi*) is necessarily the basis for the object;

mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are co-existent with it; therefore, they are established as branches. Desire (*chanda*) and resolve (*adhimokṣa*), however, are not subsumed under the four conditions; thus, they are also not branches.

For instance, while desire and resolve are useful toward an object during the stage of preliminary application (*prayoga*), they have no further function now that this is the fundamental [stage]. Therefore, they do not exist [as branches].

These are the auxiliary functions. Among the eleven wholesome factors, faith (*śraddhā*) and heedfulness (*apramāda*) may serve as the preparatory application (*prayoga*). Furthermore, within the fundamental factors, there are no four [auxiliary] meanings.

Diligence (*vīrya*), by its nature of urgency, does not accord with the gateway of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Since joy (*prīti*) and so forth already exist as factors for benefit, there is no need for pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) or the three roots.

These [latter] accord with the arousal of karma; this [state] is exclusively tranquility (*śamatha*). Shame (*hrī*), embarrassment (*apatrāpya*), and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) are able to restrain evil.

Because it is ethical discipline (*śīla*), there are no four meanings [of "dhyāna"] in the case of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If one follows the Hīnayāna, wholesome states consist of only ten; since they lack non-delusion (*amoha*), there is no need for such a distinction.
Inner serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is faith (*śraddhā*). The intention of that school is as follows: the faith of the second dhyāna can be free from defilement across all realms and stages.

Upon its first arising, great faith is produced, thinking: "I am now able to be free from the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); I can likewise be free from those of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*)."

The defilements of the first dhyāna can certainly be abandoned; since I am already able to abandon the defilements of the first dhyāna, I will necessarily abandon them up to those of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Since one has not yet attained the firm conviction regarding the higher stages when first attaining the first dhyāna, and what is subsequently attained in the third and fourth dhyānas is no longer "initial," the second dhyāna alone possesses its own factors (*aṅga*).
Now, examining this school's position: if they provide such an explanation, then within the second dhyāna there would be no counteractive factor (*pratipakṣa*) at all. This is because...
Faith can only serve as the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the subsequent state of being free from defilement; it is not the actual antidote (*pratipakṣa*) in this context.

Furthermore, joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) are likewise not capable of acting as the antidote; to claim otherwise would be a great error. Therefore, according to the Mahāyāna, the triad of mindfulness (*smṛti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) constitutes the essence of internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), which is precisely the antidote.
Moreover, when *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) is established as being subsumed within the fundamental dhyāna, there is a bliss belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmika-sukha*). Second...

The three dhyānas—both the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental states (*maula*)—all possess mental intention (*āśaya*); therefore, they are not the same. Next, regarding the four indeterminate factors:
since sleep (*middha*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*) are dharmas belonging only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are not established as branches (*aṅga*).

The two types, vitarka and vicāra, are established as branches because they serve as antidotes to the vitarkas such as malice (*vyāpāda*) within the desire realm; thus, they are established in the first dhyāna. Next, by means of...

Regarding the questions and answers that definitively explain the mutual relationship between the various factors (*aṅga*): vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha do not logically exist as they progress upward through the stages;

therefore, no questions or answers are provided for them. Furthermore, for example, while the first dhyāna has three factors as its essence, and the initial stage of concentration likewise corresponds with these three factors, why are they not established as distinct factors?
Answer: Because all desire, ill-will, and so forth belonging to the desire realm should logically be overcome by the wholesome vitarka of the first dhyāna.
[It is] because they are governed [by vitarka]. Thus, those three factors are obscured by vitarka. Therefore, the *Samuddeśa* (Xianyang lun), fascicle 19, states:

"Because they are induced through the gateway of vitarka and vicāra, although they exist, they are not mentioned; furthermore, as they serve no further purpose, they are not established as constituent factors.

If that is so, since the faculty of joy (*prīti-indriya*) already exists within the first and second dhyānas to serve as a factor of benefit, why is pleasure (*sukha*) still required? Answer: Because the gladdening of body and mind are distinct, it is not [redundant].

This is analogous. If one follows the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) school, which holds that faith (*śraddhā*) constitutes the essence [of the first dhyāna], why is it not established as a factor (*aṅga*) there as well?
Answer: It is as previously stated; according to the intention of that school, great faith arises for the first time within the second dhyāna.

Furthermore, according to the Small Vehicle, the bliss (*sukha*) of the first two dhyānas is the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Since the stage of the higher realms also certainly possesses pliancy, why is it not [established as a factor] in the higher stages?
It is established as a factor (*aṅga*). The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vasubhāṣya), fascicle 80, states:

"In order to counteract the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the two groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) and the body they induce within the desire realm, *praśrabdhi* (serenity) is established in the first dhyāna.

In order to counteract the heaviness of the two groups of consciousness and the body they induce in the first dhyāna, *praśrabdhi* is established in the second dhyāna. In all stages above these, there is no such heavy consciousness to be countered."
Furthermore, because the body induced by it possesses a state of heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), it is not established [as such].

This implies that consciousness relies upon the five sense-faculties, and since the body associated with them possesses an unfitness for action (*akarmanyatā*), *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) is established as its antidote; one should cultivate pliancy as the remedy.
Since these aforementioned stages lack this quality, they instead employ equanimity (*upekṣā*) as the antidote. In the two stages above those, joy (*prīti*) causes agitation.
Therefore, because it abandons non-clarity and lacks purity, it cannot be established as a factor (*aṅga*). Question: In the third dhyāna, wisdom (*prajñā*) is established as a factor;
why is it not so established in the higher and lower stages? Answer: According to the Mahāyāna, vitarka depends upon wisdom for its establishment.

Since the first dhyāna already possesses internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), which contains wisdom, and the second dhyāna likewise possesses it, the reason wisdom is not established as a factor in the fourth dhyāna is that the fourth dhyāna abandons... [text ends]

Because equanimity (*upekṣā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are mutually contradictory in their characteristics, wisdom is not established [as a distinct factor] there. If that were so, the same would apply to equanimity and wisdom in the third dhyāna.

The answer is: since they are not particularly superior and lack the characteristic of mutual contradiction—just as slight cold and warmth do not constitute a great contradiction—it is stated in the *Vyākhyāyukti* (or *Xianyang shengjiao lun*) regarding the fourth dhyāna: "This very equanimity and mindfulness are extremely well-purified. Thus it is revealed.
[The commentary] concludes: The intention is that because equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) are supreme, there is no "clear comprehension" (*saṃprajanya*).

The intention of the *Vibhāṣā* is that the first dhyāna is obscured by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); the second dhyāna is obscured by exultation (*prīti*); and the fourth dhyāna is obscured by the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Therefore, in none of these is wisdom (*prajñā*) established as a factor (*aṅga*). As stated in the eightieth [section], one cannot elaborate further here. Next, we shall distinguish between the inclusion and exclusion [of factors]. If according to the Small Vehicle...
In the [Abhidharma] *Madhyama*, the four factors and five factors each have a single dharma as their essence; there is no sense of separation or combination.

However, in the Mahāyāna, vitarka and vicāra are either metaphorically established upon volition (*cetanā*), or upon wisdom (*prajñā*), or as a combination of volition and wisdom; therefore, they must be distinguished.

Furthermore, inner serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) has three dharmas as its essence, which should likewise be distinguished—namely, that within the desire realm, desire, ill-will, and so forth, as well as vitarka, are also metaphorically [established].

Since it was established [as a separate factor] previously, it should likewise be established here in the first dhyāna as an antidote. Furthermore, because there is exultation (*prīti*) and the present wisdom (*prajñā*) is luminous, they are combined and termed *vitarka*.
Within the second dhyāna, inner serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is established [as a single factor]. Upon reaching the third dhyāna, it is then opened up into three factors.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Xianyang shengjiao lun*) explains its own commentary, stating: "In the second dhyāna, there is the activity of the essential nature of exultation (namely, joy...)"
[It is so called] because it is enveloped and obscured by a small portion of the mental factors (caitta) that are afflictions (namely, joy and greed).

Therefore, it is designated collectively by the name "inner serenity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*)—meaning that the mental factor of serenity in the meditative absorption does not intermingle with the savoring of feeling (*vedanāsvāda*).

In the third dhyāna, since those small portions of mental factors that are afflictions have all been removed (because joy is concordant with craving, and that stage has already been abandoned), its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are revealed—namely, the three dharmas of equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
In the fourth dhyāna, this very equanimity and mindfulness are extremely pure and clearly manifest;

therefore, among the various meditative absorptions, they are distinguished according to their respective characteristics (that is, in the fourth dhyāna, because equanimity and mindfulness are supreme, they manifest their own intrinsic nature. Because it would conflict with wisdom, correct knowledge is not established as a factor).
The section on the establishment and refutation of categories is concluded. Next, the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) shall be briefly explained.
As in the previous chapter on the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) regarding the precept against great falsehood, these have already been briefly expounded.

Nevertheless, although the *Mahāvaipulya-karma-phala-śrī-mālā-sūtra* also establishes factors (*aṅga*) for the formless absorptions, other sūtras and śāstras do not establish such factors. Thus, it is said in the sūtras concerning these eight absorptions and the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

These constitute the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*). This means that when noble beings (*ārya*) wish to elicit various qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they must first cycle through these nine attainments, bringing them to a state of extreme proficiency; only thereafter do they elicit the various virtues. Hence, they are called the "nine successive attainments.

Furthermore, the first eight of these attainments are of three types: (1) those associated with the taste of meditative absorption (*āsvādana-samprayukta-samādhi*), (2) pure attainments (*śuddha-samādhi*), and [3] untainted attainments (*anāsrava-samādhi*).

Regarding the three untainted meditative attainments (*anāsrava-samāpatti*), both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools maintain this principle. Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 162) states:

"There are eight attainments, namely the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments. There are three types of attainment, namely those associated with relish (*āsvādana*), the pure (*śuddha*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Among these, the first seven each possess all three types; the eighth possesses only two, namely excluding the untainted. Commentary: This refers to the fact that while the first seven stages of meditative absorption can be experienced with relish, as pure, or as untainted, the eighth—the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)—lacks the untainted variety because it is not a state of active mental engagement.

This means that among the eight meditative attainments (*dhyāna*), only the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) lacks the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*); therefore, the treatise excludes it. "Associated with relish" (*āsvādanā-samprayukta*) refers to being associated with craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Craving is able to sustain the mind, causing it to flow toward objects; because its characteristic conforms to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it alone receives this name.

That is to say, one emerges from pure concentration (*śuddhaka-dhyāna*) and enters the eight concentrations associated with relish; by means of a mind of relish, one takes the concentration as an object and gives rise to greed, just as in the case of the desire realm.

Regarding "arising from the realms" (*dhātu-ja*): it refers to the frequent arising of craving and attachment, which subsequently causes one to fall. The savoring of meditative concentration (*samādhi-rasa*) is likewise so, for it is a condition for retrogression and falling away.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Attachment to the flavor of dhyāna is the bondage of a bodhisattva. According to the Mahāyāna, there are four kinds of concentration.

1. Attachment predominant in dhyāna; 2. Views predominant in dhyāna; 3. Pride predominant in dhyāna; 4. Doubt predominant in dhyāna. These are the afflictions produced by the four neutral roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*), as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, fascicle nine.
That is to say, the four delusions of the *manas* are called the neutral roots, which are able to produce attachment, views, pride, and doubt within the sixth consciousness.

The fourth [root] is the root of ignorance (*avidyā-mūla*). Regarding "life and doubt": [this refers to the fact that] the *manas* clings to the continuity of life and harbors doubt regarding the cessation of existence.
This is the superior [category]. The details are as explained therein; since this is not of primary importance for the characteristics of the Vinaya, it is not set forth extensively here.

Regarding "pure concentration" (*śuddha-samādhi*), it refers to the wholesome, contaminated state of mind in meditative absorption. As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (163) and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (28), pure first dhyāna is of four types:
namely, the part conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*), the part conducive to maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*), and the part conducive to progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*).

Regarding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*): if one abides in the stage of retrogression (*hānabhāgīya*), one mostly regresses; if one abides in the stage of maintenance (*sthityābhāgīya*), one mostly does not regress;
if one abides in the stage of excellence (*viśeṣabhāgīya*), one mostly attains further excellence and proceeds toward higher meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).

If one abides in the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), one is mostly able to enter the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and so forth, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). This should be understood accordingly; that is to say, "penetration."

The divisions exist only within the four dhyānas. As for the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), it is the untainted mind that performs the contemplation of the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).

According to the Mahāyāna, however, it is not restricted to these sixteen aspects. Within this, both the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted concentrations possess all four or five branches (*aṅga*) as appropriate;
the concentration associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samprayukta*) does not establish such branches. This is explained in detail in works such as the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

The *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Abhidharmasamudaya*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, and other treatises also explain this. Now, in analyzing how a bodhisattva is about to achieve perfect awakening, it is based on pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*) that they induce the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Furthermore, while śrāvakas can enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) by relying generally on the universal stages (*mahābhūmika*), a bodhisattva must rely exclusively on the fourth dhyāna to enter the path of seeing.
This is because the fourth dhyāna excels in both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). Thus it is said:
The six stages consist of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the four fundamental dhyānas.

Furthermore, when practicing the preparatory applications (*prayoga*) for the first eight concentrations, one abandons the afflictions of the lower stages; these are exclusively termed "preparatory" (*sāmantaka*) during the eight paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the [first] eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
As for the ninth path of liberation, it may either enter the fundamental concentration or not; this should be understood according to the specific case.

If one does not enter the fundamental [dhyāna], it is nonetheless subsumed under the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*). According to the Mahāyāna, the ninth liberation (*vimokṣa*) invariably and definitely enables entry into the fundamental dhyāna.
Furthermore, among the eight dhyānas, the preparatory stage of the first *dhyāna* is precisely the "not-yet-attained" concentration (*anāgamya*).
There are also cases where the "not-yet-attained" is not subsumed under the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), as in the case of... [as in the case of] the complete...
Regarding "bondage": one who has first given rise to the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana*) gradually enters the clear observation (*abhisamaya*).

Subsequently, during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one gives rise to the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*navānantarya-mārga*) to sever the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Therefore, it should be understood that the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) which serves as the basis for that person's path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is not subsumed within the nine paths of uninterrupted transition;
this is to be known accordingly. The first dhyāna possesses applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*); through further superior cultivation, one subsequently attains progress.
The meditative concentration that is without vitarka and with only vicāra is called the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*). This is also subsumed under the first dhyāna.
Having cultivated and attained this concentration, one passes away from here and is reborn in that celestial realm as a Great Brahmā King (*mahābrahman*).

Because it is distinguished by the three stages—having both vitarka and vicāra, having no vitarka and only vicāra, and having neither vitarka nor vicāra—it occupies an intermediate position; hence its name.

The intermediate dhyāna, from the desire realm up to the first dhyāna, is called the stage with vitarka and vicāra. That which is the intermediate dhyāna itself is called the stage with no vitarka and only vicāra.
From the second dhyāna upwards, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, is called the stage with neither vitarka nor vicāra.
Furthermore, the four fundamental dhyānas are termed "abiding in happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) in the sūtras and śāstras because...
Because one experiences much pleasure while abiding in this meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) arising in dependence upon it is called the "path of ease" (*sukhamārga*).
The intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the lower three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) also give rise to the Noble Path;

however, because concentration and wisdom are not in equilibrium, its arising is difficult, and it is therefore called the "path of suffering" (*duḥkhamārga*). For a detailed analysis, one should consult the various treatises; this is a brief understanding of the matter.

Next, following the commentary (*śāstra*), the first section on the text of the First Dhyāna has three parts. Regarding the "three [aspects]" mentioned above: although the analysis of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) has already been explained, the similarities and differences between that and this Vinaya text have not yet been compared.
Furthermore, this analysis of characteristics comprehensively examines the removal of hindrances (*vighna-nivāraṇa*), the factors of benefit (*anuśaṃsa-aṅga*), and the sources from which they arise;
it does not intend to restrict the explanation solely to the four or five factors of the third and fourth dhyānas.

This is because, according to the commentaries on various treatises, the four branches and five branches are not distinguished [in this context]. This should be understood according to the specific textual passages. For instance, regarding the description of the first dhyāna, the text states:

"Having removed sensual desires, unwholesome states, and evil dharmas, with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and with joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind, one dwells sporting in the first dhyāna.
This refers to the sūtra cited in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, which says: "Free from sensual desires, unwholesome states, and evil dharmas; with *vitarka* and *vicāra*; free from..."

One gives rise to joy and bliss and dwells fully endowed with the first dhyāna (by extension, "joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind" refers to the joy and bliss born of seclusion; "sporting in the first dhyāna" refers to dwelling fully endowed with the first dhyāna).

Regarding the commentary’s explanation of "one-pointedness of mind" as the samādhi that serves as the basis, it does not necessarily correspond exactly [to the original intent], according to the meaning of this passage.
This provides a comprehensive explanation of the characteristics [of the meditative states], rather than a restricted analysis of the meaning of the five factors alone.

Therefore, "dwelling in full possession" (samyakpratiṣṭhita) generally indicates the first dhyāna, wherein one attains mastery over calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā), as has already been cited above.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains this as being able to dwell correctly for up to seven days without difficulty; all subsequent passages should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the statement that "initial investigation of phenomena is called *vitarka* (applied thought) and so forth," this can be asserted according to the *Tattvasiddhi* and the Mahāyāna schools.

However, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, since both *vitarka* and *vicāra* (sustained thought) exist within a single moment of mind, one cannot say that repeated examination is what constitutes *vicāra*.

Regarding the statement that "because of the presence of vitarka and vicāra, there is no inner serenity (adhyātmasamprasāda) and so forth," this is a brief explanation of what is excluded and what is established. This also constitutes a single characteristic;
if explained extensively, it is as interpreted in the section on exclusion and establishment above.

The text on the second dhyāna states: "Having abandoned applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one attains internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*); [the translator has inserted the character 'clarity' here;

it should be read as 'internal purity'] with joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind, being mindful without applied or sustained thought, sporting in the second dhyāna. This is the same as the sūtra cited in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which says:

"With the cessation of applied and sustained thought, there is internal purity" (which corresponds to the Vinaya version: "having abandoned applied and sustained thought, one attains internal clarity"). "The mind is one-pointed" (in the Vinaya, this is 'mindfulness') and is without applied or sustained thought.

(The Vinaya says: "without directed thought or sustained examination"). "The joy and bliss born of concentration" (in the Vinaya, this refers to joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind). "Abiding fully in the second dhyāna" (the Vinaya says:
"sporting in the second dhyāna"). The commentary explains that this can be understood.
Regarding the text on the third dhyāna, it says: "Having removed joy, one experiences physical pleasure; one attains the bliss seen and protected by the Noble Ones, and sports therein."
The Third Dhyāna. This refers to the sūtra cited in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, which states: "Detached from joy (*prīti*), one dwells in equanimity (*upekṣā*);

with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension (*samprajanya*)—[these two terms are omitted in the Vinaya]—one experiences happiness with the body (*kāyena sukhaṃ pratisaṃvedayati*). This is what the noble ones describe as dwelling in equanimity" [the Vinaya adds:

"this is what is seen by noble wisdom"; "noble vision" (*āryajñānadṛṣṭa*) is precisely this]. [Alternatively, as cited in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, it says: "The noble ones proclaim that one attains and dwells fully in the third dhyāna, which is the blissful abiding of equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-sukha-vihāra*). The Vinaya states: "This is what is seen by noble wisdom. This is [the meaning].

The Noble One has declared that what is seen by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*)—that is, the noble one—is bliss. This is the "abiding in bliss through equanimity and mindfulness. The subsequent explanation is excellent. In the *Prakaraṇāryavācā*, equanimity and mindfulness are employed as the antidote (as already analyzed above).
Regarding the third dhyāna, abiding in its full possession, it may be understood according to the preceding [explanation] in the Vinaya.

The text on the fourth dhyāna states: "Having already abandoned pleasure and pain, and having previously transcended sorrow and joy, one dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.

This is the same as the sūtra cited in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which says: "With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, one enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. [The commentary] states: "Purified" constitutes one [factor].

"Mind" (*citta*) here does not mean [the mind-organ] (*manas*). What is intended by this statement is that because equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) are pure, one must not provide a mistaken interpretation.

Regarding the phrase "because they oppose the two types of distraction from the outset," the traditional exegesis explains: the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are called external distractions.

The joy (*prīti*) of the first and second dhyānas is termed "internal distraction. The first dhyāna marks the beginning of the remedy for external distraction, while the third dhyāna marks the beginning of the remedy for internal distraction;
therefore, each possesses five factors (*pañcāṅga*).

Regarding the phrase "because it opposes the end of the two types of distraction": this refers to the first three dhyānas. Accordingly, these are the states where external and internal distractions have ultimately ceased;
therefore, the second and fourth dhyānas do not require five factors as their antidotes. This meaning is identical to what is stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 80:
"Furthermore, in order to counteract the greed for the objects of the five desires within the [desire] realm, the first dhyāna is established."
The third dhyāna is also established as having five factors in order to counteract the five categories of gross attachment and delight belonging to the second dhyāna.
Since neither the first nor the third [dhyānas] possess such objects of counteraction, both the second and the fourth [dhyānas] are established as having four factors (as stated in the treatise).
From here begins the second section, on abandoning afflictions to attain Buddhahood. Previously, the four dhyānas were explained to clarify the meditative concentrations that serve as the basis;

logically, these should have been explained together with the stages that arise in dependence upon the four *dhyānas*, such as the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)—namely, *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*—followed by entry into the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and finally the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and the realization of the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).

However, in the present text, only the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) are mentioned, intending to signify the exhaustion of outflows, which encompasses what was previously discussed regarding the path of seeing.
Because [these qualities] have already been explained in detail elsewhere, they are not fully analyzed here.
Regarding the phrase "the gates of all merits are perfectly bright, clear, and luminous," the intent is to reveal that the Buddha-body is endowed with infinite common and uncommon virtues.

As for "common virtues," these refer to the immeasurable liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the absence of strife (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), and so forth. [This refers to] the virtue of being free from suffering.

As for this, it is as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on Yoga) regarding the one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-guṇa*) [in the first twelve divisions of the teachings].
Such qualities are truly boundless; however, we shall here briefly analyze three of them—the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*)—by means of six topical sections:

first, listing the three names; second, explaining the individual names; third, clarifying their essential nature (*svabhāva*); fourth, explaining the general name; fifth, clarifying their causes and origins; and sixth, an exegesis following the text. Listing...

Regarding the three names: as stated in the chapter, first is the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*), second is the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and third is the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (27) and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (102) state: "First is the clear realization of the knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyāvidyā*); second is the clear realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānasākṣātkriyāvidyā*)."

The third is the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyā*). To explain these specific names, as the treatise states: "That which illuminates the past is called the knowledge of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*);
that which illuminates the good and evil of the future is called the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); that which illuminates present matters is called the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

This reveals that the three samādhis encounter the three time periods (*tryadhvan*), and are thus named "knowledge of former abodes" and so forth. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "The supernormal power of recollecting former abodes (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*) remedies ignorance regarding the prior limit (*pūrvānta*)."

The supernormal knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) remedies ignorance regarding the future limit (*aparānta-moha*). The supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion [of outflows] (*kṣayajñāna*) remedies ignorance regarding the intermediate limit (*madhyānta-moha*).

(That is to say, among the six supernormal powers, three are able to remedy ignorance regarding the three limits; therefore, they are established as the "Three Clear Insights" [*trividyā*]. Furthermore, "the intermediate limit" clarifies that the afflictions and karma produced during this present single lifetime are made to be permanently severed; thus, it is called "remedying. The *Chapter* [refers to this] as "the present," which likewise clarifies the present of this single lifetime.

Furthermore, regarding the interpretation: as the *Chapter* states, "the matter has passed away into the past," etc., it should be understood accordingly. Alternatively, one may apply this in terms of the retribution based on the faculties.

"Retribution" refers to celestial retribution; "roots" refers to the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Question: Since the Bodhisattva’s divine eye is attained through cultivation (*bhāvanā-labdha*), how can it be categorized as retribution?
Answer: Within the Buddha-body, it is metaphorically designated as "celestial"; thus, the eye within the celestial body is called the "divine eye.

(Alternatively, this explanation may not be logically sound, and there is no need to justify it). Regarding the "afflictions of the five dwelling-grounds," this appears in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*: first, the dwelling-ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).

The stages (*bhūmi*): second, the stage of abiding in views (*dṛṣṭi-ekadeśa-vāsa-bhūmi*); third, the stage of abiding in desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāma-tṛṣṇā-vāsa-bhūmi*); fourth, the stage of abiding in desire for the realm of form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā-vāsa-bhūmi*);

fifth, the stage of abiding in desire for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā-vāsa-bhūmi*). Regarding these, traditional exegesis has stated: all afflictions of the desire realm, excluding ignorance (*moha*) and the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*), are called the stage of abiding in desire for the realm of sensuality.

All delusions of the realm of form, excluding ignorance and views, are called the stage of abiding in desire for the realm of form. As for the delusions of the formless realm, excluding [ignorance and views]...

Ignorance (*moha*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*) are the dwelling grounds of craving for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-tṛṣṇā-vāsabhūmi*). Ignorance within the three realms is the dwelling ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*);
views within the three realms are the dwelling ground of views (*dṛṣṭi-vāsabhūmi*). Now, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle nine:

among all the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the seeds of views, doubt, ignorance, and so forth, are collectively termed the dwelling ground of ignorance. All seeds of the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision [of the truths] within the three realms are called...
One sees that there is a single abiding ground (*sthāna-bhūmi*), which is to be severed as a single unit and receives a single name.

This refers to the seeds of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; these constitute the remaining three abiding grounds. Therefore, that treatise asks:

"If the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) include views, doubt, and so forth, how can their seeds be described in the sūtras as the 'abiding ground of ignorance' (*avidyā-sthāna-bhūmi*)? [The answer is: Because ignorance is predominant, they are collectively termed "ignorance," and not because other factors are absent.

[The text says] "There are no [further] views, etc. (This is the answer). Just as with the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa*), one establishes the names for the four *ālayas*—the view-ālaya, desire-ālaya, form-and-formlessness-ālaya, and existence-ālaya.

How could there not be further [afflictions] such as pride (*māna*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)? (This refers to the other four *ālayas* as examples; that is, within the view-ālaya there are also pride and so forth, and the same applies to the other three. To state the overall meaning:

the first one is specifically the seed of the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), while the remaining four are specifically the seeds of the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*). This is [the point].

The active manifestation or the locus where they reside is called the "ground of abiding" (*sthiti-bhūmi*). However, upon examining the scriptural texts of the Vinaya, [the author] himself explains the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna*) by means of the three outflows (*traya-āsrava*).
Therefore, there is no need to laboriously analyze the five grounds of abiding (although the five grounds of abiding are indeed with-outflow, the text clarifies them by analyzing the three outflows).
Third, regarding the analysis of its essential nature (*svabhāva*): as the chapter states, "If one examines the nature of this illumination, it is solely the nature of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*).
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*’s exposition of its nature: the first two are conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). As for the third, it is either of the nature of six or ten types of wisdom.

(If it takes the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) as its object, it is then of the nature of only six wisdoms—namely, conventional, exhaustion, non-arising, dharma, inferential, and cessation wisdoms. If it is said to arise within the body of one whose outflows are exhausted, then it is of the nature of ten wisdoms—namely, those six plus the wisdoms of suffering, origin, the path, and the knowledge of others' minds.)

If one distinguishes according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the human eye and its cognition are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). This is because they are the wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Among the five consciousnesses, there is only that which is innate virtue (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*). If it belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it does not arise when transcending a level.

If it belongs to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is necessarily not produced by a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*). Therefore, from a concentrated mind, only the indeterminate arises; this refers to the following:

These are the neutral fruits of supernormal power (if according to the Mahāyāna, they are both wholesome and neutral). The remaining two types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) are exclusively of a wholesome nature.

Regarding the fourth point, the explanation of the name: the treatise states, "Because there is nothing that is not illuminated within the objects of the three periods of time, they are called the 'Three Clear Knowledges' (*tisro vidyāḥ*).

This is an etymological explanation based on enumeration (*saṃkhyānvaya-nirukti*). Fifth, regarding the clarification of their arising: the question is asked, "For what purpose does one train in these three?"

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 102, and the *Nyāyānusāra*, fascicle 76, both explain: "The supernormal power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānābhijñā*) involves recollecting the suffering of oneself and others regarding the past limit;
the supernormal power of knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānābhijñā*) involves observing the suffering of other bodies regarding the future limit.

Through this, one develops revulsion toward the manifold sufferings of birth and death and gives rise to the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānābhijñā*). This is precisely what the *Abhidharmakośa* describes as the remedy for ignorance regarding the three time periods. Thus it is said.
This establishes the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*). Sixth is the word-by-word commentary on the text. Regarding the passage stating "by means of the fourth dhyāna":
although the fourth dhyāna is not explicitly mentioned in the Vinaya, it is spoken of in the oral tradition of the Vinaya as "faultless," "abiding in firmness," and so forth.

Upon examining various sūtras and śāstras, these are all characteristics of the fourth dhyāna; the following sections should be understood accordingly. There are eight matters and six types of companionship. This...
According to the commentary on the tenth chapter of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which is the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* section;

however, it is a separate translation from the same original text as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, translated by Dharmakṣema), among the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Buddha, this refers to the power of knowledge consisting in the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*).

Regarding the eight types of objects and the six types of common associates: according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter forty-nine, these are termed the "eight bases of discourse" (*aṣṭau vyavahārapadāni*).

Among the categories of distinctions, the six types of recollection constitute the "briefly summarized modes of practice. (Commentary: The meaning here is that the eight types of distinct categories of conventional designations are called the "objects of practice" (*gocara*).
The six common characteristics are subsequently termed the "common associates" (*sahacara*). This is the intent of the *Yogācāra*.

It is said that "name" refers to the sphere of activity of verbal expression (*nāma-vyavahāra*). Briefly, there are six kinds of modes of activity within this sphere. This intent is identical to what is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Regarding "conventional designations" (*saṃketa-nāman*): in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, these are termed "invoking provisional names. Provisional names (*prajñapti*) is precisely the meaning of conventional designations (*saṃketa*).

That is to say, they are established as verbal expressions through the enumeration of conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-prajñā*). [Some do not [contradict this], and thus they take the commentary to mean "secular surnames."]
[This is] an error). Regarding the statement that there are "six kinds": first, conventional names; second, physical forms such as those of the *kṣatriya* caste;

third, parents; fourth, food and drink; fifth, good and evil (which the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* calls prosperity and decline); sixth, lifespan (if one examines the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the meaning will become clear of itself). The commentary states:

"Since these should be combined with the three [factors] among the eight, namely lifespan and so forth, there are six kinds"—this is the explanation of the Sub-commentator (*Śu-shu-zhu*). Furthermore, it says: "The eight kinds [become] the six kinds."
"Others and oneself speak thus," and so forth, refers to the sequential passages of the treatise.

This is a re-explanation of the reasons provided after the eight and six [categories] have been enumerated within the treatise; that is to say, it is because of the meanings of the six and eight types previously listed.
Regarding others and oneself, one makes such statements as, "This is my name," and so forth. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"Based upon these eight bases of conventional expression (*vyavahārapada*), worldly people engage in six types of abbreviated discourse regarding themselves and others.
Furthermore, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, one should say: "This is my name; this is that person's name; I am a Kṣatriya," and so on.
"He acts for the sake of the kṣatriyas and so forth," and so on, as explained at length. In the current text of the *Bhūmisaṃgraha*, the translator has omitted those names;
that [omission] is merely one side of the text concerning those kṣatriyas and others.
Next, regarding the listing of the eight matters following the phrase "the name is so-and-so": first, the name is so-and-so; second, the surname is so-and-so;

third, born in such a manner; fourth, eating such food; fifth, the lifespan is such (in the world one should live for a hundred years, yet due to what one has personally induced, one lives for only fifty);

sixth, the limit of the lifespan is such (that is, as in the world where one should live for a hundred years, or in the Northern Continent where one should live for a thousand years, etc.); seventh, the duration of remaining in the world is such.

(Regarding "prolonging or abbreviating"): When it is said that the Bodhisattva attained this first clarity during the first watch of the night while experiencing such suffering and pleasure, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 103, states the following:
Regarding the arising of the three insights during the first, middle, and last watches of the night: this was for the purpose of successively subduing the demonic adversaries.
