This refers to when the Bodhisattva, having sat beneath the tree, vowed to attain *bodhi*. The Māra King was struck with alarm and fear; he quickly emerged from his palace and said to the Bodhisattva:
"You should rise from this seat. This is a time of turbid evil; you ought not to realize awakening. You should instead accept the position of a Wheel-Turning King in this present life."
The Bodhisattva said, "What you have just said is like trying to entice a child; it is impossible for me to rise from this samādhi.

Māra said, "If you will not follow my words, I shall cause you to see what terrifies you. The Bodhisattva replied, "By holding a single *paṃcavārṣika* (unrestricted) great assembly, you attained this celestial body.
As for the number of great assemblies I have held, they are difficult to know; how much more so my other merits? (Because of this contemplation...)"
Because past causes must give rise to past wisdom, Māra knew he was no match and each returned to his palace.

Desiring to observe what he would do next, [the Bodhisattva] further gave rise to the divine eye (this constitutes the subduing of the celestial Māra by means of two types of clarity). He further reflected on the conditions by which Māra’s faction gives rise to evil;

knowing it arises from afflictions (*kleśa*), and having become weary of afflictions, he subsequently exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) (this is the subduing of the *kleśa-māra*, and it also constitutes the subduing of the *skandha-māra* and the *mṛtyu-māra*). As for those who remove obstructions, they obstruct clarity.

This "obstruction" (*yǒng*) is precisely the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). In the Hīnayāna, it is termed "non-defiled ignorance" (*akliṣṭājñāna*). Regarding the removal of the "obstruction of nature" (*xìng zhàng*):

"nature" here refers to that which is defiled and capable of obstructing noble wisdom; this is the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*). In the Hīnayāna, it is termed "defiled ignorance" (*kliṣṭājñāna*).
Master Chongshi also stated that these two obstructions are removed. Now, upon detailed examination, the meaning of "removing the obstructive obstruction" accords with [the former].

As for the principle that "the obstacle of nature (*prakṛti-āvaraṇa*) is excluded," this is not logically tenable, because it is clarified here that [this stage] is not subsumed under the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*).

Therefore, it is best to correlate it with the two paths—the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)—within the context of obstructing [the outflows]. (The obstacle of nature may be explained further in the section on the exhaustion of outflows.

Next, regarding the passage on the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), there are three parts as mentioned above: first, citing what precedes to introduce what follows; second, presenting the object to manifest the wisdom; third, the explanation.
The reason for this is as follows: if one were to expand upon the passage concerning death, stating that "one falls into the hells" and so forth, this would also imply birth;
thus, it would contradict reason.

Conversely, if one were to expand upon the passage concerning birth, stating that "at the end of life, one is born in the heavens," this would likewise entail death. Therefore, [the text] must be understood as it stands.
Regarding the section on the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), the chapter states: "The text cites the objects [of cognition] to clarify the internal content, which consists of four parts.

First, taking the Four Noble Truths as the object; second, severing the outflows by means of seeing the truths; third, attaining liberation by means of severing the outflows; fourth, because one is already liberated, the four knowledges reach their ultimate consummation.
The explanations for these are all as presented in the chapter and can be seen by consulting it.

Regarding the initial statement that "the mind takes the truths and so forth as its object," a close examination of the meaning of the text suggests it can be explained according to Mahāyāna doctrine.
The phrase "the mind takes the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows as its object" reveals that it takes the *tathatā* (suchness) of the four truths as its object.

"Regarding 'knowing the truths as they truly are, such as suffering,' etc.: because one knows the reality [of things], this contradicts the characteristics of the four truths. This collectively reveals fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

As for 'having attained the noble truths and knowing them as they truly are,' etc.: this restates that, by virtue of having attained the aforementioned fundamental wisdom, one further gives rise to..."

Subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is like [the knowledge of] outflows (*āsrava*) and the accumulation of outflows (*āsrava-samudaya*), and so forth (this meaning is necessary). This is precisely the difference between the fundamental [knowledge] and subsequent knowledge regarding their objects (*ālambana*) within the truths (*satya*).
As for "severing outflows by seeing the truths," it means being able to see and know the principle of the Four Truths; it does not mean seeing [them] during the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
[This is] the Truth (*satya*). (This follows the previous explanation according to the Commentary as before).
Regarding the phrase "He forms such knowledge," which cites the preceding contemplation of the Truths (*satya*) and raises the aforementioned cessation of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*):

now, upon careful examination, the text "he forms such knowledge" cites the two types of wisdom previously mentioned—namely, the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "thus observing the liberation of the mind from the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*)," this reveals the wisdom regarding the outflows that are to be abandoned.

As for the three outflows, the twentieth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states in verse: "The afflictions of the desire realm, together with the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*)—namely, anger, concealment, envy, vexation, lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, restlessness, sleep, and regret—are called the ten envelopments;

excluding delusion (*moha*), these are termed the outflow of desire. The outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) pertains to the two upper realms and consists solely of the afflictions, excluding delusion."

They are combined into one because they are both indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), inward-directed, and belong to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*). Ignorance (*avidyā*) is treated as a separate outflow (*āsrava*) because it is the root of all forms of existence.
[The prose commentary asks: "Is it not the case that the two types of envelopments—sloth (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—also exist in the higher realms?
Why are they not mentioned here? The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr say: "Because those envelopments in those realms are few and lack autonomy."
Furthermore, it is said: For what reason are the *anuśayas* of the two realms combined and designated as a single "outflow" (*āsrava*)? Because they share three common characteristics:

they are both of the same indeterminate nature (the afflictions of the upper realms are exclusively obscured-indeterminate), they operate toward internal objects (arising by taking the internal body as their object), and they arise based on the meditative stages (*samāpatti-bhūmi*). Due to these three similarities, they are combined into one.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 47, provides one explanation stating: "The meaning of 'stream' (*srotas*) is the meaning of 'outflow' (*āsrava*), just as water flows from a spring or milk [flows from a cow]."

Milk flows from the breasts. In this way, for sentient beings, the various outflows (āsrava) stream forth through the gateway of the six sense bases. Regarding [the causes such as] inversion and negligence, they are explained at length as in that [text].
Furthermore, the meaning of the three outflows in the Mahāyāna differs; fearing prolixity, I shall not describe it here.

Regarding the statement, "Having already attained liberation, the knowledge of liberation arises," this sequentially reveals the two types of liberation: the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

As for the phrase, "Based on *nirvāṇa*, it is said that the causes and conditions for birth throughout the three periods of time are eternally severed," and so forth, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (Chapter 37) states:
Because he has eternally severed the causes and conditions for birth throughout the three periods of time, he declares of himself: "My births are exhausted.

Furthermore, because he has severed the body of the five aggregates within the three realms, he proclaims: "My births are exhausted. And because the holy life (*brahmacarya*) he has cultivated is now complete, he says this.

He proclaims: "The holy life (brahmacarya) has been established. Furthermore, having abandoned the path of training (śaikṣa-mārga), it is also called "established," for that which was originally sought has now been attained today;

therefore, he proclaims: "What was to be done has been accomplished" (kṛta-kṛtya). Having cultivated the path and attained the fruit, it is also called "accomplished," because he has obtained the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
He proclaims: "I have exhausted all fetters of existence (bhava-saṃyojana). For this reason, he is named an Arhat.

Arhat (the above is the careful transcription of the scriptural text). Within the [four] verses, "birth is exhausted" corresponds to the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*); "the holy life has been established" corresponds to the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*);

"what was to be done has been accomplished" corresponds to the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); and "there is no further existence" corresponds to the knowledge of the exhaustion of the origin (*samudaya-kṣaya-jñāna*).

Furthermore, it is said: "One should simply say that the Path attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and so forth. This meaning is difficult to express; the sense of the exhaustion of the causes of the origin is what is termed "exhaustion."

Regarding "knowledge" (*jñāna*): the meaning of the cessation of the fruit of suffering is termed "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*) (this interpretation follows the Mahāyāna). Logically, it should only state the meaning of the exhaustion of the cause;

what need is there to subsequently state the meaning of the cessation of the fruit of suffering? Therefore, the answer is given: by citing the exhaustion of the fruit, one reveals the extinction of the cause.
Both of these [positions] are consistent with reason. As for Master Chong’s (Chengyou) arbitrary citation of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 102, to refute this meaning:
he attempts to undermine a great principle with a minor and heterodox school; this is utterly contrary to correct reasoning (I cannot elaborate further).

Regarding the statement "the remaining two passages can be understood": the four preceding passages collectively constitute the second section, which presents the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) to manifest [the wisdom].

In the present passage, the timing of the attainment constitutes the third section. These three preceding sections further belong to the second part, which presents the objective sphere to manifest the wisdom.
From here on, the third part—beginning with "For what reason" (*tat kasya hetoḥ*)—explains the grounds for the attainment. The current commentary specifically points to the time of attainment.
The following refers to the other two [types of people].
Regarding why this distinction is made in contrast to those who see and hear, the *Jushelun Baoshu* (Commentary on the Treasury of Abhidharma) states:

"The Dharma Master Shouji says that since ancient times, the masters of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma have all maintained that the difference between seeing and hearing refers to the varying capacities of sentient beings; thus, some may 'see' more, while others may 'hear' more."

This is insufficient; logically, it should not be so. From the initial birth and renunciation, through the attainment of enlightenment and the turning of the Dharma wheel, these events should logically be seen as occurring at the same time.

How could there be any discrepancy? He then extensively cites sūtras and śāstras to provide a harmonious interpretation; as the wording is complex and voluminous, it cannot be recounted in full. To briefly state his intent:
first, by calculating the date of the *nirvāṇa* and tracing back to the attainment of enlightenment, it is clearly known that the month of Jǐnyín (the second lunar month) is the correct one.

It is established that he attained enlightenment on the eighth day of the second month. Second, by tracing backward from the day of his enlightenment, it is clearly known that he must have turned the Wheel of Dharma on the eighth day of the eighth month.
Furthermore, as for the backward calculation, according to the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (which is the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* cited in this very commentary;
this method and its intent were understood by [certain] people, and thus it was renamed the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*) and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, both state that it was the eighth month.

The turning of the Wheel of Dharma occurred on the eighth day of the eighth month. According to the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, four months prior to the turning of the Wheel, he first cultivated the faculties of the five individuals.
Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there were fifty-seven days prior to the invitation by Brahmā. Calculating these periods together, they total six months.

It clarifies that King Dīpaṃkara renounced the world and attained enlightenment. Regarding the second person of value, one should know that from the passage "The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara thereafter" onwards, it concerns his external transformation and acceptance of offerings.
This second major section is divided into five parts; the first clarifies the time when the Brahmin was performing a sacrificial rite.

Migāra the Māṇava shifted twelve deformities and was reborn in a superior realm, departing after receiving offerings. (The twelve deformities are: first, a hunched back; second, protruding ribs; third, a goiter; fourth, jaundice; fifth, a jaundiced head; sixth, blue eyes;

seventh, saw-like teeth; eighth, black teeth; ninth and tenth, crooked hands and feet; eleventh, a body not equal in height to others; twelfth, a protruding pelvis. Regarding the sixfold trembling of the earth at the time he moved his seat, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 12, states:

first, "trembling" (*calana*), which means shaking; second, "leaping up" (*prākampa*), such as rising in the east and sinking in the west; third, "rising" (*samprakampa*), meaning ascending upward; fourth, "surging" (*vedhana*), meaning bulging upward; fifth, "shaking" (*kṣobha*), meaning descending downward... [text continues].

He departed. (The "six roars" refer to the sound of his roar. Second, from "Mīmāṃsaka the Brahmin returned to the great kingdom of Pāṭaliputra" onwards, it extensively explains how Mīmāṃsaka offered his hair as an act of worship, and how he received a prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha.

Third, from "at that time, thousands of ministers and hundreds of millions of people" onwards, they made offerings to his hair. Fourth, from "the price-seeker should know" onwards, [it concerns] the twelve fetters of ugliness.
The causes and conditions of enmity. Fifth, the convergence of past and present to prove that hair and nails can produce merit and benefit (*maṇava*;

in Sanskrit *maṇavaka*, here translated as "youth of pure conduct"). Regarding the statement in the chapter, "The fifth section may be understood," it refers from the passage beginning "At that time, the two brothers who were merchants" onwards;
as explained in the preceding commentary, the fifth section, from "At that time, the merchants" onwards, concerns the matter of making offerings through ritual prostration.

Having finished, he respectfully requested to withdraw. This is it. In the sixth assembly, that of the Dragon Kings, after the Buddha had arisen from samādhi, the Dragon King praised the Buddha with a verse.
That verse is identical to the verse spoken by Upānta in the "Instruction on the Precepts" above.
"Those who gather and benefit others" means to receive and provide for their welfare.

Regarding the principle of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), its essence has existed from of old. This meaning is intended to rely on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, chapter twenty-seven, which states that there are two kinds of ultimateity (*atyanta*):
first, the ultimateity of adornment (*vyūha-atyanta*), which refers to the six *pāramitās*; second, the ultimateity of finality (*niṣṭhā-atyanta*).
[The section] concludes. This refers to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) attained by all sentient beings; it is intended to reveal that *tathatā* (suchness) is the basis for both delusion and awakening.
The nature of *tathatā* has never changed since antiquity. Therefore, the tenth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"The basis of delusion and awakening refers to *tathatā*, because it can serve as the root of both delusion and awakening. All defiled and pure phenomena arise in dependence upon it. The noble path transforms it, causing one to abandon the defiled."
Purity is attained. (Commentary: Although the essence of *tathatā* is neither defiled nor pure, it serves as the actual nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) for both defilement and purity;
therefore, based upon *tathatā*, defilement and purity arise.
"Discussing by relying on characteristics" refers specifically to discussing by relying on the characteristics of defilement and purity.

"Not seeking through calculation and so forth" means that, in establishing any principle, there are generally three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): first, inference (*anumāna*); second, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Regarding the three types of scriptural authority (*āgama-pramāṇa*): this True Suchness (*tathatā*) is beyond the reach of verbal teachings; therefore, it is said that it is "not to be sought through scriptural authority" and so forth.

As for "realizing the essence of Perfect Enlightenment and reaching the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) fruit": this means being able to realize the Bodhi of Perfect Enlightenment—that is, awakening to the unconditioned principle within the state of fruition.
"Enveloped by darkness or fetters" reveals ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Grasping at clear characteristics" refers to the arising of wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) due to that ignorance.

Regarding the term "those of divergent livelihoods" (*anyājīva*), because they sustain themselves through such [wrong views], it is explained that maintaining and nourishing wrong views constitutes a divergent livelihood. Now, to examine this in detail: the preservation and cultivation of wrong views is what constitutes a divergent livelihood.
Because the true principle of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) gives rise to the root of both defilement and purity, it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Furthermore, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the twelve links of dependent origination are named "Buddha-nature" (*buddhadhātu*), and Buddha-nature is named "emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

This also clarifies the basis for delusion and awakening. It is by depending upon this true nature that the twelve links of dependent origination, such as ignorance (*avidyā*), arise; yet the nature of this dependent origination is not... [inherently existent].
It is apart from *tathatā* (suchness). However, because foolish commoners are unable to comprehend it, they undergo transmigration.

Regarding "being deluded about the cause of the One Vehicle" and so forth: failing to realize the nature of dependent origination is called being deluded about the cause; failing to realize *nirvāṇa* [is called being deluded about the result].
This is called "delusion regarding the fruit.
It refers to those who are unable to cultivate the habitual tendencies of the pure portion (*śukla-pakṣa*).

Through the repeated application of the principles of the objects of observation, they are thus able to gradually diminish the defiled seeds and gradually increase the pure seeds within the *ālayavijñāna*, until finally they can give rise to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and directly realize the Truth.
Principle: One becomes a sage by severing delusions. Now, because one is deluded regarding the Truth, one cannot achieve the "perfumed cultivation" of the pure portion.

Regarding the afflictions of the four abodes: as previously explained in the discussion on the meaning of the five stages of abiding, these are the four abodes excluding the stage of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
The statement that "craving is exhausted because ignorance has been forever lost" specifically reveals the *avidyā-vāsabhūmi* (the ground of the dwelling of ignorance).
The "causal vehicle" refers to the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), while the "fruition vehicle" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This is based on the tenet of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
That which is cherished by the body of the ignorant and dark refers to ignorance residing within the body and obscuring right view.
Regarding "entering the mundane mind," the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 99) states: "The Tathāgata’s untainted mind and mental factors..."

Furthermore, those previously unobtained contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are not objects currently apprehended by the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
However, regarding those previously obtained contaminated minds and mental factors that the Buddha wishes others to know, they are known immediately.

That is to say, if the Buddha wishes to make those of dull faculties know his mind, rather than those of sharp faculties, then even Sarpadāsa and others will know the Buddha’s mind; yet Śāriputra [would not].

You disciples are all unable to know it. If one wishes to cause those in the animal realm and so forth to know the Buddha’s mind—rather than those in the realms of humans or devas—then the animals and others will indeed know the Buddha’s mind, while humans and devas do not.
According to the Mahāyāna, the Buddha possesses no contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds or mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*);
nevertheless, he is able to manifest what appears to be contaminated phenomena. Thus, the tenth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The Unsurpassed..."
The Awakened One possesses inconceivable supernormal powers; therefore, he is able to manifest formless phenomena.
Were it not so, how could the minds of śrāvakas, animals, and others be identical to the Tathāgata’s mind? For even Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment do not know the Tathāgata’s actual mind.

Regarding the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇa-sampad*): "abandonment" refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because it manifests through the elimination of afflictions. Since the attainment (*prāpti*) of this has arisen within the body, it is said to be "accomplished.
The "perfection of knowledge" (*jñāna-sampad*) refers to the knowledge capable of realization; that is, the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).

"One who has once attained the conceptual understanding of the One Vehicle" refers to one who, in the past, conceptually contemplated the True Principle and thereby planted the seeds for the Mahāyāna cause.
"That which transforms into a small fruition" is as described in the *Bunyō-kyō* (Sutra on the Ornament of Original Acts) and other texts;
it concerns the case of Śāriputra, who, due to the conditions of having given his eyes in the past, regressed from the bodhicitta. This is precisely that matter.
Regarding "those who remain here according to their vows," this refers to the Buddha’s vow: "I shall not rise from this vajrāsana until I have attained perfect enlightenment.
This seat is located in the kingdom of Magadha.

Regarding the recollection of merit (*guṇānusmṛti*): among the six recollections, the Buddha constitutes one. This means that by taking the Jewel of the Buddha as an object, one gives rise to thoughts in accordance with it, thereby increasing one's merit.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*), fascicle 2, states: "For example, like a great dragon... [omission] ...and only then does he preach the Dharma."
Regarding the statement that they are combined into nine because each has superior, middling, and inferior [capacities]: [those born in] the world (inferior birth) have dull faculties (middling);

those who fear sin (superior, slightly less than superior) are many (middling) and difficult to save (inferior); those who are long [in duration] (inferior) have sharp faculties (middling) and are easy to save (superior).

This is like a man with sight in the world observing three distinct things in a pond: the earth, the water, and the flowers (the three: ground, water, and flowers). Zongchong says: "However, this is intended to reveal that there are [various capacities] among those to be converted."
Sentient beings differ in their dispositions and belong to distinct categories; this is not intended to clarify the three vehicles or the nine natures.

If one were to divide them into nine based on the three vehicles, it is unclear upon what principle or teaching such a classification is made. If there is no principle or teaching to rely upon, it must certainly be the mere fabrication of the transmitter’s own mind.
Furthermore, the Buddha observes all those to be converted in their entirety, without discriminating between those who follow a vehicle and those who do not, as follows:
How can this passage be interpreted as teaching according to the vehicles (yāna)? Therefore, we know that the ancient explanation does not accord with the ultimate intent.
We hope that those of wisdom will contemplate the text to attain realization. Now, examining the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it says:

"Reflecting upon the skillful means employed by the Buddhas of the past, I too, having now attained the Way, should likewise preach the three vehicles. ... [and so on] ... until: "Having contemplated these matters, he immediately proceeded to Pāṭaliputra."
"Na" is precisely the explicit teaching. When the Buddhas appear in the world, they invariably act to transform sentient beings, enabling them to escape birth and death;
because they possess both compassion and wisdom, this is the principle.

Regarding the fact that the matter of the five bhikṣus can also be understood in this way: it was because people might suspect that the Buddha had learned this Dharma from the five bhikṣus and therefore now first delivered it to them, that [the Buddha] first delivered it to them to dispel such external doubts.
The Venerable One said: "Previously, by the side of Lake Anavatapta, the Buddha practiced the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and so forth."

One might require the resolution of these doubts: "The five men came first; they practiced self-starvation under the Buddha. Since the Buddha originally did not learn the Dharma from these five men, what need is there to resolve these doubts? This is not so.
If one explains that the intention of the exhortation regarding cause and effect can be understood, then it should be known as follows:

In the past, they falsely clung to the "sphere of nothingness" (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and so forth as *nirvāṇa*, and they clung to self-starvation and the like as the causes of *nirvāṇa*. Now, by citing the culmination of the four knowledges (*jñāna*), he refutes their clinging to the result;
by citing the cultivation of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), he refutes their clinging to the cause.
"Yùzhī-bōluó" (欲之波羅) means "to reach" (*yāti*). "To reach" means "to go.
Regarding the Buddha’s response in verse, the fifteenth verse of the *Pañcavargika* states: "All-knowledge is supreme; it is without burden and without bondage.
My practice was not dependent on a teacher; I spontaneously realized the Noble Path. It is peerless and without equal, capable of bringing the world [to liberation]."
Peace and happiness! At Vārāṇasī, the drum of the Dharma of the Deathless (amṛta) shall be struck.
Regarding those who rely on the Āgamas as the "Four Questions," some say that within these there are eight questions, of which five are spoken of verbally.

There are three [objections] regarding the mind. Regarding the five [objections] concerning speech, they consist of two difficulties and three questions. The three questions have already been explained in the commentary. As for the two difficulties:
first, his sense faculties are tranquil, which raises the difficulty that the Buddha lacks the quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), appearing as if he were a fool who startles people;

second, his countenance is serene and joyful, which raises the difficulty that the Buddha lacks the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), appearing as if he were a person possessed by greed. Regarding the three [objections] regarding the mind: first, [the question] asks where...

[He] departed. Second, what did he do? Third, was it for his own benefit or for the benefit of others? In the response, eight points are provided. "All-knowledge as supreme" answers the first question.
"Liberation from all sensual desire" answers the second question. The two lines beginning with "Spontaneously" answer the question of what dharma was studied.
"I too [have] one verse" answers the question of who the teacher was. "I am [the one]"—one verse—answers the question of from whom [he received it].
"Who is it that studies?"—this refers to the three [aspects] within the meaning of the response regarding a single verse.

"Ling (泠) and ever serene": the character *ling* has been used for a long time; it describes the state of being *lingran* (泠然), which means clear and cool. It may also be understood as the sense of awakening and realization (*jiewu*).

"Victorious" (*jina*) means "to cease. This reveals that the Buddha’s wisdom and virtue possess the function of cessation; it is not merely a definition of the character itself (in the text, "I have severed all fetters" does not refer to the character *jina*).
The verse says: "That which is beyond words" refers to the Brahmin’s silent comprehension of the meaning (which differs from the Udāyin of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, who did not accept it).
Regarding the essence of the cause of the Middle Way: this refers to the Eightfold Noble Path, which is called the "essence of the cause" because it is able to lead toward the fruit of Nirvāṇa.
Regarding "those who practice the tranquility of nirvāṇa and so forth," the phrase "and so forth" includes the conduct of a śramaṇa.

As for the Eightfold Noble Path, although it was briefly explained in the introduction to the preceding verse, one should now provide a detailed exposition of right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
The Commentary states: "As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says, 'Bodily action produced by untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is right action,' and so forth.

This intention is intended to demonstrate that the three—vocal action, livelihood, and [right action]—are the precepts concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*). It does not necessarily constitute a direct explanation of the meaning of right action and the others.
*Shizongyi Ji*, Fascicle Seven, Part One;
*Shizongyi Ji*, Fascicle Seven, Part Two.

Regarding the fourth section, "The Separate Exposition of the Text," this provides a brief analysis of the chapter on the meaning of the Four Noble Truths through a fivefold classification. First, the Establishment...

The sequence is established as follows: first, the general introduction; second, the explanation of names and the discernment of the essence; third, the discernment and exposition of the truths and delusions; fourth, the methods for their abandonment;
and fifth, the aspects of the mental application toward the truths.
Regarding the sequence of the establishment [of the truths]: the commentary (*śāstra*) divides the text into four sections; this section explains it according to the first section. Question:

Based on what meaning are the four truths, such as suffering (*duḥkha*), established? Furthermore, based on what meaning are they presented first as suffering and then as origin (*samudaya*), and so forth, as explained at length?
Answer: As the commentary states: "Although the truths are four, [they are established] because they pertain to life, things, and birth. This is the reason.
In this context, the intended meaning is that there are causes and effects for both the mundane and the supramundane; thus, they are opened up to form four [truths].

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 77, poses an objection: "If they are established based on cause and effect, then the truths should be five, because the causes and effects of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are distinct.
Since they are already established as two, the various uncontaminated paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) also possess causes and effects and should likewise be divided [into separate truths]."

Second, cessation is established as the fifth. Thus, there are five truths (meaning that within the truth of the path, there are four causes—namely, the homogeneous, the associated, the co-existent, and the enabling—and furthermore, three fruits:
the outflowing, the virile, and the dominant; whereas within the truth of cessation, there is only the fruit of disconnection; thus, there are five truths). The intent of the treatise explains:

within the untainted path, both causal nature and fruitional nature are all practices leading toward the cessation of suffering, and are therefore collectively established as one. If that is so, then regarding the causal nature within tainted phenomena...
And their fruits all tend toward saṃsāra; they too should be unified. Answer: Because of the opening and closing of their aspects (*ākāra*), there are only the Four Noble Truths.

That is to say, the contaminated fruit possesses four kinds of aspects, namely suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth; the nature of the contaminated cause further possesses four kinds of aspects, namely origin (*samudaya*) and so forth.
The uncontaminated cause and fruit together constitute four aspects. Due to this opening and closing, there are only four truths. Now...

In detail: that school is greatly mistaken in its arduous efforts. This is truly because they take the aggregate of suffering (*duḥkha-skandha*) as a single entity, and then divide it into two truths based on the distinction between cause and effect.
Consequently, by analogy with the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), they would also have to divide it into two truths based on the distinction between cause and effect.

Now, according to the Mahāyāna, although the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) is the Truth of Suffering, karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) are the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). Since these two entities are distinct, [the division into two truths does not apply].
One must not take the principle of a single essence as a precedent and cause the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) to be bifurcated into two truths.
Therefore, within the mundane realm, only the nature of the causes and effects of maturation (*vipāka*) is established as Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its Origin (*samudaya*).

Within the supramundane realm, the nature of the causes and effects of the means of penetration and the principles penetrated is established as the two gateways of Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*). Although their names are similar, the two...

The meanings are vastly different; how can they serve as a parallel? There have been some Dharma masters who cite the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* to explain Mahāyāna doctrines, but they have utterly lost the intended meaning.
In this present commentary, I follow the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* school while judging it to be identical to the Mahāyāna. Next, regarding the determination of the sequence:

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 78, states: Question: For what reason does the World-Honored One first teach the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and so forth, up until finally teaching the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*)?
Answer: This is taught in accordance with the sequence of the phrasing. There are three types of sequence: first, the sequence of origination;
second, the sequence of ease of exposition; and third, the sequence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Herein, it is based on the sequence of ease of exposition.
Furthermore, this is stated in reference to the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
That is to say, at the stage of clear realization, one first realizes suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth, up until finally realizing the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*); therefore, it is said thus.

Among the four truths, the truth of suffering is coarse and is thus realized first, gradually proceeding until the truth of the path, which is subtle. The Venerable Pārśva said: "The practitioner of meditation knows the five..."

Having understood the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*) as being like a disease, an abscess, and an arrow, one next seeks their cause and knows it to be the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).

Next, one seeks the state of non-abiding and knows it to be the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). Finally, one seeks the remedy and knows it to be the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). The *Abhidharmakośa* (Chapter 22) also states:
"They are explained according to the sequence of the stages of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). (The intent of the commentary is the same as that of the *Abhidharmakośa*.)

Second, regarding the explanation of names and the discernment of essence: first the explanation of names, then the discernment of essence. These were presented in a disordered manner within the commentary;
I shall now distinguish them separately. First, as for the explanation of names, there are three layers: (1) the explanation of the specific names of the four [noble truths] beginning with suffering;

(2) the explanation of the name "truth" (*satya*); and (3) the explanation of "Noble Truth" (*ārya-satya*). Regarding the explanation of the specific names of the four beginning with suffering, as the commentary states: "Suffering is defined by its nature of oppression."

"Artha" means meaning. "Samudaya" means accumulation. "Nirodha" means tranquility. "Mārga" refers to that which leads universally. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (77) states that the Venerable Pārśva said: "Oppression is the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha*);
arising and growth is the characteristic of origination (*samudaya*); tranquility is the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha*); and transcendence is the characteristic of the path (*mārga*).
Based on these four characteristics, the four names are established. Question: Regarding the four noble truths, each has four aspects (*ākāra*). What are they?

Furthermore, take for example the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*): it possesses four aspects—first, suffering; second, impermanence (*anitya*); third, emptiness (*śūnya*); and fourth, non-self (*anātman*).

This applies even up to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), each of which likewise possesses four aspects. For this reason, they should also be called the "Truth of Impermanence," or the "Truths of Emptiness" and so forth, as well as the "Truths of Cause" and so forth, or the "Truths of Tranquility" and "Truths of Suchness.
Why, then, are they designated only as the Truths of Suffering, Origin, Cessation, and Path? The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 79, answers this as follows: [text continues].
It should have been stated as the "Truth of Impermanence" and so forth; that it was not so stated is an incomplete teaching (*śeṣavacana*).

Furthermore, since it has already been stated as "suffering," one should know that it has thereby already been stated as the Truths of Impermanence, Emptiness, and Non-self, and so on up to the Truth of the Path. This should be understood by analogy.
Moreover, this designation "Truth of Suffering" is a traditional transmission; it is an ancient formulation [handed down] from the Buddhas of the past.
The sands of the Ganges all use names of suffering to represent the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Now, the Buddha is likewise so;

one should understand that this applies up to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) as well. According to the fifth chapter of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Four Truths" (*Catuḥsatya-parivarta*), each of the four truths is individually listed with forty names.
Having listed them, it further states: "These four truths have forty billion hundred thousand nayutas of names. Following [this principle]...

For the sake of those sentient beings who are to be disciplined, it is spoken thus. In this manner, throughout the hundreds of thousands of billions of immeasurable and incalculable worlds in the ten directions, the names spoken by the Buddhas are each as numerous as these.
Since the sūtras and śāstras are thus, let us for now rely on what is manifest and simply explain the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Regarding the second explanation of the term *satya* (truth): as the commentary states, these four kinds are all truly so and not erroneous; furthermore, there is no other path.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 77, says: "The meaning of reality (*bhūta-artha*), the meaning of truth (*tattva-artha*), and likewise the meaning of non-perversion (*aviparyāsa-artha*)."

The meaning of being non-deceptive is the meaning of *satya* (truth). Question: If that which has the meaning of reality, up to the meaning of being non-deceptive, is called *satya*, then the four perversions (*viparyāsa*) and deceptive speech would not be included within the category of *satya*. The intention of the *Mahāvibhāṣā* in explaining this is as follows:

they are called "perversion" and so forth by virtue of one specific sense, yet they are also subsumed under *satya* by virtue of another specific sense. That is to say, while they are falsely conceived as permanent when they are actually impermanent...
"Permanent," and so forth, up to "self"—to falsely conceive that which is not-self as self due to a perverted understanding is called "perversion.

Furthermore, because this [perception] possesses the nature of a cause and the nature of a fruit, it is subsumed under the Truths; the same applies by extension to deceptive speech. In the commentary (*śāstra*), there is further clarification regarding what is not a Truth:
namely, that this differs from ordinary beings who falsely conceive suffering to be pleasure, for they are deluded regarding the Truth of Suffering.
Furthermore, those who take atoms, the nature of the world, or Īśvara as their cause do so because they are deluded regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

Those who take the two kinds of emptiness as cessation refer to those such as Ārāḍa Kālāma, who cling to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)—these two forms of emptiness—as *nirvāṇa*;

this is because they are deluded regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). In reality, the false conceptions of non-Buddhists regarding the characteristics of *nirvāṇa* are manifold; however, for now...
To take the two types of emptiness as objects of false conceptualization is to mistake them for cessation (*nirodha*).

To regard the precepts of the "black chicken" and so forth as the Path is to be deluded regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*); because of this delusion, these are not truths at all. As for "subtle atoms" (*paramāṇu*):
they are like the Lokāyata (in Sanskrit, *Lokāyata*, or *Lokāyati*; here translated as "Conformist to the World"). They maintain that all [phenomena]...

Phenomena such as form and mind all take the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) as their cause. Furthermore, within these four great elements, that which extracts the vital essence and possesses the capacity for cognitive reflection (*ālambana-cintana*) constitutes the mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*).
This is just as, although all material forms are composed of the same great elements, it is the lamp that emits light.
The others are not so; therefore, there is no logical error in asserting that among the four great elements (mahābhūta), there is that which is capable of cognitive reflection.

If one discusses material phenomena (rūpadharma), it is universally established that the four great elements constitute their substance. Furthermore, it is like the Vaiśeṣika school, which maintains that eternal, discrete atoms (paramāṇu) serve as the cause.
The receptacle world was thus formed. At the beginning of this eon of formation (*vivartakalpa*), there appeared a non-Buddhist practitioner when the human lifespan was immeasurable years.
Because he agitated the minds of people, he went among humans to beg for food during the night; consequently, the people of that time called him "owl" (*ulūka*).
He was also named *Kaṇāda*, which means "eater of rice-grains. This man’s appearance was ugly and his hair was disheveled; those who saw him were struck with fear.

Thereafter, he ceased begging for alms altogether; instead, at the sites where grain was pounded and winnowed outside, he would scoop up a measure of rice from among the husks and chaff to sustain his life.
For this reason, he was called the Rishi who Eats a Measure of Rice (Śāli-bhikṣu). He was also known as Vaiśeṣika;
in Sanskrit, it is *Vaiśeṣika-śāstra*, which is translated here as "Excellence" (*Vaiśeṣika*). His former name was Vaisesi.
He composed the *Ṣaṭpadārthasastra*. Because this treatise is preeminent, it is named the *Vaiśeṣika* (the Doctrine of Distinction) after its subject matter.

The six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) are as follows: 1. **The Category of Substance** (*dravyapadārtha*): This refers to earth, water, fire, air, space, time, direction, mind, and self (nine entities constituting its essence).

2. **The Category of Quality** (*guṇapadārtha*): This refers to color, sound, odor, taste, tangibility; number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction; beauty and ugliness; pleasure and pain; and aversion.

The categories of affection, delusion, wisdom, diligence, and negligence (having twenty-one factors as their essence); the categories of the three types of action, taking, abandoning, contracting, and extending (having five factors as their essence);
and the category of Great Existence (*mahāsattā*), which refers to the fact that substance, quality, and action are not non-existent, because it is by virtue of this Great Existence that they exist.

Apart from substance (*dravya*) and the others, there exists a separate real entity (ten categories in total): the fifth is the category of "sameness-and-difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*). For example, regarding earth, which is characterized by solidity, there is the sense of sameness [with other earth];

yet, as for this solidity, there is the sense of difference [from water and so forth]. This sameness-and-difference of earth is such that it is earth and not water; the same applies to water and the others.

However, apart from substance and the rest, there exists a separate real entity (which, according to the various dharmas of sameness and difference, possesses numerous entities). The sixth is "inherence" (*samavāya*).

The meaning of a phrase (*pada-artha*) refers to a collection of dharmas. By means of a conjunctive phrase, it is like a bird flying through the air that suddenly reaches a tree branch and remains there without departing;
it is by means of a conjunctive phrase that it causes [the collection] to abide. (This also consists of multiple entities.

However, within the actual phrases, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)—earth, water, fire, and wind—and their subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) are both permanent and impermanent. That which is permanent, at the time of the initial destruction, disperses individually.
Abiding thus, when the kalpa is about to form, two by two they couple and produce a single *paramāṇu*. Yet that *paramāṇu* is equal in measure to its parents.
From these pairs of *paramāṇus*, grandsons are produced in turn, until finally coarse material forms arise, forming the great earth and so forth.
Once the "Son" has departed, that is impermanence. Next, we shall distinguish the nature of the world (*loka-prakṛti*).

In various sūtras and śāstras, it is sometimes called *pradhāna* (the Supreme Nature), sometimes called *prakṛti*, sometimes called *avyakta-tattva* (the Unmanifest Truth), and sometimes called *svabhāva* (Self-nature).

These are all one and the same; this refers to the calculation of the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists. In Sanskrit, it is called *Sāṃkhya-śāstra*; here it is translated as "Number Theory" (*Sāṃkhya*), meaning that which is produced.
This treatise arises from the category of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*) and also gives rise to the category of wisdom; therefore, it is called *Sāṃkhya*.
It is also named *Kapila* (formerly translated as *Kāpila*). This is because this person’s head and face were both yellowish-red, and he was named after this feature.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 39, his name is *Jātiśroṇa*. He composed the *Tattvasamāsa-śāstra* (this).
It is said that he observed and extensively analyzed the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).

Fearing that his teachings would perish after his death, the seer went to the abode of Maheśvara and requested the method for prolonging life. Maheśvara replied, "Beneath Mount Vindhya there is the *āmalaka* fruit;
when it is not yet ripe, its color is blue-green, but when it reaches maturity, its color becomes yellowish-white."
When first eaten, its taste was sour and bitter; after eating it, drinking water tasted as sweet as honey. Therefore, it is called *yukanzi* (the "remaining-sweet" fruit).
"If you eat this fruit, you shall attain long life. At that time, the rishi took it and ate it, yet his mind remained undecided, and he further requested the essential method [for longevity].
Viśveśvara said, "Transform it into a stone, and you shall be able to dwell for a long time. He then transformed it accordingly.
The stone was about the size of a single bed and was located in a grove of *āmalaka* trees beneath Mount Piṇḍa.
Later, after a thousand years had passed, the Bodhisattva Dignāga appeared in the world and extensively composed various treatises to refute that school.
When the followers of that school were unable to defend themselves, they went together to the site of the stone and inscribed their own treatises upon it.
When he first began to write upon the stone, there were those who could understand the text after it had lain there for one night, while others found it increasingly difficult;

some did not begin to comprehend it until seven days had passed. After [Song] took up the brush again to rewrite it, they could no longer understand it at all. The stone then perspired, let out a roar like thunder, and shattered of its own accord.
As for the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*) established by that school, although they appear as minor matters in various treatises...
Regarding the distinctions, according to the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*, there is one verse which says: "From Prakṛti arise, in succession, Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, and the sixteen;
within the sixteen are five, from which the five great elements arise. (Commentary: The first is the truth of Prakṛti, which is the primordial nature (*pradhāna*).
This has the three qualities (*guṇas*)—sattva, rajas, and tamas—as its essence. That is to say:
"Sattva" has three meanings: first, yellow; second, greed; and third, pleasure. Next, "rajas" also has three meanings: first, red; second, hatred; and third, suffering.
Next, "tamas" also has three meanings: first, black; second, delusion; and third, equanimity. To explain them collectively:
yellow, red, and black are the qualities of form (*rūpa-guṇa*); greed, hatred, and delusion are the qualities of mind (*citta-guṇa*); and pleasure... [is the quality of sattva].
The quality of "suffering" (*duḥkha*) is the virtue of experience. This state has two aspects: first, it remains dormant and unarisen within the state of primordial nature (*prakṛti*);
second, within the twenty-three principles beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), it becomes awakened.
This second great principle arises through the transformation of primordial nature, just as a seed gradually swells when it is about to sprout. Second...

Third is the truth of self-conceit (*asmimāna-satya*). This refers to the arising of pride based on relying upon a self; it takes this [reliance] as its essence. This, in turn, arises from the aforementioned "great" [pride].
Fourth is the sixteenth truth, which arises from the aforementioned self-conceit. Regarding the sixteen: first, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); [second], sound; [third], touch; and so forth.

Three colors, four tastes, and five fragrances—these five each possess only their own substance and their own capacity; therefore, they are so named. Second, the five faculties of cognition (the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose): these five are able to cognize their respective objects.

These are called the five faculties of cognition (*pañca-jñānendriya*). Third are the five faculties of action (*pañca-karmendriya*): first, the tongue; second, the hands; third, the feet; fourth, the male and female organs; and fifth, the organ of excretion (*mahā-visarga*), by which one expels feces. These five are termed the five faculties of action.

Fourth is the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*). When added to the preceding, they total sixteen. Furthermore, when the fundamental nature (*svabhāva*) and the great ego (*mahāhaṃkāra*) are added, they constitute the nineteen principles (*tattva*).

Fifth are the five gross elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*). From among the aforementioned sixteen, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arise. That is to say, from the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), the gross element of space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*) arises.
Tangibility produces only the wind element; color produces only the fire element; taste produces the water element; and fragrance produces only the earth element.

(These five added to the previous nineteen constitute the twenty-four *tattvas*). These twenty-four are all "mine" (*mama*); together with the *tattva* of the divine self (*puruṣa*), they total twenty-five.
This means that because the divine self desires to enjoy objects, it subsequently enters into union with primordial nature (*prakṛti*). It is by virtue of this [union] that...
The transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) gives rise to the remaining twenty-three principles (*tattva*), which are for my enjoyment.
It joins male and female to produce offspring and so forth. I am the enjoyer, not the agent; the other twenty-four [principles] are solely agents, not enjoyers.
This is explained in detail in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā-bhāṣya*. Formerly, within this non-Buddhist school, there was a community...

He arrived at the Kāñcanamālā Garden, wearing a fire bowl upon his head and wrapping his abdomen with iron plates. He struck the drum of the Wheel of Sound and commanded the monks to engage in debate.
There was a monk from East India who debated with this non-Buddhist. The latter established that the world is eternal; the monk challenged him, saying:
"It must certainly undergo extinction now, because the world is destroyed at the end of a kalpa; thus we know for certain that it is extinguished now. He...
The opponent raised an objection, saying: "In the future, it will certainly not perish, just like the mountains and such things we see now.

At that time, the king [dealt with] these non-Buddhists in such a way that he caused this monk to suffer humiliation while riding a donkey. The king held the non-Buddhists in high esteem and presented them with seventy *kāra* of pure gold.

Because of this gold, there arose the *Saptati-śāstra*, consisting of seventy verses of verse-form (*gāthā*) which extensively set forth their school’s tenets; it was titled after the gold and served to propagate their views.

Later, when the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu appeared in the world, he composed the *Paramārthasaptati* (Seventy Verses on Ultimate Truth) to extensively refute that school and rescue the doctrine of the former Saṃgha.
At that time, the king held Vasubandhu’s treatise in high esteem and commanded the people of the land to propagate it widely.
Thereupon, Vasubandhu raised the corpse of the Sāṃkhya master and, having proven his point, lashed its bones with a whip; thus there arose the Dharma...
The Master said: "Vasubandhu practiced the ancient five-limbed discipline until his bones were revealed as a mark of his virtue;
Dignāga first codified the three-part logic, roaring over stones to manifest his capability. These are the facts regarding them. Next, to examine those who take Īśvara as the cause:
there are naked heretics in the West, also known as ash-smearing heretics, as well as certain Brahmins and the followers of the Yellow [Tirthikas], who hold this view. Their school..."
Regarding Maheśvara, he has two abodes: one is in the north of the Snowy Mountains (Himavat), and the other is on Mount Malaya in the southern ocean.
Formerly, in the kingdom of Mālava, there were two brothers who served Maheśvara. They went together to the Snowy Mountains seeking an audience with that deity.
Upon reaching the mountain, they suddenly saw a brāhmaṇa who said, "Maheśvara resides in your country."
"Why do you not pay homage to Śākyamuni Buddha? His brothers replied, "We have followed our ancestral tradition and worship only the celestial deities.
Relying upon his power as a brahmin, he transformed himself into the form of a deity, with three eyes on his face and four arms appearing, or sometimes eight arms.
He said to his brothers, "You should return to your kingdom to the east of the Bodhi tree and fashion an image of Śākyamuni subduing Māra."

To the south of the Bodhi tree, there is another pond that provides relief for those suffering from thirst and exhaustion. This school, based on this, maintains that there are two abodes, considering it to be unerring.

Furthermore, there are three bodies: first, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), whose essence is eternally all-pervading, its measure equal to empty space, and capable of giving rise to the myriad things;
second, the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which resides above the Form Realm heavens; and third, the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which assumes various forms according to circumstances.
They teach and transform sentient beings within the six realms of existence. Furthermore, they calculate that the Brahma King is able to produce all things;
as the Bodhisattva Deva states in his *Treatise on Refuting the Small Vehicle Nirvana of the Non-Buddhists*: "From the navel of the god Nārāyaṇa, a great lotus flower was produced."
Upon a lotus flower, Brahmā, the progenitor of all things (Brahmā being the ancestral father of the myriad things), was born.
That Brahmā created all sentient and insentient beings (meaning he fashioned all things, both animate and inanimate). From the mouth of Brahmā were born the Brāhmaṇas;
from his two arms, the Kṣatriyas; from his two thighs, the Vaiśyas; and from the two soles of his feet, the Śūdras. Such are their false reckonings. Its...
The varieties are numerous; they cannot be recounted in full. These views are all formed because the causes for rebirth are not fully understood, leading to such speculative calculations.
As for those who take the crow or the cock as the path, the phrase "and so forth" includes the precepts of the ox, the dog, and others.
This false speculation arises from two causes: first, through divine vision, they see sentient beings being born directly into the heavens from among crows or cocks; second, by...
This is an irrational reflection, a false conception. In the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 114, it is stated that there were two non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*).
One was named Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who observed the cow-vow; the other was named Ajita Keśakambala, who observed the dog-vow.
At different times, both went to the place where the Buddha was. After they had exchanged various words of affection and mutual greetings, at that time, Pūraṇa...
Cunda had previously asked another question: "Where will this Śrenika, who has observed the dog-vow and completed his training, be reborn?
The Blessed One replied, "Desist; do not ask. Yet he requested it a second and a third time. Out of compassion, the Buddha said, "Listen attentively.
If one observes the dog-vow without deficiency or transgression, they shall be reborn among dogs. If there is deficiency or transgression, they shall fall [into the lower realms]."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, he wept with such choked sobs that he could not restrain himself. The World-Honored One said, "My speech has ended;
there is no need to ask further. Now you have indeed harbored resentment. Then Pūraṇa said, "It is not because that man is destined for rebirth in the realm of dogs that I weep.
Rather, I have long observed the 'cow-vow' (go-vrata), and I fear that I too shall likewise come to pass. I only pray—"

"Great Compassionate One, please explain this for me. The World-Honored One replied (as should be understood according to the preceding account): "All of these arise from a failure to understand the true path. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* further states: Question:
How is it that observing the vows of a cow or a dog is called being without deficiency or transgression? Answer:
Acting in accordance with the laws of a cow, and acting in accordance with the laws of a dog, is called being without deficiency or transgression. Such false conceptualizations are not the truth.

Third, regarding the explanation of the Noble Truths (*āryasatya*): Although the commentary briefly raises a provisional inquiry and lists the names based on the second [truth], the text itself analyzes them.

For now, I shall provide a preliminary exposition according to the commentary’s interpretation of "noble" (*ārya*). One attains understanding by realizing [the truth]; thus, it is called "noble. This includes attaining understanding by abandoning the origin (*samudaya*), attaining understanding by realizing cessation (*nirodha*), and so forth.
Now, following the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, I shall briefly present three explanations. The first states: It is called a "Noble Truth" because it is accomplished by the noble ones (*ārya*).

"Accomplishment" (*pariniṣpatti*) is simply another name for "attainment" (*prāpti*). If that is so, since ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) also accomplish suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), why are these not called the "Truths of Ordinary Beings"?

Answer: The Noble Ones (*ārya*) fully accomplish all four [truths]; therefore, they alone are named the "Noble Truths. Question: There are also Noble Ones who do not fully accomplish all four, such as at the time of the Patience regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe-dharmajñānakṣānti*).

At that moment, one attains only a single momentary path (*mārga*), and at that time, one has not yet realized cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Thus, it is known that they have not yet fully accomplished all four. Answer: Following this, they will necessarily fully accomplish them.
Regarding the Four Truths: ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) never possess all four at once; therefore, they should be called only "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*).
Second, it is said that the Venerable Saṃghavasu stated: "While the Buddha was in the world, ordinary beings and noble ones engaged in debate with one another."

Ordinary worldlings claim that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are permanent, blissful, pure, and self (*ātman*). Noble ones (*ārya*) claim that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Each asserts their own words to be the truth. The Buddha resolved this by declaring: "The words of the noble ones are the truth."
Because the noble ones (ārya) directly know, see, and realize the truths such as suffering, what they declare to be truth is that which the noble ones proclaim based on their realization;
therefore, it is called the "Noble Truth" (*āryasatya*). Third, the Venerable Vasumitra states: "Only the noble ones penetrate [these] through noble wisdom; therefore, they are called Noble Truths.
(This corresponds to the subsequent explanation in the *Śāstra*). According to the Mahāyāna, the Buddha-body is consistently and exclusively the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).
They are subsumed within the [Four] Truths. However, while the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) resembles suffering and its origin, it is in reality neither suffering nor its origin.

For this reason, with respect to the other two types of vehicles (the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha), one may say that all four [truths] are established; yet if one considers the Buddha-body itself, only the latter two are established. The remaining two interpretations do not contradict the Mahāyāna.
Next, regarding the analysis of the essence [of the path], three schools of tenets are briefly presented: first, that based on the Sarvāstivāda; second, that based on the Sautrāntika;

and third, that based on the Mahāyāna. First, concerning the Sarvāstivāda, there are three internal meanings: first, according to the actual principle (*tattva*); second, according to the superior teaching (*praśasta-vacana*);
and third, according to a specific gate (*paryāya*). Regarding the actual principle, as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 77: "According to this explanation, if one follows..."

The five aggregates of one's own continuum, those that fall within the five aggregates of another's continuum, and all aggregates—whether categorized as sentient or insentient—are entirely suffering and constitute the Truth of Suffering. Question:

Since those falling within the continuum of another and those categorized as insentient do not exert pressure upon one's own continuum, for what reason does the practitioner also contemplate them as suffering? Answer: Because from beginningless time...
Regarding all sufferings that arise, ignorance is produced; as an antidote to these, wisdom must be produced.
Therefore, one should contemplate them universally. How much more so when they afflict oneself: for instance, if one is struck or touched by another, great suffering arises;
likewise, if wood or stones fall from the sky onto one's own body, great suffering also arises. Since there is such affliction, one should contemplate [them] as...

Suffering (the above constitutes the Truth of Suffering). If it falls within one’s own continuum or another’s continuum, whether pertaining to sentient or insentient beings, all causes of the aggregates are suffering;

this is the Truth of Suffering (this distinguishes the Truth of Origination). If it falls within one’s own continuum or another’s continuum, the exhaustion of the aggregates of sentient and insentient beings is all cessation;
this is the Truth of Cessation (this distinguishes the Truth of Cessation). If it falls within one’s own continuum... (and so forth).
The aggregates of the insentient are the remedy; all of these are the Path, and thus constitute the Truth of the Path. (Commentary:

All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) of the three natures, such as the wholesome and so forth, when considered from the perspective of being the result (*phala-bhāga*), constitute the essence of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*)—this applies to the four fruits: the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

When considered from the perspective of being the cause (*hetu-bhāga*), they constitute the essence of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*)—this applies to the six causes. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* (Chapter 22) states: "In this context, the nature of the fruit refers to the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*)."

That which is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). The appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*) that have the nature of being causes are called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), because they are capable of producing [suffering].
Due to this distinction between cause and effect regarding suffering and origination, although their names differ, there is no difference in their substance (the text is easy to understand).

All contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, according to their falling within the three periods of time, are infinite in number. At the time of attaining liberation, one realizes disjunction (*visamyoga*) for each of those quantities; such is disjunction.

This is another name for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). As for the number of these unconditioned phenomena, it is equal to their numerical quantity, and they constitute the essence of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

All the untainted noble paths (*anāsravamārga*), whether in training (*śaikṣa*) or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), present within the bodies of the noble ones of the three vehicles, along with their associated and concomitant dharmas, constitute the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
When practicing meditative cultivation, all of these are taken as objects of observation. Although the objects are thus, regarding one's own person—

The noble path arising therein does not necessarily arise instantaneously, due to the distinction of vehicles (*yāna*) and the distinction of faculties (*indriya*), as well as because its magnitude is vast throughout the three periods of time.
Since the essential natures of this cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are entirely distinct from one another, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The two truths of cessation and the path also differ in their substantial entities. Regarding the second point, the explanation based on superiority, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (78) states concerning the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*): [text continues]
What is it? As stated in the Sūtra: "The suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death;

the suffering of encountering the unpleasant, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; in brief, all five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are suffering. (Commentary:

Although the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging does not differ from the preceding [seven sufferings] in terms of its breadth or narrowness, the former seven sufferings fall within the contemplation of a single object and are likewise the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*); such is their characteristic.
It is narrow; however, it is spoken of specifically because it is manifested through its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), in order to engender revulsion [toward it].

Alternatively, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) may also be narrower than the previous category, because the former includes insentient things while this refers only to sentient beings. Regarding the five aggregates of clinging, the first chapter of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* explains:

"Afflictions (*kleśa*) are called 'clinging' (*upādāna*). Because they arise from clinging, they are called 'aggregates of clinging. Furthermore, because the aggregates belong to clinging, they are also so named."
The aggregates of grasping (*upādāna-skandha*). Alternatively, the arising of the aggregates through grasping is also called the aggregates of grasping.

According to the Mahāyāna, as stated in the first chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, "grasping" refers to desire and craving (*chanda-rāga*). "Desire" means seeking; it draws forth and takes up future aggregates, causing them to arise and manifest.

"Craving" means stained attachment; it clings to present aggregates within one's current existence, preventing their relinquishment. Therefore, they are called the aggregates of grasping. This is now being explained.
This is a minor point; let us follow the previous explanation for now. Next, to distinguish the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), the *Vibhāṣā* states:

As the Sūtra says, "All craving (*tṛṣṇā*), craving for renewed existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*), craving accompanied by delight (*nandī-sahagata-tṛṣṇā*), and the craving for this and that (*tatra-tatrābhinandinī-tṛṣṇā*)—these are called the Noble Truth of the Origination of Suffering."

(Commentary: All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) are the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). Now, four types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are explained; these are taught according to their predominant aspects. Regarding these four cravings:

craving that arises conditioned by the present and conditioned by one's own person constitutes the first two types of craving. Craving that arises conditioned by the present and conditioned by future requisites [constitutes the remaining two].

Regarding the establishment of the latter two types of craving and the subsequent analysis of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "As it is said in the Sūtra:

'Whatever craving there is, craving for renewed existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*), craving accompanied by delight (*nandī-sahagata-tṛṣṇā*), and craving for this and that (*tatra-tatrābhinandinī-tṛṣṇā*)—the complete abandonment, relinquishing, and casting off of these is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

(Commentary: In reality, the cessation of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) is termed the Truth of Cessation; however, here it is explained according to what is predominant. All [four types] are included.

Having extinguished the four types of craving, the Truth of the Path is next explained. The *Vibhāṣā* states: "As it is said in the Sūtra, the Noble Eightfold Path is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

(Commentary: In principle, the Truth of the Path actually encompasses both associated (*samprayukta*) and concomitant (*anuvartaka*) dharmas; however, for the time being, we speak only of the eight branches because they are preeminent.

Just as the eight branches do not include the mental king (*citta-rāja*), nor feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth, it is therefore not [the case that the Truth of the Path is limited to these alone].

This concludes the principle. Third, regarding the analysis according to specific categories: both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools teach that one contemplates the eleven links of dependent origination in reverse order to give rise to the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths.
Thus, in total, forty-four types of knowledge are established. For instance, regarding the four types of knowledge arising from old age and death:

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 110, states: "Knowledge of old age and death (is knowledge of the Truth of Suffering); knowledge of the origin of old age and death (is knowledge of the Truth of Origination);

knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of old age and death (is knowledge of the Truth of Cessation); and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of old age and death (is knowledge of the Truth of the Path).

Birth, existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and formations—each of these likewise leads to the four knowledges. This should be understood according to the detailed explanation. That treatise explains as follows:

There are forty-four types of knowledge, all of which pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). However, they do not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*). Regarding these Four Truths alone, there are eleven layers.

To speak briefly, taking old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) as the essence of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), one takes the branch of birth (*jāti*) as the essence of the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), because it is the cause that accumulates old age and death.
Their cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) thereto constitute the remaining two truths; this is the first layer. Furthermore, by means of...

The *jāti-aṅga* (birth-link) constitutes the essence of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). The *bhava-aṅga* (existence-link) constitutes the essence of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), because it serves as the cause of origination for the *jāti-aṅga*.

The other two [Truths] may be understood accordingly. This applies even down to the *saṃskāra-aṅga* (volitional formations), which is established as the Truth of Suffering, and the *avidyā-aṅga* (ignorance), which is established as the Truth of Origination;

the other two are to be understood by analogy. Since there is no further factor subsumed under the links of dependent origination that could serve as a cause for ignorance, it does not exist [as a separate link].

Regarding the four knowledges (*jñāna*), if one wishes to further investigate the meanings of their distinct categories, they are so numerous that I shall here merely briefly indicate their general outlines.
Second, concerning those who rely on the Sautrāntika school: initially, following various masters, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* was taken as representing the Sautrāntika; however, this shall later be...

A separate exposition of the Sautrāntika doctrine follows. For now, according to the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), as the commentary states: "The essence of the Truth of Suffering consists of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhāḥ*).
This intention is to clarify that the matured fruit (*vipākaphala*) is taken as the dharma that constitutes the Truth of Suffering.

Therefore, the second chapter of the *Tattvasiddhi* says: "Because these five things give rise to the causes and conditions for the acquisition of a body, they are called the five aggregates of clinging. (Commentary: This refers to seeking the five [objects].

Because they are the basis for the occurrence of the aggregates (*skandha*), they constitute the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*). Since the name is derived from the cause, they are called the "five aggregates of clinging" (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Next, regarding the analysis of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*): as stated in the commentary, the essence of the Truth of Origination refers to karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and so forth;
