Regarding the third, the "dharma-gate of falling into [the specific]," this refers to pointing out the substance by way of a concrete instance.

This refers to what is called a "grave offense" (*ānantarya*) within the Vinaya: namely, one who has previously committed a heavy precept, such as violating a nun, or engaging in matters such as sexual intercourse with a pure seed (*viśuddhabīja*).

Combining these two preceding types is termed "defining the essence by means of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-nirdeśa*); the third gate is termed "defining the essence by pointing to specific instances" (*vastu-nirdeśa*).
Regarding the statement that the eunuchs (*hōmon*) and others take the three aggregates as their essence: the physical form is matter (*rūpa*); furthermore, there is the internal mind;

and when one distinguishes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and so forth, these are the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). (That is to say, one [aggregate] encompasses two [aggregates]: mind and the three non-associated formations.)
"The other nine are analogous to form" means that the boundary, the monk, the thief, the destroyer, as well as the five heinous crimes, and both informative and non-informative karma are like form.
"The other two are also thus" refers to the eunuch and the hermaphrodite.
Regarding those [karmas] that extend to both body and speech: these are the four pārājika offenses and the four ānantarya crimes (excluding the schism of the Saṃgha).
As for that which is non-manifest (*avijñapti*) and is subsumed within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*):

according to the Sarvāstivāda school, non-manifest karma is subsumed within the *dharmāyatana* among the twelve spheres (it is included within the aggregate of form [*rūpaskandha*] among the five aggregates; this is precisely what is called "form subsumed under the sphere of phenomena"). In the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is also subsumed under the sphere of phenomena, yet it is not form.
It is not subsumed under the aggregate of mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
Regarding the statement that its essential nature is "opposition" (*pratigha*): "opposition" here refers to karma itself.

Regarding the statement that its functional meaning is subsumed under feeling (*vedanā*): the principle of obstructing ethical discipline (*śīla*) is termed "meaning"; this "meaning" is itself the "function," as there is an obstruction to ethical discipline.
For this reason,

if one bases the definition of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) on the first two [categories], since those first two are called "characteristics of phenomena" (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) as their defining essence, they are so named;
furthermore, these names are also established according to the principle of the differentiation of the characteristics of phenomena.

The three types of non-humans—namely, eunuchs (*pandaka*) and so forth—are so called because they lack the meaning of "other" (i.e., a true human being). "And so forth" includes animals and those with dual sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*).
Regarding the five causes for the maturation of an action, "action" refers to the essential substance of the act itself.

Other realms of existence do not perform these nine types of karma. Since other realms lack the precepts, how could there be "extreme offenses" (ānantarya-karma)? Treatises such as the *Abhidharmakośa* further state that other realms lack the five immediate transgressions (*pañcānantarya*).
Regarding the destruction of the Three Jewels by a nun-thief, this refers to those who are capable of receiving [the precepts]; it does not apply to other realms where such capacity is absent.

Therefore, it is also not mentioned. Just as with the seven-day medicine (*saptāha-bhaiṣajya*), there are many faults: there is the fault of residual contact (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), the fault of not being accepted, and the fault of taking it at an improper time (*akāla*). Furthermore, there are many other faults such as keeping it for too long.

However, [in this case] only two faults arise: namely, the fault of being at an improper time and the fault of keeping it too long. The meaning of the analogy is that it is difficult to store both [types of medicine] simultaneously.

It is precisely because of the obstruction of the precepts (*śīla-āvaraṇa*) that those two types of yellow [robes] do not arise; just as [the offense of] "excessive" or "at the wrong time" arises precisely from the verbal rule (*vāk-dharma*), whereas the faults of "residual contact" (*avaśeṣa-sparśana*) and so forth do not arise from the verbal rule.

Regarding "the Saṃgha consists of only eleven [members]": Question: If one possesses a thieving mind and lacks the precepts, how can they be called a member of the Saṃgha? Answer: This refers to the general characteristics;

it is spoken of as being similar in appearance to a member of the Saṃgha. (The eleventh: the verse says: borderers, nuns, low-caste, schismatics, yellow-robed, the five heinous crimes, and those with two sexual organs. Furthermore, regarding nuns, the schismatic is excluded. When a nun establishes herself as the principal or an associate, she cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
she merely accumulates defilement and does not constitute a heinous crime. (The tenth: the verse says: borderers, outcasts, thieves, schismatics, yellow-robed, the four heinous crimes, and...)

[The second category refers to] those with both sexual organs. The [remaining] three categories each have nine [exclusions]. Furthermore, excluding those who have committed an internal offense (one who has not received full ordination does not constitute an "internal offender"). The nine are stated in verse as follows: border-dwellers, nuns, thieves, eunuchs, the four pārājika offenses, and those with both sexual organs.

Regarding the second point, "the laity follow the eight [cases]": furthermore, excluding the extreme offenses (ānantarya), the verse says: "Nuns, thieves, eunuchs, the four ānantaryas, and those with both sexual organs."

Regarding the statement that "the bhikṣu [who commits an offense] is based solely on ten [factors]," this refers to the essential nature (*tattva*) and is spoken in reference to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and so forth.

If that were the case, then eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and those with dual sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*) would have no precepts. Answer: This is stated based on their initial state prior to any subsequent transformation. (The "ten" are summarized in verse as:

*pārājika*, *bhikṣuṇī*, *saṃghabheda*, *paṇḍaka*, the five *ānantarya* [sins], and *paṇḍaka-saṃghabheda*; the four, two, and two *ubhayavyañjana* are named as the "six"). (The "six" are summarized in verse as: *pārājika*, *saṃghabheda*, *paṇḍaka*, *saṃghabheda*, shedding blood [from a Buddha], and the two *ubhayavyañjana*).

The matters concerning nuns are only nine. (The verse says: "Borderers, schismatics, eunuchs, the four pāyattikas, and those with two sexual organs—these are called the five. The verse says: "Borderers, schismatics, and eunuchs, shedding [blood], and those with two sexual organs.")

The nine matters concerning *śikṣamāṇā* and so forth (the verse says: borderers, nuns, thieves, eunuchs, shedding blood, and the two sexual organs—these are called the five. The verse says: borderers, thieves, and eunuchs, shedding blood, and the two sexual organs).
The names and the entities together constitute eight [factors] (the verse says: a nun, a thief, and a eunuch; shedding blood, causing a retrograde flow, and being of both sexes).

The remaining eight factors are restricted in meaning (the verse says: a borderland, a nun, a thief, and one who has caused a schism within; the three types of killing, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha).
Regarding the four offenses such as [the offense against] a nun, the term "etc. includes the three types of killing.
"Excluding two as before" means excluding the [offenses of] shedding blood and causing a schism in the Saṃgha, as previously stated.

As for the question of why all thirteen [offenses] are inquired about together: if they must be inquired about together, what was the purpose of the preceding analysis of whether their essential nature exists or not? Answer: Although...
General Question: If one relies on the ultimate principle (*yathārtha-tattva*), it is not necessarily the case that all [offenses] constitute an obstruction to the precepts (*śīlāntarāya*).

For example, the schism of the Saṃgha by a *bhikṣuṇī* does not obstruct the precepts; therefore, one must distinguish whether the essential substance (*svabhāva*) exists or not. The rest should be understood accordingly. In the commentary on the twenty-third section of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it says:
"Because the Buddha has already entered *parinirvāṇa*, one follows the established texts. Thus, we know that thirteen factors must be fully present.
Question: The ancients used the meaning of "extraordinary" (*bāhya*) to explain the term "extreme" (*anta*). Thus, all thirteen types [of precepts] should be called "extremes.

Therefore, the full meaning was established to distinguish them and establish their names. Regarding the full meaning, the verse says: "Internal, *ni*, common, defeating the thief; not common, yellow."

The three types of killing, as well as [killing] those who are not animals and those with two sexual organs, are finalized by excluding the shedding of blood (the Commentary states: because it possesses four meanings, it first receives the designation of a "limit" (*sīmā*).

First, one has previously obtained the internal Dharma (*adhyātma-dharma*); now, this distinguishes those outside the assembly (*saṃgha*; "internal Dharma" refers to having previously received the Buddha’s precepts). This excludes those who have committed offenses against *bhikṣuṇīs*.

Second, it applies equally to both the *saṃgha* and *śrāmaṇeras*, as they equally obstruct leaving the household life (*pravrajyā*). This excludes the two types of "breaking" (*bhedana*) and those with a "thief's mind" (*caura-citta*). The two types of "breaking" are restricted to the *saṃgha*, while the "thief's mind" is restricted to [the *śrāmaṇera*].)

Only the śrāmaṇera is not subject to the same obstacles. Three [offenses] are common transgressions; they exclude the eunuch (*paṇḍaka*), the three types of killing, and the two sexual organs of non-animals.
These seven apply to all seven classes of practitioners; therefore, four are ultimate offenses (*anantarya*). Excluding the shedding of blood, there is an objection:

"The latter four prohibitions for bhikṣuṇīs do not apply to śrāmaṇeras, thus they lack the second criterion and should not be included among the 'borderline' (*prādeśika*) offenses. If this is granted...

Regarding what is included within the *pārājika* offenses: there are two types of intent to commit a transgression. Why would these not be included among the *pārājikas*? He immediately offers this defense:

"When a nun commits any of the eight grave offenses (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), none are designated as *pārājika*. Furthermore, even if a nun who has not committed an offense and remains pure renounces her precepts and wishes to become a laywoman again, she is still not permitted to receive ordination once more."
What is the use of discussing "limits" (*anta*)? The Master’s intention now is this: you use "extraordinary" (*bāhyārtha*) to explain the meaning of "limit," and thus there are many contradictions.
I now explain the term "limit," and thus there are contradictions regarding that limit. These thirteen are specific designations for the essential nature;
they are explained by using the names of the difficulties themselves as the extraordinary [explanations]. Therefore, there is no need for further elaboration.
Regarding the difficulty of being categorized as one who cannot receive the precepts despite undergoing the ritual procedure for requesting them from the Saṃgha:

if that were the case, then those who are underage and thus cannot receive the precepts should also be categorized as difficult cases. Therefore, it should be explained that being categorized as a "difficult case" here requires the presence of two conditions.

First, although one possesses all the requisite conditions and performs the ritual acts of empowerment, the precepts are not generated. Second, their essence is fundamentally empty from beginning to end and cannot be altered or transformed.
For instance, although the precepts are not generated for one whose age is deficient, the harm [of such deficiency] awaits the completion of the years; this is not "fundamental emptiness.
It is like all that is blue, all that is yellow, all that is black, all that is red, and all that is white—the triangular eye and the *mili* eye.

Although these cases involve the formal ritual procedure (*vidhi*) for conferring the precepts, it is possible for them to obtain the precepts. For instance, those who are blind or deaf may not obtain the precepts;

yet even for those born blind, there is still the possibility of improvement. How much more so for those who are temporarily afflicted! In such cases, it is appropriate that they be permitted to undergo transformation and once again become pure vessels.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (T. 1425), fascicle 23, states: "Regarding the blind: if they can see the lines on their palms, or if they can distinguish the days [of the month]."
Once they have already been ordained, they should not be expelled. Regarding the deaf: if they can hear loud voices from a distance, they may be ordained.
Regarding the mute: they cannot speak; they communicate by gesturing with their hands. They should not be granted ordination. Once they have already been ordained, they should not be expelled.
This is because, according to this Vinaya, they would be unable to request the precepts. (The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 29, states that there are four [such cases]).
People abandoned them. Those from families prone to strife entered Vaiśālī and encountered their former enemies. One man grasped a bow; another drew the bow;
one shot but did not kill; another shot and severed the life-faculty. Of the latter two, those who have not yet gone forth should not be allowed to go forth and should be expelled.
As for the former two, those who have already gone forth should be left as they are; if they later commit [an offense], [they should be dealt with accordingly].
"Evil! They should be expelled. Regarding such evil persons, if they transgress the *vinaya*, people all explain it thus: "In this context, these two individuals are fickle and lack resolve;

therefore, their expulsion is prescribed. Now, examining this closely, it may be that for these two, because they directed their minds toward the object [of ordination] without being able to reach a definitive resolution, they did not obtain the precepts.
Although the previous two individuals were likewise indeterminate, they had not yet made a final decision.

Because they have fixed their resolve to kill, why is it that advancing [the precepts] is not permitted? In reality, if four people can take an object as their focus and make a firm determination, they too should obtain the precepts;
however, for now, I shall explain this according to one general characteristic. In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Vinayaviniścaya*), twenty types of persons do not obtain the precepts.

The five types of eunuchs (including those born so, castrated, jealous, [70], and [2] female); the five acts of immediate retribution; a nun who has defiled herself; one who makes a vow saying "I am not a bhikṣu" (a "vow" here refers to what is called a *pāṭidesanīya* in this Vinaya;

that is, declaring oneself to have committed a grave offense and thus no longer a bhikṣu constitutes a transgression); one who stays by theft (*caura-vāsika*); a nāga (encompassing all animals); a yakṣa (encompassing all non-humans);

a mute person; a deaf person; a person who is both mute and deaf; one who does not request the precepts; and one who is obstructed (meaning one who is barred by a formal announcement). The commentary states: "No."
Seeking the precepts is likewise not permanently fixed; other cases should be understood accordingly. The *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) states:

"If a śrāmaṇera falsely represents himself as a 'Great Wayman' and receives the prostrations of a great bhikṣu, may he later receive the full precepts? The answer is: "He may not. The commentary states: "It simply says he may not."
It is not the case that one cannot attain the precepts simply because one cannot speak;

this need not be considered a difficulty. As for the "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*): the three miserable realms (hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals); the northern continent of Uttarakuru (where there is no Buddha-dharma);

the long-lived heavens (the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception with its eighty thousand *kalpas*, and the Heaven of No-thought with its five hundred *kalpas*, where people mostly cling to the notion of permanence); being before or after a Buddha (when a Buddha has not yet appeared, or after his parinirvāṇa); and having incomplete faculties (such as being blind, deaf, or mute). Regarding those who fight... [text fragment].
[Receiving the Way]. Because worldly wisdom and eloquence often lead one to fall into false views. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, Chapter Two, "Chapter on the Four Dharmas," states:

"Four wheels can increase wholesome dharmas: first, dwelling in a good place; second, relying on virtuous people; third, personally formulating right vows; and fourth, possessing roots of goodness from past lives.

Regarding "dwelling in a good place," this refers to residing in a central land, free from the five difficulties (which are the first five among the eight previously mentioned). Regarding "relying on virtuous people," it means being born...

To be born in the era of a Buddha (avoiding the sixth difficulty), and for those who have planted roots of goodness not to be deaf or mute (avoiding the seventh difficulty). Now, before [the next section], a verse is said:

In the three miserable realms, [beings] have long lifespans in the north; their faculties are distinguished as being either present or absent. In favorable states, the first five [faculties] are impaired; those who encounter [the path] plant the seeds for the remaining three through aspiration.
Those with incomplete faculties and the like do not at all seek or beg; even if they were to beg, such acts as cutting off one's ears would likewise not constitute a violation of the precepts.

Regarding the remaining nine karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*): among them, the four types of destroying [the community] by means of a schism, weapons, thieves, or robbers are bodily and vocal actions;

therefore, they are called "karmic obstructions. This distinguishes the three obstructions; that is, these are the characteristics of the three obstructions according to their categories, rather than being the actual substance of the three obstructions themselves.
The essential nature of the three obstructions is as explained in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, which will be cited later.

If one considers those that obstruct hearing, reflection, and cultivation, only the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) cause one to definitely receive their retribution in the very next life; thus they are called the "group of the wrongly fixed" (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*).

Therefore, in this present life, it is certain that the Noble Path and its preparatory practices (*mārga-prayoga*) will not arise. Question: Among the nine types of karma, the Vinaya texts also state regarding those who have committed the offenses of [killing] a relative, a monk, a thief, or a schismatic: "In..."

Within my Dharma, there is nothing that can provide further benefit. How could it not be said to obstruct hearing, reflection, and cultivation? Answer: This is based on the majority of cases where no further benefit is obtained.
However, if one should encounter a Buddha, a great Bodhisattva, or the like, who instructs one to repent and eliminate [the offense], one may still avoid falling [into the lower realms].
Therefore, they are said to be included within the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*), and thus are not specifically mentioned here.

If one were to discuss this in a general sense, it means that these thirteen grave offenses (*ānantarya*) are not being treated in isolation; rather, it is a general discussion on the meaning of the three obstructions (*trividha-āvaraṇa*) as found in the sūtras and śāstras.

As the seventeenth verse of the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The three obstructions consist of the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), the persistently active afflictions (*paryavasthāna-kleśa*), and..."

All evil destinies, the northern continent (Uttarakuru), and the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*). (The commentary states: This distinguishes the essence. The prose explanation of the five *ānantarya* [acts of immediate retribution] may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the explanation of the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*): there are two types of afflictions. First, those that are frequently practiced, meaning afflictions that arise constantly. Second, those that are intense, meaning afflictions of the highest degree.)
It should be understood that herein, only those afflictions that are habitually active (*paryavasthāna*) are termed "afflictive obstructions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

For instance, in the case of eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*) and so forth—where "and so forth" refers to the five types such as those born as castrated (*jāta-ṣaṇḍha*)—because these afflictions are habitually active, they are difficult to subdue and eliminate; therefore, they are designated as obstructions.

Although superior-grade afflictions may be intense and sharp, they are not constant and are thus easy to subdue and eliminate. Among the inferior grades, even though the habitually active afflictions are not intense, [they are still considered obstructions].

Yet they are difficult to subdue and eliminate because they operate constantly, making it hard for one to find an opportunity; from the lower grade they give rise to the middling, and from the middling they further give rise to the upper, thereby preventing the path of subduing and eliminating them from arising.
Therefore, among the afflictions, those that follow their respective grades—whether lower or upper—and are frequently active [are the most difficult to overcome].

The afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is so named. The three evil destinies in their entirety, humans of the Northern Continent (*uttarakuru*), and the gods of the Unconscious Heaven (*asaṃjñisattva*) are called the ripening hindrance (*vipākāvaraṇa*;

formerly termed the "retribution hindrance"). What dharma constitutes this hindrance? It refers to that which obstructs the noble ones (*ārya*) and obstructs the roots of goodness consisting in the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the noble path.

(To distinguish the breadth and narrowness [of these categories], the verse of the treatise says: The immediate [karmas] exist in the three continents, not elsewhere; nor among those such as the *śaṇḍha* (eunuchs) and others. Because they have little benefit [to others] and little sense of shame (*hrī*). Other hindrances pervade all five [destinies].

[The text says: "Destinies. (The commentary states: Only humans in the three continents possess the karma of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*). This excludes those in Uttarakuru, other destinies, other realms, as well as *ṣaṇḍha* (eunuchs) and the like.

This is because those such as the *ṣaṇḍha* belong to the class of those who merely experience [the fruits of action] and are by nature extremely volatile; they are incapable of definitively giving rise to an extremely evil intention.
Furthermore, their parents bestow little kindness upon them, and because their physical bodies are deficient, they lack the dominant conditions [necessary for such karma]. Since...

Because they have received little kindness from them, those [beings] possess a sense of shame and abashment (*hrī-apatrāpya*) toward their parents (in the verse, "shame" [*lajjā*] refers to this very *apatrāpya*).

Since they lack the manifest, predominant forms of shame and abashment, it can be said that they are "corrupted" and thus commit an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*). Regarding the other obstructions that pervade all five destinies:

among the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), there is no distinction made between the five destinies; at first glance, this seems broad. However, because it refers only to those who habitually practice [afflictions], their number is extremely small; therefore, it is narrower [than the previous category].

This is the retribution. Among the obstacles of maturation (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*), the three evil destinies in their entirety, the northern continent among humans, and the Heaven of Non-perception are also included within the five destinies;
however, this [classification] is the broadest.

There are only those cases where expulsion may or may not be carried out. According to this Vinaya, all five [offenses] require expulsion; however, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, three out of six require expulsion and three do not, as will be explained below.

Other cases may be understood by analogy. If one transforms into an animal, it is said that the precepts are lost; yet if an animal transforms into a human, how could they possibly receive the precepts and so forth?
Third, regarding "stealing": this refers to stealing the form of the Dharma.

Regarding the statement that "if one goes to the place of one person or two people and steals by means of a hand-to-hand transaction, it cannot constitute theft," the intention of the commentator’s refutation is as follows:

when one goes to the place of one person, including oneself makes two; this refers to stealing from a single individual. It can be understood that the same applies when going to the place of two people.
Regarding "only stealing from one's counterpart" within the fifth and sixth [of the] two [sets of] sentences: this means that within the fifth and sixth sentences, there are four objects [of theft].

If one reaches the former [stage], it is a fixed case of stealing from one's counterpart; if one reaches the latter two, it constitutes stealing from the communal property (*saṃghika-dharma*). Question:

Why is there no mention of "reciting the *Prātimokṣa* together" or "performing *karmavācanā* together" among the six sentences? Answer: Because these do not exist [in those specific cases], there is no such sentence. How, then, is the *Mahīśāsaka-āgama* (Gārgya) to be reconciled?

The *Gāthā* contains no text [addressing this]. How, then, can it be reconciled with the statement that "separate dharmas do not constitute [an offense] through concealment"? Why would a thief need to conceal?

Regarding the three types of theft mentioned in the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), its seventeenth fascicle states: "There are three kinds of theft: first, stealing the form; second, stealing the combination;
third, both stealing the form and stealing the combination. What is stealing the form? It is to emerge on one's own without a teacher."

Regarding the family [of monks]: not according to the seniority of a bhikṣu’s ordination age, not receiving prostrations according to the proper sequence, not participating in the monastic legal procedures (*saṃghakarma*), and not accepting any offerings—this is "stealing the form.

What is "stealing the harmony"? There is a teacher who has left home and received the ten precepts, but before he has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), he travels to another region where he is ten years of seniority;
there he receives prostrations according to the sequence, enters the monastic *poṣadha*, and participates in all formal acts (*karmavācanā*).
To receive the offerings of the faithful from others in succession is called "stealing harmony. What is "stealing both"?

To leave the household life on one's own without a teacher, yet to receive seniority in succession, participate in all formal rituals (*karmavācanā*), and receive the offerings and prostrations of others—this is the form of stealing both.
Such a person may obtain ordination.
In Sanskrit, this is called *paṇḍaka*; here it is translated as "eunuch" (*huángmén*). Regarding those who are eunuchs by birth: in Sanskrit, this is called *śaṇḍha-paṇḍaka*.

This refers to those who, from birth, do not possess a fully developed male organ and therefore cannot procreate. Regarding those who are eunuchs by castration: in Sanskrit, this is called *ṣaṇḍha-paṇḍaka*. *Ṣaṇḍha* here means "cut";
these are those who have been subjected to punishment. Regarding those who are eunuchs through envy: in Sanskrit, this is called *īrṣyā-*.
The *īrṣyā-paṇḍaka* (envy-impotent). *Īrṣyā* here means "jealousy. One who becomes a eunuch refers to one whose sexual organ becomes incomplete and so forth.
The half-month eunuch is called *pakṣika-paṇḍaka* in Sanskrit; *pakṣika* here means "half" (or "assisting").

For half a month he is capable as a male, and for half a month he is incapable (this refers, for the time being, to males; if it concerns a person with both sexual organs, where for half a month they act as a male and for half a month as a female, this is also included herein).

In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, section twenty-three, there are six types of eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*). Regarding those who are "born" [eunuchs], the explanation is the same as in this *vinaya*. As for those who are "crushed" (*nirbhinna*), they were crushed while young.

As for those who are "castrated," it refers to when kings or high ministers take them into their service and excise their male organs to serve as gatekeepers (the term *kliba* in this *vinaya* refers to this).

"Dependent on another" means that because of the contact of the preceding person, the body arises (the male organ being what constitutes the arising of the body). This is similar to the explanation in this Vinaya commentary regarding envy.

In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter twenty-one, the section on "eunuchs" (*pandaka*) is explained in the same manner as this Vinaya. Regarding "eunuch" (*paṇḍaka*): what is meant by a "natural eunuch" (*jāti-paṇḍaka*)?

It refers to one who, due to another's sexual contact with his body, functions [only] through that part of the body. This explains the "natural eunuch" (the phrase "functioning through that part of the body" means the arousal of the male organ).
What is meant by a "diseased eunuch" (*roga-paṇḍaka*)? It refers to one whose [organ] is decayed, or smeared, or infested by worms; this is the diseased eunuch. (The Chapter states: fifth...)

Regarding this family, it is not so. They say: "He was a eunuch due to illness. Although he was previously granted ordination and received full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*), if he is fallen, decayed, or infested with worms and is 'immovable'—meaning his male faculties do not arise, which is termed 'immovable'—he is permitted to remain [in the order] despite being immovable.

That which is able to prevent the arising and non-extinction of the substratum of feeling refers to the formal manifestation within feeling; both are without manifest action (*avijñapti*).

Various Admonitions (a monk who disregards the admonition of the Saṃgha; a nun who disregards the admonition of the Saṃgha; thus they have long been so). Emission (the Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense for monks; the Pāyattika offense for nuns); Physical Contact (the Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense for monks; the Pārājika offense for nuns); Soliciting Food (the Pācittika offense for monks; the Naiḥsargika-Pāyattika offense for nuns); and the Seven Methods of Extinguishing Disputes (Saṃghadisesa).

The existence or non-existence [of these rules] differs (such as washing beyond the prescribed limit, which exists for nuns but not for monks; or initiating [the recitation] at twilight, which exists for monks but not for nuns).

Regarding the phrase "because it possesses three meanings," etc.: when one is ignorant [of the precepts], there is no offense of *duṣkṛta*. Later, if one learns and knows [the rules], one also possesses these three meanings; since the *duṣkṛta* has already arisen, for what reason must it be confessed?

It is because awakening and delusion differ from the path of suppression (*vītarāga-mārga*). Because that [ignorant person] has turned their back on themselves [by failing to learn], [the path of suppression does not exist for them, and thus there is no transgression of a precept, nor is there an offense of ignorance].
Second, ignorance does not continue; this distinguishes them from those who do not study, whose offenses continue without being extinguished. Third, delusion and awakening...

Although they may be distinguished by time, those who equally possess the practice differ from one who has passed away; for one who has passed away, there is no continuity [of the precepts], and thus they are not vessels for the Path.
Regarding the transgressions of the higher [vows], the words of others and the teacher state that if one is ignorant, there can be no confession, because there is no interruption [of the vow].

Later, if one studies and comes to know [the rules], the understanding immediately reverses the error, and furthermore, confession is not required. It is difficult for a teacher to pass away [in such a case], for once the understanding has reversed the error, the principle allows for it.

It is the same for the rest. One might ask: "If one has given rise to a sense of regret (*kaukṛtya*), does it not need to be eliminated? Now, by analogy with the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), where what was severed is reconnected, such a principle might be acceptable.

But once an unwholesome karma has already arisen, does it not need to be eliminated? If there is no object for confession, then further confession is unnecessary—just as in the case of the *śauca* (cleansing) precepts and so forth.

Regarding the ritual performed for a *bhikṣuṇī*, she is expelled and transformed into a *saṃgha*; how could there be a case of a *bhikṣu* performing a confession before a *bhikṣuṇī*? The other sections should be understood accordingly.

When a *bhikṣu* commits four kinds of offenses, these refer to the lower four categories [of the *Prātimokṣa*], because the first category [the *pārājika*] shares the same precepts and cannot be confessed.

Regarding the bhikṣuṇī who commits the five [offenses]: (The latter four pārājikas for a bhikṣuṇī are different from those of a bhikṣu; thus, when the sexual organ changes, the offense is extinguished.
One who is not a bhikṣu is precisely a bhikṣuṇī. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle 8, states: "If a man has many offenses, he loses his male organ and transforms into a female organ.
If a woman possesses many merits, she transforms into a man. Furthermore, if two bhikṣus dwell together, and at midnight one bhikṣu...

If one’s gender changes and becomes female, one incurs the offense of *sahaseyya* (sleeping together) in its entirety. If one becomes aware [of the offense], one should bring it to the attention of the bhikṣuṇīs and others.
When departing, one must not go with only two people; if four or five bhikṣus are available, only then may one go together with them.

One should travel by carrying a torch or a staff for illumination when going to a nunnery. If the distance is great, such as being outside a village or crossing a river, if one leaves the group behind, there is no [offense].
This constitutes an offense (meaning that if a nunnery is distant, one may not place it too far away; however, there is no offense if it is situated among the assembly of bhikṣus).
After the Tuoba clan of the Later Wei moved the capital from Beida Prefecture to Luoyang, in the second year of the Xiping era, a woman named Wang Changpu, aged nineteen, was transformed into a man.

The fifth is the *pratisaṃdhāna* (reconnection). The initial act is called *pañcāhika* (the five-day rite); once the preliminary concealment has been completed, the subsequent granting of six nights is termed *pratisaṃdhāna*.

The expiation through the six nights and so forth should be understood according to the explanation. A commentary manuscript states: "There is no need for the character 'you' (有) [in the phrase] 'not-yet-possible' (不須可有)"; the character 'you' is an error.
There is a commentary which states: "It is not necessary for them to continue the procedure alternately, because the fundamental offense has already been extinguished.
Those that differ regarding the Saṃgha are the six precepts concerning leakage, touching, the two types of coarse misconduct, and the two types of buildings;

therefore, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, even if one changes while the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra*) is not yet completed, or changes while the *parivāsa* probation is not yet completed, both remain pure dwellers. If a nun changes [status], she likewise remains a nun."

The different explanations refer to: (1) a person crossing over; (2) a female thief; (3) understanding and lifting [the precepts]; (4) the ten precepts, such as the four *pārājika* offenses (*ādi* including the two acceptances, the two practices, the three abandonments, the [four] truths, and the four [realizations]).
If one undergoes transformation (a change of status) before the half-month penance has been performed or before the period of impurity is complete, one remains pure in conduct.

If the offense was committed by those who have likewise transgressed—referring to the seven precepts such as matchmaking and slandering (the "etc. including the four formal admonitions)—the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If a bhikṣu commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, even for ten or five years" (the commentary above is identical). Furthermore, another commentary states that it is not necessary to calculate the duration in years for the continuity [of the penance], because the fundamental offense has already [been addressed].

Because the [period of] extinction has ended. For this reason, according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, even if one changes while the six-night penance (*ṣaḍ-rātra*) is not yet completed, or changes while the *parivāsa* penance is not yet completed, both remain pure and abide [in the community].
The same applies to a nun who changes. If they have committed the offense together, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"If a bhikṣu commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, even if ten or five years [have passed]—the above cases are likewise."
Regarding the statement that "a *bhikṣuṇī* who previously concealed [an offense] does not need to undergo concealment again," the eighth fascicle of that treatise states:

"If a *bhikṣuṇī* at that time practices the act of matchmaking and conceals it without bringing it forth (not bringing it forth means not confessing), and subsequently changes her gender to become a *bhikṣu*, she need not confess or undergo the six-night penance for the offense of a minor transgression (*duṣkṛta*).

(Matchmaking is a shared precept; yet it is said that both methods need not be performed. This is likely because they belong to different schools. The passage cited in this chapter should be this very text; it is absent elsewhere.)"
Regarding those who "falsely enter" while not possessing the required qualifications: there is no offense for falsely entering [the community].

However, to indiscriminately enter among the pure assembly while lacking the necessary qualifications—for instance, in the case of a *bhikṣuṇī* who, although she has already undergone concealment (*praticchādana*) previously, now enters the *saṃgha* for the first time, yet has not yet undergone concealment within the *saṃgha*—is therefore called "not possessing [the qualifications].
(If she were to undergo concealment upon reaching the *saṃgha*, she would likewise be required to perform the formal act of concealment.)
If, regarding different offenses, there are seven types of emotional transgressions (*kleśa*), we shall now examine them in detail. As for the sense of "sameness," all seven are applicable.

For instance, when one encounters teachings that are either Dharma or non-Dharma and gives rise to the seven emotional transgressions, all seven are indeed the same. However, if one distinguishes between what is different, then they do not apply to all seven;

that is to say, the first six apply to both common offenses (*sādhāraṇa-āpatti*) and uncommon offenses (*asādhāraṇa-āpatti*), whereas the seventh, the evil view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), is definitely [uncommon].
The offenses are identical; it is certainly not the case that they differ in principle. To distinguish the different characteristics of the first six [offenses]:

for instance, if one intentionally instructs and disturbs the monastic community, one is subject to the *tajjaniya-kamma* (reprimand); or if one uses harsh speech, defiles a family, or commits evil conduct, one is subject to the *pabbājaniya-kamma* (banishment).

Or, because of frequent transgressions such as the emission of semen (*āśrava*), one may be granted the disciplinary treatment (*niśraya-karma*). Or, because of the words of others, one may be barred from approaching [the community].
It is precisely due to these circumstances that one neither confesses nor sees [one's fault]; therefore, it is permissible that there may be differences in the offenses committed.

Chong says: "These seven *karmas* are methods for treating persons; there is no offense that they do not treat. If the offense has been expiated, what measure is there for the dharma? This is what is meant by "according to the confession" (this objection).

First, regarding confession: once the offense has been extinguished, the disciplinary rule (*dharma*) remains. By this analogy, it should be understood that although the offense for which the sense-faculties were transformed has been extinguished, the remedial rule does not lapse.

since the rule still exists, what loss is there? (The intention of this commentary is difficult to grasp, as it alone permits that the rule prohibiting approach does not lapse. Now, examining this in detail: although the offense has been extinguished through prior confession, it is for the purpose of prevention.

To create anew; the methods of treatment do not cease. Regarding the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), since the offense has already been extinguished, there is no principle for further creation; thus, the method of treatment is concluded.

As for the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* stating that when a bhikṣu transforms into a bhikṣuṇī, his three robes and medicines lose their consecrated status (*paribhoga-vināśa*), this is a case of interpreting the text according to its underlying meaning rather than taking it literally.
[This is] a record [from] that treatise (the eighth fascicle).

When a bhikṣu has received food, if a bhikṣuṇī now touches it, the formal acceptance (paribhoga) should immediately be lost.

The following is as in the commentary.

as stated in the third fascicle of the *Śāstra*, "If a layperson serves as the preceptor (upādhyāya) and confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon a layperson, does the recipient obtain the precepts? *Khwan-yen* (the character *khwan* is pronounced with the "gu" and "chien" finals; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "eyes turned upward"; the *Erya* states that a horse with one white eye is called *jian*; *jian* and *khwan* are homophones; the Vinaya text writes it as *jian*, which is incorrect).

they consorted with non-human beings and bore children. Thus, the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks delighted in committing offenses. Good people were unwilling to dwell near such individuals; when they saw these people, [they would avoid them].
He thought to himself: "My fine disciples have all abandoned me and departed. I should instead ordain this man so that he will not abandon me.

He then ordained him as a monk. Regarding the passage in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Fenben), chapter fifteen, concerning the ordination of those whose hands and feet had been severed, and so forth, as described above:

"to obtain a harsh destruction of the auspicious marks" means to break open the body, thereby destroying the auspicious marks of the physical form. This is stated in the aforementioned text of that Vinaya.
It is not as auspicious to save people according to the formal rules. Furthermore, regarding the aforementioned passage on saving those in debt, it was told to the bhikṣus:

Therefore, it is said, "as explained above."
Regarding the expression "extremely old," it is stated only in the *Twenty-three [Karmavācanās]*: "Those who are too old are over seventy.

If one is seventy years of age or older and is healthy enough to perform various religious duties, permission is granted for them to go forth. As for those who are too young:

if they are under seven years of age, or if they are exactly seven years of age but do not yet discern between good and evil, they should not be ordained. If they are seven years of age and understand what is good and what is evil, they should be permitted to go forth.
(Those who violate this rule all commit an offense of transgression.)

as explained previously regarding the five points on being "without organs," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* judgment is cited: if the arm or other limbs are severed, it is likewise not incurred; however, if they are entirely removed, it is logically also not incurred. As for those who are mute or deaf:
As in the thirteen difficult points (*duskarapada*) above, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* is cited for judgment;

the remaining *pāyattika* offenses are to be explained by analogy. There are also nine procedures: first, requesting the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); second, establishing the *śrāmaṇera* in his place; third, appointing an instructor (*śikṣācārya*);

fourth, going to examine him; fifth, summoning him into the assembly; sixth, instructing him to request ordination; seventh, the formal announcement by the preceptor; eighth, examining for obstructing conditions (*antarāyika-dharma*); ninth, the actual [ordination].
The *Jñapti-caturtha* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations). The verse says: "Requesting, appointing, sending, summoning, begging, the motion, and the *jñapti-caturtha*.

Therefore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* states that whenever one wishes to receive the precepts, one must first have the Dharma explained. Regarding the way the Dharma is explained, it should accord with the capacities of the listeners and address their essential needs;
it is absolutely forbidden to merely recite a fixed text. I shall now briefly describe this according to the *Nanshan-jie-mo-ben*.
He said: "You should say to them: 'Sentient beings of the six realms mostly possess obstacles to the precepts; only humans may receive them.

You should give rise to the superior mind—that is, to rescue and gather all sentient beings above yourself and deliver them through the Dharma. Furthermore, the precepts are the root of all virtues and can [accomplish all good]. "
It serves as the direct cause for the three vehicles. Furthermore, the precepts are a treasure within the Buddha-dharma that is not found in other paths;

they can also protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma so that the True Dharma remains for a long time. Moreover, through the majestic power of the *karmavācanā* and the great strength of the Sangha, the supreme dharmas of the Dharma-realm can be raised up and placed within your own body and mind.

You should receive this with single-minded attention and careful heed. (The manuscript further states: "To summarize, it does not go beyond the sentient and the non-sentient, nor emptiness and existence.")

Regarding the two truths, the principle of cessation, and *nirvāṇa*, these constitute the three clusters of precepts and lead to the three gates of liberation. Now, upon careful examination, this statement is truly a great error; I shall not labor to refute it at length.

"Seeking by inference to know" refers to the mention of the candidate's name. "From such-and-such a person, [I] shall forever receive [the precepts]" refers to the mention of the request for a teacher.
"Now from the Saṃgha, I beg" refers to the formal petition. "Such-and-such a person as Upādhyāya" refers to the mention of the Upādhyāya’s name.
From "Having spoken for oneself" onwards, the two masters are cited for interrogation. From "When the time has arrived" onwards, the formal motion (*jñapti*) is concluded.

The *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure) is to be understood accordingly. Regarding the first general point: in the text, the initial phrase "not a son of the Śākya lineage" serves as a general heading to establish the fundamental thesis.
Regarding the subsequent specific [explanations]: from the phrase "you must all not... onwards, the four precepts are listed individually. Each contains five parts.

First, up to the point concerning "impure conduct," the practice of restraint and observance is presented. Second, from "if a bhikṣu... onwards, the fault of committing an offense through transgression is shown; this includes the application of the teaching, the metaphor, and the synthesis.

Within the teaching, there are three parts: first, "if a bhikṣu" identifies the person capable [of the act]; second, it correctly clarifies the commission of the offense; third, "not a śramaṇa... [identifies the consequence].
The Gate (Mendō) clarifies their faults and deficiencies; it should be understood that each case conforms to the three [preceding] principles.
Third, you are of middle or inferior capacity regarding the timing of upholding [the precepts]. Fourth, "one must not be equal" refers to examining the sincerity of one's resolve to uphold them.
Fifth, one declares oneself capable of upholding them.

The remaining text is the same as the preceding section. This is also an explanation according to the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*. The explanation in the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* states: Next, the practice of the four reliances (*catur-ārāma*) and contentment is explained.

Within this, there are two parts: first, the general summary by the *bhikṣuṇīs* to manifest the benefits; second, the specific enumeration of the four dharmas beginning with "the bhikṣus rely on discarded rags" (*pāṃsukūla*).
Regarding the first reliance, there are two sections: first, the superior grade; second, the opening section beginning with "if one obtains surplus gains," which includes the lower grades within it.
The superior grade text consists of five parts: first, the essential nature upon which one relies; second, from "relying on this" onwards, the manifestation of its basis and its coverings;

third, the citation of the time period; fourth, the careful maintenance of the mind; and fifth, the self-declaration of being capable of maintaining it. Regarding the medicinal reliance, Chong states:

"Traditionally, this has been interpreted as the impurities of the internal body. However, if Western Indian monks consume [such things], they are not tolerated by the community. Therefore, the current correct interpretation is..."

[The author] explains: These are discarded medicines. Now, examining this in detail: the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) of the Western Regions hold heterodox views and harbor resentment toward the Buddha-dharma;

even those who have left the household life and study their doctrines include both internal and external paths. The World-Honored One, being well-acquainted with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and understanding the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings, has established exceptions.

Within the *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra* (the *Lüeshi yiqieyoubu zonglun shi*), he establishes a great allowance (*mahāpavāda*) and thus permits it. This is also mentioned at the end of the fifth hundred fascicles of the *Wubai wen*.

Opening this as a medicine, I cannot provide an exhaustive account. Next, the general conclusion and exhortation consists of two parts: first, concluding that the conditions for receiving [the precepts] are complete;
second, from "You should well receive... onwards, raising the benefits to encourage upholding [the precepts]. This section has three parts: first, the present entrustment to encourage upholding;
second, from "As for other matters you do not yet know... onwards, entrusting [the disciple] to the two teachers to provide instruction at appropriate times; third, from "From now on... onwards...
The following is for the purpose of protection. The *Zengsan* (Increase of Three) states: "There are three dharmas for which one should perform the *karmavācanā* of release:

that which should be seen, one sees; that which should be confessed, one confesses; and that which should be relinquished, one relinquishes. For these, one should perform the *karmavācanā* of release.

The *Wufen* (Five-Part Vinaya) mentions "expulsion," which refers to this very *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment). "Lowering the mind" refers to this very *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension).

Regarding the statement that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for receiving the precepts entirely lacks immeasurable matters: before the initial section [of the Vinaya] was established, the *karmavācanā* had not yet been instituted.

How, then, could there be knowledge of the thirteen *antarāyika-dharmas* (obstacles)? Why did Ānanda ask about them? Now let us examine this further. It is as when the three-fold proclamation (*tri-vācanā*) was established.

It is also said that after the prohibition, the term "receiving full ordination" (śīlāṃga-samādāna) was applied. For example, immediately upon the establishment of the thirteen grounds for disqualification for an ordaining preceptor (ācārya), one could no longer receive the full ordination from such a person;

thus it is called "after the prohibition. This does not mean that the five categories of offenses (pañca-pārājika-ādi) were established, nor does it refer to the examination of the disciple regarding the thirteen grounds for disqualification.
Regarding the opening of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*): because this is the fundamental [authority], and fearing that obstacles might arise, the Buddha permitted it.

As for the objection that other teachers are not fundamental and thus should not be permitted—[the response is: the preceptor is indeed fundamental; yet even so, fearing obstacles, the Buddha permitted it.
Since others are not fundamental, why would one not fear obstacles? To permit them as well is illogical. This should be further...
The commentary states: Because the Upādhyāya acts on behalf of the Saṃgha, the Sage permitted it; for other monks, their essential nature must be that of the Saṃgha, and thus it was not permitted.

Regarding the statement that "fifteen kinds of *poṣadha* are extensively explained," the previous critic argued: "If only the abbreviated recitation were intended, one could say there are fifteen;

however, since it now explicitly clarifies the three methods such as the mental recitation (*manasikāra*), it should therefore be said that 'three kinds of *poṣadha* methods are extensively explained.'"

"From the *Sūtra* up to the *Upadeśa*, they may be explained according to one's inclination. Since the Buddha permitted the explanation of the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), [it follows that... compared to this...
The Buddha said, "I am still hesitant. If I were to explain the phrases in full and in their proper sequence, the text would be so voluminous that I fear it might cause weariness and distaste.
If, however, I were to briefly compile the excellent words and essential meanings, I do not know how to proceed. The Buddha then said, "Listen, monks.
You may briefly cite the essential words and sublime phrases from within the sūtras to directly reveal their meaning."
Regarding the term "half-chant" (*bāng bèi*) in the *Śāstra*: it is called a "half-chant" because its expression of meaning is incomplete.

For example, there are three verses praising the Buddha’s three bodies (*trikāya*). Within these, the passage from "The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body" (*rúlái miàosèshēn*) to "incomparable and inconceivable" (*wúbǐ bùsīyì*) praises the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
"The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise" praises the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body); whether form or mind, both are without end.
"All dharmas are eternally abiding" praises the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* (dharma body); it is the true basis of all dharmas, eternally abiding and profoundly still.
Nowadays, there are those who compose only a single verse; therefore, it is called a "half-chant" (*ardha-bhāṣita*).
(All cases are to be understood accordingly).
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'if there are many preachers of the Dharma' and so forth in the sixth [section], the Vinaya text mostly reads 'few preachers of the Dharma.
It appears that the reading 'few' is an error."

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter sixteen, states: "When laypeople wish to scatter flowers, they may do so as they please. If the flowers fall upon the head or the robes of a bhikṣu, he should brush them away.
If they fall upon a high seat, there is no fault. (The remainder is as cited in the commentary.)

As for the question regarding why the formulation of the precepts required repeated requests and so forth: it refers to the fact that within the introduction to the Vinaya, when the precepts were first requested and expounded, the origins (*nidāna*) of each precept involved citing transgressions and making repeated requests;
yet, when it comes to the current recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), why are they not requested again before being promulgated?

First, regarding the explanation of the second [point], namely "because this is the thesis (*siddhānta*) being expounded," although it has already been explained in the Commentary (*śāstra*), I shall further assist in clarifying it.
This refers to the text of the second chapter among the eight chapters, which says: "Venerable sirs, I now wish to recite the *Prātimokṣa*.
This refers to the precepts (*śīla*).

The Commentary states: "This is an explanation by way of changing the name. Regarding 'liberation in various places' (處處解說): among all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*), there is dissociation from them in various places; this is what is called 'individual liberation' (*prātimokṣa*) in the *Miśrakābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*."
The text states: "One maintains one's own deportment and dwelling, practices the roots of goodness, and brings together all wholesome dharmas to achieve samādhi.
The commentary says: "This praises the great merit of the Prātimokṣa in generating goodness and extinguishing evil. This is the previous change of name."
This clarifies the meaning of "protection. Because it protects, it gives rise to the wholesome and extinguishes the unwholesome (thus, *śīla* has the meaning of protection).

These two passages explain the term *pratimokṣa-śīla* from the preceding chapter. (The Commentary states: "Therefore, it says, 'I now wish to speak,' etc. The intent of the Commentary is to cite this text to prove that the teaching which expresses [the meaning] is also called *mokṣa*).
The text says: "I shall now explain the fetters (saṃyojana) as they are to be aroused, set forth, revealed, and analyzed again and again. The commentary states:
"This is specifically to provide the bhikṣus with the rules and methods for the exposition of the fetters."
The *wenyan* (text) states: "Therefore, O Venerable Ones, I shall now recite the precepts. The *shu* (commentary) says: "The formal establishment (*jie*) of the recitation is for the sake of benefit.
This means that the Buddha established the ritual procedure for the recitation, commanding the reciter to announce to the assembly that they shall recite.
The two preceding passages explain the phrase "I now wish to recite" from the previous section. (Next, the explanation of the text summarizes the intent of the commentary to form a concise meaning.)

Regarding "maintaining one's own deportment and dwelling place," this refers to guarding and upholding the characteristics of the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), thereby causing one to remain free from the seven transgressions.

Since the precepts are the very basis upon which such maintenance relies, they are called the "dwelling place" (the Commentary states: "accomplished by the Dharma-nature" means accomplished by the Dharma of the precepts).
This dwelling place is the root of practice and is also the primary head; that is to say, it is the foremost of the adornments of the collected wholesome concentrations (*samādhi*).
As for the path encompassing the three [lower] categories, this refers to the three dharmas summarized therein, which are explained in the commentary immediately following.

Regarding the "recitation and conclusion concerning the transgressions and the compliant": this refers to reciting the names of the four *pārājika* offenses and concluding by stating that they have been "already explained," followed by asking, "Are you pure?

This is called "compliant. To further say "no" is called "transgressive. (This explains the text of the precept: "Venerable sirs, I have already explained the four *pārājikas*, and so forth... Are you pure in this regard?")

Regarding the phrase "it shall be explained extensively below": as in the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Miscellaneous Khandakas), there are five dharmas that should be brought into harmony, which correspond to the three types of assemblies such as "those who should come" (*āgantuka*) and so forth.
This meaning is also explained in the section on Campā and elsewhere. Furthermore, within this exposition on the *Poṣadha* (Recitation of Precepts):

Initially, based on the necessity of gathering [the community] in one place, the *Poṣadha-hall* (Sīma) was established for the recitation of the precepts. Furthermore, because monks were sleeping in their individual cells, the procedure of *jñapti* (formal announcement) to assemble the assembly was prescribed.

Moreover, because sick monks were unable to attend, the granting of consent (*chanda*) and other such measures were established; all of these share the common purpose of assembling [the community] in one place.

This principle is also the same as the one [previously discussed]. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 23, states: "In all open places, one sits such that the outstretched hands do not reach one another;
in all covered places, one must not be beyond the range of sight or hearing. To be beyond this is not called 'having received full ordination'. (Commentary:

It has been traditionally transmitted since ancient times that "in private places one does not leave the range of sight and hearing, and in open places one does not leave the range of outstretched hands"—this refers precisely to the present passage.

This is explained in terms of being distant from the obstacle. Because the precepts are impure, meditative concentration does not arise; because there is no concentration, the Noble Path does not emerge.
Therefore, it is said to be "distant."
The practice within existence is not the dharma of severing delusions through emptiness or signlessness.
Regarding the textual phrase "listening to the sound of chanting while reciting the precepts," this refers to slightly modulating the tone, which is equivalent to chanting.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* does not permit this, as cited in the relevant chapter; therefore, it differs from this Vinaya.
The text states: "Regarding 'reciting the precepts on the poṣadha day,' the old name for *poṣadha* is translated as 'pure abiding' (*jìngzhù*). Master Jìng (淨) of the Tripiṭaka says:
*Poṣadha*—*poṣa* has the meaning of 'nurturing' (*chángyǎng*), and *dha* has the meaning of 'purity. Thus, it means 'to nurture deeply.
This intends to clarify the nurturing of wholesome dharmas and the purification of the transgressions of broken precepts."
In the text, Kapphiṇa says, "I am always foremost in purity. The intended meaning is: "The original purpose for instituting the recitation of the precepts was to cause one to abandon transgressions.
Since I have eternally severed the afflictions of breaking the precepts, there is no need for me to go. This is as stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (T.1421), fascicle 16;
it is the same as this Vinaya. If one follows the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (T.1425), fascicle 27, it states that the Venerable Aniruddha did not [go].
"Come," the monks called out. He replied, "The World-Honored One has taught that purity is the *poṣadha*. As for me, I am already pure in this world; I will not go.
When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said, "Go and summon him. Do not use your divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)."
Because this elder lost his physical eyesight, he encountered perilous mountain paths and, after enduring extreme suffering, fell over.
According to this Vinaya text, this constitutes a punishment for not being permitted to employ supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
The passage concerning the formal establishment of the *śīla-saṃghārāma* (precept hall) refers to the initial procedure for performing the ritual within the *prakṛtisīmā* (natural boundary).
As for the commentary cited there, it is the *Tattvārthā-śāstra-ṭīkā*.
Regarding the seventeen types of *parivāsa* (probation), they are summarized in this verse: "Round, cornered, water,
mountain, rock, Moon, nature, enclosure, gate, earth, The four, two, nuns, laymen, wall, full, Insane, and so forth—
these are the types of probation."

The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* verse states: "Furthermore, there are five types of *mānāpya*" (the term *mānāpya* is translated as "separate residence"; its explanation is as in the chapter). "Loss" (*śīla*) refers to a transgression. The treatise itself explains:

1. Breaking the territory (*kṣetra*): This refers to when a king does not permit the demarcation of a territory to establish a separate residence (*pṛthag-vāsa*). Such a demarcation is not valid. 2. Breaking the monastery (*saṃghārāma*): This refers to cases where it was previously a pure dwelling (*śuddha-vāsa*), or entirely pure, or where one has heard of a breach at the boundary.

To attempt to demarcate a separate residence within these three types of gardens is also invalid. 3. The meaning of the [three] gardens is as explained above regarding the precept on being separated from one’s robes. Regarding the characteristics of the three types of separate residences: joining them into a single characteristic means that two boundaries share a common stone as their marker. If one attempts to demarcate both sides [separately], this too is invalid. If...

1. Formed by two sides of a single mountain; because the boundary markers (*nimitta*) are large, they extend halfway across the separate dwelling (*pṛthag-āvāsa*), meaning the markers overlap. 2. A separate dwelling surrounded by a separate dwelling; that is, it does not remain on its own natural ground. The commentary states:

There are seventeen types of separate dwellings (meaning there are seventeen variations according to the topography). Once the boundary markers have been established, one first binds the *poṣadha* boundary, and subsequently binds the *cīvara-sthāpana* (robe-deposit) boundary to stabilize it;

this applies to all seventeen. 1. The Long-Circular Separate Dwelling: (In the middle it is narrow and long, with circular ends; the distance between them is one *zhang* or five *chi*. Stones are placed around the perimeter to serve as boundary markers. 2. The Four... [text fragment]

1. Corner Isolation (shaped as a square with four corners). 2. Water-wave Isolation (the terrain is subtly curved, like fine ripples on water). 3. Mountain Isolation (using mountains as a boundary). 4. Mountain Isolation (using mountains as a limit).

1. The *pañcagiri-pratiprasthāna* (separate residence of five rocks): using five mountain crags as the boundary. 2. The *ardhamāsa-pratiprasthāna* (separate residence of half a month): shaped like a half-moon. 3.

The *svabhāva-pratiprasthāna* (separate residence by natural feature): where there is a mountain or water that serves as a limit for the *araṇya*. 4. The *cakravāḍa-pratiprasthāna* (separate residence of the Iron Ring Mountains): first establishing small separate residences—three or four in number—and then demarcating a large boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) outside them, opening a space of one or two paces as "natural ground" (*prakṛti-bhūmi*), just as the Cakravāḍa mountains encircle the four continents.
5. The *ekadvāra-pratiprasthāna* (separate residence with a single gate): opening a gate on one side like a street; the ground within the street is the "natural ground. If the gate...

10. Crossing the Sky (k'ung): This constitutes two distinct boundaries; it is only because one does not cross over that it is termed a single gate. 11. Separate Residence in the Ten Directions (shih-fang tu-pieh-chu): The walled cities and towns of each respective direction are combined into a single boundary. 12. Separate Residence in the Four Quarters (shih-i ssu-hsiang pich-chu):

The roofs of the houses join together around the four quarters. 13. Separate Residence by Two Lines (erh-sheng pich-chu): When a boundary is established within a city wall, it may be difficult for the monks to discern, or they may be unwilling to grant their consent (*ch'ü-yü*).

Unfold the cord and encircle the place where you wish to establish the boundary. If you intend to establish boundaries of varying sizes at that location, two markers must be set; if you do not establish a small boundary, only one sign is required. Wrap the cord around the two markers and lead it out beyond the city wall for half a *yojana*, where a separate small boundary is established by likewise encircling it with the cord and setting up two markers again.

All the monks within the city wall gather at the outer boundary; first, they dissolve the *acelaka-sīmā* (the "not-parting-from-robes" boundary), next the *unmatta-sīmā* (the "insane" boundary), next the *bhikṣuṇī-poṣadha-sīmā* (the boundary for the nuns' confession), and finally the *bhikṣu-poṣadha-sīmā* (the boundary for the monks' confession). [This is done] for fear...

Because of prior binding: first a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) was established, and later a large boundary (*mahāsīmā*) was established for both the interior and exterior of the city wall. When the boundaries were established simultaneously, the cord used for the demarcation was removed. If the assembly was gathered within the city wall, those outside the wall must also grant their consent (*chanda*), lest the Dharma-affairs be disrupted;

therefore, it is necessary to dig up and destroy the ground outside the city wall or plant thorns so that the monks cannot enter. (The two cords were connected, and this became the name). Thirteen: the separate residence of bhikṣuṇīs (established for the sake of binding the nuns).

Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows: When a nun relies upon the boundary of the monks (*bhikṣu-sīmā*) and performs a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), she must inform the community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*) and obtain their consent before it may be carried out. However, if a nun establishes her own boundary within the monks' boundary and subsequently performs a ritual there, she does not need to inform them again.

Regarding the fourteenth [category], the *upāsaka* in separate residence: this refers to one for whom the Saṃgha has performed a formal ritual of establishment. If such an establishment does not exist, when an *upāsaka* comes here to receive benefits, receive the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*), or perform the Uposatha (*poṣadha*), one must take the consent (*chanda*) of an *upāsaka* from another location.

If such a boundary exists, it is not required). Fifteen: Separate residence by means of a fence or wall (using a fence or wall as the limit). Sixteen: Perfectly circular separate residence (shaped like the surface of a mirror). Seventeen:

Separate residence for those who are insane (insane bhikṣus cannot be restrained or recorded; the Saṃgha performs the *karmavācanā*. If he is not among the assembly, he must remain within the boundary; if he leaves the boundary, [the procedure is invalid]).

When the Saṃgha performs a *karmavācanā*, the Saṃgha immediately incurs an offense. Therefore, the boundary is established by meeting at the location where one has become insane. When the ritual is being performed, the insane person is within the boundary. Paramārtha says: "This is inexplicable. This person is within the boundary and does not grant their consent (*chanda*) to the Saṃgha; yet it is said that the Saṃgha incurs an offense."

How could it be permissible to cross the boundary? On the contrary, one incurs an offense. Furthermore, it is because the boundaries should not be contiguous). The above coarse points are all from the treatise itself; the annotations are all composed based on the meaning of that commentary.

Regarding the other two minor boundaries (*kṣudrakasīmā*): it is difficult to recite the *Poṣadha* for the sake of generating the wholesome; it is difficult to perform the *Pravāraṇā* for the sake of extinguishing evil.

(The formula for the boundary for the *Poṣadha* states: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Now there are this many bhikṣus assembled. If the time has come for the Saṃgha..."). The formula for the boundary for the *Pravāraṇā* states: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The seating places of the bhikṣus are already full. Up to these seating places of the bhikṣus, if the time has come for the Saṃgha..."

Establishing the names of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is too prolix for this section. It should rather state: the common realm (*sabhāga-dhātu*) of person and dharma; the common realm of dharma and food (*āhāra*);
the distinct realms of dharma and food; and the distinct realm of dharma with the common realm of food—this is preferable.

Regarding the establishment of a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) for the purpose of receiving the precepts (the text for establishing it during a time of difficulty states: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This Saṃgha has assembled in one place to establish a small boundary. If the time is right for the Saṃgha...")
This is not as it is usually explained; the general intent regarding the matter of receiving the precepts is that one should not [use them].
Regarding the question of Upāli in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: among those twenty-two cases, there were various bhikṣus in a village where no monastery (*saṃghārāma*) existed.
Regarding the initial construction of a monastic dwelling (the phrase "etc. refers to the absence of the question posed by the Upāsaka):
As for the "eight trees apart" mentioned in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, that Vinaya’s eighth fascicle states: "The measurement of a bow is five cubits;
one *āmalaka* tree is planted every ten bows. When seven *āmalaka* trees are aligned at such distances, the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) performed therein is called a 'well-executed ritual.'"
[The text] "Mò" (Grinding/Polishing). Although the various characteristics of the assembly differ, there is no separate offense for the assembly.

As for the statement in the chapter that it is "eight trees," this is likely because this Vinaya defines the clothing boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) as eight trees, intending to bring [the two systems] into accord. Since that text is already explicit, one must not arbitrarily reconcile them.

Nanshan calculates it by means of seven trees: eight *cubits* (*zhù*) make one *elbow* (*zhǒu*); a *bow* (*gōng*) is nine feet (*chǐ*); six feet make one *pace* (*bù*). Thus, it is one and a half paces. Seven...
The tree measures thirty-two *dhanus* in total, which amounts to sixty-three paces (*padas*). There is no need to calculate according to the figures in the chapter.
Three thousand paces equal ten *li*; six hundred paces equal two *li*.
Regarding the *araṇya* boundary as seen in the treatises, that is the seventeenth [case], which concerns the assembly of the Saṃgha when there is danger.
This has already been explained in detail in the section on the *kuṭī* (small dwelling) precept. One *paṭṭhāra* is fifty-four feet (*chi-cun*).
The commentary states that this amounts to three hundred and fifty-two feet and eight inches; here, three hundred feet constitute fifty paces, and furthermore, forty-eight...
One *chi* equals eight paces and four *cun*.
As it is stated in the *Śāstra*, it is likewise said in its seventeenth fascicle: "One may not establish a boundary (*sīmā*) over any river or stream.

Regarding the natural boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*) within water: if one throws water or throws sand [beyond a certain point], that which lies outside [of this]—these waters are solely based on the natural gathering [of elements]."

Regarding "the boundary marker is wide but the assembly area is narrow": this refers to cases where, although the boundary marker is wide, the space for assembling the Sangha is narrow, because it is established at a distance from the marker.
For example, at a marker set one hundred *li* away, only seven trees are assembled; or at a marker set ten paces away, only seven trees are assembled. Now, let us examine this in detail.
The boundary markers are wide while the defined area is narrow; even so, one must certainly gather everyone within the markers.

This means that when the ritual of binding the boundary is about to be completed, if there are monks within the markers, it logically constitutes a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*), and thus the ritual action cannot take effect. This is similar to how obstacles such as impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*) prevent the arising of the precepts.
The basis for communal harmony is the regulation that one does not act separately from the community; this is termed "communal harmony.
Regarding not obstructing the affairs of the Saṃgha: once the boundaries have been established, one understands what it means to assemble accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "one should strike the *gandī*": the *Zhang* (Commentary) states that this refers to striking a *qing* (stone chime).

This is an interpretation based on meaning. Tripitaka Master Jing says: in Sanskrit it is called *gandī*; there is no direct translation for it here, so it is named according to its function. A wooden mallet is used to strike the wood;
alternatively, the *gandī* itself may refer to the wooden block being struck. To distinguish its shape: it is like a pestle for beating silk, five or six feet long, made of light-sounding wood.
Positioned at both ends, they are separately fashioned as wooden mallets approximately one chi in length, with slender handles and thick heads.

When it is time to strike the gong, the ritual officiant (formerly known as the *vinaya-dhara*) takes the long pestle in his left hand, holding it horizontally by its narrow middle section in front of himself, while grasping the mallet with his right hand to strike outward.
As for the manner of striking: it begins slowly and lightly, gradually becoming more rapid and forceful.
