When the sound is about to end, it gradually becomes fainter and finally subsides; this is called one "penetration" (*tong*). Repeating this up to three times is called three penetrations.
At the final penetration, immediately after the sound has subsided, strike the bell three times, or twice, or once, to signify that the sound has ceased.
Whether three, two, or one, ensure these strikes remain constant and do not alter their number. The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "As explained in the *Vinaya-viniścaya-uttaragrantha* (*Weiyi jing*)."
In the lower fascicle of that sutra, it says: "There are five matters for the *gaṇḍī*: first, the regular assembly;

second, the morning meal; third, the midday meal; fourth, evening—when the trays are set down and the vessels are gathered; fifth, all [meals] at improper times. Furthermore, there are seven rules... (and so on, until) "...the seventh is calling the *śrāmaṇera*.

(This likely refers to calling the *karmadāna* or a junior attendant, but the transcription was incorrect during the translation from the foreign language, and the scribe erroneously recorded it. Although Nanshan cited this, he was unable to explain it. Furthermore, the sutra...
Regarding what is called "the time for the regular assembly": first, one must begin with a small sound and gradually increase it to a loud one, striking twenty times;
then, gradually decreasing the volume, strike ten more times; finally, strike three times loudly. This is the same as what the Tripitaka Master Jing explained.

Now, examining this further, [Master] Yong previously did not rely on that sūtra when establishing his doctrine, stating: "The first three strikes are called the 'bell to alert the assembly,' meaning they serve to alert the disciples to prepare themselves."
Regarding robes: next, as for the "long strike," it is called the "bell that summons the assembly," meaning it leads the assembly to assemble.

As for the "striking after covering [the bell]," it is called the "bell for quieting the assembly," meaning that once they have assembled, one sits in silent stillness. Only when the sound of the bell has ceased does one perform the Dharma service.
Formerly, at Dong Chan Ding Temple in the Western Capital, there was a monk named Zhixing who would always strike the bell with a sincere and pure mind. Later...
Regarding the account of being moved by spirits and ghosts to receive thirty bolts of silk, and the practice of "striking three times":
the tradition explains that this refers to striking from a small to a large pitch, ceasing, and then striking again for three major beats.

This is consistent with the principle that within the "long strike" itself, the three rounds are inherently complete. For further details, one should consult the *Nanshan Sengtu Bian* (Discriminations on the Monastic Diagrams of the Southern Mountain). Now...
Regarding this dharma, it is in fact not a scriptural text.
As for the "four [aspects] of the initial text and meaning," the subsequent commentary states: "By first adding three meanings, they become four."
"Binding first and then opening" means that after the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) has been bound, the boundary for the observance site (*sīmaṇḍala*) is opened.
"Excluding the inner ground" means that outside the observance site, one leaves the natural ground intact, as it remains within the boundaries of the great boundary.
Therefore, it is called "internal ground.
Regarding these eighteen and twelve collected [factors]: in the preceding text of this *Khandhaka*, there are eighteen characteristics.
As that text says: "Whether in an empty space, at the foot of a tree, on a mountain, in a valley, or in a rock cave"—searching through that text, there are eighteen.
The character "ge" (this) is correct. Twelfth: this refers to the passage in this very text which says, "In the east there is a mountain called Mount [Name]," and so forth;
this is the twelfth.
As for the thirty *cheng*: one *cheng* is fifteen *jin*, totaling four hundred and fifty *jin* (which can barely be three feet in circumference).
"Excluding scattered stones" refers to small, level, scattered pebbles.

The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle 17, states: "Regarding road-boundaries: paths leading into fields, paths for going to wells to fetch water, paths for going to rivers to fetch water, and dead-end roads—none of these may be used as boundaries" (the commentary notes that this is because such paths are separated by fields and the like). A "dead-end road" refers to a distance of three paces.
After five paces, the path was cut off; this is it.
As for the "ant-mounds," they are abundant in the land of Wu; the large ones are like burial mounds.
Regarding the twenty-eight characteristics in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says: whether it be a wall (*yuan*), or a grove, or a tree, or a mountain...
"Rock," "road," "river," or "pond"—the phrase "water waves abiding separately" and so forth includes the remaining sixteen [elements]. To explain the meaning:
these natural boundaries correspond to the circular enclosure (*parikṣepa*). Now, a diagram is provided to demonstrate this for those who have not yet realized it. Now...
Approximately sixty-three paces constitute one *dharma* (unit of measurement). Calculating from north to south, there are two such units of sixty-three paces;
the same applies to each direction from east to west.
(Regarding the previously mentioned "threefold markers": the outer boundary of the *śīmaṇḍala* constitutes one marker, and the inner boundary of the *mahā-sīmā* constitutes [the second].)
One marker: the outer boundary of the great precinct (*mahā-sīmā*) constitutes one marker; thus, they together form three. The text states:

"A circle is drawn measuring seventy-three paces. Now it is sixty-three paces. This refers to the distance from the body to each of the four sides where the *saṃgha* sits—sixty-three paces on each side.
Calculating both sides together, this totals one hundred twenty-six paces; this is the aforementioned red circle. From here...

Beyond this, although there may be other monks who do not disrupt the Dharma-activities, when the Saṃgha first assembles at the boundary (sīmā) to perform the formal act of binding it, there must likewise be sixty-three [monks] on each of the four sides.
This diagram is intended merely to clarify the locations for their placement;

do not think that the assembly of monks can be conducted in such a manner without being divided and gathered together. Since this has already been clarified, other sites such as araṇyas should each follow what is appropriate.

The same applies. If [the site] is in an open, unobstructed space, one should demarcate it in a circle as before. If it borders another boundary (*sīmā*), there is no need to demarcate it in a circle, because other boundaries do not need to be gathered together.
Although the commentary (*śāstra*) instructs that the large boundary (*mahāsīmā*) be established first, in current practice one must first establish the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*);
one must not stubbornly adhere to the commentary and refuse to change. This shall be further discussed later.

Regarding the fact that the *Pañcavargika-mātṛkā-śāstra* always prescribes the demarcation of the *sīmā* (boundary) first: the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter sixteen, states, "Having already demarcated the *kṣetrasīmā* (monastery boundary), one further demarcates the *saṃghārāma-sīmā* (monastic precinct boundary).

The *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, fascicle two, states, "The method for demarcating boundaries is to first demarcate the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*) and subsequently demarcate the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*)."
The *Five Hundred Questions* states: "Some first establish the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) and subsequently establish the ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*).

To receive the precepts therein—as Kumārajīva mentioned (referring to Saṃghavarman; this was Kumārajīva’s own teacher)—one fears that no result will be obtained. Yet it is said that they were unaware of this beforehand."

It is the same as when [the rule] was not yet established; by relying on this path, one may still have a chance for success. (Shu says: Since the various texts are thus, one must first demarcate the *sīmā* (boundary).

Regarding the explicit explanation of the proclamation of the boundaries (*sīmā*): although the method for establishing the boundary of the *śīmaṇḍala* appears later in the text, when discussing the actual performance of the rite, it is necessary to establish the smaller boundary first;
therefore, we shall now first distinguish the proclamation of the characteristics of the *śīmaṇḍala*. First, the Saṃgha must be assembled and seated within the boundary.

A monk who is naturally clear-minded and prudent should be appointed; it is extremely unwholesome to wait until the moment the matter arises to then change the person. One should strike the wooden gong.

With palms joined, standing, he should proclaim: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, the resident bhikṣu, shall announce the boundaries of the small *sīmā* (boundary) for the four directions for the sake of the Saṃgha.

Starting from this stone at the southeastern corner—the eastern corner on the southern side—one follows the cord westward down to the southwestern corner stone—the southern corner on the western side.
From here, following the cord, one goes down to the northwestern corner stone—the western corner on the northern side."
The corner: proceeding downward from the east, along the inner side of the small wall to the northeastern inner corner;

from there, proceeding southward along the wall to the stone at the southeastern corner, facing east—this is the complete description of the outer boundary of the *śīmaṇḍala* (three times [recited], though Chong says once; for now we follow the old tradition). Next, perform the *karmavācanā* for delimiting the *śīmaṇḍala*, as explained in the subsequent text.

Note that the gate of the *śīmaṇḍala* follows its winding contours; these are to be mentally excluded. (Note: Regarding the recitation count, while the text mentions three recitations, Master Chong asserts it should be one. For the present purpose, we shall follow the traditional practice. Furthermore, the location of the *śīmaṇḍala* gate should be adjusted according to the actual curvature of the site, with such irregularities being mentally set aside.)
Next, the boundaries of the great precinct (*mahā-sīmā*) are proclaimed. The Saṃgha must assemble within the markers of the great precinct;

however, those who are elderly or infirm may remain on the site of the precept platform (*sīma-maṇḍala*), as this constitutes a separate boundary that does not invalidate the ritual proceedings. The *Śāstra* states: "First proclaim the outer markers, and next proclaim the inner markers.

All schools follow this practice. However, Nanshan says: "One should first proclaim the inner markers. There is no fixed principle [regarding which comes first]; nevertheless, it is customary to proclaim the outer markers first.
The principle is somewhat more extensive. Since the internal boundary is clearly marked by its characteristics, one should say: "Venerable Sangha, listen!
I, the resident bhikṣu, shall proclaim the characteristics of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) for the four directions of the Saṃgha. First, I shall proclaim the external characteristics:

starting from the southeastern outer corner of the large courtyard wall of this monastery, following the wall westward and downward, reaching the outer edge of the earth on the eastern side of the main gate, and proceeding along its winding turns."
Reaching the inner edge of the eastern jamb of the door, one proceeds westward along the inner edge of the threshold.
Reaching the inner edge of the western jamb of the door, one follows the curvature outward until reaching the outer edge of the western jamb’s plaster.
From there, one descends along the wall to the southwest outer corner. From there, one descends along the wall to the northwest outer corner. From there, one proceeds eastward along the wall.
Proceeding down to the outer northeast corner, one follows the wall southward back to the outer southeast corner; this constitutes the outer boundary.

Next, the inner boundary is proclaimed: from the outer southeast corner of the small wall, one passes through it to the west, follows the inner face of the main enclosure wall to the west until reaching the inner southwest corner, and from there exits north along the wall. One then passes through...
To the small wall. Reaching the outer northwest corner of the small wall, one proceeds alongside the small wall eastward down to its outer northeast corner.
From there, one proceeds south along the wall, returning to the outer southeast corner of the small wall. This constitutes the boundary markers for the interior of the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).
This serves as the interior marker; that serves as the exterior marker. This completes one circuit of the interior and exterior markers of the Great Boundary.

Regarding the three proclamations (Nanshan says: there may be three cycles of internal characteristics and three cycles of external characteristics, each being announced separately). As for the method of announcing the characteristics:

whether there are gates, alleys, or various winding passages, the community of monks should examine them together before the announcement and explain them in detail for the sake of the Saṃgha. Since such characteristics and objects are numerous, there is a fear that confusion will arise;
therefore, the monks should collectively deliberate on what is appropriate and establish names for each, ensuring they are distinct and clear so as to prevent disorder.

It is easy for the monks to identify [the boundary]. Furthermore, if the wall outside serves as the mark for the exterior boundary, when the proclamation reaches the gate, any irregularities or curves must be removed.

This is intended to prevent the situation where, during the *karmavācanā*, a monk arrives at the gate; if these [irregularities] were not removed, that location would then be considered within the boundary.

This would then constitute a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*). If one were to take the interior of a wall as the external boundary, even when reaching the gate, one must remove any curves or recesses;

for there is concern that during the summer retreat, monks might leave early and wait for dawn beneath the gate, and if they were to mistakenly enter within, it would then become outside the boundary.

The "Heavenly Brightness" (Tianming) [period] marks the breaking of the summer retreat. Furthermore, when a sick person has given their consent (*yuyu*) for the ritual proceedings and subsequently wanders outside the gate, upon returning they must come back again;

since they have already crossed the boundary, they have lost their consent, and thus the monastic rule (*saṃghadharma*) is broken. Therefore, both [the boundary and the consent] must be re-established.

Again, there is a discussion stating that one should take the exterior of the temple’s main wall as the defining mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Should a bhikṣu happen to come and sit upon the wall, that itself constitutes the boundary.
Regarding the "internal" [announcement]: because one fears that the matter of the Dharma might be disrupted, it is best to take the inner face of a large wall.

As for the four phrases within the *jñapti* (formal motion): first, the announcement to the assembly requesting their attention; second, the statement of the cause and origin of the matter; third, the time for the formal procedure having arrived, exhorting the assembly to be patient and deliberate;
fourth, the presentation of the action to be performed, concluding the *jñapti* formula.

"Fearing that it might be applied indiscriminately to individuals" means that it would be applied indiscriminately to individual persons (for the purpose of boundary-delineation is fundamentally for the sake of the *saṃgha*). "Relying on a single text" means that in current practice, the names [of the individuals] are not recited.

"Regarding two dwelling places" means that regarding the ritual for food (*āhāra-vidhi*), the two share the same boundary (the text for the ritual of food for the two sharing the same boundary states:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Regarding the characteristics of the boundary as described, if the time has come for the Saṃgha... at this place and that place, we establish a common distribution of offerings (*ekapiṇḍapāta*) and a common recitation of the precepts (*ekapoṣadha*). This is the formal motion (*jñapti*)."*)
Regarding "establishing the same [status] for those in different boundaries," this refers to the rule for summoning [monks] to the *sīmā* (boundary).

The reason this can be known is that one incurs an offense by preaching the *Poṣadha* (confession) alone; therefore, the rule establishes the requirement to summon them. The *Karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), however, is the reverse of this.
Now, upon careful examination, it may also be said that the *Poṣadha* inherently includes the same *Karmavācanā*, whereas the *Karmavācanā* does not necessarily include the same *Poṣadha*. This...

This is also well-explained. Later, the difficulty regarding the specific matter is raised: "If that is so, how can it be reconciled? The answer is as stated in the chapter. Regarding the term "excessive and unrestrained" (*làn cháng zì*):
"excessive" refers to the necessity [of using] the twelve months at all times.
Regarding the expression of consent according to the specific matter: for example, when performing the *karman* of censure against someone, the person giving consent says:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [name], express my consent for the *karman* of censure."

Regarding the difference between what comes first and what comes later: within the ritual of establishing a boundary (*sīmābandha*), one first states, "Within these four boundaries, I establish the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*)," and only afterwards does one specify the matter by saying, "For the purpose of reciting the *Poṣadha* together," and so forth.

In the case of granting consent (*chanda*), one must first specify the matter by saying, "For such-and-such a monastic affair," and only afterwards say, "I grant my consent and purity. The meaning here is that one specifies the matter before performing the formal act of establishment.

The *dhātu* (element) follows later. Calling out the matter (*vastu*) to grant consent (*chanda*) occurs before the granting of consent; therefore, they are not analogous. Now, upon detailed examination:

although calling out the matter for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) is indeed a calling out of the matter, its meaning of "concord" (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*) is the same as that of other dharmas. However, calling out the matter to grant consent fundamentally contradicts the original intent [of concord].

Therefore, it is distinguished from other dharmas and is certainly not accomplished. Furthermore, calling out the matter to grant consent is merely for the sake of a single assembly; how could one also allow...?

If one performs the recitation of the precepts once and the binding of the boundary once, and furthermore refers to the specific matter while conveying the consent (*chanda*), the Buddha has prescribed that this incurs an offense.
How could it be that referring to the specific matter while binding the boundary is not an offense as prescribed by the Buddha?

The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views), volume seventeen, states that water washes away [the boundary] to form a pit, as cited in the relevant chapter. The intent of this section is to determine whether the non-informative (*avijñapti*) arises in a continuous succession within the ground where a boundary has been established.
The commentary states: "Our current interpretation is not so. For generally speaking, what is called "non-informative" refers to bodily and vocal karma;
how could insentient matter achieve non-informative karma? If this is the case, how does one reconcile this with the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* (Good Vision)? Answer:
This refers to that which occurs within the limits [of a formal boundary], not to what arises subsequently.

For instance, although non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) does not exist upon the physical substance of items such as robes, medicine, or alms bowls, it nevertheless arises within the bodies of those who perform the ritual acts.

Likewise, even though there is no non-informative matter in the mere maintenance of precepts, the performance of those precepts gives rise to non-informative matter; the same principle applies to the demarcation of boundaries (*sīmābandha*). One should understand other cases by analogy with this.
Regarding "water washing away trees and so forth to form pits": the formation of pits has already been cited previously. Furthermore, the *Śāriputrābhidharma* (or *Jianlun*), fascicle 17, states:
"If there is a stone mountain that is broad at the top and narrow at the base, and one establishes a boundary (*sīmā*) upon it, if there are bhikṣus below, it does not obstruct [the boundary].

This is based on the time when the boundary is being established; since the boundary arises in dependence upon the actual ground, the Saṃgha is below and thus not within the boundary. Moreover, if after the boundary has been established, water pierces the earth to form a hole.

Regarding the non-destruction of the characteristics of the boundary (meaning the non-loss of the boundary): A bhikṣu possessing supernormal powers may dwell in the air within a cave or beneath the ground; he must not perform separate ritual acts [there].

Although it is calculated by principle that there would be no boundary in the air, in reality, the boundary exists in the actual locations on the four sides as well as above and below; thus, it remains within the designated area, and therefore ritual acts are performed there.

This is different from being in the open air, where there is no boundary on the four sides or above, and thus ritual acts are not performed there. Furthermore, if a large tree branch extends beyond the boundary from atop a *śīma* (ordination platform), [the same principle applies].
If a bhikṣu is above and obstructs the performance of the ritual, he should be called down.

If a bhikṣu with supernormal powers is in the open air or mid-air, provided he does not obstruct the ritual (if the corner of his robe touches the ground, he should be called down). Regarding the phrase "high, low, etc. in the text: being upon a tree is considered "high."
"Below ground" refers to what is beneath. Within a cave, the space may be shallow or deep; the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* has been personally examined, yet there is no such text [regarding this].
However, the *Pañcaśata-praśna* states: Question: "If all the *bhikṣus* have departed and only a *śrāmaṇera* remains, does the boundary (*sīmā*) still exist?

Answer: "If there is even a single *upāsaka*, the boundary is not destroyed; how much more so with a *śrāmaṇera*. If they have all departed and not a single person remains for one night, the boundary is destroyed."

(Commentary states: Because the characters used for "question" were identical, the Master of the Commentary mistakenly cited them. If one follows the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Seeing), that which is "resembling non-loss" refers to the previously cited scriptural passage stating that one knows its location and erects pillars to form a pavilion;
this means it resembles something that has already been occupied by people.

Regarding the restoration of old monasteries (*vihāra*), the text on the ritual for medicinal substances states: "At that time, the bhikṣus did not know which places were pure grounds (*śuddhasthāna*).
The Buddha said: 'They should be demarcated. If there is doubt that a pure ground previously existed, it should be released; however, [once released], it may be demarcated again.

At that time, the bhikṣus were restoring an old monastery and did not know whether they could establish it as a pure ground. The Buddha said: "It may be established as such. (The above is complete; I have relied strictly upon [the original text]).

[Text]. Chongyun said: "The various masters of antiquity have all used [the terms] incorrectly. In the following passage, where it says 'doubtful as to whether there is a pure place,' since there is none, it says 'there is';
and where it says 'there is,' it says 'place. It is not known whether this constitutes the establishment of a pure ground (*śuci-bhūmi*).

The Buddha said: 'It may be so established. This is the text of our own school (*sva-nikāya*), yet even here they err; how much less could they fully comprehend the texts of other schools? The *Shiyi* (Supplement) states: 'However, within the main text...'"

One suspects there may be a pure site, but since there is none, it is said [it cannot be used]. This is explained at length, even unto the Buddha’s words that one may [use it] provided it is made [pure].
Since it was already intentionally established and the boundaries were clearly demarcated, how can you falsely cite this as proof that the [status of the site] is not lost? Now, consider this:

since it says, "not knowing which place is a pure ground," it is clear that this location had previously been abandoned by people; this sufficiently demonstrates it is an old monastery (hālā). Why must you insist so narrowly on your position? Furthermore...

Therefore, when a monk in an old monastery (purāṇārāma) did not know whether he could establish a *śuddha-bhūmi* (pure ground), the Buddha directly ruled that it was permissible to establish such a pure ground.

Thus we know that within an old monastery, the rules governing the boundary (*sīmā-dharma*) are not lost; for it is only by relying on the rules of the boundary that the establishment of a pure ground is permitted.

[If one were to argue: "Because there are those who are ignorant of the teachings, they do not know which place constitutes a pure ground"—then by what logic can one know that their own school’s interpretation is correct and my school’s interpretation is incorrect? Furthermore, there is another refutation, as in the [previous] refutation.
The confused explanations need not be elaborated upon here.

Regarding the *Dharmaviniścaya-sūtra* (or *Dharmakṣaya-sūtra*), which mentions "the four matters pertaining to the Saṃgha," this refers to the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (boundary enclosure); in principle, there can be no *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) therein.
As for the statement that "the matter arose concerning the five bhikṣus," this merely refers to the practice of receiving precepts in border regions. However, as for the ritual of the *sīmāmaṇḍala*:
As stated in the eighth fascicle of the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*: "The smallest [mandala] can accommodate twenty-one people. Master Jing of the Tripitaka said: "Its dimensions are barely over one zhang;
if it were any wider, it would be difficult to assemble the sangha. Its original Sanskrit term is *maṇḍala*, translated as "altar site" (*tánchǎng*).
It is also called *kṣudra-sīmā* (or *kuṭṭarika-carma*), translated as "small boundary" (*xiǎojiè*). This is currently the standard practice in the Five Regions of India.

This area should measure approximately one *zhang* or more. Beyond the one *zhang*, bricks are to be piled around the perimeter in two or three layers, four or five feet wide, and plastered with lime mortar to serve as seating for people.
Outside this inner ring of bricks, bricks are to be stacked continuously to form a wall, two or three *zhang* high and about one and a half feet thick.
Within this enclosure, a *caitya* (translated here as "congregated form," referring to the stūpa) is to be installed upon the altar.
To pile bricks and stones to form a high mound is precisely what constitutes a Buddhist stūpa. It should be approximately one *zhang* in height, with a *śarīra* (relic) enshrined within;

this is the proper ritual protocol. As for the location of the entrance, it may be made wherever convenient. In former times, the Vinaya Master Sengyou piled stones to create a square altar and donned blue and yellow robes.
Whomever resided there would practice his methods. [The authorities] ordered that he be removed from office, fearing that his conduct constituted an introduction of illegal practices.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter sixteen, states: "He addressed the bhikṣus: 'I permit that those who wish to receive the precepts be placed outside the boundary of the ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*), where they are within sight but beyond hearing.
One should request a group of ten [monks] to be on the ordination platform; a single formal motion (*jñapti*) shall appoint a teacher to go and instruct them.

Once the instruction is completed, he should return. (Commentary: According to this, it is also permissible to inquire about the obstructing conditions (*antarāyika-dharma*) while outside the boundary."
Regarding the statement that "a *sīmā* (boundary) is not established if there is no dwelling place," the eighth fascicle of the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* asks:
"What is meant by a 'difficult dwelling' (*duskarāvāsa*)? It answers: "When a powerful king establishes [a dwelling] upon another's *sīmā*, it is therefore called a 'difficult dwelling.

One should say to those residing there: 'Do not build a dwelling here'... (and so forth)... even if one intentionally builds it improperly, and after three admonitions it remains improper, if the community..."
Many monks who possessed a sense of shame and remorse tore down this hall, leaving only the Buddha Hall and the Bodhi tree. (Commentary:
Thus we know that there is no *śīmaṇḍala* (ordination platform) where people do not reside.

Regarding the explanation of "sharing the same great boundary" (*mahā-sīmā*): the previous explanation of the great boundary stated that the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony) possesses two aspects; "sharing" refers to sharing within the same boundary or across different boundaries, as both are governed by the same regulations.

Regarding *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts), there is only the sharing of the same boundary; since there is no regulation against summoning those from different boundaries, it is unnecessary to say "the same *karman*.
Now, since the establishment of the *sīmā-bandha* (boundary enclosure) involves doubt regarding the *karman*, for this reason, "the same *karman*" is not mentioned.

This refers to the *mṛṣṭa* (polishing). Regarding the fact that the texts for the remaining three [procedures] and the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (boundary site) are all omitted: this means that for the two types of food-rites (*bhojanavidhi*) and the other three, as well as the *sīmāmaṇḍala*, there are no texts for the formal resolution (*visarga*).

Regarding the statement that "the time has arrived" will be explained below during the recitation of the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*): in the preceding ritual for the formal establishment (*bandhana*), the phrase "the time has arrived" and so forth is placed after the mention of "being of one accord" (*ekavācaka*) and other such terms;

however, in this present ritual for the dissolution (*mokṣaṇa*), the terms "being of one accord" and so forth are recited prior to "the time has arrived. By analogy, it should be understood that the same applies to the boundary of the Precept Platform (*śīlā-maṇḍala*).
Regarding the phrase "those that require explanation and those that do not": this comprehensively clarifies all meanings that require explanation.
As for the two-fascicle *Karmavācanā*, it refers to the ancient manuscript of the *Karmavācanā* whose title reads "Compiled by the Tripiṭaka Master. This is it.

The first section has four parts: (1) binding the sameness of the Dharma-food; (2) binding the sameness of the food while the [Dharma] is distinct; (3) binding the distinctness of the Dharma while the food is the same;

(4) citing the first two cases of sameness and explaining them as two types of distinction (that is, citing the initial sameness of the Dharma-food within a single boundary, which one now wishes to resolve into the distinctness of the Dharma and the food).
Regarding "one must bind the intention," etc.: the term "etc. includes the explanation of the names. As for "one must intend": in a single location, there is food but no proclamation.

Regarding the preceptor (*śāstṛ*): first, there is the case where there is a preceptor but no food; since these two factors require one another, the two are established as being "the same" (*dvaya-samāna*).

To explain the terminology: when the common dharma and the common food coincide, it is called "the two being the same. Other cases are explained by analogy to this. Furthermore, the text also contains four [sections].
Since there are four major sections, this is now a sub-section. Because the number four is the same, it says "also.

Regarding the phrase "the concluding dharmas are also four," etc.: previously, the conclusion of the *mahā-sīmā* was divided into four textual parts: first, appointing the person who proclaims the boundaries; second, the actual proclamation of the boundaries;
third, appointing the person who performs the formal act (*karma*); and fourth, the actual performance of the formal act. This present case is likewise the same, as explained before.
This is divided into two parts: first, citing the past as one [point] and distinguishing it as two; second, manifesting that the present desire is equal to the former, as previously stated.
Regarding the phrase "guarding the dwelling place," it means that at the time of performing the ritual, one desires that [the assembly] not be gathered [in a crowded manner].

Regarding the statement "the next two categories of fetters should also be treated thus": this refers to cases where the phenomena (dharma) are identical but the nutriment (āhāra) differs, and cases where the phenomena differ but the nutriment is identical.

Just as the first category—where both phenomena and nutriment are identical—should be explained as having two distinct types, so too should these be explained; however, the text is abbreviated and lacks the explanation for the phenomena.
That text also consists of four parts: first, citing the initial two [sections] as being identical; second, from "At that time, the bhikṣus... onwards, revealing the present distinction;

third, from "The Buddha said... onwards, explaining the previous identity; and fourth, from "In accordance with that... onwards, opening the present distinction and concluding the formal act (*karmavācanā*).

In examining the traditional practices of those who perform these rites, I have observed that within a single monastery—whether it be a large *ārāma* or a small boundary (*sīmā*)—multiple boundaries (*sīmā*) may be established.

As for this: taking food from within the *bhaktasaṃsṛṣṭa* (food-sharing) boundary and carrying it outside the monastery grounds (*ārāma*), or even into the interior of the temple within a separate boundary, all are said to constitute the offense of theft (*steya*).

Now, upon careful examination, this is not so. Since the matter concerns a single monastery, they share the same status as one family; how could mere separation by boundaries constitute a restriction?
Furthermore, regarding those who share the same *dharmasaṃsṛṣṭa* (dharma-sharing) boundary, they do not dissolve the old boundary but simply establish the sharing of food directly.

Thus we know that it is not because the substance of the boundary (*sīmā*) restricts food that one discusses the "commonality of the Dharma" (*dharmasāmagrī*) while distinguishing the boundaries for food.

One must understand that after establishing the old boundary, one further binds a new boundary for the commonality of the Dharma. Therefore, we know that the original intent of binding a boundary is for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of food. By investigating through this, [the truth becomes clear].

Therefore, it is known that there is no offense. If one were to say that the boundary is strictly restricted to specific food, then should two monasteries happen to establish a single common boundary, food would necessarily be shared between them.
If such sharing were permitted, it would conversely incur the offense of theft.

This might perhaps be acceptable; however, upon careful examination, it is not so. According to principle, one should permit four persons who act in accordance with the Dharma to go outside the boundary in secret and quickly perform the formal act of demarcation (*sīmā-bandha*). As for the assembly of the Saṃgha, it should still follow the usual procedure.
This is because if many people were to depart at once, evil persons would become aware of it.

Regarding the phrase "contact does not constitute contact," etc.: the "etc. includes the case where one with a malicious mind interprets another's pure ground; this does not constitute an interpretation of purity.

A malicious cessation constitutes contact-food (*āhāra*), yet it does not constitute a malicious contact. It is because the designated location is unknown that the prohibition does not constitute a prohibition. (Now, taking "non-constituting" as the common example:
if one were to take "malicious mind" as the common example, one would have to admit that a prohibition spoken with a malicious mind within the boundary does not constitute a prohibition.)

Regarding the phrase "reducing one dharma and entrusting it to the lower prohibition": this refers to the *Adhara-Pratibandha-khandaka*. It is heard that there are monks from another realm who take pleasure in quarreling and intend to come here.
The Buddha permitted the reduction [of the assembly] to perform two or three *poṣadha* ceremonies. If the *poṣadha* should be recited on the fifteenth day...
If the date is reduced by fourteen days, and it should be the fourteenth, reduce it to the thirteenth. If [the new arrivals] arrive today, the *poṣadha* should be performed promptly.

If they have already entered the boundary, the resident monks should provide them with bathing water so that they may bathe; meanwhile, the resident monks should secretly go outside the boundary to perform the *poṣadha* ceremony.
If this is not done, the Buddha has permitted performing the *poṣadha* later; one should then perform a *jñapti* (single motion). From...

From the white fortnight until the black fortnight, if he still does not go while being waited for, a second white fortnight should be observed. If he still does not go while being waited for, one should know that the Dharma is more powerful and that they must be brought into harmony.
The distinction between "small" and "large" can be understood thus: the fourteenth day is small, and the fifteenth day is large.

Regarding the necessity of employing the dual counting method: the method for counting the long dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) involves staining [the count] black, while the method for counting the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) involves staining it white.
As stated in the chapter of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Ji-lü), number twenty-seven, if such [substances] are available, one should sprinkle fragrant liquid upon the ground and so forth.
"Those who are guests" refers to those who are all bhikṣus. Regarding "the meaning applies to both realms":
within the natural boundary (jñapti-kṣetra), one may only perform the ritual of *poṣadha* by means of face-to-face interaction; the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) is not permitted.

Regarding the three positions for one who possesses the precepts: in the position of the Saṃgha, the precepts are recited; whether it be a large assembly or a single individual, the precepts are not recited.
The distinctions between these characteristics are not set forth within this chapter.
Within the Sangha, there are four distinctions: recitation by ten people, twenty people, four people, or five people;

as well as mental recitation (*manasikāra*) and so forth. These may be called *poṣadha*, but they cannot be called "reciting the precepts" (*śīla-vyākhyāna*). (This is not distinguished within the [relevant] chapter.)
Therefore, regarding those cases where only a *jñapti* (motion) is required: because the matter is easily settled through its formal execution, it is accomplished by the *jñapti* alone.

The same applies to the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism): when the Saṃgha appoints a person to perform the threefold proclamation, it is called "extensive" (*vistara*); when there is a twofold or single proclamation, it is called "abbreviated" (*saṃkṣepa*).
For four or fewer persons, there is only the face-to-face invitation (*pratyakṣapravāraṇā*), and no further discussion of "abbreviation" is necessary.
Regarding "not following the previous standard," it is unnecessary to follow what was distinguished in the four preceding sections.

The chapter states, "each and every point may be understood as usual. Furthermore, regarding the subsequent statement, "the abolition and establishment may be understood," one should first strike the bell.
Everyone recites their own verse on hearing the bell. As stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 23:

"Having subdued the enemy of Māra’s power, and having eliminated all fetters without remainder, the ghaṇṭā is struck in the open air; let the bhikṣus who hear it assemble. All those who wish to hear the Dharma," [should likewise come].
Having crossed the ocean of birth and death, they hear this wondrous sound; all shall gather here together. Next, the bhikṣus, maintaining their dignified deportment, advance slowly into the hall.
They pay homage to the Buddha with reverence, kneeling on their right knees and joining their palms, reciting these verses:
"Your precepts are pure like the full moon; Body and speech are bright and stainless. The great assembly is harmonious, free from conflict."

Only then may one participate in the common *poṣadha*. Having recited this verse, they sit upright in sequence. Furthermore, within the hall, it must first be swept and sprinkled with water, and clean mats must be spread.
Incense burners, counting sticks, tables, high seats, and lamps and candles should be arranged so that the scene is solemn and dignified.
A young person should be appointed to announce the proceedings (*śrāvaṇa*), and three or five young bhikṣus, or perhaps śrāmaṇeras, should be assigned to assist.

Prepare what is required. Each person shall maintain their proper decorum and avoid confusion. The *karmadāna* first takes pure water to wash his hands and then distributes it to the others to be offered to the Saṃgha.
When receiving the pure water, each person shall recite this verse: "The water of eight virtues purifies all defilements;
Washing my palms, I offer it with a heart free from attachment to the stūpa. Upholding the prohibitive precepts without transgression, [May] all sentient beings..."
It is also like this. One person should hold a clean cloth, grasping the upper end with the left hand and holding the lower end with the right hand, and present it to the assembly of monks.
The same applies to the scented bathing water and the cloth. The *karmadāna* then washes his hands with the scented water, next takes the perfumed water, and goes before the *sthavira*.
He pours the water onto the *sthavira’s* palms, hands him the counting sticks (*śalākā*) for the bath, and each recites a verse: "The noble Saṃgha of Arhats has assembled."
The assembly of ordinary beings gathers in harmony. With scented water they bathe and purify the counting sticks (*śalākā*). Through the *poṣadha*, they deliver sentient beings.
If the Elder (*sthavira*) is unable to bathe, the *karmadāna* bathes the sticks himself; when the scented water remains, he has others distribute it to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha receives the scented water, and each recites this verse: "Scented water perfumes and bathes away all defilements; The Dharma-body is perfected, replete with the five parts."

May Prajñā illuminate perfectly and liberation be fulfilled; may all sentient beings gather together as one in the harmonious fusion of the Dharma-realm. The procedure for the bathing cloth follows the above.

However, the water and hot liquid are intended solely for rinsing the hands and must not be used for rinsing the mouth. Once the *vina* has finished distributing the bathing sticks (*yuchi*), he proceeds to the side of the *jingchui* (the wooden mallet for signaling silence).
Holding the stick in his left hand and grasping the mallet by its handle with his right, he must first apply pure incense and the two waters to the handle as well.
Bathe them to make them clean. Strike once and chant: "Venerable Sangha, listen! Who among the assembly is junior? Let the junior one receive and protect [the items]. (Recite this three times.

This is said because they are collected and protected; alternatively, it is said: "And provide for the collection of the tally-sticks" (*śalākā*). (The meaning of "collecting and protecting" is as previously established.

As this practice has been followed for a long time, it is not abandoned. Again, strike once and chant: "Venerable Sangha, listen! The pure Great Śramaṇa from outside enters. (Recite this three times. Some say:)

This refers to calling for Piṇḍola. However, according to the Vinaya, those who harbor enmity should not be assembled; furthermore, when summoning the monks at the boundary (sīmā), it does not restrict this to noble ones (āryas).
Some add one more announcement here: "Those who have not yet received full ordination, depart. In the *Caturvargika-vinaya-karmavācanā*, the preceptor himself drives them out;

there is no need for the Karmadāna (Vina) to falsely order them to leave first. If someone recites the precepts from another school and the Karmadāna drives them out, this is perfectly correct. This is because...

The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* of other schools lacks the text regarding expulsion; therefore, the *karmadāna* (Venerable One) must first announce the expulsion. Furthermore, some say that those who are impure should depart;
this is likewise correct, as there are three inquiries within the body of the *Prātimokṣa* itself. Again, he strikes for silence and says: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Those among the assembly who are junior have already been gathered and protected; those outside who are pure great śramaṇas have also [been accounted for]."
[The assembly] enters. Both internally and externally they are tranquil, free from all obstacles, and fit for the casting of voting sticks (*śalākā*).
They shall perform the *poṣadha* extensively. The Saṃgha should mindfully perform the *poṣadha*. I, the bhikṣu [Name], for the sake of the *poṣadha*, cast this voting stick.

May the elders, the middle-ranking, and the junior monks each receive their voting sticks in due order according to the Dharma. (The words "receiving the voting stick according to the Dharma" are recited three times. Furthermore, he receives the voting sticks of those who have been entrusted with their own. Having made this proclamation:
Having arrived before the Saṃgha, they prostrated themselves on their right knees in order from the top seat and offered [the tally].
The Elder (Upādhyāya) likewise bared his right shoulder, knelt on his right knee with palms joined, and the remaining monks simultaneously followed the ritual of the Elder.
When taking the tally, each held it upon the crown of their head and recited this verse: "The tally of adamantine, unimpeded liberation is as difficult to obtain and encounter as a golden fruit."
"I now receive this with joy upon my head; may all sentient beings do likewise.

Thereafter, the person collecting the tally-sticks proceeds before the Saṃgha and receives them while kneeling on their right knee (*hu-kuei*). Those returning the tally-sticks place them back with their hands and recite this verse:
"Endowed with purity, I receive this tally; Endowed with purity, I return this tally. Firm in joyful relinquishment, without transgression. (1)
All sentient beings are likewise so. Once the counting sticks (*śalākā*) have been returned, fearing that they may become exhausted by the delay, each is permitted to sit down again.

In this manner, it proceeds in turn until the entire assembly of monks has finished. Having collected the sticks, one goes to the place of the *sthavira* (senior monk), kneels on the right knee (*hu-kuei*), and hands them over to him, instructing the *sthavira* to count them.

As stated in the *Zhi san shi si* (The Thirty-fourth [Section]): "Once the *śalākā* have been washed with scented water, they should be distributed; one person shall go [to distribute], and one person..."

[The procedure for] distributing the voting sticks (*śalākā*) is as follows: one must not walk with the head covered or the shoulders covered. One should remove one’s leather sandals and bare the right shoulder; the person receiving the voting stick should do likewise.
First, the voting sticks for those who possess full ordination (*upasampadā*) are distributed, and subsequently those for the novices (*śrāmaṇera*).

Once they have been distributed, one should announce: "There are this many persons who have received full ordination, and this many novices. Thus there shall be this many people. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter sixteen, states: "No..."
[The Buddha asked: "Who knows who should perform [the counting]? The Buddha said: "Let a junior bhikṣu perform it. If he does not know how to perform it, one should select someone who does.
A bhikṣu then cast the voting sticks (*śalākā*) for the Saṃgha. The Buddha said: "They should be handed over by hand. Once collected, they were not counted; once counted, they were not announced.
The Buddha said: "Once they have been collected, they should be counted; once counted, they should be announced. The announcement should state:
'There are so many bhikṣus and so many śrāmaṇeras; in total, there are so many who have left the household life. The karmadāna shall again strike for silence and say: 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Then he proceeds to distribute the śrāmaṇera voting-slips (reciting this three times). He must circulate among the monks everywhere, announcing aloud, 'Śrāmaṇera voting-slips,' for fear that a bhikṣu might receive a proxy from a śrāmaṇera; therefore, it is necessary to circulate them everywhere. Once the distribution and collection are finished, they are returned to those responsible for the count."
The *karmadāna* comes forward and kneels on his right knee to count the number [of monks]. The presiding elder informs him, who then returns to strike the signal for silence and proclaims:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen! At this single residence, for this single poṣadha, there are such-and-so many monks and such-and-so many śrāmaṇeras, totaling such-and-so many persons.
We, pure renunciants, perform the poṣadha in harmony. Above, we accord with the Buddha’s teachings; in the middle, we repay the four debts of gratitude."
For those below, who are sentient beings, each should recite the pure and wondrous verses from the sūtras. The verses say: "Pure as the full moon, one attains the *poṣadha* through purity;
when the karma of body and speech is pure, this is truly in accord with the *poṣadha*" (from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, fascicle 26).

Venerable Nanda then comes before the *sthavira*, prostrates, kneels with his right knee on the ground, joins his palms, and requests: "Today is the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight; the assembly..."

"The Sangha is in harmony. Great Virtue, out of compassion, please recite the precepts for the assembly. The Elder replies, "Very well. The *karmadāna* (Vina) then makes the proclamation according to the usual procedure.
If [the Elder] is unable, he should announce: "Regarding this matter of the recitation of the precepts, such-and-such a person should perform it;

however, because of old age and illness, my strength is insufficient. I shall therefore request the next seat [to act]. The *karmadāna* then requests two or three people in succession. If they are all...
The one who declines returns before the *sthavira* and says: "All those from the seat next to you downward have declined, stating they are incapable;
I await the instructions of the *sthavira*. The *sthavira* declares: "Let whoever is capable be appointed. The *karmadāna* strikes for silence and says: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.

The Saṃgha appoints the Vinaya-master [Name] to recite the precepts for the assembly. The Vinaya-master [Name], with a pure voice, shall ascend the high seat and accept the invitation. The Vinaya-master then ascends the high seat and accepts the request.
Having paid homage to the Buddha, he knelt with his right knee on the ground and said: "The bhikṣu [Name] bows his head in prostration and respectfully addresses the Great Assembly:
'I have been appointed by the Saṃgha to recite the Prātimokṣa; fearing there may be errors, I pray that those who join me in the recitation will provide guidance.

Having performed one prostration, he rises and slowly ascends the seat. Next, he performs a *brahmaghoṣa* chant as is customary. Then, the one reciting the precepts dismisses the śrāmaṇeras; the śrāmaṇeras..."

Having finished reciting the ten numbers before the Sangha, one returns to the room to perform one's duties; there is no need to trouble the masters with fruitless efforts toward heterodox views, for there are only twenty-three.
Because of the presence of those who dwell as thieves [among the monks], one uses the ten numbers to test whether they are right or wrong.
These "ten numbers" are simply ten methods of increasing numerical categories; they do not follow a fixed sequence.
As for the statement that "desire" (*chanda*) means "longing" or "need," this is not so. Here, "desire" refers to delight, approval, and acceptance.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* says: "Delight, sympathetic joy, and commonality.

In Sanskrit, it is called *chandāruci-yami* (where *chanda* means "desire," *aruci* means "to speak," and *yami* means "I"; thus, "I speak of desire"). This means that at the time of performing a ritual action, one delights in, desires, and accepts it.

In Sanskrit it is *ī* (pronounced with a third tone); here it means "desire. This refers to the desire of longing and seeking. In Sanskrit it is *kāma* (pronounced with a fourth tone); here it also means "desire.
This refers to the desire for the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). The Sanskrit pronunciations differ, and their meanings likewise vary.
Nevertheless, the dharmas to which they correspond number only one hundred and forty-four. Some commentaries state that there are only one hundred and one. Now...

“Detailed examination: ‘One hundred and forty-four’ refers to the claim that the ritual for establishing boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) is excluded from the *dharmas* [of the *Karmavācanā*]. This interpretation is incorrect.

In the *Jie-mo-shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), the Master himself enumerates one hundred and forty-five types of *karmans*. Among these, the rituals for establishing large and small boundaries constitute eight items.
For what reason would he exclude only one such *karman*? Therefore, it should be stated: however, as for the rites that ought to be performed, their...”
It is exactly one hundred and thirty-six [days]. The commentary above and below contains this numerical error; it should be understood accordingly. Furthermore, by further reasoning:
when performing the *parivāsa* (probation) for six nights, if there is someone who comes to announce [the matter], it is logically unnecessary to assemble the *saṃgha*.

If the announcement is made at the time of the *poṣadha*, or if it is announced to the *saṃgha* every day during the six-night period, it is likewise necessary to solicit the consent (*chanda*) and inquire about harmony (*sāmagra*). Although this announcement...
This is not subsumed under the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), yet it still requires the expression of consent (*chanda*).
Regarding the two subsequent positions that lack the method for expressing consent—namely, the positions of face-to-face (*saṃmukha*) and mental recollection (*manasikāra*)—it is as follows.

Regarding the "one hundred forty-four triads": these consist of the single *śukra* (white), the two *śukra*, and the three *śukra*. A commentary states: "The first is the position of the three *śukra*.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action) encompassing the three: within the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), there are both [the *śukra*] and the *karmavācanā*; because they occur together with the *karmavācanā*, they constitute the three.

Regarding the two restricted [procedures], *Poṣadha* (Recitation of Precepts) cannot be combined with *Pravāraṇā* (Invitation to Criticism), and *Pravāraṇā* cannot be combined with *Pariśuddhi* (Declaration of Purity).

This means that the two methods of *Poṣadha* and *Pravāraṇā*, which are to be maintained and practiced by the two types of Saṃghas mentioned previously, were established by the Buddha as practices to be performed constantly.

Regarding whatever matters from previous events that require something necessary, one may act according to their explanations as they please. This extends even to all ritual matters, such as the six-year staff and the water-strainer;
for anything that must be performed, it is permitted to grant one's consent (*chanda*).

If both "when it is necessary" and "when it is not necessary" involve a combination of permission and prohibition, this means that within both the cases where it is necessary and where it is not necessary,
there is both the permission to grant one's consent (*chanda*) and the prohibition against not granting one's consent (for failing to grant consent constitutes a *pāyattika* offense).
If matters such as the breaking of precepts are entirely unaccomplished, the person in question has committed a lie;
however, the formal act (*karman*) of the Saṃgha remains valid because that person’s mind does not oppose the Saṃgha (this principle is certain).
Regarding "the permanent and the impermanent": "permanent" means constant. This refers to the statement that the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) is a constant practice.
All other dharmas are termed "impermanent.

As for "each being explained in relation to the five": it is said that the *poṣadha* (confession of precepts) and the *pravāraṇā*, as well as the *pravāraṇā* and the *pāriśuddhi* (declaration of purity), do not both take place simultaneously.
Regarding the statement that it is "neither twenty-three people, because for the fivefold proclamation by monks and nuns, [the number] is sufficient or insufficient":

since it was previously stated that two [people] are not suitable for the three lower assemblies, it would logically follow that both monks and nuns together could constitute the quorum for bestowing ordination. Why, then, does it now state "twenty-three"?

Among those twenty-three [members], the four assemblies including the bhikṣuṇīs are all included in that number. Thus, by analogy with the monks, these [bhikṣuṇīs] are capable of bestowing [the precepts].

Does this not contradict the previous statement that both [assemblies] must be complete to constitute the capacity to bestow? Therefore, the present explanation states: the previous mention of "both being complete" refers to the respective assemblies themselves;

the current mention of "twenty-three" means that within that number, the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs is insufficient to constitute the noble Saṃgha. Hence, [the requirement for completeness] applies to the specific assembly in question.
It is not that [the recipient] is able to grant it. When the *bhikṣuṇī*s perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*), one should speak in the opposite manner; thus it is called the "fivefold recitation.

However, regarding the twenty-three [members], excluding the five such as the *parivāsa* (probation), this refers to the number of those who should speak. Excluding the twenty-eight, in the present case of granting consent (*chanda*), there are only twenty-three;
in substance, they are not those who can grant it. This is because the four assemblies, including the *bhikṣuṇī*s, constitute a different assembly (*anyasaṃgha*); hence, it is cited.
The five types of persons who are to be expelled (*pārivāsika*) and those subject to the thirteen difficulties (*trayodaśa-āpatti*) are not, by their very nature, members of the Saṃgha;

therefore, regarding the person concerned—from oneself up to the Saṃgha—they are clearly not capable of bestowing [the ordination]. For this reason, based on their essential nature (*svabhāva*), they are all incapable of bestowing it. As for those in *parivāsa* (probation) and so forth, their nature is that of pure monks;
therefore, based on their essential nature, they are all capable of bestowing it. Within this, there are three categories of distinction. First, those with supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*)...
First, if the person happens to enter the boundary, it constitutes a valid giving. Second, in the case of disappearance or being out of sight and hearing, it certainly constitutes a valid giving.

Third, regarding separate residence: if [the recipient] extends their hand beyond [the donor's reach], it certainly constitutes a valid giving; if they are outside the boundary, they may still enter the boundary.

Thus, the capacity to bestow [the fruit] is established. By examining the commentary (*śāstra*) and observing it closely, one will fully understand this meaning. In the section on Campā below, there are twenty-eight individuals;

however, two of them do not count toward the total body [of the group]. This is summarized in a verse: "The remaining [twenty-three] are cited as those who attained extinction with difficulty (i.e., twenty-three);
the 'hidden spirit' and 'separation from the field' (these five, together with the above, constitute twenty-eight)."

Regarding the fact that the four monastic ranks, when viewed in relation to one another, possess mutual inclusion, there are two meanings. First, according to the analysis of their characteristics: the higher [ranks] can accomplish the requirements of the lower;
therefore, a community of twenty monks fully includes the *chanda* (consent) of all four monastic ranks. Within a community of ten monks, the *chanda* of three ranks is included.

For communities of five or four monks, it should be understood accordingly. The lower [ranks] cannot accomplish the requirements of the higher; therefore, a community of four [monks] [includes only its own rank].

Regarding purity (*viśuddhi*), it does not include the invitation for mutual confession (*pravāraṇā*) and so forth. For a group of five persons, it includes the invitation for mutual confession and the formal acceptance (*jñapti*), but does not include the removal of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*).

For a group of ten persons, it includes only the formal acceptance, but does not include the removal of offenses. For a group of twenty, it includes only the removal of offenses. Regarding the second point, the classification according to function:

the group of twenty has the function of removing offenses, because the invitation for mutual confession, the formal acceptance, and so forth do not depend upon it. The group of ten has the function of conferring ordination (*upasampadā*), because [the sūtra] says...
Since [those such as] those who act at will do not depend on this, one should understand that for the five and four persons, it is the same.

For this reason, with respect to the side of "having dependence," they are said to be included; with respect to the side of "not depending," they are said to be not included. Regarding the twenty-seven persons, the verse says:

When life has ended, the remaining formal acts (*karmavācanā*) cease. Upon entering a separate faction of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the boundary of the *śīmaṇḍala* is dissolved at the appearance of the dawn light.

Regarding the "difficulty of suspension" (*duṣkṛta-samudghāta*), the text states that "the remainder specifically refers to persons," namely twenty people. The verse says: "Life ends, difficulty, suspension, and cessation" (the suspension is divided into three types).
Regarding the requirement for a quorum based on the actual person (*pudgala*): some say this interpretation is incorrect.

They argue that if one does not speak for oneself, the quorum is fulfilled even when granting consent (*chanda*), whereas if one does speak for oneself, it does not constitute a fulfillment of the quorum or the consent. Now, upon careful examination, the principle that the quorum is determined by the actual person must indeed be so;
for if the person is impure, the sense of communal harmony (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*) cannot arise. (The text contains this statement; it is appropriate to return to the traditional reading.)
Regarding the passage "as when the path is distant, the boundary is established," etc., the intent is to challenge the ancient masters.

Since they held that the *jñapti* (formal motion) was lost as soon as one saw someone who had departed from the assembly, the present author now challenges this by citing the aforementioned text concerning the distant path and the establishment of boundaries:

if one goes on the fourteenth day for the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day and is unable to receive the *chanda* (consent), it is simply because the subsequent text states that there is no other expedient means available to receive the *chanda* while staying overnight.
Therefore, the preceding text states: "One must not receive the *chanda* (consent). However, if one does not stay overnight, it is logically permissible to grant it.

Since the *chanda* is granted from afar, it is clear that [the recipient] has already departed beyond the sight and hearing of the person who granted the *chanda*. Thus, one cannot say that [the validity of the *chanda*] is lost simply because one leaves the sight and hearing of the person who granted the *chanda*.
As for the ancient masters who held the view that the intention of not delivering the *chanda* results in its loss upon leaving sight and hearing, they further explained "leaving" as follows:

There are four kinds of seeing and hearing: first, concealment; second, reaching and emerging; third, obstruction by a barrier; and fourth, sitting at a distance. When first receiving [the precepts], one is separated from the patient’s sight and hearing;
when reaching the halfway point, one is separated from the companions’ sight and hearing. In these two cases, there is only the single type of concealment.

Upon arriving among the Sangha, all four types are present (as the subsequent text states: "If one reaches the halfway point, or if one arrives among the Sangha, it is likewise; they should be understood according to their respective applications"). Now, the Master...

If it is argued that the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) constitutes a difficulty, this reasoning is likely incorrect. Since the supernormal power belongs to a different realm (*dhātu*), the mind is not questioned therein.

Now, although one is separated from seeing and hearing, there is no impediment to being within the same realm; how then could these two cases be considered analogous? Nevertheless, upon examining this explanation, there is indeed some truth to it.

One should understand the Master’s correct interpretation as it appears in the commentary (*śāstra*). Chong says: "Being separated from seeing and hearing" refers exclusively to the restriction of time; [in such a case] speech and reception cannot be obtained.
Because it is apart from seeing and hearing. Within the community of the Middle Way, even if one departs from the conventional path, the *kāmacchanda* (desire) is not lost.
Since the holding of desire is already a mission involving coming and going, how could one lose that desire immediately upon departing from the path?

If this is so, why does the text say "it is also thus"? Answer: In truth, it should indeed be excluded. However, looking back generally at what precedes, it says "it is also thus. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that in all three stages...
Regarding the clarification on receiving [the precepts]: since it was so at the initial reception, it is likewise for those in the midst of the Saṃgha.

To reflect upon one's transgressions and accord with the text, this interpretation is superior. The statement of the ancient masters that there are four types of "separation from seeing and hearing" is also not correct.

Now, examining the matter: if one constantly passes through various places along a path, one certainly loses the *chanda* (desire/intention). As stated in the precept regarding visiting other households before or after a meal: "If..."

If a bhikṣu, having entrusted his *chanda* (consent) with the intention of going to a village, returns on the way; or if he does not go to the place where he entrusted it, but instead goes to other houses;
or if he entrusts it to reach a householder’s home, or even a storehouse, a lodging at the edge of a village, or a *niḷa* (monastery);
or if he returns from those very places, such as a householder’s home—he loses the previous entrustment in each case and must entrust it again. [The procedure for] entrusting is as follows:
Even in minor matters, there are still many such errors; how much more so now when one harbors desire? How could one possibly attain the direct path while remaining apart from the constant Way?

Within the *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha*, it is stated that even by ascending two steps at once, one loses one's desire; thus we know it is extremely difficult. (To "ascend two steps" means to leap over two rungs at once.)
"One succeeds and two do not succeed. As the subsequent text states: "There are three kinds of madness and delusion:
first, whether one remembers or does not remember when the *poṣadha* is being recited; second, remembering the *poṣadha* and coming; third, not remembering the *poṣadha* and not coming.
(The first and third do not constitute the holding of the *chanda*; the second does. This is the interpretation established by the Master of the Commentary.)"

Regarding the twenty-one cases where both [the offender and the victim] are the same, the verse says: "The arena, the difficult-to-lift, the extinguishing, the spirit, and the hearing" (these are seven-character lines).
"Śikṣamāṇā and the two others" refers to including the śrāmaṇerī as well.
Regarding the two [cases] beginning with *parivāsa* (probation), the term "etc. (*ādi*) includes *antarāyika* (concealment).

As for "the suspension of the religious life (*pravrajyā-utsarga*) may be understood," this is based on the analogy of death (meaning: if one has returned to the assembly, then it is not a suspension of the religious life; if it is a suspension of the religious life, then there is no sense of returning to the assembly).

"Entering among the non-Buddhists and so forth": the "and so forth" includes entering other sects (since those who do not come and go [regularly] are not included; if they were to gather there, they would not be considered "entering among the non-Buddhists," etc.).
One interpretation states that this refers to performing rites in a place of concealment, which means being separated by obstructions and remaining hidden.

Regarding the passage: "When many are gathered and the sick person is unable to give their consent (*chanda*), etc."—this is intended to establish the textual passages concerning those who are ill, those who have departed from the boundary (*sīmā*), and so forth.

As for the phrase "the first is according to the previous explanation," the text is again divided into four parts: (1) [from the beginning] up to "thus it is well"; (2) "the light illness gives consent" [from the following section]; (3) "unable to... [and so on]; and (4) "assisted by others."

Regarding the passage on "going to the assembly" (*赴集*) [the section beginning with "At that time, the various..."]: regarding the passage on "the increase of illness surrounding [him]" (*病增圍繞*) [the section beginning with "If there is..."]: regarding the passage on "many being ill and leaving the boundary" (*病多出界*):

the first text is further divided into three parts. First, there is the necessity of assembling due to a specific cause. Second, from "At that time... onwards, the circumstances are presented to the Buddha. Third, from "The Buddha said... onwards, the permission to grant *pārisuddhi* (purification) is granted.

Within this, there are again three parts: first, the granting, the establishing, and the non-establishing; second, the maintaining of the establishing and the non-establishing; third, the explaining of the establishing and the non-establishing.

Within the middle [section], there are again three: first, the granting upon hearing; second, if one explains, then the five types are listed below; third, if one does not explain, it is the opposite of the above and constitutes non-establishing.
That which is performed by the Saṃgha is intended to signify purity; it should be practiced constantly by the Saṃgha and is not merely a matter of formal procedure.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (T. 1425), fascicle 27, states: At the time of the *poṣadha*, there were many who gave their consent (*chanda*) but few who assembled.

Furthermore, the number of monks giving their consent was equal to those who had assembled. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "From this day forward, when those who can give their consent are numerous or equal [to those assembled], one shall perform the *poṣadha*."

[The term] *vye* [means] "should assemble. That many [monks] generally do not have the fault of being separate is as previously cited from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*: "In a concealed place, one does not depart from seeing or hearing," and so forth.
As for the text stating, "the second monk speaks on behalf," if one follows the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter nineteen, it says that if [a monk] forgets, a bystander should speak on his behalf.

[The preceptor] shall grant [the instruction]. If three [recitations] are forgotten, another person should be assigned to continue the recitation in sequence. However, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (27) states: "If one forgets while reciting, others may provide the instruction.
If one causes [the recitation] to be performed during the *poṣadha*, it constitutes a transgression. This differs from both the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and this [own] Vinaya.
That Vinaya further states: "From this day forward, if one is unable to recite [the precepts] in reverse order, or if one forgets them while reciting, they may be restored.

To recite in reverse order constitutes a *vyatikrama* (an offense of transgression)—provided it was done intentionally. It also states: "To transfer one's *chanda* (consent) is not termed 'giving *chanda*'; this differs from the present Vinaya.
If one follows the eighth fascicle of the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, regarding the seven formal acts (*karmas*) associated with the procedure: "The one who receives the *chanda* speaks once..."

The person [conveys it] in this manner, successively speaking to a seventh person; all obtain what they desire and receive the purity of the *chanda*. This is called the "Dharma of Sevenfold Correspondence.
Following this, the transmission of the *chanda* may extend up to the seventh person. Furthermore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states:

"On the day of the *poṣadha*, if there is a black wind and rain, or fire, or bandits, and the bhikṣus are all startled and dispersed, it is not considered that the *chanda* was brought to the assembly. If...
When there is one person present, this is called "arriving at the Saṃgha.
To explain this extensively and directly, the intent is to simplify it as the four [procedures], such as the *chanda* (consent) and so forth.
Regarding the point that the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is not immediately broken: tradition says this is not so; logically, the retreat should be broken, as it differs from the *chanda* procedure.
Regarding the seven remaining conditions: furthermore, among the middle four, each has the character "ruò" (if), while among the latter three, each has the character "huò" (or).
(However, although there are two difficulties regarding the [different] coverings, having two [cases] is not a difficulty; therefore, they are combined into one.)
The text states, "The *poṣadha* night has already been long. This means that those who have committed offenses spend half a month in repentance to cultivate the roots of their precepts;
because the offenses to be repented are many, the night has become long. According to the *Pravāraṇā* rules below, it says:

"If the time spent on giving is excessive," which is traditionally explained as meaning that when a donor gives, they offer many blessings and prayers. Now, examining this in detail, as in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*...

The ninth point states: If there is preaching of the Dharma or formal discussion, or if many verses are being recited as an offering, such that the recitation of the precepts cannot be accommodated, it is permitted for the *poṣadha* to be held until the following day.
This is in accord with the intent of this Vinaya.

Regarding the partial citation of the latter four: these represent the remainder of the preceding seven. Since all four types—intermediate and inferior—involves staying late into the night, one fears violating the rule against spending the night [in seclusion];
therefore, one must perform a brief recitation.

Regarding the "Extensive Recitation of the Vinaya of the Precepts" (*Guǎngsòng jiè píní zhě*): this is one fascicle concerning the precepts. It consists of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya) in sixteen sections, comprising five types of recitations for the confession of precepts (*poṣadha*).

From the introduction up to the thirty rules on forfeiture and transgression (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*), it states: "The remainder is what the Saṃgha regularly hears. (The remainder is as detailed in the chapter. As for the differences in wording:

that [text] has only one set of five, whereas this has three sets of five. In the third of the first five sections of this Vinaya, the recitation extends to the thirteenth rule; in the third section of that Vinaya, the recitation extends to the two indeterminate rules [*aniyata*]).

Regarding the "Nidāna" (Introductory Sections) two and five: first, the introduction; second, up to the eight *śaikṣa* rules; third, up to the seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; fourth, up to the thirty-five *pāyattika* (prātideśanīya);
and for the second set of five, up to the eight *pratideśanīya*, it should be understood accordingly.
If one recites the original words again and exceeds [the limit], the *Śīla-vinaya* (or *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*) volume twenty-seven states:

When the bhikṣus were performing the *poṣadha*, they recited until reaching the *pāyattika* [offense]: "Having cut it, having broken it, having pulled it out, it is a *pāyattika*. While this was being recited, the thieves completed their task;
the reciter remained silent. After a short while, the thieves emerged. He recited it again, and so on up to three times. The thieves then thought to themselves: [End of provided text]
