The fourth section, which briefly explains the texts concerning shared property, exists in all schools. Regarding those who die while living alone, their robes and bowls are to be given to the first group of five monks who arrive.
Such various texts cannot be recorded in full; they are recorded here in brief to demonstrate their similarities and differences.
Among them, some employ formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) for distribution, while others simply permit the taking of the items as they are. Since there are these commonalities...
This is a different matter; at first glance, it is difficult to grasp its meaning, and thus I wish to analyze it briefly through three sections:

first, setting forth the correct principle; second, exposing past errors; and third, explaining according to specific instances. Regarding the setting forth of the correct principle, there are generally two approaches to discerning the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*):

first, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), discerning that all phenomena lack a fixed nature; and second, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), wherein some phenomena possess a fixed nature while others do not.

Regarding the nature [of these matters]: now, within the context of the conventional gate, one must distinguish between what is determinate and what is indeterminate—namely, whether the property of a deceased person belongs to the Saṃgha, its lightness or gravity, or other possible exemptions;
whether it possesses a fixed nature or lacks a fixed nature. Why is this so? Because the nature of such objects is inherently without an owner;
rather, based on the principle that the five groups [of monks] constitute a single family, once a person has passed away, it is adjudicated as entering the five [groups].

Once the assembly has determined that an item has been brought in and its ownership has been established, if one steals or damages it, the value is calculated to determine whether the offense is grave.

However, within this category of "brought in," there are further distinctions between those that are indeterminate and those that are determinate. Regarding the indeterminate: these may be either light or grave, resulting in further variations or exemptions;
they lack a fixed nature and exist solely because the Buddha established different legal classifications for them. For instance, [in the case of] the Sangha...

The distinction between light and heavy offenses is determined as follows: although the Dharma resides with the Buddha, the adjudication is carried out by the Saṃgha according to the circumstances, such that the gravity of the offense is not fixed.
For instance, at times a fan may be judged as a heavy offense, while at other times it may be judged as a light offense; the underlying principle is explained below.

Furthermore, there are cases where the Buddha himself personally adjudicates, granting permission for an individual to take something that would otherwise be prohibited, as in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.

Regarding the Vinaya: when taking items such as those belonging to one who has drowned or those considered "refuse" (pāṃsukūla), as well as the property of śrāmaṇeras according to the Mahāsāṃghika, there are many such categories.

Thus, it is known that these objects do not have a fixed nature. Because they lack a fixed nature, when determining their gravity, what might be light may enter the category of heavy, or what is heavy may enter the category of light;
however, as long as it merely violates the Buddha’s teachings, there is no grave offense. This is provided that the Saṃgha has adjudicated and declared the item to belong to its respective owner.
Once the determination has been made, there is subsequent mutual loss; this refers to the calculation of the value.

After the determination has been finalized, because the nature of each individual item is fixed, one should understand from this that within the process of adjudication, there are further meanings of "fixed" and "unfixed," which differ from the tenets established by various masters of antiquity.

Regarding those who were alive, the benefit accrues based on their reliance [on the Sangha]; after death, light items are definitively the property of the *pratyutpanna* (the present assembly). As for all [other] possessions...
Regarding heavy objects, they definitely belong to the permanent endowment (*saṃghika*). If monks were to judge them among themselves, calculating their value would constitute a *pārājika* offense.

The difficulties and contradictions in this matter will be analyzed in the subsequent section. Since it is known that the nature of these objects has no fixed ownership, the correct principle here should open six categories, which can be combined into three pairs:
namely, through one perspective they are said to be ownerless, while through another perspective they are said to have an owner. Furthermore, by...
By one method, it is described as light property; by another method, it is described as heavy property. Furthermore, by one method, the taking of non-existent things is permitted;
by another method, the taking of existent things is prohibited. In what sense is it said to be "without an owner"?

This means that when one investigates through reasoning and scriptural authority from various perspectives, since living beings already have the bhikṣu as their master, if the Saṃgha were to seize them, it would constitute an offense in every case.
Regarding the ultimate penalty: if one dies suddenly, [the property] is immediately assigned to the community.

If it is argued that because death is for the sake of principle, this object must belong to the community, then after a layperson dies, it should likewise belong to the Saṃgha; why then is it exclusively ordained that it belongs to the community only for a bhikṣu?
If it is argued that a layperson does not receive the benefits of the Saṃgha, and therefore after death their property does not belong to the Saṃgha or the bhikṣus—[this argument is flawed].

Furthermore, a bhikṣu should not receive *ni-li* (inheritance). After his death, the property does not belong to a bhikṣuṇī. For what reason, then, is there sometimes property that belongs to the community of bhikṣuṇīs?
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-one, states: "There was a dwelling place where a bhikṣu had passed away, but no other bhikṣus were present."

The bhikṣuṇīs should divide [the inheritance]. If a bhikṣuṇī passes away and there are no other bhikṣuṇīs present, the bhikṣus should divide it; this is largely consistent across all Vinayas, and thus one [view] is untenable.
Furthermore, if while alive one does not rely on a non-Buddhist community to obtain benefits, after death, those benefits should likewise not belong to them.
For what reason is there a case where property belongs to the assembly? As the following text states: "If one goes from this group to that group and dies before arriving, the Buddha said:
'Give it to whichever place he desired. Both [of these cases] are impossible. Furthermore, while living, one does not rely on the fourfold assembly to obtain benefit;
thus, after death, the property does not belong to the fourfold assembly. For what cause would property sometimes enter the fivefold assembly? This is the following text.
It is said: There was a bhikṣu traveling among the people of Kośala who, upon reaching a place where no other bhikṣus resided, passed away.
If there were members of the fivefold assembly of renunciants who arrived first, they should be given [the deceased’s belongings]. Zongchong said:

"However, since laypeople do not understand internal monastic law, I fear they might misappropriate the property of the Saṃgha; therefore, one should send it to those who arrived first. Once those who arrived first have received it, they must examine and inquire into the matter.

Answer: If the bhikṣu knows the location of his original monastery, he should send it to that monastery. If he does not know, it shall enter the inventory of the nearby monastery; the same applies to the death of a bhikṣuṇī.

Furthermore, if one takes [the property], it must necessarily undergo the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). Since it is already monastic property, how could it be entered [into the inventory] arbitrarily? An objection is raised:
Is it because the Buddha’s decree establishes it as monastic property, or is it because its nature is fixed such that it naturally belongs to the Saṃgha? If...

As for the Buddha’s ruling that this is property belonging to the Saṃgha: why would it not have entered [the Saṃgha] immediately upon his ruling? If you say its nature is fixed, then it should naturally belong to the Saṃgha;
the portion for the Bhikṣuṇīs of the *Pañcavargika* should return to their original monastery. This third point is untenable.

Due to these many reasons, we know that the nature of this object is such that it has no fixed owner; therefore, according to the presence of conditions, it enters and belongs to whoever possesses those conditions. Why, then, do other schools explain it differently?
Regarding those things that have an owner: since one has already received benefits by relying on the two Sanghas while alive, after one’s death, one no longer possesses them as an owner.

Therefore, the Buddha commanded that they be entered into the Sangha for communal use. As stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fascicle 57: "The Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī."
When Baddhānanda died, his robes and bowl were worth three hundred thousand *suvarṇas*. His ministers and kinsmen all came to claim them. The Buddha said:

"Those who provided Baddhānanda with food and clothing should receive them; as for those given by the Saṃgha, they belong to the Saṃgha. This is as explained at length in the sevenfold passage cited above.
In this context, their inclusion in the Saṃgha is due to the Buddha’s adjudication; it does not mean that their nature was originally [inherently] belonging [to the Saṃgha].

Regarding the Sangha: once the Buddha has adjudicated that an object belongs to the Sangha, its ownership is fixed within the Sangha; however, regarding its weight (the gravity of the offense), whether it is given to the Sangha or to an individual, and whether there is a formal legal procedure (*dharma*) or not, the nature [of the act] is indeterminate.

Because the ownership is definitively fixed with the Sangha, if one steals this object, the offense is established by calculating the value based on what was or was not obtained from the assembly of monks.
Therefore, scriptures and treatises such as the *Śraddhākarman-sūtra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* all state that [this constitutes] theft.

Regarding the property of a deceased bhikṣu: before the *karmavācanā* has been performed, one incurs an offense by [taking it] with respect to the Saṃgha of the ten directions (this meaning applies to incurring an offense in relation to the five groups of practitioners throughout the ten directions).

Furthermore, due to variations in gravity or lightness, whether it is committed with another person, or whether the factor (dharma) exists or does not exist, the nature [of the offense] is indeterminate.

Therefore, if one judges them interchangeably, they do not constitute a grave offense. How is it known that the natures of gravity and lightness are indeterminate? It is as stated in the *Gāthā-śāstra*:

He immediately permitted the division of gold; however, among the four divisions [of the Vinaya], this was prohibited and not allowed. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the division of fans is permitted, whereas in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, it is not heard of as being allowed.

Examples such as these all arise from differences in the capacities of those to be trained (*vineya*). The Buddha fundamentally established both permissions and prohibitions in accordance with these capacities. Since there are thus both general permissions and specific prohibitions, [the rules must be applied accordingly].

This demonstrates that phenomena lack permanence. There are also separate provisions [in the Vinaya] that permit not taking things that do not exist; how much more so regarding matters of light and heavy offenses? If their nature were fixed, how could they be established as such?

Light and heavy offenses are originally of an indeterminate nature. Even if one were to sever them alternately, how could one incur the offense of *pārājika* (defeat)? [Ancient legal judgments state that one incurs a heavy offense.]
(As will be extensively refuted later). How is it categorized as a light object through another method? It is because the nature of this object is indeterminate;

at times it acts as an impediment, yet it is also permitted to divide gold into pure portions for acceptance. This is an expedient allowance, just as in this Vinaya, the acceptance of money for medicine, housing fees, and similar items is permitted.
Now, this case is likewise: if gold is scarce at the residence where one stays, and there is a faithful offering...
It is entirely absent. Because the sudden lack of necessary provisions and conditions obstructs the Noble Path, it is therefore permitted to be classified as an "obscuration" (*nīvaraṇa*).

As stated in the *Dharmatrāta-śāstra* (The Treasury of the Transmission of the Dharma): there are those who ought to enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*), yet because they lack the necessary provisions and conditions, they are unable to do so.

For such circumstances, it should be permitted [to consume water]. (Consult the text for the continuation. Consequently, according to this sutra, those who do not cultivate the Path are not permitted to drink water, nor is the earth allowed to be traversed by them.

If it is for the sake of liberation, [the Buddha] permitted it in all cases (as verified in the *Buddhapiṭaka-tantra*). Why, then, is it described as a "heavy object" (*gurudharma*) through another method?

That is to say, regarding one's dwelling where pure wealth is abundant and faithful offerings are easily obtained, if one accepts gold and silver—receiving them with a greedy mind like the five physicians of the sun—one is not a śramaṇa.
Since there are established texts in the Vinaya and explicit judgments in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is therefore determined to be a heavy offense.
How is it that the non-appropriation of things (*avastu-parigraha*) is explained through another method? It is also because the nature of such objects is indeterminate.

For example, when a monk dies on the road, his belongings are given to the five classes of monastics; this is because the original donor intended them for the sake of śramaṇas. Furthermore, items such as robes and bowls are not for the use of laypeople.
If he were to use it immediately, it would fruitlessly diminish the donor's intention to give; furthermore, when he wears it, it would serve as a distinctive mark of his status.

Because there are many such faults, it is given as previously described. Once it has been received as previously described, it serves as a repayment of kindness; for if it were not repaid, who else would be willing to come?
Therefore, this scripture provides an exception that reverses the many previous prohibitions. That is to say, it allows for the merit of giving to arise continuously and constantly.

Furthermore, it prevents laypeople from using [the items] as markers of their status or as clothing, while also providing for the monastic community; since these are necessary requisites for the path, they are permitted. As for those who died by drowning:

Fearing that [the property] might be lost through injustice or negligence, and in order to prevent such loss, one should likewise open [the inheritance]. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is stated that a śrāmaṇera must repay the kindness of his teacher’s instruction;

cases such as these should be applied according to the specific circumstances. Question: When a bhikṣu passes away, is it also permitted for the teacher to take [his belongings]? Answer: In principle, it should also be permitted.

However, for now, based on the absence of explicit scriptural injunction (*avijñapti*), it is judged that he may not take them. Chong says: It should be left to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) to dispose of them and give them to the Saṃgha; it is not [permitted for the teacher to take them].

Regarding the entry into the *upādhyāya*: An objection is raised that since the text pertains to the *upādhyāya*, it should immediately be given to the Saṃgha; taking it with the notion that it is discarded refuse (*pāṃsukūla-saṃjñā*), it should not be taken as one's own.
Why, then, does another section establish a formal rule for taking it? This refers to the exclusion of cases where there are no formal rules regarding the objects.

In principle, it should be equally distributed and used within the Saṃgha; because the Dharma manifests equality, it is necessary to restrict the procedure to the formal rule. Thus, the preceding six sections consist of alternating prohibitions and permissions, which are not fixed.

Following and complying with the teachings, none are at fault. Although the various sections attributed to Mañjuśrī appear to be contradictory, if one seeks their fundamental intent, they all converge upon the absence of coming.
These were all spoken by the World-Honored One according to the specific capacities of his audience; as the provisional openings differ, sectarian attachments arise.

However, if one focuses solely on the essence of the precept-receiving body (*upādāna-kāya*), disputes will naturally be resolved. Furthermore, it is said: "Adhere to the object and consult the text; do not look to the opinions of others. This approach is sufficient to eliminate offenses.

"Sin. The ultimate punishment suffices to eliminate it; the deep delusions from the past are likewise removed. It further states: "Now there exists the *dāna* practice and the Vinaya teachings, which are divided into complete sections according to the treatises (*śāstra*).

This is because the bhikṣus were previously born among the gods, and thus human requisites are not what they find comfortable. [They] constantly bestow grace..."
The Buddha ordered Ānanda to provide all the requisites for the gods from among those available in the heavens; thus, in a single night, he attained the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).
It was through this that the *Qu* (the *Vinaya* of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda*) was opened. Those belonging to the *Fenquan* (the *Sarvāstivāda*) school falsely propagate an incomplete teaching.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that such is the teaching of Māra. Furthermore, it asks: "How can one receive the precepts according to this Vinaya yet employ that *Fenquan* [tradition], abandoning the established prohibitions to adopt [their errors]?"

[The Master] said: "I have not yet discerned whether the capacity for understanding and the application of the teaching are unimpeded. I have consulted extensively with various masters, and they all state that if one calculates the money [involved], it constitutes a grave offense.

If it were determined by the judgment of the Buddha or the Sangha, on what basis would one calculate the value [of the object] and thereby commit a *pārājika* offense? Furthermore, regarding the distinction between what is inherently fixed as contrary to the Sūtras and Vinaya:

If that [position] were correct, then this school would have committed a *pārājika* offense; if this [position] were true, then that school would have committed a grave offense.

"In the future, there will be twenty schools among my disciples that will be able to cause the Dharma to endure. These twenty schools will all attain the four fruits;
the Tripitaka will be equal, without superior, middling, or inferior distinctions—just as the taste of the ocean water is no different. As it says in the verse:"
The Mahāsāṃghika school branches out into seven divisions. (And so forth... "There is neither 'is' nor 'is not'; I speak of what will arise in the future. Furthermore, Nanshan says:
"If one examines this according to the substance of the precepts received, the disputes will naturally dissolve. He also says:

"How can one rely on this Vinaya to receive the precepts, yet employ the complete [rules] of that other division? Now, I shall likewise pose a counter-objection: For what reason does that school permit the ascent to the state of non-existence?

[In] the *Śikṣā*, this particular section alone prohibits entry into the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*). Furthermore, if one accepts [the precepts] based on that [text], it is permitted to take them as they are opened [in other texts].

Why, then, does this specific acceptance alone exercise exclusive control? Moreover, if that acceptance of the precepts permits both partial and complete [observance], how could this acceptance alone constitute a demonic teaching (i.e., a false doctrine)?

[For it is stated that] "one may accept [them] after performing the purification ritual," and all textual sources permit this. Furthermore, the title of the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* reads: *Sarvāstivāda-mātṛkā*.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "For what reason is it judged that [the rules] for the Śākya-vaṃśa are not [identical]? This is not reasonable; therefore, we shall now provide a detailed explanation.

The permissions (*anujñā*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) are essentially the same as the established regulations (*vinaya*). One may simply adopt or reject permissions and prohibitions according to the occasion; one should not adhere to biased practices based on narrow attachments.

Whether the nature of an object is grave or light is determined by the Buddha and the Saṃgha. Depending on whether it is light or grave, one deliberates upon the matter at hand, thereby eliminating both extremes. And so forth.

These two points are established. For instance, regarding the distribution of fans: since they are not required during the winter, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) requires that they be included among the heavy items.

However, when the summer heat inevitably arrives, even the absence of such items becomes a matter of necessity; thus, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü) classifies them as items subject to distribution. Furthermore, this applies to water jars and wash-basins.
Since all people already possess [it] beforehand, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* judges that it should not be divided. However, if they did not previously possess it, its division for use is permitted;

thus, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* allows for the taking of two *sheng*. These examples are numerous, but they may be universally explained according to the circumstances; in all cases, there is no contradiction.
From this, one should know that judging [the gravity of offenses] as contrary to the intent of the teachings does not constitute a transgression.
Third, regarding the explanation according to specific matters: this refers to determining whether an offense is grave or light based on the category of the object involved.

Although the texts of the various schools do not provide a fixed standard for gravity or lightness, there are distinctions between the hidden and the manifest within the principles of the *dharmalakṣaṇa*. "Hidden" refers to those cases where exceptions are made; "manifest" refers to those cases that are generally applicable.

Therefore, to distinguish between the partial and the complete, it is termed "crooked" (*kuṭila*) and "universal" (*sādhāraṇa*). This serves to clarify the pure substances and determine them as universally applicable.

Regarding the opening [of a rule] for what lacks a formal basis and the restriction for what has a formal basis, one should understand that the distinction between the crooked and the universal follows this same principle. Where there is necessarily a crooked occasion, one should not prohibit it.

For example, regarding the prohibition against eating meat, it is determined to fall under the five types of wrong livelihood (*pañca mithyājīva*); because these are light offenses and belong to the category of the indeterminate (*aniyata*), they are permitted according to what is allowed.

Furthermore, in accordance with the Noble One’s intention, regarding the establishment of the regulations for light and heavy items based on common practice: since their nature is not fixed, one should seek the Buddha’s intent.
That is to say, items that are light by nature, essential to the person, necessary as requisites for the path, and which do not incur public reproach—these all constitute light items.
Apart from these, anything that increases the burden of possessions or intensifies greed, and which invites external reproach and disgrace, all constitutes "heavy property.

Why is this so? Because those who have left the household life share the same Dharma and, in principle, are as one in birth. Once a person has passed away, their assets and wealth are to be distributed. This is analogous to when a single member of a secular family passes away;
their assets and clothing are shared among those currently living together. The Buddha’s intention was likewise so, for the purpose of benefiting his disciples.
One may only use what is necessary; all that can be divided should be distributed, while that which cannot be divided should be stored for the use of the community.

From this, one should know that there is no teaching permitting the sale [of such items]. Yet in current practice, people sell them to take money, performing this act without any valid or exceptional justification.
This is most improper. Furthermore, for this reason, it is not because one gained benefit while alive or relied upon the Saṃgha that the community must seize [the property] upon his death.
Consequently, even the shrouding of the corpse must conform to the teachings; how could one allow it to remain exposed, thereby abruptly obstructing human sentiment?

However, since the body perishes and is as common as tiles or wood, it is of little benefit to provide much for it; one should follow what is appropriate with moderation. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If a bhikṣu passes away and his body is left exposed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; it should be covered with clothing. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-eight, states:
"When a bhikṣu is traveling in the wilderness and encounters a sick bhikṣuṇī, he should attend to her," as explained in detail therein. If the bhikṣuṇī passes away, she has... [text ends]
Regarding the robes and alms bowl, one should hire someone to perform the cremation; this is the ultimate principle. There is no need for laborious scrolls.

As for oxen and livestock, grain and silk, money and wealth, tiles, wood, rafters and beams, basins, jars, cauldrons, and protective vessels—if one were to enumerate each item individually, the accumulated words would become excessive.

To cling to objects and rely on texts, there will inevitably be errors in those words. Why is this so? Because objects have no fixed standard and their uses are not constant. [The text ends with] "the brush."

This has been written for a lifetime, yet it cannot be fully exhaustive. I have heard that when the virtuous elders of the capital once gathered to deliberate and judge matters of gravity and lightness, there was a small copper dish within a begging bowl, which people of the time called the "Dish of Sentient Beings.

Since it is not recorded in the scriptures and does not appear in the commentaries or digests, I have long hesitated; no one dared to definitively categorize it. Then, one master said: "For now, let us classify it as light. Furthermore—
Someone asked, "By what principle or teaching is this based? The Master replied, "As long as one enters into a state of lightness, why worry about having committed an offense?

Even if there were an offense, such a person would naturally remain constant. Furthermore, there are those who carry prayer beads while harboring doubts; how could every such category of object be recorded in detail?
One should simply seek the underlying intent and achieve understanding according to the specific circumstance. For instance, keeping a shallow dish does not invite reproach. If, however—

What is necessary for saving the age must enter the light category without error; if it were truly useless, it would not enter the heavy category. When one understands and integrates matters in this way, all things will be free from obstruction.
By verifying the mind and following the teachings, one will not be blamed in the future; yet if one indulges in greed and delusion, there will surely be long suffering on the perilous path.

Once the underlying intention has been understood, one may then employ the records of various masters to reach a judgment. Should they not record it, one should resolve it through the aforementioned intention;
only then will one have fully exhausted the principle. (Next, follow the commentary for the explanation.)
Regarding the "six items": according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter twenty-eight, it states that one should first provide the six items to the monk who has been attending to the sick;

as for other minor articles, the Saṃgha should take note of them. These six items are: the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, the *antarvāsaka*, the alms bowl, the water-strainer, and the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*).
According to this *Vinaya*, the meaning of the "six items" is established as follows: namely, the robes, the bowl, the sitting mat, the needle case, and the container for the robes.
Regarding the "storage vessels" (to be explained in detail later).

As for the "six domestic animals," Zheng Xuan states: "The six domestic animals are the six natures; that is to say, oxen, horses, sheep, dogs, pigs, and chickens constitute the six domestic animals."
Regarding secular scholars: although the commentary specifies six categories, the intent here applies to all types of animals.
Among them, those such as oxen and horses that are capable of performing labor for the Saṃgha and do not involve scandalous faults may, by definition, enter the Saṃgha.

As for chickens, dogs, pigs, sheep, parrots, and the like, they provide no benefit to the Saṃgha and need not be kept in cages; if they are able to fly and sustain themselves, they should be released.

Release them. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Tridharmaka-vinaya), chapter thirty-three, it is not permitted to accept such gifts; therefore, they should be released (as cited above in the section on the precept against stealing).

As for animals such as cats and wildcats, if the Saṃgha keeps them collectively, they collectively incur the offense of killing. Such practices exist [among various schools], and one brings calamity upon oneself.
All such animals should be released and must not be given away as gifts. Therefore, within this context, one should make fine distinctions and should not treat all cases as the same.
The judgment is that this constitutes a grave offense. The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Combine the first six into three; combine the lower nine with the tenth; and leave the remaining five as five.

Thus, they are judged by way of nine categories. (There is also a version of the *Śū* which states: "Combine the first six into three; return the lower seven to seven. Thus, they are judged by way of ten categories. This version of ten categories was the original draft of the *Śū*, but the author later revised it and did not adopt it.
This means that the category of "warm" (*uṇha*) and the category of "blue" (*nīla*) are treated as a single item, as are the separate rooms and the items belonging to those rooms.
They constitute a single unit. Axes, adzes, and similar tools, as well as heavy objects, constitute a single unit. Because these six units are similar in pairs, they are combined.
The ninth is the "blue person" (nīlapurusa), and the tenth is the "cart and litter"; their types are similar, and thus they are also combined into a single unit.

"Those items of the same type as previously mentioned bags" refers to the aforementioned coarse screens and so forth; these are simply of the same category as the previously mentioned articles of adornment, and none of them should be divided.
Regarding "ten *lǐ* or more than half a *shēng*" in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this refers to twenty-eight [measures]; all horn-based objects should not be divided, with the following exceptions:
Regarding items of half a *sheng* or less, all leather goods should not be divided, with the exception of bags for holding ghee or oil that hold half a *sheng* or less.
Furthermore, all iron, copper, stone, and ceramic items—except for those holding two *sheng* or less—should not be divided.
The Master of the Southern Mountain (*Nanshan*) says: this *vinaya* mentions "bottles" (*ping*) but does not specify their capacity in *sheng*, which has led to...

The *Chuanxi* (Tradition of Practice) states that when items are cut off [from the community] and subsequently recovered, they should be recited from below and their distribution determined accordingly. Regarding nuns, they must perform the ritual of *śuddhika* (purification) before keeping such items;

for monks, however, they may store them as they please. Now, examining this closely: if one were to divide items based on having performed the *śuddhika* ritual, then since money and precious objects are also permitted to be kept through *śuddhika*, their division should likewise be allowed.
Therefore, it is clear that the underlying intent has not been fully understood.
Regarding the eighth, *elāpattra*: according to the thirteen chapters, it is the eighth; however, according to the nine gates, it is the fifth.
Nanshan says: "Elāpattra refers to the *ūrṇa* mark on the Tathāgata’s shoulders, which are like those of the *elāpattra* deer king;
thus we know this refers to the skin of this deer."
*Moro moro* are both names for beasts; they resemble tigers or rhinoceroses, with thick skin and soft fur, and are found in the Western Regions.
Since they do not exist here in this land, their original names have been retained. Why did the ancients speak of "step-screens" (*bu-zhang*) and so forth?
The Master of Nanshan explained the ancients' intention as follows: First, *ilī-ā-dha*—is this not the appearance of a screen? Next, *mo-mo-zhu-lo*—is this not...?
It is not a large or small canopy (*vitāna*). A canopy resembles a hat; therefore, it is called *maura*. To use this for the purpose of a canopy—how laughable!
This has been extensively refuted by Nanshan (*Daoxuan*) in works such as the *Qingzhong yi* (*Ritual of Light and Heavy Matters*).

Regarding the *kūlū* (woolen rug): Master Nanshan stated, "In the past, I considered its measurement to be the same as that of the three robes (*tricīvara*), and thus categorized it among light items.

Blankets made of [*li*-*mu* + *tuo*] wool and the like were all treated according to this precedent. During the Qianfeng era, a celestial being appeared in a vision and said, 'This is specifically permitted for use in cold, snowy countries;

it is not permitted in the Central Kingdom, as the Central Kingdom already possesses the Dharma-robes (*dharmakāya-cīvara*), which are all classified as heavy items. Now, upon detailed examination..."

His intention was that since this country already possesses dharma-robes, [the *chīvara-āvaraṇa*] need not be worn; this clearly indicates it must be used when entering a crowded place. However, upon careful examination, even Arhats alone possess ignorance;

how much more so for those devas and humans whose wisdom is inferior to that of human beings—it is not sufficient to rely on them. Furthermore, the *vraṇapracchādana-cīvara* (wound-covering robe) does not necessarily have to be determined as prohibited according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the ninth section on slaves and servants: according to the thirteen chapters, this corresponds to the ninth;
however, according to the nine sections, it should properly constitute the sixth section, combining the ninth and tenth chapters."
The Commentary states: "Regarding the twelfth, the 'Iron' [offense], according to the thirteen chapters it is the twelfth; according to the nine gates, it is the eighth.
Since there is no textual authority for its inclusion here, there is no hindrance to its being included; it is better that it be included among the light offenses.
Regarding "giving to one who is able to make offerings," this refers to the case where the person [receiving] is alive. If the object consists of ordinary wealth, it may be classified as light;

however, if precious ornaments are included, it is classified as grave. This applies when one has already made a firm resolve to relinquish the item for the purpose of making an offering and then gives it to the person who makes the offering.
The phrase "the following section divides the *kubjara* vessel" refers to the text immediately following this.
Regarding the statement from the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, the third fascicle of that work says: "There was a bhikṣu who lived alone in a separate dwelling. He fell ill and passed away.
All the robes, bowls, and requisites belonging to this bhikṣu should belong to the *saṃgha pratyutpanna*" (the above is the text of the treatise).

The commentary’s main intent is as follows: when a person dies in private or in a secluded place, they belong to the category of those present at the time of death, precisely because there is someone to guard them.
As for one who dies within a village, they belong to the fivefold assembly (pañcavarga). Therefore, that treatise states:
"If a bhikṣu dies alone in the house of a layperson within a village, and subsequently the fivefold assembly arrives, whichever group comes first shall take possession of his belongings."
Regarding the statement that one "dare not give a *fei-yi* (non-garment) to a bhikṣuṇī," some say:
since the preceding text states that one makes a bowl-sack (*pātra-kośa*) from a *fei-yi*, we know that a *fei-yi* is not necessarily a bowl-sack. Now, examining this closely:
a *fei-yi* generally encompasses everything that is not used as clothing; thus, even a bowl-sack is a *fei-yi*.
Regarding the phrase "the tree of non-anger": it is so named because it causes people to rejoice.
The word "de" (的) means "to clarify" or "to manifest"; it refers to seeing clearly and with certainty.
Regarding the statement that Mahānāman was his maternal grandfather, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Wufen lü), fascicle 21, states:
"At that time, the Śākya kingdom still adhered to its ancient custom of not entering into marriage alliances with those of a different clan. King Prasenajit, relying on the strength of his army..."
A messenger was sent with this message: "If you do not grant me your daughter in marriage, I shall destroy your kingdom.
The Śākyas deliberated together, asking, "What means should we employ to dissuade that fierce tiger while not violating the ancient customs of our nation? They all agreed:

"We must select a beautiful maidservant of excellent appearance, adorned to the utmost extent of the world, and designate her as being of the Śākya clan, and then give her to him. Acting according to their plan, they immediately—
[He] was given [in marriage] by King Prasenajit, who received him with full ceremony and welcomed him as his brother-in-law. Later, a son was born whose countenance was exceptionally beautiful;
he was named琉璃 (Rāhula). (The above is from the Vinaya text. Therefore, in the present text, Mahānāman is designated as the maternal grandfather.

Regarding the statement that the fruit of the meditative state (*dhyāna-phala*) created in the past is [the result], the *Ekottarika Āgama* (Zengyi Ahan), fascicle 26, states: [The Buddha] addressed the bhikṣus...
“Kāśyapa, in the past, there was a fishing village in Rājagṛha. At that time, there was a period of extreme famine.
The people went to the pond to catch fish for food. Among them were two fish who made a vow to take revenge.
At that time, there was a young boy in the village about eight years old; he neither caught fish nor took life. However, when the fish died upon the bank, the boy—”
The boy was exceedingly joyful. At that time, the people of the city of Yecheng are now the Śākyas. The fish was King Virūḍhaka. The young boy was the Buddha.
Because I laughed at him then, I now suffer from a headache as if pressed by a stone, as if my head were bearing Mount Sumeru.
(Pañcavargika-vinaya 21) Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha: "Please allow me to manifest an iron cage to enclose him."
In the great city, the Buddha said, "By what power of your supernatural abilities could you possibly alter this fixed retribution?
The Buddha prophesied that in seven days, Virūḍhaka would suffer the sin of harming the disciples, and his kinsmen, both great and small, would likewise lose their lives.

Upon hearing this, the king thought to himself, "The Buddha’s words are never empty. Other sufferings may yet be endured, but I fear only being consumed by fire. He immediately took his kinsmen and boarded a boat to enter the river. Seven...
When the date arrives and the waters rise and submerge [the area], everyone will die at once.

To prevent the indiscriminate taking of property by those who are not relatives, if one permits great relatives to take miscellaneous small items, there is a fear that this might extend to minor relatives who take small things.
In truth, even minor relatives are strictly forbidden from taking anything at all.

Regarding the five hundred offenders: the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states that when the Buddha saw this man's illness, he led the fourfold assembly and, emitting a great radiance, went to where the patient was and said, "I now requite your kindness; I now requite your kindness. He then took a water jar in his hand.

He sprinkled the medicine upon the sick man’s body, and his illness was cured instantly upon contact with his hand. The bhikṣu said, "Though the physical illness has been cured, the mental affliction has not yet been removed.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he immediately attained arhatship, becoming endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.

The bhikṣus asked the Buddha, "What was the cause for [the man] previously speaking of repaying a kindness? The Buddha said, "Long ago, there was a certain kingdom that had a deep [connection] with a *pañcaśatika*..."
They recognized each other’s minds and entrusted him with the administration of punishment. Those who had obtained the goods were immediately released;

those who had not obtained them were subjected to various forms of harsh treatment, some even resulting in death. At that time, there was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who had committed a minor offense and was to be punished.
At that moment, five hundred people saw that he was a virtuous man and immediately ordered his release. Those five hundred at that time are these current sick people. For this reason...
He said: "Relieve him of his heavy burden" (verify the text). The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or relevant Vinaya commentary), fascicle 28, states:

When traveling through a wilderness, one must not abandon a fellow bhikṣu; one should take him along and carry his robes and bowl for him. If he is unable to walk, one should hire a vehicle or beast of burden.
One must not load a cow-drawn cart or a donkey and the like; rather, one should load a bull or a stallion. If he is ill...
For those who are deeply free from conceptual discrimination, proceeding by means of a vehicle is without fault. However, if a vehicle cannot be obtained, one should leave behind a caregiver.
You, O caregiver, when I have reached the village, shall seek out a vehicle to come and meet me. One should also leave behind provisions so that those staying behind do not lack for sustenance.
If each person says, "Who can abandon body and life in the wilderness? and no one is willing to stay, then [the journey] cannot be undertaken.
He then departed. [The patient] should construct a hut and a bed of grass, prepare a fire, and provide water and wood.
He should leave behind *tatkālika-bhaiṣajya*, *yāmika-bhaiṣajya*, *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*, and *yāvajjīvikabhaiṣajya*. He tells the sick person: "Venerable one, remain at ease.

I shall go to the nearby village and seek a vehicle to come and fetch you. Upon reaching the village, he must not circumambulate the stūpa, but instead inquire after the health of his preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and *ācārya*.
"Lī! You should tell the bhikṣus in the village: 'There is a sick bhikṣu in the wilderness; let us go together to welcome him back.
If they ask where he is, you should answer, 'In such-and-such a place. If they say, 'That place is full of tigers and wolves; we fear he will be devoured,' [you should respond accordingly]."
"Of ten thousand, not one remains. Although I have heard these words, I cannot stay; I must go to see him.
If I see crows or birds from afar, I must not yet return; I must reach his location. If he has already died, I should make offerings to his corpse.
If he is alive, I should bring him to a village and say to the resident monks: "Venerable sirs, this is a sick man from such-and-such a place whom I found in the wilderness."
Having made the offerings, they have now arrived here; let the Elder look after them next. If he does not look after them, he commits a *vinaya*-offense.

If there are no monks present, he should tell the lay follower (*upāsaka*): "There is a sick monk in the wilderness; lend me a vehicle to go and welcome him. Having welcomed him, he brings him to the donor’s house.

One should set aside a separate place for those with obstacles and jointly encourage them regarding robes, medicine, food, and so forth. If a visiting bhikṣu arrives, one must not immediately say, "You must look after this patient.
Instead, one should say, "Welcome," take over the carrying of his robe and bowl, and provide various offerings. Having done so, one should say, "I have looked after this patient for a long time;
it is now your turn to look after him. If a bhikṣuṇī is ill, one must not abandon her and depart. The method of attending to her is as described above.
Except for holding or lifting [the patient], if it is necessary to massage or apply oil to the body, one should request a woman to do so.
If there is no permanent resident [nun] available, and the patient possesses robes and a bowl, one should hire someone to perform the cremation; if the patient has none, one should simply depart.

If there are laypeople who find this objectionable, if one can maintain the perception of the ground [as empty], one should carry the body to a distant place. This is the third section of *Śrī-utpatti*, concerning the time of attending to the sick.

One should not give rise to weariness. If one has no property of one's own, one should seek it by going out in the four directions; if one cannot obtain it through seeking, one may take the property of the Triple Gem.

Once the debt has been assigned, it shall be repaid tenfold according to worldly custom, in accordance with King Aśoka’s True Dharma. If one is unable to repay it, one should instruct them as follows:

"You have incurred a great debt to the Triple Gem that you cannot repay; therefore, you should be encouraged to cultivate the path so as to attain the fruits, from the stage of Stream-enterer up to the fourth fruit."
If one can sincerely resolve upon the Bodhicitta; or if one causes a thousand people to develop pure faith in the Buddha-dharma;

or if one destroys the grave wrong views of a single person—these two types of individuals both obtain immeasurable benefit (meaning this applies to each individual case, not necessarily to those performing both).
The *Śāstra* says: "If one is ill and lacks medicinal decoctions, one may offer flowers, fruits, food, or drink to others to seek in exchange for medicinal decoctions."
Regarding the offense: the phrase "sitting in stillness to quiet the inner mind" refers to contemplating such reflections as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and death;
one should not be filled with panic or fear, nor should one be solely terrified of death. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle 20, states: "One cannot constantly contemplate impermanence."

Regarding the general explanation of the established principles (*siddhānta*): the principle of simultaneous arising should be understood by taking the higher category; the principle of assignment should be understood by taking the lower; the principle of gravity should be understood by taking the higher;
and the principle of distribution should be understood by taking the lower. All of these must be clearly comprehended.
"Reverently receiving and being mindful of me" refers to the thought of cherishing and loving one while alive.
"Without the fatigue of [physical] labor" means there is no labor such as massaging and so forth.

Laypeople do not have the labor of explaining the Dharma to śrāmaṇeras, which is said to be one-third [of the total labor], and so on; these are all [treated] according to the *Pañcavargika* and the *Dharmaguptaka*.

This is the tenth section. The *Zhi* (祗) states, volume thirty-one: "If a bhikṣu passes away or enters parinirvāṇa, one should not immediately close his door" (*Zhang* [the commentary] says this question does not rely on the text). This refers to the disciple who relies [upon him] (as can be understood).
The measured shadow should be aligned; it is exactly thirty-one units. It says there: "Either one encounters death but not the *karmavācanā*, or one encounters the *karmavācanā* but not death;
or one encounters both death and the *karmavācanā*" (it lacks the fourth case, presumably because it is too obvious to be mentioned).

Regarding the number of persons: for those above the rank of *saṃgha*, they must necessarily be present at the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). For three persons or fewer, both types of boundaries apply.
In the texts, there are only two cases; the case of appointing a person is omitted from the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation).
As it is said regarding the distribution of offerings received by the Saṃgha, one should speak as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. A certain bhikṣu has passed away at this residence.

Whatever robes or non-robes he possessed should be divided among the Saṃgha present here. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent that these items be divided among the Saṃgha present at this residence.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). The ritual act (*karman*) is completed according to the motion."
Regarding the performance of the three methods: for four persons, it is the *karmavācanā* (formal act) method; for three or two persons, it is the method of mutual agreement (*dvaya-sammata*).
However, as for rewarding with robes, this refers to taking the reward collectively; because it is not possible to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) in such cases.
Regarding the fact that objects have qualities of being desirable or undesirable, it is as explained in the following text: one should look at the superior items and the three types of robes;

the middle and inferior ones are to be understood by analogy. As for the second text, which addresses objects through five gates, these five gates are precisely those found within the aforementioned categories of meaning.
The third is the analysis of the substance (it is better to explain the text using the fourth section). Regarding the third, which concerns qualities (*guṇa*):
this text refers to the third [section], which is the fourth section within the aforementioned categories of meaning (*artha-mukha*).
"Those who hope for wrong livelihood" refers to those who, by means of this [acceptance], hope for clothing, food, and so forth. "Delighting in merit" means seeking merit for oneself;

therefore, one should not accept [such things]. If one accepts them, it does not constitute the meaning of seeking merit. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Wufen lü), fascicle 20, states: "There were certain caregivers..."

The section on the three gates of entrustment (*śāsanā*) is explained according to its meaning; now, the text will be interpreted line by line. Regarding "entrusting without requiring formal instruction" (*śāsanam vinā śāsanam na prayojanam*):

this means that it does not depend upon a formal act of entrustment. Furthermore, within this gate, there are three phrases in total: first, entrustment (*śāsanā*); second, instruction (*śāsana*); and third, both entrustment and instruction (*śāsanā-śāsana*).
The fourth phrase is missing; it may be found by searching for it.
"That which cannot be moved or transferred" means it is not like silk cloth, which can be taken up and carried away by hand.
Furthermore, "that which has no alteration" is so called because it causes [the mind] to become resolute. If one uses the second [phrase], etc., among the three phrases...
The second [point] verifies the remaining two phrases. The subsequent phrase, "just as with that which has not been purified," is likewise so (both are merely thirty-one).
Regarding the procedure for granting [the property] by means of a *pañcavācikā jñapti-dvitīya* (a motion followed by two announcements), the *Mahā-vibhaṅga* (Twenty) states:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu named So-and-so has passed away here. Whatever robes or non-robes he possessed during his lifetime should be divided among the present Saṃgha. We now grant them to So-and-so.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let it be so announced. The formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is completed according to this announcement.
Regarding the differences from the *Ji-lü* (Mahīśāsaka-vinaya): it is not the case that one must perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*) differently [to obtain the cloth].

As for the *Wufen-lü* (Mahīśāsaka-vinaya) stating "covering it with a robe," this refers to the twenty-one articles of clothing. Now, examining this in detail, it is determined that one should use the deceased person’s own robe to cover it.
One must not use the *kāṣāya* (monastic robe). [This means one need not offer it to the Sangha; currently, the Tripitaka Master also permits using the deceased's belongings for funeral rites.
The text says "jieshu" (*jiéshù*; the second character is pronounced *róng* as a variant; it refers to woolen cloth. The correct radical form is [茸*毛]. *Ji* refers to woven woolen fabric).
Regarding the five types of patched robes (*pañca-paṭapilotikā*): they are composed of patches of five colors.
"Obtained by begging from a seller" means obtained by begging from a householder who is not a relative.
In the text, first the forfeiture for an offense (*nissaggiya*) is explained; second, the absence of the *pārivāsika* (probationary) robe is explained; third, the [absence of the]... is explained.

First, regarding giving away a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* robe to others (the commentary states: "one does not commit a minor offense [in this case], as wearing it constitutes a minor offense"). Fourth, clarifying the permission to wear robes that have been confiscated (the sub-commentary states:

Fifth, clarifying buying and exchanging (the commentary states: "as for what was previously prohibited, this refers to the third section above; as for the subsequent permission to wear them, this refers to the fourth section"). Sixth, clarifying pure donation (*śuddhaka-dāna*).
These [points] are not explained within the chapter. At the very end of the chapter, the sequence for the non-appearance of the *pārivāsika* is explained.

This is similar to the doubt regarding the five matters. In the aforementioned section on leather articles (*carma-vastu*), it was permitted to receive a second leather sandal and to bathe repeatedly, as well as to use leather bedding.

A certain bhikṣu heard of this in another region; later, when he obtained a robe at his residence, he refused to accept it, fearing he would commit an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

The Buddha permitted that once robes have been received into one's possession, they may be kept for up to ten days; if this period is exceeded, they must be relinquished and then confessed. (The commentary states:

After one has departed, if someone gives a robe to them, or entrusts it to a disciple, or entrusts it to a fellow resident, then from the day of that entrustment onward, even if many days pass, there is no violation of the rule against keeping an extra robe. Because the original circumstances were not clearly understood, [the monks] questioned the World-Honored One. The Buddha then resolved the matter: once the robes have been received into one's possession, only then does the ten-day count begin.

In the present case, since the doubt was not manifest at the time of receipt, does one incur a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense? The Buddha likewise adjudicated that this is not a violation, as in the preceding passage. The sixth rule: The Method for Protecting Bedding and Requisites.

In the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, it is stated: "When moving bedding, if one fears that the body [of another] will be exposed," this refers to cases where, due to civil unrest, one fears being seen by others;
thus, one covers [the body] with ten layers of cloth or places it beneath a layer of cloth. Other people should not drive such a person away. This may be seen clearly from the text.
This text opens with the permission to receive summer robes (*kathina*), which ought to be explained first. The intention is as follows: the initial provision is a general permission;

it is because of this that there subsequently arises the specific case of robes obtained by the *saṃgha* present before one's eyes. Therefore, the section on the permission should stand at the very beginning. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 27, states:
"After the last month of the summer retreat, Upananda went on an inspection tour of the various monasteries, wishing to know in which places [the robes] were being stored."
While the resident bhikṣus were receiving many offerings of robes and requisites, two elderly bhikṣus saw them coming from afar;

they rose to greet them and, after a brief silence, asked, "Have the monks here received any offerings of robes? They replied, "We have. [The elders asked,] "Has it been divided yet? They replied, "It has not been divided.
The two elderly bhikṣus asked, "Are you able to divide it? They replied, "We are able. [The elders said,] "In this matter, a formal ritual (karmavācanā) must be performed. Thereupon—
He takes the robes and divides them into three portions. He places one portion between those two bhikṣus and stands himself between the other two portions, saying:
"Listen to the *karmavācanā*. You two have one portion; likewise you have [another] three—namely, the two portions together with mine."
"In this way, I have three [shares]. He asked, "Is this *karmavācanā* valid? They replied, "It is excellent.

He said, "Elder, our various robes and belongings have not yet been divided. Vatsa said, "I shall give you my share; one who knows the Dharma should give a fine robe. The other said, "I shall give it.
Then Vatsa took a high-priced robe from the collection, placed it in one spot, and having divided the remainder into two parts, he gave them away.
He himself carried many robes into the Jeta Grove. After the Buddha had even rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, at a bend in a river, there were two otters. They caught a large carp in the river but could not divide it. A jackal came along, saw them, and said:"
"Nephew, what shall we do with this? The otter said, "Uncle, here is a carp.
Can you not divide it? The jackal replied, "I can. At this point, a verse should be spoken. The jackal divided it into three portions and asked, "Who among you likes to enter shallow water?
He answered, "It is I, the otter" (referring to a specific otter). "Who can enter deep water? He answered, "It is I, the otter. The jackal said, "Listen as I recite a verse."
"If they enter shallowly, the tail should be given; if they enter deeply, the head should be given; as for the flesh of the body in between, it should be given to one who understands the Dharma.
The Buddha said, "The two otters were two elder bhikṣus, and the jackal was Bāṣpa. Having rebuked them, he established a precept, saying:
"One must not receive a share of robes from other locations; to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense."
Regarding the phrase "entrusting for the sake of taking [alms]" and so forth, some say there are three reasons: first, the person is not within the boundary (*sīmā*) of the donated object;

second, they do not share the same physical body in receiving the alms; and third, there is the labor of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). If that were the case, then one who has performed labor outside the boundary should also be permitted to entrust [alms] and so forth.
The answer is: because the other two conditions are lacking, one may not entrust for the sake of taking and so forth.

This is consistent with the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. The twenty-eighth fascicle of that [vinaya] states: "Regarding 'impermanence,' it means death. One should not receive a share of the summer retreat robes.
Even if they have already been collected but not yet divided, if at the point when one's life is about to end, one entrusts them to a certain person, they should be given to that person after death.

This is called 'impermanence. (That vinaya has a separate chapter on "Impermanence, Breaking the Retreat," etc., which states: "One should not receive [them]; this is the explanation of the chapter on impermanence. The twentieth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "There is..."
"O Bhikṣus, when the offerings for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) have been received but not yet distributed, if someone passes away, the Buddha said:

'If [the deceased] had already given [his share] to others during his lifetime, it should be granted to them by means of a formal announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). If he had not already given it to others during his lifetime, it should be divided among those present. (The above two passages are from the Vinaya texts).

As for the statement in the *Śāstra* that 'one should take one-fifth,' etc., this is an error. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* agree on this point; that is to say, [the former view] is not established."
"Entrustment. This should also be divided among the monks. If the entrustment is successfully established, it belongs to the person to whom it was entrusted.
Regarding the phrasing "whether accepted or not accepted," etc., this explains the meaning of the formal act (*avijñapti*).
This is truly "cutting it with every stroke. An ancient source says: "The text speaks of mental intention; thus one should know the ritual procedure (*vidhi*).

If this is so, why does the text state that one should not receive a share of robes in a different location? Answer: This is because [the recipient] is present at the time [of the distribution]; therefore, the rule was established to prohibit it. If this is so, why is there mention of "entrusting" [the robes]? Answer:
It is like when distributing the belongings of a deceased person; if one does not coincide with the formal motion (*jñapti*) or if both [parties] are absent...
[The Sangha] is not present. [The property] should not be received. If one seeks medicine for a sick person, or departs for the sake of stūpa affairs, it should be given [to them].

(This text appears in volume thirty-one. Since the property of the deceased is not encountered by the Sangha at that time, yet they are permitted to give it away, what harm is there in the Sangha being absent at that time and being permitted to entrust it?
If this is so, why is there only the method of mental intention (*manasikāra*)? Answer: As stated above, it is because the Sangha does not obtain it at an improper time.
In the midst [of the assembly], three dharmas are possessed. Regarding the property of the deceased, it is based on the existence of *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).

Now, this case involves only the *cittānujñā* (mental authorization) method, as it is a condensed abridgment of the five types of formal acts (*pañca-uddharaṇa*). As for the phrase "knife by knife," it refers solely to those who care for the sick;

although they may leave and receive a reward, others who are not caring for the sick may not leave at all. At present, when the Sangha acquires [property], if individuals depart from among the entire Sangha, their departure is permitted.
"Entrusted for retrieval. How could these be similar? This is also a fragment. The aforementioned "bestowing of the Dharma" refers to a fragment.
Thus concludes the two major sections of the text.
"Essence is exclusively one" means that among the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), it is exclusively non-attachment (*alobha*).

"According to the implements of giving" refers to the various implements of bodily and vocal actions. "Not considering the internal" means this does not refer to giving away one's own body, flesh, and so forth;
rather, it signifies that the category of giving is not exhausted [by these alone]. This is the explanation of the text according to the second method.

The "last two groups of monks who obtain" refers to those who obtain [the gains] at the proper time and those who obtain them at the improper time. The "first two counted individuals" refers to those who appear at the proper time and those who appear at the improper time.
The phrase "in terms of meaning, they include the last three" refers to the three lower assemblies.
The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views), fascicle 17, states: "There are fifteen locations where one may receive offerings. First, regarding the *śīma-āyatana* (boundary site):

as previously explained [in this treatise itself, referring to the section on the *Poṣadha* rules], it is the smallest area sufficient for twenty-one persons and so forth, established by formal ritual. If someone says they are giving a gift to the *śīma-āyatana*, the *poṣadha-sīmā* (confession boundary) cannot be established there.
Second, regarding the *gocara* (domain): it may be in the lecture hall, or in the dining hall, or at the place where robes are distributed. It continues: "In these two cases..."
The stone-throwing boundary: according to the size of the territory, there is always a stone-throwing boundary; both the monks and the area where the stone was thrown share in the distribution.
Third is the *poṣadha* boundary: if one is within the *poṣadha* boundary, all should share in the distribution;
they also share in the same *lābha* (alms) boundary. This is called the *poṣadha* boundary. Fourth is the *acīvarāpavādana* boundary: entering the *acīvarāpavādana* boundary...

Within [the boundary], all should receive their share; they may obtain both the benefits of the *poṣadha* boundary and the *lābha* (material offerings) boundary, except that within the *poṣadha* boundary, there are village boundaries where this is not permitted.
This is called the "boundary for not losing one's robes" (*acīvarāpanāśa-sīmā*). Fifth is the *lava* boundary:
if a king or a high minister intends to provide a dwelling place for a bhikṣu, whether it extends for ten *yojanas*, or if they erect a pillar or establish a landmark.
Marking these boundaries: if there is any act of giving, it all belongs to my monastery; this is called the *rāva* boundary (*rāva-sīma*). Sixth, the village boundary (*grāma-sīma*):
because there is a market, it is called a village boundary. Within a village boundary, there may be a *poṣadha* boundary (*poṣadha-sīma*), whether large or small.
Seventh, the hamlet boundary (*kheṭa-sīma*): that which lacks a market is called a hamlet boundary. Within a hamlet boundary, there may be a *poṣadha* boundary.

Both large and small [measures] are permitted. Eighth, the "territorial boundary" (*janapada-sīma*): there are cities and towns called "territories," and within these territories, all [measures] are permitted.
Ninth, the "Avaṇḍala boundary" (*avaṇḍala-sīma*): this refers to the boundary of an *āraṇya* (wilderness hermitage). It is permitted within the *āraṇya* area, but not in other places.
Tenth, the "water-throwing boundary" (*udaka-kṣepa-sīma*): this is the boundary of a boat; it is permitted once one has entered within the water-throwing boundary.
It is obtained; it is not obtained in other places. Eleventh, regarding the "village boundary" (*grāma-sīman*): following the east and west of a city is called the village boundary;
within the village boundary, a demarcated area (*sīman*) may also be established. Twelfth, regarding the "Nara boundary" (*nara-sīman*): this refers to the boundary of a kingdom;
one may also establish a demarcated area for a single kingdom such as Nara. Thirteenth, regarding the "Araja boundary" (*araja-sīman*): [it refers to] a single king...
That which is administered is obtained by the community of monks of the entire territory; this is called an *ārṣabha* boundary (*ārṣabha* being translated here as "king").
Fourteenth, the island boundary (*dvīpa-sīmā*): a single island within the ocean is called an island boundary.

If it is said that a gift is given to the communities of monks of two islands—Sīhala Island (Lion Island) and Jambudvīpa—the property should be divided equally between them, according to how many monks there are in each. [In the case of] Jambudvīpa...
There are five [groups]. One hundred thousand people from Siṃhala Island also constitute half of that number. Regarding the fifteenth, the boundary of the Cakravāḍa Mountains:

this refers to the boundary of the Cakravāḍa Mountains. (It is further stated: When the gong is struck to assemble the community, if external bhikṣus arrive and enter while holding hands in a continuous line, even if they extend for as far as one hundred yojanas, those at the front who have entered the boundary, the last ones also obtain [the status of being within the assembly]. Why is this? Because they are connected by hand-holding.
Because they have been severed, they are summarized in a verse as follows:
The field, the environment, the clothed one, and Rāva; The village, the town, the country, and Aparānta;
The water-thrown, the rural district, and the realm of the Nārakas; Araṭṭa, the continent, and the Iron Ring Mountains.
Regarding "attaining [the boundary] by one section or attaining it by two sections": if both orders of the Saṃgha are present on the fifteenth day, they must both divide into two parts.

If only the monks or only the nuns enter the island boundary (*dvīpa-sīmā*), they should likewise divide into two parts, as clearly stated in the treatise (*śāstra*). This is because the boundary is defined in relation to the island;
for all other cases, the principle is to calculate the division based on the number of people. Those who perform the same ritual action (*karmavācanā*) are one hundred.

First, it refers to obtaining property by participating in the administration of the Dharma together with others. Second, regarding "two groups," this is like the two groups of nuns receiving ordination;
because of that, they receive offerings. According to the underlying principle, this is also a matter of dividing the property among several people.

Regarding the fifth major section on the Dharma of Pure Giving (*śuddha-dāna*): the preceding textual analysis states that from the fifth [section], "Winter Month," onwards, it concerns the practice of receiving and utilizing pure gifts according to the Dharma.

Xiūbù and others; these are all translations of names found in the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), volume seventeen. Regarding *màntù*, the *Jian* says: *nàtù* is a foreign medicine; there is no [Chinese] equivalent.

Regarding "the first must be both": the meaning of the commentary (*shu*) is that whether it is "all-encompassing" (*zhou*) or "one's own" (*zi*), if either one is lacking, it necessarily is not included herein;

The entire monastery is designated as a "pure kitchen" (*śuddha-karmānta*). Within every room, both raw and cooked food may be stored; since the monks do not guard the food overnight, there is no fault of hoarding.
This tradition has been handed down in the Western Regions (India), whereby the entire monastery is collectively established as a pure kitchen.

If one wishes to restrict this to only a single section, it remains within the bounds of what is permitted. Regarding the statement that the north-eastern side is considered "lower," the intention of the ancients was that in the Western Regions, many [monasteries]...

Since these take the lower wind, those opening to the south have the kitchen to the west of the gate, while those opening to the east have the kitchen to the south of the gate.

after the boundary has been established according to the *Caturvarga*, there is the fault of "storing cooked food overnight" (*sāyantanapāka-doṣa*); therefore, it is necessary to establish a "pure area" (*śuddhasthāna*). (As for the permission to establish a pure area:

A brief analysis: In the eighth fascicle of the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, among the six types of places (*sthāna*), there are similarities and differences. First, the impure ground (*aśuci-bhūmi*), which refers to locations such as latrines.
Second, monastic dwellings (*vihāra*), intended solely for staying overnight. Third, the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), intended solely for the performance of formal legal acts (*dharmakarma*).

In this context, with the exception of the *kalpiya-śālā* (the clean kitchen), it is the same location as the other five. Regarding the four *kalpiya-śālās*, they appear to be outside the boundary (*sīmā*).

Fifth is the *poṣadha-sthāna*, which is the hall for reciting the precepts (*pravāraṇā-śālā*). Sixth is the *acchinna-cīvara-sīmā* (the boundary where robes are not lost); this must be established upon a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).
That treatise permits the performance of the formal ritual for establishing the *kalpiya-śālā* within the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*). This is the second passage from that treatise.
One should first set aside a location for the pure kitchen (*kalpi-kuti*); only after that may one designate the locations for the monastic dwellings (*vihāra*) and so forth.

If one has forgotten to do so and there is no other available ground, one must first dissolve the large and small boundaries (*sīmā*), then designate the pure kitchen, and only after the pure kitchen is established may the various other boundaries be designated.
(This must necessarily be done in this manner; it does not mean that the purity [of the site] is thereby excluded.)

Regarding "attaining [the boundary] both before and after": whether at the initial time of constructing the monastery or at a later time, the formal ritual (*vidhi*) for binding [the boundary] is accomplished in all cases.

This differs from other schools (*nikāya*), which require that the night must not have passed. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "If there is doubt, one should release [the boundary] and then bind it again.
Thus, we know that multiple releases and bindings are permitted. (Master Jing [of the Tripitaka] also does not permit the night to pass; this must surely be a difference between the schools.)
Regarding the question, "If one area was previously excluded and now another is also excluded, does this mean that area was already occupied by the Saṃgha?

This refers to a case such as when the pure ground (śuddhasthāna) to the southeast was previously excluded, and now the pure ground to the southwest is also excluded; yet that southwestern ground had already been occupied by the Saṃgha.
The meaning of the answer is that since the southeastern area was already excluded at the former time, the southwestern area was then occupied according to the Dharma; now [it is likewise].
The method of explanation being concluded, one may therefore further establish a pure kitchen (*śuddhāgāra*).
Regarding the procedures for the assignment and the formal ritual of binding (*bandhana*), as stated in the text, these reveal the specific rules of one's own school (*sva-nikāya-dharma*).

If it is a single monastery (*ekavihāra*) where there is only a third [person], this should be analyzed according to four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): there may be a monastery that is not the third [person].

"Blue" (*nīla*) refers to this. There is a third case which is not "blue," namely where the text says there are no fences or enclosures. There are cases where both [conditions] are met, which are easy to understand;

and there are cases where neither is met, such as when pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) is demarcated within a remote boundary (*viviktasīmā*). Now, this commentary adopts the third case to explain the preceding question.
The intention here is to distinguish that although it functions by the power of being "blue," it is said to exist; therefore, it says: "If it is a single *nīla*... only.
There is a third [position]: that which does not exclude what is produced by the power of non-blue [factors] exists upon the blue.
Just as when one designates something as pure, it is not produced by the power of the blue; how could this exclude its existence upon the blue?
If the single realm were merely the agent, it would exist upon the blue; as in the fourth [case], there would be no force to constitute the third.
The remainder may be understood through reflection.
If one explains this comprehensively, it is stated generally based on both those with power and those without power.

Regarding the first two pure stages (śuddhāvāsa) being common to both locations, one should likewise state that the third is restricted to spontaneous [arising], while the fourth is restricted to formal ritual action (karmavācanā).
Regarding the second [case] in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: it refers merely to the location. "Li-chang" (利昌) is the same as "Licchavi.

"Clouds arising at the wrong time" means that it has already passed the hour of noon. King Bimbisāra served as the monastery administrator (*vihārasvāmin*); after his death, King Ajātaśatru took his place.
[The Vinaya in Five Sections, Chapter Twenty-two. Various bhikṣus fell ill during the autumn season.

To prepare medicinal decoctions and food appropriate for their ailments, they entered villages both at the proper time and at improper times, whereupon they encountered difficulties. There was a weaver who had built a hut along the road and was weaving within it.

[The Buddha] permitted it. This Buddha allowed the construction of a *śuddhasthāna* (pure house) in the residences of laypeople. Consequently, it disturbed the two [neighbors] and interfered with the master’s weaving.
The weaver thought to himself: "I originally worked for the sake of weaving; now that I can no longer weave, I shall instead offer this to the Saṃgha to serve as a *śuddhasthāna*."
He immediately gave it to the Saṃgha. The Buddha said: "It is permitted to prepare food within a pure building (śuddha-veśman) donated to the Saṃgha;
