however, those who hope for [the merit of] the Saṃgha must exclusively prepare it upon pure ground (śuddha-bhūmi). This refers to 'purity. Taking the food there renders it pure; staying overnight there constitutes an offense.

It is not the case that if one is on pure ground, the gathering of the Saṃgha to perform formal acts (dharmakarma) is permissible; if the Saṃgha arrives there, it constitutes an offense. This is the meaning.

It is said: "Because it is considered to be included within the act of eating, it therefore further constitutes an obstruction (*āvaraṇa*). Since there is no sense of being 'included' with respect to the Saṃgha, the sense of obstruction naturally ceases to exist.
Most people of this time understand this incorrectly and waste their efforts; one should simply say, "The twenty [rules] are finished.

Regarding the phrase "purification through assignment" (*uddhāra-viśuddhi*) in the commentary, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Jianlun), fascicle 17, states: "If, at the time of first erecting a sturdy pillar, a bhikṣu holds the pillar and speaks..."
The Saṃgha establishes a *kappiya-kuṭi* (a house for pure goods) in this manner. Even if only a single pillar is mentioned, it becomes a *kappiya-kuṭi*.

If the house is already built, one should summon the householder and say to him: "This house is not yet purified; you must establish it as a *kappiya-kuṭi* for the Saṃgha. The donor then speaks these words:
This purified house is offered to the Saṃgha; it may be used at their discretion, and thus it becomes a purified house.

If a house has already been built but lacks an owner, an elder from the village should be summoned and requested to serve as the master of purification for this house, which has not yet been purified.
If the donor does not understand, one should instruct them to perform this purification: "This is a purified dwelling; it is offered to the Sangha for their use as they please.
By doing so, one incurs no offense regarding storing food overnight within or cooking within.

Regarding those who have not yet reached the required age and thus cannot undergo the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of boundary-establishment: examine the twenty-second chapter of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* in detail.
If one has not yet reached the [required] age, one may not undergo the formal act of boundary-establishment either; it would be too cumbersome to explain this in full.

Regarding the detailed explanation of exchanging unequal items as is customary: for example, at a certain residence that was previously not designated as pure, a Vinaya master arrives and, in order to establish it as a pure area (*śuddhasthāna*), instructs them to perform an exchange for purity (*parivartana-śuddhi*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), chapter sixty, states:

"Various bhikṣus were passing through a great marsh when they begged for food from some merchants. The merchants said, 'Do you not know that food is difficult to obtain here? Why do you not [exchange it]...'"

[The monks] carried [the food] themselves. They informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I allow you to carry your own provisions. You may exchange them for pure food from others; only then is it permitted to eat it. If not exchanged, it is not permitted to eat it.
When the bhikṣus wished to exchange [their food] but the other party would not give it, saying, "What is wrong with the food you have that you must exchange it?", they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, give it because it is pure. After giving it, they did not return it. They informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "One should beg for it. The *Samayabhedoparacanacakra-śāstra* (Jian lun), fascicle 16, states:

"If many bhikṣus are traveling together and there is only one junior śrāmaṇera, the bhikṣus may carry their own provisions. When it is time to eat, they may divide the food among themselves, setting aside a portion for the śrāmaṇera.
Having set aside his portion, they say to the bhikṣus: 'I have now taken this portion for the śrāmaṇera; I shall now take it and give it to the second elder. As it says.
These successive exchanges of food are all without offense. If a śrāmaṇera does not understand the rules, a bhikṣu may personally take food and exchange it with the śrāmaṇera;
in this manner, they may successively exchange items with one another. This does not constitute the offenses of "staying overnight" or "impurity through contact.
If a bhikṣu is carrying rice while traveling and a śrāmaṇera is too young to prepare the meal, the bhikṣu may prepare it himself, provided he does not light a fire.
Fire: [The Buddha] instructed a śrāmaṇera to kindle it. When the food was cooked, he exchanged portions as before; thus, there was no offense for making the food oneself.

If the Buddha emerged [from the earth], a bhikṣu must not blow upon it with his breath nor use an object to fan it; in all such cases, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense (the above is from the *Śāstra*; since blowing with breath and so forth constitute "defiled contact," if the food is exchanged for pure food, one should likewise be permitted).

Only this Vinaya and Śāstra permit exchange for purity (*parivartana-śuddhi*). Since it is stated that when a bhikṣuṇī gives [food] to a bhikṣu, it is not "defiled contact" (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*), [the same applies here].
If there are remnants of food such as rice, flour, or sauce remaining, they may be rendered pure by exchanging them for an equivalent measure of grain or other goods through successive trade.
Earthenware vessels should be rinsed with water to remove their greasy residue; bronze and stone vessels should be polished further; wooden vessels should be scrubbed with soap-nuts (*gaurasarṣapa*).
Storage pits are purified by being re-plastered with mud; iron implements are purified by heating them. In these cases, they both attain the status of being "pure.

Regarding the phrase "the names of the offenses and their ranks are equal," this means that those who commit the offense are equally guilty of a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). This is the intended meaning of this single *khandhaka*.

The Great Commentary clearly explains four points. In the preceding passage, Ānanda cooked for himself; here, among these six sections, the middle section clarifies contact (*sparśa*), and the fourth clarifies the two internal factors.
The remaining sections are cited because they are mutually dependent.

The substance of bodily action refers to manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*). As for the substance of nutriment, among the four great elements and the four derivative elements, what constitutes its substance?

Therefore, we shall now directly examine this by way of analogy with human beings—whether they possess the requisite capacity or not—and their locations—whether pure or impure ground—just as in the case of touch.
In the following passage, because the bhikṣus moved the vegetables so that they might grow anew, the Buddha permitted them to eat them.

Thus we know that while growth is not yet complete, they continue to regenerate from moment to moment and thus do not constitute an unwholesome contact (*duḥsparśa*). Once growth is complete and there is no further generation, this constitutes contact. This should also apply to [the case of] overnight [vegetables].
One must know that regarding the binding [of food]: if it is bound before it has reached the point of being "cooked" (i.e., prepared for consumption), it becomes pure through the binding.

However, if it has already been fully cooked, the binding does not constitute purity, because it has already become "overnight" (sustha) [and thus defiled]. (The method of binding is inherently established; yet the substance itself has already become overnight.)

Regarding the statement that among the four cases, those that are both impure and not yet cooked may not be eaten: it should be said that they must become pure before they may be eaten as something desirable.
Now, upon closer examination, it is simply by transforming the raw into the cooked that something is termed "self-cooked," not because of the presence of the nature of being raw.
For instance, although rice and flour lack the nature of being raw, cooking them is nonetheless not permitted; this is because such preparation invites censure.
Therefore, it is said that "touching" refers to impurity. In the subsequent text, there is the case of a bhikṣu who, having previously harbored mutual resentment,
touched another’s food with the intention of causing him to become impure, and so forth.

Regarding items such as those suspended [from a cord]: the following text states that if there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle pure items), one is permitted to suspend the vessel containing clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
As for the two types of "contact" mentioned above: first, grasping an item without having formally received it; second, losing the formal reception (*parāmarśa*) of the item.

Regarding "it can be known from the detailed exposition": since it is stated that one must distinguish [the objects] according to the specific case, and as there are immeasurable cases among the utensils used for food, the details should be understood by analogy with the extensive explanation.
Regarding "the door-bolt and so forth," the *Kuti-dharmas* (Rules on Lodgings) below states: "That bhikṣu was doubtful; he did not take hold of or grasp the door of the Saṃgha..."
Regarding hooks, flutes, rings, ladles, antlers, bronze hooks, or bathing benches: when the Buddha said they may be held, this was based on the condition that they were free from oily food residues.
If they were stained with oily food, they would constitute a case of defilement.
Regarding the four faults that apply both at the beginning and the end: if there were no medicinal dharma-food, the principle would be the same as [ordinary] food;

in that case, the four faults could arise at all times, whether it be the proper time or not. However, since we now distinguish the medicinal dharma-food from ordinary food, the two cases are not the same.

Regarding "that which produces what is produced": this refers to fruits, vegetables, and the like. Regarding "that which produces what is ripened": this refers to rice, flour, and the like (fruits must be purified by fire;

otherwise, one commits the offense of destroying what is living. Rice and flour must be purified by fire; otherwise, one commits the offense of destroying what is living. Therefore, they are discussed separately).
Regarding the phrase "should be the same as cooking for oneself": if judged by the act of preparation, it should indeed be the same as cooking for oneself; this applies exclusively to raw food.
However, since the holy teachings universally prohibit touching [food] with one's own hands, this rule applies to both raw and cooked food alike; thus, they are not the same.

"Regarding 'the specific [case] of the arising and exhaustion of arising': this refers to the arising of the characteristic of arising within the process of arising, which exhausts the total maturation and restraint.
'If [it occurs] through spontaneous hand or mouth' speaks in terms of the forfeiture of the undertaking through spontaneous action. 'The prior self-restriction of the equipment'..."
"Self-cooked" means cooking for oneself.
Regarding the contrast between the pure and the impure, this refers to pure ground and impure ground.
Regarding the two methods of making pure, these are the formal act of assignment (*āveṇika-karman*) and the formal act of ritual procedure (*jñapti-karman*).
Regarding "not being included within the purified ground (*pariśuddha-bhūmi*)," this means that not being included constitutes a separate location.

However, if it is uncertain whether [the food] was left overnight, even if the person providing the food and the food itself are both situated within two purified grounds, the fault of leaving [food] overnight still occurs.

If the food is prepared in two separate locations and the person is outside the area of purity, then there is no fault of "overnight storage" (naihastika). If both the food and the person are naturally pure and remain together, there is still no fault of overnight storage.
If the food is outside the area of purity while the person is inside, there is logically no doubt that it is permissible.

Regarding these three points: first, the distinct offenses and their definitions; second, the discernment of their essential nature and characteristics; and third, the clarification of what is permeable and what is obstructed.
Next, as for the explanation of the text, it shall be interpreted by drawing upon the six preceding sections.
The meaning is the same as "newly acquired from another": this refers to falling [into impurity] without being aware of it, yet suddenly finding oneself on pure ground.
If one reverses the previous statement, both become impure; that is to say, reversing the preceding clause means intentionally wishing to cause the fall.

Therefore, it is impure. If one reverses the second case, that is, when the root of the tree is in impure ground while the fruit falls onto pure ground, yet there is the further condition of having been stored overnight together with [impure things], then even though the fruit has fallen onto pure ground, it is nonetheless impure.
If one explains according to the literal text, two propositions are established; however, if one explains contrarily, it is because the meaning of the phrases is similar.
Regarding the first proposition, as for that which is "impure" due to being unripe: if something is entirely in the stage of impurity while still unripe, it is nevertheless pure;
how much more so when discussing their mutual interpenetration?
Regarding the second phrase, "ripening" (*pakva*): once ripened, it becomes pure or impure according to the boundaries of the pure or impure ground.

This text first clarifies that "pure by way of being injured" refers to the five parts being damaged; "pure by way of not being fit for planting" refers to the five parts not yet having become seeds—that is, they have not yet ripened and are not yet capable of serving as seeds.
Regarding the phrase "if one is purified, that is sufficient": this means that if they are gathered in one place, joined together without interruption, then purifying one is sufficient.
If they are severed, each must be purified individually.
As for the expression "food, unbroken fruits, etc.," it refers to food that has first been purified by fire and then grows again; although it has grown again, [it remains pure].
This does not violate the rule regarding the arising of the formal act (*dharmotpāda*). This [section] is introduced to resolve a doubt.

"Encountering conditions" means non-contact. The intended meaning is as follows: although one has previously received [the formal act], because one has not yet performed the purification (*pariśuddhi*) to make it pure, this constitutes losing the reception due to encountering conditions;
one may then receive it again without it constituting an improper contact (*duṣṭa-sparśa*), for the text permits eating. Washing root vegetables with water [is likewise permitted].

To explain the meaning of this chapter: Previously, it was purified by fire; now it is further treated with water. One might fear that the water will extinguish the fire, leading monks to harbor doubts and so forth.

Now, it is said that this is not the case. "Purifying with water" refers specifically to the fivefold water-purification (*pañcaka-vāri-pariśodhana*), which means rubbing [the garment] within the water.
Thus, purity is attained.

Although the text states that the bowl must be slightly separated from the food vessel and the *śocana-kuśa* grass, this means one should momentarily withdraw the bowl to separate it from the pure grass used for receiving food.
Even if one places many items upon it, as long as they are received in this manner, it does not constitute a violation through contact.

Regarding the fact that there are several interpretations: according to one ancient master’s explanation, "storing overnight" refers to what is common (meaning that people eat together in the same place, though only one person may have formally accepted the food).

When a boundary (*sīmā*) exists, it destroys the purity of the ground; when no boundary exists, the food is encompassed [by the rules]. Therefore, the characteristic of "cooking" constitutes an offense [only when cooking for oneself within such a context]. If one says, "I am merely looking after this," then because the cooking is distinct [from one's own], one does not commit the offense of cooking.

If the food is encompassed by a boundary, there is no "internal cooking," and thus one does not commit the offense. Furthermore, another interpretation states: "Storing overnight" refers to the person.

Eating in the same place incurs heavy censure; therefore, it constitutes an offense of eating stored food (*śayyāsana*). Supervising the cooking process does not involve a prolonged duration, and the locus of the fault is minor;
thus, there is no offense. There are two further interpretations as set forth in the chapter.
This refers to an impure location where there is no bhikṣu present and no prior transgression. It is distinguished from "cooking in the presence [of a bhikṣu].

Regarding "a bhikṣu being difficult to trust," it is because one fears the violation of eating at an improper time. Regarding "fearing censure or suspicion," it is because one fears external slander regarding eating at an improper time.
The phrase "not cooking in the presence [of a bhikṣu]" and so forth distinguishes this from "cooking in the presence. However, as for the statement that there is no scriptural evidence:
Regarding the certainty within the context of cooking: if there is a distinct *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible) present, there is evidence that the food has been cooked by fire.

However, within what has been stored overnight, one cannot be certain that a *kappiya-kāraka* is present; therefore, it is said there is no evidence. Nevertheless, even if such evidence were present, how could one thereby escape transgression?
For now, based on this uncertainty, it is stated that there is no evidence. Both the act of cooking and the supervision of the cooking do not constitute the conditions for internal cooking.

These two phrases are intended to re-examine the case of "touching. The three phrases concerning "erroneously receiving oil" and so forth are combined into one, while the phrase for "not forming a valid statement" and the phrase for "forgetting the act of receiving" constitute the second.
Regarding the eight types of matters, there are five because the four types of *vighasa-kalpa* (rules for leftover food) are combined into one, thus making five.
As for the inclusion of "unwholesome contact" (*duṣṭa-sparśa*), it is not counted within that enumeration.
Regarding "the remnants of what was previously impure": this means that what has already been permitted is not to be permitted again.

Regarding "external loss of food" as opposed to "internal [loss]": from "storing overnight" (antarāvasita) as opposed to "not stored overnight," up to "not performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* rite" as opposed to "performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* rite"—in all these cases, it is permissible for others to damage or consume the food.

Regarding the fear of causing harm through external application: it is feared that one might not eat [the food] but instead apply it externally, thereby committing the offense of destroying living beings.
According to the principle, if one wishes to eat raw vegetables, one should purify them with fire oneself; only then will one avoid the destruction of life.
Regarding the "interval between the pure and the impure": when one is pressed between the two realms, it may also be termed an "interval.
Why labor over a separate explanation? In the fourth section of the text: first, a visiting bhikṣu arrives from outside; second, he sets out to leave the boundary.

Regarding the anus, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states that one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. One must always be cautious regarding the principle of such intervals. This also applies to cases such as being inside a boat.
This constitutes an offense. However, if other medicines do not cure it, then [the use of] this is permitted.
● Regarding the *Kathina* section:
according to the commentary on the *Vyākhyāyukti*, *kathina* is translated as "solid" or "firm. When this robe is made, there are many [benefits].
It is established; therefore, it is called "solid and firm. All solid things are termed *kaṭhina*.
For example, if a person’s afflictions (*kleśa*) are powerful and intense, such a person is called a "person with a *kaṭhina* mind. Regarding the term "difficult to sustain":

it is like a poor person who lacks the means of livelihood and finds it extremely difficult to survive. If a poor person is able to give material goods and they enter into this *kaṭhina* robe, [they gain] merit.
As for the karmic fruit: it is superior to making other kinds of offerings with a heap of robes as large as Mount Sumeru.
Because the Buddha specifically distinguished the poor and commanded them to practice this giving, he singled out the poor; they are called "those who live in difficulty."

The chapter says, "Rewarding the virtuous," etc. It is traditionally said that this meaning is not a direct translation. As for "punishment" (*fà*), it refers to those who establish [the *kaṭhina*] later;

because the text states there is a five-month period for the *kaṭhina* for those who establish it earlier, whereas there is no five-month period for those who establish it later, one knows they do not obtain the benefit.

Nanshan says: those who establish it earlier receive it on the sixteenth day of the seventh month; therefore, the text says it is relinquished in the fourth month of winter. As for those who establish it later...
From the seventeenth day of the seventh month until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, one may receive [the robes] every day;
therefore, the text says, "received on that very day, not having passed a night. If this is so, why does the text say, "there are *kāṭhina* [robes] for five months"?

An ancient commentator explained: "Although the month is not full, what prevents one from receiving them? (This refers to those who settle later, who would otherwise receive only four months of benefit). Now, examining the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, fascicle ten...

8. One may not perform the *pravāraṇā* later. According to the seventh fascicle of the *Vinaya-śīla-vibhāṣā*, there is no *pravāraṇā* for one who has broken [the precepts]. If the *pravāraṇā* is performed later or in another location, it does not count as having received [the invitation] for one who is under suspension (*nigarhaṇīya-karman*).
For now, following the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*, this view is preferable.
Regarding the five matters, "not losing the robe" means that while it is permitted to be separated from the *saṃghāṭī*, it is not permitted to be separated from the other two.

As for the *Kāśyapīya* and *Dharmaguptaka* Vinayas, there are commentaries which state: "According to the *Kāśyapīya* and *Dharmaguptaka* Vinayas, [the rule] is similar and both are permissible. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 39, also says:
"If one is observing the *parivāsa* (probation) in another location, one may not receive the *kaṭhina* robe in this location. Furthermore, regarding one who is practicing *mānāpya* (penance)...
One must not accept [the invitation]. Other *karmas* (formal acts) are absolutely not permitted.
However, as for the requirement of five persons: one who has been appointed is excluded from the count of the *saṃgha* (monastic community), and thus does not enter into that number.
Regarding "among the four types of Saṃghas," this is as explained in the section on the four meanings of the Saṃgha in the *Campa* [Vinaya].

Since the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* does not prescribe appointing a separate person to guard the robes, a single individual may alone receive them (those who seek to distinguish [the meaning] according to the text refer to those of wrong livelihood, etc.).

The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 18, states: "To whom should the Saṃgha grant the *kaṭhina* robe? It should be granted to one whose robes are worn out. Those whose robes are worn out are many. (It continues further...)

One must not give [the robe] to one who is stingy or greedy (this applies by analogy; this refers to the person who holds the robes, not the person who distributes them, as with those whose robes are ruined, etc.).

This Vinaya merely mentions appointing a person through *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), as stated in the passage below: "If one obtains an unfinished robe, one should, within the assembly of monks, perform a *karmavācanā* to appoint a *bhikṣu* to make it.
The *Jianlun* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 18, states: "In the past, the Tathāgata Padma was surrounded by sixteen thousand *bhikṣus*..."
Regarding the joint making of the *kaṭhina* robe (which is done out of respect for this robe): the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten-Recitation Vinaya), fascicle six, states in the twenty-ninth [section]:
"One should give it to four monks who are capable and proficient, and have them wash it (2), cut it (1), dye it (3), pin and stitch it (4), lay it out securely (5), and measure it (6).
One should bring mindfulness to each of these steps, thinking: 'I shall receive this robe as the *kaṭhina* robe,' and one must not fail to generate these six [thoughts]."
Regarding the mind, it is not termed "properly received" (*samyak-parigṛhīta*). In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter fifty-four, within the section on the "Difficult Questions of Upāli," it says:

"At the time of washing; at the time of dyeing and cutting; at the time of pinning and joining; at the time of sewing together; and at the time of measuring—among these six [stages of] mental states, 'sewing together' is precisely 'peaceful and secure' (*kṣema*).

Master Jue remarked: "That Vinaya lacks the term 'peaceful and secure'; this refers to the text of chapter fifty-four. However, it does appear in the text of chapter twenty-nine; therefore, one should have verified this."
Regarding "the substance must be as it is": this does not refer to the six processes such as rough examination, spreading out, stretching, rolling, cutting into ten sections, and sewing.
The text states that one should first say: (1) wash, (2) dye, (3) stretch, (4) roll and treat, (5) cut into ten sections, and (6) sew and treat.
Regarding the method for inserting the inner lining: observe the text; since these are robes offered by a donor (*dānapati*), they must be lined and then purified (*pariśuddha*).
If they are refuse-rags (*pāṃsukūla*), they are purified after being washed.
Regarding "because it maintains the opening": this is the most important among the openings; hence it is called "maintaining the opening.

As for the five types of wrong livelihood, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dazhidu lun), fascicle 22, states: first, in order to seek gain and offerings, one constantly assumes a dignified demeanor and falsely manifests extraordinary signs;
second, in order to seek gain, one speaks of one's own virtues; third, in order to seek gain and offerings, one forcibly encroaches upon others... [and so forth].

1. To predict good or bad fortune; 2. To seek gain and offerings by speaking loudly and manifesting an air of authority to inspire awe in others; 3. To seek gain by claiming to have attained supernatural powers in the past to move people's hearts and incite them to give; 4. To seek gain and offerings by raising one’s voice and displaying an imposing demeanor to cause others to revere them;
5. For the sake of seeking gain, to recount past acquisitions to stir the human heart and rouse it to practice giving.
The remainder can be understood as follows: the previous analysis consisted of seven items and five items, both of which have already been explained; these may be found by consulting them.
Thus, the sixth and seventh [items] are what are referred to here as "the remainder."
Regarding the phrase "the other two may be known": prior to the aforementioned categories of meaning, there are likewise three types of robe substance (*cīvara-dravya*).

First, the robe substance is appropriate; second, the robe substance is inappropriate; third, taking up the previously mentioned appropriate substance, it accords with the Dharma and is fit for acceptance.
Since the first has already been explained, the latter two are indicated briefly; hence it says, "the other two. (The remaining explanations may all be found by consulting the preceding sections.)
Regarding the phrase "dwelling outside the boundary and receiving one's own robe": this refers to personally receiving robes offered by donors and the like.

As for the fourfold text on the formal reception of a robe: if one intends to perform the ritual, and if one obtains a robe that has not yet been finished, some say that according to the *Jian lun* (Visuddhimagga), it should be made collectively by the entire Saṃgha.
This is not so; according to this Vinaya, one must appoint a person through *karmavācanā*. How could this be?
This constitutes a formal *karmavācanā* assembly; therefore, it is unnecessary to follow the *Jian lun*.

One should appoint a person from within the *saṃgha* via *karmavācanā* to perform the task (the text for the *karmavācanā* shall be explained later). Once appointed, they must complete the work on that very day.

If a finished product is obtained, it should be taken and crosswise extended to a length of two chi, with one seam; likewise, five such pieces with four seams are placed inside a fine chest and presented to the *sthavira*.

[The document] is placed before [the assembly], or before the person authorized to perform the *karmavācanā*. The *Ji* (祇) states: "It should be placed within a casket; various flowers should be scattered upon it. Next, the formal motion (*jñapti*) for the harmony of the Saṃgha is performed.
First, the bell should be struck to assemble the community and have them sit in one place (those subject to the disciplinary act of *karmavācanā* should properly sit separately;

those such as the *pārivāsika* and others who have been separated from the group may sit together again, provided they do not speak; this constitutes non-acceptance [of the motion]. There is no need for them to sit separately. Even if they are separated, it still constitutes non-acceptance; thus, everyone must be fully assembled, or else provide their consent (*chanda*). Otherwise, the procedure will not be valid). Request.

If one wishes to ask about the harmony [of the assembly], the response should be: "The *kaṭhina*-robe acceptance *karmavācanā* has been performed. The one performing the *karma* should then perform a single motion (*jñapti*), as in the initial text.

(Having performed the motion, one should ask the Saṃgha: "Who is able to hold the *guṇavat-cīvara* for the Saṃgha? The capable person should respond: "I, so-and-so, am able to hold it. Next, one performs a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to appoint the holder.
If there is a separate question and answer, one should respond by saying: "The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for appointing the person to hold the *guṇavat-cīvara*."

Regarding the Dharma, it is as stated in the second passage. The chapter says: "The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* distinguishes virtuous qualities. In the twenty-ninth [section] of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the five virtues are first established:

being free from attachment and so forth, and knowing how to receive [the robe]. This is for the sake of the Saṃgha receiving the *kāṭhina* robe. (Having finished reciting these two sections, the chapter immediately poses a question and answer, saying: Question: Why are those who have previously been appointed [to oversee] the *pravāraṇā* [sent]? Etc.)

Having completed his appointment, he rises from his seat and goes before the Saṃgha. Having paid homage to them, he kneels with his palms joined before the *karmācārya* (the officiant of the ritual) and listens to the *karman*.
The Saṃgha then performs the *karman* and entrusts the robe to him. If there is a separate question-and-answer session, the answer is:
"The *karman* for the entrustment of the *kaṭhina* robe. The text of this *karman* is that which constitutes the third [section]. However, in the text, who...

The passage beginning with "May the elders consent" consists of a few missing phrases; that is, it is slightly deficient in this dwelling place. These are present in the ancient *karmavācanā* manuscripts.
Although they are missing from the formal ritual (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), the meaning can still be understood. It would also be well to complete them so that the text is sufficient.
The fourth section of the text is divided into three parts. Regarding the first of these three:

once this person has been formally entrusted with the robe by the Saṃgha, they should immediately take up the robe-casket with both hands, proceed before the Elder (sthavira), kneel with palms joined at the crown of the head, and present it to the Elder.
The Elder likewise receives it, places it upon his head, and returns it to the person. This is repeated three times. Finally, the casket is placed before the Elder.
He brushes aside the flowers with his hand so they open, and with his right hand he grasps the robe. He takes up four folds at once and places them in his left hand.
Approaching the senior monk (*upādhyāya*), as soon as the senior monk sees him coming, he must kneel on his right knee; the other monks do likewise.

The senior monk extends his hand, and the person immediately takes one fold of the robe and presents it to the senior monk. He then steps back one fold and hands it to the second senior monk, proceeding in the same manner.
In this manner, they proceed by turns until reaching the fourth seat, then return again to the second seat and the third seat.
During this interval, holding the robe in their hands, they say: "This robe is accepted by the community of monks for the purpose of making a *kaṭhina* robe," and so forth, as written.
Thus concludes the first section. Next is the second section. Once that person has finished making this statement, these four elders should immediately speak in unison, saying:
"The recipient has properly received [the robe]," and so forth. Thus concludes the second section. Next is the third section.
That person holding the robe shall answer, "So be it. Then, the person holding the robe shall rise and proceed to the fourth seat.

Take one robe and fold it into four layers. Next, proceed before the fifth-ranking elder and pass it on in succession, following the same procedure as before, until the monks from the highest to the lowest seats have all received the robe.
Then, the person holding the robe comes before the presiding elder, holds the robe while kneeling with knees apart, and addresses the Sangha, saying:
"The Sangha has now reached a state of harmony and completed the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe. This is the explanation.

The third section concludes. Regarding "each of the three times has three": in the preceding analysis of the chapter, these were determined to be future; the text contains three instances of this. Now, as for the present, there are again three instances of the present.
As for the past, there are again three instances of the past. By means of these three instances of the present, one fulfills the requirements for receiving a virtuous robe. However...
It is for the sake of fulfillment that nine phrases are spoken.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-two, states briefly that there is no formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for appointing a distributor. It says: "Once the robe-custodian has received [the robes], he should wash, dye, beat, and sew them on that very day.
If he cannot accomplish this alone, the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) to appoint one or two [assistants]."
Third, even if many bhikṣus assist him, they shall proclaim: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! We now appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so and so-and-so to make robes.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). The formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is accomplished according to this motion.
If one follows this Vinaya, it should be stated only when the time has arrived: "I appoint such-and-such bhikṣus to assist such-and-such bhikṣu in making robes;
the motion is as follows. This is because in the *Pañcavargika*, once the time for all formal acts (*karmas*) has arrived, there are no further words, and one simply says, "The motion is as follows.
Thus, one knows that this is not the same as the formal procedures (*karmas*) of this Vinaya. People [should] understand this by way of its meaning.

The same applies. If the entire community is dispatched, regardless of whether there are assistants, one should say: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let it be announced thus regarding the robe.
The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is accomplished according to the announcement (*jñapti*). (This [method] is preferable for those who perform the subsequent dissolution.)

To explain the ritual procedures for the assembly of the Saṃgha, one should first understand that within this Vinaya, the texts concerning Campā and other locations explain the meaning of "harmony" (saṃghasāmagrī) through three aspects:
namely, those who ought to come must come; those who ought to give their consent (*chanda*) must give their consent;
and those present who ought to be censured must not be censured. Furthermore, the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states: "There are five matters by which the Saṃgha should be harmonious. What are these five?"

If it is in accordance with the Dharma, there should be concordance through five things: remaining silent, giving one's consent (*chanda*), hearing from a trustworthy person, or having previously sat silently within the assembly; by these five matters, there should be concordance.

Regarding the phrase "it is not that those who have gathered for the prior *saṃgha* assembly do not include those who have conveyed their consent (*chanda*)," this means that within the gathering for harmony—where the threefold gathering and fivefold concordance are already fully established—it was previously shown to manifest the "consent" that maintains the transmission of consent. Now, however, it speaks of the "consent" for the formal debate (*pravāraṇā*).

Therefore, beyond the two meanings of "gathering for the *saṃgha*" and "harmony," it is explained once more. The commentary states: "Alternatively, 'gathering for the *saṃgha'* refers to the initial [assembly]."

Third: "Now, this granting of consent (*chandadāna*) is gathered solely by the mind" (there is also a commentary manuscript that omits this latter explanation). This intention is meant to clarify what was previously stated regarding the gathering of the Saṃgha.
However, within the three types of assemblies and five kinds of harmonies, this refers specifically to the inclusion of the three assemblies and the four harmonies;
thus, "giving consent" (yuyu) here refers to giving consent within these three and five.
Regarding the statement that "the latter two [cases] are but one": at the end of this *khandhaka*, there are two kinds of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*):

first, when the robe-holder goes abroad overnight; second, when the Saṃgha as a whole departs together. Since the text mentions their departing together, and because this is essentially no different from the "departing together" mentioned among the eight cases above, it is said that they are "but one.
To explain this himself, he says: "As for 'departing together,' it is identical to the meaning previously stated. Furthermore...
There is a commentary manuscript which states: "In these two passages, there are four types of relinquishment (*prahāṇa*). The first eight are divided into two:

the first six involve relinquishing through the mind, while the latter two involve relinquishing through ritual action (*karmavācanā*). The final two are themselves two [distinct types]; therefore, they are collectively treated as four relinquishments.

Now, upon careful examination, although these four relinquishments follow the original commentary manuscript, their meaning is superior. This is because, among the eight, those described as "commonly emerging" refer to the intermediate cases.
"Abandoning. [The phrase] "at the end, they exit together" refers to the completion of the fourth month;

therefore, it is not the same [as other cases]. "Speaking of them separately as ten" means that the latter two and these eight combine to make ten. "According to the specific matters, they are many" means...
Because the arising of the intentional resolve (*saṃkalpa-citta*) is indefinite as to its degree, there are thus discrepancies that result in many formulations.

Regarding the first six among the eight cases where the treatise states that the intentional resolve is lost: one searches throughout the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (14), the third chapter of the *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra*, and the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*, yet none of these contain a textual judgment that the first six involve the loss of the intentional resolve. Nevertheless, upon examining their meaning, it is evident that this is indeed the case.

This is essential. As for those who argue that the term used here is "lun" (論), meaning it refers to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), and that it is an error to treat it as "lun" (論) [in the sense of a formal treatise]:

if we now examine the twenty-ninth chapter of the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, it lists eight grounds for relinquishment (*aṣṭau tyāgāḥ*): first, the completion of the robe; second, the completion of the requirement; third, the announcement; fourth, hearing; fifth, the loss of the vow through the arising of the thought [of returning];

sixth, the passing of the time limit; seventh, the transgression of the boundary; and eighth, the time of relinquishment. Although it enumerates these eight, there is likewise [no mention of the term "lun"].
The scriptural text states that there are six essential points of mind (*cittotpāda*). However, this is a mistaken citation by the commentators (*śāstrakāra*).

Nevertheless, in wishing to explain the text, one must first understand that all these essential points of mind arise from the initial resolve (*cittotpāda*), thinking: "If I remain as I am or have not yet completed [the practice], I shall require the five benefits."

If I have resolved with determination to go forth permanently from the boundary, or if I have finished making robes and no longer require the requisites, yet at a later time I actually do go forth permanently, or if I have finished making robes and my essential resolve has been fulfilled, at that moment [the robe] is lost; this applies to cases where the work is not yet finished, and so forth.
Based on this, one should understand that (if the essential items are absent, the vow is lost only when the time limit is reached).

That is to say, regarding "one who lacks the two lower robes," the meaning of the commentary is: if one lacks the *saṃghāṭī*, the reception [of the precepts] is not valid from the outset; it is clearly understood that "having completed the making" refers to having made the two lower robes.
Now, upon careful examination, this also applies generally to other surplus robes (*atireka-cīvara*); there can be "completion and relinquishment" without being restricted solely to the lower robes.
Regarding the two robes, there is none [to be forfeited]. The following cases are all analogous.
As for the phrase "hearing of the relinquishment," the commentary (*shū*) explains it in a way that is easy to understand; I shall now provide another interpretation. This is explained as follows:

one might suspect that because he went out with the community of monks within the boundary (*sīmā*), his robe could be said to have been lost. However, since he was outside the boundary and did not go out together with the community of monks, he should be entitled to the full limit [of the period]. Therefore...
The commentary explains: "Upon hearing it, it is immediately lost.

Regarding the second passage, concerning the "first two, the six, etc.": there exists an ancient version of the Vinaya that contains only eight rules of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), omitting this section beginning with "the first two, the six," and so forth.
Consequently, tradition has passed down that the virtuous masters of former generations took the six phrases from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitation Vinaya).
The following [passages] have been omitted and set aside. Now, upon examining the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the text from the sixth section onward differs from this;
it should not be considered a mistaken transmission. However, regarding the four Vinayas, the first was translated by Buddhayaśas during the fifth year of the Hongshi era of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Later, in the eleventh year of the Hongshi era, Zhi Falin returned from the West and re-collated them once more. This [text] appeared within that later collated version.

The following is the text. Within the text there are two sets of six. In the first set of six, everything is presented in detail; that is, the essential points are set forth, while the remainder is omitted with a reference back to what precedes.
In the second set of six, the essential points are presented in full, while the remainder is omitted with a reference back to what precedes. This can be seen by examining the text.

Regarding the statement that "raising the pair of 'sage' and 'abandonment' may consist of five or six [categories]": previously, one had not yet attained [the goal] and sought it, yet there was still hope for abandonment because the result had not been achieved;
now, having already attained it and sought it, the purpose has been fulfilled and no further hope is entertained. From what, then, could one speak of "abandonment"?
Therefore, it cannot constitute "hopeful abandonment. Since it cannot be so constituted, one must invariably eliminate hopeful abandonment. Thus it is said.
Regarding the further removal of the five essentials such as "expectation" (*āśā*) and so forth, there may be five or six [stages].

In this case, since "expectation" cannot be maintained from the outset, if one removes it as the first of two pairs, one must likewise remove that "expectation. This constitutes the three-fold threefold removal.

However, when the first removal is completed (as expectation is logically impossible), the second removal is not yet completed (as expectation is logically impossible), and by the third removal, [the sequence] is lost.

(To expect this is to sever the connection; logically it is impossible). Fourth, "departing from hearing" (to expect this is to sever the connection; logically it is impossible). Therefore, the Commentary states:
"If one takes 'departure' as the primary term, it can only result in four, five, and so forth. This refers precisely to this principle.

Regarding the phrase "because it is encompassed within the meaning": [The opponent] asks, "If 'attainment' and 'non-attainment' are combined, there ought to be the severance of expectation (*āśā-prahāṇa*) based on the aspect of non-attainment.

Although the intent of the Commentary (*ṭīkā*) is currently stated in this way, in the fifteen phrases of the following section, it fully distinguishes the meanings by means of the three gates, such as attainment and so forth.

Within those three gates, the Commentary itself admits that the severance of expectation is maintained. (If one wishes to defend the Commentary, for now, it is based on what has already been attained...)

Having obtained the edge of the robe, there is necessarily no further expectation. The subsequent text concerns the time of receiving the robe, based on what has already been obtained and what has not yet been obtained, such that at a later time, a separate expectation arises of its own accord. Question:

Among these three sets of six, why does the text suddenly exclude "disappointment" (*viṣāda*) and "interruption" (*cheda*), etc., without following a sequential order? Answer: This merely indicates the general direction; it is not necessary to provide a comprehensive explanation.

Regarding the statement in the commentary on the fifteen phrases, "Because there is only one [case] outside the boundary, there are only fifteen," this refers to the fact that there is but a single instance beyond the *sīmā*.

The same applies to the veneration of Śākyamuni. Now, to examine this in detail: the objection states that among those who go out together, if one was originally not within the boundary (*sīmā*) and only temporarily went out before returning, this constitutes being outside the boundary.
Within such cases of being outside the boundary, one must likewise admit that the person originally resided outside the boundary.
This is a phrase concerning being outside the boundary. To enter briefly and then exit is a phrase concerning being inside the boundary.

If one says that being inside contradicts the name "outside," then being outside should likewise contradict the name "inside. Why then is it permitted that being inside and exiting together constitute two distinct phrases?
Furthermore, should the phrases outside the [eight] realms not be treated as equivalent to a single phrase? Moreover, the text explicitly states that there are eight "interchanges" (*vyatyaya*).

For what reason, then, are the eight above now divided and combined to become fifteen? Since the locations of the combinations and interchanges have entirely different characteristics, this is not logical.

Now, examining the above text in detail: within the two sets of six, three essential elements are excluded in each. That is to say, from the first set of six, the "abandonment of despair" is excluded;

from the second set of six, the "abandonment of hope" is excluded; and from the current [third] set of six, the "abandonment of loss and despair" is excluded. These constitute the eight abandonments (*aṣṭau upekṣāḥ*).
Excluding three and five from the remainder, one multiplies this number five by three to form fifteen; that is, it becomes fifteen.

This means that, according to the twelve phrases below, where three times four equals twelve, one should likewise apply this analogy here, allowing the multiplication of three and five to constitute fifteen.
Furthermore, regarding the first five [cases], one obtains the robes as expected; the next five do not obtain the robes as expected; and the final five obtain what is expected in combination.
These are distinguished according to the three categories beginning with "not yet obtained," which together constitute the full fifteen cases. Question:

Among the three sets of five, since "obtaining what is expected" and so forth all refer to what has already been obtained, how can you allow for the category of "robes not yet obtained"? Answer: The three categories beginning with "not yet obtained" [are as follows]:...
Based on the initial reception, there is a subsequent arising of a distinct seeking for fulfillment, such as obtaining what was desired and so forth.
If one explains it in this way, it clarifies that within the two sets of six mentioned above, two from each are excluded; next, among the fifteen, three from each are excluded;
next, among the twelve, four from each are excluded; and next, among the nine phrases, five from each are excluded. This is the meaning.

This is necessarily so; it can be seen by examining the text. What has preceded consists entirely of the removal [of defilements] based on the essential mind. In the subsequent two sets of five, one method of operation is excluded.
Since its meaning differs from what precedes it, it does not follow the previous pattern, but rather constitutes a "six-fold six-fold" removal.

Regarding the statement that there are four [categories] because one excludes three and attains cloth, and because hope is severed upon attainment, and because attainment and non-attainment are combined:

this means that within each of the twelve [cases], one must individually and fully analyze them according to the three gates of "attained," "not yet attained," and so forth, in order to fully establish the two sets of four.
That is to say, the three categories of "completed," "incomplete," "not yet completed," and "lost" are analyzed according to the gate of attaining cloth.
And yet it exists. Therefore, the Commentary states: "The other three exist because they obtain the robe.
Regarding the phrase "in terms of severance, based on not obtaining [the robe]," the single phrase "in terms of severance" applies to both the gate of non-obtainment and the gate of obtainment.

If that is so, since the first four sections of the text state that one "obtains" in relation to the robe, how can it be said that this refers specifically to the gate of non-obtainment? Only then... [text ends].

"Regarding 'the severance of expectation' (*āśāccheda*): the answer is that it refers to the time when one first receives [the robe]. Because one has not yet obtained the robe from the Zhang family, one hopes that one will certainly obtain it;

later, when it is not obtained, this is called the 'gate of non-obtainment' (*alābha-mukha*), whereby the expectation is severed. However, the expectation for the receipt [of the robe] originates from the place of the Wang family."

Furthermore, one may initiate separate requests and indeed succeed in obtaining them; thus, there is the attainment of what was hoped for. These twelve phrases are formulated with reference to many people.
If they were applied to only one person, there would be an increase or decrease in the requirements. What logic is there in applying them to many? They simply clarify the case of twelve individuals.
Therefore, regarding one person’s request for three types of robes, it refers, for example, to requesting cotton cloth, requesting silk, and requesting [wool].
*Zhou*. Alternatively, one may expect that four essentials arise for each of the three types of robes within a single family, thus resulting in twelve.
(This explanation regarding the three families is also logically sound; it is fully set forth in the *Shu* [Commentary] according to a single family.)
Regarding the phrase "the other two categories are likewise": this refers to the two sections concerning robes and so forth that have already been discussed.
Within the two sets of five statements, the expression "it is also thus outside the boundary" refers specifically to the statement concerning going beyond the boundary.
That [passage] specifically concerns the seeking of robes; this is the analysis of the boundary (*sīmā*).

That is to say, the textual structure of the preceding twelve phrases is also a requirement arising from other regions, and according to principle, there should likewise be the fault of being outside the boundary (*sīma-bahis*). However, that [text] explains it for the time being by way of the seeking of robes.

Regarding the *Kauśāmbī-vastu* (The Section on Kauśāmbī) within the *Vibhaṅga* (Explanatory Treatise) concerning the Vinaya masters, the eighteenth [chapter] states: In the monastic residence of Kauśāmbī, there were two bhikṣus;
one was a Vinaya master and the other was a Sūtra master. The Sūtra master entered the latrine and, having finished using the washing basin, did not...
The Vinaya Master entered the latrine and saw that the water had not been drained; he asked, "Who entered the latrine and failed to drain the water? The Sūtra Master replied, "It was I.
The Vinaya Master said, "Do you recognize your offense? He replied, "Truly, I did not know. The Vinaya Master said, "You have committed a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
The Sūtra Master said, "If I have committed an offense, I should confess it. The Vinaya Master asked, "Was this done intentionally?"

The Sūtra Master said, "It was not intentional. The Vinaya Master said, "If it was not intentional, there is no offense. The Vinaya Master returned to his room and said to his disciple, "The Sūtra Master does not know whether an offense has been committed or not.
Upon hearing this, the disciple told the Sūtra Master's disciple, "Your teacher does not know whether an offense has been committed or not.
Having heard this, [the Sūtra Master's disciple] reported it to his own teacher. The Sūtra Master then said to his disciple: "This..."
The legal expert previously stated there was no offense, yet now he states there is an offense; the legal expert has spoken falsely.
When the legal expert’s disciples heard this, they reported it to their teacher, and as it spread from one to another in this manner, a great dispute arose.

Regarding the inclusion of "not shaving the hair" and so forth, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*), fascicle three, states: "As for what constitutes an offense and what does not:

the shaving of hair and clipping of nails was not originally proscribed. Although the Buddha stated that one commits an offense against the precepts [if one neglects them], he also said that 'hair and nails possess life'; therefore, not shaving or clipping them does not constitute an offense. (The above is the text of the treatise.)
Regarding "the same matter being seen differently": this refers to cases such as the act of not shaving, where one person sees it as an offense while another sees it as non-offensive.

"Action-arising from dispute" (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha-vastu*) means that action (*vastu-kriyā*) is itself a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). Dispute regarding a ritual (*karmādhikaraṇa*) is precisely a dispute regarding a matter (*vastv-adhikaraṇa*);

a dispute regarding a matter has no separate essence other than being subsumed within a dispute regarding speech (*vādādhikaraṇa*). That is to say, disputing over other principles is termed a dispute regarding speech. Dispute...

*Karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical action) is termed a "dispute over matters" (*vastu-vivāda*). This refers to cases such as when, regarding a single formal act (*karmavācanā*) based on the teachings, one person says it is valid while another says it is invalid;
this is also a case where the matter is one and the views differ. This is explained in detail below according to the method of reduction.
Therefore, when the Buddha exhorted them, saying, "If you two are as I have described," the phrase "you two" refers to both the agent and the object.
Within the text, the single expression "for what reason" (kiṃ kāraṇam) contains a dual meaning; thus, in this narrative, it is divided into two parts for the sake of explanation.
This is because it penetrates and connects both the passages concerning those who do not dwell together and those who dwell together.
As for "each having three [parts] which can be known," this refers to the three sections consisting of the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Regarding the phrase "because it explains the subsequent meanings of the agent and the object of accomplishment," "subsequent" refers to the section on exhortation (*codanā*).

As for the concern that this might not be analogous to the present text: if that were so, how would the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* respond to this objection? Could one possibly be permitted to subvert the Vinaya texts?
Nevertheless, observing the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-three, it states: "One who commits [this offense] with a loud voice incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), etc."
Although the bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s words, they did not cease their dispute and proceeded to perform separate monastic acts (saṃghakarma) within the same boundary.

The Buddha spoke again, saying: "If the Saṃgha has already been split, and they perform separate formal procedures (karmavācanā) within the boundary in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, this is also called a successful procedure (siddha-karman).
Why is this so? There are two kinds of dualities regarding different views and non-concordant residence; there is that which is inherent..."
They form a separate residence (*nānāvāsa*). There is a formal monastic procedure (*saṃgha-karman*) by which they are made to live separately.

Although the bhikṣus hear the Buddha’s words, their quarreling does not cease (as stated in the Vinaya text). Since they continue to quarrel despite having heard [the teaching], it is clear that those who previously acted according to the Dharma and achieved [their goal] belong to the faction that acts according to the Dharma (*yathādharma-pakṣa*).
This immediately reveals that the Buddha rebuked the faction that acts contrary to the Dharma (*ayathādharma-pakṣa*); that is to say, between these two factions, one must certainly exist.

No; it is not because these are words of simultaneous praise. If one were to provide such an interpretation, it would also accord with this [current] interpretation, yet it would still be inconsistent.

Regarding the two passages concerning the third and fourth [items], they can be understood as follows: the third is the repeated petition to the Buddha, while the fourth is the instruction on the location for installation.
The five points that may be understood are as follows: first, [the rule] regarding non-Buddhists, which exhorts one not to expose the faults of others;

second, the exhortation to reflect that those who have committed offenses may possess great power and influence, and one should fear that they must be exposed and disciplined; third, the three passages beginning with "If we ourselves...
and so forth, which are treated identically to the preceding section.
Regarding the statement that the written words are the companions of King Changsheng (Long-life), the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that he was formerly a minister of King Changsheng.
As for the "wash-water of the sword," this refers to the child’s desire to arouse desire in his mother; it is moved by a fierce and violent nature.

Regarding the phrase "the subtle eye seeks out the parents": according to the *Zilin* (Lexicon Forest), "subtle" (*wei*) means hidden conduct; according to the *Erya*, "hidden" (*wei*) means to conceal or lurk.
The subsequent verse states, "knowing thus, not seeing. This refers to knowing through correct principle (*yukti*), hence it says "knowing as such. It may also be understood as "thus."

Regarding "like one who knows": ancient scribes used the character *ér* (而) in place of the character *rú* (如). It should be stated as "thus knowing" (*rúshì ér zhī*); "like" (*rú*) is not "seeing" (*jiàn*).
Furthermore, there is a commentary manuscript that says: "Thus, like knowing, it is not seeing" (*rúshì rúzhī fēijiàn*); this [version] omits one instance of the character *rú*.
Those who harbor the three poisons within their breasts—according to treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the three poisons are also called the "three arrows.
That which can destroy the three virtues refers to greed and the other [poisons].
"Releasing [the restraint of] body and speech" refers to the arising of bodily and vocal karma from the three poisons.
"Defilements arise from the mind" means that harm is one of the six defilements. As the twenty-first verse of the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

The afflictions (*kleśa*) are six: *styāna* (sloth), *pradāsa* (malice), *upanāha* (enmity), *śāṭhya* (deceit), *māyā* (guile), and *mada* (arrogance). The commentary states: when one intends to harm another, this constitutes being associated with the affliction of *styāna*;
thus, it results in self-injury. Alternatively, one may rely on the seventh fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, which states that there are three types of *styāna*:
namely, greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*). This is because they manifest the impure characteristics of transgressing the precepts.
Regarding "shàn zì liáng hé shàng jiàn zhí jí zhě" (善自良合上箭執急者): it should be stated in full as "hé shàng shàn zhí jiàn zhí jí" (合上善執箭執急), consisting of five characters.
As for the character "zhào" (兆), the *Guoyu* commentary states: "Zhào means 'to see'."
Regarding the statement that "the opposite of the previously mentioned conditions can be understood": (1) the previous case of violating the precepts is now defined by the Buddha;

(2) the previous case of the three acting together to raise a formal accusation is now taught as the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense involving contact; (3) the previous case of being unwilling to submit to one's guilt is now addressed by the procedure of *pratyosāraṇīya-karman*.

Regarding the question of what precedes and follows: if the preparation has not yet been completed, may one subsequently perform the formal reconciliation? The Buddha replied that this is not permitted.
If the preparation has already been completed, it should be understood that the opposite is the case.

Regarding the single matter of the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*): after performing the *jñapti* (the formal motion) for an untimely assembly as described in the preceding text, one immediately recites the *Prātimokṣa*.

For the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, one may either use the standard *jñapti* without deviation from the usual form, or one may use the *jñapti* for the untimely recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* found in the subsequent text.
Since this performs the act of the *Poṣadha*, it is said that "one may perform the *Poṣadha*."

The "announcement" (*jñapti*) refers not to the announcement for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha-vācanā-jñapti*), but may instead refer to using the standard announcement to perform the *poṣadha*.
These two methods constitute a single ritual procedure.
Regarding *anupada*: tradition says it refers to questioning a Brahmin; it is a precept of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*). Now, examining this in detail:

*anu* is translated as "following" (*sui*), and *pada* is translated as "phrase" (*ju*). This means that one must not follow behind a virtuous bhikṣu while engaging in speech, conversation, or question-and-answer exchanges.
Regarding the "wicked horse" who does not distinguish between the matter and the offense once the business is concluded: I have now examined this in detail.

If, after the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (monastic offense) has been transformed [into a lesser offense], the matter and the offense are not distinguished—as in the case of Chanda—one applies only the *brahmadanda* (the highest penance). It is only when one commits a *pārājika* (offense involving expulsion) such that the matter and the offense are not distinguished that one treats them with harsh abuse, as shall be explained in the eighth supplement below.
This is the method of management for those who can bring forth what has been taught.
"Standing alone and transcendent beyond that" means that "that" refers to the worldly conventions of that world.
Regarding the two types of transgressions, these are the transgressions of both abstention and performance.

Regarding the restatement of the previous clauses on non-transgression, the intent is to state that transgression is the first and non-transgression is the second; this refers to the three preceding persons. The aforementioned text lists five types.
Regarding the offender, their release can be understood accordingly.

As for the statement that "one who possesses faith is able to receive," it means that because the leader of the assembly possesses virtue, those with faith are enabled to receive his verbal instructions.

For the sake of the Saṃgha, one who is capable of speaking is dispatched. This person is a virtuous member within the Saṃgha; with the intention of serving the Saṃgha, they are exhorted to dispatch the leader of the assembly.
Having accepted the dispatch, this leader is capable of conveying the words of the Saṃgha.

● Regarding the *Campa-khandhaka*, the "Request for Clarification on the Three Superior Matters": these are the three matters concerning the clarification of doubts regarding the superior [matters]. First, the request to know whether an offense has been committed or not;

second, the request to know whether an action constitutes a formal censure (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) or not; third, the request to know whether a formal ritual act (*kamma*) has been validly accomplished or not.
Since ancient times, the text has been divided into two parts. Master Yuàn (願) of the Vinaya school stated: "The first part briefly clarifies the right and wrong of persons and dharmas;

this constitutes the establishment of the thesis (*siddhānta*) in response to specific conditions. This master’s intention was that within this *Khandaka*, the thesis clarifies the seven types of wrong.

When it comes to the section on the seven wrongs below, he says, "This modifies the original thesis. His meaning was that the seven are subsumed into four; therefore, he speaks of "responding" [to the conditions].
This is based on the establishment of the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Regarding the "seven non-[valid] cases," this refers to the passage concerning the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) acting contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya.
As for the eighth, ninth, and even the cases of being expelled whether one understands or not: the eighth is difficult to accomplish when the matter arises; the ninth...
"The multitude together disputes what is wrong," and so forth, up to "whether [the offense] is resolved or not resolved," refers to the tenth and twelfth textual passages.

The meaning herein is to clarify that the eighth point, which is difficult to establish, is definitively situated within the two faults of person and dharma; the ninth point concerns the certainty of the dispute among the multitude.

Regarding the legal procedures for settling disputes, if they are performed incorrectly, they constitute a "human error" (*puggalāparādha*). If ten or ten monks do not perform the procedure as required, it is likewise a human error.
Alternatively, if one treats others with disciplinary measures when such action is improper, this too is a human error. It is clear that in all these cases, there is a human error.

Alternatively, it may be that within each respective category there are both concise and extensive versions. The three, four, and eight sections that single out and explain only their names are the concise versions of their respective categories.

The remaining eight sections of text, which explain both [the name and its characteristics], are the extensive versions of their respective categories. Furthermore, among the four "non-[realities]," the first non-reality can subsume the two types of "semblances";

since it does not stop at merely listing their names, it is concise. Among the seven [categories], the first non-reality is not included; because the following three are set apart from it, it is extensive.
Furthermore, it contains many other "non-[proper]" cases. The ancient masters held that there were only seven types of "encounters" (yù), namely those between persons and dharmas.

Now that there are fifteen, among them there are instances of mutual application, repeated application, indirect non-exclusion, and matters concerning the establishment of boundaries for persons. Thus it is.
Although the text does not explicitly distinguish between the realms and the non-realms, they are nonetheless included by virtue of their implicit extension through the underlying meaning.
Therefore, this *Khandhaka* contains a great deal of material concerning the "non-" (i.e., the non-realms), rather than being restricted solely to persons and phenomena.

Regarding the two pairs of dharmas: as stated in the text, there is the *adharma-karman* (illegal formal act) and the *bhinnasaṃgha-karman* (formal act performed by a divided assembly)—this constitutes one pair.
There is the *dharma-karman* (legal formal act) and the *saṃghasāmagrī-karman* (formal act performed by a harmonious assembly)—this constitutes the second pair.

Furthermore, regarding those who uphold the Dharma before the assembly and find it difficult to accomplish their tasks when faced with actual matters—this refers to "grinding words" (which, if carried to its extreme, leads to harm).
Apart from these, the six types of phrasing that manifest non-characteristics are the phrases consisting of five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, and eleven syllables.
Regarding the seven differences in views: in the following section, there is a case where a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed by a separate assembly that is not in accordance with the Dharma;

all of them dispute it together, some saying it is "unlawful and separate," some saying it is "unlawful and harmonious," some saying it is "resembling the Dharma and separate," and others saying it is "resembling the Dharma and harmonious."
Some say it is established; others say it is not established. Of the first seven [cases], two are statements of the Dharma (*dharmavāda*).

If one examines the upper and lower [texts] and finds fourteen kinds of what is not [the Dharma], I shall now examine this in detail. For the time being, based on the extant text itself, fourteen are mentioned.

However, if one further infers through reasoning, regarding the tenth and eleventh, since the two methods of "expelling" (*udrāha*) and "driving away" (*nirghāta*) are explained as opening up two types of "what is not," they should likewise [be included].

In the *Bhikṣu-vinaya-vaibhāṣika*, there are one hundred and one *karmavācanās* (formal procedures). Each has its proper application; to fail to perform what should be done and instead do what is improper results in immeasurable faults, as can be understood by reflection.

Question: Among the seven types of improper actions (*saptavidha-adharma*), it is already stated that "reproving without ceasing" refers to the sixth section below, which is designated as the seventh.
This is not so. Regarding the "six virtuous bhikṣus" and so forth, who are the twenty-eight persons mentioned above, this refers to the second section of the text below.

In that Vinaya passage, it is explained that one neither attains the full number [of the quorum] nor may one censure [the assembly]; yet, twenty-eight persons are enumerated. Furthermore, it is explained that one does attain the full number.

They are also included among those who may be rebuked. The six persons, beginning with the "virtuous bhikṣu," are listed as follows. Twenty-eight persons are grouped together in a verse: "Remaining, accusing, extinguishing, and difficult;
Spiritual power, concealment, separation, and the field. (From here, the text proceeds to the second section; consult the Vinaya itself.
Regarding the six persons beginning with the "virtuous bhikṣu": first, the virtuous bhikṣu; second, one dwelling within the same boundary; third, one who does not [use] spiritual power...
1. The feet are off the ground. 2. The four [factors] are not concealed. 3. It is not apart from seeing and hearing. 4.
Even when speaking to bystanders (this also appears in the second section below; one will find it by consulting the Vinaya itself).
Answer: Regarding the "four groups of monks" mentioned below, the primary focus is on the "fewer than twenty-three" who are insufficient to constitute a formal assembly;
these are included within this context. Now, in this section concerning the full *ākrośana* (reproval), the twenty-eight individuals are specifically enumerated.

As for why they are insufficient, it is because this text does not mention that one person is missing, and thus they are deemed insufficient. This refers to the fifth section below, which clarifies the assembly of monks. In terms of...
Regarding that which is "fulfilled": it refers to the state of the fourfold Saṃgha; specifically taking a small degree of cessation, it is termed "insufficient.
As for the statement that twenty-three [assemblies] are "incalculable," because they are no different from the "small" [degree], they are likewise included within this "small" category.

It is called "insufficient" because, with respect to the fourfold Saṃgha that fulfills it, one speaks of only twenty-one persons. Question: Regarding the two preceding passages, what is the intention for requiring the reference to "that which can fulfill"?

The objects to be fulfilled (*pūraṇīya*) and the meanings [of the terms] are distinct. Answer: Since the subsequent passage is intended to clarify that the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of the four types of *saṃgha* differ, it explains their meaning by way of the objects to be fulfilled.
If one were instead to explain the meaning by way of those who fulfill them (*pūraka*), how could one possibly come to understand the complete essential nature of the four *saṃghas*?

Now, in the preceding passage, the intent is to clarify those who fulfill them; among those capable of fulfilling and those capable of reproving, there are individuals who possess the capacity to fulfill and reprove, or there may be...

It does not establish the fulfillment or the censure. If one were to clarify the meaning by way of that which is fulfilled, how could one possibly understand the meaning of whether the fulfillment and the censure are established or not?
Therefore, the commentary subsequently states: "By means of fulfillment and non-fulfillment, one contrasts them with censure and its inappropriateness;
the meanings explained are also different. Regarding what is appropriate, it refers to the sense of "attainment" or "fulfillment," etc., which differs from what follows below.
Regarding the seven types of illegal [procedures] listed in the preceding six sections:

these refer to the seven types of illegality—excluding the fifth, the "illegality of the *vinaya*," and so forth—among the fourteen types of illegality distinguished in the preceding commentary, as well as the other seven types of illegality that were previously enumerated.
This appears in the second, third, fourth, seventh, tenth, eleventh, and sixth sections of the text.
As for "speaking from the point of origination," it means speaking by taking the six deviations as the starting point.
Regarding the phrase "the essence is not different from the seven," this does not mean it is not different from the seven sections of the text. However, the commentary (*shu*) states:
"Because the fifth section directly clarifies the application of the *saṃgha*," intending thereby not to distinguish [the error] within the fifth section. Now, upon examining the text:
Regarding the statement that "one person being missing is contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya," this is none other than the first of the seven [cases] within the sixth section.

However, these fifteen instances of what is contrary [to the Dharma] should be explained such that all are subsumed under the single category of "contrary"; that is to say, they are to be subsumed according to their respective applications.
First, it is not so. "Not so" means that not everyone possesses all fifteen [dharmas]. For instance, regarding those who do not fulfill [the requirements], such as those who rebuke what is improper:
