To explain the three turnings and three subsequent turnings by way of these latter six, this interpretation follows the *Vibhāṣā* (46), the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (21), and the seventh chapter of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.
As for "turning" (*vartana*), it is like a hand turning a wheel; thus it is called the "agent of turning. As for "subsequent turning" (*anuvartana*), it is like the wheel [following the hand].

It is that which follows and turns [along with another]. For example, because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises first, one subsequently clings to the self as being either annihilated or eternal;
thus, this view of a self-identity is the "primary mover" (*pravartaka*), while the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is that which "follows and turns.

Furthermore, because the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arises first, one subsequently clings to those very precepts and observances as being superior; thus, this clinging to precepts and observances is the primary mover. Its...

The adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is that which follows along with the primary [view]. Furthermore, just as one first doubts whether the Truths and Jewels exist or not, and from this arises the definitive view that they do not exist, it is for this reason that doubt is said to be the "primary mover" (*pravartaka*) and wrong view is the "follower" (*anuvartaka*).

Since it is known that the follower arises by virtue of the primary mover, when the primary mover is severed, the follower is also severed. Question: Since there is no adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) under the Truths of Origination and Cessation, why is this so?

By whom, then, is that adherence to views abandoned? Answer: It is abandoned simultaneously with the abandonment of the underlying attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) associated with suffering.

Since that attachment to precepts and observances is a pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*), when the cause is abandoned, the effect is also abandoned accordingly. From this, one should understand that "simultaneous abandonment" does not necessarily mean they must be abandoned at the exact same moment;
rather, it means they are abandoned in succession because one contemplates them in sequence at the time of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*). One should reflect upon this.
Explanation: Thus far, we have understood the general characteristics as they are. To distinguish them specifically, this reveals the abandonment of the eighty-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*).

For instance, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the cessation of suffering within the three realms; thus, there are three [instances]. The clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is abandoned through the cessation of suffering and the path within the three realms.

These are the six [factors]. Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is abandoned through the four truths of the three realms; these are twelve [factors] (the preceding total is twenty-one; the five [factors] conducive to the lower realms have already been explained).

Extremist views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are abandoned through the truth of suffering in the three realms; these are three more. The view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are abandoned through the four truths of the three realms;
together they constitute twenty-four. Including the aforementioned extremist views, this makes twenty-seven. Combined with the previous twenty-one, the total is forty.

Eighteen [factors] (the above constitutes the opening of the five views and doubt into forty-eight). Greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance—excluding those abandoned through cultivation and restricting them to those abandoned through vision—further comprise forty.
For instance, greed, pride, and ignorance consist of thirty-six when combined across the four categories of the three realms.
Hatred is abandoned only by the four categories of the desire realm; thus, they total forty. When combined with the previous forty-eight, [they become ninety-six].
This totals eighty-eight. Question: If one calculates based on the three turnings and the three subsequent turnings, there are only forty-eight;
how then can these manifest the forty [afflictions] such as greed? Answer: These are also permitted to be included within the three subsequent turnings.

For example, suppose a person, having already grasped at the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), feels greedy attachment toward this view, and furthermore, gives rise to hatred and resentment toward the views of others, relying upon this very view.

They give rise to pride. Furthermore, since these afflictions are all associated with delusion (*moha*), the four—greed and the others—arise in accordance with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
One should understand, according to the preceding principle, that greed and the others also arise upon the views of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

However, while the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views, and false views are invariably and definitely categorized as "concomitant" (*anuvartin*), it is not so determined for greed and the others.

As for the "affiliations" (*pratisaṃyukta*), let us set them aside for now as they are not being discussed. In reality, these are also included within the category of "concomitant transformation" (*anuvartaka*). Therefore, the *Chapters* (*Zhāng*) state:
"This is precisely eighty-eight.

Regarding the phrase "one kind, etc.," both the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* contain this passage; however, the intent of the citation in the *Chapters* relies upon...

*Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*. Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Moreover, this sutra briefly reveals the gateway and the ladder [to liberation]—that is to say, it speaks of the abandonment of the three fetters.

Among the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), there are those that belong to only one category (*nikāya*), those that pertain to two categories, and those that pertain to four categories."

If one speaks of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it should be understood that this refers collectively to a single category (namely, the inclusion of the two types of extreme views across the three realms, totaling six).
If one speaks of the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it should be understood that this refers collectively to two categories.

Although there are no other afflictions apart from these that pertain to both categories, the clinging to precepts and observances is nonetheless termed "pertaining to both categories" (totaling six across the three realms). Furthermore, "precepts" refers to those [mental factors] associated with and co-arising alongside that clinging to precepts (that is, the complex of mental states associated with the clinging to precepts).

If one speaks of "doubt," it should be understood that this is a general statement encompassing all four categories (which includes false view, adherence to views, as well as greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance;

among these, excluding hatred, the remainder pervade the three realms, totaling seventy-two; adding hatred makes seventy-six; adding the previous two sets of six makes eighty-eight). All of the above are the doctrines of the Sarvāstivāda.
However, according to the *Mahāyogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 29, the Blessed One said: "The permanent abandonment of the three fetters constitutes [the first fruit]."
Regarding the first fruit: there are three types of fetters based on three categories that obstruct the Noble Path, preventing it from arising.
First, within the category [of the view of self], there is the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Because of this view, one fears *nirvāṇa* and does not proceed toward the Noble Path.

Second, based on the category of evil doctrines and discipline (*vinaya*), there is the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Because of this clinging, although one has already set out [on the path], one acts...
1. Deviation: It does not give rise to the noble path. 2. Based on the category of the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, there is the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Because of this clinging, although one has already set out [on the path], one acts with deviation and the noble path does not arise. 3.

Based on the category of the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, there is the affliction of doubt (*vicikitsā*). Because of this, although one has already set out and does not act with deviation, [the noble path does not arise].

Because they have not yet become habituated to the right path, they harbor hesitation and doubt regarding the objects of knowledge—the truths to be seen as they truly are—which obstructs the arising of the Path.

This is explained at length in that [text]. In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, there is an interpretation concerning their identity or difference; its intent is the same as that of the Mahāyāna, though I cannot elaborate on it here.
In the *Wénzhōng míngxué* (The Explanation of Learning in the Text), it says: "If a bhikṣu fully maintains the *prātimokṣa*, etc. Cóngshǒu says:

"This very passage is used to explain the preceding section on 'how one learns the precepts' and 'the training in higher morality,' and so forth; therefore, it is called 'learning. Furthermore, it states:

'The old interpretation [compares this] to an ordinary person (*bāwài fánfū*) who exclusively applies himself to guarding and maintaining [the precepts], and so on at length. This interpretation is incorrect, as it directly contradicts the clear instruction [of the Buddha]. Next, below..."

In the text itself, he offers his own analysis with such wild and reckless abandon that the arguments above and below are inconsistent. For a long time, no one has awakened to this, and thus it has flowed far and wide.
Now, regarding the details of his establishment and refutation, they are like those in the *Pomiji* (Refuting Deluded Records); I shall not discuss them at length here.

Nevertheless, although that master of ours makes these statements, he still does not understand the intent behind establishing the Three Learnings (*tri-śikṣā*). This meaning is fully explained in the sixteenth and seventeenth [chapters] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

The intermediate explanation. Regarding the general meaning: the basis of training is primarily the distinct analysis [of phenomena]. Having relied upon pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), one next cultivates the training in concentration (*samādhi*).
However, since the four dhyānas are the most excellent basis for all meritorious qualities, they are specifically established as the training [in concentration].

Because one relies on this superior concentration to give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) state and eternally exhaust all afflictions, it is established as the training in wisdom (*prajñā*)—and this is exclusively untainted. Although [the three trainings] are thus established...

This is superior because it does not exclude the discipline that arises simultaneously with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) from being subsumed under the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).

Nor does it exclude the untainted (*anāsrava*) concentrations and so forth from being subsumed under the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*). Furthermore, it does not exclude the tainted (*sāsrava*) states and so forth from being subsumed under the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).

Therefore, in the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the three groups of pure precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*) are established as the training in ethical discipline; [this includes] the four types [of samādhis], such as the Mahāyāna-prabhāsa and others.

Taking superior concentration as the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), and taking the three types of wisdom—preparatory, fundamental, and subsequent—as the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*):

how could this be merely a restrictive interpretation of this specific passage? It is truly because one has not understood the distinction between the universal and the restricted, or the superior and the inferior, that one takes [the meaning] arbitrarily. (However, from the perspective of the Śrāvaka, it is appropriate to establish [the trainings] according to what is predominant, as is done in the Vinaya.)
Regarding the cultivation of the two right efforts (*samyak-pradhāna*), they are also termed the four right abandonments (*samyak-prahāṇa*) or the four right strivings (*samyak-saṃkrama*).

For details, see the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* 41, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 29, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* 2, and the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* 10. Here, I shall briefly cite from the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*:
First, for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, one generates desire and exerts effort to rouse oneself.
1. Mindfulness of the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*). 2. For the sake of preventing unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising—the rest is as explained before.
3. For the sake of causing unarisen wholesome states to arise—the rest is as explained before. 4.

For the sake of establishing, not forgetting, and further cultivating and increasing wholesome states that have already arisen—the rest is as explained before. These four are themselves mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).

The essence of diligence within the middle [category] establishes four types based on its differing functions within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), just as a lamp has four distinct functions in one instant:
namely, consuming the wick, exhausting the oil, burning the vessel, and dispelling darkness; this should be understood according to the commentary.

Regarding the six phrases concerning the hindrance of greed (*rāga-nīvaraṇa*) mentioned previously, if one examines the meaning of the text, the pair of "existence" and "non-existence" serves to distinguish the observation of active manifestations (*samudācāra*).

The pair of "not yet arisen" and "subsequently arisen" differs according to whether it refers to permanent abandonment (*prahāṇa*) or suppression (*vibhava*). The next two [factors] are the right abandonments (*samyak-prahāṇa*).

Regarding the omission of the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): some versions of the Vinaya contain it, but upon examining its intent, it is based on the principle that the factor of joy exists in the first and second dhyānas;
if one is in a higher stage, there is no factor of joy, and this is not a case of intentional omission. Furthermore, upon examination...

The meaning of this passage is as follows: Within the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), the initial clarification of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) and the cultivation of the four right efforts (*catvāri samyak-prahāṇāni*) reveals the first fruit [of the path].

Having first entered the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), one subsequently advances in cultivation to sever the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This is precisely what is meant in the sūtras and śāstras by "cultivating calm abiding (*śamatha*) based upon insight (*vipaśyanā*).
The subsequent passage concerning the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*) and the arising of the four right efforts reveals the [attainment of] transcendence.
One who has realized the third fruit has already attained the four dhyāna concentrations; now, severing the remaining fetters, they cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment.
This is precisely what is meant in the sūtras and śāstras by practicing vipaśyanā based upon śamatha.
"Omitting the fifth" means that within this text, there should be six phrases. It is logically appropriate for "having already produced mindfulness and awakening" to be the sixth;
however, the fifth—causing what has not yet arisen to arise—is missing. Thus, it consists of five. There are also versions of the Vinaya text that contain all six phrases.
Now, inferring its meaning: the pair of existence and non-existence is distinguished by whether [the seeds] are currently active or not.

"Unarisen" and "arisen" are distinguished by whether they have not yet been cultivated or have already been cultivated. "The already-arisen being fully cultivated and the unarisen being brought to birth" refers to their extensive manifestation.
...and causes the seeds to sprout. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 76, states: "Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras that there are three kinds of seeds:

first, those that do not lead to birth; second, those that lead to birth; and third, those that lead to superior birth. Worldly people all desire the second and third types of seeds—those that lead to birth and those that lead to superior birth.
Within the Buddha-dharma, however, one desires only one type: that which leads to birth [in the sense of liberation], for [the others] do not exist..."
Because there is a Victorious One (Jina) who is the Buddha, there are five types of "sons of the Buddha": those born from the Buddha’s own mouth, ranging from the *srotāpanna* up to the *arhat*;

and the *dharmatā-bodhisattva* (referring to those from the first stage, the *bhūmi*, onward). A *pratyekabuddha* cannot be born from the Buddha’s mouth, because they attain the Way when no Buddha is present.
Therefore, those whose outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted are "born in accordance" [with the Dharma]. Now, examining the meaning of the text, it cites three categories of worldly beings.

"Son, contemplate within the Buddha-dharma so as to seek one who is equal to the Son. This is because all those who have attained the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are equal to the Buddha in their body of liberation (*vimukti-kāya*).
(According to the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this is how it should be understood.)

if these are not obtained, it cannot be healed. Second, whether they are obtained or not, the illness is in no way curable. Third...
Whether one attains it or not, all can be cured. It is the same for all sentient beings:
if they encounter a virtuous friend, they are able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; if they do not encounter such a friend, they cannot give rise to it.

This refers to those from the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the *arhat* and *pratyekabuddha*; although these two types encounter virtuous friends, they still cannot give rise to it. This refers to the *icchantika*.

"Ti. Third, whether one encounters [the conditions] or not, all are capable of generating [the resolve]. 'Taking' refers to the Bodhisattva. Now, observing this Vinaya, it does not necessarily coincide with the Sūtras;

The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, fascicle five, states directly: "The dharma of a bhikṣu is that he himself must not dance, nor may he teach others to dance;

"No bhikṣu whatsoever shall sing, dance, or perform as an entertainer. There were six groups of bhikṣus who moved about like dogs circling their dens; the Buddha did not permit this.

First, regarding the miscellaneous explanation of various practitioners: therein, at the beginning, there are four sets of four that are not explained in this chapter.

The second five teach others to be endowed with the fivefold Dharma-body. Within the third five...

(3) Teaching the abandonment of evil views (4). In the fifteenth set of five, (1) knowing one has not committed an offense, (2) [knowing] the light [offenses], (3) the heavy [offenses], and (4) extensively reciting the Vinaya.

Twenty-fifth is "Firmly Abiding in the Vinaya" (the first). Within the first five [sections], one fully maintains the two hundred and fifty [rules] (the first), and does not resolve matters of impurity (the second). Altogether, the total number above is fifty-six.
If the nineteenth, "Skillfully Reciting the Vinaya," is excluded, there are fifty-five. As for why this chapter mentions fifty-seven, it is because of the twelfth...

This is understood.

however, according to the intent of the commentary, following the *Upasampadā-kaṇḍa*, the *śikṣamāṇā* and *śrāmaṇerī* are combined into one, thus making eight sets of five. In substance, there are fourteen items: the first five are complete, while the second...

One should completely abandon this [view] (this treatise clarifies the matter of abandoning the precepts). These five dharmas of the Upādhyāya in this Vinaya correspond to those two sets of four lines;

they comprise the entirety of the seven hundred [stanzas] that constitute the fundamental essence of the precepts. According to the above discussion regarding the "Section on the True Doctrine" (*śarīra*), it would be better to exclude the two types of *saṃgīti* (councils) that belong to the subsequent sections.

The five kinds of "thieving mind" (*caura-citta*), when examined according to the text, appear to be distinctions within the "stealing mind" (*steya-citta*) rather than distinctions among the afflictions (*kleśa*).

This is as in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, where an elder (*mahallaka*) acts as a gatekeeper for others, inciting them to steal property while believing himself to be without fault, or using things interchangeably while claiming he is without fault;
the characteristics of these cases are explained in detail in the aforementioned section on the precept against stealing.

Regarding the meeting with the "three preceding" [categories] to give rise to the seven afflictions: first, the five offenses; second, the five regulations; third, the collection of the five offenses.
Thus they are called the "three preceding.

As for those who commit an offense and perform confession through mental recollection (*svacitta-smaraṇa*) and so forth, this is as explained above in the section on the precept concerning extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), within the chapter on the Differences in Interpretation.
The *Wen Zhong Zi* commentary states: "As explained in the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Section on Reprimands), this refers to the thirty-five matters consisting of seven sets of five.
These are collectively termed 'matters contrary to the seven sets of five outside the boundary. If these were not bound together as a collective, it would be like..."
Receiving offerings and support while residing where there are no bhikṣus constitutes three matters; when these are now combined into a single category, it is called one type.
Regarding "when censuring another, one should also examine oneself through five matters," this means one should reflect:

"In censuring another, I am not providing him with the *karmavācanā* or the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*," and so forth, as explained at length. Therefore, one should not hastily censure another without having a virtuous companion.
Now, to examine this in detail: perhaps it is because the passage on the "sevenfold observation" briefly cites the general characteristics.
Just as one fears that evil spirits might find an opportunity at a place where corpses lie, so too does one fear that evil people might find an opportunity when seeing wicked men.
The phrase "allowing evil spirits an opportunity" means fearing that they might find such an opportunity.
"Leaving behind a rain-bath robe" or "giving food to one who is ill" refers to that which cannot be accomplished by one's own power.
Among the six types of diminution (*apacaya*), the text states that joy and anger constitute one [category]. "Not relinquishing" refers to further stubborn adherence as another [category].
As explained above in the Kauśāmbī-khandhaka: 1. A bhikṣu commits an offense. Another bhikṣu says to him, "Do you see your offense?
If he says he does not, [the other] says, "If you see your offense, you should confess it. 2. The full explanation continues until: "If you see your offense, you should confess it before the Saṃgha.
3. And so on until: "You should confess this within the Saṃgha. 4. Punishment by verbal abuse. 5. [And so forth.]
...up to the point that one should perform the disciplinary procedure of "not seeing" (*adarśana*). As explained at length therein, if one does not know the Sūtras, such questions will arise:
"Venerable One, what is this matter? What is its meaning? Thus, one is unable to analyze it. For example, if someone asks:
"In the Sūtras it is well taught that the nature of offenses is entirely empty; yet now you raise my offense—what is the meaning of this? It compels me to confess."

Yes. You should provide a detailed analysis. The sūtras state that the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) refers to the contemplation of principle (*li*). Since you have not yet eliminated delusion, how can you speak of emptiness?

Furthermore, the emptiness of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) serves only to eliminate afflictions; how could it ever discard conventional activities? Only after one has abandoned such activities can one discuss emptiness.

If emptiness were to discard activities, emptiness would obstruct existence, and thus it would fail to be emptiness. Because it would fail to be emptiness, one ought logically to perform repentance. If [one does not...]

If existence were obstructive, it should not obstruct repentance; since it does not obstruct repentance, one must still repent. Whether one advances or retreats, the difficulty remains; there is no escaping the transgression committed.
If you further argue that emptiness does not obstruct existence nor does it obstruct emptiness, and thus neither requires nor precludes repentance—why then do you cling to a self?
Now I insist on repentance. To distinguish this further: if you do not repent of emptiness, you contradict...

I repent my emptiness; therefore, the Saṃgha must certainly discipline you. In the second fascicle of the *Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra*, there are sixteen matters each for preaching the Dharma and listening to the Dharma.

There are twenty different ways of combining and opening [the categories], and there are also slight differences in their sequence (which can be seen below). First, teaching at the proper time (*kāla-vāda*). According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, this means being well-established in dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), which is called "timeliness.

This refers to the rule that if one is seated on high and the listener is on low ground, one should not preach the Dharma to them, as detailed in the *Pratimokṣasūtra*. Why is this so? Because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas revere the Dharma. Second, teaching with a sincere mind (*adhyāśaya-vāda*). In the *Yogācāra*, this is called "revering the Dharma. causing the listener to give rise to a sense of extreme preciousness toward the Dharma. Third, teaching with equality (*samatā-vāda*). According to the *Yogācāra*, this means preaching all dharmas without interruption. Its meaning is...

It is said: The person before had already attained the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) upon hearing the Dharma, yet they wished to advance further to seek the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*). [The teacher] did not allow them to advance, causing an interruption; now, however, it is made continuous. (4) *Andha-saṃnipāta-vyākhyāna* (Explanation by Harmonious Union).

(5) *Arthānugama-vyākhyāna* (Explanation according to the Meaning). In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, this is called "conformity. how could these cited words necessarily all be drawn down [to apply to the subsequent context]? Therefore, it certainly contradicts reason.

Regarding the phrase "totaling fourteen or fifteen": previously it was stated that there are two sets of five, such as the full observance of the two hundred and fifty [rules], together with seven sets of five from among the prohibitions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), and five sets of five such as the unwholesome and wholesome; these total fourteen.

However, since these categories of unwholesome and wholesome do not constitute separate divisions, they naturally form ten sets of five; thus, the expression "five sets of five" is used here merely for the sake of grouping them together.
"However, there are only ten sets of five dharmas. This is the Master of the Commentary’s (Shuzhu) definitive interpretation.

That is to say, among the previous fourteen [sets], the four consisting of the unwholesome, wholesome, and so forth, are excluded; all others state that there are fourteen, which is superior because the preceding text contains no sense of subtraction or addition.
How could the words of the text also speak thus [of ten]? Therefore, it is known that the former explanation is superior. Now, examining the preceding text, it clarifies...

Regarding the statement that "the five types of illegitimate formal accusations (*adharma-udghāta*) are countered by the five types of legitimate formal accusations (*dharma-udghāta*)," for what reason does it say there is no sense of benefit or harm?
Generally speaking, throughout the preceding and following sections, there are eleven sets of five; the Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) correctly explains ten of these sets of five.
In the preceding text, there is one set of five, which states: "The Buddha told Upāli: 'You all must not repeatedly bring formal accusations against others. Why is this...'"
Therefore, regarding the mention of others: if one's own physical deportment is impure, that speech arises: "Venerable sir, first make your own body pure. Second, regarding the purity of speech:
the same applies to the third, the purity of livelihood. Fourth, regarding the proclamation of what has not been studied or recited from the Sūtras, that speech arises;
if one is learned and has recited them, that speech does not arise. Fifth, regarding the proclamation of what has not been studied...

The *Vinaya*: giving rise to that speech and reciting what has been heard without giving rise to that speech (the commentary here states: "The five [factors] of physical purity mentioned above are precisely these").
Together, they constitute eleven.

Regarding "and these first five": this refers to the former set of five among the two sets of five—such as fully maintaining the two hundred and fifty precepts and so forth—which were detailed previously.
As for "wisdom that knows the Abhidharma-piṭaka and the like [of great learning]," it is because within the aforementioned five types of physical purity, [the former] is lacking.
Regarding "knowing the Abhidharma": this refers merely to having extensive learning (*bahuśruta*); thus, it brings wisdom and the like into accord with that extensive learning.
As for the statement that "the four dharmas below are all for the sake of benefiting others," it is as previously stated in the text: "there is the desire to benefit [others]" (this is the first).
Causing growth (the second). Repentance (the third). Purification (the fourth). These four items below are all for the purpose of benefit.
Regarding the two sections on increasing by ten and seventeen, one shall see their characteristics in the text that follows.
Regarding the absence of a third alternative such as "and so forth" to exclude [other possibilities], this refers to cases such as "both real and unreal.
Because these would manifest multiple propositions, the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) is placed [at the end].

Regarding the "sixfold increase" based on the factors of the action (*karmapatha*), the object (*ālambana*), and the conditions (*pratyaya*): the six types of offenses that arise, as well as the act of stealing, are termed the "factors of the action.
A valuable object is the "object. The six roots of contention, such as the intent to steal, are the "conditions. The six factors, such as the age at birth, are the "designations."

Regarding the explanation of the eight conditions of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), this has already been fully explained above in the commentary on the introductory verses and within the analysis of the meaning of the Vinaya.

Specifically, to these six [conditions], two additional phrases are added, as that treatise states: "There are [actions] arising from the mind but not from body or speech, such as the various offenses of the mental ground (*cittabhūmi*).
Furthermore, one phrase states: "There are [actions] not arising from body, speech, or mind, such as when one first speaks to another person."
"Great falsehood. That person did not understand [the meaning]. This person had already countered the three preparatory stages (*prayoga*).
Later, if that person subsequently understood the words, this person would incur a *pārājika* offense (as stated in the treatise). Master Yue-si said:
"If one has already countered the three preparatory stages, one must cease the action. If one does not cease the action, it is not a 'severed continuation,' and thus there is no confession."
The legal procedure is not established. When one later incurs the *pārājika* offense, it arises immediately from the mouth and so forth; how then could it be "neither"?

The Vinaya Master’s intention is that when wishing to confess, one must say to the person before them: "I previously spoke falsely; I now wish to confess. This would constitute the cessation of the act.
Now, upon careful examination, this is not the case. How could it be permitted that at the time of confessing a minor falsehood, one must report [the matter] to every single person who was deceived?

Furthermore, whenever one speaks of "the matter of cessation" (*nirodha-vastu*), it refers to the fact that the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) has already ceased; this is what is termed "the matter of cessation. How could it be necessary to wait for the retribution to be known before it is called "the matter of cessation"?

For example, if one instructs someone to commit murder or theft, but the act is not yet completed, and that person repents immediately after being sent away—this is still merely the preparatory stage and cannot yet be called "cessation";
thus, the matter of cessation must indeed be present. Since the present case is different from this, how can you cite such a fallacious analogy? Moreover, this is a treatise (*śāstra*).

[This is] the text. How could one dare to falsely refute it? Therefore, those who rely on the treatise are correct. The section on purifying the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-pariśuddhi*) and the preceding *Adhikaraṇa-śamatha-vastu* have already been explained.
As for the "eight plus eight," totaling eighteen, this refers to the eight horses, the eight persons, and the eight such as the mass of fire, when separated out.
The metaphorical [classification] of three becomes ten; combined into one, it is eight times eight.

Regarding the formal accusation according to the regulations (*vinaya*), this is not so. This refers to Maudgalyāyana’s initial occasion of accusing someone of an offense. To have used his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) for the accusation would constitute a violation of the regulations.

The aforementioned *Śīlaskandhaka* (Chapter on the Recitation of Precepts) concludes with the regulations concerning self-accusation; immediately following that, the text in question should logically occur here.

Having extensively explained the eight similes below, there subsequently follow eight unique passages that correspond to them. Furthermore, these eight additions should likewise have had those eight unique passages;
it is simply that the compilers arranged them out of order, or perhaps this has been so for a long time.

The *Bānyè* (Brahma-leaf) has been inverted, resulting in such omissions as the upper and lower sections being conflated. When reciting the *Poṣadha*, one must be pure; it is necessary to clarify the administration of discipline.

The omission of the text on "abusive speech" (*durvacana*) is logically improper. Furthermore, regarding the increase in the number [of offenses], the omission of the eight extraordinary texts is likewise improper.

Moreover, in ancient exegeses concerning the matter of offenses, the treatment of "abusive speech" was not cited; this interpretation also leaves room for further refinement. Now, in our current exegesis, we shall not cite it. In response:
When a monk commits an offense, the Sangha is fully aware of it. If he has committed an offense of the first category (pārājika), both the bridle and the tether are cast away;

for such a wicked person is not permitted to uphold the Dharma or perform acts of formal exclusion (nāśanīya). If he has committed an offense of the lower categories, he is to be treated through the "silent exclusion" (tūṣṇīka-pravāsanīya) according to the Brahma-faring rules, as was the case with Channa’s use of evasive speech.
Regarding the bhikṣu who was censured by Maudgalyāyana at that time, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* simply states that he had committed an offense involving theft.
[The Buddha] rose. Since he was one who had committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), how could those of antiquity have erroneously explained this meaning?

Furthermore, one must examine the two passages above and below—concerning the World-Honored One’s dwelling place, the bright and dark fortnights, the timing of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), sitting in the open air, and so forth—as well as the mention of "accusing of an offense" (*āpatti-udbhāvana*).
These are sufficient to clarify that the original intent of the two texts is continuous.
Regarding the four types of those who practice association: there are twenty-eight [verses] on nirvāṇa. The Lion’s Roar addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, as previously stated in the analogy of the mango fruit, there are four kinds of people. There is one whose conduct is subtle but whose mind is not upright or true (ripened on the outside but raw within)."

There are those whose minds are subtle but whose conduct is not upright or real (where the external is raw while the internal is ripe). There are those whose minds are subtle and whose conduct is also upright and real.

There are those whose minds are not subtle and whose conduct is not upright or real. Regarding these first two types, how can they be known? The Buddha said: "Good son, [it is known by their speech]."
The analogy of the mango fruit concerns two kinds of people and others; it is indeed difficult to know them. Because they are difficult to know, I have said in my sūtras:

"One should dwell together with them. If one does not know them while dwelling together, one should live with them for a long time. If one still does not know them after living together for a long time, one must rely on wisdom.
If one’s wisdom does not know [the truth], one should observe deeply. By means of such observation, one will come to know whether a son of good family observes the precepts or violates them.

When these four matters are present, one dwells with him for a long time; through the observation of wisdom, one may subsequently discern whether he maintains the precepts or violates them (as stated in the sutra).
Because they together protect the Buddha-dharma, it is said that "those who act as well-wishers" (kalyāṇamitra) are meant. Now, examining this in detail, regarding that...
Regarding the person who committed the offense, the disciplinary method is applied; this method is then used as an analogy for the *kuṭilā* (well-ran).
One does not expect others to call it *kuṭilā*.
Fifth, "abusive speech" (*pāruṣya*) is the primary condition; this may also be taken as the whole. As stated in the text above: "uttering irrelevant speech" (*anyavāda*).

Answer: What is there that is not included? One should simply exclude the eighth case, because at that time it was not necessarily the case that the act of abandoning the precepts had already occurred.

[The cases include] "immediately giving rise to anger," "remaining silent," and so forth. As for the phrase "since his knee was injured," this means that having already committed the offense himself, he further slanders another.

That which can be understood through the combined analogy refers to a collective synthesis; thus, the scriptural text also says "it is likewise. Blood boils and flows from the face because one knows for oneself that there has been an offense.

One abandons the precepts and ceases the path because one fears not reaching the end [of the practice]. The mind is liberated through the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) because the noble ones advance upon the Path.
One is far removed from dust and defilement because one proceeds from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) to that of a noble one (*ārya*).

[The ten items] increase. The text says: "One follows the requirements of the Dharma and the Saṃgha" (since one follows them, one should not obstruct them); "one does not criticize the requirements of the Dharma and the Saṃgha" (the preceding *Khandhaka* on Obstructing says:

"one does not oppose the requirements of the Dharma and the Saṃgha"); "one does not fall into the midst of criticizing the requirements of the Dharma and the Saṃgha" (the preceding text says: "in the midst of speaking without opposing the requirements of the Dharma and the Saṃgha").

Furthermore, there are three additional "increases of ten. These ancient masters, drawing from the five types of upholders of the Vinaya within the aforementioned "increase of five," explain this passage by taking the three distinct qualities—extensive recitation of the *Vinaya*, abiding in the *Vinaya* without wavering, and being well-able to eliminate disputes—and applying them to the preceding [five points on] pure conduct.
One must personally distance oneself from what is difficult, suspicious, or censurable (referring to the five points of prior purity), and furthermore, benefit those who have been formally accused.
(This refers to the five constant virtues mentioned later).

Regarding the "increase of twelve" or "possibly three": as in the "Exhortation to Study" below, these were non-existent in antiquity but exist today; this shall be understood when we reach that section.
Regarding "roots of contention" and "non-roots of contention": as in the case of the middle path of renunciation, non-ill-will (*avyāpāda*) and so forth are not roots of contention;
conversely, those [opposites] are roots of contention.

Regarding the sequence where "non-" comes first and "as" follows in the analysis: one should examine the intent of the chapter. The intention is to state that within the analysis of the roots of contention, first—

"Non-accordance" (*na-yathā*) refers to what follows in the text below: "If, wherever a bhikṣu may be, he does not engage in quarreling or contention"—the opposite of the preceding phrase constitutes "accordance" (*yathā*).
If it is not so, then there is the triad of cessation and the triad of increase; these are invariably termed "non-accordance."
"How can there be such a thing? This refers to the statement that "one who has not heard the sūtras does not see them. Not seeing the sūtras is precisely what makes it appropriate to hear them;
this is the intended meaning of the commentary (*shu*). Furthermore, the text says, "One who is not widely learned does not know the *vinaya*.
In the commentary, "not knowing the *vinaya*" is extracted separately as the fifth [point].
Furthermore, as for those who say that the matters mentioned above were debated by the two masters Piṇḍola and Śūra, they speak in common on this point.
Regarding "taking up the recollection," this includes, by extension, the offenses of non-delusion (*amūḍha-vinaya*) and the determination of the location (*sthāpanā-vinaya*).

Next, the twenty-second [section] consists of six items, beginning with "respect" (*satkāra*). These are combined into one [category]. Next are three items, beginning with "breaking the precepts" (*dauḥśīlya*).

Next are the three faculties (*indriya*), and next are the five virtues (*guṇa*); thus, there are twelve [items in total]. Regarding the phrase "having respect but no affection" (*satkāra-vinā prema*), if there is a textual error here, some versions of the Vinaya also state:
"no respect but having affection," which is not an error. Upon careful examination, these two versions of the Vinaya differ in this way.
There is also the view that it merely concerns what is appropriate; this is the opinion of Vinaya Master Yun.
Regarding the previous instruction to first present two phrases from among those mentioned: as in the preceding single phrase, within the seven [categories], the first and the [second] are missing.
5. Furthermore, regarding the second phrase, both the first and third [phrases] should likewise be cited.

As for "counting the months of the womb, moisture, and so forth": the *Pravāraṇāvastu* contains a passage permitting [the calculation of years from] the womb, moisture, and so forth; the *Upasampadāvastu* also contains such a permissive passage.
Although the two texts are identical in wording, their meanings differ. In the *Pravāraṇāvastu*, it does not permit [the use of these months] for determining the age of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
Regarding the method of receiving the precepts: this is intended to clarify how a disciple attains the precepts (the intent of the commentary is thus).
Among those who are "intermediate" in both person and dharma, they commit many offenses yet attain much of the dharma. In the text, there are seven phrases:

the first four manifest what is correct, while the latter three clarify what is not. Within the first four, the first three are incomplete, whereas the fourth clarifies the teaching, though it remains incomplete.
In the middle [of the discussion], suppose that as in the first case, one commits two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and conceals both. That person remembers one offense but does not remember the other;

they then request from the Saṃgha the practice of penance (*parivāsa*) regarding the offense they do remember. While practicing it, they further remember the second offense. The Buddha permitted that they be granted the second concealment (*praticchādana*) in accordance with what they have remembered.
However, the intent of this passage is that from the time the offenses were committed, both had already become concealed; it is only upon reaching the point of requesting [the penance] that...

At that time, he then falsely claimed one [offense]. Therefore, both offenses were subject to concealment (*paticchādana*). Regarding the three subsequent phrases concerning the arising of non-virtue, the first phrase states:
"One commits two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; one remembers one offense and does not remember the other.

Both request concealment from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants concealment for both. A visiting bhikṣu then rebuked him, saying: "It is well for one who remembers to receive concealment, but for one who does not remember..."

This constitutes concealment of unwholesome conduct; the Saṃgha should perform the *jīva-kṣānti* (confession of restoration). However, this is not the same as the case where one remembers one thing but forgets another.
From the outset, the intention to commit the offense was already present; how could this be the same as previously requesting [the precepts] while remembering them falsely?

It is simply that the assembly of monks did not understand the meaning of the teaching, and thus falsely clung to the previous passage regarding "remembering one and forgetting one. The Buddha permitted [the confession] according to what is remembered, granting the Dharma in both cases. I...

Now, furthermore, the phrasing is also the same for both "recalling one" and "not recalling one. Since the phrasing is identical, both should be subject to concealment (*paticchādana*), resulting in an increase of seventeen.
Regarding benefit and loss: within the aforementioned increase of seventeen, one should cite the virtues [of the practitioner].
The twelfth [point] is benefit; this is further correlated with the five constant virtues. Within these, there is also benefit. What is the distinction? Furthermore...
There are two [types of] real and unreal, and two [types of] loving-kindness (*maitrī*), etc., all of which are distinguished below.
Regarding "each observing one's own body" in the *Ekottarika-āgama* (Sūtra 17): because of a lack of virtue, one should only observe oneself.
This is as explained in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* within the section on the precept against admonishing those of evil character.

[The *Ekottarika-āgama*, Chapter Twenty-two] states: "Regarding those who arrive later and sit later," Yunshou explains that they are those who first gather and initiate a dispute, and only afterwards sit down;
for them, a judgment is made to resolve the matter. One must possess these qualities to be able to preside over an assembly and adjudicate according to principle.
Now, examining the text, since it explicitly states that one does not engage in the same business as this faction or that faction, we know from this that [this applies] to all [cases].
At that time, those who arrived later sat behind; this signifies that they did not follow [the preceding group].
The fundamental principle is profound and mysterious, difficult to fathom through ordinary sentiments.
Thus, following my own humble views, I have completed this compilation. Although the benefit may be slight, I hope it will bring about the two benefits for self and others.
May it cause the thousand lights to blaze ever more brightly throughout the long night.
End of Volume Ten of the *Shishuōyìjì* (Notes on the Adorned Meaning of the Doctrine).
